exp.0:0:
It says this book begins with the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah. He came from a family of priests who lived in Anathoth, a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, near Jerusalem. The name "Anathoth" in the verse is the older spelling of Anatot.

The book introduces its author and says where he came from. The verses that follow explain that God spoke to him during the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, up until the fall of Jerusalem. That is, Jeremiah served for about forty years in very difficult times. It is not known with certainty whether this Hilkiah is the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's time; many doubt it, and the Bible does not confirm it.

God does not call perfect people, but people with a concrete history, with family and with a place. He can use your origin, your work, and your surroundings to speak. Today, ask him how he wants to use what you already are and where you are.
exp.0:4:
God says that he knew Jeremiah before he was formed in his mother's womb. Before he was born, God set him apart, meaning he dedicated him for a special purpose. And he appointed him as a prophet to the nations.

The LORD speaks, and he addresses these words to Jeremiah, a young man from a priestly family who lived in the final years of the kingdom of Judah, until the fall of Jerusalem. God calls him to a difficult task: to speak his message to a people who had turned away from him. Jeremiah answers with fear, saying that he is too young and does not know how to speak, but God does not change the call.

For today: God knows you and has valued you from the beginning, before your achievements or your failures. When you feel that you do not measure up to what he asks of you, remember that his calling comes with his support. Take the first step by trusting him.
exp.0:10:
God speaks to Jeremiah and asks him a simple question: "What do you see?" Jeremiah answers that he sees a rod of an almond tree, that is, a branch from that tree. The old wording in the text is a matter of spelling and grammar, not a difference in meaning.

The Lord speaks with Jeremiah, who had just been called as a prophet. God had just placed his words in Jeremiah's mouth. Then he goes on to say that he is quick to carry out his word. Many explain that in Hebrew the word for almond sounds something like the word for watching or staying awake, but that connection is an interpretation, not something the text states outright.

Today we can learn to look closely at ordinary things, asking God to teach us something through them. We can also trust that God keeps what he says, even when it takes time to be seen.
exp.0:12:
God spoke to Jeremiah a second time and asked him what he saw. He answered that he saw a boiling pot, tilted toward the north. The word "north" in the verse is the direction the pot faces, so the pot appears to be pouring over toward the south.

God speaks to Jeremiah at the beginning of his call as a prophet. Through this vision he announces that a disaster will come from the north upon Judah and Jerusalem because of their disobedience. The verses that follow explain it as nations that would come to surround the city. Tradition often connects this with Babylon, although the text here speaks in general of kingdoms from the north.

For today: God warns us in love before the consequences arrive. If today you feel that He is calling you to correct something, do not put it off; respond with humility and trust that He remains faithful.
exp.0:14:
God says that he will call all the peoples of the kingdoms of the north. They will come, and each king will set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, around its walls and against the cities of Judah. It is an image of armies surrounding and taking the city.

The LORD speaks to the young Jeremiah at the beginning of his calling as a prophet. He showed him a boiling pot tilting from the north, a sign of a judgment that is drawing near. According to the text that follows, the cause is that the people left God and worshiped idols. Many think it refers to Babylon, although the text does not name it here.

God does not ignore sin, but neither does he act without warning: he sends his prophets to call people to repentance. Today we can listen with humility when his Word corrects us, and return to him before the consequences arrive.
exp.1:2:
God says that Israel was holy to Him, that is, a people set apart and dedicated. He compares it to the firstfruits, the first produce of the harvest, which belonged to God. Those who devoured Israel, meaning those who took advantage of it or attacked it, will be held guilty, and God promises that evil will come upon them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He tenderly remembers Israel's early days, when it followed Him through the wilderness like a faithful bride. This sets up a contrast: soon God will ask what wrong they found in Him that led them to turn away. It is an accusation, but one spoken with a tone of grief.

For today: God sees us as something precious and set apart for Him, not as an object of no importance. Today you can remember your first love and give God the first of your time, even if it is only a few minutes of prayer at the start of the day.
exp.1:4:
God asks his people a question: what fault or injustice did their ancestors find in him that they should go so far from him? They followed what is worthless, that is, empty idols and things without value, and they ended up empty and without purpose.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He reminds them that Israel was set apart for him, that he brought them out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, and brought them into a fertile land. The question does not seek information; it is a painful complaint that shows how unjust their turning away from him was.

For today: when something pulls us away from God, it is wise to ask ourselves whether he truly gave us anything better. Remembering his past faithfulness helps us return to him and not chase things that leave us empty.
exp.1:12:
God says that his people committed two evils: they abandoned him, who is the fountain of living waters (water that flows and gives life), and they began digging their own cisterns, that is, pits for storing water. But those cisterns are broken: they have cracks and do not hold the water.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, his people. He rebukes them for exchanging their living God for idols and human alliances that could not help them. Not even the pagan nations change their gods, and yet Israel exchanged the true one. The following verses show the consequences: invasion and destroyed cities.

For today: we all seek something to quench the thirst of the heart, such as success, money, approval, or pleasure. Those things can be useful, but they fail when we ask them for what only God gives. Today, before you run after something to feel full, take a few minutes to pray and read the Bible, returning to the fountain.
exp.1:13:
These questions sound harsh. God asks whether Israel is a servant or a slave born in the house, that is, someone without rights who can be mistreated. Since he is not, God asks why he has been given over to plunder, that is, why he is seized and stripped like an animal that has been hunted.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he said that his people committed two wrongs: they abandoned him, the fountain of living water, and dug broken cisterns. The question leads us to think that Israel was not destined to be a victim, since it was his son and chosen people. The verses that follow describe invaders who laid the land waste, and many understand that this was the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: when you feel that life is wearing you down, ask yourself honestly what things you are relying on for support apart from God. Return to him in prayer and in his Word, for only he gives water that never runs out.
exp.1:16:
God asks his people a question that already contains its answer: was it not your own choice to abandon the Lord that brought these troubles upon you? He says this while reminding them that he himself had been leading them along the way.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. The verses before describe ruin and humiliation, and they mention Egypt (Noph and Tahpanhes were Egyptian cities). Judah sought security in alliances with Egypt and Assyria instead of trusting God. The Lord shows them that their problem was not bad luck, but having left him.

For today: when something in your life falls apart, ask yourself honestly whether you have been looking for support in other things before looking to God. Returning to him with humility is always possible.
exp.1:22:
God asks his people how they dare to say they are not defiled and have never gone after the Baals, which were false gods of the Canaanites. He asks them to look at their conduct in the valley, probably a place where idolatry was practiced; some think of the valley of Hinnom, though this is not certain. He compares them to a swift young camel that runs back and forth without direction, driven by its desires.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was denying its idolatry, even though its actions showed it. Earlier, God had said that its sin was engraved, meaning marked deeply and impossible to hide or wash away with simple rituals.

Today we can ask God to show us our hearts honestly. Instead of making excuses or comparing ourselves with others, let us acknowledge what we have done and return to him, for he forgives the one who repents.
exp.1:28:
Another phrase means that they betrayed or deliberately failed in their commitment. God tells them that all of them, without exception, have been unfaithful to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people worshiped idols of wood and stone, but when distress came they asked God for help. They defended themselves by saying they had done nothing wrong, and God responds by showing that their guilt is real and obvious.

For today: when God corrects us, it is easy to look for excuses or to argue. We can instead pray sincerely, acknowledge where we have failed him, and return to him, for he remains good and waits for us with patience.
exp.1:36:
It says that Judah will go out from Egypt with their hands on their heads, a gesture that normally shows grief, shame, and defeat. The reason is that the Lord has rejected the things they trusted in, that is, whatever they were placing their security in. Therefore they will not prosper in them, meaning things will not go well for them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people claimed to be innocent and sought alliances with foreign powers, such as Assyria and Egypt, instead of turning back to God. He warns them that these alliances will leave them ashamed. Scholars understand the gesture of the hands on the head as a sign of mourning or humiliation.

Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our security: money, work, influence, or our own righteousness. All of these can fail. The wisest course is to acknowledge our faults with humility and to trust God first.
exp.2:1:
God tells his people to look up at the hills, where worship of other gods was carried on, and to find a single place where they have not given themselves to idolatry. The high places were elevated sites where pagan worship took place. Judah sat along the roads like a nomad waiting in the desert for travelers, so the people sought allies and false gods. The verse speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness, and of land made dirty and unclean.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah. He uses the image of a broken marriage: the people have abandoned their God. Even so, the verse before invites them to return. The drought that follows is understood as the consequence of that unfaithfulness.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts. Honor him with sincerity, recognize those things, and return to him, who continues to call with love.
exp.2:9:
Here, the verse says that although Judah saw the punishment that fell on her sister Israel, she did not turn back to God with her whole heart. She only pretended, going along with it without sincerity. The point is that Judah's repentance was only on the surface.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been taken into exile because of her unfaithfulness, which the Scripture describes as spiritual adultery. Judah, the southern kingdom, saw this and yet carried on just the same. It is likely that this refers to shallow religious reforms, though scholars interpret it in different ways. God wants a true change.

For today: God is not satisfied with rituals or pleasant words. We can honestly ask ourselves whether our faith comes from the heart or is only a matter of habit, and ask him to give us a genuine repentance.
exp.2:14:
God promises that he will give his people leaders who think and feel as he does. "Feed" here means to care for and nourish, the way a shepherd looks after his sheep. In this verse, that nourishment is knowledge and understanding for living well.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been unfaithful to him, like a wife who leaves her husband, and had gone after other gods. Even so, God calls them to return and promises to restore them. This promise shows that his desire is to heal and guide his people, not only to rebuke them.

For today: value leaders who teach God's Word with truth and humility, and pray for them. And remember that God himself wants to nourish you with his wisdom if you return to him with sincerity.
exp.2:17:
This verse promises that, in a future time, Judah and Israel will no longer be divided. They will walk together, and they will come back united from the land of the north, which is an old way of saying the north. They will return to the land that God gave as an inheritance to their fathers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were divided into two kingdoms and had turned away from God. Israel had already been taken captive northward, to Assyria. God calls them to return and promises restoration, forgiveness, and unity. Interpreters differ on when it is fully fulfilled: some think of the return from exile, others of a future fulfillment.

For today: God heals divisions and brings back those who were lost. Ask Him to help you seek reconciliation with someone you have grown distant from.
exp.2:20:
What it says: A voice is heard on the bare hills, a weeping and a pleading of the children of Israel. They weep because they have turned aside from the good way and have forgotten the Lord, their God. Going astray is living in a crooked manner, far from what is right.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had betrayed him like an unfaithful wife, worshiping false gods on the high places. Many understand this weeping on the hills as the people's repentance, which the following verse confirms when God calls them to return and heal their rebellion. Some also see it as a lament of grief over their sin.

For today: When you notice that you have drifted away from God, do not hide or make excuses. Return to Him sincerely, with tears if needed, because He promises to heal those who come back.
exp.3:0:
God speaks to Israel and says: if you truly want to return, come back to me. If you put away your abominations from my sight, meaning the idols and practices that God detests, you will no longer wander from place to place, without direction or security.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had turned away from God and were seeking other gods. The verses that follow call for a sincere commitment: swearing by God in truth, with judgment and righteousness, and preparing the heart the way one prepares a field, without sowing among thorns.

For today: returning to God is not only feeling sorry, but letting go of whatever has taken his place. Ask him to show you one specific thing you should leave behind, and take that step today with sincerity.
exp.3:2:
God tells the men of Judah and Jerusalem to prepare their hearts like a field. Breaking up fallow ground means plowing land that has become hard or left unused so it is ready. Thorns are the weeds that choke the seed. There is no point in sowing before the ground has been cleared.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He calls His people to truly return to Him, not merely with words. Right after this, He asks for a change within, a renewal of the heart, and warns of coming judgment if they continue in their evil ways.

For today: before seeking new spiritual goals, ask yourself what thorns are in your life, such as resentments, habits, or excuses. Bring them honestly before God and let Him remove them, so that His Word can bear fruit in you.
exp.3:7:
God calls his people to put on mourning clothes, to weep, and to cry out in pain. Sackcloth was a rough cloth worn in times of grief or repentance. To lament means to mourn with songs or weeping, and to howl means to cry out in intense anguish. The reason is that the Lord's anger still remains upon them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the kingdom of Judah, warning that an invader is coming from the north, described as a destroying lion. The people had rejected God and still believed that everything would turn out fine. That is why the warning is serious, and weeping is the appropriate response.

Today, when God shows us that something is wrong in our lives, it is not wise to downplay it or distract ourselves. We can stop, confess with sincerity, and return to Him, trusting that his mercy remains open to those who humble themselves.
exp.3:9:
Jeremiah cries out to God in pain and surprise. He says that the Lord has deceived this people, because they were promised peace, and now the sword has reached the soul, that is, to the very depths of life. Jerusalem is Jerusalem.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, distressed by the judgment that is coming upon Judah. Interpreters explain his words in different ways: some think the false prophets proclaimed peace in God's name and the people let themselves be deceived; others think Jeremiah voices his complaint in very strong language, without really accusing God of lying. In both cases, the people ignored the warnings.

Today, let us not trust comfortable messages that avoid the truth. Let us seek God's Word with humility, even when it corrects us, and bring our complaints to Him with sincerity, as Jeremiah did.
exp.3:10:
It says that a time is coming when people will speak of Jerusalem and its people in this way: a dry, scorching wind will blow from the bare heights of the desert upon "the daughter of my people," a tender way of naming God's people. Winnowing was throwing the grain into the air to separate the chaff from it, and cleansing was making it pure. But this wind is not for that purpose: it is too strong and only destroys.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The people believed that everything would be at peace, and false messages reinforced that belief. But God announces an invasion that many understand to be that of the army of Babylon, which comes from the north. Jeremiah himself is distressed by this word. The wind represents judgment for the people's unfaithfulness, not a gentle correction.

For today: let us not trust in an easy peace that avoids the truth. Let us ask God to show us honestly what we must correct, and return to Him while there is still time.
exp.3:16:
This verse says that the enemy armies will surround Jerusalem like the watchmen who guard a field or a harvest: they keep watch on every side and do not let her escape. The reason is clear: the city rebelled against God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Before this verse, it is announced that an army is coming from far away and that the warning of danger runs from Dan to Judah. God explains that this is not bad luck: the people turned their back on him. Afterward, the prophet shows grief over what is coming.

For today: when something in your life goes wrong, do not stay only with the complaint. Ask God to show you whether there is something you should correct. He corrects with pain, but he always invites you to return to him.
exp.3:26:
God says that a very great punishment is coming: the whole land will be laid waste and emptied. But he adds a limit: he will not make a full end. He will not destroy it completely or finish it off entirely. "Desolate" means ruined and left empty. Although the judgment is harsh, God leaves open a hope that a remnant will remain.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had turned away from him and were living in wickedness. Jeremiah describes the judgment as a vision of desolation: no people, no birds, cities in ruins. Many understand that it refers to the invasion that would come from the north, although the text presents it in very broad and symbolic language.

For today: God is serious about sin, but even when he corrects, he does not stop being merciful. If you are going through a painful consequence today, remember that God disciplines to restore, not to destroy you. Return to him with humility and trust.
exp.3:27:
This verse says that the earth will mourn and the sky will grow dark. God gives the reason: what he has said and decided, he will carry out. The phrase "will mourn" means the earth will be in grief, the way people mourn when they lose someone they love. "I have not changed my mind, nor will I turn back" means that God will not change his plan or reverse his decision.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Judah for its idolatry and rebellion, described as a land laid waste by an invading army. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. Notice that God had earlier said he would not make a full end, meaning he will not completely destroy his people. His judgment is serious, but it leaves a door of hope open.

For today: God means what he says, both when he warns and when he promises. Do not take him lightly; it is better to respond in time with humility and return to him, for he is merciful.
exp.3:28:
At the sound of the horsemen and archers approaching, the whole population flees the city, the verse says. They hide in the thickets (very dense woodland) and climb up onto the rocky crags. The cities are left forsaken, meaning abandoned, with no one living in them at all.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Judah for its rebellion. The nearby verses describe an invading army from the north. The text does not name it here, and many connect it with Babylon. God says he will not change his mind about what he has announced, but also that he will not bring a complete end, that is, total destruction.

For today: we should not trust in appearances or in false securities. It is better to turn back to God sincerely while there is still time, since his warning comes from his desire to restore.
exp.3:29:
This verse speaks to Jerusalem (Judah) as if she were a woman who has already been ruined. It asks her what she will do now. She dresses herself in bright red clothing, adorns herself with gold jewelry, and paints her eyes dark, but all of it is useless. Her lovers, that is, the nations she sought alliances with, despise her and want to kill her.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had turned away from Him and trusted in other nations. God had already announced judgment, and the invading army was drawing near. Many understand the lovers to be those allied nations, although the text expresses this in poetic language.

For today: no appearance, success, or human support can replace a sincere life with God. If today we trust more in what looks good on the outside, let us return to Him with humility.
exp.4:4:
It says that the prophet thought to seek out the great ones, that is, the leaders and important people, to speak with them. He expected that they, at least, would know the way of the LORD, that is, what God requires and how he judges. But he discovers that they too had broken the yoke and burst the bonds. The yoke and the bonds are the straps with which an ox is joined to the plow; here they stand for obedience to God.

The one speaking is Jeremiah. Earlier he thought that the poor did not understand God because they lacked instruction. Then he turns to the leaders, but they too were unwilling to submit. For this reason God announces judgment: it was not ignorance, but rebellion.

For today: knowing what is right is not enough. Knowing the Bible, or holding a position of responsibility, calls us to obey. Let us ask God for a heart willing to accept his correction, rather than hardening ourselves.
exp.4:7:
This verse compares the people of Judah to well-fed horses that, as soon as morning comes, are full of desire. Each man went after his neighbour's wife without any restraint, like a horse that whinnies and charges with no bridle to hold it back.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just said that the people abandoned him, swore by false gods, and fell into adultery. God had given them abundance, but they used it to sin. For this reason he asks whether he should not call them to account. Some understand the adultery literally and others also as spiritual unfaithfulness; the text allows both readings.

For today: what God gives us, such as health, work, or well-being, should lead us to thank him and to be faithful, not to live without control. Ask him to help you care for your marriage and to respect the marriages of others.
exp.4:9:
God says that an invading army is to climb up the city's walls and destroy it, but without finishing everything off. The phrase about not making a full end means: do not wipe it out completely. He also commands them to take away the battlements, the projecting tops or parapets of the walls, because those defenses are not the Lord's: they do not belong to him and have no backing from him.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. First he describes a society marked by unfaithfulness and wickedness, and then he says the people rebelled and denied God, believing that no harm would come. Many understand the invaders to be the Babylonians, although the text does not name them here. The judgment is serious, but it is not total.

For today: let us not trust in defenses that God does not stand behind, such as pride, religious habit, or self-sufficiency. If God corrects, it is so that we will return to him, and even in discipline there is mercy.
exp.4:14:
God tells Israel that he will bring against them a nation from distant lands. He describes it as strong and ancient, a people whose language you will not understand. Strong means powerful, and ancient refers to a people with a long history. The phrase about not understanding means you will not know their language.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had rejected his warnings, saying that no harm would come. So the judgment would be a foreign invasion. Many understand that it refers to Babylon, though the text does not give the name. Hearing a language you cannot understand was a sign of being left without protection and without a home.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly. He corrects because he wants us to return to him. If you feel his call today, do not harden your heart; ask him for forgiveness and trust in his mercy.
exp.4:15:
It says that the arrows of this enemy people are as deadly as an open grave, ready to swallow everyone. The quiver is the case where the arrows are kept. And "mighty men" means that all of its soldiers are strong and fearless.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel had turned away from Him and did not believe that punishment would come. God announces that He will bring a foreign nation, whose language they do not know, as a consequence of their rebellion. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here.

For today: God is serious, but He is also patient. If there is something in your life that He has pointed out to you several times, do not ignore it. Today you can return to Him with sincerity, before the consequences arrive.
exp.4:16:
It says that an invading people will devour everything Israel had worked for: the harvest, the bread meant for their sons and daughters, the flocks and herds, and the vines and fig trees. Even the fortified cities, where the people felt safe, would be destroyed by the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that a foreign nation, whose language they do not know, will come as a consequence of the people having abandoned him to serve other gods. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. The following verse makes clear that God would not destroy them completely.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether it is your work, your savings, or your strongholds. All of that can fail, but God endures. Trust in Him first, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.4:21:
God asks his people whether they do not hold him in awe. He set the sand as the boundary of the sea, by a law that lasts forever. The waves rise and roar, but they cannot cross that limit.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He calls them foolish because, although they have eyes and ears, they do not understand. God reminds them of his power in creation to show that he deserves reverence, and that they have a rebellious heart that turns away from him.

For today: when you feel that your life is like a stormy sea, remember that God sets limits on what seems unstoppable. Respecting him and trusting him gives you peace, and it invites you to return to him with a sincere and humble heart.
exp.4:23:
They never stopped to think, in their heart, "Let us now reverence and honor the Lord our God." He is the one who sends the early rain (the autumn rain, for sowing) and the late rain (the spring rain, to ripen the harvest). He also keeps the set weeks of the harvest. Here, "fear" means reverence, not just being afraid.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of having a rebellious heart. Just as the sea respects the limit of sand that God set for it, the people should have respected their Creator. But they took the blessings for granted and forgot who gave them.

For today: let us not take our daily bread for granted. Before eating, or when receiving good news, pause for a moment and thank God, aloud or in your heart. This simple gratitude keeps us humble and close to Him.
exp.4:27:
They have grown fat and sleek. That means they lived well fed and looked prosperous. "They have gone beyond the deeds of the wicked" means their evil went past every limit; they were worse than ordinary wrongdoers. They did not plead the cause of the orphan or the cause of the poor, that is, they did not do justice in the courts, and still things went well for them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses his people of getting rich through deceit and of taking advantage of the weakest. The next verse shows that God will not overlook this: he will call them to account.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat those who cannot defend themselves. Think of a vulnerable person near you, such as a child, an elderly person, or a worker who is underpaid, and look for a concrete way to help them or to speak up on their behalf.
exp.4:29:
This verse says that something horrible and scandalous is happening in the land. The colon at the end announces that what this terrible thing is will be explained right away.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah. Earlier He accused the rich of growing fat while they did not defend the orphan or the poor. What follows in verse 31 reveals the matter: the prophets prophesied falsely, the priests ruled by their own authority, and the people loved it that way. The most serious thing was not only the sin of the leaders, but that the people accepted it.

For today: let us not accept comfortably what sounds good but is not true. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and let us defend, with concrete actions, those who have no voice, like the orphan and the poor.
exp.5:0:
This verse is a war alarm. God tells the people of Benjamin to flee from the middle of Jerusalem. They are to blow the horn (the ram's horn or trumpet) in Tekoa and raise a signal of smoke in Beth-haccerem. "North" is where the danger comes from, and great destruction comes with it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who was from the tribe of Benjamin. Judah had refused God's calls to return to Him. Tekoa and Beth-haccerem were places near Jerusalem, and they were used to send warnings. Scholars often connect the danger from the north with Babylon, although the text presents it in general terms.

Today we can learn to take God's warnings seriously. It is not wise to wait until the crisis arrives: listening in time, repenting, and returning to Him with humility is an act of wisdom.
exp.5:8:
He says that God, the Lord of hosts, will go through Israel the way a vineyard is gone over again after the harvest. The word "glean" means gathering again what was left behind, cluster by cluster. The phrase "the remnant of Israel" refers to those who were still left.

Then the grape-gatherer (the one who harvests grapes) is commanded to pass his hand over the branches once more and put whatever he finds into the baskets.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The people kept on in injustice and would not listen. The image suggests a very thorough judgment: no one would escape by going unnoticed. Scholars disagree about who receives the command, whether Jeremiah or the invading army, but the underlying message is the same.

For today: do not put off God's correction. If something in your life troubles you as you read his Word, listen to it with humility and change in time, while there is still grace to return.
exp.5:9:
Jeremiah asks to whom he can speak so that someone will listen. He says the people's ears are closed, shut up, as if they were not ready to receive anything from God. The word of the Lord strikes them as a reproach: they see it as something shameful or something they look down on. They take no pleasure in it.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. God had warned the people many times, but they remained hardened. Jeremiah feels the weight of speaking and not being heard, and in the verses that follow he says he is full of the anger of God.

For today: ask yourself whether you truly want to hear God or only want to hear what pleases you. Ask him for a heart willing to receive his word, even when it corrects you.
exp.5:11:
This verse announces a harsh judgment. The houses, the fields, and even the wives of the inhabitants will pass into the hands of others.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had rejected his word, regarded it as shameful, and did not want to hear it. Moreover, from the least to the greatest, everyone was seeking gain, and the leaders deceived with a false peace. Many understand this as a warning that was fulfilled with the Babylonian invasion.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God corrects us. If his word makes us uncomfortable, it is better to listen and change in time, rather than soothing our conscience with false calm.
exp.5:17:
God calls all the nations to listen. The opening words are an invitation to pay attention. The second part is hard to translate: some understand it as addressed to the congregation or assembly (perhaps of the nations), and others render it in different ways. Even so, the central idea is clear: pay attention!

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people rejected the good ancient path and would not heed the watchmen who warned them. Therefore God makes the nations witnesses that the punishment coming is the consequence of their rebellion. Moreover, he rejects their sacrifices, because they were religion without obedience of the heart.

For today: it is not enough to practice religious acts if we do not listen to God. Today you can stop, read his Word, ask yourself what he asks of you, and then obey him simply, without hardening your heart.
exp.5:19:
This verse says that God does not value lavish offerings when the heart is far from him. The costly perfumes that came from distant lands were prized goods, and Sheba is usually placed in the south of Arabia, though its exact location is debated. Whole burnt offerings were sacrifices burned completely on the altar. The idea that God does not accept them, and that they do not please him, is what the verse conveys.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah kept performing their rituals in the temple, yet they rejected God's word and his law, as the preceding verse says. For that reason God announces judgment. The sacrifices could not cover their disobedience.

For today: before looking for impressive things to offer God, such as songs, services or donations, check whether you truly listen to him and obey him. God seeks a sincere heart, not merely a good religious appearance.
exp.5:20:
God says he will put stumbling blocks in front of his people, that is, things that will make them fall. The fall will reach everyone: fathers and sons together, and also the neighbor and the one who lives nearby. "Neighbor" here means a close associate or fellow person. "Perish" means to die or be destroyed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the invasion of Judah. The people did not listen to his word, they despised his law, and they thought sacrifices and incense were enough, even though their hearts were far from God. The verses that follow announce an army coming from the north. Scholars debate exactly who that people was, but the text presents them as an instrument of judgment.

For today: God is not satisfied with religious practices if there is no sincere obedience. It is worth asking ourselves whether we truly listen to his word and live it, and do not merely keep customs.
exp.5:25:
It says that God's people should dress in sackcloth, roll in ashes, and mourn with the deepest grief, as one who has lost his only son. Sackcloth and ashes were signs of mourning and repentance. The word "suddenly" is what the verse says about the invading army that is about to come upon them without warning.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The verses before this one describe fear and anguish in the face of an enemy coming from the north. Judah had rejected God's warning, so the call is to grieve in earnest, not to pretend. The text that follows shows that Jeremiah was to examine the people's wickedness.

For today: do not minimize your mistakes or get used to them. When you see something that pulls you away from God, come to Him with humility and a sincere heart, before the consequences arrive.
exp.5:29:
This verse says the people will be called "rejected silver," that is, silver with no value, which is thrown away because it is no good. The reason is that God himself has rejected them. The word "rejected" means cast aside or set off to one side as something no longer useful.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares Judah to a metal that is put through the fire to be purified. But however hard the refiner worked, only dross was left: the people did not give up their wickedness, and their leaders kept deceiving and corrupting. That is why the people were rejected as worthless. Some scholars see here a judgment that announces the coming invasion of Babylon.

For today: it is not enough to look valuable on the outside. God looks for a heart that lets itself be corrected. When He confronts us, it is wise to answer Him with humility and repentance, instead of hardening ourselves.
exp.6:3:
It says not to trust in deceptive words. The people repeated three times "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, is this," as a formula of security. God calls that idea a lie: the belief that the temple would protect them no matter how they lived.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who preached at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people worshiped there, but they oppressed the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, and followed other gods. God asked them to change their conduct, not merely to keep up their religious observances.

For today: attending church or using spiritual phrases is not enough to feel secure with God. Today you can ask yourself where in your life you truly need to obey, for example by treating with justice and kindness those who depend on you or who have less than you.
exp.6:7:
It says that the people trust in false words that are of no use. To trust in something means to place one's security in it, and the verse's point is that these words bring no benefit at all. In other words, they felt safe because of things that were not true.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people kept repeating that the temple would protect them, while they went on stealing, murdering, swearing falsely, and worshiping Baal. God asks them to change their way of living, to care for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, and to return to Him.

For today: let us not put our trust in religious phrases or in attending church as if that alone guaranteed us anything. Let us examine whether our lives reflect what we say we believe, and ask God to correct us with sincerity.
exp.6:26:
God tells Jeremiah to repeat to the people everything He has told him, but He warns him ahead of time that they will not listen to him. Even if he calls out to them, they will not answer him.

God speaks to Jeremiah in the temple in Jerusalem, where the people relied on rituals while they lived in injustice and idolatry. God had sent prophets to them again and again, and they stiffened their necks, meaning they became stubborn. Jeremiah receives a difficult assignment: to speak without any guarantee of being heard. The text does not say the message is not worth delivering, but that the people's hearts were closed.

Today it reminds us that obeying God does not depend on the results. If you share the truth with love and people do not pay attention to you, do not be discouraged. Remain faithful, pray for those people, and trust that God is working in hearts.
exp.6:29:
God says that the people of Judah did evil in His sight. They placed their detestable idols and practices inside the temple, the house that bears God's name, and so they defiled it, making it impure and unclean.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who preached in the temple at Jerusalem. The people felt secure because they had the temple, yet they still did not obey. The verses that follow mention Topheth, a place where they sacrificed their children, something God never commanded. For this reason He announces judgment.

For today: it is not enough to appear religious or to attend church. God looks at the heart. We can ask ourselves whether there is something we have placed in the position that belongs to Him alone, and give it to Him sincerely.
exp.6:30:
This verse says that the people of Judah built places of worship on high ground in Tophet, in the valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. There they burned their sons and daughters in the fire. The high places were elevated sites for worship, and Tophet is the name of the place. God says he never commanded this, and it never even came into his mind.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had already filled even the temple with pagan ideas, and now they were sacrificing children. Because of this, God announces judgment: that valley would be called the Valley of Slaughter. Scholars agree that this was a serious pagan practice, though they debate the details of how it was carried out.

For today: let us not invent ways of worshiping God according to our own customs. Let us compare what we do with what he teaches in his Word, and protect the youngest from anything that harms them.
exp.7:0:
This verse announces a very harsh judgment. God says that, at that time, enemies will open the tombs of Jerusalem and bring out the bones of the kings, the princes, the priests, the prophets, and the ordinary people. Being left in one's grave was a great dishonor, because in that culture a proper burial was very important.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had turned away from God and worshiped the sun, the moon, and the stars, as the following verse says. This announcement is a warning about the consequences of that sin. Many understand it to refer to the invasion by Babylon, although the text does not give exact details.

For today: whatever we put first in life ends up ruling over us. Today you can ask yourself to whom or to what you are giving your trust, and return to God with humility while there is still time.
exp.7:5:
God says that he listened with close attention, but heard no one speaking what was true. No one repents of his wickedness or asks himself, "What have I done?" Each one keeps going his own way, like a horse that charges into battle without thinking or pulling back.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. God has just asked why his people do not return to him, even though whoever falls gets up again. Here he describes the hardness of their hearts: they have heard warnings, yet they keep moving forward without reflecting.

For today: before we hurry on with our own habits, it is good to stop and ask ourselves honestly, "What have I done?" If God shows us a mistake, we can repent quickly and return to him, who welcomes with grace whoever comes back.
exp.7:9:
God says he will give their wives to other men, and their fields to new owners. The reason is that everyone, from the lowest to the highest, is driven by dishonest gain. Greed means wanting to get ahead at any cost. Even the prophet and the priest, who should be leading the people, act deceitfully, practicing lies and fraud.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the Babylonian invasion. The people boasted of having God's law, but they did not live by it. This warning announces the consequences: the loss of families and land. Many understand it to refer to the conquest and the exile.

For today: it is not enough to own a Bible or hold a religious position; one must live with integrity. Examine your dealings, your work, and your money today, and ask God to help you correct any deceit or hidden greed.
exp.7:15:
From the region of Dan, in the far north, the snorting of the enemy's horses was heard. The strong sound a horse makes when it breathes is what this describes. The neighing of his strong ones made the whole land tremble. The invaders came and devoured the harvests, the riches, the cities, and the people.

The prophet Jeremiah announces God's judgment on Judah for its sin. The people expected peace, but terror arrived. Many understand the enemy from the north to be Babylon, although the text does not name it here. In these verses the voices of the people, of God, and of the prophet, who grieves over what is coming, are mixed together.

Today: do not trust in excuses or in human refuges. If God corrects you, return to Him soon and with sincerity, before the consequences reach your door.
exp.7:16:
God says he will send venomous snakes against his people, and that no charm will be able to stop them. Charms were words or practices used to calm snakes. The verse's word for these snakes is one that the verse says was the name of a feared serpent, though it is not known for certain which species is meant. The verse is figurative language for a punishment that cannot be escaped.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had fallen into idolatry and did not want to return to God. Before this verse, the arrival of an enemy army from the north is described. Afterward, the prophet shows his deep sorrow for his people.

For today: we cannot deceive ourselves with a false peace while we remain far from God. He calls us to return in time, with humility and repentance, because his heart also suffers for us.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that the pain is so great that the heart feels without strength.

The speaker is Jeremiah, the prophet, although some think the voice of God is also heard, feeling the pain of his people. The text does not make this fully clear, and it is interpreted in several ways. Judah faced judgment for its idolatry, and an invasion from the north was announced. Jeremiah does not speak coldly: he grieves over the ruin of his people. That is why he is known as the weeping prophet.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain before God. You can bring him your sadness honestly, and also learn to feel compassion for those who suffer the consequences of their own mistakes.
exp.7:19:
It says the harvest is over and the summer has ended, that is, the seasons when the fruit is gathered and the crop is expected. Even so, the people still are not saved, that is, not rescued from their distress. "Harvest" here means the gathering of the grain.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks with grief for his people, who suffer because of their idolatry and are under threat of judgment. The voices in the verse may be those of the people lamenting, although some think Jeremiah is expressing them on their behalf. The opportunities have passed and the rescue has not come. Afterward the prophet asks whether there is no balm and no physician to heal.

For today: do not put off turning back to God, because opportunities do not always come again. If you sense his call today, respond with humility and do not wait for the summer to pass.
exp.7:21:
Jeremiah asks whether there is no balm in Gilead, that is, a resin used as medicine, and no physician there. If there was a remedy and a healer, why did the people not recover? "The daughter of my people" is a tender way of referring to Judah, seen as a wounded daughter.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, grieved by the sin and suffering of his people. Times of judgment were coming, and they still would not turn back to God. Gilead was a region known for its balm. Some understand the question to point out that God offered healing, but the people would not accept it.

For today: if you are wounded inside or by your own mistakes, do not stay silent or hide it. God offers forgiveness and healing, so come to Him in prayer and also seek the help of fellow believers and trained people.
exp.8:0:
Here the prophet wishes that his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain, so that he could weep day and night. He mourns for the slain of the daughter of my people, a poetic way of referring to the whole nation of Judah.

Jeremiah speaks, the one many call the weeping prophet. God had given him the task of warning Judah about its disobedience. The verses that follow speak of lies, unfaithfulness, and a people who did not know God. The slain may refer to those who would fall in the judgment that was drawing near; scholars mainly understand it this way. Jeremiah suffers with his people, even though he must announce the punishment to them.

For today: when we see sin and pain around us, let us not remain in criticism or indifference. Let us ask God for a sensitive heart, one that prays and weeps for others, and that is firm in the truth with love.
exp.8:1:
He says that the prophet wishes he had, out in the wilderness, a lodging place of wayfaring men, that is, a simple shelter where travelers spend the night. He wants to go there and leave his people behind. The reason is that he sees them as adulterers, unfaithful to God and to one another, and as an assembly of treacherous men, people who betray and break what they have promised.

The speaker is Jeremiah, the prophet who suffers for his nation. In the verse before, he wished he could weep day and night for the dead of his people. His grief is mixed with weariness at so much lying and betrayal. Many understand that it also reflects the grief of God himself.

For today: when it hurts us to see injustice or unfaithfulness around us, let us not flee in bitterness. Let us bring that pain to God in prayer, and ask him to keep us sincere and faithful, even when others are not.
exp.8:9:
The prophet Jeremiah speaks, and in many passages he seems to express the grief of God as well. Judah was living in lies and betrayal, as the previous verse says. That is why God announces judgment: the land would be left in ruins. Even so, the message is not cold, but full of sorrow over what sin destroys.

For today: God does not rejoice in the damage that sin causes. We can ask Him to make us honest in our words, and to let us feel the pain that He feels, instead of being indifferent.
exp.8:10:
God says that Jerusalem will be turned into heaps of ruins, a place where serpents live, that is, wild animals that take over what has been abandoned. He also says that the cities of Judah will be laid waste, that is, destroyed and empty, without any dweller, meaning without any inhabitant.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had abandoned God's law and had not obeyed his voice, as the following verses explain. This announcement of judgment speaks of the destruction that would come at the hand of Babylon. Jeremiah says it with sorrow, since the text shows mourning and weeping over the land.

For today: God takes obedience seriously, but he also warns us with love. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something he has told us in his Word that we are setting aside, and turn back to him with sincerity.
exp.8:12:
God answers the question of why the land was left in ruin. The reason is that the people abandoned his law, the law he had set before them. They did not listen to his voice, nor did they live according to it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, the text asks who is wise enough to understand why judgment would come upon Judah and Jerusalem. God himself gives the answer: it was not by chance, but the consequence of disobedience. The following verse adds that they followed their own stubborn hearts and the Baals, false gods.

For today: it is not enough to have God's Word within reach; we must listen to it and put it into practice. You can choose one concrete command from the Bible that you have been putting off, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time to pray, and begin to obey it today with humility.
exp.8:14:
God says that he will feed his people wormwood and give them water of gall to drink. Wormwood is a very bitter plant, and gall is a bitter, poisonous liquid. They are images of suffering and pain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before Judah was taken into exile. God explains the reason: his people abandoned his law, did not listen to his voice, and followed their own desires and the Baals, false gods. The verses that follow speak of scattering among the nations and of the sword. This is not a whim of God, but the consequence of persistent rebellion.

For today: when we turn away from what God says, we usually reap bitterness. Today we can ask ourselves what stubborn desires of the heart we are following, and return with humility to his Word, which invites us to repentance.
exp.8:16:
God says that people should think carefully about what is coming, and that the mourning women should be called, that is, women who were paid to weep at funerals. He also commands that the skilled women be sent for, women who were good at singing laments. It is a command for them to come and wail.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. Because of the people's disobedience, God announces punishment, scattering, and death. The call to the mourning women shows that the disaster will be so great that a public mourning will be needed, as for a whole nation that is dying. The prophet himself weeps with pain in this book.

For today: God invites us to take sin and its consequences seriously, without hardening the heart. Today we can acknowledge our faults with humility, grieve what hurts, and return to God in time, trusting in his mercy.
exp.8:18:
This verse describes a cry of mourning heard from Zion, that is, Jerusalem. The people weep because everything has been destroyed, and they feel shame and bewilderment. A lament is a song of grief, and to be bewildered means to be ashamed and confused. They ask why they had to leave their land, and they say that their own homes have cast them out, as if they could no longer live in them.

God himself speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Just before this verse, he calls for skilled women to come and wail at funerals, because a great calamity is near. Many understand that it foretells the invasion and exile brought on by the people's sin, although the text presents it as an advance lament.

For today: when a loss leaves you confused, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it honestly to God, and also examine your heart, asking him to guide you back to himself.
exp.8:20:
This verse describes death as if it were a thief that climbs in through the windows and slips into the houses. It reaches even the palaces, which seemed like safe places, and it takes away the children playing in the streets and the young men gathering in the squares.

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. God asks him to call for the women who mourned the dead so that they may teach a funeral song. In this way God warns that the judgment for the people's unfaithfulness is real and will reach everyone, regardless of their position.

For today: let us not trust in our security, wealth, or strength, because life is fragile. The verses that follow say that what truly matters is to know God. Today you can take a few minutes to thank him for your life and to ask him to teach you to live with humility and to value those you love.
exp.8:22:
God says that no one should take pride in their wisdom, their strength, or their wealth. Here, "boast" means to show off or to feel secure and superior because of something. These three things, wisdom, courage, and riches, were what the people believed would protect them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was living in sin, and judgment was drawing near, with death and destruction, as the verses before it show. Neither the wise, nor the strong, nor the rich would be able to save themselves. The verses that follow say what is truly worth rejoicing in: knowing God, who acts with mercy, justice, and righteousness.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust. Studies, work, or money are good, but they are not our foundation. Make time to know God through his Word and in prayer, because that is where true security is found.
exp.8:25:
God says he will hold accountable Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and the peoples of the desert, those who live in the farthest corners, probably those who shave the sides of their heads or live in remote areas. "Uncircumcised" means not having been circumcised. All these nations are uncircumcised in the body, but Israel is uncircumcised in the heart: their inner self has still not surrendered to God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Several of those peoples practiced circumcision, and yet God treats them alike with the uncircumcised. Judah trusted in that outward sign as a guarantee, but lived without mercy, judgment, or justice. For this reason God announces that he will visit them all alike.

For today: a religious sign is not enough, such as being baptized, attending church, or knowing the Bible. Ask God for a sincere heart and examine whether your life reflects mercy and justice toward others.
exp.9:8:
It says that idols are made from costly materials: beaten silver brought from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz. A craftsman and a founder work the metal, and then they dress the image in cloth of dark blue and purple. All of it is the work of skilled hands, yet it is still human work.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, sent by God to Judah. He mocks the idols of the nations, which tempt his people. Tarshish and Uphaz were distant places from which precious metals came, though no one knows for certain where each one was. The contrast comes right after: the LORD is the living God, not a fashioned figure.

For today: let us ask which beautiful and well-made things, such as money, success, or image, we are treating as if they could give us security. Only God, who made us, deserves our trust.
exp.9:10:
This verse says that the false gods, the ones that did not make the heavens and the earth, will disappear from this world. The word "perish" means to be destroyed or to cease to exist. It is a forceful statement about the difference between the true God and idols.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people, who lived surrounded by nations with idols of silver, gold, and wood. The verses before this one mock those images made by craftsmen. It is notable that this verse is written in Aramaic, not in Hebrew, as if it were a message meant for neighboring peoples to understand. Scholars explain this in different ways.

Today we do not carve statues, but we can put our trust in things we make ourselves: money, success, or recognition. Ask yourself where you are placing your security, and turn your trust back to the Creator.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that God, with just his voice, causes the heavens to fill with water. He lifts up the clouds from the ends of the earth, makes the lightnings together with the rain, and brings out the wind from his treasures, that is, from his storehouses. The words "the ends of the earth" refer to the most distant places.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. Just before this, he says that the false gods did nothing, and afterward he mocks the cast idols, which have no breath in them. By contrast, he presents the true God as the Creator who governs nature.

For today: when you feel that your life is moving through storms or things beyond your control, remember that the God who commands the wind and the rain cares for you. Trust in him and do not place your security in money, success, or passing things.
exp.9:13:
Jeremiah 10:14 says that the person who worships idols acts without understanding. This verse says such a person becomes foolish and stops reasoning. A "knowledge" here means understanding or insight. A cast image is a figure of molten metal poured into a mold, and the one who makes it is the metalworker. The metalworker should feel shame, because his work is a deception: the figure has no breath, that is, no life in it.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, sent by God to warn Judah not to imitate the religions of the surrounding nations. Just before this, the text shows the Creator who made the earth, the heavens, the rain, and the wind. The contrast is strong: the living God creates, while the idol is made by human hands.

For today, let us ask what we put in the place of God, such as money, success, or image. These things promise security but have no life. Let us return to trusting the Creator, who hears and sustains.
exp.9:16:
It says that someone must gather up their belongings from the countryside or the surrounding lands. It speaks to a woman who lives in a fortified place, that is, a walled city. The goods here are her possessions or the things she kept outside. The command is to bring them into the city because something serious is approaching.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah trusted in its walls and in its idols, but God announces that a siege and exile are coming. The woman represents Jerusalem, or its people. Many scholars read it this way, although the text does not say so in so many words.

For today: let us not place our security in what we build, save, or own, because that can fail. Let us learn to heed God's warnings in time and to trust in Him, who is the Maker of all things.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that a report is coming, a great roar from the north. The phrase used for the report means a rumor or news that spreads, and the word for "north" is an old term. That army will turn the cities of Judah into desolate places, so abandoned that only snakes will live in them (other versions say jackals).

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah before the invasion by Babylon. The verses just before show Judah mourning like a tent that has been torn down. It says that their leaders, called shepherds, were foolish and did not seek God, and for that reason the people were scattered. Many understand the north to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here.

For today: when we make decisions, let us seek God first, and not only our own wisdom. If we are leaders at home, in the church, or at work, let us care humbly for those who depend on us.
exp.9:24:
Here the prophet asks God to pour out his anger on the nations that do not know him and do not call on his name. The reason is that those nations ate up and devoured Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, and made their home desolate.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of his people, before or during the Babylonian invasion. He has just acknowledged that a person does not control his own path, and he has asked for correction that is just, not destruction. Now he cries out for God to act against those who attacked Israel with cruelty. It is a prayer of pain, and this kind of cry also appears in some of the psalms.

For today: when you suffer injustice, you can bring your pain honestly to God and leave justice in his hands, instead of taking revenge yourself.
exp.10:0:
This verse is the introduction to a new message. It says that God spoke to Jeremiah.

The one speaking is Jehovah, the God of Israel, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. From the verses that follow, we see that God asks him to remind the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem of the covenant they had with Him. Scholars disagree about the exact moment this message refers to, so it is not wise to claim a specific date. What is clear is that God speaks to call His people to obedience.

For today: before looking for what to do, let us learn to listen. Take a few minutes to read the Bible with an open heart, asking yourself: "Lord, what do you want to say to me, and how can I obey you today?"
exp.10:1:
Here God commands that the words of "this covenant" be heard, that is, the solemn agreement He made with His people. And it is not enough to hear them: they must go and speak them to everyone, to the people of Judah and to those who lived in Jerusalem.

God speaks to Jeremiah, His prophet, and charges him to proclaim the covenant He had made with Israel when He brought them out of Egypt. From what follows in the chapter, the people had stopped obeying, and God was reminding them of what they had promised. It is not known with certainty which exact moment of Jeremiah's ministry this message corresponds to; some connect it with the reforms of King Josiah, but there are different opinions.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we merely know God's Word or truly listen to it in order to obey it. We can also ask with whom we might share what God has taught us.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that God commands Jeremiah to speak to the people on his behalf. The message is serious: "Cursed be the man that obeys not the words of this covenant." "Man" here means any person among the people, and "cursed" means that they are under the consequences of having rejected God. "Covenant" is the solemn agreement between God and his people.

The LORD speaks, and Jeremiah must repeat it to the people of Judah and of Jerusalem. This covenant had been given to their ancestors when God brought them out of Egypt. God reminds them that he kept his part faithfully, and asks them now to obey him. Scholars debate the exact moment when Jeremiah delivered this message, so it is not wise to state it with certainty.

Today we can remember that obedience to God springs from gratitude for what he has already done for us. We can ask him today to help us obey him in something specific.
exp.10:5:
In this verse, God orders Jeremiah to proclaim aloud, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, the words of the covenant. Proclaim means to announce publicly. Hear, and do them mean to listen and to put them into practice. Hearing is not enough: God asks for obedience.

The one speaking is God, and he gives the task to the prophet Jeremiah. The covenant is the commitment God made with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt: they would obey, and he would be their God. Jeremiah had already given his answer. The verses that follow explain why the message was urgent: their ancestors did not obey, and the people were still walking the same path.

For today: hearing God should lead us to act. Choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know, and decide today on one concrete step to live it out.
exp.10:8:
God tells Jeremiah that he has discovered a common plot and rebellion among the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks to the prophet Jeremiah. He had warned their fathers, from the time he brought them out of Egypt, to obey him and keep his covenant. Now the people were repeating the same disobedience: it was not just an isolated mistake, but a shared decision to return to idols. That is why God announces that judgment will come.

For today: disobedience sometimes becomes a collective habit and stops seeming serious to us. Ask yourself humbly which practices accepted around you move away from what God says, and ask him for the courage to listen to him and obey, even when others do not.
exp.10:11:
This verse says that when disaster comes, the people of the towns of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go out to cry for help to the false gods to whom they burned incense. But those gods will not be able to save them when they need them most.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had broken the covenant that God made with their ancestors, and had given themselves over to idolatry. God announces that the evil will come, and shows with irony that the idols they chose have no power to rescue them.

For today: it is easy to trust in things that seem to give us security, such as money, success, or the approval of others. When crises come, only God truly sustains. It is worth asking ourselves what we trust in first, and returning to Him with sincerity before the storm arrives.
exp.10:12:
It says that Judah had as many false gods as it had cities, and that in Jerusalem there were as many altars as there were streets. Those altars were for Baal, a Canaanite god who was very popular at that time.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had broken their covenant with Him and worshiped idols everywhere. For this reason God announces a punishment: when trouble comes, they will cry out to those gods, and those gods will not be able to save them. It is a serious warning to a people who did not want to return to God.

For today: examine what you place your trust in, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Anything that takes the place of God can become an idol. Give that place back to Him today in prayer.
exp.10:13:
God tells Jeremiah that he should no longer pray for the people of Judah. He warns him not to raise a cry or a prayer on their behalf, because when they call to Him in their distress, He will not listen to them.

God is speaking to his prophet Jeremiah. Judah had broken the covenant: they filled the cities and streets with altars to Baal and to other gods. This command is very harsh and shows how serious their persistent rebellion was. God had warned them many times, but they did not change. Now, only in the crisis, they wanted to seek Him.

For today: God does not want us to seek Him only when trouble comes. True faith is cultivated every day, with obedience and sincere repentance. Let us not wait for pain before returning to Him; let us draw near today with humility.
exp.10:14:
God asks with sorrow: what is my beloved people doing in my house, when they have committed so many wicked deeds? The holy flesh refers to the offerings from the temple sacrifices. God says that those offerings will not be able to remove the punishment, because the people were glad and boasted in their wickedness. The text is difficult, and some translators understand it in different ways, but the general sense is clear.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had as many gods as it had cities, and it worshiped Baal, and yet it kept going to the temple as if nothing were wrong. God had already said that he would not listen to their pleas, because religion without obedience is of no use.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or to perform rituals. God seeks a faithful heart, one that turns away from what is evil and loves him alone.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that God, who planted his people like a tree, now announces disaster against them. The phrase about pronouncing it is explained as meaning that he has declared a punishment. The cause is the wickedness of Israel and Judah, who brought harm on themselves, that is, they hurt themselves through their own choices. Burning incense here means offering it to the idol Baal, which is the act that provoked the Lord to anger.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, delivering God's message. The people had made a covenant with him, but they broke it by worshiping false gods. The image of the green and beautiful olive tree shows how greatly the Lord had blessed them. Scholars understand the fire mentioned in the previous verse as a reference to the judgment that was coming, though the details are interpreted in different ways.

God has given us everything good that we have. It is worth asking ourselves what things take the place that belongs only to him, and returning to him sincerely before those things do us harm.
exp.10:18:
Here Jeremiah says that he felt like a gentle lamb being led to the slaughter. He did not realize that some were scheming against him. Those who plotted did so in secret, planning evil, and they wanted to destroy him along with everything his life produced. They wanted to cut him off from the living, so that no one would remember his name.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. God had shown him that there was a conspiracy, and it is later known that these were his own fellow citizens from Anathoth. They rejected his message, which called the people to abandon the worship of Baal. They wanted to silence him so that he would prophesy no more.

Today, if you suffer opposition for doing what is right, you are not alone. Jeremiah did not take revenge on his own, but placed his cause before God. You can do the same: pray sincerely, remain faithful, and trust that God sees what others do in secret.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that God speaks about the men of Anathoth, the town of Jeremiah. They wanted to kill him (they were seeking his life, that is, seeking to take his life), and they told him: "Do not prophesy in the name of the Lord, or you will die by our hand." In other words, they wanted to silence him with threats.

The Lord speaks, and he is answering Jeremiah after Jeremiah discovered the plot. The people of his own town, probably even people close to him, rejected God's message and wanted to silence the prophet. Jeremiah had placed his cause in God's hands, and here God answers him and announces that he will judge those who threatened him.

For today: if you are rejected for obeying God or speaking the truth, even within your own family or community, do not stay silent out of fear, and do not take revenge. Entrust your cause to God, as Jeremiah did, and trust that he sees and judges with justice.
exp.10:21:
God announces that he will punish the men of Anathoth, that is, call them to account for what they have done. The young men will die by the sword, and their sons and daughters will die of hunger. It is a very harsh announcement of judgment.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The neighbors in his own town, Anathoth, wanted to kill him so that he would stop prophesying. Jeremiah placed his case in God's hands, and God responds with this sentence. Some scholars connect it with the invasions that came upon Judah, but the text does not detail how it was fulfilled.

For today: when someone rejects you or attacks you for doing what is right, do not seek revenge. Commit your cause to God, who sees the heart and judges with justice. Remain faithful and let Him work.
exp.11:0:
Jeremiah acknowledges that God is righteous, yet he dares to bring a complaint before Him. He wants to speak with God about matters of justice. His question is: why do the wicked prosper, and why do those who act treacherously live at ease? Here, bringing a complaint before God means presenting one's grievance to Him, and acting treacherously means with betrayal or a lack of faithfulness.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, in the midst of his ministry in Judah. He was suffering rejection and opposition for proclaiming God's message. So, with pain and sincerity, he lays his confusion before God. The verses that follow describe people who speak of God with their mouths, but keep Him far from their hearts.

For today: when injustice confuses you or hurts you, you do not have to stay silent. You can bring your questions to God with honesty and respect, as Jeremiah did, trusting that He is just even when you do not yet understand.
exp.11:5:
They say that even Jeremiah's own relatives, his kinsmen and the house of his father, have dealt treacherously with him. They rose up against him and cried out after him, that is, they accused him and pursued him loudly. God warns him: do not trust them, even when they speak with kind words to you, that is, do not put your faith in them even when they speak to you in a pleasant way.

Here God answers Jeremiah's complaint about the wickedness of the people. It is thought that his relatives were from Anathoth, his hometown, though the text does not say this in detail. God tells him that the opposition will be harder and closer than he imagines, and that he must prepare himself to remain faithful.

For today: when someone very close to you wounds you, do not be surprised or stop obeying God. Be wise about whom you trust, ask for wisdom, and rest in God, who never betrays you.
exp.11:13:
Thus says the Lord concerning the wicked neighbors, the nations close by that attacked and harmed the land God gave Israel as an inheritance. God promises to uproot them from their land, that is, to drive them out of it. He also says he will pluck Judah out from among them, which can be understood as rescuing Judah from those nations.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had been judged, and the neighboring nations took advantage of its fall. But God does not leave them unaccountable: they too will answer for what they did. The verses that follow show that, after the judgment, God will show mercy and restore those who turn back to him.

For today: God sees injustice and also offers a new beginning. We can trust that he executes justice without our taking revenge ourselves, and we can draw near to him with humility, knowing that his mercy remains available.
exp.11:15:
