It says that if the neighboring nations of Israel carefully learn the ways of God's people, and swear "As the Lord lives" sincerely, just as they once taught Israel to swear by Baal, then they too will be prospered, or made to grow strong, in the midst of his people. "Swear" here means committing oneself to God as the true God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on the wicked neighbors who harmed Israel and led them into idolatry. But he also leaves open a door of mercy there: if they turn back to the Lord, they will be received. If they do not, the following verse speaks of their destruction.

For today: God offers a new opportunity even to those who have harmed us or led us astray. We can pray for them and live with integrity, so that our example invites them to know the Lord.
exp.12:0:
God tells the prophet Jeremiah to buy a linen belt, that is, a sash of fine cloth, and to put it around his waist. The waist, or the lower part of the back, is the place where the belt goes. He is also told not to wet it, that is, not to wash it or put it in water.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is his messenger. God often teaches through symbolic actions, so that the people can see a message and not only hear it. Here a lesson begins about Judah and its relationship with God. The full meaning is explained in the verses that follow, so it is good to read them calmly. Some scholars debate details of how this action was carried out, but the central message is clear.

For today: obey God even when you do not yet understand the reason. Often he explains his purposes later, while you take the first step of trust.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah a second time. The word "came" in the verse is how the message reached him, and "the word of the Lord" is God's message. Jeremiah had already obeyed the first instruction, to buy and wear the linen belt, and now he receives new instructions.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking, and God is the one giving the message. All of this is part of a sign God uses to teach Judah. The linen belt represents something close to God, and the text explains this later. Some scholars debate whether the journey to the Euphrates was real or a vision, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: God keeps guiding us step by step. Be faithful in obeying what He has already shown you, and stay alert and ready to listen for what He asks of you next.
exp.12:3:
Here God asks Jeremiah to take the linen belt he bought, the one he wears around his waist, and go to the Euphrates River. There he must hide it in a hole in a rock.

The Lord speaks, and gives an order to his prophet Jeremiah. It is a symbolic action, like a parable acted out. Later in the same chapter, God explains that the belt represents Judah, a people who were meant to cling to him but became proud. Some debate the exact location of the Euphrates, since it is far away, and it is not certain whether this was a real journey or a vision.

For today: God wants us close to him, like a belt held snugly against the body. We can set aside a moment each day to pray and read his Word, so that we do not drift away from him.
exp.12:8:
God says that just as the linen belt hidden by the Euphrates rotted and became useless, He will cause the pride of Judah and of Jerusalem to rot. Pride means thinking more of yourself than you should and refusing to submit to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had been commanded to use a linen belt as a sign for the people. God wanted to show that Judah, made to stay close to Him, had drifted away by refusing to listen and by following other gods. The text does not make clear whether the trip to the Euphrates was literal or a vision, and scholars understand it in both ways.

Today, pride pulls us away from God and ruins us from within. We can ask God in prayer where we struggle to listen to Him, and obey Him with humility.
exp.12:9:
God says this people is evil because they refuse to listen to his words, follow the wishes of their own stubborn heart, and go after other gods, to serve them and bow down before them. So they will be like this waistband: good for nothing.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had asked him to take a linen waistband, hide it by the Euphrates River, and later it rotted there. Through that sign he shows that Judah, which should have clung to God like a waistband to the waist, was ruined by its pride and disobedience.

For today: God wants us close to him, not just out of habit. If we stop listening to his Word and follow only what our heart dictates, we wear ourselves down from the inside. Today you can set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and obey one concrete thing.
exp.12:12:
God says he will fill all the inhabitants of the land with a staggering confusion: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the people of Jerusalem. This is not about drunkenness from wine, but a picture of God's judgment: they will be confused, stumbling, unable to defend themselves.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, with the image of the linen belt, God had reminded them that he had bound his people to himself so that they would honor him, but they would not listen. The image of the wineskin full of wine announces that this judgment will reach everyone, without exception, not even the leaders.

For today: let us not trust in our position or our religion; let us listen to God with humility and obey while there is still time.
exp.12:19:
Look up, it says, and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given to you, the flock that was your pride? That people is no longer there, for it was taken into exile.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jerusalem, and probably the royal house, before Judah fell to Babylon. Many understand that the invaders were coming from the north. God warns that the ruin is not an accident, but the result of a persistent wickedness, as the following verses say.

For today: if God has entrusted people to us, such as children, students, or a congregation, let us care for them with faithfulness and humility. Let us not wait until a crisis arrives to turn back to God; let us listen to his correction in time.
exp.12:22:
It says that just as a dark-skinned person cannot change his skin, nor a leopard remove its spots, neither can the people do good on their own, because they are accustomed to doing evil. The word "Ethiopian" here renders the Hebrew term for a man from Cush, that is, the region south of Egypt. "Skin" is the outer covering of the body. "Accustomed" means used to something.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. After many warnings, the people kept on with idolatry and injustice. God uses this image to show how deeply rooted their sin was, and that punishment was drawing near.

For today: bad habits are hard to break by willpower alone. Recognize your need, ask God to transform you, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.13:1:
It says that all of Judah is in mourning because of the drought. And from Jerusalem rises a cry, a plea for help.

God speaks to Jeremiah because of a great drought. The verses that follow show nobles, servants, and farmers ashamed because there is no water and no harvest. Jeremiah presents this crisis as a painful situation, and in the context of the book many connect it with the people's turning away from God, though here the emphasis is on the suffering.

When crises come, we should not hide our pain. We can present it honestly to God, cry out to Him, and examine our hearts so that we return to Him with humility.
exp.13:2:
The verse tells how the nobles of Judah sent their servants to fetch water. The servants went to the pools, or water reservoirs, but found nothing. They returned with their vessels empty. They felt shame and dismay, and they covered their heads, a gesture of grief and humiliation.

God spoke to Jeremiah because of a great drought. All the people were in mourning. Here it is shown that not even the rich and powerful were spared from the scarcity. In other passages of Jeremiah, this drought is connected with the sin of the people, although this verse only describes the distress.

For today: when our resources run out and nothing we have is enough, we can set aside pride and seek God with humility, recognizing that only he can give what we truly need.
exp.13:5:
It says that even the wild donkeys, which usually endure drought well, climbed onto the hills and gasped for air like jackals. Their eyes grew dim, meaning their strength of sight failed, because there was no grass left at all.

Jeremiah describes a great drought in Judah. Shortly before, he speaks of the cracked ground, the ashamed farmers, and the does who abandoned their young. Soon the people acknowledge their sin and cry out to God. Many understand this drought as a consequence of the people's disobedience, although the text here mainly describes the suffering and the prayer that follows.

When things dry up inside or outside us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can do what the people did: recognize our need, be honest about our failings, and cry out to God, who is our hope.
exp.13:7:
Jeremiah speaks to God in pain. He calls him the hope of Israel and the one who keeps his people in distress. But he complains: why does God seem like a stranger passing through, or a traveler who stops only for a night, with no intention of staying? The word "stranger" means someone who is only passing through.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, pleading for the people during a terrible drought. He acknowledges that they have sinned and asks God to act for the sake of his name. His complaint expresses what he feels, not necessarily what God is really like. Later, God answers that the people had turned away from him.

For today: when you feel that God is distant, do not stay silent. Bring your complaint to him with honesty and humility, acknowledge whatever needs correcting, and trust that he remains your hope.
exp.13:12:
Jeremiah says to God, in distress: "Ah, Lord God!" because the prophets are telling the people that there will be no war or famine, but a secure peace. The word "sword" stands for war itself. The phrase "peace" can also be understood as a steady and lasting peace.

Jeremiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks in a time of drought and threat. God had already told him not to pray for a people who did not want to return to Him. Jeremiah responds by pointing out that other prophets say the opposite. God clarifies that those prophets speak lies in His name, although He did not send them.

Today, not every message that sounds encouraging comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and seek the truth even when it is uncomfortable, because God calls people to repentance before He gives firm comfort.
exp.13:13:
God answers Jeremiah and tells him that the prophets who speak in his name are lying. He did not send them, he did not command them, and he did not speak to them. What they announce is a false vision, divination, a thing of nothing, and a deceit that comes from their own heart.

Jeremiah had interceded for a people suffering from drought and famine. God tells him that he will not listen to their fasting. Jeremiah complains that the prophets promise peace and no war. Here God speaks and makes clear that these promises do not come from him. For that reason the people, who believed the deception, will also face the consequences.

Today it is wise to compare what we hear, even when it sounds spiritual or encouraging, with what the Bible says. That someone uses God's name does not prove that they speak on his behalf. A pleasant word is not always true.
exp.13:16:
God tells Jeremiah to say these words to the people: let their eyes overflow with tears day and night, without stopping. The "virgin daughter of my people" is a poetic way of speaking of Judah, like a beloved young woman. She is broken, that is, shattered, struck with a very heavy blow.

Jeremiah speaks, yet his words reflect God's own grief. There is drought, hunger and war, and false prophets had promised peace when God had not sent them. Even so, the message of judgment does not come from a cold heart, but from someone who weeps for his people.

For today: when someone suffers the consequences of their mistakes, we can speak the truth without harshness or pride. Let us ask God for a heart that weeps with those who suffer and also prays for them.
exp.14:0:
God tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel, two great intercessors for the people, were to stand before him pleading for them, his decision would not change. The phrase about casting them out of his sight means that God commands Israel to be sent away. The phrase about his will not being toward this people means that at this time he will no longer show compassion to them.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah in the midst of a drought and a crisis in Judah. Moses and Samuel had interceded for Israel before (Exodus 32; 1 Samuel 7). Here God shows that the people had persisted so long in their idolatry and disobedience that judgment was already decided. The verses that follow describe death, the sword, famine, and captivity.

For today: the prayers of others are valuable, but they do not replace our own repentance. Do not delay turning to God; today you can draw near to him with sincerity and obedience.
exp.14:1:
This verse says that when the people ask, "Where shall we go?", Jeremiah is to tell them the words of God: each person will receive the fate that falls to them. Some will die of disease or plague, others by the sword, others by famine, and others will be led away as captives to another country. The word for "sword" here means war or the blade of battle.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had rejected God for a long time, and the passage points to the sins of Manasseh as part of the cause. God says that not even Moses or Samuel, great intercessors, would change the situation. Some understand "death" to mean plague; the text does not make this clear.

For today: do not take lightly God's voice when He calls you to return to Him. You can pray sincerely today, acknowledge something you have neglected, and ask Him for help to change, because His patience is real, but it must not be mistaken for permission to stay as you are.
exp.14:2:
God announces that he will send four kinds of punishment upon his people: the sword that kills, the dogs that tear apart, and the birds and the beasts that devour and leave everything ruined.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the time of Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had rejected God again and again. Not even the prayers of Moses and Samuel, great intercessors, would change the decision. The text mentions the sins of Manasseh, a king who led the people into idolatry and violence.

For today: God is patient, but he takes seriously the sin that is not abandoned. Let us not wait for the consequences to arrive. If there is something God has shown you that you should leave behind, do it today with humility, trusting in his forgiveness and his mercy.
exp.14:10:
The Lord tells Jeremiah that surely what remains of him will turn out for good, that is, that his life will end in something good. He also promises that even the enemy will come to seek him and to plead with him in the difficult time and on the day of distress. The remnant, what is left over, is the part that survives.

Jeremiah has just complained to God: they curse him and see him as a man of quarrels, even though he never harmed them. Here God answers him with a personal promise. Translators and scholars understand this verse in several ways, since the Hebrew text is difficult, but almost all agree that it is a word of comfort for the faithful prophet in the midst of rejection.

When you suffer for doing what is right and feel alone, bring your complaint to God honestly, as Jeremiah did. He listens, answers, and promises to care for your future. Trust that the end of the one who is faithful to him is in his hands.
exp.14:11:
This verse asks a question: can anyone smash iron, iron from the north, or bronze? The expected answer is no. The phrase "from the north" is not part of the question's wording in the verse you are reading, so the question stands on its own. Scholars interpret it in two ways: as a reference to Babylon, which would come from the north with great force, or as an image of Jeremiah's firmness, since God made him strong.

Jeremiah complains to God because everyone rejects him for preaching a hard message. God answers him that his life will have a good ending. Then God announces judgment on the people for their sins. The text is difficult, and there is no single explanation that is certain.

For today: when people reject you for doing what is right, do not rely only on your own strength. God sustains those who are faithful to him, and you can bring your complaints to him honestly, as Jeremiah did.
exp.14:13:
God says that he will cause the enemies of Judah to carry the people away into a land unknown to them. The reason is that God's anger is like a fire that has been kindled and will burn against them. The phrase about making them pass over is about being taken away or carried off to another place. The word for the people carried away refers to being taken as captives, and to handing over to plunder.

Here God speaks to the people of Judah through Jeremiah. They had fallen into idolatry and disobedience, and God announces the consequences. Some scholars see here a reference to the exile in Babylon, but the wording of this verse presents certain difficulties, and for that reason there are different ways of translating it.

For today: God speaks with seriousness about sin, but his warnings aim to wake us up in time. If today you feel that God is calling you to change something, do not harden your heart; return to him with humility, because his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.14:14:
Here Jeremiah speaks to God with honesty. He tells God that He knows his situation, and he asks Him to remember him, to visit him (that is, to step in and look after him), and to avenge him (to do justice against those who persecute him). He also begs God not to let him suffer while God delays His anger, because he is bearing reproach and contempt for being faithful to Him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, rejected and mocked for announcing God's message to a people who did not want to hear it. This is one of his most intimate outpourings. The verses that follow show that he loved God's word, but he felt alone and wounded by the mission.

For today: when you suffer for doing what is right, you can pray with complete frankness, without hiding your pain. Hand over to God your desire for justice, instead of taking it into your own hands, and trust that He sees your faithfulness.
exp.14:16:
Jeremiah says he did not join the mockers for their amusement, nor did he think himself superior for being a prophet. He preferred to remain alone, because God had filled him with bitterness, a deep indignation and sorrow. Being filled with anger here is the sense of what the verse describes.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a sincere complaint to God. He had received the word of the Lord with joy, but announcing it brought him mockery, rejection and loneliness. His pain was great, and he even dares to ask God whether He has left him without help. God answers by calling him back to Himself and to remaining firm.

For today: if obeying God brings you loneliness or mockery, do not hide your pain. Tell Him honestly, and ask Him for strength to remain faithful without being carried along by the crowd.
exp.14:17:
Jeremiah asks God why his pain does not end. He speaks of a wound that is hopeless, without any prospect of healing, and that refuses to be cured. Then he dares to ask God whether he will be to him like something false, a deception, like a stream that dries up and gives no reliable water just when it is most needed.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He had been faithful: he received God's word with joy, did not join with the mockers, and stood alone, filled with indignation at the sin of the people. Even so, he suffered rejection and persecution. That is why he complains with honesty. God does not rebuke him harshly, but calls him to trust again and promises to be with him and to protect him.

You can bring your complaints and doubts to God with sincerity, without pretending. He listens, corrects with love, and reminds you that he remains with you, even when the pain lasts longer than you expected.
exp.14:18:
God tells Jeremiah that if he turns back to Him, He will restore him and he will continue to stand before Him and serve Him. If he separates what is precious from what is worthless, he will speak as the mouth of God. Restoring means bringing back to its place, and what is worthless is that which has no value at all. In the end, the people must turn to the prophet, and not the prophet to the people.

The Lord speaks, answering Jeremiah, who has just complained bitterly. He feels alone, wounded, and rejected for preaching an unpopular message, and he even asks God whether he will be like a stream that dries up. God does not scold him harshly, but calls him to regain his confidence and faithfulness. Then He promises him protection.

For today: when you feel tired from doing what is right, tell God your pain honestly, but do not give in to whatever pulls you away from the truth. Ask Him to help you distinguish what is valuable from what is empty, and to speak with firmness and love.
exp.14:19:
God promises Jeremiah that he will make him like a wall of bronze, strong and impossible to knock down, standing against the people. They will fight against him, but they will not be able to defeat him, because God will be with him to keep and defend him.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah, who felt hurt and worn out by the rejection of his people. He had come to doubt God, calling Him unstable waters. God asks him to return to Him and speak the truth, without giving in to the pressure of the people. Then He gives him this promise of firmness.

For today: when you do what is right and others criticize you, do not depend on your own strength. Come to God honestly, even with your doubts, and trust that His presence sustains you. Being firm does not mean there will be no opposition, but that you will not be alone.
exp.15:3:
This verse announces a very harsh judgment on Judah. Many will die of terrible diseases, and no one will mourn them or bury them. Their bodies will be left lying like refuse on the ground, and they will become food for birds and wild animals. There will be war and famine.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He is commanded not to marry or have children, as a living sign of what would come upon that land. The people had abandoned God and followed other gods, and God withdraws his peace. Many understand this as a warning given before the fall of Jerusalem, although the text does not give details of each scene.

For today: God is serious about sin, but his warnings are meant to bring us back to him. Today you can ask yourself what you have put in God's place, and, in prayer, return to him sincerely before the harm grows.
exp.15:4:
God tells Jeremiah not to enter a house where there is mourning, not to go and weep with the family or offer them comfort. The reason is that God has taken away his peace, his mercy, and his compassion from this people. It is a harsh sign that the judgment is already unavoidable.

The Lord speaks to his prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had rejected God again and again. That Jeremiah should not take part in the mourning was a public sign: there would be so many deaths that no one would be left to bury or comfort the dead. Scholars understand in different ways whether this also protected Jeremiah or only announced the judgment.

For today: God calls us to listen to him in time, before we harden our hearts. Today, through Christ, we can draw near to his mercy with confidence. Let us not let it pass; let us come to him with humility, and also comfort those who are suffering.
exp.15:5:
It says that in the land of Judah people of every age will die, great and small, and no one will give them a proper burial. No one will mourn for them. Wailing aloud, cutting the skin, and tearing out the hair were gestures of grief, as when one wounds oneself or pulls out one's hair.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had left God for idols, and judgment was coming because of their rebellion. God forbids Jeremiah to attend funerals and feasts, as a sign that there would no longer be peace or comfort for that generation. Many understand that this points to the invasion of Babylon.

For today: God is serious about sin, but He still calls people to repentance. Do not harden your heart; if God shows you something, return to Him today, while there is still time for mercy.
exp.15:6:
This verse says that when judgment comes, people will no longer be able to observe the customs of comfort for the dead. Sharing a meal with mourners, and the cup that was offered to them to encourage them, even when they had lost a father or a mother, will be impossible. There will be so many deaths that not even this will be possible.

God speaks through Jeremiah before the fall of Jerusalem. He orders the prophet not to attend funerals or feasts, as a living sign for the people. God says he has taken away his peace because of Judah's persistent disobedience. It is a serious warning, not a mockery of grief.

Today, we can see how valuable it is to be present with someone who suffers. If you have the opportunity today to comfort someone with a meal, a visit, or a prayer, do it, and remember that true peace comes from God.
exp.15:9:
God tells Jeremiah that when the prophet announces the punishment, the people will ask him in amazement: "Why has the Lord pronounced all this great evil against us? Or what is our iniquity? What is our sin that we have committed against the Lord our God?"

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah before the fall of Judah. God orders him not to attend feasts or times of mourning, as a sign that the end of joy in that land is coming. God already knows that the people will not acknowledge their guilt. In the verses that follow, he answers them: their ancestors abandoned him to serve other gods, and they have done even worse, following their own stubborn hearts.

For today: it is easy not to see our own sin. Let us ask God to show us honestly where we have drifted away from him, and let us listen without becoming defensive.
exp.15:13:
This verse says that God announces a change. Until now people swore by saying, "The Lord lives, who brought up Israel out of Egypt." But days will come when that will no longer be the main saying.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just announced the exile because of the people's idolatry and hardness of heart. Even so, before finishing the warning, God adds a promise: there will be a return. What follows compares it with the exodus, but presents it as a deliverance that will be remembered even more, coming from the north and from other lands.

For today: God disciplines, but He does not abandon. If you are going through the consequences of your own mistakes or those of others, remember that He can open a new path. Trust in His faithfulness and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.15:16:
God says that his eyes are fixed on all the ways of his people, that is, on the way they live. Nothing they did escaped him, and their wickedness cannot be hidden from his sight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises to bring Israel back from the lands where it had been scattered, but first he explains that the punishment is just: the people filled the land with idolatry, and God saw all of it. So judgment comes first, and restoration follows.

For today: we do not live hidden before God, and that can bring us either fear or comfort. We can stop pretending and honestly confess to him what is in our hearts. The One who sees us completely also offers forgiveness and a new beginning to anyone who turns back to him.
exp.16:0:
This verse says that the sin of the people of Judah is not something temporary or easy to erase. It is written as if with an iron tool and a diamond point, that is, carved into hard stone. That sin is marked on the heart of the people and also on the horns of their altars (the reference to the altar's corners is what the verse describes).

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who warns Judah before the judgment. The people practiced idolatry at altars and high places, and their children followed the same custom. That is why God announces that there will be consequences.

For today: do not downplay the bad habits of the heart, because they become custom and are passed down. Ask God to renew your heart and to teach you to leave in your family a mark of faith, not of sin.
exp.16:1:
Here the text says that the children of Judah fondly remember their altars and their groves, which were sacred poles or trees used to worship idols. Those places stood beside leafy trees and on the high hills, where that false worship was practiced.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just said that Judah's sin is engraved as with an iron chisel on their heart. The children inherited idolatry from their parents and felt it as part of their identity. That is why the judgment announced afterward would come.

For today: what we repeat and love over time is engraved on the heart. It is worth asking ourselves which inherited or learned "altars" are occupying God's place in our lives, and asking him to write his truth on our hearts.
exp.16:5:
This verse describes how the person ends up who trusts only in human strength and turns away from God. He will be like a dry shrub of the desert. He will not notice when something good arrives. He will live in dry, barren places, in a land without people where nothing grows.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had put their security in alliances with other nations and in their own strength, and had left the LORD. God warns them with this image of the desert, which contrasts with the tree by the water in the following verse.

For today: when you face pressure, do not place all your hope in money, connections, or your own effort. Make prayer and trust in God your first support, and you will see your life take root where there is water.
exp.16:6:
Blessed is the person who trusts in the Lord, that is, who places his security in Him. The word "man" here refers to any person, and "trusts" means has confidence. The second part reinforces this: the Lord Himself is his confidence, not just one more help among others.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on what God said to the people of Judah. Just before this, God warns against trusting in other people and in one's own strength (flesh is his arm). That mistake is compared to a dry bush in the desert. This verse presents the contrast, and then the one who trusts in God is compared to a tree by the water.

For today: when a great worry comes, before looking only for human solutions, pray and hand it over to God. Asking others for help is not wrong, but let your final rest be in Him.
exp.16:13:
Here Jeremiah asks God to heal him and to save him. He says that if God does this, he will truly be healed and saved. He ends by saying that God is his praise, that is, the reason for his gratitude and trust.

The text does not make clear whether the healing is physical, emotional, or spiritual.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He has just said that those who turn away from God will be put to shame, because they abandon the source of living water. Right after this, he reports that people mock him and ask him where the word of the Lord is. For this reason he prays out of his pain, seeking from God what no one else can give him.

When you feel hurt, tired, or criticized, make a simple and sincere prayer like this one. Do not depend only on your own strength or on the opinion of others. Bring your need before God and trust that he alone can give you true healing and salvation.
exp.16:14:
Here Jeremiah reports what the people say to him in mockery: "Where is what God says will happen? Let it happen now!" They doubt God's word because they still do not see it fulfilled. The phrase "let it come now" means "let it come right away, let it be fulfilled this very moment."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, in Judah. He had announced judgment because of the people's disobedience, but time went by and nothing happened. That is why they mocked him. Jeremiah, hurt, brings his complaint to God and asks him to heal and sustain him, trusting that God knows he spoke with sincerity.

For today: when God seems slow, or when others mock your faith, do not lose heart. Bring your pain to God honestly, as Jeremiah did, and keep trusting that his word is true, even when his timing is not yours.
exp.16:17:
Jeremiah asks God that his persecutors be put to shame and dismay, and that he himself not be. He asks that God bring upon them the day of evil, that is, a time of calamity, and that God destroy them with a complete and severe punishment.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here; he suffered mockery and threats for announcing God's word to the people. Earlier he says that he did not seek to be a prophet for his own pleasure, nor did he desire disaster; he only spoke what God gave him. This prayer is very harsh, and some see it as a desperate cry for justice rather than as a model of revenge.

For today: when you are hurt for doing what is right, you can tell God honestly your pain and your anger. Then leave justice in his hands and do not take revenge yourself.
exp.16:19:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the kings of Judah, to all the people, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem who pass through the city's gates. The verse's word "hear" means listen closely and pay attention.

Here the Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He sends him to stand at the gates, where all the people came and went, so that no one could say they did not hear. The message that follows is about keeping the Sabbath and not working on that day, as God had commanded their ancestors.

For today: God speaks clearly and wants his word to be heard. We can set aside a fixed time each day, or each week, to pause, read the Bible, and listen with humility, ready to obey what God shows us.
exp.16:23:
It says there will be blessing if the people obey God. Dios's wording is rendered here in plain terms: God asks them not to carry burdens through the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath, but to set that day apart for Him and do no work at all.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. Shortly before this, he says that their ancestors would not listen and stiffened their necks, meaning they were stubborn. The sabbath was a sign of Israel's covenant with God. The text then promises that the city would remain standing and that the people would come to worship in the temple.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and put God first, without letting work and hurry push Him aside. Christians understand differently how the sabbath applies to them, but the principle of trusting God in rest still holds.
exp.16:24:
God promises that if the people obey and keep the Sabbath, kings and their princes will continue to enter through the gates of Jerusalem, riding in chariots and on horses, seated on the throne of David. The men of Judah are the people of Judah, and the inhabitants are those who live in the city. The city will remain forever as long as there is obedience.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had become stubborn and refused to listen. God offers them a choice: obey and receive blessing, or disobey and see the city burned, as the following verse says. The Sabbath was a sign of trust in God.

For today: God invites us to trust Him and not to live enslaved to work. Set aside a regular time to rest, pray, and thank Him, believing that He sustains your life.
exp.16:25:
This verse describes a promised blessing. If the people obey, people from everywhere will come to the temple: from the cities of Judah, from the areas around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the plain, from the mountains, and from the south, the region toward the Negev. They will bring burnt offerings, sacrifices, grain offerings, incense, and sacrifices of praise, that is, gratitude expressed to God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Before this passage, God asks the people to keep the Sabbath without carrying loads or doing business. If they obey, Jerusalem will remain and its worship will flourish. Then comes the warning: if they do not obey, there will be fire. God offers them a clear choice, and the Sabbath reveals whether their hearts are faithful to him.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest from your work and give thanks to God. That rest can become your sacrifice of praise: singing, praying, and acknowledging that he sustains your life.
exp.16:26:
This verse is a warning. God says that if the people do not obey him by keeping the sabbath as a holy day, and keep carrying loads and bringing things in through the gates of Jerusalem on that day, he will send a fire into those gates. That fire will destroy the palaces and will not go out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message addressed to the king and the people of Judah. The verses before this one promise blessing if they obey: the city would remain and people would come to worship. This verse shows the other side: disobedience would bring judgment. The sabbath was a sign of the covenant between God and his people.

For today: God invites us to set aside time to rest and to remember that he is our provider. You might reserve one unhurried moment each week, free from work and rush, to pray, rest, and be with your family or your church.
exp.17:2:
Jeremiah obeys what God commanded him: he goes down to the potter's house, the craftsman who makes clay vessels. There he sees him working at the wheel, the spinning device on which the clay turns while the potter shapes it.

God himself had told Jeremiah to go there, to give him a message. Jeremiah was a prophet in Judah, a people who had turned away from God. The Lord uses an everyday scene as a visual lesson, which is explained in the verses that follow: he has the right to deal with his people as the potter deals with the clay.

For today: God often speaks to us through the simple things of each day. Today, as you look at your work or your home, ask him to teach you something. And let him shape you with trust.
exp.17:3:
It says the potter was working a clay vessel, and it was spoiled in his hands. But he did not throw it away: he began again and remade it into another vessel, as seemed good to him.

God sends the prophet Jeremiah to the house of a potter to teach him something. Then God applies the scene to Israel: the people are like the clay in his hand. In the verses that follow, we see that God can respond according to how the people respond, whether with repentance or with rebellion.

For today: if something in your life has been broken, such as a failure or a mistake, it does not mean that God is finished with you. Humbly surrender what you are to him, allow yourself to be corrected, and trust that he can form something new and good.
exp.17:4:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that, after what Jeremiah saw in the potter's house, a message from God came to him. The verse's quoted wording is an old way of saying "came to me," which is already how the verse reads, so no separate comment is needed.

Here the narrator is Jeremiah, and he presents God as the one who is about to give the verse. First the prophet watched the potter remake a damaged vessel. Then God shows him that this scene is a lesson for Israel: He can deal with His people according to His justice and His purpose, and the people need to return to Him.

For today: before drawing quick conclusions about what we are going through, it is worth pausing to listen to God in His Word. He can give meaning even in broken situations, and He invites us to let ourselves be shaped with humility.
exp.17:5:
God asks whether he does not have the right to deal with Israel as the potter deals with his clay. He says the people are in his hand, just as the clay is in the hand of the craftsman.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah saw a potter remake a damaged vessel, and through that picture God explained his message to Judah and Israel. The verses that follow make clear that this is not a blind fate: if a nation turns away from its wickedness, God changes his mind about the punishment. Scholars understand that expression in different ways, but all see an invitation to return.

We can allow ourselves to be shaped by God with humility. If something in our life has been broken or needs to change, it is not too late: God can form us again, and we are called to respond with a willing heart.
exp.17:10:
God tells Jeremiah to speak at once to the people of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The message is that God is preparing a punishment against them, but He offers them a way out: that each one turn from his evil way and correct the way he lives and acts.

The Lord speaks after Jeremiah has watched the potter remake a damaged vessel. God teaches that He responds according to the attitude of the nations: if they repent, He holds back; if they harden themselves, judgment comes. That is why the warning is also an invitation. Nevertheless, the people answered with stubbornness.

For today: when you feel God correcting you, do not take it as rejection, but as an opportunity. Think of one specific habit you need to change, and take a step today to leave it behind, without waiting for tomorrow.
exp.17:11:
This verse says that the people of Judah responded with hopelessness and stubbornness to God's call. They said there was no point in trying, and they chose to follow their own plans and do what their evil heart asked of them, without caring what God said.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, right after the image of the potter who can reshape the clay. He offers Judah a way out: turn from their wrong path and improve their deeds. But the people reject the invitation. Here we do not hear God, but the voice of the people, who shut the door to repentance.

For today: when we feel that change is pointless, or we prefer to keep walking our own way, let us remember that God still invites us. Today we can listen to his voice and take a concrete step toward correction.
exp.17:13:
God asks two questions whose answer is "no": will the snow of Lebanon stop being there? Will the cold waters that come from far away dry up? These things are constant and reliable. Note: the Hebrew of the first sentence is difficult, and translations understand it in several ways.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah. The people had said they would follow their own plans and their stubborn hearts. God contrasts the faithfulness of nature with the unfaithfulness of his people, who had forgotten him to go after empty things, such as idols.

If creation is so constant, how much more can we trust God. Today we can ask ourselves: do I follow my impulses, or do I stay firm in God? Let us return to him with humility and steadiness each day.
exp.17:14:
God says that his people have forgotten him. Instead of worshiping him, they burn incense to emptiness, that is, to empty idols that are of no use at all. That idolatry makes them stumble on their paths, and it turns them away from the old, well-tested paths of their ancestors' faith. So they walk on untrodden trails, paths no one has traveled before and no one knows where they lead.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the kingdom of Judah. Shortly before, he compares the faithfulness of nature, like the snow of Lebanon and the cold waters, with the unfaithfulness of Israel. It is a call to return, but also a warning of judgment, as the verses that follow show.

For today: when you notice that other things are taking God's place, such as success, money, or the approval of others, stop and return to the basics: prayer, his Word, and simple obedience.
exp.17:15:
It says that, because they had abandoned God, the land of Judah will be left in ruins. The phrase about constant hissing refers to mocking or horrified whistles that will be heard again and again. Anyone who passes by there will be astonished and shake his head, a gesture of pity or scorn at seeing such a disaster.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares the steady faithfulness of nature, such as the snow of Lebanon and the cold flowing waters, with the inconstancy of his people, who forgot him and burned incense to empty idols. The old paths are the road of faithfulness that their ancestors walked. The verse announces the consequences of leaving that road.

For today: God calls us to return to the firm and tested character of his Word, instead of chasing empty things that promise much and hold up nothing. Today you can ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart, and turn back to him.
exp.17:16:
It says God will scatter them with strength, like the east wind, a wind from the east that is dry and destructive. He will let them flee before their enemies. "I will show them the back, and not the face" means that God will turn away from them and will not look on them with favor. "The day of their calamity" is the time of their ruin and disaster.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had forgotten him and were offering incense to empty idols. Because of this, they had turned away from the ancient, faithful paths. God announces the consequences of that abandonment. The following verses show that the people, instead of repenting, wanted to attack the prophet.

For today: when God corrects us through his Word, it is better to listen with humility than to defend ourselves or silence the one who speaks to us. Returning to God in time prevents much pain.
exp.18:0:
God tells Jeremiah to go to a potter and buy a clay jar, one of those that are already made and fired. He also asks him to take with him some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests, that is, respected leaders who will serve as witnesses to what is about to happen.

The Lord speaks and gives his prophet Jeremiah an order that will be a living lesson. The verses that follow say that he will go to the Valley of Hinnom and there announce a judgment on Jerusalem. The jar will be a visible sign of that message. The details of the gesture are better seen in the rest of the chapter.

God sometimes speaks to us in ways that can be seen and touched. Today we can ask him to help us not to be only hearers, but to take his word seriously and let it correct our course before it is too late.
exp.18:5:
God says that days are coming when this place will no longer be called Tophet or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. Tophet was the site within that valley, near Jerusalem, where sacrifices were made. "Slaughter" announces that the place would be marked by death and judgment.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The people had abandoned him, worshiped Baal, and burned their children in the fire, something God never commanded. They filled the place with innocent blood. That is why the name of the place would change: what they used for sin would be remembered for punishment. In context, this announces the fall of Jerusalem before its enemies.

For today: God takes injustice and harm to the innocent seriously. Let us ask him to deliver us from following customs that seem normal but dishonor him, and to return to him with humility.
exp.18:6:
God says that he will make void, or bring to nothing, the plans and decisions of Judah and Jerusalem. They will fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hands of those who seek their lives, meaning those who want to kill them. Their bodies will be left unburied, as food for the birds of the heaven and the beasts of the earth.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. There the people had worshiped Baal and offered their children in the fire, something God never commanded. This message is a judgment for that idolatry and violence. It was fulfilled with the siege of Jerusalem by Babylon.

For today: the best plans without God do not hold up. Before deciding, ask yourself whether your path honors God, and return to Him with humility when you have gone astray.
exp.18:7:
God says he will leave Jerusalem turned into something that astonishes and terrifies. A horror is something that causes dread, and a hiss is a whistle of scorn or amazement. Those who pass by there will be stunned and will hiss when they see all its plagues, that is, its wounds and disasters.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who carries a clay jar to the Valley of Hinnom. There the people had practiced idolatry and shed innocent blood. God announces judgment because Judah turned away from him and would not be corrected. The jar that would later be broken would be a sign of that destruction.

For today: God is patient, but he takes seriously sin that does not change. Today you can ask yourself whether there is something in your life that God has shown you and you have ignored. Respond with humility and repentance while there is still time.
exp.18:8:
It says that God will allow Jerusalem to be surrounded by its enemies, and that the hunger will be so terrible that people will come to eat their own sons and friends. The siege is the encirclement of the city; the extreme distress is the anguish of being pressed on every side; those who seek their lives are the ones who want to kill them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who announces judgment on Judah. The people had abandoned God, worshiped idols, and shed innocent blood in the valley of Ben-hinnom (see the verses before). This warning matches what is later described in Lamentations and in other texts about the siege of Jerusalem. It is presented as a consequence of rebellion, not as a desire of God to see them suffer.

For today: do not take God's warnings lightly. When He points out a wrong path, returning to Him in time is an act of mercy, not of weakness.
exp.18:10:
God commands Jeremiah to say that He will break Jerusalem and its people, the way one breaks a clay pot that can no longer be mended. The place called Tophet was in the valley of Hinnom, and the burying in that place points to so many deaths that there will be no more room to bury anyone.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Jeremiah had broken a clay jar in front of the elders as a sign. The people had left God, worshiped idols, and burned incense to the stars. In Tophet, according to the text, innocent blood had been shed. The punishment came with the Babylonian invasion.

For today: God takes injustice and idolatry seriously, but His warnings are also an invitation to return to Him. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts, and repent sincerely while there is still time.
exp.18:13:
Jeremiah returns from Topheth, the place where God had sent him to prophesy. Then he stands in the courtyard of the house of the Lord, that is, the temple court, and speaks to all the people.

Here the narrator of the book tells what Jeremiah did. In Topheth, a valley where false worship was practiced, the prophet had announced judgment. Now he carries that message to the temple, where the people gathered, so that everyone may hear it. What follows is God's warning because of their stubborn hearts.

For today: God sometimes asks us to speak the truth in uncomfortable places, not only where it is easy. We can ask him for courage and love to say what is true with humility, while remaining faithful to him.
exp.18:14:
Thus says the Lord of hosts, meaning the Lord of all power, that he is going to bring upon Jerusalem and its surrounding towns all the punishment he had already announced. The reason is that the people have hardened their necks, a way of saying they were stubborn, like an ox that refuses to bow its neck to take the yoke, and so they would not listen.

Jeremiah had just broken a clay jar in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, next to Topheth, as a sign of the judgment to come. Then he returns to the temple and speaks to all the people. He does this because God commanded him to. The people had worshiped false gods, and the earlier warnings meant nothing to them.

God speaks before he acts, and his warnings are a sign of patience. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something God has told us in his Word that we have been ignoring. Listening in time, with humility, prevents much pain.
exp.19:0:
Pashur, son of Immer, was a priest who served as the chief governor, or the leading officer, in the house of the Lord. One day he heard Jeremiah speaking out the message God had given him.

The verse here is that the title used for Pashur does not mean he was a king's son, but someone with authority, like the head or overseer of the temple.

The book of Jeremiah tells what happened after the prophet declared God's judgment on Jerusalem because of its disobedience. Pashur, because of his religious office, was responsible for keeping order in the temple. Instead of listening with humility, he responded with anger, as the verses that follow show: he struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks.

For today: holding a religious position or being respected does not make us immune to error. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen to his Word, even when it troubles us or corrects us.
exp.19:1:
Pashur, a priest with authority in the temple, struck the prophet Jeremiah and left him bound in the stocks. The stocks were an instrument of punishment that held the body fast to humiliate and cause pain. They stood at the high gate of Benjamin, on the way up to the temple.

Jeremiah had just announced that God would bring judgment on Jerusalem for its disobedience. Pashur, in charge of order in the temple, would not listen to that message and tried to silence it by violence. Even so, the public punishment did not change what God had said, and Jeremiah went on speaking the next day.

Today, speaking the truth in love sometimes brings rejection or mockery. Let us ask God for courage to be faithful, and for humility to listen when his Word corrects us, neither silencing it nor resisting it.
exp.19:7:
Here Jeremiah says that every time he speaks on God's behalf, what he announces is destruction and ruin for the people. So instead of bringing him honor, the word of God brings him shame, insults, and mockery every day.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking just after the priest Pashur beat him and put him in the stocks for prophesying. Jeremiah feels exhausted and even confused with God, and he opens his heart to him with complete honesty. His message was unpopular, and he was paying the price.

For today: if being faithful to God costs you mockery or misunderstanding, do not pretend it doesn't hurt. Tell God about your weariness as Jeremiah did, and ask him for strength to keep being honest and faithful.
exp.19:10:
He says that God stands with Jeremiah like a strong and fearsome warrior. Because of this, those who persecute him will stumble, that is, fall and fail, and they will not be able to overcome him. They will be deeply ashamed because their plans will not succeed. Their shame will be a lasting disgrace that no one will forget.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He was tired of being mocked for proclaiming God's message. Even his friends hoped he would be proven wrong so they could take revenge. He wanted to stay silent, but the word of God burned inside him. Even so, in the midst of fear, he expresses his confidence that God defends him. How and when this would come about in his life, the text leaves in God's hands.

When you feel rejected for doing what is right, do not rely on your own strength. Ask God to sustain you, and trust that He is your defense.
exp.19:11:
Jeremiah speaks to God, whom he addresses as the Lord of hosts. He says that God tests the righteous, that is, examines them thoroughly. Jeremiah refers to the innermost part of a person, meaning the thoughts and the feelings. He asks to see God's judgment on his enemies, that is, for God to act justly. He says he has laid his cause before God, meaning he has entrusted it to him completely.

The prophet Jeremiah is the one speaking. His own friends were watching him and waiting for him to fall, because he announced harsh messages from God. He feels persecuted, but he trusts that God is on his side.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, tell God everything honestly, hiding nothing. Instead of taking revenge yourself, leave your cause in the hands of the one who knows your heart and the hearts of others as well.
exp.19:13:
He says Jeremiah wishes the day of his birth were cursed and never remembered with joy. It is a very strong expression of pain. The phrase about the day he was born means the day he came into the world. He does not curse his mother or God, but the day on which he was born.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking here, after being beaten and put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur for announcing God's message. He has just praised God, and suddenly he expresses his anguish. This mix of faith and despair may surprise us, but the Bible presents it with complete honesty. Job also spoke in a similar way.

For today: if you are exhausted or discouraged, you do not have to pretend to be strong before God. You can tell him honestly what you feel, even the darkest things. And seek the support of trusted people who will listen to you and walk with you.
exp.19:16:
He says that Jeremiah wished God, or whoever helped him, had put him to death before he was born. In that case his mother would have been his grave, and her womb would have stayed pregnant forever, so that he never came into the world. It is a very strong way of expressing deep pain.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah. He had just been beaten and placed in the stocks for preaching God's message (Jeremiah 20:1-2). He feels rejected, mocked, and worn out. His words are a sincere outpouring, almost a poetic lament. We do not know that God agreed with him in this; the Bible only shows his honest complaint.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you do not need to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Jeremiah did. Then seek support from people you trust, and keep trusting that God hears you.
exp.20:1:
Here King Zedekiah sends word asking the prophet Jeremiah to inquire of God on their behalf. Babylon, led by King Nebuchadrezzar, is attacking them. The king hopes God will do a miracle like those of the past, that God will act as he did before, and that the enemy army will withdraw. The word "perhaps" shows that he is not sure. "He" refers to Nebuchadrezzar.

The speakers are Zedekiah's messengers, Pashhur and Zephaniah, sent by the king. Jerusalem is surrounded and the king is afraid. But he seeks God only when danger arrives, without having turned to Him before. God answers through Jeremiah that He will not do what they hope, but that judgment will go forward.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis before seeking God. Let us draw near to Him with humility and sincerity from now on, without asking Him to approve what we have already decided.
exp.20:2:
Here Jeremiah answers the king's messengers. He tells them to carry a message to Zedekiah, and that message comes from God.

Context: Babylon, under King Nebuchadnezzar, had Jerusalem under siege. Zedekiah sent Pashur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to inquire of God, hoping for a miracle like those of the past. Jeremiah speaks as a prophet, and what follows is not what the king hoped for: God says he will not fight on their side, because the people had turned away from Him.

For today: It is easy to seek God only when we are in trouble and to expect him to give us the answer we want. It is better to approach Him with humility and be willing to listen, even when His word confronts us and calls us to change.
exp.20:10:
Here the verse says that God commands Jeremiah to speak directly to the family of the king of Judah. "Hear the word of the Lord" is an order: listen to what God says. "The house of the king" refers to the king and his family, the ones who governed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was surrounded by the armies of Babylon, called the Chaldeans, and God had already announced judgment. Before giving his sentence, he calls the rulers to listen. Next he asks them for justice: to defend the one who is oppressed. This shows that the responsibility of the leaders was great.

God expects that those who have authority or influence, in the home, at work, or in the church, will listen to his word before deciding. Today we can ask ourselves: am I using what I have to care for the one who suffers, or only for my own comfort?
exp.21:5:
God compares the royal house of Judah to Gilead and to the top of Lebanon, places known for their forests and their beauty. They were like a treasure to Him. Yet the word "but" here is the key: despite that value, God warns that He will leave the house in desolation, with cities that have no inhabitants.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the kings of Judah. He had offered them a condition: if they practiced justice, the throne of David would remain firm; if not, ruin would come. Many understand that Gilead and Lebanon allude to the splendor of the palace, which was built with cedar wood.

For today: privileges and positions do not replace obedience. God loves us and gives us gifts, but He expects us to live with justice and humility. Today you can ask yourself: am I trusting in what I have, or in listening to and obeying God?
exp.21:7:
This verse says that many people from other nations will pass by this city in ruins and will ask one another why God did such a thing to a city so great. The word "nations" is used here for the peoples around them, and the one who walks alongside you, a companion, is the person who goes with you.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the royal house of Judah. He warns them that their palace, beautiful as Gilead and Lebanon, will be destroyed. The verses that follow give the reason: they abandoned the covenant with God and served other gods. Many understand that the "city" is Jerusalem, although the text does not name it here.

For today: our decisions reveal what we love. Today you can examine which things you give first place and return to God sincerely, before what has been neglected becomes ruin.
exp.21:8:
This verse is the answer to the previous question. When people ask why God let Jerusalem fall, others will say it was because the people abandoned the covenant, that is, the commitment of faithfulness they had to the Lord. Instead, they worshipped other gods, that is, gods of other nations, and served them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the royal house of Judah. He warns them that the city will be destroyed. What matters is that the cause is not bad luck or only politics, but the unfaithfulness of the people and their leaders. God had warned them before this outcome.

For today: God invites us to care for our faithfulness. Today "other gods" can be good things that become first in our lives, such as money or success. Ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.21:9:
It says that it is not worth weeping for the one who has already died, nor finding comfort for him. Rather, one should weep with great sorrow for the one who goes away into exile, because he will never return or see again the land where he was born.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had left the covenant with God and worshiped foreign gods. The following verse makes clear that the one carried into exile is Shallum (also called Jehoahaz), son of King Josiah, taken captive. Josiah, already dead, was spared from seeing that ruin; Shallum would live through the loss. It is an announcement of God's judgment on the people.

For today: the decisions to turn away from God have painful consequences. Today you can return to Him sincerely, before the pain arrives. We can also accompany with compassion those who suffer deep losses, not only those who have already rested.
exp.21:18:
He says that King Jehoiakim will not have a dignified burial. He will be treated like a dead animal: they will drag him out and throw him outside the gates of Jerusalem, without honor. The phrase about being buried like a donkey means his body would be left without any ceremony, the way a donkey's would be. The word for wrongdoing refers to injustice or harm done to others.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, ruled with greed, violence, and oppression, very unlike his father. God announces that no one will mourn him. Scholars agree that this is a severe judgment; the Bible does not clearly describe how it was fulfilled, and some understand it as an expression of the dishonor that awaited him.

For today: power and wealth do not cover up injustice. Examine whether your decisions, at work or at home, treat others with justice and respect, and ask God for a humble heart that listens to his voice.
exp.21:21:
It says the wind will carry off all the leaders of Jerusalem, as if they were worthless chaff. "Shepherds" here means the rulers and guides of the people. "Lovers" are the allied nations Judah trusted in, instead of God. Those allies will go into captivity, and the people will feel shame and confusion for their wickedness, that is, their evil.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Jerusalem, pictured as a woman. She did not listen to the voice of God, either in good times, and she sought security in other nations and in kings who fell. Some scholars see here an announcement of the fall before Babylon; the text gives no further details.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we truly trust. God speaks to us in good times, not only in crises. It is wise to listen to him before everything starts to totter.
exp.21:23:
God swears by his own life, which is the strongest oath possible. He says that even if Coniah were like a signet ring on his right hand, the most valuable and closest place, he would still pluck him off from there. The signet ring here was the king's seal, a symbol of authority. Coniah is another name for Jehoiachin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had lived in injustice and idolatry, and God announces that Coniah, king of Judah, will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and taken captive to Babylon, together with his mother. His office would not protect him from the consequences.

For today: no position, success, or religious closeness frees us from being accountable before God. Rather than relying on what we are, it is wise to live with humility, listen to his correction, and turn back to him in time.
exp.21:24:
God tells Jeconiah, king of Judah, that he will hand him over to those who want to kill him, the very people he is afraid of. They are Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and the Chaldeans. The phrase about those who seek his life means that they are trying to take his life. The phrase about those whose face he fears means that he is terrified of them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was a king who trusted in his power and his security. God warns him that even if he were as precious as a signet ring on his right hand, God would still tear him off. According to the context, he was taken captive to Babylon, and God judges him for the wickedness of his reign.

For today: do not place your security in your position, your money, or your reputation. All of that can disappear. Seek each day to humble yourself before God and to obey Him, because only in Him is true firmness found.
exp.22:0:
This verse is a strong warning from God. "Woe" expresses grief and condemnation. The "shepherds" are the leaders of the people, and the "sheep" are God's people. "Destroy and scatter" means that they ruin them and leave them dispersed, without care or direction. "Pasture" is the flock that God himself looks after.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The shepherds were the kings and rulers of Judah, and possibly other leaders as well. Through their bad example and their neglect, the people were lost and ended up scattered. The verses that follow say that God will hold them accountable, but he also promises to gather those who remain and bring them back to their land.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the church, the family, or the workplace, care for them with humility and truthfulness. And if leaders have failed you, remember that God is the Shepherd who does not abandon his people.
exp.22:2:
God promises that he himself will gather the sheep that were left of his people, that is, a remnant, from all the countries where he scattered them. He will bring them back to their folds, which are their homes or their land. There they will grow and multiply, that is, they will be fruitful and numerous.

The Lord speaks, and he does so in the midst of a severe warning against the shepherds, the leaders of Judah, who neglected and scattered the people. God confronts them, but also promises that he will not abandon his sheep. Afterward he announces new shepherds and a just King, a descendant of David. Christians see in him Jesus.

For today: if you have felt lost, far away, or hurt by bad leaders, remember that God cares for his people and knows how to gather them. You can return to him with confidence and seek a community where you are cared for with truth and love.
exp.22:3:
God promises to give his people good shepherds, who will care for them and feed them. Thanks to them, the sheep will no longer live in fear, nor be frightened, nor will any of them be lost.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The leaders of Judah had scattered and neglected the people, and God is going to judge them. Afterward he promises to gather the survivors and bring them back to their land. The next verse points to a just King, a descendant of David, whom many Christians understand as a sign pointing to Jesus.

For today: God cares for those who are looked after and for those who look after others. If you have some responsibility over others, in your family, your church, or your work, serve them with tenderness and justice. And if you feel lost, trust that the Good Shepherd is searching for you.
exp.22:4:
This verse promises that God will raise up, from the family of King David, a righteous Branch: a descendant like a new shoot growing out of a stump. He will be a King who prospers and who will rule with righteousness and justice throughout the land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The kings of Judah had failed as bad shepherds, and the people were scattered in exile. God promises to gather his sheep and give them good shepherds. Christians see Jesus in this King; the original text speaks of a future descendant of David, and Jews understand it in other ways.

For today: when you see injustice or leaders who fail, do not lose hope. Trust that God keeps his promises, and try to treat others with justice in your own surroundings.
exp.22:10:
God says that both the prophet and the priest are profane, that is, wicked or false in the way they live and serve. The most serious thing is that God found their wickedness even in his house, in the very temple, where reverence and truth were supposed to be.

Here the Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The prophet is distressed, almost reeling, over the corruption of the religious leaders. The land suffers because of the people's wickedness, and the guides who should have led them were leading them down the wrong path. That is why judgment comes upon them.

For today: it is not enough to be in religious places or to hold a spiritual office. God looks at the heart and at daily life. We can ask him to examine us and make us honest, and pray for those who lead in the church, that they may live with integrity.
exp.22:14:
God announces a punishment for the false prophets of Jerusalem. He will make them eat wormwood, a plant with a very bitter taste, and drink bitter, poisoned water. These are images of suffering and judgment. The reason is that from them came a false religion without sincerity, which spread throughout the land.

The one speaking is the Lord, through Jeremiah. These prophets claimed to speak for God, but they lived in lies and adultery. Moreover, they encouraged the wicked with false promises of peace, so no one repented.

For today: it is not enough for someone to speak about God with confidence. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible and to consider whether that teaching leads us to change our lives or only leaves us feeling comfortable with our sins.
exp.22:18:
It says that God's judgment comes like a strong storm, and that it is already prepared. The storm will fall on the wicked, that is, on those who persist in evil without repenting.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At that time, several false prophets were telling the people that they would have peace and nothing would happen to them, even though they lived following their own desires. God makes clear that He did not send them and did not speak to them. His warning is serious, but it also shows that God does not ignore lies or injustice.

Today it invites us not to seek only words that comfort us, but the truth of God. Before accepting a message, we can compare it with the Bible, pray, and examine our hearts with humility, ready to correct our course.
exp.22:22:
It says that God is not a God limited to one place. The phrase that means "near" is not something your verse uses, and the phrase that means "far" is also not used, so these explanations are dropped. God asks whether he is only near and not also far away. The answer is clear: he is everywhere and sees everything.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. He condemns the false prophets of Judah, who claimed to have messages from God without having been sent by him. They presented their dreams as if they were divine word. They believed their lies would go unnoticed, but God reminds them that nothing is hidden from him.

For today: since God is near and far, nothing we do or say escapes his sight. That invites us to be sincere, not to use his name to back up our own ideas, and to test every teaching against the Bible. It also comforts us: he is always near us.
exp.22:23:
Here God asks whether anyone can hide in secret places so that He will not see them. And He answers with another question: does He not fill heaven and earth? The word "fill" in this verse is the key idea: God is present everywhere and sees everything.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At that time there were prophets who spoke lies in God's name and presented their dreams as if they were divine messages. God reminds them that He hears them and sees them, even though they think their deceptions go unnoticed. Moreover, if they had truly stood in His counsel, they would have turned the people away from their evil ways.

Today we can live with sincerity, knowing that God sees even what no one else sees. This should not frighten us, but encourage us to be honest with Him and always to speak the truth.
exp.22:27:
This verse says that a prophet who has only a dream should tell it as a dream, and the one who has received the word of God should announce it faithfully. The chaff is the dry husk that is left over; the wheat is the grain that gives food. God asks: what does the useless have to do with what gives life? They are very different things.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. At that time, several prophets said that God spoke to them in dreams, but they announced falsehoods that comforted the people. In this way they led the people away from God, as had happened earlier with Baal. God does not condemn every dream, but condemns speaking in his name without having his word.

Today we can examine what we hear or teach. Compare every opinion, feeling, or experience with the Bible. Whatever does not agree with it, do not present as the word of God.
exp.22:29:
God says he is against the prophets who "steal" his words, meaning they take them. Each one takes them from his neighbor, repeating what another said and presenting it as if it came from God.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. In that time, many prophets said they had a message from God, but they gave their own dreams and borrowed phrases, and they promised false peace. God confronts them because they deceived the people and he had not sent them. His true word is like fire and like a hammer, not like straw.

Today we can be careful not to repeat beautiful phrases as if they were the word of God without checking them. Before we teach or share something, let us compare it with the Bible, and speak with humility and truth.
exp.23:0:
God showed Jeremiah a vision: two baskets of figs set in front of the temple. This happens after Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried into captivity Jeconiah (son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah), the leaders of the people, the officials, and the craftsmen and smiths.

The Lord speaks, and Jeremiah tells it in the first person. This takes place around 597 B.C., when a first group of the people was taken into exile. God uses the image of the figs to explain what He thinks of those who were taken away and of those who stayed behind. The verse only sets the scene; the verse comes later in the chapter.

For today: God does not judge only by appearances or by difficult circumstances. A painful situation may not be a sign of rejection on His part. We can trust that He sees us with care and that He keeps working even in hard times.
exp.23:4:
God tells Jeremiah that, just as good figs are precious, He will look with favor on the exiles of Judah. The people carried away into exile are the ones taken from their land, and the Babylonians are the ones who carried them off. God affirms that He sent them there for their good.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah after Babylon had taken the king and many leaders of Judah captive. God uses two baskets of figs: the good ones represent the exiles, and the bad ones represent those who stayed behind or fled. The promise is that He will watch over them, bring them back, and give them a heart to know Him.

For today: even when a crisis seems like punishment or total loss, God may be working for our good. Trust Him and turn to Him with all your heart.
exp.23:6:
God promises to give his people a new heart so that they truly know him. Here, "know" means a close relationship, not just having information. Then they will be his people and he will be their God, because they will return to him with their whole heart, that is, with complete sincerity.

God speaks through Jeremiah after Babylon took the first exiles of Judah captive. In a vision of two baskets of figs, the good figs represent those exiles: God did not abandon them, but would watch over them and bring them back. The bad figs represent King Zedekiah and those who stayed behind or fled to Egypt.
