Today, we cannot change our own heart by sheer willpower alone. We can ask God to renew it and return to him sincerely, even in difficult times.
exp.23:7:
It says God will make Zedekiah, king of Judah, like the bad figs, so rotten that they cannot be eaten. The same will happen to his officials, to those who were left in Jerusalem, and to those who went to live in Egypt.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs: some good, representing those carried off into exile in Babylon, and some bad. Zedekiah and the others felt secure, but God says their stubbornness would bring judgment. Interpreters agree that the image contrasts those who accepted correction with those who rejected it.

For today: let us not trust in our position or in appearances. God looks at a heart willing to listen and turn back to Him. When He corrects us, accepting it with humility can be the path to a new life.
exp.23:9:
God says he will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, that is, war, lack of food, and deadly disease. This will continue until they are consumed, that is, until they disappear from the land that he had given to their fathers and to them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. In the vision of the two baskets of figs, the bad figs represent Zedekiah, his princes, and those who remained in Jerusalem or went down to Egypt. They did not listen to God, and for that reason this judgment would come. Historians and the biblical texts connect this with the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon.

For today: God speaks in earnest when he calls us to return to him. Let us not harden our hearts. If today you sense his voice, respond with humility, trusting that he corrects in order to restore those who repent.
exp.24:0:
This verse presents a message from God to Jeremiah, addressed to all the people of Judah. It says that it came in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and that this same year was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon.

Jeremiah was a prophet who spoke in a very tense time. Babylon was becoming the dominant power, and Judah still would not listen to God. The following verse says that Jeremiah had been warning the people for about twenty-three years, but they did not pay attention to him. That is why the date is recorded so carefully: God speaks within real history.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to God in time. Often he speaks to us through his Word, through wise counsel, or through our conscience, and we put it off for later. Today is a good day to obey with humility.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that God sent all his prophets, again and again, to speak to his people. The phrase rising early and sending them means that he did it with persistence, starting early and never tiring. To incline the ear means to truly pay attention. The people heard the sounds, but they would not listen.

Here Jeremiah speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. He has been warning them for twenty-three years, since the thirteenth year of King Josiah. God was asking them to turn away from their evil ways and give up their idols. He reminds them that other prophets had also spoken, but the people paid no attention.

For today: God keeps speaking with patience. Today you can ask yourself whether there is something he has shown you in his Word that you have put off for later. Listen with humility and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.24:4:
God, speaking through his prophets, kept calling the people again and again: "Give up your evil ways and your wicked deeds, and live in the land that the LORD gave to you and to your ancestors forever."

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. For twenty-three years he warned them, along with other prophets, but they would not listen. The call was an invitation to repentance: if they turned back to God, they could remain in their land. The phrase "forever" is understood as tied to their obedience, and some interpret it in different ways.

For today: God keeps calling with patience, not in a hurry to punish. If there is something in your life that you know does not please him, do not wait any longer. Listen to him today, take a concrete step of change, and trust that his mercy receives you.
exp.24:8:
God says that he is going to send and gather all the peoples from the north, along with Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, whom he calls his servant. They will come against Judah, against its inhabitants, and against the surrounding nations. The destruction will be complete: the land will be left as an object of mockery, a thing that people stare at in astonishment and whistle at in amazement, and as ruins that remain desolate forever.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. For years he had called the people to turn away from their evil ways and give up their idols, but they would not listen. That is why judgment is coming. Calling Nebuchadnezzar God's servant does not mean that he was righteous; it means that God was using his power to carry out God's purpose.

For today: God speaks with patience and does not stay silent about what harms us. If you feel today that he is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Listening in time is a sign of humility and spares you greater pain.
exp.24:9:
This verse says that God will remove from the land the sounds of daily life and of celebration: joy, weddings, the noise of the millstones (the stones used to grind grain for bread), and the light of the lamps in the homes. In other words, everything would fall silent and dark, like an abandoned place.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and the neighboring nations. For years the people refused to listen to his warnings or to give up idolatry. That is why God announces that he will use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, as his instrument of judgment. He then notes that this domination would last seventy years, and that Babylon too would be judged.

For today: God speaks with love before he corrects, and listening to him in time spares us much pain. Today you can open the Bible with a heart ready to obey, and give thanks for simple things, such as food, light, and shared joy, which are his gifts.
exp.24:13:
It says that Babylon, which had conquered and enslaved other peoples, would also be brought low. The phrase about other nations using them as servants means that other mighty nations and kings would make them serve them. The idea of repayment means giving a fair reward, and the phrase about according to their deeds indicates that the punishment would match what they had done.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had gone for years without listening to his warnings, and God announced that Babylon would be his instrument of judgment for seventy years. But Babylon would not go free either: its pride and its violence would also be judged. Scholars understand in different ways how these seventy years were fulfilled, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees every injustice and does not forget it. We can trust that he judges with justice, so there is no need for us to take revenge. And he invites us to live with humility, treating others as we would want to be treated.
exp.24:14:
God tells Jeremiah to take from his hand a cup full of the wine of his anger. He is to make all the nations to whom God sends him drink from it.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks and gives his prophet a command. Jeremiah lived in days of great wickedness, and God warns that judgment would reach Judah and also other peoples. The cup is a picture of the punishment each nation would have to drink. Some scholars understand that Jeremiah did this in a vision, and others that it was a spoken message. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God is just with everyone, not only with a few. This invites us to live with humility, to listen to his correction in time, and to turn back to him before our hearts grow hard.
exp.24:15:
The nations will drink from the cup of God's judgment. When they drink it, they will stagger, lose control, and be driven out of their minds because of the sword that God sends against them. "Sword" here means war. The word being explained refers to confusion and desperation, like someone who is drunk.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around 605 BC. Judah and the neighboring nations had lived in idolatry and injustice. God uses the image of a cup of bitter wine to show that the punishment would reach everyone, beginning with Jerusalem. Scholars understand the cup as an image, not as a literal drink.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not overlook our choices. Today you can examine your life honestly, turn away from what displeases God, and return to Him, for He is patient and always offers forgiveness to those who turn back to Him.
exp.24:24:
It says that God will also make the kings of Zimri, of Elam, and of the Medes drink the cup of his judgment. The word for north is used here for the direction the verse refers to. Zimri is a little-known place, and it is not known for certain where it was. Elam lay east of Babylon, and the Medes lay even further to the northeast.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, sent by God. In this chapter, the LORD announces that Babylon will be his instrument of punishment. The cup is an image of divine judgment, which reaches first to Judah and then to many nations. With this, God shows that he rules over all peoples, not only over Israel.

For today: no human power is beyond the reach of God. If you trust in kings, money, or fame, remember that only God is secure. Live with humility and obedience, knowing that he is just and also merciful to whoever turns back to him.
exp.24:26:
God commands Jeremiah to tell the nations to drink until they are drunk, vomit, and fall, never to rise again. It is an image: the cup stands for God's judgment, and the sword is the war that He allows. "Drink" is not an invitation to sin, but to swallow the consequence to the very end.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Babylon posed a threat. Earlier, God had shown this cup of His anger to Judah and Jerusalem, and then to many nations. God judges everyone, not only His own people. Some details, such as the exact identity of the name in this passage, are understood in several ways; many see it as a coded name for Babylon.

For today: God takes sin seriously, beginning with His own people. Instead of justifying ourselves, we can ask Him to correct us and turn back to Him with humility.
exp.24:28:
God says that his judgment begins with Jerusalem, the city that bears his name. If he punishes his own people first, the other nations cannot imagine they will go free. "Unpunished" means left without punishment. "Sword" stands for war and destruction, and "the inhabitants of the earth" are the peoples of the world as it was known then.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the Babylonian invasion. For years Judah had rejected the calls to return to God. The cup they drink is a picture of divine judgment. The verses that follow show that God is the Judge of all nations.

For today: bearing God's name is not a license to live as we please, but a call to live with greater sincerity. We can ask him to examine our hearts and correct us without delay when he speaks to us.
exp.24:29:
God says that, like a lion, he will roar from heaven, from his holy dwelling, and his voice will be heard with force. "Roar" is the word used for a loud, deep cry. The ones who tread the grapes in the winepress are those who stomp on the grapes to get the wine; they sang and shouted while they trod. In this way, God will make his judgment heard against all the inhabitants of the earth.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah and commands him to announce this message. It comes after the image of the cup of God's anger, which the nations must drink. God begins the judgment with his own people, the city that bears his name, and then it reaches the other nations. Scholars often see here a judgment against wickedness and injustice.

God is holy and just, and he does not ignore evil. This invites us not to take his patience lightly, but to examine our hearts, repent, and return to him with humility.
exp.24:30:
It says that the noise of God's judgment reaches the most distant places on the earth. God has a dispute, that is, an accusation, against all the nations. He is the Judge of every person on the earth, of all humanity. The wicked are those who live without respecting God, and being given over to the sword means they will be handed over to the sword.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, a few years before Babylon conquered Judah. God had already warned that he would judge his own people, and here he makes clear that no nation will be free from giving him an account.

For today: God judges with justice, and no one escapes his gaze. This invites us to examine our hearts with humility, seek his forgiveness, and live with reverence toward him, without thinking ourselves free to answer before our Creator.
exp.24:33:
This verse says that the shepherds and the principal ones of the flock, that is, the rulers and leaders of the people, must cry out loud and roll in the dust, as was done as a sign of mourning. Their time is over: they will be slaughtered and scattered. They will fall like a pleasant vessel, an expression usually understood as a precious and delicate vessel that breaks when it falls.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After years of warning Judah and the nations that they would not repent, he announces a judgment that will come from afar. The "shepherds" are the leaders, and their guilt is greater because they were meant to care for the people and did not.

Whoever has some authority, in the home, the church or the workplace, must care for those they lead with humility, because they will have to give an account to God.
exp.25:1:
The Lord tells the prophet Jeremiah to stand in the court of the temple and speak to all the people who come from the cities of Judah to worship. He must tell them everything God has entrusted to him, without leaving out a single word.

The Lord speaks at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, a king who did not faithfully follow God. The people kept going to the temple, but their lives were not changing. God sends his message in the hope that they will repent, as the following verse shows.

For today: when God shows us a truth in his Word, we should share it with love and honesty, without trimming it to look good. We can also ask ourselves whether our lives match what we say at church.
exp.25:6:
This verse tells us that the priests, the prophets, and all the people heard Jeremiah while he spoke in the temple. "The house of the Lord" is the temple in Jerusalem. The verse's word "heard" means they listened closely.

God sent Jeremiah to stand in the temple and warn the people that, if they did not obey, the temple would become like Shiloh, a place of worship that had been destroyed. God reminded them that he had sent prophets again and again, and they had not listened. Listening was not the same as obeying: they soon seized Jeremiah and demanded his death.

For today: hearing the Word of God is not enough; we must let it correct us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, so that we may receive with gratitude even what makes us uncomfortable.
exp.25:9:
When the princes of Judah heard about these things, they left the king's house and went up to the house of the Lord, and they took their seats at the entrance of the new gate of the Lord's house. This verse says that the leaders of Judah, the officials of the land, found out what was happening to Jeremiah. They left the king's palace, went up to the temple of the Lord, and took their seats at the entrance of the new gate, as if to hear the case and reach a decision.

Jeremiah had just announced in the temple that, if the people did not repent, Jerusalem would be destroyed as Shiloh had been. The priests, the prophets, and the people seized him and demanded his death. The officials came as authorities to judge. They would sit at the gates because legal matters were usually handled there, although the text gives no further details.

When someone tells us something uncomfortable, we should not react with anger. Before we judge, let us listen calmly, seek the truth, and compare what is said with what the Word of God teaches.
exp.25:13:
Jeremiah tells the leaders and the people: "I am in your hands; do with me whatever seems good and right to you."

Jeremiah had preached in the temple that Jerusalem would be destroyed if the people did not change. Priests and prophets demanded his death. He defends himself before the officials: he does not take back his message, and he trusts that God will look after him. Right away he warns them that killing an innocent man would bring guilt upon them. The officials and the people acquit him.

For today: we can speak the truth with humility and without fear, leaving the outcome in God's hands. Whoever obeys God does not need to fight with pride or stay silent out of fear.
exp.25:14:
Jeremiah warns them firmly: if they kill him, they will be shedding innocent blood, and the guilt would fall on them, on the city, and on its inhabitants. He affirms that the Lord himself has sent him to speak these words to them.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, before priests, prophets, officials, and the people. They had seized him and were demanding his death for announcing that Jerusalem would be destroyed if they did not turn back to God. Even so, he does not defend himself out of fear: he places himself in their hands, but reminds them that his message came from God and that they could still repent. The officials and the people declared him innocent.

For today: God calls us to speak the truth with humility and courage, even when it costs us. He also invites us to listen to correction carefully, without attacking the one who brings it.
exp.25:16:
Some of the elders of the land stood up and spoke to the whole assembly of the people. "Assembly" here means a gathering, and "elders of the land" refers to older men who held authority and respect in the community.

Jeremiah had just preached in the temple that Jerusalem would be destroyed if the people did not repent. The priests and prophets demanded his death, but the princes and the people said he did not deserve to die. Then the elders step in and recall the case of Micah, who in the days of King Hezekiah said something similar and was not put to death. In this way they support Jeremiah with an example from history.

Today, when someone speaks an uncomfortable truth, it is good to listen with humility and not react with anger. And when we see injustice, we can raise our voices with wisdom, as these elders did.
exp.25:17:
It says that Micah, a prophet from the town of Moresheth, spoke in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. His message from God was harsh: Zion, that is, Jerusalem, would be plowed like a field, the city would become heaps of ruins, and the mountain of the house would be like wooded high places overgrown with thickets.

Here some of the elders of the people are speaking. Jeremiah had just announced something similar in the temple, and the priests and prophets wanted to kill him. The elders recall the case of Micah (Micah 3:12) to defend Jeremiah: Hezekiah did not kill Micah, but listened, feared God and prayed, and God did not bring the punishment that had been announced.

A hard word from God can be an opportunity to turn back to Him. Before rejecting the one who corrects us, it is wise to listen with humility, examine our hearts, and pray.
exp.25:18:
Here the elders defend Jeremiah with a question: did King Hezekiah put Micah to death for prophesying disaster? No; rather, Hezekiah feared the Lord, that is, he held him in reverent awe, and prayed. Then God relented, that is, he changed course and did not send the punishment that had been announced. That is why they ask: if we harm Jeremiah, will we not bring great evil upon ourselves?

Jeremiah had announced in the temple that Jerusalem would be destroyed if the people did not return to God. Priests and prophets wanted to kill him. These elders recall what happened about a hundred years earlier with Micah, who said something similar. They understood that a harsh warning can be an opportunity for change.

For today: when a correction makes us uncomfortable, let us not react with anger. Let us listen with humility, pray, and ask God to show us whether we should change.
exp.25:22:
They sent men who brought Uriah back from Egypt, where he had fled, and took him before King Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim killed him with the sword and had his body thrown into the burial place of the common people, the cemetery of the poor and dishonored.

The narrator, who tells the story, relates what happened to Uriah, another prophet who announced the same message as Jeremiah against Jerusalem. He is mentioned to show the real danger Jeremiah faced. When Jeremiah speaks in the temple, some want to kill him, and Uriah's example shows that the king had already silenced a prophet through violence.

For today: telling the truth can cost dearly, and the powerful sometimes punish it. Even so, this scene invites us to be faithful to God with courage and not to measure success by human recognition. God does not forget those who suffer for obeying him.
exp.26:2:
God commands Jeremiah to send messages to five neighboring kings: Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. The messengers those kings had sent to Jerusalem, to King Zedekiah, would serve to carry the word back.

Straps and yokes of wood, like the ones put on oxen, are the items Jeremiah was to place on his neck as a sign.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Those kingdoms were planning to rebel against Babylon, and God warns them, through a symbolic action, that by submitting to Babylon they would avoid a greater harm. Notice that the text mentions Jehoiakim at the beginning but speaks of Zedekiah, so some scholars believe there is a variant or a copying error in the name.

For today: before we cling to our own plans, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are listening to what God says, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.26:4:
God says that he made the earth, the people, and the animals. He did it with his great power and with his outstretched arm, which is a way of speaking of his strength in action. Furthermore, he gave it to whomever seemed meet to him, that is, to whomever he was pleased or willed.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Envoys from neighboring kingdoms had come to Jerusalem, probably to plan a rebellion against Babylon. God orders them to tell their kings that he is the Creator and that he decides to whom he gives dominion. Therefore, for now, Nebuchadnezzar would have that power.

For today: trust that God remains Lord over all, even when the world seems confused or unjust. Instead of depending on your own plans or on the powerful, pray, surrender to his will, and rest in his sovereignty.
exp.26:6:
The passage says that many nations will serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his grandson, until the time comes when Babylon itself will be judged. Then other peoples and powerful kings will subdue her. The word "nations" in the verse above is the same word used for peoples in other translations, so both mean the same thing.

Through Jeremiah, God speaks to Judah and to the neighboring kings who wanted to rebel against Babylon. God affirms that He governs history and that, for a time, He allowed the power of Babylon. Its dominion would have a limit. The false prophets said the opposite and gave false hope.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever; only God remains. This invites us to be humble, not to trust messages that only tell us what we want to hear, and to seek God's voice with sincerity.
exp.26:8:
It says that the people should not listen to those who speak to them in God's name or in the name of hidden powers and assure them that they will not have to submit to Babylon. Those who foretell the future by omens are among the kinds of speakers named there; those who practice magic or spells are another; and those who try to uncover what is hidden are another. The phrase about dreams refers to the dreamers who presented their dreams as messages from God.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah and to the neighboring nations, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. He had allowed Nebuchadnezzar to dominate the region. Many false prophets promised an easy way out, but God warns that those words were lies and would lead the people to lose their land.

For today: let us not believe a voice simply because it sounds spiritual or because it comforts us. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, pray with humility, and be willing to hear also what we do not want to hear.
exp.26:11:
Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah to bring his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, that is, to submit to his rule and serve him and his people. In this way he will be able to live.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah was under pressure from Babylon, and some prophets were saying that they did not have to submit. Jeremiah states that this is a lie. God wanted them to accept this discipline in order to avoid death by war, famine, and plague. This applies to that specific historical moment, not to every government of every age.

For today: sometimes the wisest course is not the most comfortable one or the one we most like to hear. Before following a voice that promises easy solutions, let us ask God for humility, compare what we hear with the Bible, and be willing to obey even when it costs us.
exp.26:13:
Here God warns the people not to listen to the prophets who were saying, "You will not have to serve the king of Babylon." The sentence that quotes their words is rendered here in plain terms, and the phrase about prophesying falsehood means that they speak falsehood in God's name. According to God, those messages did not come from Him.

Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks in the time of King Zedekiah of Judah. Babylon already controlled the region. Jeremiah urged the people to accept that yoke, that is, to submit, in order to save lives. The false prophets offered easy hope and said that everything would soon return to normal. But God's message was harder and more true.

For today: do not believe something just because it sounds pleasant. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray asking for discernment, and accept God's truth even when it costs you, because His correction seeks your good.
exp.26:15:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the priests and to all the people. He warns them not to listen to the prophets who promise: "Soon the vessels of the Lord's house will be brought back from Babylon." God says that is a lie.

Jeremiah speaks in Jerusalem, shortly after Babylon carried away part of the temple's articles and some of the leaders. Many wanted to hear that everything would be set right quickly. But God commanded them to accept Babylon's rule for a time, so that lives and the city could be saved.

Today we can learn not to believe something just because it sounds pleasant. Before accepting a spiritual message, it is wise to compare it with the Bible, pray with humility, and ask whether it calls us to obey God, even when the truth is hard.
exp.26:17:
Jeremiah says that if those prophets truly speak on behalf of God, then they should pray to the Lord that the sacred objects still left in the temple, in the king's palace, and in Jerusalem will not be carried off to Babylon.

Jeremiah speaks to the people, the priests, and King Zedekiah. False prophets were promising that Babylon would soon return what had already been taken. Jeremiah challenges them: if they truly listen to God, let them pray to prevent another loss. He insists that they submit to Babylon and live.

Today we can learn not to believe only what sounds pleasant. Before following a teaching, compare it with the Bible and seek God in prayer. God's truth is sometimes hard, but it leads us to life.
exp.27:0:
This verse sets the scene. Jeremiah tells us that in the fourth year of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, in the fifth month, a prophet named Hananiah, son of Azur and a native of Gibeon, spoke to him in the temple. He did so in the presence of the priests and all the people.

Jeremiah is the one speaking, telling the story in the first person. Judah was under pressure from Babylon, and some of the treasures of the temple had already been carried away. Hananiah presents himself as a prophet of God and gives a message that the people wanted to hear. The next verse announces a swift deliverance. Later in the chapter, the text shows that his message was false.

For today: not every pleasant message comes from God, even when it sounds religious and is delivered in a sacred place. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and ask God for wisdom to discern.
exp.27:1:
Here speaks Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, and he says that the LORD, the God of Israel, has already broken the king of Babylon's yoke. The yoke was the wooden piece placed on oxen to bring them under control; here it stands for Babylon's rule over Judah.

This happens in the fourth year of King Zedekiah, in the temple and in front of the priests and the people. Hananiah promises that within two years the vessels of the temple and the exiles would return. But Jeremiah had announced that submission to Babylon would be long. The chapter shows that Hananiah was not speaking on God's behalf, even though he used God's name.

Today, not every message that sounds encouraging comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray calmly, and prefer the truth, even when it costs you, over easy promises.
exp.27:7:
Jeremiah tells Hananiah that the prophets who came before, both his own and Hananiah's, announced hard things: war, affliction, and pestilence (that is, diseases that killed many people). They spoke of many lands and great kingdoms, and their message was usually a warning.

Jeremiah is speaking in the temple, in front of the people. Hananiah has just announced that God would break the power of Babylon within two years and that everything would soon be restored. Jeremiah replies with respect, but he reminds him that earlier prophets often brought difficult messages. For that reason, whoever announces peace should wait for events to confirm it.

For today: let us not accept a message simply because it sounds pleasant. Let us compare what we hear with the whole of Scripture, and be patient to see whether it comes true. Let us seek the truth of God, even when at times it is uncomfortable.
exp.27:10:
Hananiah says before all the people that God will break the yoke of the king of Babylon from all the nations within two full years. Then Jeremiah simply goes away.

Hananiah is a prophet who contradicts Jeremiah. Jeremiah had announced that Judah должна submit to Babylon, and to show it he wore a wooden yoke. Hananiah breaks that yoke and promises a quick deliverance. Jeremiah does not argue at that moment; he withdraws, and shortly afterward he receives an answer from God.

For today: an encouraging message does not always come from God. Before believing an easy promise, compare it with what the Bible teaches, pray calmly, and take time to discern.
exp.27:11:
This verse tells how Hananiah, who claimed to be a prophet, broke the wooden yoke that Jeremiah wore on his neck. After that, God spoke to Jeremiah. "The word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a message.

Jeremiah wore the yoke as a sign that Judah had to submit to Babylon. Hananiah said, in God's name, that Babylon would fall within two years. Jeremiah went away without arguing any further, and then God gave him an answer. In this way we see that God himself corrects falsehood, and his servant does not need to win by shouting.

For today: not every message that sounds cheerful and claims to come from God is true. Test it against the Bible, pray calmly, and patiently wait for God's direction.
exp.27:12:
He says God sends Jeremiah to go to Hananiah and give him a message. Hananiah broke wooden yokes, but God says that now iron yokes will come, much harder and impossible to break. The yoke is the piece placed on the neck of working animals; here it stands for submission to Babylon.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Hananiah, a prophet, had announced that Babylon would fall within two years, and he broke the wooden yoke that Jeremiah was wearing as a sign. But God had not sent him. His false hope did not remove the punishment; it would make it heavier.

Today, listening only to what comforts us can turn out to be very costly. Before we believe a pleasant message, let us compare it with the Bible and ask God for a humble heart, ready to hear the truth even when it hurts.
exp.27:13:
This verse says that God himself, the Lord of hosts, placed an iron yoke on all those nations so that they would serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The word "nations" here refers to the peoples and kingdoms surrounding Judah. A yoke is the wooden frame placed on the neck of working animals. God adds that he has also given the beasts of the field to Nebuchadnezzar.

Jehovah speaks through Jeremiah. Hananiah, another prophet, had broken the wooden yoke that Jeremiah wore as a sign, and had promised that Babylon would soon fall. God answers that this false hope would only bring a heavier yoke, one of iron. The people were to accept the judgment that was coming.

For today: sometimes we prefer to hear words that comfort us rather than the truth that corrects us. Ask God for the humility to listen to his voice, even when it is difficult, and trust that his correction seeks our good.
exp.27:16:
This verse tells us that Hananiah, the prophet who had spoken in God's name without God having sent him, died that same year, in the seventh month. In this way the warning Jeremiah had given him two months earlier came true. The seventh month refers to a month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly between September and October.

The narrator recounts the end of a confrontation. Hananiah had announced that Babylon would fall soon and that the exiles would return right away, and he had broken the wooden yoke that Jeremiah was wearing as a sign. Jeremiah replied that God had not sent him and that his message was false. The people were trusting in a promise that God had never given.

For today: it is not enough for a message to sound pleasant or hopeful. We should compare what we hear with God's Word and ask him for wisdom. This keeps us from trusting empty words, and it reminds us to speak with responsibility whenever we mention God's name.
exp.28:1:
This verse is a parenthesis that tells us when the letter was written: after King Jeconiah left Jerusalem. Leaving with him were the queen mother, the court officials (the royal attendants), the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen and the smiths (according to others, the blacksmiths or locksmiths; the term is understood in several ways).

The one speaking is the narrator, who places the letter of the prophet Jeremiah. This happened around 597 B.C., when Nebuchadnezzar carried the most capable people of the kingdom off to Babylon. Jeremiah writes to the exiles to bring them God's word in the midst of their grief.

For today: God does not forget those who live through circumstances they did not choose. Even far from what is familiar, we can receive his word, pray, and keep trusting in him.
exp.28:16:
God announces that he will send three blows upon the people who remained in Jerusalem: war, hunger, and disease. He compares them to figs so rotten that they cannot be eaten.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. A group had already been taken captive to Babylon, and those who stayed in Jerusalem, including King Zedekiah, considered themselves the favored ones. Moreover, they were listening to prophets who promised a swift peace. God tells them that his judgment is coming because they did not listen to the true prophets whom he sent to them again and again. The image of the figs appears in more detail in chapter 24.

For today: when God speaks to us, whether through his Word or through wise counsel, it is wise to listen in time and with humility. Feeling secure is not the same as being right with God. He corrects because he wants to heal us, and his mercy remains open to anyone who turns back to him.
exp.28:18:
God explains why the punishment is coming: his people did not want to hear his words. He sent them through the prophets, sending them early and often, which is a way of saying he did it with persistence and from the beginning, without growing tired. At the end he repeats the charge that they would not hear, so the accusation reaches those who were listening to him at that very moment.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. He addresses Judah, and especially those taken into exile in Babylon. He announces beforehand that those who stayed in Jerusalem would be like bad figs, too spoiled to eat. The cause is not bad luck, but a long refusal to heed God's warnings.

For today: God keeps speaking with patience. Today we can set aside time to read his Word carefully and obey what we understand, without putting it off until later.
exp.28:19:
This verse is a direct call from God to the exiles of Judah who live in Babylon. The word "hear" in the verse conveys what the original text meant, and the people who were carried off by force to another country are the ones being addressed. God asks for their attention, because what follows is important.

It is the Lord who speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah, who writes to the exiles. Many of them were listening to false prophets who promised a quick return. God reminds them that the exile came because His people ignored the true prophets He sent to them again and again. Now He invites them to listen once more.

For today: even in difficult situations, God asks us to listen to His voice with humility. Before following any spiritual message, compare it with the Bible and ask yourself whether it truly reflects what God has said.
exp.28:24:
This verse begins a message that God sends through Shemaiah of Nehelam. God says that Shemaiah sent letters in his own name to all the people in Jerusalem, to the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, and to all the priests. Letters means written messages, and Jerusalem is the city in which those people lived.

Jeremiah had written to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to settle there and wait. Shemaiah, one of those exiles, answered with letters of his own to oppose Jeremiah and to pressure the priests to silence him. God responds to that action, because Shemaiah was speaking as though he had authority without having been sent by God.

Today we can learn not to speak in God's name carelessly. Before advising or correcting others, it is good to compare what we say with the Bible and to pray with humility.
exp.28:29:
This verse is simple: it says God spoke to Jeremiah again. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" is an older way of saying that God gave him a message. It is a brief introduction to what follows.

Jeremiah had written a letter to the exiles in Babylon, and a false prophet named Shemaiah had sent them letters saying the opposite. The priest Zephaniah read that letter to Jeremiah, and then God gave him an answer. Here God is the one speaking, and Jeremiah is the messenger. The message that follows condemns Shemaiah for giving false hope.

For today: before believing any spiritual message, compare it with what God has said in his Word. Words that sound encouraging do not always come from God, and his truth sustains us even when it is hard.
exp.29:2:
It says that God promises a time is coming when he will change the fortunes of his people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah and commands him to write his words in a book. The people were under judgment and faced exile, or were already suffering it, and they needed hope. What was written would serve as a witness for the future. The words that follow speak of fear and anguish, so this promise comes in the middle of hard times. Some interpreters see it fulfilled in the return from Babylon, and others see a greater fulfillment still further ahead.

When everything seems lost, God remains faithful to what he has promised. You can hold on to his Word and wait with patience, knowing that he does not forget his own.
exp.29:3:
This verse says that what follows are the words God spoke about Israel and Judah. It works as an introduction: God wants his message to be clear and clearly identified. "Israel" refers to the northern kingdom and "Judah" to the southern kingdom.

Here the Lord speaks, and he commands the prophet Jeremiah to write his words in a book. The people were under the weight of judgment and exile, but God promises that one day he will bring his children back to the land he gave to their fathers. The verses that follow show that before this restoration there will be a time of distress.

For today: God speaks to us and wants his Word to be kept and read. We can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and write down what God tells us, trusting that his promises are fulfilled even after difficult times.
exp.29:5:
It says that God invites the reader to ask an absurd question: whether a man can give birth. Yet the prophet sees men with their hands on their loins (the waist or the lower part of the back), like a woman in labor. Their faces are pale with fear. It is an image of very deep terror and anguish.

Jehovah speaks through Jeremiah to the people of Israel and Judah. A time of great distress is announced, probably tied to the fall before Babylon, although some also see in the passage a future fulfillment. But the immediate context is one of hope: God promises to deliver Jacob and break the yoke of his servitude.

Today, this text reminds us that God does not ignore our moments of fear and pain. Even when everything seems like anguish, he can turn them into a path toward deliverance. We can pray with honesty and wait in his promise.
exp.29:7:
God promises that, on that day, he himself will break the yoke that weighs down his people. The yoke is the wooden piece placed on the necks of working animals. The straps that hold it in place are the ties that fasten it on. Foreigners are the peoples from other nations. The promise is that they will never again be enslaved.

The LORD of hosts speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people were suffering under foreign rule and in exile, and before this promise a time of great distress is described. Yet God announces deliverance. The verses that follow say they will serve the LORD their God and a king from the line of David. Some see this fulfilled in the return from exile, others in Christ.

For today: if you feel bound by fear, guilt, or some heavy burden, you can trust that God knows how to break chains. Bring that burden to him in prayer today, without fear.
exp.29:15:
He says God will bring justice on the enemies of his people. Those who "devour" (eat up, destroy) will be devoured; those who afflict (cause suffering) will go into captivity; those who trampled will be trampled; and those who plundered will be plundered.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel, who was suffering the consequences of its sin, as God's discipline. Even so, God does not forget his people. This verse opens the promise of restoration: after the punishment comes healing, the return from captivity, and the rebuilding of the city.

For today: when others have harmed you, do not take revenge with your own hands. Trust that God sees, judges with justice, and also heals. And if you have failed, remember that his discipline is not the end, but the path toward his restoration.
exp.29:16:
God promises to bring healing and to mend the wounds of his people. The word "Outcast" means someone who has been rejected or thrown away. The nations mocked Zion, saying that no one cared and that no one sought her. Here the verse's "but" marks the point where God answers that scorn with a promise of restoration.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people in exile and wounded. Earlier the text says their suffering came because of their sins, but now God changes course: he will punish their oppressors and bring his people home. The verses that follow speak of rebuilding the city and of joy returning.

For today: when others make you feel discarded or worthless, you do not have to accept that label. God does not define your worth by what others say. Bring your wounds to him honestly, even the ones you yourself caused, and trust that he can heal and raise you up again.
exp.29:18:
God promises that out of the people will come thanksgiving, and the voice of those who make merry will be heard. He also promises to multiply them so that they will not be few. He will glorify them, so that they will not be small.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel were in captivity, wounded and looked down upon, and others were saying that no one cared for Zion. In the middle of that pain, God announces healing, return, and rebuilding. This promise was first read as hope for the return of those who had been exiled, and many Christians also see in it a foretaste of the restoration God gives in Christ.

For today: if you are going through a season of hurt or loss, do not hold on only to what others say about you. God knows how to restore. Learn to give thanks to him now, because praise can be a first step of hope.
exp.29:22:
It says that God's judgment comes like a strong storm, already prepared, and it will fall on the heads of the wicked. The first quoted phrase in the source means that it is ready. The word for the wicked there refers to people who live without respect for God and practice evil. The word translated here as the verb to rest means that it will remain, and that it will fall with weight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a passage of comfort for Israel. Before this, he promises to restore his people, give them a ruler of their own, and renew the relationship: "You shall be my people, and I will be your God." The judgment on the wicked shows that God does not ignore injustice. The next verse says that his anger will not cease until he has accomplished his purpose. Some see this fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also look toward the future.

Today we can trust that God sees evil and will bring about justice. So we do not have to live with resentment or take revenge. It also reminds us to examine our own hearts and to draw near to God with humility.
exp.30:8:
God says that his people will return from exile weeping, but that he himself will bring them back with mercy. He will lead them beside streams of water, along a straight path where they will not stumble. He is their Father, and Ephraim, a name that here stands for the people of the north, is his beloved firstborn son.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was scattered by exile and defeat. This passage is part of a promise of restoration: God will gather the weak and the strong, the blind, the lame, and women who are expecting children. Some think the weeping is from repentance, others that it is from joy or from sorrow along the road; the text allows several readings.

If you feel far from God or have stumbled often, you can return to him with your tears. He does not reject you; he receives you as a father, guides you, and sustains you on the way.
exp.30:11:
This verse says that God's people will return to their land and praise with joy on Mount Zion, that is, Jerusalem. "They will rush to the goodness of the Lord" means they will go eagerly toward the good things God gives: grain (the bread), wine, oil, and animals. A "well-watered garden" is a garden that is full of life, well cared for with water.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been scattered into exile, and God promises to gather them and care for them like a shepherd with his flock. It is a message of comfort and hope for a wounded people. Christians often also see here a foreshadowing of the fullness God gives in Christ, although it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: if you are tired or hurt, remember that God knows how to restore. Go to Him with confidence, give thanks for what He gives you each day, and let Him care for you like a well-watered garden.
exp.30:13:
It says that God will give the priests such abundance that they will be fully satisfied, like someone who eats until they are full. The verse's word for filling up here does not speak of drunkenness, but of filling completely. The word for fatness refers to the best and richest part of the food, especially in the sacrifices. All the people will be satisfied with God's goodness.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter announces the restoration of Israel after the exile. The people had suffered greatly, but God promises to bring them back, turn their weeping into joy, and give them provision and comfort. The priests were the ones who lived from the offerings of the temple, so the promise includes that worship would flourish again.

Today we can remember that God not only forgives and restores, but also provides generously. When we go through sorrow or scarcity, we can come to Him with confidence and gratitude, trusting that He will satisfy us with His goodness.
exp.30:14:
God says that a voice was heard in Ramah: a very bitter weeping. It is Rachel, weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no longer there. "Weeping" means crying, and the phrase about them being lost or dead refers to those who were taken away and no longer present.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to a people wounded by the fall of Judah and the exile. Rachel, mother of the tribes of Joseph and Benjamin, appears as a mother who weeps for her children carried far away. Ramah was in the territory of Benjamin. Matthew 2:18 quotes this text in connection with the grief over the children of Bethlehem. But in Jeremiah, the pain comes with a promise: the children will return.

Today, God does not ask you to hide your pain or hurry your mourning. Weep honestly before Him and do not isolate yourself. Trust that He sees your loss and can sustain you with hope.
exp.30:19:
God asks whether Ephraim is not his precious son, his dear child. He says that every time he speaks of him, he remembers him with affection. Because of this, his heart (his inmost feelings, the deepest part of his being) is moved, and he promises to have mercy on him.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Ephraim represents the northern kingdom, Israel, which was in exile. Shortly before, the people had wept with regret, acknowledging their rebellion and their shame. God responds with tenderness, not rejection. Then he invites them to come home by the way they had traveled.

For today: when you feel ashamed of your mistakes, do not run from God. Come close to him with sincerity, because he does not look at you only as someone who failed, but as a beloved child whom he wants to forgive and restore.
exp.30:23:
This verse says that when God brings his people back, the people of Judah will again live in their land. Not just in one place, but in all its cities. It mentions farmers, that is, those who work the land, and shepherds who go out with their flocks. The word rendered "dwell" in the verse above is the word the verse glosses; no further gloss is needed here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter is part of the promises of comfort for Israel and Judah after the punishment of exile. God announces that he will turn their captivity into blessing. What is described is a simple, ordinary life: work, fields, livestock, and peace. Some see here a promise about the return from exile; others also see a foretaste of the final restoration. Scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: God knows how to restore the everyday as well. If you are going through a hard time, trust that he can give you stability again, and give thanks for daily work as a gift from him.
exp.30:28:
It says that a time is coming when people will no longer repeat a well-known saying. Sour grapes are green grapes, very acidic. The sensation after eating them, when the teeth feel sensitive and uncomfortable, is what the saying points to. The saying meant that children suffered the consequences of what their parents had done.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people battered by exile. Many used this saying to say: "We are paying for the sins of our ancestors." God promises to restore his people and announces a new covenant, in which each person will answer to Him for themselves. Interpreters debate how much of the saying was an excuse and how much was real pain; there were probably both.

For today: even if our family has left us wounds, we do not have to use them as an excuse. We can ask God for healing and decide with Him on a new path, taking on our own responsibility.
exp.30:29:
It says that each person will answer for their own sin. The verse's word for the unripe grapes would be sour grapes, very tart green grapes, and the feeling of their sourness set on the teeth is the bitter sensation that is felt in the teeth. The word "set on edge" in the verse refers to that same feeling. It was a popular saying: the parents eat the sour fruit and the children's teeth ache. God says that this will no longer be the case: each person will face the consequences of their own wrongdoing.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who were suffering in exile. Many thought they were paying only for the mistakes of their ancestors. God promises to restore them and announces a new covenant, one that is more personal. Some think that he does not deny that the decisions of some affect others, but rejects using that as an excuse.

For today: do not blame your past or your family to justify your mistakes. Acknowledge your responsibility, ask God for forgiveness, and trust that he can give you a fresh start.
exp.30:30:
God announces that days are coming when he will make a new covenant, that is, a new agreement, with all his people: with Israel (the house of Jacob) and with Judah. The name of God is "the LORD," and the promise comes from him and does not depend on human effort.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were living through a hard time, with judgment and exile, because they had broken the earlier covenant made in the days of Moses. Even so, God does not abandon them. He promises them a fresh beginning, in which his law will be written on the heart and there will be a close relationship with him.

For today: even if you have failed or feel far from God, he still offers a new beginning. Christians see this covenant fulfilled in Jesus. Ask God to change your heart from within, not only your behavior on the outside.
exp.30:31:
God says that the new covenant will not be like the one he made with Israel's ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt. He speaks of taking them by the hand, the way a father guides a child. They broke that covenant, even though God was a faithful and committed husband to them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a time of crisis for Judah, when the people had been unfaithful. Even so, God promises something new. The verses that follow explain that this covenant would work in the heart and would bring forgiveness. Christians see its fulfillment in Christ (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8).

For today: our relationship with God does not rest on our own strength, but on his faithfulness and his forgiveness. When you fail, return to him with confidence and ask him to transform your heart.
exp.30:34:
This verse presents God as the Creator who sustains the universe. He gives the sun to light the day, and sets the order of the moon and the stars for the night. He also divides the sea, that is, he stirs the waters so that its waves roar. "The Lord of hosts" is his name, a title that speaks of his power over all that he has made.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just promised a new covenant, in which his law will be written on the heart and sin will be forgiven. To give Israel assurance that he will keep that promise, he appeals to the faithful order of creation. The verses that follow say that as long as that order endures, Israel will not cease to be his people.

Today, when you doubt God's promises, look at the sun and the stars. The One who sustains them every day is also faithful to forgive you and to fulfill what he has said.
exp.30:35:
God says that if the laws that govern the sun, the moon, the stars, and the sea were to stop working, then the descendants of Israel would also cease to be a nation before Him. "Descendants" means offspring, and "cease" means to stop existing. Since that does not happen, the promise will not fail either.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in crisis and exile, and God promises them a new covenant, in which everyone will know Him and He will forgive their sin. To assure that He will keep this promise, He uses the steady order of creation as a sign. Many Christians also see here an announcement of the work of Christ.

For today: when you doubt that God is faithful, look at the sunrise and remember that He sustains creation and also sustains His promises. Rest in His faithfulness, not in your own strength.
exp.30:36:
God says that it would be as impossible to measure all the heavens above or to search out the foundations of the earth to their depths. In the same way, it is impossible for him to reject the descendants of Israel completely. Although they had done wicked things, he affirms this.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were under judgment and suffering exile because of their unfaithfulness. Even so, in this passage about the new covenant, God assures them that his commitment to them will not come to an end. What follows announces that Jerusalem will be rebuilt for him.

For today: when you feel that your failures are greater than God's patience, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your perfection. Return to him with sincerity, trusting in his promise and not in your merits.
exp.30:39:
This verse says that the whole area of the valley where dead bodies and ashes were, and the fields as far as the Kidron brook and the Horse Gate on the east, will be set apart for God. "Holy" means set apart for the Lord. And it will never again be uprooted or destroyed.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces the restoration of Jerusalem after the punishment. The valley is probably the Hinnom Valley, a place associated with death and idolatry, although some scholars debate this. Even the most defiled place will be made clean. Some see a future fulfillment here, while others see a spiritual promise in the new covenant.

For today: God can make holy even what seems dirtiest or most lost in your life. Give him your story, including your most painful parts, and trust that he restores and sustains.
exp.31:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah on a specific date: the tenth year of King Zedekiah of Judah, which matched the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The word "Lord" in this verse is the name of God used in this translation.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. According to the verses that follow, Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonian army, and Jeremiah was imprisoned because he had announced that the city would be handed over to Babylon. Scholars usually place this around 587 BC, although the exact dates can vary depending on the calculation.

For today: the Bible places God's word within real events and difficult moments. When life feels enclosed or without a way out, we can remember that God continues to speak and act in the middle of crisis. Look for his voice in Scripture and trust that he does not lose control.
exp.31:5:
Here Jeremiah tells that God spoke to him. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to me" means that the Lord gave him a message. The verse only sets up what God is about to say next.

Jeremiah the prophet speaks, and he is shut up in the courtyard of the prison because he had announced that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon. The Babylonian armies were already surrounding the city. In that dark moment, God speaks to him about a family field in Anathoth, which a cousin will come to offer for sale.

For today: God knows how to speak to us even in difficult times. When everything seems closed off, we can stop, listen for his voice in his Word, and trust that he is still guiding our path.
exp.31:7:
Jeremiah tells us that his cousin Hanameel came to the courtyard of the prison, just as the Lord had already told him he would. He asked Jeremiah to buy his field in Anathoth, because Jeremiah had the family right to acquire it. The word "redemption" here means buying back a property so that it does not leave the family. When Jeremiah saw that everything was happening just as God had said, he knew the message came from Him.

Jeremiah was in prison, since Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. God announced this purchase to him as a sign: although destruction and exile would come, one day the people would again buy and farm the land. Many understand this as a promise of hope.

For today: when God confirms his word step by step, we can trust him even in difficult times. Dare to take steps of faith, knowing that he keeps his promises.
exp.31:9:
Jeremiah describes how he closed the deal for buying the field. He wrote the deed of sale and sealed it so that it would be protected. He had some witnesses confirm the transaction, and he weighed out the silver on a scale, because that was how payment was made back then.

Jeremiah was a prisoner in the courtyard of the guard while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. His cousin Hanamel offers him the field, and Jeremiah recognizes in this the word of God. Buying land at that moment was a sign that, after the punishment, God would once again give hope to his people.

Today, this verse encourages us to act with order and honesty, even when things seem lost. We can trust God's promises by faithfully doing what is ours to do: keeping agreements, being clear, and acting with hope.
exp.31:13:
God tells Jeremiah to take the two documents of the purchase of the field: the sealed copy, which was the official one and was kept closed, and the open copy, which could be read. They were to be stored in a clay jar so that they would last for many days.

Jeremiah is held in the courtyard of the prison while the army of Babylon surrounds Jerusalem. God had asked him to buy a field from his cousin Hanameel, something that seemed absurd in the middle of the war. Jeremiah gives the documents to his assistant Baruch, and God explains that this purchase is a sign: one day people will again buy houses and fields in this land.

For today: even when everything looks lost, God invites us to plant hope through concrete steps of faith and obedience, trusting that He does what He promises.
exp.31:16:
Jeremiah begins his prayer by acknowledging who God is. He says that the Lord made the heavens and the earth by his great power and by his outstretched arm, a way of speaking about his strength in action. And he concludes that nothing is too hard for him, that is, nothing is impossible or too great for him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. Babylon had Jerusalem under siege, and everything seemed lost. Even so, God had told him to buy a field from his cousin, and Jeremiah obeyed and handed the deed of sale to Baruch. Afterward, puzzled, he prays. That purchase was a sign that one day the people would live again in their land.

When the situation looks closed, we can do as Jeremiah did: before listing the problems, remember who God is. Praying this way does not deny the difficulty, but it places it under the power of the One who created all things, and it helps us keep obeying with hope.
exp.31:18:
He says that God is great in his plans and wonderful in what he does. His eyes are open, that is, he sees everything that people do. For this reason he gives to each person according to their way of living and according to the fruit of their deeds, in other words, the consequences of what they have done. The word "counsel" here means his purposes and his wisdom.

Jeremiah is praying to God. Babylon has Jerusalem under siege, and the prophet is a prisoner. Even so, God had asked him to buy a field, and Jeremiah prays by remembering who God is: Creator, faithful and just, the one who brought Israel out of Egypt.

For today: when you feel confused or see injustice, remember that God sees everything with clarity and nothing escapes him. You can trust that his plans are wise. It also invites you to live with honesty, knowing that your decisions matter before him.
exp.31:19:
This verse says that God performed signs and wonders, that is, miracles and astonishing deeds, in Egypt. It says those works continued to be remembered down to the present day, both in Israel and among other nations. In this way God made himself a name, a reputation that was still alive in the time of Jeremiah.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, in prayer. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and he is a prisoner. God had told him to buy a field, something that seemed absurd at that moment. Jeremiah recalls what God did in the past, such as the exodus, to support his confidence that God can keep his promises.

For today: when everything seems to have no way out, remember what God has already done in your life and in his Word. Recalling his past faithfulness can give you the courage to trust him today.
exp.31:21:
This verse says that God gave the Israelites the land of Canaan, just as he had promised with an oath to their ancestors. The phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey" is a way of saying the land was fertile and abundant.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, in a prayer to God. Jerusalem is surrounded by the army of Babylon (the Chaldeans), and Jeremiah remembers God's faithfulness in the past. Then he acknowledges that the people disobeyed, and that is why the punishment came.

For today: when you go through difficult moments, remember how God has kept his promises to you. And ask him for help to respond with obedience and gratitude, not with indifference.
exp.31:22:
They came in and took possession of the land that was promised to them, but they did not listen to God's voice or live according to His law. They did not do what He commanded them. Because of this, God allowed all that disaster to fall upon them.

The prophet Jeremiah is the one speaking, praying to God. Babylon (the Chaldeans) had surrounded Jerusalem, and Jeremiah had bought a field by God's command. He remembers God's faithfulness in the past and acknowledges that the punishment came because of the people's disobedience. Then he asks, troubled, why God had told him to buy a field in the middle of that disaster.

For today: when we face difficult times, we can pray honestly, remembering what God has done and acknowledging our failures. Obeying Him is not a burden but the way to live well with Him.
exp.31:23:
They say the Babylonian armies have already raised siege ramps and are attacking Jerusalem. Soon the city will fall into the hands of the Chaldeans, who are the Babylonians. Inside it the people suffer because of war (the sword), hunger, and disease (the pestilence). What God had announced is coming true, and Jeremiah acknowledges it.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, in prayer to God. Jerusalem is under siege, and God had asked him to buy a field, something that seemed absurd. Jeremiah remembers that the people disobeyed, and that is why the punishment came. He appears confused: why buy land if everything is being lost?

For today: when things make no sense, pray honestly. God is not offended by your questions. Bring your confusion before Him and keep obeying, trusting that He has a greater plan than what you can see.
exp.31:24:
Jeremiah speaks with God and expresses his confusion. He reminds God that he was told to buy a piece of land, to pay for it with money, and to have witnesses sign the purchase. But now the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, are about to conquer the city. It seems strange to him to buy something that appears to be lost.

Jeremiah is in prison while Babylon besieges Jerusalem. God asked him to buy the field of his cousin Hanamel as a sign that, after the punishment, the people would return to live in their land. Jeremiah obeyed, but he prays honestly and without understanding everything. God answers by reminding him that nothing is hidden from him.

For today: when God's instructions seem to make no sense, you can obey and also express your doubts with sincerity. He is not bothered by your questions, and his promises still stand even when the situation looks dark.
exp.31:27:
God announces that he is going to hand Jerusalem over into the hands of the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, and of their king Nebuchadrezzar. He says the city will be taken.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah while Jerusalem is under siege and King Zedekiah has the prophet imprisoned. Shortly before this, Jeremiah bought a field as a sign of future hope. God reminds him that he is the God of all flesh and that nothing is hidden from him. The judgment comes because the people fell into idolatry and wickedness.

For today: God speaks the truth even when it hurts, and he also keeps promises of restoration. We can trust that he sees everything, so it is wise to turn to him honestly, hiding nothing, and to wait for his mercy.
exp.31:28:
This verse says that the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians who were already attacking Jerusalem, will enter the city and set it on fire. They will also burn the houses where the people offered incense to Baal and poured out drink offerings of wine or other drinks to false gods, which provoked the anger of God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and Jeremiah is in prison. God makes clear that this fall is no accident: the people had long been given over to idolatry, and the flat roofs of the houses were places where this worship was practiced.

For today: God sees what we do even on the rooftops, in what is hidden. It is worth asking ourselves what things are occupying the place that belongs to Him, and turning back to Him with sincerity before those things destroy us.
exp.31:31:
This verse says that God is about to punish the city for all the wickedness of his people. It names everyone: the kings, the princes (leaders or officials), the priests, the prophets, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. "Provoke me to anger" means to stir up his anger. No one was left out: both the leaders and the ordinary people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon, and God explains why he allows that situation: the people had turned their backs on him for generations, even after receiving constant teaching and after defiling the temple with idols. Even so, in this same chapter God promises to restore his people.

For today: instead of blaming only others, we can examine our own hearts with humility. If we acknowledge our failings and return to God, we find his forgiveness and his loving correction.
exp.31:33:
This verse says that the people of Judah set their abominations, that is, their idols and detestable practices, inside the temple in Jerusalem. That was the place where God had put his name. By doing so they defiled it, that is, they made it unclean and dishonored it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon, and Jeremiah was in prison. God explains why judgment is coming: the people, their kings, priests, and prophets did not listen to his warnings, though he spoke to them again and again. Even so, in this same chapter God promises to restore his people.

For today: God wants first place in our lives, which is now his house (1 Corinthians 6:19). We can ask ourselves what things we have let into our hearts that compete with him, and ask him for forgiveness and help to remove them.
exp.31:34:
This verse says that the people of Judah built altars to Baal in the valley of Hinnom, a place near Jerusalem. There they made their sons and daughters pass through the fire as an offering to Molech, a false god. God makes clear that He never commanded this, and that it never came into His mind that they would do something so terrible. The word "abomination" means something deeply detestable.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. He reminds them that although He taught them again and again, they turned their backs on Him and refused to correct themselves. Even so, the passage that follows announces that God will bring them back.

For today: we should measure our customs by what God says, not by what most people do. If there is something that harms others, and God does not endorse it, we must leave it behind and return to Him in humility.
exp.31:35:
Here the verse says that God, the Lord of Israel, speaks about Jerusalem. The people repeat that the city will be handed over to the king of Babylon and will die by the sword, the famine, and the pestilence.

Jeremiah speaks during the time of Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. He was imprisoned, and God had commanded him to buy a field as a sign of hope. Before giving that hope, the Lord acknowledges the cause of the judgment: idolatry and the sacrifice of children to Molech. Then, in the verses that follow, he promises to gather his people and bring them back.

For today: God is honest about the consequences of sin, but he does not stop there. If you are going through a painful consequence, do not lose hope. Acknowledge your mistake and trust that God can restore.
exp.31:42:
In the very land that people today see as a destroyed and empty place, handed over to the Babylonians (the Chaldeans), fields and property will once again be owned. A portion of land, held and passed down to one's children, is what is meant here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and the people feel that everything is lost. Even so, Jeremiah buys a field at God's command, as a sign that there will be a future. God promises that just as He allowed the punishment, He will also bring the good He has promised, and that the people will return from captivity.

For today: when a situation seems empty or without a way out, do not take what you see as the final word. You can take small steps of faith and obedience, trusting that God is faithful and can raise up hope where today you only see ruins.
exp.31:43:
In the future, it says, people will once again buy fields with money. They will draw up a deed of purchase, seal it, and call in witnesses. This will happen in the land of Benjamin, around Jerusalem, in the towns of Judah, in the hill country, in the lowland plains, and in the south (the south is the Negev). Bringing back the captives means returning the exiles to their land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon (the Chaldeans) is besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah is in prison. Even so, God commanded him to buy a field as a sign. It seemed like a pointless purchase, since the country was about to be conquered. But God promised that, after the punishment, he would restore his people.

For today: when everything seems lost, you can take small steps of faith based on God's promises. He is faithful and can restore hope where today you see only ruin. Trust and act with patience.
exp.32:4:
God says that the houses of Jerusalem were torn down, and that the people went out to fight against the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). Those houses would be left full of the bodies of the dead. The phrase about filling them means the houses would be packed with corpses, and striking down the enemy is the picture of the destruction. The phrase about God hiding his face means that God withdrew his favor and his protection. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some scholars understand it in somewhat different ways.

The words come through Jeremiah, who was held prisoner while Babylon was laying siege to Jerusalem. God explains that the city is suffering because of its persistent wickedness, not because He has forgotten it without reason.

For today: the harsh consequences of sin are real, but they are not God's final word. Right after this, He promises healing, peace, and restoration. If you are going through a hard time, be honest with God, acknowledge whatever you need to, and cry out to Him. He invites us to do so and promises to answer.
exp.32:5:
God promises to bring health and medicine to Jerusalem. He says he will heal his people and show them abundant peace and truth. The phrase about bringing up healing means that God makes healing spring up or come forth, the way a wound is bound up. Here "reveal" means to make known, and "truth" points to something firm and trustworthy.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who was imprisoned at the time. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and the houses were being torn down. God says this punishment came because of the people's wickedness, but it does not end there: immediately he promises to bring them back from captivity, cleanse them, and forgive them.

For today: even when you feel that everything has collapsed, whether because of your own mistakes or because of circumstances, God does not shut the door on you. You can draw near to him with sincerity, ask for forgiveness and healing, and trust that he knows how to rebuild what seemed lost.
exp.32:7:
This verse says that God promises to cleanse his people from all their wickedness. "Cleanse" means to purify, like washing away a stain. He also promises to pardon all their sins, both those of disobedience and those of turning away from God on purpose. God does not make light of what happened, but he offers to erase it completely.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was in ruins and many had been taken captive, something the Bible connects with their sin. Even so, in the midst of that pain, God announces healing, peace, and restoration. Forgiveness is the foundation of that new stage: first he cleanses the heart, and then he rebuilds what was lost.

For today: if you feel that your mistakes are too big, bring them to God with sincerity. He offers cleansing and a fresh start. Confess what weighs on your conscience and receive his forgiveness without continuing to carry the guilt.
exp.32:8:
God says that Jerusalem, his restored people, will be for him a name of joy, praise, and glory before all the nations. Those peoples will hear of the good that God does for them, and they will fear and tremble, meaning they will be amazed and filled with awe at so much goodness and peace.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who was then imprisoned, while Jerusalem was suffering destruction and the people were living in exile. In the midst of that pain, God promises to bring them back, to cleanse them from their sin, and to forgive them, so that their restoration will display his mercy.

For today: when God forgives you and lifts you up, your life can speak of his goodness. Tell someone, with humility and gratitude, the good that he has done for you.
exp.32:11:
