God says that this place, now a desert with no people and no animals, will once again be full of life. There will again be shepherds' huts, that is, simple shelters where shepherds look after their flocks. The image speaks of peace, ordinary work, and everyday life restored.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah at a time when Jerusalem and Judah had been destroyed by the Babylonian invasion, and the people were either in captivity or on the way to it. In the middle of the ruin, God promises to bring them back and restore joy. Many understand that this was fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also see a greater fulfillment in Christ.

For today: when something in your life seems empty or lost, do not treat that scene as the final word. God can raise up the simple and ordinary once again. Trust Him and take one small step of faith today.
exp.32:12:
This verse lists several regions of Judah: the cities of the mountains, the cities of the lowland, the cities of the south, the land of Benjamin, and the places around Jerusalem. In all of them, God says, flocks will once again pass under the hands of those who count them, that is, of the shepherds who number their sheep. Counting the flock is a sign of peace and prosperity.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who is in prison while Jerusalem is under attack by Babylon. It is a message of comfort for a people who will be taken into captivity. God promises to restore the desolate land and then announces the Messiah, the Branch of righteousness from the line of David.

For today: when everything seems ruined, God can still give back the ordinary and the simple. Trust that he keeps his word, and praise him now, even in the middle of trial.
exp.32:17:
God promises that there will always be Levite priests standing before Him to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices every day.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who is in prison and writes to a people discouraged by the fall of Jerusalem. God promises restoration: a king from the line of David and a priesthood that continues. Christians often see here a sign pointing to Christ, the King and High Priest; others understand it in a more literal way. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if God keeps His promises even when everything seems lost, we can trust Him. Today, in the middle of your difficulties, come to God in prayer every day, with thankfulness and hope.
exp.32:21:
It says that God will make the descendants of David, his servant, and the Levites who serve him grow until they are as countless as the stars of the sky and the sand of the sea. The phrase about the stars is explained here as referring to the host of heaven, meaning the stars themselves.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who is in prison, while Jerusalem falls to Babylon. The people feel that God has rejected the two chosen families: the royal family and the priestly family. God answers with a firm promise, comparing his covenant to the order of day and night. Christians often see here a announcement fulfilled in Christ, although there are different ways of understanding it.

For today: when your situation seems lost, remember that God is faithful to his promises even when you cannot see how. Trust his word and keep serving him with hope.
exp.32:22:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that God spoke again to Jeremiah. The word "Moreover" links it to what came before, and the phrase "the word of the Lord came to" shows that what follows is not the prophet's own idea but a message that comes from God.

Jeremiah was speaking to the people in a very hard time, when Jerusalem had fallen and many believed that God had abandoned them. God himself speaks and promises that he will not forget his covenant with David or with the Levites. He will soon answer those who said that God had rejected the two families he had chosen.

For today: when you feel forgotten or doubt God's promises, do not rely only on the opinions of other people or on your circumstances. Take time to listen to what God says in his Word, because he remains faithful.
exp.32:23:
God asks Jeremiah whether he has taken notice of what the people are saying: that the two families the Lord chose, he has now rejected. "Notice" here means to perceive or realize. "Rejected" means cast off or abandoned. So that people despises God's people and no longer regards them as a nation.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah when Jerusalem has fallen or is about to fall, and the people are discouraged. There is discussion about which "two families" is meant: many believe they are Israel and Judah, others the line of David and that of the Levites. God answers with promises: just as day and night remain, his covenant with Jacob and David will stand, and he will restore their captivity with mercy.

For today: when others say your situation has no remedy, or you yourself think it, remember that God's faithfulness does not depend on opinions or circumstances. Trust his word.
exp.32:24:
Here the verse says that God has a covenant with day and night, that is, the fixed order of creation. He himself set the ordinances of heaven and earth. The verse stands as an open condition, and the next verse completes it: if that order could fail, then God would cast off Jacob and David.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah during the time of exile. The people were saying that God had rejected Israel and Judah, the two families. God answers with a comparison: his faithfulness toward his people is as certain as the dawn and the dusk. He promises to restore them and to show mercy.

For today: when you feel that God has forgotten you, or that your failures have ruined everything, look at how the sun rises every morning. Let that order remind you that God keeps his promises. Trust his faithfulness more than your feelings.
exp.33:0:
This verse introduces a message from God to Jeremiah. It says that the word came when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, with his whole army and the kingdoms and peoples under his rule, was attacking Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. The verse shows the attack as happening at that moment, and the verse of the wording is given in the note below.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in the last days of the kingdom of Judah, when Babylon was already surrounding the land. Soon after, God tells him to carry a message to King Zedekiah: the city would fall and he would be captured. The text presents this as the result of the people's disobedience, although the details of each cause are explained in other parts of the book.

For today: God speaks clearly even in times of crisis. When everything seems to be falling apart, it is worth listening to his Word with humility, even when it is not what we want to hear, and trusting that he is still in control.
exp.33:3:
God speaks to King Zedekiah.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God while the army of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. The message is serious: the city would fall and the king would be taken away as a prisoner. But God leaves a door open to repentance. Some scholars think that the promise of dying in peace depended on Zedekiah obeying; the Bible does not fully make clear how it was fulfilled.

For today: even when we face the consequences of our mistakes, God continues to speak to us with mercy. If He shows you a hard truth, listen with humility; His correction always comes with an opportunity to return to Him.
exp.33:9:
This verse tells that the leaders and all the people heard about the agreement made in Jerusalem: each person would let go their male and female servants, and would no longer use them as slaves. They obeyed and let them go.

King Zedekiah made this covenant when Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Babylon. God, through Jeremiah, was reminding them that the law of Moses commanded that enslaved Hebrews be set free. It is not known with certainty why they did it at that time; some believe it was out of fear of the danger. Sadly, they later changed their minds and enslaved them again.

For today: obeying God is not only making a good decision in a difficult moment, but keeping it when the pressure passes. Ask God for the steadiness to fulfill what you have promised.
exp.33:10:
Here, the people and officials of Judah turned back on what they had done. They had first set free their Hebrew servants, but afterward they changed their minds. They made the men and women they had released come back, and they forced them into slavery again.

Jeremiah records this during the siege of Jerusalem by the army of Babylon. King Zedekiah and the people had made a covenant before God to free their Hebrew brothers, as the law of Moses required. Many believe they did it out of fear of the crisis, and when the pressure eased, they broke their word. God answers by reminding them of his covenant with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

For today: keeping what we have promised to God and to others, even after the trouble has passed. We might ask ourselves whether our obedience is sincere or only appears when we are afraid.
exp.33:11:
This verse is a brief introduction. It says that God spoke to the prophet Jeremiah. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah" means that the message did not come from Jeremiah himself, but from God.

Here the narrator speaks, and then God speaks. The princes and the people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but afterward they changed their minds and enslaved them again. God intervenes to point out that betrayal, recalling the covenant he made with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt.

For today: God sees whether we keep what we promised. Before going back on a commitment, especially one that protects another person's dignity, it is good to remember that God listens and expects faithfulness.
exp.33:18:
This verse lists those who passed between the parts of the divided calf: the princes of Judah and of Jerusalem, the eunuchs (court officials), the priests, and all the people of the land. All of them took part in the covenant, and for that reason all of them would be held responsible.

God speaks through Jeremiah while Babylon threatens Jerusalem. The people had freed their Hebrew slaves, as the law required, but then they enslaved them again. Passing between the halves of an animal was a solemn way of swearing a covenant, and here that oath was broken.

For today: if we promise something before God, we ought to keep it. It is worth reviewing what promises we have made, and being faithful, especially when keeping them costs us something.
exp.33:21:
God says that he will bring the Babylonian army back to Jerusalem. They will fight against the city, capture it, and burn it. He will also leave the cities of Judah desolate, without a single inhabitant.

God speaks through Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. King Zedekiah and the people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but then they took them back into slavery. In this way they broke their covenant with God. Here he announces the punishment for that disobedience. The Babylonians had withdrawn for a time, but they would return.

For today: when we give our word to God or to others, we must keep it. If we fail, God invites us to repent quickly and to make things right with sincerity, not to remain in empty promises.
exp.34:1:
God tells Jeremiah to go and find the Rechabites, a family that lived as nomads, and to bring them into the temple, into one of its side rooms. There he is to offer them wine to drink. The words "speak to them" simply mean inviting them, and the name of God is the Lord.

The one speaking is God, in the time of King Jehoiakim of Judah. The Rechabites, by command of their ancestor Jonadab, never drank wine. God wants a public test: they obey a man even when wine is offered to them, while the people of Judah do not obey God. This contrast is made clearer later in the chapter.

For today: ask yourself whether you are as steady in obeying God as this family was in keeping their promise. Choose one specific thing God has asked of you and carry it out this week, even if there is pressure or temptation around you.
exp.34:2:
Here Jeremiah tells that he obeyed God's command. He gathered Jaazaniah, his brothers, all his sons, and the whole family of the Rechabites.

Jeremiah speaks, and he does so by the command of the LORD, in the days of King Jehoiakim of Judah. God wanted to use the Rechabites as an example. Later it is seen that they were faithful to the command of their ancestor not to drink wine, and that faithfulness stood in contrast with the disobedience of the people of Judah.

For today: God values steady obedience. We can ask ourselves whether we are as firm in obeying God as others are in keeping their commitments. Today you can choose one concrete way to obey him better.
exp.34:4:
Jeremiah tells us that, inside the temple, he set before the Rechabites pots full of wine and cups, and told them to drink.

Jeremiah speaks here on God's command. The Rechabites were a family who, by the order of their ancestor Jonadab, lived in tents and did not drink wine. They had come to Jerusalem fleeing from an invading army. God uses this test to show a contrast: they obeyed a human father, but Judah did not obey God.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we are as faithful to the Word of God as this family was to its commitment. Constant obedience, even when temptations are in plain sight, honors God and strengthens our character.
exp.34:5:
The Rechabites answer that they will drink no wine. The reason is that their ancestor Jonadab, son of Rechab, commanded them that neither they nor their sons should ever drink wine.

Here the family of the Rechabites speaks, the same people the prophet Jeremiah tested in the temple when he deliberately offered them wine. God uses this scene as an example: they faithfully obeyed a human father for generations, while Judah did not obey God, who spoke to them again and again. The point is not to teach that all wine is sin, but to show faithfulness.

For today: ask yourself whether you are as steady in obeying God as these men were in keeping their commitment. Choose one specific thing God has shown you today and carry it out firmly, even when no one sees you.
exp.34:6:
This verse records the command that Jonadab, ancestor of the Rechabites, gave to his family: not to build houses, not to sow seed, not to plant vineyards or own them, but to live in tents all their lives. In this way they would live many years in the land where they were foreigners.

Here the Rechabites speak, explaining to Jeremiah why they refuse the wine he offers them. God used this scene to contrast their faithfulness to a human command with the disobedience of Judah toward Him. Scholars do not know for certain why Jonadab gave those rules.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we are as steadfast in obeying God as these men were in obeying their father, and let us practice that faithfulness in one concrete decision this week.
exp.34:7:
Here the Rechabites explain that they have obeyed their ancestor Jonadab, son of Rechab, in everything he commanded them. They have never drunk wine, neither they, nor their wives, nor their sons and daughters.

The people speaking are the Rechabites, a family that lived in tents. God asked Jeremiah to bring them into the temple and offer them wine. They refused. God used their faithfulness as a contrast: they obeyed a man, but Judah did not obey God.

Today, this passage invites us to ask whether we are consistent in obeying God. We can choose a clear command from the Bible that we have neglected and commit to keeping it with perseverance this week.
exp.34:8:
It says that the Rechabites did not build houses to live in, nor did they have a vineyard, nor any land of their own, nor a field sown with seed.

Here the Rechabites speak, a family that God sets forth as an example before Judah. They explain that they obey their ancestor Jonadab, son of Rechab, who ordered them to live in tents and not to drink wine. They kept that command for generations. They took refuge in Jerusalem only because of the invasion by Babylon. God uses their faithfulness to show that Judah did not obey Him.

For today: ask yourself whether you obey God with the same steadiness that others show in keeping a promise. Choose today one single instruction from God that you have put off, and begin to carry it out faithfully.
exp.34:9:
They say they live in tents, not in fixed houses, and that they have kept everything their ancestor Jonadab commanded them.

These are the Rechabites, a family whom Jeremiah tested by offering them wine. They refused, because Jonadab, son of Rechab, had given them rules of simple living. When the Babylonians invaded, they took refuge in Jerusalem. God uses their faithfulness as an example to rebuke Judah, which did not obey its Lord.

For today: if this family was so steadfast in keeping the word of a human father, how much more should we obey God? We can choose today a clear command of Jesus and practice it with firmness, even when it costs us or others do not do the same.
exp.34:10:
This verse tells how the Rechabites, a family that lived in tents, had to take refuge in Jerusalem when King Nebuchadnezzar invaded the land. They were afraid of the army of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) and of the army of Syria.

The Rechabites are the ones speaking, answering Jeremiah. Their ancestor Jonadab had ordered them not to build houses, not to sow fields or plant vineyards, and they had obeyed him for generations. They made only one exception because of the war, and even so they remained faithful in everything else. God uses them as an example to rebuke Judah, which did not obey its God.

For today: if a family kept the word of a father faithfully for years, how much more can we obey God with steadfastness. Ask yourself today which clear command of God you have set aside, and take one concrete step to fulfill it.
exp.34:11:
This verse is a short phrase that marks a turning point. It says that God spoke to Jeremiah. The wording "came" is the older form of the verb, and it is simply a way of saying the word of the Lord arrived to him. Up to this point, the Rechabites had been telling how they obeyed their ancestor Jonadab. Now God himself takes up the word to say something.

The one speaking is the Lord, and the messenger is the prophet Jeremiah. The Rechabites had come to Jerusalem fleeing the Babylonian army, but they remained faithful to the command not to drink wine or live in houses. God uses this example to show that the people of Judah were not obeying him, even though he spoke to them again and again.

For today: before giving a lesson, God invites us to look closely. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his voice in the Bible with the same seriousness that others keep a promise made to their family.
exp.34:13:
It says the commands of Jonadab, son of Rechab, were carried out faithfully. He ordered his sons not to drink wine, and to this day they have not drunk it, out of respect for their father. But God spoke to the people of Judah, rising early and speaking to them again and again, and they would not listen.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The Rechabites had kept their ancestor's custom for generations. God uses them as an example to show Judah its disobedience, even though He is far more worthy of being obeyed than any human father.

For today: if there are people who faithfully keep a family rule, how much more should we listen to and obey God! Today you can choose one instruction from the Bible that you have let slip by and put it into practice with consistency.
exp.34:14:
God says that he sent all his prophets to his people, again and again and with urgency. His message was: leave your evil way, correct your actions, and do not follow other gods. If they obeyed, they would keep living in the land God had given them. But they did not incline their ear, that is, they did not want to listen.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. God uses the example of the Rechabites, who faithfully obeyed their ancestor Jonadab in not drinking wine. If they honored the word of a human father, how is it that the people did not obey the God who had cared for them and spoke to them with such patience?

Today, God still speaks with patience, above all through his Word. A practical application: set aside a moment each day to read it and ask yourself what concrete change it calls for. Then obey without putting it off.
exp.34:16:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts and God of Israel, is going to bring upon Judah and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem the punishment he had already announced to them. The reason is simple: God spoke to them and they did not listen; he called them and they did not answer.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. In this chapter, God holds up as an example the Rechabites, a family who faithfully kept the command of their ancestor Jonadab not to drink wine. If they obeyed a man, how much more should the people obey God, who had sent them prophets again and again?

For today: when we sense that God is speaking to us through his Word or through our conscience, we should not delay our response. Listening and obeying humbly today is better than hardening the heart.
exp.34:17:
Jeremiah speaks to the family of the Rechabites and tells them what God thinks of them. God commends them because they obeyed Jonadab, their ancestor (the word "father" here means the founder of the family). They kept all his commands and carried them out just as he gave them.

God himself had tested the Rechabites by offering them wine, and they refused it out of loyalty to their ancestor's command. Jeremiah uses their example to make a contrast: they obeyed a man, but Judah did not obey God, who spoke to them again and again. After this comes a promise for that family.

For today: if the Rechabites' loyalty to a human command was so firm, how much more should we listen to and obey the voice of God? Today you can choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice with steady commitment.
exp.35:0:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and king of Judah, God spoke to Jeremiah. The verse says that the word came to Jeremiah from the Lord. The Lord is the name of God.

The one speaking is God, who gives a message to his prophet Jeremiah. From the verses that follow we see that he will ask Jeremiah to write on a scroll everything he had already said to him. The fourth year of Jehoiakim is usually placed around 605 BC, although the exact dates can vary depending on the calculation. God wanted the people to listen, to turn back, and to be forgiven.

God does not tire of speaking to us or of offering us a way out. Today we can open his Word with a willing heart, asking ourselves which path we need to change, and trusting that he wants to forgive.
exp.35:1:
God tells Jeremiah to take a scroll, that is, a long sheet rolled up that was used for writing, and to put in it everything God has said to him. It includes messages for Israel, Judah, and the other nations. It covers the period from when Jeremiah began to speak, in the time of King Josiah, up to that moment.

The Lord speaks in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. Jeremiah had spent years warning the people, and now God wants his words set down in writing. According to the verses that follow, the hope was that the people would listen, turn away from their wrongdoing, and that God would forgive them. His Word was not only meant to condemn, but to give an opportunity to return.

God does not grow weary of speaking to us or of offering forgiveness. Today we can read the Bible with a willing heart, asking ourselves which path we should change. Listening to God in time is always better than ignoring him.
exp.35:3:
Jeremiah calls for Baruch, the son of Neriah. Baruch was a scribe, that is, someone who knew how to write. While Jeremiah speaks to him, Baruch writes on a scroll everything that God had said to the prophet. A scroll was a long sheet of papyrus or leather that was rolled up.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks during the time of King Jehoiakim, about twenty years after his ministry began. God wants his warnings to be put in writing, because Jeremiah was prevented from going to the temple. God's aim was not only to punish: he wanted the people to listen, to turn back, and to receive forgiveness.

For today: God takes care that his word is preserved and reaches people. We can value it by reading it carefully and, if something corrects us, responding with humility. We can also write down what we learn so that we do not forget it.
exp.35:5:
Jeremiah tells Baruc to go to the temple and read aloud the scroll on which he wrote what God had spoken to him. He is to read it before the people gathered on the day of fasting, and also before those who come in from the cities of Judah. A scroll was an ancient book made from a long strip rolled up.

The speaker is Jeremiah, God's prophet, who is in prison and cannot enter the temple. For that reason he sends his assistant Baruc. God wanted to warn the people of his judgment, in the hope that they would turn back. This is believed to have taken place in the time of King Jehoiakim, although the exact details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: God still uses ordinary people to share his Word. If he places in your heart to say something true and good, do it with courage and humility, even when others cannot or will not.
exp.35:7:
This verse says that Baruch, the son of Neriah, did exactly what the prophet Jeremiah had commanded him. He read aloud from the scroll the words of the Lord in the Lord's house. The verse uses the name "the Lord" for God, and the scroll is the same writing that appears throughout this passage.

Jeremiah could not enter the temple, so he entrusted Baruch, his secretary, with reading what God had said to him. This took place on a day of fasting, when many people had gathered. The purpose was that the people would listen, repent, and turn away from their wrong ways, because God had announced serious judgment.

For today: Baruch's obedience was simple and complete, even when the message was difficult to deliver. We can ask God for the courage to do what He asks of us, without changing or softening His word.
exp.35:8:
It came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month. They announced a public fast, meaning a time of going without food in order to seek God. The people of Jerusalem were called to it, along with those who came from the other cities of Judah.

Jeremiah had received words from God warning of judgment on the people. He could not enter the temple, so his helper Baruch was to read the scroll aloud. The text does not say who ordered the fast, but it gathered many people, and so it was a good moment for them to hear the message.

Today, when we humble ourselves before God, we should also be ready to listen to his Word and obey it. Praying without listening is only half done.
exp.35:9:
Baruch, Jeremiah's assistant, read the book of the prophet's words aloud. He did it in the temple, in the room of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, who was a scribe (the one who wrote and handled official documents). That room was in the upper court, near the new gate, and all the people could hear.

The writer tells how Baruch obeyed Jeremiah's command. Jeremiah could not enter the temple, so Baruch read on his behalf. It was a day of fasting, so many people from Jerusalem and Judah had gathered. It was a good moment for them to hear God's message, which called them to turn back to Him. This public reading would carry the news as far as the officials and the king.

Today too it is fitting to give others the Word of God faithfully and boldly, without changing or softening it. And when we hear it, let us not let it pass as if nothing happened: let us ask God for a heart ready to obey.
exp.35:11:
He went down to the king's palace, to the secretary's room. There all the leaders were gathered, the princes, that is, the senior officials of the kingdom. Several are named: Elishama the scribe, Delaiah, Elnathan, Gemariah, Zedekiah, and the rest. A scribe was an official clerk of the government.

The narrator tells what happened after Baruch read aloud in public the message from God that Jeremiah had dictated. Micaiah, son of Gemariah, heard the reading and went to tell the officials. Some names, such as Gemariah and Elnathan, also appear in other accounts in the book, but we do not know for certain what each of them thought.

For today: when you hear the Word of God, do not keep it to yourself just because you heard it. Micaiah carried it to those who needed to know. Share it with wisdom and respect with someone who needs it.
exp.35:13:
Here the princes, who were the high officials of the kingdom, send a man named Jehudi to fetch Baruch. They ask him to bring the scroll, that is, the rolled-up book in which were written the words of God that Baruch had already read to the people. Baruch takes it in his hand and goes with them.

The narrator recounts what happened after Micaiah reported to them what he had heard. Jeremiah, the prophet, had dictated those words to Baruch, his scribe. The officials wanted to hear them for themselves, because they were a serious message from God to Judah.

For today: when we hear that God's Word says something important, it is good to listen to it personally and attentively, without relying only on what others tell us. Let us open the Bible, read it calmly, and let it speak to us.
exp.35:17:
Baruch answers the officials that Jeremiah was dictating all these words to him with his own mouth, and that he was writing them with ink in the book, that is, in the scroll. He invented nothing; he only put in writing what he heard.

The officials of Judah had just heard the scroll read and were frightened, because they knew King Jehoiakim would not receive a message of judgment well. That is why they ask Baruch how he had written everything down. He, a faithful scribe, explains his role clearly. Then the officials advise him to hide with Jeremiah, for they feared the king's reaction.

Today we can learn to be faithful and honest with the truth of God: to convey it as it is, without adding or taking away, even when it causes discomfort. God cares for those who are faithful to him, even in difficult times.
exp.35:18:
The leaders of the kingdom tell Baruch to go and hide along with Jeremiah, and to make sure no one knows where they are.

These officials had just heard God's message written on the scroll. They were frightened and decided to report it to King Jehoiakim. They knew the king could react violently against the prophet and his scribe, so they advised them to protect themselves. The text does not say whether they fully believed the message, but it does show that they wanted to look after them.

Today we can learn that obeying God does not always mean exposing yourself without wisdom. Sometimes prudence, such as withdrawing from a dangerous conflict, is a way of caring for the life and the mission God has given us. Let us pray for discernment to know when to speak and when to take shelter.
exp.35:19:
This verse says that the officials went to the king, who was in the court, and left the scroll stored in the room of Elishama the scribe. Then they told the king, in person, everything the scroll said. The king's court is the palace yard, and the room is a chamber.

The scroll contained God's messages that Jeremiah dictated and Baruch wrote down. The officials were frightened when they heard them and decided to inform King Jehoiakim. Before this, they advised Baruch and Jeremiah to hide, perhaps because they feared the king's reaction. The Bible does not explain this in detail, so it is a reasonable assumption.

When God speaks to us through his Word, it is not wise to cover it up or soften it. We can carry it with honesty and respect, and humbly ask ourselves how we will respond, because ignoring it is also a decision.
exp.35:20:
This verse says that King Jehoiakim sent a man named Jehudi to bring the scroll. Jehudi took it out of the room (the chamber) of Elishama, the secretary or scribe, and read it aloud before the king and all the princes (the high officials) who were standing beside him.

The scroll contained the words God had given to Jeremiah, and Baruch had written them down. The princes, frightened by the message, told the king, and they advised hiding Baruch and Jeremiah. The account does not explain everything the king was thinking when he asked for the scroll, but what follows shows that he did not want it in order to obey it.

Today we can ask ourselves how we receive the Word of God. We can listen to it carefully and still not let it change us. Let us ask God for a heart ready to obey, especially when his message makes us uncomfortable.
exp.35:21:
This verse describes the scene: King Jehoiakim was sitting in the winter house, a part of the palace used during the cold months. It was the ninth month (roughly November or December), and in front of him was a brazier, a vessel with coals to give warmth.

God had told Jeremiah to write his warnings on a scroll. Baruch wrote them down, and now they were being read to the king. The author mentions the fire on the hearth in detail because it will be key: the king will burn the scroll in that fire. This shows that he heard the word of God but did not want to obey it.

For today: we can be very close to the Word of God and still harden our hearts. When something in the Bible makes us uncomfortable, instead of burning it or ignoring it, let us ask God for a humble heart that listens and changes.
exp.35:22:
King Jehoiakim would listen as the scroll was read, and each time Jehudi had read three or four sections of it, the king would cut off those sections with a knife and throw them into the brazier, a kind of fire pan set on the hearth. He kept doing this until the whole scroll had been burned.

In context, God had told Jeremiah to dictate to Baruch his warning messages for Judah, in the hope that the people would turn back from their wrongdoing. It was winter, and the king was sitting near the fire. Instead of trembling before the word of God, as one would have hoped, he despised it and destroyed it. The verses that follow say that there was neither fear nor repentance.

For today: when the Bible makes us uncomfortable or corrects us, the temptation is to silence it or ignore it. Better to ask God for a humble heart, one that listens, acknowledges its mistake, and changes.
exp.35:23:
This verse says that King Jehoiakim and his servants heard all the words of the scroll and were not afraid. Neither did they tear their garments. In that time, tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief, humility, and repentance. Here "servants" means his officials or attendants.

Jeremiah had dictated to Baruch the messages of God, warning of judgment if the people did not return to Him. The narrator contrasts this reaction with that of King Josiah, who did tear his garments when he heard the law (2 Kings 22). Jehoiakim chose to burn the scroll rather than listen.

When the Word of God confronts us, we can harden ourselves or respond with humility. Today, instead of looking for excuses, let us ask God for a tender heart willing to change.
exp.35:26:
This verse says that God spoke again to Jeremiah after King Jehoiakim had burned the scroll. That scroll contained the words Baruch had written while Jeremiah dictated them.

The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a new message. A scribe is someone who writes out or copies texts.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and then God addresses Jeremiah. The king rejected the warning and destroyed the scroll, but God protected Jeremiah and Baruch. Right away he orders them to write another scroll with the same words. Burning the paper did not change what God had said.

For today: do not be discouraged if someone rejects or scorns what is true. God's word endures. Perhaps today your task is to keep obeying with patience, trusting that God cares for his message and for those who are faithful to him.
exp.35:27:
God tells Jeremiah to take another scroll and write down again all the words that were in the first one, the one King Jehoiakim burned. The word "write" here means that Baruch, the scribe, would put them down in writing again, as he had done before.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah after the king burned the scroll containing messages of judgment. Jehoiakim was angered by the warning that Babylon would come, and he tried to silence it by destroying the document and seeking to arrest the messengers. But God hid them and ordered the writing to be made again. The passage shows that burning the message does not cancel it.

For today: God's truth does not depend on being accepted. If there is something in his Word that makes you uncomfortable, do not hide it or ignore it; instead, listen to it with humility and let it correct you in time.
exp.35:30:
God says that he will punish Jehoiakim, his children, and his servants for their wickedness. "Punish" here means to come and call them to account, that is, to bring judgment. "Descendants" means offspring, and "men" refers to the men. God will also bring upon Jerusalem and Judah the evil he had announced, because no one would listen to him.

God speaks through Jeremiah. King Jehoiakim had burned the scroll with the prophet's warnings, as if destroying the message could cancel it. God answers that his word still stands, and that the king and the people would face the consequences of rejecting it. Then Jeremiah writes another scroll, and the word of God continues.

Today we might ask ourselves whether there is something God tells us through his Word that we prefer to ignore or silence. It is better to listen in time and correct our course, because God is patient, but his warnings are real.
exp.35:31:
Jeremiah takes another scroll, that is, another book in the form of a rolled parchment, and gives it to Baruch, his scribe or secretary. Baruch writes again, taking dictation from Jeremiah, everything that King Jehoiakim had burned. Moreover, many other similar words were added.

God had commanded Jeremiah to put his messages in writing to call Judah to repentance. King Jehoiakim cut up the scroll and threw it into the fire, showing contempt for the message. God responds by ordering that it be written again and announcing judgment on the king and on the people who refused to listen.

For today: the Word of God is not destroyed because someone rejects it. If what God says makes us uncomfortable today, instead of ignoring it or pushing it away, we can listen to it with humility and respond with repentance and obedience.
exp.36:0:
This verse says that Zedekiah, son of Josiah, began to reign over Judah. He took the place of Coniah (also called Jehoiachin or Jeconiah), and it was Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, who set him on the throne. The verse shows Nebuchadrezzar's authority in appointing him.

The one telling the story is the book of Jeremiah, which recounts these events as history. Judah was already under the power of Babylon, so Zedekiah was a subject king, not an independent one. The verses that follow explain why this matters: neither the king nor the people paid attention to the words that God gave through Jeremiah, even though they later asked him to pray for them.

For today: let's not wait until we are in trouble to seek God. Listening to and obeying his word in time is worth more than asking for prayer when it is already too late.
exp.36:2:
This verse says that King Zedekiah sent two men, Jehucal and Zephaniah the priest, to ask Jeremiah to pray to the Lord for them. The phrase "to the Lord our God" is the wording it quotes. Asking for prayer is what the king wanted.

The writer tells how Zedekiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made king, did not listen to the word of God that Jeremiah spoke to him. Now Jerusalem is surrounded by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). When the army of Egypt approaches, the Chaldeans pull back for a while, and the king wants the prophet to pray. He asks God for help, but without changing his heart or obeying.

Today we can notice how easy it is to ask for prayer only when we are in trouble, while ignoring what God has already told us. Praying is good, but it goes hand in hand with listening and obeying. Today, ask God for help, and also decide to do what you already know He is asking of you.
exp.36:4:
The army of Pharaoh of Egypt had come out to help Judah. When the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), who had surrounded Jerusalem, heard the news, they withdrew from the city.

The one who narrates is the writer of the book of Jeremiah. King Zedekiah, who was weak and undecided, asked the prophet for prayer, but he did not want to obey his message. When the Chaldeans left, the people may have thought the danger had passed. However, God said through Jeremiah that Egypt would return to its own land and that Babylon would come back.

For today: do not confuse a passing relief with the true solution. When a crisis passes, do not stop seeking God or obeying Him. He wants us to trust in Him, not only in human help.
exp.36:5:
God spoke to the prophet Jeremiah at a specific moment. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a direct message. The phrase is only an introduction: the important part comes in the verses that follow.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). When the army of Egypt arrived, the Chaldeans withdrew for a time, and the people and King Zedekiah were filled with false hope. The king sent to ask Jeremiah, and God answered that Egypt would return to its own land and that the Chaldeans would come back. Jeremiah speaks what God says, not what the people want to hear.

When circumstances seem to improve, that does not always mean the danger has passed. Let us seek the word of God sincerely, even when it is hard to hear, and not simply trust in what looks like momentary relief.
exp.36:6:
God commands Jeremiah to give an answer to the king of Judah, who had sent to ask him what was going to happen. The message is that the army of Pharaoh, which was coming to help Jerusalem, had already returned to Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (Babylonians), but when the Egyptian army came near, the Chaldeans withdrew for a time. King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah to pray and consult God, hoping for good news. God answers him that this help would not last and that the Chaldeans would return.

Today, we often place our hope in human help that seems secure, but it can fail. We can accept help with gratitude, but our firmest trust must be in God, and we should listen to his truth even when it is not what we hoped to hear.
exp.36:7:
It says that the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, will come back. They will attack Jerusalem, capture it, and burn it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to King Zedekiah. The Babylonians had stopped besieging the city because the Egyptian army was approaching. The people felt relieved and thought the danger had passed. But God warns them that this lull is temporary and that the announced judgment still stands.

A passing calm does not always mean the problem has been resolved. When God speaks to us through his Word, it is better to listen and correct our course than to trust human solutions or momentary relief. Today we might ask ourselves: is there something I need to acknowledge before God, instead of ignoring it?
exp.36:8:
God warns the people not to deceive themselves. Some were saying, "The Chaldeans have already left; we are safe." But God says it is not so: they will return. Here "deceive" means to fool your own selves, to mislead your own hearts. "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing King Zedekiah. Babylon had besieged Jerusalem, but it withdrew for a time when the army of Pharaoh came from Egypt. The people felt relief and believed the danger had passed. God tells them that Egypt will not save them and that the city will be taken.

For today: a temporary relief does not always mean the problem has been resolved. Before we put our trust in something, it is wise to listen honestly to God and to correct what He points out to us, rather than comfort ourselves with illusions.
exp.36:9:
What it says: God declares that the fall of Jerusalem is certain. Even if the people managed to defeat the whole army of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and only wounded men were left, those wounded men would rise up from their camp and burn the city.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to King Zedekiah. The Chaldeans had lifted the siege because the army of Pharaoh of Egypt was coming, and the people thought the danger had passed. God warns them not to deceive themselves: the Chaldeans would return, because the judgment had already been decided.

For today: It is easy to trust in temporary relief and to believe that everything is fine. God invites us to listen to his truth even when it is uncomfortable, and to turn back to him with honesty, instead of leaning on false hopes.
exp.36:11:
It says that Jeremiah went out of Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin. The final phrase is difficult: "to separate himself thence in the midst of the people" can be understood as wanting to separate himself from the people, or as going there to receive a portion of his inheritance. Scholars translate it in different ways, so there is no single certain reading.

Context: The Babylonian army (the Chaldeans) had stopped besieging Jerusalem because the army of Egypt was coming. Some thought the danger had passed. But God, through Jeremiah, warned that the Chaldeans would return and burn the city. When Jeremiah went out, a guard accused him of defecting to the enemy, and they arrested him unjustly.

For today: Even when you are honest, sometimes you will be misunderstood or accused without reason. Jeremiah answered with the truth and remained faithful to God. Do the same: speak the truth calmly and trust that God sees.
exp.36:12:
This verse tells that Jeremiah came to the gate of Benjamin, one of the gates of Jerusalem. There a captain of the guard, named Irijah, stopped him. He accused him of going over to the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians.

A narrator recounts the events. The Chaldeans had stopped besieging Jerusalem because the army of Pharaoh was coming. Jeremiah was going out toward the land of Benjamin, probably on some personal matter, and the captain thought he was a traitor. Jeremiah had announced that Babylon would win, and for that reason they suspected him. But he denied the accusation.

Today, we are sometimes judged unfairly or accused without reason. Jeremiah remained faithful to God even though others did not understand him. We can speak the truth, keep calm, and trust that God knows our heart.
exp.36:13:
Jeremiah tells Irijah that it is false, that he is not defecting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians, who had Jerusalem under siege). But Irijah, an officer in charge of the gate, does not believe him. He seizes Jeremiah and brings him before the princes, that is, the leaders of the government.

Jeremiah was a prophet of God, and he had warned that Jerusalem would fall. For that reason many regarded him as a traitor. He was heading toward the land of Benjamin, and the officer assumed the worst. The princes grew angry, beat him, and locked him in a makeshift prison. This shows that speaking God's truth is not always well received.

For today: sometimes we will be judged unfairly even when we are sincere. We can answer with truth and calm, and trust that God knows our hearts, even when others do not believe us.
exp.36:15:
This verse says that Jeremiah was put into the underground prison and into the cells, which were small rooms or narrow chambers. He stayed there for many days, that is, for quite a long time. The word for the prison means a dark, enclosed dungeon.

Jeremiah was a prophet of God in the final days of Judah, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. He was accused of wanting to defect to the Chaldeans, but he denied it. The princes grew angry, beat him, and imprisoned him. His punishment came because he spoke what God commanded him, even though no one wanted to hear it. Later, King Zedekiah secretly sent for him to ask whether there was any word from God.

For today: being faithful to God can cost us misunderstanding or rejection. If this happens to you, do not lose heart. Remain honest, and trust that God sustains you, even in long and difficult times.
exp.36:20:
This verse tells that King Zedekiah answered Jeremiah's plea. He had him taken out of the house of Jonathan and placed in the courtyard of the guard, a more open and less dangerous place. There they gave him a loaf of bread each day, taken from the bakers' street, until the city's bread ran out.

Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians. Jeremiah had announced that the city would fall, and for this reason he was accused and locked in a damp dungeon. He asked the king not to send him back there, for he feared he would die. Zedekiah, though weak and fearful, granted him some relief.

For today: God can care for us with simple provisions, even when the situation remains difficult. Jeremiah was not fully freed, but he received daily bread and protection. We can trust God day by day, and remain faithful to the truth even when it costs us.
exp.37:0:
This verse tells us that four men heard what Jeremiah was saying to all the people: Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashur. "Heard" here means they heard it with their own ears. What Jeremiah said appears in the next verse.

The prophet Jeremiah was speaking in Jerusalem while the city was surrounded by the army of Babylon. He was announcing God's message: whoever surrendered would live, and whoever stayed would face grave danger. These four were officials of the kingdom. According to the text that follows, they became upset with his message and asked that he be put to death. We see that later, not in this verse.

For today: hearing is not the same as obeying. We can listen to a hard truth and become angry, or we can let it correct us. Let us ask God for a humble heart to receive his word, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.37:2:
This verse says that God announces, through Jeremiah, that Jerusalem will certainly be handed over to the army of the king of Babylon, and that this army will capture it.

Jeremiah speaks to the people while Babylon has the city under siege. Some officials hear him and become angry, because they believe his words discourage the soldiers. Jeremiah does not speak for personal gain or out of disloyalty, but repeats what God has shown him, even though it costs him rejection and nearly his life.

For today: speaking the truth in love can be costly, but it is better than lulling others to sleep with pleasant words. It also invites us to listen with humility, even when the message is uncomfortable, because God corrects in order to give us the chance to change.
exp.37:5:
The verse says that they took Jeremiah and put him into the cistern-pit of Malchiah, son of Hammelech, which was in the court of the guard. They let Jeremiah down with ropes. There was no water in it, only mud, and Jeremiah sank into the mud.

The officials of the king were angry because Jeremiah was prophesying that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon. They said his words discouraged the soldiers and the people. King Zedekiah, weak and fearful, gave them permission to do with him as they wished. Jeremiah suffered for speaking what God had commanded him.

For today: speaking the truth with love can bring misunderstanding or rejection. Even so, God does not abandon those who are faithful to him; in the next verse he sends unexpected help through Ebed-melech. Today we can stand firm and trust God.
exp.37:8:
Ebed-melec tells King Zedekiah that the men who threw Jeremiah into the dungeon have acted wickedly. A dungeon is a dark prison, a pit or cistern under the ground. He warns that the prophet would die of hunger there, because there was no more bread left in the city.

Ebed-melec speaks as an Ethiopian who served in the palace. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians and there was a shortage of food. Some officials, angered by Jeremiah's messages, had put him into a cistern full of mud. Being a foreigner and of humble position, Ebed-melec dares to speak before the king, who was sitting at the Gate of Benjamin.

Today we can learn that speaking up for someone who suffers injustice is an act of faith. We may have no power or influence, but God can use our voice and courage. Ask yourself: whom can I defend this week?
exp.37:9:
This verse tells that King Zedekiah gives an order to Ebed-melech, a man from Ethiopia who worked in the palace. He orders him to take thirty men and bring the prophet Jeremiah up out of the dungeon, which was a cistern or deep pit, before he dies.

King Zedekiah is speaking in the middle of the siege of Jerusalem. Jeremiah had been thrown into the pit by his enemies for announcing messages from God that they did not like. Ebed-melech dared to speak up for him before the king. There is debate about why the king changed his mind so quickly; the text only shows that he gave in.

For today: when you see an injustice, do not stay silent. Ebed-melech, with no power or fame, spoke with courage and helped. Ask God whom you can defend or help this week.
exp.37:10:
What it says: Ebed-melech gathered the men the king had given him and went to the palace, to a room under the treasury. There he took old, worn-out clothes and torn rags. Then he lowered them with ropes to Jeremiah, who was in the dungeon, a deep cistern full of mud.

Context: The narrator tells how Ebed-melech, a foreign official in the court, rescues Jeremiah. The leaders had thrown him there for announcing God's message, and the prophet could have died of hunger. Ebed-melech spoke with the king, obtained permission, and acted quickly.

For today: Ebed-melech did not only speak, he also did something concrete and careful. The rags were there so the ropes would not hurt Jeremiah. We can help others with simple actions, thinking of their pain and without waiting for someone else to go first.
exp.37:11:
Here Ebed-melech, a man from Ethiopia who served in the king's house, gives Jeremiah an instruction. He asks him to put the old, torn rags under his armpits, and under the ropes. This way the cords would not hurt his skin as he was pulled up. Jeremiah obeys.

It is Ebed-melech who speaks, the one who intervened to save the prophet, who was in a cistern or pit full of mud and close to dying. The king had given him permission to bring Jeremiah out. The text does not say why he was the only one who acted, but his courage and compassion are evident.

Today we can learn that love is also shown in small details. Ebed-melech not only rescued Jeremiah, but also took care that he would not suffer further harm. Ask yourself who you can help, and how to do it with tenderness and attention.
exp.37:12:
This verse tells how Jeremiah was pulled alive out of the cistern. The men drew him up with ropes from the dungeon, which was a deep, dark cistern used as a prison. Afterward, Jeremiah remained imprisoned, but now in the court of the prison, a more open place and far less deadly.

The narrator recounts what happened. The leaders of Judah had thrown Jeremiah into the muddy cistern for predicting the fall of Jerusalem. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian who served in the palace, spoke on the prophet's behalf before the king and rescued him. He put old rags under Jeremiah's arms so the ropes would not hurt him.

For today: God can use unexpected people and simple gestures to care for his own. Ask yourself whom you can help today with a practical act of compassion, even if no one notices.
exp.37:13:
This verse tells how King Zedekiah secretly had the prophet Jeremiah brought to a certain entrance of the temple, a place we cannot identify with certainty. He said to him, "I will ask you a thing; hide nothing from me."

Jeremiah had just been rescued from a muddy cistern by Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian official. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. Zedekiah was afraid and wanted a word from God, but he was a weak king, pressured by his leaders. Jeremiah distrusts him and reminds him that he had not listened to him before.

For today: we often want to hear from God, but only if the answer suits us. Let us ask God not only for counsel, but also for a heart willing to obey him, even when it costs us.
exp.37:16:
Here Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah, on God's behalf, that there is a way out: if he surrenders and goes out to the princes of the king of Babylon, his life will be spared, Jerusalem will not be burned, and his family will also live.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet at a very hard moment: Babylon had surrounded Jerusalem. The king, out of fear, consults him in secret. Jeremiah asks for assurance because he had already been punished for saying uncomfortable things. Even so, God's message offers mercy. Later on, Zedekiah does not obey, out of fear of the people.

For today: when God shows us a path of humility and obedience, even when it costs our pride, it is better to follow it than to let fear of what others will say make the decision for us.
exp.37:18:
King Zedekiah of Judah confesses to Jeremiah that he is afraid. He fears that the Jews who had gone over to the side of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) will hand him over to them, and that they will mock him and mistreat him.

Jeremiah had just passed on a message from God: if the king surrendered to the leaders of Babylon, he himself would live, his family would be spared, and the city would not be burned. The king wanted to obey, but he was held back by fear of the people and of what they would say or do. Jeremiah answers him at once that they will not hand him over.

Today too we can know what God wants and still hesitate out of fear of mockery, rejection, or the consequences. This story invites us not to let human fear make our decisions for us, but to trust the word of God and take the step of obedience, even when it costs us.
exp.37:19:
Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah that the Jews who had defected to the Babylonians will not hand him over to them. He asks the king to listen to the voice of the Lord, that is, to obey what God says through the prophet. If he obeys, things will go well for him and his life will be spared. The phrase about his life surviving means that he will keep his life.

Jeremiah speaks during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. The king is afraid of his own countrymen and does not dare to surrender. Jeremiah urges him to give himself up to the Babylonian officials, just as God had indicated, so that he and the city might be saved. Interpreters see here a genuine offer from God, which the king had to decide whether to accept.

For today: sometimes fear of what people will say weighs more heavily than the voice of God. Before deciding, stop, listen to what God says in his Word, and obey with confidence, even when the path is frightening.
exp.37:20:
It says that if King Zedekiah refuses to surrender and go out to the officers of Babylon, God has shown Jeremiah what will happen. It is a serious warning: there is one good choice and another that brings suffering.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks with the king during the siege of Jerusalem. Zedekiah was afraid of his own people and of the mockery of the Chaldeans. Jeremiah offers him a way out: obey God and save his life, his family, and the city. Then he describes, as a vision, the consequences of resisting.

For today: sometimes we know what God asks of us, but fear of what others will say holds us back. Obeying may seem humiliating, but it is safer than giving in to fear. Ask God for the courage to obey him today, even when it costs.
exp.37:25:
King Zedekiah tells Jeremiah what he should answer if the officials ask him what they discussed in private. He should say that he begged the king not to send him back to Jonathan's house, so that he would not die there. The word "return" is used here for going back to a place.

The king speaks with Jeremiah in private. Zedekiah is afraid of the officials, who already wanted to kill the prophet. Jeremiah had been held prisoner in Jonathan's house, a place in poor condition. The answer the king suggests is partly true, since Jeremiah had indeed asked for this before, but it does not tell the whole conversation. Some scholars see here discretion in the face of a real danger; others notice the king's weakness.

For today: one can keep discretion without lying, and under pressure it is wise to act with prudence, yet with honesty and courage, trusting that God cares for those who are faithful to him.
exp.37:26:
The verse tells how the princes came to Jeremiah and asked him what he had said with the king. Jeremiah answered them just as the king had instructed him. Then they left him alone, for the matter was not perceived, meaning that no one else knew what had really been discussed.

This passage is told by the narrator of the book. King Zedekiah had called Jeremiah in secret, and he feared the princes, who wanted to kill the prophet. Jeremiah had asked not to be sent back to the house of Jonathan, where he had nearly died. His answer was true, though he did not tell them everything. Some scholars see prudence in this; others debate whether it was the best course.

Today we can learn to be prudent and honest at the same time. We do not always have to tell everything, but we should take care that what we say is true. Let us ask God for wisdom to speak with sincerity and to protect what ought to be kept.
exp.38:2:
The princes of the king of Babylon came into Jerusalem and took their seats in the middle gate. Several officials are named there. The word "sat" here means that they sat down, which is to say, they took control. Some of the names might be official positions, such as Rabsaris and Rabmag, and it is not certain what they mean. The name Nergal-sharezer appears twice, and it is not clear whether these are two people or a repetition.

The account tells of the fall of Jerusalem, which Jeremiah had announced for years. The Babylonians laid siege for a long time and then broke through the wall. That gate was probably a place of authority, and from there the invaders began to rule.

For today: God always fulfills what He says. If His Word warns us of something, it is wise to listen in time and correct our course with humility, before the consequences arrive.
exp.38:3:
What it says: When Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his soldiers saw that the Babylonians had already entered Jerusalem, they fled by night. They went out through a gate between two walls, near the king's garden, and the king took the road toward the wilderness, that is, toward the valley of the Jordan.

Context: The passage comes from the book of Jeremiah, describing the fall of Jerusalem after a long siege. Jeremiah had warned for years that God would allow this defeat and that surrendering was the best way out, but the king would not listen. Afterward, the Chaldeans caught up with him near Jericho.

For today: Running away from the consequences does no good when we would not listen to God's voice before. Today we can obey in time, acknowledge our mistakes, and return to Him in humility, because His word guides us better than our fear does.
exp.38:4:
The army of Babylon pursued King Zedekiah, who had fled from Jerusalem, and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho. They captured him and brought him before Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah in the land of Hamath. There Nebuchadnezzar passed judgment on him and pronounced his punishment.

The text is narrative; God does not speak directly here. After a long siege, Jerusalem fell. Zedekiah tried to escape at night, but he was caught. Jeremiah had warned many times that surrendering to Babylon was the way to save lives, and the king would not listen. Here what had been announced comes to pass.

For today: when God warns us through his Word, it is wiser to obey in time than to try to escape the consequences. Ignoring his voice out of fear or stubbornness only makes the fall more painful.
exp.38:5:
This verse says that the king of Babylon had the sons of King Zedekiah killed in front of their father, in a place called Riblah. He also ordered the death of all the nobles of Judah.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks, recounting the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Zedekiah had tried to escape at night, but he was caught near Jericho. Jeremiah had spent years warning that surrendering to Babylon would save lives, but the king refused to listen. This scene is the sad fulfillment of those warnings.

For today: ignoring the truth out of fear or stubbornness often costs far more than we imagine. We can ask God for a humble heart that listens in time, even when the advice is hard.
exp.38:6:
This verse tells of the sad end of King Zedekiah. The Babylonians put out his eyes and bound him with fetters, which were metal chains for the feet, to take him away as a prisoner to Babylon. The last thing he saw before he was blinded was the death of his sons.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks, recounting the fall of Jerusalem. God had warned through Jeremiah that the city would fall if the king did not surrender to Babylon. Zedekiah would not listen and fled, but the Chaldeans caught up with him near Jericho. In this way what the prophet had said came to pass.

For today: ignoring the voice of God out of fear or stubbornness brings painful consequences. Today we can listen to his Word with humility and obey it in time, trusting that his guidance seeks our good.
exp.38:12:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, sent for other important officers: Nebushasban, Nergal-sharezer, Rabsaris, Rabmag, and the rest of the king's princes. "Captain of the guard" was a high-ranking military leader. The names Rabsaris and Rabmag seem to be official titles, though it is not known with certainty what exact functions they held.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book, who recounts what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar had given a special order: to take care of Jeremiah and not harm him. These officers gather to carry it out, and they bring the prophet out of the courtyard of the prison to hand him over to Gedaliah.

For today: God can care for His own even in the midst of chaos and by using unexpected people. If you are going through a hard situation today, trust that God is still at work, even when you cannot see how.
exp.38:13:
The verse says that the Babylonian officers had Jeremiah brought out of the court of the prison. They handed him over to Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, so that he would take him home. There Jeremiah lived among the people, now free from the prison.

The narrator tells what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar had ordered that Jeremiah be cared for, and his officers carried out the order. Jeremiah had announced this judgment for years and had been mistreated because of it. Gedaliah came from a family that had earlier protected the prophet (Jeremiah 26:24). The Bible does not explain all of Babylon's reasons, but the text shows that God looked after his servant.

God can care for those who are faithful to him even in very difficult times and through unexpected means. Today we too can keep obeying with integrity, trusting that God knows how and when to bring us relief.
exp.38:14:
This verse says that God had already given Jeremiah a message while he was still held in the court of the prison. The phrase "the word of the Lord had come" means that God had spoken to him before the Babylonians brought him out.

The author presents this detail as a step back in time. Jerusalem had already fallen, but the text recalls a promise made earlier to Ebed-melech, the Ethiopian who had defended Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38). The Lord is the one speaking, and he wants to show that he keeps his word to someone who acted with courage.

For today: God sees the acts of kindness we do, even when no one else notices them or when the things around us are falling apart. We can do what is right and trust that he will care for us in his own way and in his own time.
exp.38:16:
This verse is a promise from God to a particular person. It says that, on the day Jerusalem falls, God will rescue him and will not leave him in the hands of those he fears.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who was being held in the courtyard of the prison. The message is for Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian who served in the king's court. According to Jeremiah 38, he intervened to bring Jeremiah up out of a cistern. While God announces disaster on the city, he promises to look after this man. The following verse explains the reason: he trusted in God.

For today: when fear surrounds you, remember that God sees those who act with courage and trust in him. Do what is right today, even when it costs you, and leave the outcome in his hands, knowing that he cares for you.
exp.38:17:
God promises Ebed-melech that he will rescue him. He will not die by the sword; instead he will keep his life as a prize, that is, as the spoil of war: the only thing a person takes with them when they come out alive from a disaster. God gives him this reason: because he trusted in Him.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian who served in the palace, had defended the prophet when he was thrown into a cistern (chapter 38). Now Jerusalem is about to fall to Babylon, and God promises to care for him in the midst of that judgment. This is not stated in the text, but it is fulfilled within that same account.

For today: God sees acts of courage and trust, even when no one else notices them. If you do what is right and it costs you, rest in the knowledge that He cares for you. His care may not spare you every difficulty, but it will not abandon you.
exp.39:0:
This verse says that God gave a message to Jeremiah after Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, released him at Ramah. Jeremiah had been brought there in chains, bound in irons among all the prisoners from Jerusalem and Judah. The bound prisoners are the captives taken away from their land to another country.

The one speaking here is the narrator, who presents God's word to Jeremiah. Jerusalem had already fallen to Babylon, and the people were going into exile. Jeremiah had spent years warning that this would happen, and almost no one had believed him. The details of how he ended up at Ramah are told somewhat differently in the nearby accounts, so it is worth reading them carefully.

For today: God does not abandon those who are faithful to Him, even in times of grief. You can keep trusting Him and obeying His word, even when everything around you seems to be falling apart.
exp.39:6:
This verse tells that the military commanders who had been scattered across the countryside, along with their men, heard something important: the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor of the land. Furthermore, he had entrusted to him, that is, placed in his care, the men, the women, the children, and the poorest of the land, those who had not been carried away captive to Babylon.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jerusalem had already fallen, and the Babylonians left in Judah the most humble people to work the land. Gedaliah, from a respected family, stayed in Mizpah to lead them. The officers who had fled now approach to see what they will do.

For today: God cares for the most vulnerable, and those who lead should protect the weak, not take advantage of them.
exp.39:7:
This verse says that several leaders of the Jewish army came to Mizpah to meet Gedaliah, the governor. Their names are Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai, and Jezaniah son of the Maacathite, together with their men.

After the fall of Jerusalem, Babylon left Gedaliah in charge of the poor who remained in the land. These leaders had been scattered across the countryside and now came to him. The narrator only introduces them; in the next verse Gedaliah speaks and proposes that they live peacefully under Babylon.

For today: when times of crisis come, it is wise to seek the counsel of someone who leads with calm and not to act out of fear alone. But it is also good to listen carefully, because among those who come there may be both good and bad intentions, and we need to ask God for discernment.
exp.39:9:
He says that Gedaliah will stay in Mizpah to represent the people before the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) when they arrive. In the meantime, he encourages the Jews to gather wine, bread and oil, which are the fruits of the harvest, to store them in their storehouses, and to stay in the cities they had already taken.

Gedaliah is speaking, the man whom the king of Babylon appointed as governor over the few who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. The army leaders were uncertain and afraid, so he promises them that, if they submit to Babylon, they can live in peace and work the land.

For today: in uncertain times, God invites us to keep going with what is within our reach, to work with calm and to take care of what we have, instead of letting fear paralyze us. Doing well the tasks of each day is also a way of trusting.
exp.39:10:
This verse tells that the Jews who had fled to Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands heard something: the king of Babylon had left a group of people in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, as governor.

Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon. The one telling the story is the author of the book, who continues the account after the destruction. Gedaliah, from a respected family, had encouraged the people to stay, to serve Babylon, and to gather the harvest. That news reached the scattered people and gave them hope of returning.

Today, the news that there is a place to start over can encourage someone who feels far away and scattered. If you are in a season of loss, do not close the door on an opportunity to rebuild. Ask God for wisdom to take the first step with humility.
exp.39:12:
This verse tells that Johanan, son of Kareah, came with all the captains of the troops who were out in the countryside. They went to see Gedaliah at Mizpah. The fighting men are the armed men, and the word for captains here means leaders or commanders.

Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon, and the Babylonian king appointed Gedaliah as governor over the Jews who remained in the land. Here the narrator speaks, introducing Johanan, who comes to warn Gedaliah of a plot to kill him. Gedaliah did not believe them, and that had very painful consequences.

For today: when someone brings us a serious warning, it is wise to listen with humility and check it carefully. Ignoring an alert out of excessive confidence can cost dearly.
exp.40:0:
This verse tells how, in the seventh month, Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, came to Mizpah to visit Gedaliah. Ishmael was of royal descent, that is, of the king's family, and he came with ten men. There they ate bread together, which was a sign of friendship and hospitality.

The writer of the book then tells what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonians had appointed Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Ishmael visited him, but, as the account goes on, his intention was to kill him. Scholars do not know his motives for certain; some think he wanted power, or that he acted out of jealousy.

Today the passage invites us to be wise. Being kind and trusting is good, but we should ask God for wisdom to discern people's intentions, without falling into constant suspicion.
exp.40:1:
It says that Ishmael, together with ten men, rose up and struck down Gedaliah with the sword, the man the king of Babylon had set over the land as governor. The phrase about striking him with the sword means they attacked him with a sword. They did this after they had eaten with him.

It is part of Jeremiah's historical account. Jerusalem had fallen, and Babylon left Gedaliah in charge of those who remained in Judah. Ishmael was of the royal family, and the Bible does not state his motives clearly. Some think he wanted power or rejected the man who served Babylon, but the text here does not say so. Even so, the act was a cruel betrayal.

For today: trust is valuable, but we need wisdom. And when we feel jealousy, resentment, or pride, we should master it in time, before it leads us to harm others.
exp.40:3:
This verse tells us that a day had passed since the murder of Gedaliah, and that still no one had found out. In other words, Ishmael's crime was still hidden. The verse itself simply says that on the second day after the killing, no one yet knew about it.

The book of Jeremiah recounts here what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Ishmael, who was of royal family, betrayed him and killed him in Mizpah. The narrator, who describes these events, shows us how deceit and violence could stay concealed for a time. Soon eighty pilgrims arrive in mourning, and Ishmael deceives them with false tears.

For today: what is hidden does not stay hidden forever, nor does it escape God. If we are tempted to conceal something wrong, it is better to confess it and act in truth, because God sees everything and forgives the one who repents.
exp.40:4:
They said that eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria. They came with their beards shaved, their clothes torn, and cuts on their bodies, signs of mourning and grief. They brought an offering and incense to take to the temple of the Lord, which lay in ruins.

The narrator tells what happened days after the murder of Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon. No one yet knew of the crime. These men were in mourning, probably because of the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, and they were going to worship God. Ishmael deceived them and killed them. The text does not fully explain his motives.

For today: even in the midst of grief, these men wanted to draw near to God. Let us bring our pain to Him honestly, but let us be prudent and not trust blindly someone who has not shown himself worthy of trust.
exp.40:6:
It says that Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, killed the men who came to the city. He cut their throats, that is, he slew them, and threw their bodies into a cistern, which was a pit for storing water. He did this with the help of the men who were with him.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. Gedaliah had been appointed governor after the fall of Jerusalem, and Ishmael had murdered him. Those eighty men were coming in mourning, with offerings for the temple, and Ishmael deceived them with false tears to bring them into the city. The text does not explain his exact motive, and scholars only suppose it.

For today: deception can come with a friendly appearance and even with tears. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern, and never use false kindness to harm others.
exp.40:8:
