It says that Ishmael threw the bodies of the men he had killed into a cistern, that is, a large well for storing water. That cistern was the same one King Asa had made long before, when he was preparing against Baasha, king of Israel. Ishmael filled it with the dead.

The writer tells what happened after Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon. Ishmael kept killing people in Mizpah. The detail of the cistern shows that something made to protect and to give life ended up becoming a grave. The Bible does not explain here, with certainty, what Ishmael's motives were.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what God has given us for good, such as talents, influence or resources, we are using to serve or to harm. May our decisions never be born of envy or of violence.
exp.40:9:
It says that Ishmael, after killing many, took captive all who had been left in Mizpah, including the king's daughters. These were people whom Nebuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, had entrusted to Gedaliah. Ismael led them away with the intention of crossing over to the territory of the Ammonites, a neighboring people.

Context: the speaker is the narrator of the book of Jeremiah. Babylon had already destroyed Jerusalem, and Gedaliah had been appointed governor of those who remained. Ishmael murdered him through treachery. The Bible does not explain all his motives here; the text suggests he had ties to the Ammonite king, but does not detail it.

For today: violence and betrayal only bring more suffering to innocent people. When we face difficult times, let us seek God's will with humility and trust in Him, rather than settling things with resentment or ambition.
exp.40:11:
This verse tells how Johanan and all the men who were with him set out to fight Ishmael, son of Nethaniah. They found him near the great pool in Gibeon.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and was carrying off the people of Mizpah as captives toward Ammon. When Johanan heard of this wickedness, he gathered the military leaders to rescue the people. According to the account, the captive people rejoiced and turned back to Johanan.

For today: when we see injustice against people who cannot defend themselves, God calls us not to stay silent or still. We can act with courage and wisdom, defending and helping those who suffer.
exp.40:14:
This verse tells how Ishmael, the man who had murdered Gedaliah and led many captives away from Mizpah, managed to escape from Johanan. He got away with only eight men (according to the account, he had first come with ten, and two had died), and he took refuge with the Ammonites, a neighboring people.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. After the murder of Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, the people were left in great fear. Johanan rescued the captives, but Ishmael escaped without paying for his crime. This left the people frightened and close to fleeing to Egypt.

For today: injustice sometimes seems to go unanswered, and that frightens us. Even so, fear should not lead us to decide on our own. Before acting, it is wise to stop and seek God's guidance.
exp.40:15:
This verse tells how Johanan and the army officers with him gathered all the survivors they had rescued from Ishmael: soldiers, women, children, and court officials (men who served in the royal household). Ishmael had killed Gedaliah, the governor, and had carried the people of Mizpah away as captives.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. Gedaliah had been placed by the king of Babylon over the people who remained in Judah. After his murder, the people were afraid that the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) would take revenge. For this reason Johanan began to consider fleeing to Egypt, as the next verse shows.

For today: rescuing and caring for those who are in danger is good, but fear should not make our decisions for us. Before taking a major step, it is wise to pause and seek God's direction, and not simply run from what we are afraid of.
exp.42:2:
Here the men say that Baruch, Jeremiah's assistant, is turning him against them. They accuse him of wanting to hand them over to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) so that they would be killed or taken away as prisoners to Babylon.

Azariah and Johanan speak, along with other proud men. After the fall of Jerusalem, they wanted to flee to Egypt because they were afraid of Babylon. Jeremiah had told them, on God's behalf, to stay in Judah. Instead of accepting the message, they called him a liar and blamed Baruch. The Bible does not say that Baruch did anything like this; it is their accusation.

When we do not want to hear an uncomfortable truth, it is easy to blame the messenger. Today we can ask God for humility to examine his Word with sincerity, even when it contradicts what we have already decided.
exp.42:3:
This verse says that Johanan, the army commanders, and all the people did not listen to the voice of the Lord. God had told them to stay in Judah, but they did not obey.

After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and killed Gedaliah, the governor, the people were afraid of the Chaldeans. They asked Jeremiah to pray for them and promised to obey God. When God answered that they should stay in the land, the leaders said that Jeremiah was lying. Even so, they went to Egypt and took Jeremiah and Baruch with them.

Obeying God only when his answer pleases us is not true obedience. Before we ask him for direction, let us ask ourselves whether we are really willing to follow it, even when it frightens us.
exp.42:10:
God says that Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike the land of Egypt. He speaks of three fates: some for death (plague or death in general), others for captivity (being taken away as prisoners), and others for the sword. The word "sword" here means war. The repeated phrase shows that none of this can be avoided.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews had fled to Egypt, thinking they would be safe there from Babylon, even though God had told them not to go. Jeremiah performs a symbolic act with stones hidden in Tahpanhes to show that Babylon would reach even there. God calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant because He uses him as an instrument, not because Nebuchadnezzar knows Him.

For today: there is no safe refuge far from the will of God. When we seek protection in human places or powers, instead of obeying Him, we deceive ourselves. Trusting God and following His guidance is true security.
exp.43:1:
God speaks to the Jews who live in Egypt and reminds them of what they themselves saw: the destruction of Jerusalem and of the cities of Judah. Today those cities are a ruin, with no one living in them.

It is the Lord who speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah. This group of Jews had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Places such as Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros were locations in Egypt. God reminds them of the past so that they do not repeat the same mistake: worshiping other gods. The verses that follow explain that this was the reason for the punishment.

For today: learn from past experiences, our own and those of others. If God has already shown us the consequences of turning away from him, it is wise not to go back to the same path. It is better to listen to his voice and return to him in humility.
exp.43:2:
God explains why Jerusalem and the towns of Judah were left in ruins. The cause was the people's wickedness: they provoked him to anger by burning incense and by worshiping other gods that neither they nor their ancestors had known. "Other gods" means the gods of other peoples.

God speaks through Jeremiah to the Jews who were living in Egypt, in places such as Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros. They had seen the destruction of Judah, yet they continued in the same idolatry. God reminds them of the past so that they may learn and turn back to him.

For today: let us not wait to suffer the consequences before we correct our course. If anything occupies in our heart the place that belongs to God, we can recognize it today and return to him with humility.
exp.43:4:
This verse says that the people did not pay attention to God's warnings. They did not listen or take heed so as to turn away from their wickedness. They kept burning incense to other gods.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews who were living in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. He reminds them that from earlier times He sent prophets again and again, rising early and sending them with urgency. Even so, the people continued in idolatry, and that brought the destruction of their cities.

For today: God speaks to us with patience, and ignoring His voice hardens the heart. When something in your life competes with God or pulls you away from Him, do not put it off: listen, recognize it, and change course today.
exp.43:5:
It says that God poured out his anger with force on the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. Because of this they lay in ruins and empty, and they stayed that way until now.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews who had gone to live in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. He reminds them that he sent prophets again and again, but they would not stop burning incense to false gods. He tells them what happened so that they do not repeat the same mistake, and so that they see his warnings were serious.

For today: when God corrects us, it is because he loves us and wants to protect us. Let us listen to his voice in time, before the harm grows, and return to him with humility.
exp.43:6:
God asks with grief: "Why do you do such great harm to yourselves?" He warns that if they keep on this way, they will be cut down like a tree, men and women, children and infants. Nothing would be left, not a single survivor. The incense burned in worship was the offering the people made.

Jeremiah speaks for God to the Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. There they were still burning incense to false gods. God reminds them that they already saw Judah destroyed because of that same idolatry, and he does not want them to repeat it.

Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking the place of God in our hearts. Learning from past mistakes, with humility, spares us much pain. God corrects because he desires our good.
exp.43:7:
This verse is part of a question God asks the Jews who had gone to Egypt. He charges that they provoke him with the works of their hands, meaning idols made by their own hands. Burning incense is offered in worship. Shame means public disgrace, and being cut off means they would be destroyed.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group fled to Egypt and continued to worship other gods. God reminds them that this same idolatry had already brought destruction upon Judah. He warns them so that they will not repeat the mistake.

For today: we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts. Learning from past mistakes, and returning to God with humility, spares us from repeating the pain.
exp.43:9:
It says that the people of Judah, up to that day, had not humbled themselves or shown reverence for God. They also had not walked in God's law, which he had given to them and to their ancestors.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and there they were burning incense to other gods. God reminds them that the destruction of Jerusalem came because of that same idolatry, and that even so they had not learned the lesson.

For today: it is not enough to suffer the consequences of our mistakes; God invites us to acknowledge them with humility and return to him. Today you can ask him to show you something in which you have resisted changing.
exp.43:11:
God says he will take the group of Jews who decided to go to Egypt to live there, and that they will die right there, by war or by hunger, from the lowest to the highest. "Sword" means war. "They will become an oath, a horror, a curse and a disgrace" means that their fate will stand as an example of punishment and shame, something people will mention with dread.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group fled to Egypt, even though God had asked them to stay in Judah. In Egypt they continued to worship other gods. God reminds them that they did not change or obey, and for that reason he warns them of the consequences.

For today: it is not enough to look for safety far from God. If we already know what he asks of us, it is wise to obey him promptly and humbly, and not to trust in our own plans.
exp.43:14:
This verse introduces a large group that comes together to answer Jeremiah. They were the men who knew that their wives were burning incense to other gods, the women who were standing there, and all the Jewish people living in Egypt, in the region of Pathros (southern Egypt). Burning incense means giving off fragrant smoke as an offering, and "other gods" means false gods.

Jeremiah had just warned them that God would punish them in the same way as Jerusalem. They had fled to Egypt, and yet they were still worshiping idols. Now they all respond together, and what they say next is an open rejection of God's word.

For today: it is easy to close our ears when the truth challenges our habits. Let us ask God for a humble heart that listens, even when his word asks us to change.
exp.43:16:
They say the people refuse to obey Jeremiah. They insist on doing everything they promised: burning incense to the "queen of heaven" and pouring out drink offerings to her. They claim that they did this, and their ancestors, their kings, and their leaders did it too. According to them, back then they had plenty of food, were well, and saw no evil.

They are Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Jeremiah warned them in God's name to abandon idolatry. They answer with rebellion. The exact identity of the "queen of heaven" is debated; many think she was a goddess of the ancient Near East, such as Ishtar or Astarte.

Today we can learn not to measure what is true by what went well for us before. A comfortable memory can deceive us. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his Word, even when it confronts us.
exp.43:18:
What it says: The women of Judah explain that when they burned incense to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, their husbands knew about it and approved. Incense is the smoke of offerings burned on the altar; cakes are bread or pastry offered in worship; to worship her means to give her reverence.

Context: The speakers are Jews who took refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Jeremiah had called them to abandon idolatry, but they reject his message and blame their troubles on giving up this practice. The exact identity of the "queen of heaven" is debated; many connect her with a goddess of the ancient Near East, such as Ishtar or Astarte.

For today: It is easy to justify what we do by saying that everyone does it or that it has always been so. Let us ask God to show us the truth and obey him, even when custom says otherwise.
exp.43:19:
This verse is an introduction. It says that Jeremiah addressed the whole people: men, women, and all the people in general. The common people were the ordinary folk, the people as a whole. They had just answered him defiantly, and now the prophet is about to respond to them.

The Jews who fled to Egypt argued that worshiping the queen of heaven (probably a pagan goddess, though her exact identity is debated) brought them well-being. They said their troubles began when they stopped practicing that worship. Jeremiah, speaking on God's behalf, answers that the ruin came because of their idolatry and wickedness, not because they had abandoned it.

Today it is easy to blame the wrong thing when things go badly. It is worth pausing, listening humbly to God's correction, and returning to Him, rather than justifying our mistakes.
exp.43:21:
This verse says that God could no longer put up with the people's wickedness and their detestable practices. That is why the land of Judah was left in ruins, turned into a horror and an example of a curse, and without inhabitants, just as it stood at this day.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who had gone down to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. They said they were better off when they burned incense to the queen of heaven. Jeremiah answers them that the ruin of their land was no accident, but the result of their idolatry and of not obeying God.

For today: God's patience is real, but we must not mistake it for indifference. If God shows us something we need to leave behind, it is wise to repent today and return to Him with humility.
exp.43:24:
God speaks with a tone of rebuke, almost ironic. He tells them that they and their wives made promises with their mouths and carried them out with their hands: burning incense to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her. Then he tells them: "Go ahead, keep your vows and fulfill them."

Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. They insisted on continuing to worship the queen of heaven, a goddess that many scholars connect with Ishtar or Astarte, though this is debated. They believed that this worship had brought them prosperity. God warns them that their idolatry was the cause of their misfortune.

Today: a promise made to something mistaken does not oblige us to keep the error. Let us examine what we have pledged our loyalty to, and if it is not from God, let us have the humility to make it right.
exp.43:29:
God says that he will hand Pharaoh Hophra, king of Egypt, over to his enemies, to those who seek to take his life. He compares this with what happened to Zedekiah, king of Judah, whom God handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Seeking his life means trying to take his life, wanting to kill him. To hand over means that God allows him to fall into their power.

Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who fled to Egypt, disobeying God, thinking they would be safe there. God gives them a sign: if Egypt falls, they will know that his word is fulfilled and that they should not have trusted in that country. The history records that Hophra (Apries) lost his power in Egypt, though the details of his fall are told in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we trust as a refuge. Human powers change and fall, but the word of God endures. Let us seek his guidance before seeking security elsewhere.
exp.44:3:
God commands Jeremiah to tell Baruc a clear message: the Lord is going to tear down what he himself built and uproot what he himself planted, and this reaches the whole land. Uprooting means pulling something out by its roots, and the land means the whole country of Judah.

The Lord speaks, through Jeremiah, to Baruc, the prophet's scribe. Baruc was worn out and discouraged by so much suffering. God reminds him that the judgment on Judah is very great, and so he should not expect an easy life or seek personal greatness.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, we can remember that God still is the one who governs. Instead of striving for status or comfort, we can trust that He cares for our lives, as He promised Baruc.
exp.45:1:
This verse opens a prophecy addressed to Egypt. It speaks of the army of Pharaoh Necho, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish. There Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, defeated it in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is part of the oracles against the nations, that is, against the neighboring nations of Judah. Egypt was a very proud power, and its defeat at Carchemish (around 605 BC) changed the balance of power in the region. The verses that follow describe the soldiers preparing for war.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, is above God. We can trust that He governs history, and so we do not need to place our security in money, fame, or power.
exp.45:5:
It says that no one will be able to escape defeat: neither the swift nor the mighty. The swift man is the one who runs fast, and the north is the direction in the verse. Beside the river Euphrates, to the north, the Egyptian soldiers stumbled and fell.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah about Egypt. The text connects it with the battle of Carchemish, beside the Euphrates, where Babylon defeated the Egyptian army (around 605 B.C.). Earlier it mocks the great military gathering: they prepared well, but they ended up fleeing in fear. God shows that He governs over the powers of the nations, even when they seem invincible.

For today: do not place your final security in your strength, your preparation, or your resources. Do your part well, but trust in God, because He sustains what no human power can guarantee.
exp.45:8:
This verse describes the army of Egypt getting ready for war. The horses and chariots are called to advance with force, and the brave soldiers are called to come out. Cush is the region south of Egypt (often linked with Ethiopia), and Put and Lud are allied peoples who supplied soldiers. The phrase about those who handle the shield means they take up their shields, and the phrase about those who handle and bend the bow means they string their bows.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, passing on a message from God about Egypt. It refers to the battle of Carchemish, beside the river Euphrates, where Egypt faced Babylon. Egypt advances with pride, swelling like a flooding river, but the text that follows says that day belongs to the Lord, and that Egypt will be defeated. Some scholars debate details about the location of Lud.

For today: human strength, however great it may seem, does not decide the final outcome. Before you trust in your resources, plans, or strength, surrender them to God with humility and ask Him for wisdom.
exp.45:9:
This verse says that day belongs to the Lord God of hosts, and that it will be a day of judgment against his enemies. It uses a strong image: the sword devours, is filled, and is made drunk with blood, that is, there will be a great slaughter. The place is the north, beside the Euphrates River.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks of the defeat of the Egyptian army, which was thought to be unstoppable, like a river that keeps rising. Historians often connect this with the battle of Carchemish, near the Euphrates, against Babylon. The text presents God as the one who rules over the nations, even though a human army is the instrument used.

For today: no human power is above God. If something seems enormous or unjust, trust that God sees everything and has the final word. Leave vengeance in his hands and seek peace.
exp.45:17:
This verse says that God himself, the true King, swears by his own life that someone will come against Egypt. He compares this to Mount Tabor, which rises above the other mountains, and to Carmel, which stands up beside the sea. That is, the one who comes will be an overwhelming presence, impossible to ignore. "As I live" is a way of swearing an oath. "The Lord of hosts" means the Lord of all powers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Egypt had been defeated, and its soldiers were fleeing, trusting in a pharaoh who let the appointed time pass by. Many understand that the one who comes is Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, used by God as an instrument of judgment. The text gives no further details.

For today: no human power, however great, stands above God. We can rest in the knowledge that he governs history, and trust in him more than in the leaders or security of this world.
exp.45:19:
This verse says that Egypt is like a very beautiful young cow, meaning a young, strong, and well-cared-for heifer. But destruction is approaching.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on the message of the LORD. Egypt felt secure because of its wealth and power. Many understand that the enemy from the north was Babylon, which under Nebuchadnezzar advanced against Egypt. God shows that no nation is as strong as it believes itself to be.

For today: let us not put our security in what looks good, such as money, success, or fame. All of that can fall suddenly. Let us trust in God, who sustains what truly endures.
exp.45:21:
This verse says that Egypt, which was once thought to be strong, will now sound weak and frightened, like a snake that writhes and hisses while being attacked. An enemy army comes with axes, like woodcutters coming to clear a forest.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon, coming from the north, will defeat Egypt. Many understand this to refer to Egypt's defeat before Nebuchadnezzar, and some connect it with the battle of Carchemish. The Egyptian soldiers trusted in their strength, but God showed that no human power stands above him.

For today: do not place your security in your money, your work, or your own strength. All of these can fail. Trust in God first and live with humility.
exp.45:22:
He says that the enemy cuts down Egypt's forest, that is, brings it down, and that it cannot be counted because their soldiers are more numerous than the grasshoppers.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God to Egypt, after its defeat by Babylon at Carchemish. The "forest" can represent Egypt, with its people and its power, although some understand it in another way. The Egyptian soldiers seemed strong, but they fled. God shows that He rules over the nations.

For today: let us not place our security in what seems great and firm, such as money, power or fame. All of that can fall. Let us trust in God, who endures, and ask Him for wisdom and humility to live each day.
exp.45:24:
God, the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, declares that he will bring punishment on Amon of No (the name of Thebes, the great city in southern Egypt, and of its god Amon), on Pharaoh, on Egypt, on its gods and its kings, and on all who trust in Pharaoh. The word "punish" here does not mean a friendly visit, but a judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter announces the defeat of Egypt before Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Egypt seemed strong and many trusted in its power, but God shows that no king or idol can stop his plans. Then the same passage comforts Israel with the promise that it will not be completely destroyed and will rest again.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, power, or people. All of that can fail, but God remains faithful. Trust in him first.
exp.45:26:
Do not be afraid, God tells his people, and do not lose heart. He promises to rescue them from far away, that is, from the place where they are exiled, and also their children. He says that Jacob (another name for Israel) will return, will live in peace, will prosper, and no one will make him afraid.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. First he announces judgment on Egypt, which would be defeated by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The Israelites lived under the weight of exile and the threat of foreign powers. God assures them that he will not abandon them: he will discipline his people, but he will not destroy them completely.

For today: when you feel weak or far from everything, remember that God remains faithful. You can speak to him honestly, ask him for comfort, and trust that he knows how to sustain you and lead you back to peace.
exp.45:27:
God tells his people, called "my servant Jacob," not to be afraid, because he is with them. He promises to put an end completely to the nations where he scattered them, but not to Israel. He will correct Israel with measured justice, that is, with fairness and due limit. To destroy completely means to wipe out entirely, like cutting down a tree until nothing is left. Full destruction means total annihilation.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were under the threat of Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar, and many would be taken into exile. God comforts them: the punishment would be real, but it would not be the end. He keeps his promise to restore them and bring them back.

For today: when God corrects us, he does so as a Father who seeks to heal us, not to destroy us. If you are going through a hard consequence, do not think that God has abandoned you. Come to him with humility, trust that he is with you, and let his correction lead you to change and to rise again.
exp.46:0:
This verse is the introduction to a message from God. It says that the LORD gave a word to the prophet Jeremiah concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, struck Gaza, that is, attacked it or beat it down.

God is the one speaking, and Jeremiah is the messenger. Gaza was an important Philistine city. It is not known for certain which attack the verse refers to; scholars have understood it in several ways. What is clear is that the message announces a judgment that would come upon that region, as the verses that follow show.

For today: God sees the future and rules over all nations, even those that seem strong. We can trust that nothing escapes him. This invites us to live with humility and to place our security in him, not in human power.
exp.46:1:
God says he is announcing a great invasion. The waters that come from the north are waters rising out of the north, and the word "north" is the term the verse itself uses. These waters swell until they become a flood that overflows the whole land, its cities, and its people. Everything that is in it is swept along with them. The men cry out, and all the inhabitants of the land wail, that is, they cry out in pain and despair.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, and his message is against the Philistines. The waters are a poetic image of an army that advances and sweeps everything away. Many think this refers to Babylon, although the text does not name it here, and some see it differently. The passage speaks of judgment on peoples who did not turn to God.

For today: no one and nothing is beyond God's reach. We can trust that he governs history, and not place our security in things that can suddenly come to an end. Let us seek refuge in him.
exp.46:5:
This verse is a lament addressed to the sword of the Lord, which represents God's judgment carried out through war. The speaker asks how long the destruction will last and calls on the sword to return to its sheath, to rest and be still.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment against the Philistines, especially Gaza and Ashkelon. His plea comes from grief at so much ruin. But the next verse answers that the sword cannot rest, because the Lord himself sent it with a purpose. Many understand the invader to be Babylon, though the text here does not name it.

For today: we can cry out to God honestly in the middle of pain, asking him how long. We can also learn to trust that he governs history and acts with justice, even when we do not understand it.
exp.47:4:
It says that the weeping of Moab will be so great that people will go up the slope of Luhith crying. At the descent to Horonaim, even the enemies heard cries of pain over the ruin. Luhith and Horonaim were places in Moab.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing a message from God about Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Moab trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh, and for that reason judgment would come. Scholars are not certain of the exact location of Luhith, but the meaning of the verse is clear: the disaster would reach the whole territory.

For today: let us not put our security in money, in achievements, or in things that can disappear. Let us ask God to teach us to trust in Him first, and to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.47:5:
The verse is an urgent command: flee to save your lives. It asks them to be like the broom bush in the desert, a solitary shrub with thin branches and no shade, that survives on dry ground. Some understand that it speaks of someone who flees with nothing and barely holds on; others, that it refers to hiding in remote places. The original text allows more than one reading.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God, announcing judgment on Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The following verses explain the reason: Moab trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh, and not in the Lord. Because of this, destruction would come upon its cities.

For today: what we have, whether money, work or security, can fail. Today we can examine where we are placing our trust and return it to God, who does not collapse.
exp.47:6:
It says that Moab trusted in its works (its deeds, strongholds and achievements) and in its treasures, and for that reason it too will be taken, that is, conquered. Its god Chemosh will go into exile, together with his priests and his princes. A god who cannot even save himself cannot protect anyone.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment on Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. The context shows a disaster that is near: weeping, flight, and cities destroyed. Moab trusted in its wealth, its pride, and its god, and not in the Lord. Scholars agree that the message is one of judgment, although they debate the historical details.

For today: examine what your security rests on. Money, success, or prestige can help, but they do not sustain the soul. Trust first in God, who does not fail or fall.
exp.47:7:
This verse says that a destroyer will come upon every city of Moab, and no city will escape. The valley and the plain will also be ruined. The word "destroyed" means destroyed, and the plain is the open countryside, with its crops. All of this will happen because the Lord has already said it.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. The preceding text points out that Moab trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh. For that reason, the judgment would reach both the people and their gods. Scholars often connect this with the Babylonian invasion, though the text does not name the destroyer.

For today: examine where you place your security. Money, possessions, or success can fail, but God remains faithful. Trust in Him first, and use what you have with humility and generosity.
exp.47:10:
He says that Moab has lived at ease since its youth. The image is that of wine: it is left to settle on its dregs, and it is never poured from one vessel into another to clear it. Moab was never taken into captivity, and for that reason it keeps its flavor and its smell, that is, it has not changed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, with a message of judgment against Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Its comfort had brought pride and trust in its god Chemosh. The verses that follow announce that those who carry people away will come and empty its jars, that is, enemies who will shake it up. Interpreters see Babylon here, although the text does not name it.

For today: unchanging comfort can leave us hardened. Let us ask God to shake us with love, and receive with humility the trials that help us grow.
exp.47:11:
Thus says the Lord that days are coming when he will send people who pour out wine from one vessel to another, and they will make Moab leave its place, empty its vessels and break its jars, which were leather bags used to keep wine.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab had lived at ease, like wine that rests on its dregs (the sediment) and is never disturbed. That comfort made it proud and confident in its god Chemosh. With this image, God announces that this calm will end in judgment.

For today: long-lasting comfort can make us self-sufficient without our noticing. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and receive with humility the changes God allows, for at times he shakes us to draw us closer to himself.
exp.47:12:
It says that Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, its national god, because that god will not be able to save it. The comparison is with Israel, which was ashamed of Beth-el, the place where it had placed its trust. This probably refers to the golden calves that Jeroboam set up there, which failed to protect them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab had lived at ease and without disturbance, like wine that rests undisturbed in its jar. That comfort gave it a false sense of security and pride. God announces that judgment is coming, and with it will fall what Moab believed was firm: its military strength and its god.

For today: examine where you place your confidence. Money, comfort, success, or even a routine of religious habit can give us a security that does not hold up in a crisis. Rest in God, who remains faithful when everything else begins to waver.
exp.47:13:
Jeremiah asks Moab a question that sounds like a serious mockery: "How do you dare to say that you are mighty and strong men for the war?" In other words, what right do they have to boast of their strength when disaster is already coming?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Moab, a people who lived next to Israel. Moab trusted in its army, its riches, and its god Chemosh (Chêmos). God declares that none of these things will save them. The verses that follow say that their best young men will fall and that ruin is near.

For today: our strength, our money, or our abilities can fail. It is wise to examine what we truly trust in. We can work hard, but without placing our hearts in ourselves, and instead placing them in God, who sustains our lives.
exp.47:14:
It says that Moab was destroyed. Its cities were laid waste, and its finest young men were led to the slaughter. The one who declares it is the King, the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord who rules over all power.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on God's word about Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Moab trusted in its god Chemosh and in its military strength, and it boasted of being brave. The text announces that this confidence would not save it. Some historical details about how this judgment was fulfilled are not entirely clear.

Today, this verse reminds us that neither power, nor pride, nor idols can give us true security. It is worth asking ourselves what we truly trust in, and placing our hope in God, the only King who never fails.
exp.47:15:
This verse says that Moab's ruin is very close and that the disaster is coming quickly. The word for "calamity" here means total destruction or utter defeat, and it refers to the disaster that awaits Moab.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, known for its pride and for trusting in its own strength and riches. In the past they boasted of being brave in war, but God, here called King and the LORD of hosts, declares that their power will not save them. Neighboring peoples are invited to mourn their fall.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, in our strength or our success, because all of that can disappear quickly. It is wiser to live with humility and trust in God, who sustains what truly endures.
exp.47:17:
It says that Dibon, an important city of Moab, must come down from its place of honor and sit in dry ground, without comfort. The reason is that the destroyer, an invader sent against Moab, has already come up against it and torn down its strongholds, that is, its defenses.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing God's message against Moab, a nation neighboring Israel. Throughout the chapter, Moab's pride and its trust in its wealth and strength are pointed out as the cause of its fall. Interpreters do not agree on who the exact invader was, but the message is clear: what seemed firm was going to collapse.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or reputation. All of these can fail. Entrust your confidence to God and live with humility, because only He does not fall.
exp.47:20:
This verse says that God's judgment has already come upon the open plain country, that is, the flat tableland of Moab. It then names three towns that were reached: Holon, Jahazah, and Mephaath. The plain country means open, level ground, and judgment refers to the punishment that God pronounces.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah, announcing what God says about Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Specific places are named, as in a list, to show that the punishment would reach the whole territory. The prophets explain that Moab trusted in its pride and its riches. The exact location of some of these towns is not fully certain.

For today: God sees what happens in every place, even the smallest. We can examine whether we trust in our own strength or in Him, and draw near with humility.
exp.47:21:
This verse continues a list of cities of Moab on which God's judgment falls. Here the cities named are Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim. It is an incomplete phrase, which continues into the next verse. Judgment here means punishment decided by God.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and the prophet announces that its fall will reach the whole country. The text names specific places, as if to say that no one will be left unaware. It is generally understood that Moab's pride and its trust in itself were part of the reason (see 48:7, 29).

For today: God knows places and people by their names, and nothing escapes him. We can trust that he sees injustice, and we can also examine whether we are trusting in our own strength instead of in him.
exp.47:22:
This verse continues a list of cities of Moab on which God's judgment falls. Three more are named here: Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon. The names appear in an older spelling in the text this explanation is based on, but they are real places in the Moabite region. It is not known with certainty where each one was located today.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and God announces punishment for it, partly because of its pride and its trust in its own riches and fortresses (v. 7, v. 29). Naming so many cities shows that the judgment would be complete: no one would be left out, whether far away or close by.

For today: God sees and knows every place and every situation. Nothing we build to make ourselves feel secure, whether money, success, or fame, can protect us from Him. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and humbly hand that pride over to God.
exp.47:23:
This verse follows a list of Moabite cities that will be reached by God's judgment. Here Kerioth and Bozrah are named, and then all the cities of Moab are included, both far and near. In other words, none would be left out. Some believe that Bozrah here is a Moabite city and not the well-known Bozrah of Edom, although there is no complete certainty.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, carrying the message of the LORD. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, trusted in its own strength and exalted itself against God, as the following verses say. For this reason its downfall is announced.

For today: God sees every place and every attitude, however great or small they may seem. We can examine whether we trust in our own strength and, with humility, hand over to God our pride and our sense of security.
exp.47:24:
It says that Moab has lost its power. The "horn" was an image of strength and pride, like the horn of a bull or a deer. The "arm" stands for the ability to fight and defend oneself. If the horn is cut off and the arm is broken, Moab no longer has strength or defense. "Broken" means shattered.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, but what he says comes from the LORD. It is a message of judgment against Moab, a people who lived next to Israel. The verses that follow explain the reason: Moab exalted itself against God, that is, it rose up in arrogance, and it also mocked Israel. Scholars understand this language as a description of Moab's downfall, although not all of them agree on when or how it happened.

For today: human strength does not hold up when it turns into pride against God. Today we can ask ourselves what we trust in, and ask God for a humble heart that depends on Him.
exp.47:27:
He tells the people of Moab to leave their cities, which are no longer safe, and to seek shelter in the rocks and the cliffs. He asks them to be like the dove that makes its nest at the mouth of a cave, hidden and safe.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Moab was filled with pride and rose up against God, and it also mocked Israel. Because of this, judgment is coming upon them. Some understand that the invasion would be so severe that only fleeing to hidden places would offer any hope. The exact historical details of how this was fulfilled are not entirely clear.

For today: pride makes us feel strong, but humility leads us to seek refuge in God. Today you can bring to God in prayer whatever you trust in most for yourself.
exp.47:28:
We have heard of Moab's great pride. The verse piles up several similar words to stress the point: arrogance, swelling (being puffed up with oneself), pride, haughtiness, and the conceit of the heart. Everything points to an attitude of thinking oneself superior to others and not needing God.

It is part of Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Here the prophet speaks, or God speaks through him, and announces judgment. Moab had mocked Israel and felt secure, but God sees its heart. The verses that follow show that God, even so, grieves over Moab and does not rejoice coldly.

For today: pride often grows when we feel secure or better than others. Today you can ask God to show you where haughtiness lives in your heart, and practice humility by listening more and recognizing that everything you have is a gift from him.
exp.47:30:
This verse says that the one speaking is filled with grief for Moab. To howl, to cry out, and to lament are ways of weeping loudly, as was done in times of mourning. Kir-heres was a city of Moab, perhaps the same as Kir of Moab; this is not known with complete certainty. The "men of Kir-heres" are its inhabitants.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab had been very proud and trusted in its lies, and for that reason judgment comes. Even so, the text shows God (or the prophet speaking in his name) feeling sorrow over the destruction that is coming. The judgment is just, but it is not presented with joy.

For today: when we see someone fall because of their pride or their mistakes, we should not celebrate. We can recognize what is just and, at the same time, feel compassion and pray for that person.
exp.47:34:
It says that God will put an end to religious worship in Moab. There will no longer be anyone who offers sacrifices on the altars or who burns incense to their gods. It refers to the high places where the people practiced their worship.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring nation of Israel, which trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh. The whole chapter announces judgment on Moab for its pride. The verses that follow show that even the prophet feels sorrow over that destruction, with images of mourning. Some scholars also see here a historical fulfillment, although the details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: examine what you truly trust in. Whatever we put in place of God, whether money, success, or religious customs, cannot sustain us. Seek God with humility and sincerity.
exp.47:35:
It says that the heart of the one speaking sounds with sorrow, like the sound of a flute at a funeral, for Moab and for the men of Kir-heres. The reason is that the riches they had gathered were lost. The sound of the heart is a sound of grief and pain. Kir-heres is a city of Moab, and some believe it is the same as Kir-hareseth.

The one speaking is the LORD through the prophet Jeremiah, and he expresses grief over the judgment that is coming upon Moab. Earlier, their pride and their idolatry are described. Even so, a sincere sorrow is shown. Scholars debate whether the lament belongs to God, to the prophet, or to both.

For today: although God corrects pride and idolatry, his heart does not rejoice in anyone's ruin. We can pray that others will repent and feel compassion, instead of mocking when someone loses what they had put as their security.
exp.47:36:
In Moab, everyone will show their grief: heads shaved bald, beards cut off, hands marked with cuts, and rough cloth worn at the waist. Shaved means cut away or cut short.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel, trusted in its riches and its gods, and God announces its fall. These customs were signs of mourning in that time. It is striking that God says his heart will moan like a flute, meaning he grieves even over this judgment.

For today: God does not delight in human suffering, even when it is just. We can trust that he judges with truth, but we can also ask him for a compassionate heart rather than a proud one, and not place our security in material things, which pass away.
exp.47:37:
This verse says that on all the housetops of Moab and in its streets there will be nothing but weeping. The housetops are the flat roofs of the houses, where people used to gather. God says he broke Moab like a vessel that no longer pleases him, that is, it is no longer of use and it shatters.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and this message announces its judgment. The prophet even shows sorrow for them: the signs of mourning are shaven heads, wounded hands, and clothing of sackcloth. The texts speak of their pride and of how they trusted in their riches.

For today: do not place your security in what you have or in your own pride. All of that can be broken. Ask God for a humble heart, and learn to feel sorrow, not mockery, when others face the consequences of their mistakes.
exp.47:40:
It says that the cities and strongholds of Moab will be captured. The bravest soldiers, who seemed strong, will be overcome with so much fear that their hearts will be like those of a woman in labor, filled with pain and anguish. The word "taken" in the verse means seized, and the strongholds are walled places where people go to defend themselves.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD says against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The text gives as the reason that Moab grew proud against the LORD, that is, it became arrogant and rose up against God. The image of the eagle spreading its wings shows an enemy who falls swiftly. The text does not name the invader here.

For today: our walls, money, or strength do not give us true security if we live in pride. Today we can humble ourselves before God and place our trust in Him, who sustains those who seek Him.
exp.47:45:
It says that Moab is in great disaster. Chemosh was the chief god of the Moabites, and here it is announced that his people, the ones who followed that god, will be destroyed. Their sons and daughters will be taken away as captives. To perish means to be destroyed, and captivity means being carried by force into a foreign land.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, had trusted in its gods and in its pride. God announces the time of his judgment on them. But the chapter ends with hope: God promises to restore Moab in the latter days. How this is fulfilled, interpreters explain in various ways.

For today: nothing other than God can truly sustain us. Examine where you place your trust, and turn your heart back to the Lord, who judges with justice but also offers restoration.
exp.47:46:
Although God judged Moab and its people were taken into captivity, the verse says that one day their fate will change. The phrase about "the latter days" refers to the last days, or a time yet to come. With the words that close the verse, the message of punishment against this nation comes to an end.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, Israel's neighbor, is warned because of its pride and its trust in its god Chemosh. The earlier chapters describe its ruin. This verse ends with a promise of restoration. Interpreters differ about when or how it will be fulfilled: some see it in the near future, others at the end of time.

For today: God corrects, but he takes no pleasure in destruction. Even in the harshest consequences, he leaves a door of hope open. If you are going through a hard season, trust that his final word is redemption.
exp.48:2:
Jeremiah calls on Heshbon to wail because the city of Ai has been destroyed. He also tells the women of Rabbah to put on sackcloth, the clothing of mourning, and to lament. Mourning here means crying out with sorrowful songs. Running back and forth along the walls probably means running frantically from one side to the other in despair. Their king, with his priests and princes, will go into exile.

God speaks through Jeremiah against Ammon, a people neighboring Israel, who had taken over the territory of Gad. Some believe the king mentioned here is the god Milcom. It is also not certain which Ai is meant here.

Today, this passage reminds us that no power or wealth can protect us from God. We can examine whether we trust in what we have more than in Him, and live with humility and justice.
exp.48:6:
This verse is a message from God against Edom. God asks, in a tone of rebuke, whether wisdom is no longer found in Teman, an important city of Edom. He asks whether their wise people no longer know how to give counsel and whether their understanding has been ruined.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was known for its reputation for wisdom, and Teman was a symbol of that. God announces judgment and shows that not even human wisdom will be able to save them. The atmosphere is one of warning, because a disaster is coming.

For today: intelligence, experience, and good advice are valuable, but they do not replace God. Before relying only on your own plans, ask God humbly for direction.
exp.48:9:
God says he will leave Esau, that is, Edom, without protection. The word that means stripping him bare says that he will be left exposed. The places where he used to hide will no longer serve him. Esau's descendants are the ones who would have carried on his line. His brothers and neighbors, the nearby peoples, will also fall, and Edom will cease to exist as a nation.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message of judgment against Edom. This people descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob, and lived in lands that were hard to reach, where they felt safe. Earlier, God compares this judgment to grape harvesters and thieves, who leave something behind; here nothing will be left. Even so, God cares for the fatherless and the widows.

For today: do not put your security in your resources, your position, or the places you hide in. Trust in God, who sees everything and protects the weak.
exp.48:10:
It says that God invites the fatherless to be left in his care, because he will provide for them. It also promises that the widows can trust in him. Here, "preserve" means keeping alive, caring for, and sustaining.

The message comes from the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah, and it is directed against Edom, the people descended from Esau. It announces that Edom will be completely destroyed and that its capital, Bozrah, will be left in ruins. In the middle of that judgment appears this sentence. Many read it as a sign that God cares for the most defenseless even when a nation falls. Others see it as a promise addressed to the families who will suffer the loss. The text does not clarify more than that.

For today: if you or someone close to you is living through a loss or a great need, you can entrust their care to God in prayer, and at the same time be the hands that help orphans and widows.
exp.48:14:
God tells Edom that he has made it small among the nations, that is, weak and of little importance. The word "despised" in this verse means looked down on, treated as someone of no worth.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Edom, the people living next to Israel. Bozrah was one of its main cities. Edom trusted in its strongholds in the rocks and in its pride, as the following verse says. God announces that this pride will be brought low. Some understand that this was already taking place in the prophet's vision, and others that it refers to a judgment still to come; the text does not give exact dates.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, in our reputation, or in our own strength. Let us ask God for a humble heart, because He cares for the humble and opposes pride.
exp.48:18:
God says that he will come like a lion coming up out of the thick thickets along the Jordan when the river overflows, and he will attack a place that looks fine and secure, a green and safe pasture. God will make its people run away from there and will appoint whoever he chooses to take charge. He will make them run, and whoever he calls to account cannot match him or resist him.

The message is spoken by the LORD through the prophet Jeremiah, against Edom. Edom was a neighboring nation of Israel, known for being proud and secure in its mountains. God announces that its confidence will not protect it from judgment. Scholars discuss some details, such as who the one "chosen" is, but the central message is clear: God rules over the nations.

For today: do not put your security in your strength, your achievements, or your position. Trust in God, who is just and is above all things, and live with humility before him.
exp.48:19:
Here he says that God invites us to hear his plan against Edom and against the inhabitants of Teman, a city known in Edom. The words for counsel and thoughts mean purpose and decision. The phrases about what has been settled and resolved mean that he has already decided it. The expression about the least of the flock can be understood as the youngest or weakest shepherds, or as the most insignificant ones; it is interpreted in several ways. Even they will drag the people away and lay waste to their dwellings, that is, their homes and pastures.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom was a neighbor of Judah and considered itself safe and wise. God announces judgment on its pride and violence, and compares its fall to that of Sodom and Gomorrah.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, fame, or security, because God is the only one who is truly powerful. Let us receive his Word with humility and live justly, knowing that he rules over all.
exp.48:20:
The fall of Edom will be so severe that the earth will tremble, and the cry of its suffering will be heard as far as the Red Sea. It is a poetic way of saying that no one will fail to hear of what has happened.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, a neighbor of Israel, appears here under the judgment of the LORD, who is compared to a lion advancing with power. The cities of Teman and Bozrah, both Edomite, are mentioned. The text does not detail all the reasons here, but other prophets speak of Edom's pride and its violence against Israel.

Today, this verse reminds us that God is just and that no human pride is strong enough to stand before Him. We can examine our hearts, lay down arrogance, and trust in God's justice instead of seeking revenge.
exp.48:21:
It says that someone will come up and fly like an eagle, spreading his wings over Bozrah, which was an important city of Edom. On that day, the bravest soldiers of Edom will have as much fear and pain as a woman about to give birth.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, a neighboring people of Israel, trusted in its strength and its high places. God announces that he will send judgment upon them. The eagle is not clearly identified in the text; many think it represents an invading army, such as Babylon, and that God uses it as his instrument.

We can learn that no human strength, reputation, or security protects us if we leave God out. Today it is good to ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and to place our hope in the Lord, the only refuge that does not collapse.
exp.48:25:
It says that the young men of Damascus will fall dead in the city's streets, and that all its soldiers will die on the same day. The word translated as "young men" in the verse above means young people or lads. The soldiers are the men of war. It is spoken by the LORD of hosts, a title that shows his authority over every kind of power.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, within a message against several nations that were neighbors of Israel. Damascus, the capital of Syria, appears frightened and without strength, like a woman in labor. The texts do not explain each step in detail, but the message is that God judges the nations and that no strong city is outside his hand. Scholars debate which exact historical events are meant.

For today: do not place your security in your strength, your money, or your youth. All of these can fail. Trust in God, who is just and sustains what truly endures.
exp.48:26:
God announces that he will set fire to the wall of Damascus, and that this fire will destroy the palaces, or fortified houses, of Ben-hadad. The wall is the barrier that protected the city. Ben-hadad was a name used by several kings of Syria, so here it stands for his whole dynasty and its power.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, within a message against several neighboring nations. Damascus, the capital of Syria, appears as a city full of fear and defeat. The verses that follow mention Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, and many understand that he would be the instrument of this judgment, although the text gives no further details about how it happened.

For today: no human stronghold, no wealth or power, is safe before God. We can examine where we place our trust and seek refuge in him, who remains when everything else falls.
exp.48:31:
It says that the camels and the large herds of Hazor will be taken as plunder by their enemies. God says he will scatter his people in every direction, to the farthest corner, that is, the most distant remote place. He also states that he will bring ruin on them from every side. "Spoil" means what is taken away from the defeated.

The message is spoken by the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah, against Kedar and Hazor, desert peoples who lived off their flocks. They lived in confidence and without walls, but Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, planned to attack them. It is not known exactly where Hazor was; it is understood as a region of Arab tribes, not the city of Israel with the same name.

For today: wealth and a sense of security cannot protect us from everything. It is wise to trust God more than our possessions, and to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.48:33:
This verse introduces a new prophecy. God gives Jeremiah, his prophet, a message about Elam. The phrase "that came to Jeremiah" means that the word of the Lord came to him. It is placed at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, who ruled from about 597 B.C.

The one speaking is the Lord, and Jeremiah receives the message and passes it on. Elam was a nation east of Babylon, in the region of today's southwestern Iran. The verses that follow announce that God will break its power and scatter its people. It is one of Jeremiah's prophecies against the nations, which show that God rules over all peoples, not only over Israel.

For today: God remains Lord of history, even when the powers of the world seem strong. We can rest in the fact that nothing escapes his control. Trust in him, and seek to live with humility, without relying on your own strength.
exp.48:35:
It says that God will bring winds upon Elam from the four corners of the heavens, and will use them to scatter his people everywhere. "I will scatter them" is what the phrase means, as grain is winnowed to separate it. There will be so many exiled Elamites that no nation will be left where they do not go.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah. Elam was a people east of Babylon, known for its archers. God announces that he will break its bow, that is, its strength. The judgment comes because of its pride and its trust in its own power. The text does not detail all the historical events of its fulfillment.

For today: let us not place our security in our strength, money, or achievements, because everything can change. Let us trust in God, who governs the nations, and live with humility before him.
exp.49:3:
It says that when Babylon falls, God's people will come back together: Israel and Judah, who had been divided. They will not return in pride, but weeping, and they will seek the Lord, their God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Babylon. He announces that this empire will be defeated by a people from the north, and that its idols will be put to shame. Scholars understand in different ways how much of this was fulfilled with the return from exile, and how much points to a future time. What is clear is that God promises to restore his people.

For today: when you have moved away from God, sincere weeping is not the end but a good beginning. Come back to seek him with humility, and try to do it together with other believers, not alone.
exp.49:5:
The passage says that God's people were like a lost flock. Their shepherds, that is, their leaders, led them astray and took them over the mountains. They wandered from mountain to hill without rest, and they forgot their resting place, which is the fold, the safe place where the flock lies down to rest.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Babylon. He announces that Babylon will fall and that Israel and Judah, united, will return weeping to seek God. The verse describes how they were lost: their leaders misled them, and for that reason they suffered harm from their enemies.

For today: those of us who guide others, in the home, the church, or the workplace, must care for those who follow us and lead them toward God. And if we find ourselves lost, we can always return to the Shepherd, who receives us with grace.
exp.49:7:
God tells his people to run out of Babylon and out of the land of the Chaldeans. He asks them to be like the he goats, the ones that go at the front of the flock and open the way. In other words, they should be the first to leave, not left behind.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people were like a lost flock, poorly led by shepherds who had led them astray. God announces that Babylon will fall, attacked by an alliance of peoples from the north. For that reason he invites his own to leave before the judgment. Some scholars think this refers to the return from exile; others also see a broader message about turning away from evil.

Today we can ask ourselves what environment or habit draws us away from God. With his help, let us find the courage to leave that place and take the first step, even though others may still hesitate.
exp.49:8:
It says that God himself will raise up and bring against Babylon a company of mighty nations from the north (the north is the direction meant here). They will get ready for the attack, and Babylon will be conquered. Their arrows are like those of a skilled warrior who never comes back empty-handed; that is, they will not miss.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed Israel, and here God announces that this empire will also be held accountable. The verses before this one show a scattered people, and the verses that follow explain that Babylon falls because it rejoiced in destroying God's inheritance. Historians see the Medes and Persians in this, although the text gives no names.

For today: you can rest in the fact that God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered forever. This invites you to trust him rather than take revenge, and to live with humility, remembering that no one stands above his judgment.
exp.49:9:
It says that Chaldea, another name for Babylon, will be a spoil, that is, plunder that others will take. Those who plunder her will be fully satisfied, with everything they were seeking. The one who declares it is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and mistreated his people, and it felt proud and secure. God announces that he will raise up against her an assembly of nations from the north. The following verses explain the reason: Babylon rejoiced in destroying God's inheritance, that is, his people. Thus, judgment comes because of her pride and her injustice.

For today: let us not be deceived by the power of those who do harm. God sees injustice and has the last word. We can entrust our pain to him, refrain from seeking revenge, and live with humility, trusting in his justice.
exp.49:11:
It says that Babylon, here called the "mother" of its inhabitants, will be brought low and filled with shame. From being a great power, it will become the last of the nations.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, and says the message comes from the LORD. He addresses Babylon, which had destroyed Jerusalem and mistreated God's people. It mocked them and became full of pride. God announces that she herself will suffer the punishment for her arrogance and her sin.

For today: pride and cruelty may seem successful for a time, but God sees injustice. Today we can treat those with less power with humility and compassion, and trust that God will bring about justice in his time.
exp.49:12:
Because of God's anger, the verse says, Babylon will be left without inhabitants and completely destroyed. Anyone who passes by will be amazed and will whistle, that is, make a sound of mockery or horror, when they see all the wounds the punishment left behind. The word for the disasters that fell on the city means blows or calamities. Being laid waste means being torn down to ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and mistreated Israel, whom God calls his own inheritance. Babylon had filled itself with pride and joy over its conquest. Now God announces that this empire will be judged for its wickedness. Scholars understand the fall of Babylon in different ways regarding when and how it was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: God holds it accountable.

For today: do not lose heart when injustice seems to win. God sees everything and will bring justice in his time. Meanwhile, avoid pride and do not rejoice in the misfortune of others.
exp.49:16:
Israel was like a lost and scattered flock. The lions were powerful nations that attacked it. First Assyria devoured it, and last of all Babylon, under Nebuchadrezzar, broke its bones, meaning it crushed Israel and left it without strength.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon will fall because of the violence with which it treated other peoples. But the next verse offers hope: God will punish Babylon, as He did earlier with Assyria, and will bring Israel back to its land so that it may live again in peace and abundance.

For today: if you feel wounded, lost, or without strength, remember that God does not abandon His people. He sees injustice, knows how to heal, and can restore what others destroyed. Trust in His care and in His justice.
exp.49:17:
God says that he will punish the king of Babylon and his land, which means he will come to call them to account and bring judgment on them. He will do it in the same way he earlier punished the king of Assyria. "The Lord of hosts" is a title that shows God as the Lord of all power.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Assyria had devoured Israel, and Babylon had then stripped it bare, as the previous verse says. God used these nations, but they were cruel and proud. So now it is their turn to answer. The text that follows promises that God will bring his people back and forgive them.

For today: even when evil and injustice seem to win, God sees everything and will do justice in his time. We can trust him and leave in his hands what we cannot fix.
exp.49:18:
God promises that he will bring his people Israel back to their land, to their dwelling place, that is, to their home. There they will graze like sheep in good pasture, on Carmel, in Bashan, on the hill country of Ephraim and in Gilead. These were regions known for their fertile land. Their souls will be completely satisfied, meaning they will be fully content.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been like a scattered and mistreated flock, first by Assyria and then by Babylon. God announces that he will judge Babylon and that he will spare those of his people who remain. Some understand this promise as the return from exile, while others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: if you feel lost or worn out, remember that God knows how to restore. He cares for his people like a good shepherd and can give you back peace and rest. Trust in him and return to his care.
exp.49:21:
This verse describes the sound of war coming into the land, and a very great destruction. The word "destruction" conveys the idea of ruin, collapse, or a blow that leaves everything broken to pieces. It is as if one could hear the noise of an army and of a city falling.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah and announces judgment against Babylon, the power that had oppressed other nations. The verses before it mention Merathaim and Pekod, names that probably refer to regions of Babylon, though scholars debate their exact meaning. At the same time, God promises to forgive his people who remained.

For today: God sees injustice and does not allow human pride to last forever. We can rest in the fact that he governs history, and at the same time receive his forgiveness with humility.
exp.49:33:
Their Redeemer is strong; the Lord of Hosts is his name. He says that the Redeemer of Israel and Judah is strong, and that his name is the Lord of Hosts. A redeemer is one who rescues and defends his own people. He will plead their cause like a lawyer, to bring rest to the land of his people and to bring unrest and fear upon the inhabitants of Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel and Judah had been oppressed and taken captive, and their captors did not want to let them go. God promises to judge Babylon for that oppression. The verses that follow show that the judgment would reach its rulers, wise men, and soldiers. Scholars understand this as speaking of the fall of Babylon, though they do not all agree on how and when each detail was fulfilled.

When you feel trapped or unfairly treated, you are not alone. Entrust your cause to God in prayer, trust in his justice, and avoid taking revenge yourself.
exp.49:34:
God says he will send a sword against all of Babylon. The word for "sword" in the original refers to war, and the verse names the Chaldeans as the people who ruled there. The judgment reaches the common people, the princes (the rulers) and the wise men (the advisers and experts). No one is left out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Israel and Judah and refused to release the captives. God presents himself as their Redeemer, the Strong One, who defends the cause of his people. These words announce the fall of Babylon, and the Bible presents that judgment as the justice of God.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. If you are suffering or have been mistreated, you can entrust your cause to him and refrain from seeking revenge. And if you have power or knowledge, use it with humility and justice, because neither prestige nor human wisdom protects us before God.
exp.49:38:
This verse says that Babylon will become an abandoned place. Wild animals of the desert will live there, such as beasts of the wild (wild animals), wolves, and ostriches. It will never again have inhabitants, not from one generation to the next.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, a powerful, idolatrous, and proud nation that had oppressed other peoples, including Judah. The text announces its judgment with the coming of a people from the north. Scholars debate how and when all this was fulfilled, since Babylon declined little by little over the centuries.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, is eternal. We can trust that God is just and that he sustains those who suffer. It is also a good moment to examine what we put in God's place, because whatever is not God cannot give us lasting security.
exp.49:40:
Jeremiah 50:41 says that an army is coming from the north, a great nation, and many kings are stirred up from the ends of the earth. The picture is of a force gathering from distant and far-off places, drawn together from many lands to march toward Babylon.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter announces God's judgment against Babylon, a city and empire known for cruelty and pride. Many commentators connect this coming invasion with the Medes and the Persians, though the text itself does not give every detail, so it is wise not to claim more than it says.

God rules over empires, however powerful they may seem. If you see injustice or arrogance that appears to have no end, trust that God sees and acts in his own time. In the meantime, live with humility and justice, and do not rely on human power.
exp.49:41:
It says that an enemy army will come against Babylon armed with bow and spear. They will be cruel and show no mercy. The sound of their advance will be like the sea, and they will ride on horses, arranged in formation, every one ready, like one man going into battle.

Habla Jehová por medio del profeta Jeremías. Babilonia had been a proud empire that destroyed nations and carried Judah into captivity. God announces that judgment is now coming to her, and he compares it to what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. The text says the enemy comes from the north. History mentions the Medes and Persians, but the passage does not name them here.

For today: God sees injustice, and nothing escapes him. If you are suffering because of someone powerful who has abused you, you can trust that God is just. And if you have power, use it with humility and compassion, because one day you will give an account.
exp.49:42:
This verse says that the king of Babylon received news of the reputation of the people coming against him, and fear paralyzed him. His hands grew weak and lost their strength. He felt anguish and intense pain, like that of a woman about to give birth.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a power that oppressed Judah. Now God announces that a people from the north will defeat it. Many understand this to refer to the Medes and Persians, though the text does not give names here. The message shows that no empire stands above God.

For today: when you feel that someone powerful is in control, remember that God is still the Lord of history. Trust in Him, act with justice, and do not place your security in human power.
exp.49:43:
He says that God will bring an enemy like a lion that comes up out of the thick thickets along the Jordan toward a safe pasture. The reference to the Jordan's thick banks points to the crowded, overgrown edge of the river, where lions used to live. Babylon is the place that seemed secure, and God says he will make them run away from it suddenly, and he will set over it whomever he chooses. The word for calling someone to account, to demand an answer, means that no one can challenge him, not even a shepherd, that is, a ruler.
