God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon, which had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed Judah. Much of what is said here nearly repeats what was said against Edom (Jeremiah 49:19). Scholars understand the "chosen one" as a people or leader whom God raises up, commonly associated with the Medes and Persians.

For today: no human power is beyond God's reach. If you see injustice or abuse that seems unbeatable, you can trust that God governs and will do justice in his time. Meanwhile, seek to live with humility and do not rely on your own strength.
exp.49:45:
It says that when Babylon is conquered, the cry of its fall will be so loud that it will shake the earth, and its outcry will reach all the nations. The phrase "nations" in this verse is the word the verse refers to, and it simply means peoples or nations. The picture shows that the fall of this great power will not go unnoticed, but will shake the whole known world.

The one speaking throughout this passage is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces his judgment against Babylon, the proud empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed his people. God is presented as a lion that no one can stop, and he declares that no one can stand against him. Scholars often connect this with the fall of Babylon before the Medes and Persians, although some also see a broader meaning.

No human power, however great it may seem, is above God. We can trust that he does justice in his own time, and hand over with peace whatever worries us.
exp.50:5:
It says that God's people must flee from the midst of Babylon and save their lives, so as not to perish with her because of her wickedness. "Vengeance" here means justice: God is going to give Babylon what she deserves.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was a powerful empire that had oppressed other peoples, including Judah. The previous verse recalls that God did not abandon Israel and Judah, even though they had sinned. For this reason God warns them to leave before the judgment on Babylon.

For today: God invites us to move away from any environment, habit, or relationship that pulls us toward evil. Ask him to show you something concrete you should turn away from, and take a real step today to get out of it.
exp.50:7:
It says that Babylon, the great power, suddenly collapsed and was broken to pieces. It calls people to wail over her, and to take balm, a medicine to ease the pain of her wounds, in case she might be healed.

Jeremiah announces what God will do to Babylon for her wickedness. Earlier, God had used her as a golden cup that made the nations drunk. Now her judgment arrives. The verses that follow show that it was already too late to heal her. Many read the words about the balm as an ironic or sorrowful call, and not everyone interprets it the same way.

No human power lasts forever, and God remains just. Do not place your security in what seems strong, but in God. If something harmful surrounds you, ask Him for wisdom to get out of it and return to Him.
exp.50:10:
He tells them to get ready for war: to polish the arrows and raise up the shields. God himself has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes so that they will attack Babylon and destroy it. This is the Lord's vengeance, that is, justice for what Babylon did against his temple in Jerusalem.

Jeremiah announces this message to a people in exile, or about to go into exile. Babylon seemed unconquerable, but it had destroyed the temple and oppressed Judah. The text presents God as the one who directs history and uses other nations to carry out his judgment. Historians know that Media and Persia played a part in Babylon's fall, although the details are explained in several different ways.

For today: when evil seems powerful and unstoppable, remember that God sees injustice and has the final word. Trust in his justice, without taking revenge into your own hands.
exp.50:11:
It tells them to prepare to attack Babylon: raise the banner or signal of war on its walls, strengthen the watch, post sentries (soldiers who keep guard), and set ambushes, which are surprise traps. The reason given is that the Lord has decided it, and he will carry out what he said against the people of Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah announces God's judgment against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and carried the people into captivity. The text mentions the kings of Media as instruments God would stir up. Babylon, trusting in its walls and wealth, would be judged for its pride and its violence.

For today: you can trust that God keeps his word, even when it takes time or seems impossible. When you see injustice that seems to have no end, do not fill yourself with resentment; pray, do good, and wait patiently for God to act in his time.
exp.50:14:
This verse says that God is the Creator of everything. He made the earth by his strength, that is, by his great power. He established the world by his wisdom, meaning he made it firm and well ordered. And he stretched out the heavens with understanding, as one who spreads them out with perfect insight.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing God's judgment on Babylon, a rich and proud city that trusted in its treasures and its idols. The verses that follow contrast the living God, who governs the rain, the clouds and the wind, with the idols, which are a lie and have neither life nor breath.

For today: when you feel that money, power or anything fleeting gives you security, remember who holds up the world. Entrust your life to the wise and powerful God, and not to things that cannot save you.
exp.50:15:
This verse says that God, with only his voice, makes a great quantity of water fall from the sky. He lifts up the clouds from the farthest places on the earth. He makes lightning along with the rain, and he brings out the wind from his storehouses, as if he kept it in storage rooms.

The prophet Jeremiah announces God's judgment against Babylon. Earlier, God promises to send against her armies as numerous as locusts. Here Jeremiah shows who the God who speaks is: the Creator who governs nature. Then he compares him with idols, which are human work, without life or spirit.

For today: when you feel small before problems or powers that seem enormous, remember that the God who governs the clouds and the winds also cares for your life. Trust him before anything that you or other people make to feel secure.
exp.50:16:
Every person who worships idols is said to act like a fool, without knowledge. The craftsman who makes the image is the one who is shamed by it, and the carved figure is the idol itself. The cast metal idol is the image poured from molten metal. The verse affirms that this idol is a lie, because it has no breath or life in it.

The prophet Jeremiah announces judgment on Babylon. Before this verse, he speaks of the Creator God who made the earth, the clouds, the rain, and the wind. After the verse, idols are set against the God of Jacob, who is the Former of all things. The message confronts trust in false gods and reminds readers who holds the true power.

For today, let us ask where we place our trust, such as in money, success, or the approval of others. None of these has life to save us. Today we can pray and hand that worry over to God.
exp.50:19:
It says that God uses someone as his battle axe and weapons of war. With that instrument, he himself will break in pieces nations and destroy kingdoms. To break in pieces means to shatter or destroy, and to destroy means to tear down completely.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, in his message against Babylon. The verses before it contrast idols, which are worthless, with the God of Jacob, creator of all things. Not all scholars agree on who the battle axe is: some think of Israel, others of the Medes and Persians who would overthrow Babylon. In either case, the one who acts is God.

For today: God can use ordinary people as tools in his hands. Ask him to use you, and remember that the power is not yours, but his.
exp.50:27:
This verse is a command to prepare several nations and their rulers to attack Babylon. The word "Prepare" in the verse means to get ready or set in order. The verse names the kings of the Medes, their captains, all their rulers, and the whole land under their dominion. In other words, God calls a whole people with their leaders to rise up against that city.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, who announces judgment on Babylon, the powerful empire of his time. Babylon had destroyed nations and had mistreated Judah. The text presents God as Lord of history, who uses other peoples to carry out his purpose. The Medes appear here as the instrument of that judgment. Later history shows that Babylon fell, although the details of how this was fulfilled are explained in different ways.

For today: no human power is eternal, but God remains faithful. We can trust that he sees injustice and acts in his time, and in the meantime we can live with humility and hope.
exp.50:29:
This verse says that Babylon's bravest soldiers no longer went out to fight. They stayed shut up in their strongholds, without strength, so frightened that they became like women, a phrase that speaks of fear and weakness in battle. Their houses were set on fire, and the bars of their gates were broken.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what God has decided against Babylon. God calls the Medes and other nations to bring down that great city. The passage shows that no human power, however strong it may seem, can stop the Lord's plan. The exact historical details of the fall are understood in various ways.

Today we can remember that strength, money, or prestige are not a secure foundation. It is better to trust in God, who continues to rule above every human power.
exp.50:31:
This verse says that the fords, that is, the shallow places where the river could be crossed, were taken by the enemy. The reeds, which are the canes or rushes along the bank, were burned, and the soldiers of Babylon were left full of dread, not knowing what to do.

Jeremiah announces, on God's behalf, the fall of Babylon, the power that destroyed Jerusalem and led the people into exile. Many connect this with the conquest of 539 B.C., but the exact details of the fords and the reeds are not entirely clear. The message was a comfort for the exiles: God had not forgotten their suffering.

Today we can remember that no human power is eternal. If you feel oppressed or afraid before something that seems invincible, bring it to God in prayer. He sees the injustice and acts in his own time.
exp.50:32:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts, compares Babylon to a threshing floor, that is, wheat spread on the ground of the threshing floor so that it can be beaten and the grain separated from the chaff. The time has come to tread and beat it. Very soon the time of the harvest will also arrive, that is, the reaping, and with it the final judgment on the city.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a power that oppressed Judah and destroyed Jerusalem. The verses that follow show the pain of God's people. Here he promises that this injustice will not go unanswered and that Babylon's power will come to an end.

For today: when you see injustice that seems never to end, do not take revenge with your own hands. Trust that God sees, that he has his just timing, and that he cares for his own. Meanwhile, keep doing good with patience.
exp.50:33:
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, devoured and tore apart God's people. He left them empty like a vessel, swallowed them up like a monster, and filled himself with the best they had. Then he cast them out.

The verse of the words used here is as follows: to tear apart means to break into pieces; a dragon here is a great monster or serpent; and the finest things are the most valuable and refined possessions.

The speaker is Jerusalem, that is, the people of Judah, who describe their grief after the Babylonian conquest. Nebuchadnezzar plundered the city and carried many people into exile. The verses that follow show that God hears this cry and promises to defend their cause and punish Babylon.

For today: when you feel that someone has left you empty or harmed you, you can bring your complaint to God honestly. He sees injustice, and He does not ask you to take revenge yourself; He invites you to trust that He judges with justice.
exp.50:34:
This verse is a cry for justice. Jerusalem, called the inhabitant of Zion, asks that the violence and the blood she suffered fall upon Babylon and Chaldea. "My flesh" speaks of her own wounded body, and "my blood" of the lives that were taken away.

Here the people of God speak, pictured as a mistreated woman. Earlier, they say that Nebuchadnezzar devoured them and left them like an empty vessel. God answers in the following verse: he will plead their cause and execute justice. The prophets present this as God's judgment on Babylon, not as mere human revenge.

For today: when you suffer injustice, you can bring your pain to God with sincerity, instead of taking revenge yourself. He listens to the wounded and knows how to act justly in his time.
exp.50:39:
He says God will bring the Babylonians down like lambs led to the slaughter, like rams together with male goats. It is an image of weak and defenseless people walking toward their fate. The phrase "I will bring them down" is the same idea stated in the verse above. Before this they were like roaring lions, but now they will not be able to defend themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He is announcing judgment against Babylon, the proud empire that had destroyed nations and carried Judah into captivity. The verses before speak of feasts and an everlasting sleep, and the verses after refer to a code name for Babylon. The message was a comfort to God's people.

For today: do not lose heart before the power of the proud. No human power lasts forever, and God sees injustice. Trust that He governs history and acts in His own time.
exp.50:41:
The sea has risen against Babylon and covered her with the multitude of its waves. It is a poetic image: Babylon is buried and destroyed like a city under a flood.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on what God announces against Babylon, the empire that had oppressed Judah. God promises judgment for its pride and violence. The "sea" most likely represents enemy armies arriving like waves, although some understand it only as a figure of total destruction. Babylon was not literally covered by a sea, as far as we know.

For today: no human power lasts forever, however great it may seem. We can trust that God sees injustice and has the final word. This invites us to live with humility and to rest in Him when evil seems to be winning.
exp.50:43:
God says he will punish Bel, the chief idol of Babylon. "I will punish" means coming to call someone to account. The phrase about bringing out of his mouth what he has swallowed refers to the riches and peoples that Babylon had seized as plunder. In addition, the nations will no longer come to pay him honor, and his wall, the symbol of his security, will fall.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had conquered Judah and looted the temple. Bel (another name for Marduk) was its protecting god. God shows that this idol cannot defend anyone and that he rules over empires. Immediately he calls his people to leave that place.

For today: the things we place our security in, such as money, power, or reputation, can fall. Ask yourself what you truly trust in, and place your trust again in the God who endures and cares for his own.
exp.50:50:
It says that God's people feel shame and humiliation. They have heard insults, and confusion covers their faces, that is, they do not know where to hide. The cause is that foreigners entered the sanctuaries, the holy places of the temple of the Lord. Public insult is what shame here refers to, and the holy places are the sacred parts of the temple.

Here the exiles of Judah are speaking, remembering the destruction of Jerusalem and the defiling of the temple by Babylon. It is part of a message from Jeremiah announcing that God will judge Babylon. The verses before it encourage the survivors to remember the Lord and Jerusalem, and the verses after it promise that God will punish Babylon.

For today: when you feel shame or pain over what has happened, do not stay only with the wound. Bring it to God, remember who He is, and trust that He does justice in His time.
exp.50:55:
It says that a destroyer has come against Babylon. Her brave soldiers were captured, and her bow, which is her weapon and her strength, was broken. The reason is that the Lord is the God who repays, that is, a God who does justice and gives each nation what it deserves. The verse's promise that he shall surely requite means that he will pay back according to what they have done.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people, who lived under the power of Babylon. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed many peoples. The message announces that this proud empire would not last forever and that God does not forget injustice.

For today: when you see wickedness that seems to go unpunished, do not take revenge with your own hands. Trust that God is just and will act in his own time. In the meantime, try to live with humility and to do good.
exp.50:61:
Jeremiah tells Seraiah what he must say when he arrives in Babylon: a prayer addressed to God. He acknowledges that God himself announced that this place would be destroyed completely. He says that neither person nor animal would remain, and that it would be left a wasteland, desolate and in ruins, forever.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet and writes God's words in a book. Seraiah, who was traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah, was to read it aloud there. It was a message for the exiles, a reminder that Babylon, so powerful, would not have the final word. Some understand the total destruction as prophetic and gradual language; others expect a more complete fulfillment.

For today: when evil seems great and unconquerable, we can pray with confidence, remembering that God still governs and fulfills what he says.
exp.51:2:
It says that what happened to Jerusalem and Judah was no accident: God was angry because of their sin, and in the end he cast them out of his presence, that is, he removed them from their land and led them into exile. Also, King Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

This final chapter of Jeremiah summarizes the fall of Jerusalem, probably as the historical closing of the book. It tells how Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, did evil, just as earlier kings had. He rebelled against Babylon, and that brought the siege of the city. The text presents this as God's judgment for years of disobedience.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also warns us beforehand. If you feel God is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Listen to him today, with humility, and return to him before the consequences grow.
exp.51:6:
This verse says that the walls of Jerusalem were broken through and the city fell. Then the soldiers fled at night through a small, hidden gate that lay between two walls, near the king's garden. They took the way toward the plain, even though the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) were still surrounding the city.

The one telling this is the author of the book, who recounts the fall of Jerusalem in about 586 B.C. Earlier, God had warned through Jeremiah that the city would fall if the people kept refusing to turn back to Him. This chapter shows that those warnings came true. The attempt to escape did not save them, as the verses that follow make clear.

For today: running away from the consequences does not remove them. If we have done wrong, it is better to acknowledge it before God with humility and ask Him for direction, rather than looking for hidden ways out. His forgiveness is real, and He still receives anyone who returns to Him.
exp.51:10:
This verse says that the king of Babylon put out the eyes of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He bound him in chains, took him to Babylon, and kept him in prison until he died. The last thing Zedekiah saw was the death of his sons, according to the verse before.

Context: This final chapter of Jeremiah tells of the fall of Jerusalem, and it seems to summarize what is also recounted in 2 Kings 25. For years, Jeremiah had warned Zedekiah to surrender and listen to God, but the king did not obey. Here the narrator simply records the events: what God had said through the prophet came to pass.

For today: God's words are serious, and ignoring them has consequences. Today we can hear his Word with humility and obey in time, rather than hardening our hearts. His warning seeks to protect us, and it always offers a way back.
exp.51:11:
On the tenth day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan came into Jerusalem. He was captain of the guard and served close to the king of Babylon.

The account presents this as a historical record of the end of the kingdom of Judah. Babylon had already captured Zedekiah, and now its officer comes to carry out the destruction of the city. The parallel passage in 2 Kings 25:8 gives the seventh day instead, and it is not known for certain why. Some think these are two different moments of the same event. The chapter seems to be a summary added to the book, and its exact author is not certain.

Today, this passage reminds us that God speaks seriously, but he also does what he says. Listening in time is a sign of wisdom.
exp.51:15:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, left some of the poorest people in the land to work as vinedressers (those who tend the vineyards) and husbandmen (those who farm the fields). The rest were taken into exile.

Chapter 52 is a historical summary of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The one telling the story is not a prophet speaking in the first person, but the account that reviews how Babylon destroyed the city and the temple. The Babylonians probably left these poor people behind so that the land would keep producing and would not be left abandoned, although the text gives no further reasons.

For today: God sees and remembers those whom the world overlooks. Even in the midst of judgment, the poor were not forgotten, and their simple work kept the land alive. Value humble work, yours and that of others, and seek to care for those who have less.
exp.51:16:
This verse tells how the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, broke up the large bronze objects of the temple. The columns were two huge pillars at the entrance. The stands were the supports with wheels for the water basins. The "bronze sea" was a large basin of water for the priests. Then they carried all that metal off to Babylon.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, closing the account of the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. Jeremiah had warned for years that the people would suffer for abandoning God. This account shows that those warnings came true. The symbols of God's presence did not protect the people on their own.

For today: let us not trust in places, objects, or religious routines as if they were a guarantee. What God seeks is a faithful and obedient heart. Examine today where you are placing your security.
exp.51:17:
This verse says that the Chaldeans, the army of Babylon, carried off the bronze utensils that were used in the temple. The words in the verse refer to: caldrons (pots used for collecting ashes or for cooking), shovels (scoops for removing ashes from the altar), snuffers (the word is uncertain; probably bowls or vessels for sprinkling), bowls (vessels or basins), and spoons (ladles or small containers).

This is recorded in the final account of the book of Jeremiah, which describes the fall of Jerusalem around 586 B.C. The text goes through in detail what Babylon plundered, while the captain Nebuzaradan left the poorest of the people in the land. The emphasis on each object shows how much was lost.

For today: what we use to serve God can be lost, but he remains faithful. Value what you have today for serving, and trust not in places or objects, but in the Lord himself.
exp.51:18:
This verse describes the looting of the temple in Jerusalem. The Babylonians carried off the cups, the censers (for burning incense), the bowls, the pots, the candlesticks (holders for lamps), the basins (deep dishes), and the cups. Everything that was of gold and of silver was taken by the captain of the guard, that is, the chief of the king's soldiers.

It is the end of the book of Jeremiah, which repeats the account of the fall of Jerusalem around 586 BC. The narrator tells the events in detail, and many believe he adds this historical summary to show that the prophet's warnings were fulfilled. The people had trusted in the temple, but not in living faithfully before God.

For today: sacred things can be lost, but God does not depend on them. Take care of your relationship with Him, not only the outward side of your faith.
exp.51:19:
This verse describes the largest bronze objects in the temple: the two pillars, the "sea" (an enormous basin of water for the priests), and twelve bronze bulls that held up that basin. The "stands" were the supports with wheels. Solomon had made them, and the Babylonians carried them away. There were so many of them, and they were so heavy, that the weight of the metal could not be calculated.

This final chapter of Jeremiah tells, as a historical summary, the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 B.C. The captain of the guard, Nebuzaradan, plundered the temple. The scene shows the judgment that God had warned of because of the people's disobedience.

For today: What is most beautiful can disappear, and we should not place our security in buildings, achievements, or possessions. Let us set our hearts on God himself, who remains faithful even when everything else is lost.
exp.51:20:
Here, according to the text, each of the temple pillars was eighteen cubits tall (about eight or nine meters, since a cubit was roughly half a meter). A cord of twelve cubits went around it, meaning that was its circumference. The wall of the pillar was four fingers thick, and it was hollow inside.

This chapter closes the book of Jeremiah with an account of the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. We do not know for certain who wrote it; many believe it is a historical summary added later, similar to 2 Kings 25. The detail about the pillars, made by Solomon, shows how much was lost when the Babylonians destroyed the temple.

For today: what seems large and secure, such as a sacred building, can be lost. Place your trust in God himself, not in places or things.
exp.51:21:
It says that on top of each bronze column in the temple there was a decorative piece, called a capital, five cubits high (about 2.2 meters). It was surrounded by a bronze network and by pomegranates, also of bronze. The second column was the same.

Here the narrator describes the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 BC. He mentions in detail what the Babylonians carried away from the temple that Solomon built. The chapter closes the book of Jeremiah and shows that what the prophet had warned about came to pass. Scholars think the detail stresses how much was lost.

For today: beautiful and sacred things can disappear, and we should not place our security in buildings or religious symbols. Let us trust in God himself, who remains faithful even when everything else falls apart.
exp.51:22:
The passage says that on the ornaments of the bronze pillars of the temple there were pomegranates made of metal. On each side or row there were ninety-six, and in total there were one hundred around the network. Some explain that the ninety-six were seen on the four sides, and the hundred counted all the pomegranates on the ornament, but the text does not fully make this clear.

Here the narrator describes in detail what the Babylonians destroyed and carried away when they conquered Jerusalem, around 586 BC. This final chapter summarizes the fall of the city and the temple, as the fulfillment of the warnings that Jeremiah had given for years.

For today: God pays careful attention to what we do for Him, but no outward beauty can replace a faithful heart. Let us care for our relationship with God, not merely the appearances of our Christian life.
exp.51:23:
This verse tells how Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, seized Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, together with three keepers of the door of the temple.

The chapter describes the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, and the writer tells it as a historical event. Earlier, the text details how the temple was plundered, including its bronze pillars. Now its religious leaders are carried away. According to the account that follows, these prisoners were brought before the king at Riblah, where they were judged. It is a sign that the judgment announced by the prophets had been fulfilled.

For today: God takes his announced word seriously. We can listen to his Word with humility and not trust only in offices, buildings or traditions, but in a sincere and obedient faith.
exp.51:24:
At the fall of Jerusalem, the Babylonians took prisoner several important men of the city. Among them was a eunuch, an officer who commanded the soldiers, and seven men who were close to the king, that is, counselors who were always near him. They also took the chief scribe of the army, the one in charge of enlisting people for the war, and sixty ordinary men of the people.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks, recording the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon, around 586 B.C. Nebuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, removed the leaders who could organize resistance again. The text presents this as the consequence of years of disobedience, just as Jeremiah had warned.

For today: God speaks to us patiently before the consequences arrive. Today we can listen to His Word and correct our course in time, trusting in His mercy.
exp.51:25:
He says that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of Babylon, gathered the important prisoners from Jerusalem (priests, officials and other men) and brought them to the king of Babylon, who was at Riblah. "Captain of the guard" was a high military commander.

The chapter tells, as a historical account, the fall of Jerusalem in the time of King Zedekiah. Jeremiah had warned for years that the people would be judged for their disobedience and for not listening to God. Here the announced judgment is seen fulfilled: the religious and military leaders are taken away as prisoners and executed at Riblah, in the land of Hamath.

For today: God speaks seriously, but he is also faithful to his word. If today we sense his call to correct something in our lives, it is better to listen in time and return to him with humility, without waiting for the consequences to arrive.
exp.51:27:
This verse begins a list of the Jews whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away, that is, took into exile in Babylon. It says that in his seventh year there were 3,023 people. It is a brief record, with precise figures.

Jeremiah 52 is a historical appendix that reviews the fall of Jerusalem. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Some think it was Jeremiah or one of his associates. The dates and numbers differ from other biblical accounts, and many scholars explain this by different ways of counting the years. The purpose seems to be to leave a record that what God had warned through the prophets was fulfilled.

For today: God does not overlook the pain of his people, not even when it is reduced to figures. You can trust that He sees your situation, and his word deserves to be taken seriously and with humility.
exp.51:29:
This verse says that in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried away captive 745 people from Judah. Adding up all the groups mentioned, the total was 4,600 people. "Carried away" means he took them into exile in another land.

The author, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though some think this appendix was added by another hand, closes the book with a record of the exiles. The figures are lower than others that appear in the Old Testament, and it is not known for certain why; various explanations have been proposed, such as that different groups were counted. What matters is that the prophecies of judgment were fulfilled. But the book ends with hope: King Jehoiachin is released from prison.

God keeps his word, and he also holds hope for his people. If you are going through a hard season today, trust that God sees every detail of your life and can still open a door of grace.
exp.51:31:
This verse says that Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, treated Jehoiachin, the king of Judah who was in prison, well. He spoke to him kindly and gave him a place of honor, higher than that of the other kings who were also living in exile there. "Kindly" means with good and gentle words. "Throne" here means a seat of honor, a place of importance.

This is the end of the book of Jeremiah. It is not God or the prophet who speaks here, but the account reports a historical event. Jehoiachin had been a captive for thirty-seven years. After so long, a new king brought him out of prison. Many understand this as a sign that God had not forgotten his people, although the text gives no further explanation.

For today: even in long and dark times, God can open an unexpected door. We keep waiting on Him, without losing hope.
exp.51:33:
This verse says that the king of Babylon gave Jehoiachin a daily provision of food, every day, for as long as he lived, until his death. The word for this daily allowance means a portion of food or sustenance. The phrase about receiving what was needed day by day means that he received what he needed each day.

The book ends with this historical detail, probably added by whoever gathered the words of Jeremiah. It tells that Evil-Merodach, king of Babylon, released Jehoiachin, king of Judah, after about 37 years in prison. Although he remained in exile, he was treated with kindness. Many see here a sign that the line of David had not disappeared, although the Bible does not explain this in detail at this point.

For today: even in times of loss or hard consequences, God can give small reliefs and daily sustenance. Learn to recognize and be thankful for those everyday provisions, and trust that God is still at work in your story, even when the outlook seems dark.
exp.47:43:
This verse says that Moab will not be able to escape God's judgment. Whoever flees from the panic will fall into the pit, a hole dug to trap animals. Whoever climbs out of the pit will be caught in the snare, a trap made of rope. The phrase "the year of their punishment" refers to the time when God brings judgment on them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel, had become proud against God; it grew arrogant and rose up against Him. For this reason He announces its downfall. The images show that every attempt to escape only leads to another danger.

For today: let us not trust in our own cleverness or strength to escape the consequences of living in pride. It is better to humble ourselves now, ask God for forgiveness, and seek His mercy, because He is just, but He also forgives those who turn back to Him.
exp.26:0:
The verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, son of Josiah, king of Judah. The phrase "this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD" means that the message came directly from God. Zedekiah reigned from about 597 to 586 B.C.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents Jeremiah receiving a divine command. A curious detail: the verses that follow speak of several nations and their kings, and the message concerns Judah's neighbors. Scholars continue to discuss how the chapter's dating fits with the reigns mentioned elsewhere in the book, and there is no complete agreement on every point.

For today: God speaks at specific moments in history, and he expects obedience even when his message is uncomfortable. Let us ask for attentive ears to hear him.
exp.21:13:
He says this man thinks: "I will build myself a great palace with spacious upper rooms." He cuts windows into it, panels it with cedar, and paints it a bright red. "Spacious upper rooms" are tall, showy halls; "vermilion" is a very striking red, a sign of luxury.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses the king of Judah who followed Josiah, probably Jehoiakim, although the text of this passage does not say so in full. He rebukes him because he was building his palace with other people's labor, without paying the workers. The problem is not the house, but the injustice with which he was building it.

For today: ask yourself whether what you achieve or build rests on justice. Pay with honesty, treat well those who work for you, and do not seek your own comfort at the expense of others. For God, knowing him is shown in how we treat the needy.
exp.3:18:
Jeremiah speaks in a pain so intense that he feels it throughout his body. "My anguish, my anguish!" and "the pain in my chest" describe the deepest kind of suffering. His heart pounds within him, and he cannot stay silent, because he has heard the sound of the horn, the alarm of battle.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, who sees judgment coming upon Judah for rebelling against God. Some think he speaks only out of his own pain, and others that he also expresses God's grief over his people. The text allows both readings. What is clear is that Jeremiah takes no pleasure in the punishment, but suffers because of it.

For today: when you see sin and its consequences, do not react with coldness or pride. Ask God for a heart that feels pain and prays for others.
exp.5:12:
It says that everyone in Jerusalem, from the lowest to the highest, was driven by greed, that is, by the desire to gain more at any cost. And the religious leaders, the prophet and the priest, instead of guiding the people, were practicing deceit. The word "deceit" speaks of falsehood and trickery.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the invasion of Babylon. God warns that judgment is coming because corruption had reached everyone. Most serious of all, those who should have taught the truth twisted it and said that all was well, as the next verse shows: "Peace, peace; when there is no peace."

Today it invites us to examine our hearts: do we seek to gain at any cost? It also encourages us to prefer the truth even when it is uncomfortable, and not to stay silent or disguise what is wrong, whether at work, in the family, or in the church.
exp.30:5:
This verse speaks of a future day when the watchmen posted on the hills of Ephraim will call out with joy. They will say, "Arise, let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God!" The watchmen are the lookouts who kept guard from high ground, Zion is Jerusalem, where the temple stood, and Ephraim names the tribes of the north.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises to restore Israel after the exile. The northern tribes had been divided and far from Jerusalem, but God announces that they will be brought back together to worship him together. Some see here a partial fulfillment in the return from exile, and others see a fuller fulfillment still to come.

For today: God knows how to gather what is divided and far away. We can draw near to him with hope, and we can encourage others to say, "Let us go together to seek the LORD."
exp.5:7:
This verse is an urgent call from God to Jerusalem: "Be forewarned" means take this warning seriously and change your course before it is too late. God warns that if she does not do so, he will turn away from her, that is, he will withdraw from her with grief and rejection. The result would be a city turned into a desolation, a land without inhabitant.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. An enemy army is about to surround the city, and God explains the reason: violence, injustice, and robbery abound inside Jerusalem, and the people do not want to hear his word. Even so, this warning shows that God still offers a chance to return to him.

For today: when a correction makes you uncomfortable, do not reject it right away. Ask God for humility to listen, and pay attention to the Bible or to wise counsel. God corrects because he wants to restore us, not destroy us.
exp.8:7:
Their tongues are like deadly arrows: they speak deception. The verse says that with his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him. The word translated "trap" here refers to hidden schemes or plots meant to harm someone.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah lived surrounded by lies and had stopped knowing God. Therefore the Lord announces that he will melt them down and test them, as metal is purified in the fire. At the same time his sorrow shows: he weeps over what will come upon the land.

For today: let us take care that our words match what is in the heart. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that our greetings and our affection are true, and not a mask that hides resentment.
exp.13:18:
This verse is a prayer full of pain. Questions are put to God: "Have You rejected Judah completely? Do You despise Zion?" To reject completely is to cast away, and to despise is to hold in contempt. Then they ask: "Why have You stricken us so that we are beyond healing?" They hoped for peace and well-being, but no good came, and terror arrived instead. Healing is restoration, and what they got was terror.

Here the people of Judah speak, and Jeremiah is often the one who puts that prayer into words. There is drought, famine and the sword, and the religious leaders did not understand what was happening. The next verse shows that the people acknowledge their sin and appeal to God's covenant.

For today: when you suffer and feel that God is far away, you can bring him your questions with honesty. But pray also with humility, acknowledging your faults and trusting in his faithfulness.
exp.47:18:
The people of Aroer are told to stand by the road and watch closely. There they will see those fleeing and those who have escaped passing by. They are to ask them, "What has happened?" The question here is the verse's own wording, and it is the thing they are to ask.

Aroer was a city of Moab, beside the river Arnon.

This is a prophecy from Jeremiah announcing God's judgment on Moab. The prophet describes the fall of Dibon and other cities. Aroer lies on the border, so it would be among the first places to see the refugees arrive. The verses just before it speak of pride and strength being broken. Its neighbors were to mourn.

For today, let us not wait until the crisis reaches us. We can learn from what others have lived through, listen to their warnings, and correct our course in time, with humility before God.
exp.41:21:
God, speaking through Jeremiah, tells them plainly that they will die by the sword, by famine and by plague. And it will happen in Egypt, the very place they were determined to go to settle down. Here "to settle down" means to make a home there as outsiders, and "plague" refers to a contagious sickness that kills many people.

Jeremiah speaks to the people who stayed in Judah after Jerusalem fell. They had asked him to pray for them and had promised to obey whatever God said. But they had already decided to flee to Egypt, and when God told them to stay, they refused to listen. That is why Jeremiah reminds them that they had made a promise they never intended to keep.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly seek the voice of God or only want Him to bless what we have already decided. Obeying is safer than running toward what only seems like a way out.
exp.7:4:
God sadly asks why the people of Jerusalem keep turning away and staying in rebellion without ever stopping. A turning away that never ends or changes shows a pattern of disobedience that never lets up. "They cling to deceit" means they held on to lies and false feelings of safety. "They refuse to return" means they would not come back to God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he asked whether someone who falls does not get up. In other words, the normal thing is to return to the right path. But the people did not turn back or admit their mistake. God points to the birds, which know when it is time to return, while his people ignore what God asks of them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are clinging to some comfortable lie, such as excuses or bad habits. Returning to God begins with admitting, "I was wrong." He welcomes anyone who comes back sincerely.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that the people admit their sins are a real charge against them. Even so, they ask God to act, not because they have earned it, but for the sake of his own name, meaning his reputation and his faithfulness. Their wrongdoing is called iniquities, and their repeated acts of rebellion are the failures they confess. They admit that these have piled up and that they have sinned against God.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the people of Judah during a severe drought. The animals are suffering for lack of grass, and the people cry out for help. Instead of defending themselves, they confess their guilt and rest on the character of God. The verses that follow show this, with the people saying: "Your name is called over us; do not leave us."

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses for yourself. Acknowledge your sin honestly and come to God trusting in his mercy, not in your own merits.
exp.2:23:
It says that "that shameful god" has consumed everything their fathers had worked for since they were young: their flocks and herds, their sons and daughters. The phrase "from our youth" refers to the time from their early years onward. The "shameful god" is the idol Baal, whom the people served; many scholars understand the name this way, though others read it only as a term of shame.

The speakers are repentant Israelites, in a confession that the prophet Jeremiah puts on their lips. They acknowledge that worshiping the gods of the hills cost them everything and gave them nothing. That is why they end by saying that salvation is found only in the LORD.

For today: whatever we place above God, whether money, success, or pleasure, ends up costing us dearly. Today you can examine where you are investing your best strength, and return to God, who truly heals and restores.
exp.50:37:
They will roar together like young lions, and they will growl like lion cubs. The word "together" means they act at the same time, all as one, and "roar" means to make a loud, fierce, powerful noise. The image is one of strength and pride.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the Lord says against Babylon. God promises to defend his people, who had suffered at the hands of that empire. The verses that follow show that this roaring will not save them: they will be led away like lambs to the slaughter. Some understand this roaring as their arrogance, others as their despair at the fall; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by the noise and arrogance of the powerful. Their strength does not last forever. Trust that God sees injustice, and leave justice in his hands, while you keep acting with humility and uprightness.
exp.32:1:
This verse says that the one speaking is the LORD, the God who made the earth and formed it, and that he formed it in order to establish it, that is, to make it firm and secure. It ends with a statement of identity: the LORD is his name.

Jeremiah is held prisoner in the courtyard of the guard, while Jerusalem faces the siege of Babylon. The houses are being torn down, and the people feel that everything is being lost. God speaks to the prophet a second time and presents himself as Creator and Lord of history. Some understand that "it" refers to Jerusalem; others, to the land in general. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when your situation seems to be falling apart, remember who God is. Before asking him for something, pause to recognize that he made, sustains, and can restore. That brings calm to pray with confidence, as he invites in the following verse.
exp.47:26:
God asks Moab: "Was not Israel your object of ridicule? Was he ever found among thieves, that you shake your head every time you speak of him?" He adds that whenever Moab spoke of Israel, Moab shook its head in contempt. "Object of ridicule" means a target of cruel mockery. The mention of Moab shaking its head points to a gesture of scorn toward Israel, though the exact meaning of the gesture is uncertain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. Moab had become full of pride and mocked Israel when things went badly for it. God takes this as an offense against himself, since Israel was his people, and so the punishment falls on Moab.

For today: God sees how we treat others, especially when they fall or suffer. Before we mock or criticize, let us ask him for a humble and compassionate heart, one that helps rather than despises.
exp.14:8:
The mother of seven will grow faint and lose all her strength, and in the end she will breathe her last. Her sun sets at midday, meaning her happiness ends suddenly and before its time. She is disgraced and humiliated. Those who remain, God will put to the sword in the presence of their enemies.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah did not turn back from their ways, and God announces judgment for that rejection. The mother probably represents the city or the nation; many understand it this way, though the verse does not say so with full clarity.

For today: God grieves when we ignore his call, but he always invites us to return. Do not harden your heart; if God speaks to you, respond today with humility and repentance.
exp.2:3:
God invites his people to come back to him. "From this time on" means "right now, even though it is late." God asks whether they will not call out to him, saying "My Father, you are my friend from youth." Here "friend" points to the relationship that has existed since the beginning of their life as a nation. "Call out" means reaching out to him for help.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Israel, who had turned away from him by worshiping idols, which is described as unfaithfulness in a marriage. God reminds them of their sins and of the drought as a sign of judgment, yet still opens the door to repentance. His words show both grief and patience.

For today: if you have turned away from God, do not wait until you are better before returning. Call out to him today with sincerity, as to a Father who is still waiting for you and wants to be near you again.
exp.32:14:
God says he will raise up from David's family a righteous Branch. A branch is a new shoot, a sprout that comes up from a trunk that seemed dead. This descendant of David will administer justice and righteousness throughout the land. The phrase "I will cause to sprout" shows that it is God who does this, not people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were living through a very hard time, with Jerusalem threatened or destroyed and exile near. God promises to restore the land and to fulfill his good word. Christians see in this Branch Jesus, a descendant of David. Jews have understood it in other ways, as an ideal future king.

For today: when everything seems dry or without a way out, trust that God knows how to bring forth life and justice. Wait on him, and seek to live with uprightness and righteousness in your home and at your work.
exp.26:14:
God says that He never sent those prophets. They speak as if they were speaking in His name, but they are speaking falsely. And that false message would have a terrible result: God would banish the people from their land, and they would perish, both they and the prophets who spoke to them. The word "banish" here means to force out or send away, and "perish" means to die or be destroyed.

Jeremiah spoke to King Zedekiah, to the priests, and to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. Through Jeremiah, God asked them to submit to Babylon in order to save their lives. But other prophets promised that everything would soon be settled and that the objects from the temple would return. It was a comfortable message, but a false one.

Today, do not believe something just because it sounds pleasant or claims to speak for God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray for wisdom, and listen with humility, even when the truth is difficult.
exp.48:0:
God asks the Ammonites whether Israel had no sons and no one to inherit the land. In other words, the land of Gad had rightful owners. Even so, Milcom has taken possession of Gad, and the Ammonites have settled in its cities. An inheritance is land received as a family's portion.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. It is a message against Ammon, Israel's neighbor east of the Jordan. The Ammonites took over territory belonging to the tribe of Gad, probably when part of Israel was taken into exile, though the text does not give all the details. God defends what he gave to his people and announces judgment.

For today: God sees injustice, even when someone takes advantage of another person's weakness. We can trust his justice and check that we are not holding on to what does not belong to us.
exp.36:17:
Here Jeremiah asks King Zedekiah a direct question: what wrong did he do to deserve being put in prison? The phrase "I have sinned against you" is not in this verse, so I have used the wording your verse does use, asking how he has sinned against the king, his servants, or the people. The phrase "they put me" is not quoted here either, so I will simply say that he was kept in prison.

Jeremiah is a prophet of God, and he speaks with the king, who had brought him out secretly to ask whether there was any word from the Lord. Jeremiah had already told him that Babylon would rule over them. They had imprisoned him for announcing that uncomfortable truth, while other prophets spoke only pleasing things.

For today: speaking the truth with respect can cost us dearly, but it remains the right thing to do. We can ask God for courage to be honest, without hatred or pride, and trust that He cares for those who are faithful to Him, even when they suffer injustice.
exp.38:0:
In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, marched against Jerusalem with his entire army and laid siege to the city, surrounding it with troops. To lay siege to a city means to cut off its exits and its supply of food to force it to surrender.

This is a historical account within the book of Jeremiah. The narrator describes the beginning of the siege, which lasted about two and a half years, until the walls fell, as the following text shows. Jeremiah had warned many times that this would happen if the people and their leaders did not return to God. Here that warning is seen coming true. The dates are counted by the years of Zedekiah's reign.

For today: God does what he says, both his warnings and his promises. If today we feel that God is calling us to correct something, it is better to listen in time and not wait for the consequences to arrive.
exp.4:30:
The passage says that the prophets were announcing lies in God's name, and that the priests ruled by their own authority. What is most troubling is that the people loved it that way. The question "but what will you do in the end?" points to what will happen when all of this reaches its final outcome. God asks the people directly: "What will you do in the end?"

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Judah was living in injustice and idolatry. Earlier, God says that he must hold accountable this "horrible and shameful thing." The problem was not only false leadership, but also a people who preferred comfortable messages. Some interpreters understand the priests' authority in different ways, but the central idea is clear.

Today, it is good to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible. Let us seek not only words that comfort us, but the truth that brings us near to God.
exp.33:14:
God reminds the people of Jerusalem that not long before, they had done something good: they had repented and set their servants free. Each one proclaimed freedom for his neighbor, and they made a covenant before God in the house that bears his name.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. The people freed their servants, as the law required, but afterward they enslaved them again. God holds them accountable for that betrayal, because they had made their promise before him.

Today, this passage invites us to keep what we promise to God and to others. A good beginning is not enough if we later turn back. Let us ask him for help to be faithful.
exp.45:18:
God tells Egypt to pack its bags, like someone who is about to be taken away into exile. Packing for exile means gathering up the belongings of people who will be carried off to live in another land. Memphis was a great Egyptian city, and the verse says it will be laid waste, destroyed, and left with no one living there.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. This message announces that Babylon would come against Egypt. Egypt trusted in its power and its reputation, but God warns that its sense of safety was false. Scholars connect this prophecy with the campaign of King Nebuchadnezzar, although the exact fulfillment is understood in different ways.

For today: let us not place our security in money, status, or our own strength. All of that can fall suddenly. Let us seek refuge in God, who remains firm, and live attentive to his voice before trouble arrives.
exp.39:14:
Johanan tells Gedaliah, privately and at Mizpah, that he is willing to go and kill Ishmael without anyone knowing. He asks why Gedaliah should let Ishmael take his life, because then the people of Judah who have gathered to him would be scattered and the rest of Judah would perish.

After the fall of Jerusalem, Babylon left Gedaliah in charge of those who remained in the land. Johanan and other military leaders warned him that the Ammonite king Baalis had sent Ishmael to assassinate him. Gedaliah did not believe them, so Johanan insists in private, concerned to protect the people who were left.

For today: when someone warns us of a danger, it is wise to listen with humility and to examine the facts in prayer. But we also learn that sincere concern does not justify settling a problem with violence or in secret. Let us seek wisdom and just ways.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the people used their tongues the way someone uses a bow: just as a bow sends an arrow, they sent out lies. Lies win out over truth in the land. They did not stand firm for the truth, but kept moving from one evil to the next. Saying they do not take God into account means that they did not truly want to know God or consider him in their lives.

God speaks here, and he does so with the grief of the prophet Jeremiah, who weeps for his people. Judah lived with deceit, injustice and unfaithfulness. The verses that follow show that there was no trust even among brothers or friends, because lies were everywhere.

For today: truthfulness is practiced in small things. Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true and whether it helps or hurts. Ask God to teach you to speak honestly, even when lying seems easier or more convenient.
exp.15:7:
It says God commands Jeremiah not to enter a house where there is a feast, nor to sit down with the people to eat and drink. A feast means a banquet or party. "Likewise" would mean "in the same way," since earlier God had already told him not to marry and not to attend funerals.

God speaks, addressing the prophet Jeremiah. His solitary life was a sign to the people: soon a judgment so great would come that there would no longer be ordinary weddings, feasts, or funerals. God wanted the people to wake up and return to Him before it was too late.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly. Take a moment to listen to His voice and correct whatever needs correcting, instead of carrying on as if nothing were happening. He warns because He desires to restore, not merely to punish.
exp.30:37:
This verse says that days are coming when Jerusalem will be rebuilt and given to the Lord, that is, set apart for him. Its boundaries are marked: from the tower of Hananel, on the north side, to the Corner Gate, which was probably on the northwest side. The phrase "rebuilt for Me" means that the city will belong to him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the section known as "the book of comfort." The people were under judgment and would soon be taken into exile. Even so, God promises restoration and a new covenant. The verses before this one assure that God will not completely reject Israel. The boundaries mentioned show that the promise is concrete. Some see it fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also look for its fulfillment in the future.

For today: God keeps what he promises even when everything seems to be in ruins. Today you can entrust your broken areas to him and ask him to rebuild them for himself.
exp.24:37:
God comes out of his den like a lion to bring judgment. A "den" is the hiding place where the lion lives. "Laid waste" means destroyed and left in ruins. The "sword of the oppressor" and "fierce anger" speak of strong, violent judgment. In this verse, the land is ruined because of that anger. Some scholars think "the oppressor" refers to Babylon, and others to God's own judgment itself; the phrase can be understood in either way.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. This chapter closes a long warning to Judah and the nations: they did not listen to the prophets, and judgment would come. The "shepherds" are the kings and leaders, who now mourn because their people, like a flock, are being destroyed.

For today: God is patient, but he does not ignore injustice. If this gets your attention, do not harden your heart; listen to him today and turn your path around with humility.
exp.41:15:
This verse says that the things the people want to escape by going to Egypt, the sword of war and the famine, will catch up with them right there. In the verse, "the sword" is the same danger the people already fear: the sword you fear will overtake you there in Egypt. The famine will follow on their heels, not letting them go. And "you will die there" is a serious warning: running away on their own will not save them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the remnant of Judah asked God for guidance, but they had already decided to go to Egypt out of fear of Babylon. God had told them to stay in the land, and here he shows them that disobeying would not bring them safety.

For today: sometimes we look for safety in our own solution, even when God has already shown us another path. Before deciding out of fear, it is wise to pray, listen to his Word, and obey, trusting that his direction is safer than our plans.
exp.19:12:
This verse is an invitation to sing and praise the LORD. The reason given is that He rescues the life of the needy from the hands of evildoers.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah. He had just suffered blows and humiliation for announcing God's message. Even so, he expresses his confidence that God is with him. It is striking that, just after this, in the verses that follow, Jeremiah goes so far as to curse the day of his birth. This shows that faith and deep sorrow can live together in the same person. Some understand this praise as a certainty of faith, and others as a brief moment of relief.

For today: even when the distress has not passed, you can choose to praise God for what you already know of Him. Be honest with God in your pain, and also thank Him for His care.
exp.37:6:
This verse tells how Ebed-melech, a Cushite man who served as a court official in the royal palace, learned that Jeremiah had been put into the cistern, which was a deep pit. At that moment the king was sitting at the Gate of Benjamin, one of the gates of Jerusalem.

The narrator recounts how Jeremiah, for announcing God's message, was thrown into the mud by the leaders of Jerusalem. Ebed-melech, a foreigner, is the one who becomes aware of it and decides to act. The king was in a public place, where he could be spoken to.

Today, when we see an injustice, we do not need to hold an important position to speak up. Ebed-melech encourages us to raise our voices boldly on behalf of those who suffer.
exp.43:8:
Here God asks a pointed question: "Have you forgotten?" He reminds them of the wickedness of their fathers, of the kings of Judah and their wives, and of themselves and their wives, committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. "Wickedness" here means evil deeds, above all idolatry.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews who had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. There they were still offering incense to other gods. God reminds them that this same idolatry had already brought judgment on their land, and warns them that repeating it will bring them further ruin.

For today: forgetting the past leads us to repeat the same mistakes. It is worth remembering our falls with humility, and the lessons God has given us, so that we return to Him sincerely and do not insist on paths that have already done us harm.
exp.33:8:
This verse says that every Israelite was to set free his Hebrew male and female slaves. No Jew was to keep another Jew in bondage, because they were fellow countrymen. "Slave" here means a person held to forced labor without freedom. The idea of freeing them means releasing them from that service.

Jerusalem was under siege by the army of Babylon. King Zedekiah made a covenant with the people to proclaim liberty. Jeremiah receives this word from God about that agreement. Some think the people acted out of fear and convenience, since the Bible does not fully explain it. What is certain is that afterward they changed their minds and enslaved them again.

For today: keep what you promise, especially when it comes to treating others with justice. Obeying God should not depend on the pressure of the moment, but on a heart that truly respects people.
exp.20:12:
God speaks directly to Jerusalem and declares that he is against her. He addresses the city as the one who dwells above the valley and sits atop the rocky plateau, a vivid way of describing a city settled on high, rocky ground. The people feel secure and ask: "Who can come against us? Who can enter our dwellings?"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the days before Jerusalem fell. Earlier he had called the house of David to practice justice and rescue the oppressed. Since they did not obey, he now confronts them for their false confidence. Some believe the phrase "dwell above the valley" refers to the city itself; others, to its location. It is not entirely clear.

For today: do not trust in your security, your position, or your resources. Practice justice and help those who suffer, because God looks at the heart.
exp.10:10:
This verse is a warning from God. He says he is about to bring a disaster upon the people, one they cannot escape. When they cry out to him for help, he will not listen to them. Here "disaster" is the word for calamity, and "will not listen" means he will not answer their plea.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah and Jerusalem had broken the covenant that God made with their ancestors, for they went after other gods and refused to listen. For this reason the Lord announces the consequences. Then he tells them that the idols they worshiped will not be able to save them.

For today: it is not enough to seek God only when trouble comes. It is good to listen to him and to be faithful to him in everyday life, and if we have drifted away, to return to him sincerely today, without waiting for a crisis to arrive.
exp.0:16:
God tells Jeremiah to get ready and to get moving. "Get yourself ready" means he should prepare himself for the task, and "stand up" calls him to act. God orders him to tell the people everything God commands him, without holding anything back. The last sentence warns that if Jeremiah is intimidated by them, God would let him be terrified in front of them.

The Lord speaks to the young Jeremiah as he calls him to be a prophet. Judah had turned away from God to worship idols, and Jeremiah was to announce the judgment that would come from the north. God promises that he will be with him, even though they will attack him.

For today: when God asks you to say or do something right, prepare yourself with prayer and determination, and do not let fear of what others think hold you back. Trust that his presence sustains you.
exp.19:5:
Here God, through Jeremiah, tells Pashhur that he and his household will be taken away as prisoners to Babylon. There he will die and be buried, together with all his friends, to whom he had prophesied these lies. "Those who truly love you" means those who valued him or followed him. "Captives" means prisoners taken in war.

Pashhur was a priest and a senior official of the temple. He had struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks because he did not like his message of judgment. Jeremiah answers with the word of God, and this appears as an announcement of the Babylonian exile. Pashhur was saying that everything was fine, but God was saying the opposite.

For today: let us not look only for words that make us feel comfortable. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his truth, even when it hurts, because true restoration comes from it.
exp.3:21:
It says that God's people acted with foolishness. A "fool" is someone without good sense, who ignores what matters. The "foolish children" did not truly know God. They were very skilled at doing evil, but they did not know how to do good. Those who are "without understanding" are the ones who lack discernment.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. God grieves because he announces an invasion that will leave the land destroyed. The nearby verses use images of desolation, and many read them as a poetic way of showing how serious the judgment is. God explains the cause: his people did not know him.

For today: intelligence is not always wisdom. We can be very clever at business or personal advantage and still ignore God. Ask him to teach you to know him and to practice good, not just to know about him.
exp.41:4:
Here the people promise Jeremiah that they will obey everything God tells him to say. They ask that the Lord be a faithful witness against them, meaning a witness who will hold them accountable if they do not keep their word. It is a solemn vow, and their wording makes plain that they are binding themselves to act on every word God sends through Jeremiah.

The speakers are the army leaders and all the people who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. They are afraid of the Babylonians and want to know whether they should flee to Egypt. They ask Jeremiah to pray for them. Later in the text, when God answers, they do not accept his answer (chapter 43). This suggests that their promise was not sincere.

It is easy to say "I will do whatever God says" before you know what he will say. Before asking God for direction, ask yourself whether you are truly willing to obey, even if the answer is not the one you hoped for.
exp.1:30:
God calls his people to attention: "You people of this generation, consider the word of the LORD." He asks whether he has been a wilderness to Israel, an empty and lonely place, or a land of dense darkness, a place with no hope. Then he asks why his people say, "We are free to roam; we will come to You no more."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had left him to follow other gods and trust in themselves, even though he had cared for them and corrected them. His question is not seeking a technical answer; it reveals a wounded heart and shows that their abandonment had no just cause. The verses that follow show that they forgot him for a long time.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we drift away from God believing we do not need him. Remembering how he has cared for us helps us return to him with trust and humility.
exp.28:17:
God says he will pursue the people who stayed in Jerusalem with sword, famine, and plague. He will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, a curse, a desolation, and an object of scorn and reproach among all the nations where he banishes them. They will be remembered in this way wherever they are scattered.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Some of the people had already been taken to Babylon, while King Zedekiah and others stayed behind in Jerusalem. They thought they were safe, but God compares them to rotten figs. The reason is given in the next verse: they did not listen to the prophets whom God sent to them again and again.

For today: when God speaks to us, whether through his Word or through others, we should not harden our hearts or feel secure without reason. Listening and obeying in time spares us much pain.
exp.32:13:
He says that God promises to fulfill the gracious promise he has spoken to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. "Behold, the days are coming" means that the time is on its way. "When I will fulfill" means that he will make the promise come true.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem and Judah lay in ruins because of God's judgment, and the people felt that everything was lost. God answers with hope: there will be shepherds and flocks again, and a righteous branch will come, a descendant of David. Many Christians see in him Jesus.

For today: when your situation seems like a desert, do not lean on what you can see, but on the faithfulness of God. He keeps what he promises, even though sometimes it takes longer than we expect. Today, remember one of his promises and trust in it.
exp.50:13:
God makes a solemn oath, swearing by himself, which means by the most serious thing he can swear by. He promises that he will fill Babylon with men, as many as locusts, a swarm that covers everything. Those enemies will shout in triumph, the cry of an army that has won the battle.

Jeremiah announces God's judgment against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed his people. God himself speaks and declares that this rich and proud city has reached its limit: the measure of your greed. The verses that follow remind us that the one who makes this promise is the Creator of all things.

For today: no human power, however rich or strong it may seem, stands above God. We can rest in knowing that he sees injustice and fulfills his word in his time, and we can also examine whether our own greed needs to be corrected.
exp.14:20:
God promises Jeremiah: "I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless." The words "deliver" and "redeem" are the verse's own wording, and in this verse "redeem" means to free or save someone from danger.

The Lord speaks, and answers Jeremiah, who felt alone and rejected for preaching a message that no one wanted to hear. God had asked him to be faithful and not to be swept along by the pressure of the people. Now He assures him that, although they attack him, they will not overcome him, because God is with him.

For today: when being faithful to God brings opposition or loneliness, do not rely on your own strength. Pray, keep doing what is right, and remember that God walks with you and knows how to care for you, even when it is not always in the way you expect.
exp.32:25:
This verse continues the thought of the previous verse: "If my covenant with day and night does not stand, then I would also reject the descendants of Jacob and of My servant David." In other words, God is saying that rejecting them would be as unthinkable as the breaking of his covenant with day and night. Because the order of creation remains firm, God promises to restore his people from captivity and to have compassion on them.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in captivity, and some were saying that God had rejected Israel and the family of David. God answers with a promise of restoration.

For today: when you feel that your failures or your hard times have pulled you away from God, look at the sunrise and the sunset. God sustains his creation faithfully, and he also keeps his promises. Return to him with confidence.
exp.30:32:
God makes a promise of a new covenant with Israel. Instead of a law written on stone, he says he will put it in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. He says the law will be placed within the deepest part of their being, and written where their desires and choices come from. The promise ends with the familiar words he has long spoken: "I will be their God, and they will be My people."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in a time of crisis, when Judah was facing judgment for breaking the earlier covenant made at Sinai. In the middle of that punishment, God announces hope: a new covenant based on forgiveness and on a personal knowledge of God. The New Testament takes up this promise again, especially in Hebrews 8.

For today: it is not enough to keep rules on the outside. Ask God to transform your heart, and spend time in his Word so that he shapes you from within.
exp.46:2:
This verse says that the sound of the galloping hooves of the stallions, the rumbling of the chariots and the clatter of their wheels will be so terrible that the fathers, overcome with panic, will not even turn back for their sons. Their hands will hang limp, a picture of the weakness that fear brings.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the Philistines. He announces a judgment coming from the north like a flood. Scholars often see there an invading army, and many think of Babylon, although the text does not give the name. The passage shows that God rules over all nations, not only over Israel.

For today: let us not place our security in the strength, power or resources of this world, because they can vanish. Let us trust in God, who remains a firm refuge when everything shakes.
exp.33:7:
This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after King Zedekiah had made an agreement with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim liberty to them. The agreement consisted of proclaiming liberty, that is, publicly announcing that the Hebrew slaves would be set free. An agreement like this is a binding promise made between the king and the people.

The army of Babylon was attacking Jerusalem and the few strong cities that remained in Judah. Jeremiah, the prophet, spoke on behalf of God to the king. The verses that follow say that the leaders and the people obeyed and freed their servants. Historians and commentators do not agree on the exact reasons, but the danger of the siege probably weighed heavily.
