For today: doing what is right should not depend only on crises. We can ask whether there is some injustice that God is calling us to correct, and do it steadily, not only when we are afraid or under pressure.
exp.38:8:
This verse tells that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard for the king of Babylon, led into Babylon those who were left in Jerusalem. He also took the deserters who had defected to him. The phrase "carried away" simply means "took them far away," and "defected to him" means they had switched sides and joined the Babylonians.

Here the narrator of the book is recounting the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. For years, Jeremiah had warned that this judgment would come because the people had disobeyed God. The verses before this one show the ruin of the city and the capture of King Zedekiah. Then a contrast appears: the poorest people were left behind and received land.

For today: God is serious when he warns, but he also cares for the humble. Listen to his voice in time, before the consequences arrive.
exp.47:31:
God says he will weep for Sibmah, a place in Moab famous for its vineyards. He compares his weeping to that of Jazer, another town nearby. The "tendrils" are the long shoots of the vine, which spread so far that they seemed to reach out to the "sea" (probably the Dead Sea, though some understand it differently). The "summer fruit" is the summer harvest, and the "grape harvest" is the crop of grapes gathered in the fall. A "destroyer" came and swept everything away.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Moab for its pride and its trust in itself. What is striking is that God takes no pleasure in it: he says he will weep and mourn for them, even though he judges them.

For today: God is just, but he also has compassion. When we see someone fall because of their mistakes, we should not celebrate. Better to pray for that person and show a tender heart, like God's.
exp.2:11:
God tells the prophet to go and announce this message toward the north: "Come back, faithless Israel. I will no longer look on you with anger, because I am merciful. I will not stay angry forever." The phrase "toward the north" points to the direction the message is to be sent, and "faithless" describes someone who has turned away from God and remained unfaithful.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had been taken captive by Assyria, and the message is directed toward that region. Even so, God offers them the chance to return. Judah, the southern kingdom, had seen that punishment and still carried on with a false repentance. But God asks that Israel acknowledge its sin.

Today we can draw near to God without fear of eternal rejection, but with sincerity. If you have walked away, acknowledge what you did and return. His mercy is a real invitation.
exp.30:27:
This verse says that God watched over his people with the same close attention when judgment came as he now promises for rebuilding. In the Berean Standard Bible wording, God watched over them to uproot and tear down, to demolish, destroy, and bring disaster. Now God promises that same devoted care for building and planting.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel and Judah had suffered judgment, above all through the exile in Babylon. Chapters 30 and 31 are a message of comfort and hope. God announces that punishment will not be the final word, but that there will be restoration and a new beginning.

For today: if you are going through a season of loss or correction, do not conclude that God has abandoned you. He is as faithful to build up as he was to discipline. Place your ruins in his hands, trust his timing, and cooperate with what he wants to build in you.
exp.1:33:
God says that the blood of the innocent poor is found on the edges of the people's clothing, that is, in plain sight of everyone. The edges of the garment are the hems. The phrase about breaking in probably refers to a break-in, as a thief would make at night. God did not catch them hiding: the guilt was in full view.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Earlier, he rebuked them for forgetting him, something unthinkable, like a bride who forgets her dress. Now he accuses them of injustice and violence against the weak. And yet, in spite of all these things, they say: "I am innocent."

Today, let us ask God to show us whether our decisions harm others, especially the most vulnerable. Acknowledging sin with humility is better than justifying ourselves.
exp.31:30:
God says that Jerusalem, from the day it was built until now, has aroused his wrath and fury. Therefore he announces that he will remove it from his presence. The phrase about removing it means that he will take it away from before him.

God spoke through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the Chaldeans (Babylonians) destroyed Jerusalem. The people had worshiped Baal and other gods, and they had not listened to God's warnings. Some scholars understand the words "from the day it was built" as a strong expression that sums up a long history of disobedience, not as an exact date.

God is patient and speaks to us again and again, but he is not indifferent to sin. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has pointed out to me that I have let pass? Listening in time and correcting our course is a sign of humility and of love toward him.
exp.45:23:
Egypt, called here "the Daughter of Egypt," is said to be left humbled and without defense. The verse's word "put to shame" means that it will suffer disgrace and dishonor. The phrase "the people of the north" refers to a people who would come from the north and gain control over it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Egypt, a power that trusted in its own strength, will be defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who came from the north. The text compares the army to locusts and woodcutters to show that they would be many and unstoppable. God also promises that, afterward, Egypt will be inhabited again.

For today: let us not place our final trust in power, money, or prestige, for these can fall. Let us rest in God, who rules over all and also restores.
exp.28:3:
This verse is the opening of a letter. It says that the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, speaks to all the exiles who were carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon. The verse shows that God addresses this whole group of people in their exile.

The prophet Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem, after the first deportation under King Jehoiachin. The letter is carried by two men sent to Babylon by King Zedekiah. The exiles expected to return soon, and God gives them instructions for a long stay.

God can speak to us and guide us even in places we did not choose. Instead of living while waiting for everything to pass, you can serve him today and do good in your present situation, trusting that he remains with you.
exp.31:39:
It says God will make an everlasting covenant with his people, meaning a promise that never comes to an end. "I will never turn away from doing good to them" means he will not back out of it or stop doing good for them. Furthermore, God will put his fear in their hearts, a reverent and loving awe of him, so that they will never turn away from him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were about to be taken captive to Babylon because of their disobedience. Even so, God promises restoration. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of the new covenant, though this passage speaks first to Israel.

For today: if you feel weak or afraid of drifting away from God, remember that he does not only ask for faithfulness but also works in your heart. Pray each day, "Lord, keep my heart close to you," and trust that he sustains what he has begun.
exp.29:12:
It says that no one stands up to plead the people's case so they can be healed, and that there is no remedy that brings recovery. It is an image of a serious wound: no one tends to it, and no treatment closes it. To "plead your cause" means to defend or take charge of a case; "remedy for your sores" is a treatment that actually works; "recovery" is restoration to health.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Israel and Judah, who faced the punishment of exile for their sin. God describes their condition as a wound that cannot be healed by human means, and says that even their allies will not help them. But in verse 17 he promises to restore their health. He first shows the seriousness of the situation, so that the people will stop trusting in false help.

For today: when your problem has no human solution, do not fill yourself with excuses or false remedies. Honestly acknowledge your need and turn to God, who can heal what no one else can.
exp.45:25:
God says he will hand the Egyptians over to those who want to kill them: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his officers. The phrase "those who seek their lives" means they are trying to take away the Egyptians' lives. But he adds a promise: after this, Egypt will be inhabited again, as in days of old.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Egypt trusted in its pharaoh and its gods, and God announces that Babylon will defeat it. The verses that follow, by contrast, comfort Israel: although Israel will be punished, God will not destroy it completely. Some think the restoration of Egypt shows God's mercy even toward other nations; the text gives no further details.

For today: do not place your security in human powers, but in God, who governs history. If you are going through correction or loss now, remember that God's final word can be restoration.
exp.6:10:
Is God asking whether the temple, the house that bears his name, has become for the people like a den of robbers, that is, a hiding place where criminals feel safe? Then he adds, "Yes, I too have seen it," meaning that nothing escapes him. The phrase "bears my name" means that the place belongs to him and carries his name.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were stealing, murdering, and worshiping Baal, and then they came to the temple as if the building would keep them safe. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh, an earlier place of worship that was destroyed because of the people's wickedness.

For today: going to church or using God's name does not replace an obedient life. Before we worship, let us honestly examine whether there is something we need to correct, ask forgiveness for, or make right, because God sees the heart.
exp.50:54:
It says that the Lord himself is destroying Babylon and will silence the mighty voice of the city: its noise, its pride, and its power. A "roar" is a loud noise. The enemy's "waves," or invaders, will roar, and the tumult of their voices will resound like great waters, that is, like a restless sea arriving with force.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the words of the Lord. The message is addressed to Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and taken God's people into captivity. Those people needed to hear that God had not lost control and that he would bring about justice. Scholars understand in different ways how and when each detail was fulfilled, but the central message is clear.

For today: no human power, however great and noisy it may seem, stands above God. If you are suffering from something unjust today, you can trust that God sees and that he has the last word. Bring your worry to him in prayer.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that God spoke directly to Jeremiah. The phrase "The word of the LORD came to me" means that the Lord's word reached him. Jeremiah does not invent the message; he states that he received it from God. Here his account of his calling as a prophet begins.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, in the first person. Earlier, the book explained that his ministry spanned about forty years, from the reign of Josiah until the fall of Jerusalem. With this verse, he moves on to tell how it all began. What follows is God's answer, in which He speaks of His purpose, and Jeremiah's reaction, in which he feels very young.

For today: God still speaks through His Word. Before wanting to do something for Him, we can stop and listen with humility. Opening the Bible with that desire changes the way we decide and the way we live.
exp.47:19:
Moab is put to shame because it has been shattered. The call to "wail and cry out" is a command to weep out loud, with grief. "Declare by the Arnon" is the instruction to announce the news of the ruin, so the word of the downfall would reach as far as the river Arnon, which marked the border of Moab. Here the phrase "that Moab is destroyed" means that the country has been completely ruined.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, delivering God's message against Moab, a neighboring country of Israel. The passage describes the fall of its cities, such as Dibon and Aroer, and the people who flee and report what has happened. Many understand that the judgment came because of Moab's pride and its trust in its fortresses and riches, something the same chapter mentions. The exact historical details of how it was fulfilled are debated.

For today: do not place your security in your achievements, money, or strength. All of that can fall. Seek humility before God, because only in Him is there a firm refuge.
exp.45:7:
Egypt rises like the Nile when its waters swell and overflow, and its army rises with pride. It boasts that it will cover the earth and destroy cities and the people who live in them.

Jeremiah speaks of the battle of Carchemish, beside the Euphrates River. Egypt went out confident, but it was defeated by Babylon. The prophet describes that arrogance to show that God rules over the nations. The verses that follow say that day belongs to the Lord. Historians place this battle around 605 BC.

For today: human plans may seem unstoppable, but they do not have the final word. Before boasting in your strength or your plans, place them in God's hands and live with humility.
exp.6:8:
God asks his people whether they can really steal, murder, commit adultery, and lie under oath. He also rebukes them for burning incense to Baal and following other gods they have not known. "Stealing" means taking what belongs to someone else, "adultery" means being unfaithful in marriage, "swearing falsely" means lying under oath, and burning incense means offering it in worship.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people believed they were safe simply because the temple was nearby, even though they lived in injustice and idolatry. God shows them that their religion was a facade. The verses that follow say that it is not enough to come to the temple and say "we are safe" if the heart remains in sin.

Today the message is clear: attending church or speaking well of the faith does not replace an honest life. Ask God to align your actions from Monday to Saturday with what you say on Sunday.
exp.9:15:
God is not like the idols at all. The phrase "the portion of Jacob" refers to the people of Israel, who belong to God and are his own possession. He is the Maker of all things, and Israel is "the tribe of his inheritance," that is, the people who belong to him, set apart as his own. His name is the LORD of Hosts, the Lord of all power.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, sent by God to Judah. Earlier he mocked the idols made by craftsmen: they have no life and no breath. Now he sets those lifeless things against the living God. Then comes a warning that judgment and exile were drawing near, because the people had trusted in what was false.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, success, or the opinions of others. All of these fail. Rest in the God who made you and calls you his own.
exp.48:11:
God says that he will judge Edom. He speaks of the "cup" as an image of punishment, something bitter that must be drunk. If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, Edom will not escape. "Remain unpunished" means being left without consequence. "Must" means it is certain to happen.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Edom, the people descended from Esau. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and, according to other passages in the Bible, showed hostility when Judah fell. Here God announces that his judgment reaches all the nations, and the context adds a comfort: he cares for orphans and widows.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with indifference. If he judges with justice, we can leave in his hands the injustices we suffer, instead of seeking revenge, and examine our own hearts with humility.
exp.31:1:
This verse says that Jerusalem was surrounded by the army of the king of Babylon, and that the prophet Jeremiah was imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, an area under watch inside the royal palace. The word "imprisoned" means held in custody, kept from going out or coming in.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, describing the situation in which Jeremiah received a word from God, in the tenth year of King Zedekiah. The king had locked him up because Jeremiah was announcing that the city would fall into the hands of Babylon. Jeremiah was in prison for saying what God commanded him to say, even though nobody liked it.

For today: the truth of God does not lose its value by being surrounded by problems or rejection. Even when everything seems closed off, we can remain faithful and trust that God is still speaking and working. Ask him today for the courage to be honest and faithful.
exp.19:9:
Jeremiah says he has heard the whispering of many people. The phrase "Terror is on every side!" was something he had used as a warning. Now his enemies throw it back at him. They say, "Report him, and let us report him." Even his trusted friends were watching for him to fall, that is, to slip up or make a mistake. They hoped he would be deceived, overcome, and that they could take vengeance on him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. His message of judgment on Judah brought him mockery, rejection, and betrayal, even from people close to him. Just before this, the priest Pashhur had beaten him and put him in prison. Jeremiah felt worn out, but the word of God burned within him and he could not keep silent.

For today: if you are criticized or abandoned for doing what is right, do not hide your pain. Bring it honestly before God, as Jeremiah did, and ask him for strength to remain faithful. He sustains those who trust in him.
exp.2:21:
God calls his unfaithful people: "Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness." The word "return" means to turn back, to change direction. The word "heal" speaks of healing a wound of the soul. The people answer: "Here we are. We come to You, for You are the LORD our God."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been unfaithful to him, like a wife who betrays her husband, and had sought help from idols on the hills. Even so, God does not reject them: he invites them to come back. The verses that follow say that those idols are worthless and that salvation is found only in God.

For today: if you feel far from God, do not wait to get yourself in order first. Come back just as you are, with sincerity, and acknowledge that only he can heal what is broken in you.
exp.27:8:
Jeremiah says that a prophet who announces peace will only be recognized as one the Lord has truly sent if his word comes true. The verse speaks of the prophet's word coming true, so that fact is what this phrase shows. Until that happens, his message still has to be tested by time.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, in front of all the people. He had put a wooden yoke on his neck to show that Judah must submit to Babylon. Hananiah, another prophet, opposed him and promised a quick peace. Jeremiah responds calmly: the earlier prophets often warned of war and disaster, so a message of peace needed a greater test. Then Hananiah breaks the yoke.

Today, not every pleasant message comes from God. Compare what you hear with Scripture, be patient, and examine whether it comes true, without being carried away only by what comforts you.
exp.50:18:
The portion of Jacob is not like these idols, because he is the Maker of all things. The people of Israel are the tribe of his inheritance, the people who belong to him. His name is the LORD of Hosts, the Lord who commands all power.

Jeremiah announces judgment against Babylon. Earlier in the chapter, the text shows that the idols made by craftsmen are false and have no life. Here it contrasts the true God with them, and reminds his people that they are not abandoned. Who the hammer of the following verse is has been interpreted in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, success, or things we ourselves have built. God is the Maker of all things and can be our true inheritance. Trust in him.
exp.6:32:
This verse says that the bodies of the dead of Judah will be left lying out, without burial. The birds and the wild animals will eat them, and no one will chase them away. "Chase away" here means to drive them off or send them away.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had built high places at Topheth, in the valley of Hinnom, where they burned their sons in the fire, something God says he never commanded. Therefore he announces judgment: there will be so many dead that the place will be called the Valley of Slaughter. Being left unburied was a great dishonor in that time. The next verse speaks of the end of joy and of weddings.

For today: God takes human life and true worship seriously. We can examine whether what we do in the name of faith truly pleases him, according to his Word. And we can turn back to him with humility, knowing that his judgment is serious, but that he always calls people to repentance.
exp.15:10:
God tells Jeremiah what to answer when the people ask why such a great punishment is coming. The reason is that their ancestors abandoned God, followed other gods (false gods of other nations), served them, and worshiped them, that is, they bowed low before them. They abandoned God and did not keep his instruction.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. The people believed they were innocent and asked what wrong they had done. God reminds them that idolatry went back many generations, and the next verse says that they were doing even worse.

For today: it is not enough to say "I have done nothing wrong." It is worth asking ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts, such as money, success, or comfort, and listening again to his Word with sincerity.
exp.25:10:
The priests and the prophets accuse Jeremiah before the officials and all the people. They say he deserves death, because he has spoken against the city and announced its destruction. "Officials" refers to the leaders in charge. "Deserves" means they believe he has already earned that punishment. "Destruction" means the city would be stripped bare and ruined.

Jeremiah had preached in the temple that, if the people did not turn back to God, Jerusalem would become like Shiloh, a place where the sanctuary once stood and which now lies in ruins. The priests and the prophets felt attacked, since they believed the temple protected the city. They make the accusation, and the officials will act as judges.

For today: sometimes the truth that calls us to change makes us uncomfortable, and we prefer to silence the one who speaks it. Let us ask God for humility to listen to correction, instead of defending ourselves or attacking the messenger.
exp.1:7:
The verse describes the failure of Israel's spiritual leaders. The priests did not ask, "Where is the LORD?" The experts in the law no longer knew God. The leaders rebelled against him. The prophets spoke in the name of Baal, a false god, and followed useless idols.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just recalled how he rescued his people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. But the people, and especially their leaders, turned away from God and went after idols. For this reason God brings them to judgment, as in a lawsuit.

Today, it is not enough to hold an office, have knowledge, or keep religious customs. Ask yourself honestly: "Where is God in my life?" Seek to know him truly, not just to talk about him.
exp.50:12:
Jeremiah 51:13 speaks of Babylon, the city that lies by many waters (its canals and rivers) and is rich in treasures. The verse declares that her end has already come. Her greed has reached its limit, or, as the image of the thread suggests, God has measured out her life and cut it off, just as a thread is cut.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and to the nations. He announces that Babylon, which had harmed his people and his temple, will be judged. He names the kings of the Medes as the instrument of that judgment. The text presents this as the justice of God, not as a mere political event.

For today: riches and power do not protect us forever. It is worth asking ourselves whether greed is directing our decisions, and learning to trust God, to be generous, and to live with honesty, knowing that he is the true Judge.
exp.3:25:
Jeremiah says he looked and saw a vision: Mount Carmel, a fruitful hill full of greenery, had become a desert. Its cities lay torn down before the LORD, before his fierce anger. The word "torn down" in this verse means completely laid waste, reduced to nothing. The phrase "fierce anger" speaks of a very strong wrath against sin.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet, and God shows him what the land of Judah would become because of its rebellion and idolatry. It is a warning of judgment, probably through an invader from the north. But the following verse makes clear that God will not make a full end of his people.

For today: do not take lightly God's call to return to him. His patience is real, but we must not take advantage of it. Today you can examine your life, repent of what you know displeases him, and trust in his mercy.
exp.10:6:
God says that He strongly warned the ancestors of Israel, from the day He brought them out of Egypt until today. The word "warned" here means that He spoke to them with great seriousness. "Again and again" means that He kept repeating the warning, over and over, without stopping. His message was simple: "Obey My voice."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah and of Jerusalem. He reminds them of the covenant He made with their fathers when He brought them out of Egypt. He does this because the people had turned away from Him. The verses that follow show that they also refused to listen, and for that reason the consequences of the covenant they failed to keep would come upon them.

God does not speak once and then withdraw; He insists with patience because He loves us. Today we can ask ourselves: am I listening to His voice in the Bible, in prayer, and in my conscience? Listening is not enough; we must obey. This week, read a passage calmly and put into practice one thing it shows you.
exp.34:15:
This verse says that the descendants of Jonadab, son of Rechab, faithfully kept their forefather's command, which was not to drink wine. In contrast, the people of Judah did not listen to God. The phrase "carried out" in the verse means they kept the command and followed it through without changing it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. God told Jeremiah to offer wine to the Rechabites, and they refused out of loyalty to their ancestor. God uses this example to show Judah's disobedience. If a family obeyed a human forefather for generations, how much more should the people obey God, who spoke to them again and again through his prophets?

For today: look at an area where you know what God asks of you but have gradually let it slide. Choose one concrete step of obedience and take it this week, with humility and trust in his care.
exp.9:6:
Who would not fear and honor God, the King of the nations, that is, of all the peoples on earth? The phrase "this is your due" means that this fear and honor rightly belong to him. No one among the wisest of the nations, and no one in any of their kingdoms, is equal to God.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, addressing God in the middle of a message to the people of Israel. Earlier, he mocked the idols: they are like scarecrows, they cannot speak or walk, and they can do neither good nor harm. Jeremiah sets that powerlessness against the greatness of the living God, so that his people would not copy the religious customs of the nations.

For today: when you feel pressure to trust in money, success, or the opinion of others, remember that none of these compares to God. Take a moment today to thank him and to put him first.
exp.43:10:
This verse says that the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, has set himself against those who remained in Judah. "I will set My face to bring disaster" means he has decided to act against them and not in their favor. "To cut off all Judah" refers to the rest of the people who still lived there.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and there they continued to worship other gods. God reminds them that their fathers, their kings, and they themselves did not turn back from their sins or live by his law. His warnings were ignored again and again.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God corrects us. If he points out something to us, it is better to repent soon and return to him, rather than look for security somewhere else.
exp.51:9:
This verse says that the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, had the sons of Zedekiah killed right in front of their father. He also had all the officials of Judah killed, at a place called Riblah.

The verse says "slaughtered," and the verse reflects that word. "Officials" here means the leaders and authorities of the nation.

The book ends with a historical account of the fall of Jerusalem. It is told as a fact, probably to show that the warnings Jeremiah had given for years were fulfilled. Zedekiah had been king of Judah, and his flight ended in capture and punishment. Afterward his eyes were put out, so the last thing he saw was the death of his sons.

For today: This passage reminds us that ignoring the voice of God has painful consequences, and that our decisions affect others, especially our own family. Today we can listen to God with humility and obey him in time.
exp.1:1:
God tells Jeremiah to go and speak out loud to Jerusalem. The message is that God remembers her with affection. The words "devotion" and "love as a bride" are the key ideas: devotion is the eager loyalty of early years, and love as a bride describes the commitment shared before a wedding. God recalls how his people followed him through the wilderness, a place without crops and without security.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At the start of his ministry, God presents his relationship with Israel as a courtship. Before he rebukes her unfaithfulness, he recalls her first devotion. The verses that follow show that Israel was holy to God, and that those who harmed her would be judged.

Today, we can ask ourselves how our first love for God is doing. Even if we have grown cold, he remembers our beginnings with tenderness and invites us to return with confidence, without fear.
exp.47:32:
The passage says that in Moab the harvest celebration will come to an end. Joy and gladness will be removed from the orchards and fields, and the flow of wine from the presses will stop. Before, the grapes were trodden with shouts of joy; now, when people shout, it will not be a sound of happiness but a cry of distress.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel, known for its abundance and its pride. Even so, the prophet does not speak with mockery: he says he will cry out and weep for Moab. God judges, but He also shows grief.

For today: let us not place our security in what we produce or enjoy, because it can end suddenly. Let us thank God for what we have and live with humility. And if someone suffers the consequences of their mistakes, let us not rejoice; rather, let us pray with compassion.
exp.1:32:
God asks Israel: "How skillfully you pursue love! Even the most immoral of women could learn from your ways." Here the wording shows that Israel has become so practiced at chasing other loves that she is almost a teacher in the art, and even women known for their immorality could learn from her.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who runs after lovers, that is, foreign alliances and other gods, instead of returning to her Lord. She works very hard to win others over, but she has forgotten God. Some understand the "love" she pursues as political alliances; others, as idolatry. It probably includes both.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for approval or security apart from God. Striving to please everyone, or trusting in fleeting things, leaves us empty. Let us return to God with sincerity, for his love is not won by appearances.
exp.11:1:
God has allowed the wicked to prosper, like trees that are planted, take root, grow, and bear fruit. With their lips they speak of God often. But their hearts are far from Him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, addressing God. He is confused and hurt, because he sees that false people live well, while he, who serves God, suffers opposition. He acknowledges that God is just, yet he dares to ask Him honestly. In the end, God answers him, but that comes later.

For today: You can bring your doubts to God with honesty, without pretending. And examine your own heart: let your faith not be only words, but a real closeness to Him.
exp.2:18:
God says that he asked himself how he could treat his people as his children and give them a beautiful land, the most desirable inheritance among all the nations. The word "desirable" means delightful and valuable, and the inheritance is understood as the most glorious among the peoples. God hoped they would call him "Father" and never turn away from following him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been unfaithful to him, as the next verse shows, where he compares them to a wife who betrays her husband. Even so, God expresses his longing for a close relationship and announces a future restoration.

For today: God does not want only obedience, but a relationship of trust like that of a father with his children. Today you can speak to him sincerely, call him "Father," and ask him for help so that you do not turn away from following him.
exp.11:4:
If you have grown weary running with people on foot, how will you compete with horses? And if you stumbled in a land of peace, how will you manage in the thickets of the Jordan?

"Compete" means to race against someone or to face them in a contest. The "thickets of the Jordan" refers to the dense brush along the riverbank, where dangerous animals hid (some interpreters understand it this way).

Here God answers Jeremiah, who was complaining because the wicked were prospering and even his own family was betraying him. God tells him that the worst has not yet come. It is a firm answer, not one of immediate comfort, meant to prepare him for a harder ministry.

For today: small trials prepare us for great ones. Instead of giving up before the difficulties of the present, we can seek God, who strengthens us for what lies ahead.
exp.49:25:
It speaks of distant peoples, "from the farthest border," who will come against Babylon. They are told to break open her granaries, that is, the storehouses where her grain and wealth are kept. Then they must pile her up like mounds of grain, and devote her to destruction. No survivors are to be left.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD says. Babylon had been God's instrument for judging other nations, but it grew proud and mistreated Israel and its temple. For this reason God now judges her. Scholars understand this as referring to the fall of Babylon before the Medes and Persians, though some also see a broader sense of final judgment.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, stands above God. If you are suffering injustice, you can trust that God sees and will act justly in his time. And if you have some power or success, use it with humility.
exp.36:16:
This verse tells how King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah and received him in his own palace, where he asked him privately, "Is there a word from the LORD?" Jeremiah answered that there was, and told him plainly that he would be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah was God's prophet in the last days of Judah. Officials had beaten him and put him in prison for saying that Jerusalem would fall. Zedekiah was afraid and wanted an answer, but he did not dare to hear Jeremiah openly. Even so, the prophet did not change the message to save himself from prison.

For today: God's truth is not always comfortable, but it must be spoken with honesty and love. And when we seek the voice of God, let us ask for the courage to obey it, not just curiosity to hear it.
exp.4:18:
When the people ask why the LORD our God has done all these things to them, the answer is plain: you abandoned Me and served foreign gods in your own land, so now you will serve foreigners in a land that is not your own. The phrase "foreign gods" refers to the gods of other nations, and "foreigners" means people from other lands.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah, shortly before an enemy nation invades. Earlier in the chapter, the loss of crops and cities has already been announced, but God makes clear that He will not finish them off completely. The punishment is not arbitrary: it is a response to persistent idolatry. Even so, it leaves room for hope.

When something goes wrong in our lives, it is good to ask ourselves honestly whether we have put other things in the place of God. Not all suffering is punishment, but examining our hearts always brings us closer to Him.
exp.0:1:
God spoke to Jeremiah in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, king of Judah. The verse names God as "the LORD," and the phrase "the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah" means that God's message reached him directly. Josiah was the son of Amon. This verse marks precisely when Jeremiah's calling began.

The book is presented by a narrator or editor, who introduces Jeremiah as a prophet whose words come from God. Josiah was a reforming king, and many place that year around 627 B.C., although the exact dates are calculated in different ways. This verse and those that follow show that Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, until the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: God speaks at concrete moments of history and of our lives. We can approach his Word with confidence, believing that he still guides those who listen to him, even in difficult times.
exp.41:18:
God has already spoken to the people who remained in Judah, the survivors. His message is clear: do not go to Egypt. The phrase "Know for sure that I have warned you today" means they should be certain that they are being warned in earnest, right now.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in God's name. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors feared Babylon and wanted to flee to Egypt. They had asked Jeremiah to pray so they would know what God wanted, and they promised to obey. But it seems they had already decided to leave, and God warns them before they take the step.

For today: when we ask God for direction, it is good to do so with hearts ready to obey, not merely seeking his approval for what we have already decided. Listening with humility spares us from paths that seem safe but are not.
exp.31:41:
God says that just as he brought all this great disaster of destruction and exile upon his people, so he will also bring them all the good he has promised. The "great disaster" refers to the calamity they suffered, and "all the good I have promised" refers to the promises of restoration that he himself had announced.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (Babylonians), and Jeremiah was in prison. Even so, God commanded him to buy a field as a sign that one day the people would return and possess the land. The punishment was not God's final word, and his covenant remained firm.

For today: If God kept his word of judgment, he will also keep his word of hope. In the midst of trials, you can hold on to his promises and keep obeying with confidence, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.51:4:
This verse says that the armies of Babylon kept Jerusalem under siege until King Zedekiah's eleventh year. A siege means the city was surrounded by an army, with no one allowed to come in or go out.

Here the book's narrator is recounting the fall of Jerusalem. He explains that this happened because of God's anger against Judah, after many warnings that the people did not heed. Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, and the result was this long siege, which ended with famine and the city taken.

For today: the consequences of ignoring God sometimes take time, but they come. If God speaks to you through his Word or your conscience, do not wait until you are surrounded by problems to listen. His forgiveness is always near to those who repent.
exp.48:29:
God tells the people of Hazor to run quickly, escape, and lie low in deep places, such as caves or hollows in the ground. The command "Run! Escape quickly!" calls for urgent flight, and "lie low" means staying hidden and out of sight. The reason is that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, has already drawn up a plan against them and has devised a strategy to attack them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah within his messages against several nations. Hazor here is not the city in Israel, but a group of settlements of desert tribes in the Arabian desert, near Kedar. They were a peaceful and confident people, and God announces that Babylon would defeat them. The exact details of that campaign are not known with much precision.

For today: when God gives a warning, it is wise to listen and act with prudence, rather than trusting too much that everything will remain calm.
exp.40:13:
This verse says that all the people whom Ishmael had taken captive at Mizpah turned and went over to Johanan, son of Kareah. The phrase about turning and going is rendered here as "turned and went over." Johanan's coming to rescue them is why they were glad when they saw him.

This is part of the account in Jeremiah. Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and he took many people of Mizpah captive. Johanan and the military leaders pursued him and caught up with him at Gibeon. The text does not say there was a battle with the captives; they simply went over to Johanan's side. Ishmael escaped with eight men.

For today: when someone sets us free from an oppressive situation, let us thank God and turn toward what is good without hesitation. Even so, we need to ask him for wisdom about what comes next, because the rescue was only the beginning.
exp.12:5:
The passage says that a long time passed after Jeremiah hid the linen belt by the Euphrates. Then God tells him to go and get it. A "belt" here is a loincloth, and the phrase "many days later" means "after a long time." Jeremiah is to return and take back what he had hidden at God's command.

Here the LORD speaks to the prophet Jeremiah, and this action is a symbolic sign for Judah. Later on, God explains that the ruined loincloth represents the people's pride and their refusal to hear his word. Scholars debate whether the journey was physical or a vision, because the text does not make this clear.

For today: God wants us to stay close to him, like a loincloth held snugly around the body. If we drift away and harden our hearts, we wear down inside. Today you can set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and pray, so that you remain close to God.
exp.37:21:
It tells that the women of King Zedekiah's palace would be brought out before the officials of the king of Babylon. They themselves, in a tone of mockery or lament, would say that his trusted friends had misled him and overcome him. "Your feet sank into the mire" means that they left him stuck in the mud, and "they deserted you" means that they abandoned him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking to King Zedekiah while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. Jeremiah offers him a way out: surrender and live. He warns him with this vision of what would happen if he disobeyed God. The king was afraid of his people and of their criticism, and for that reason he hesitated.

For today: do not let fear of what others think keep you from obeying God. Advice that only seeks to please you can leave you stuck, but God's word, even when it is hard, leads to life.
exp.22:1:
God speaks to the "shepherds," that is, the leaders of the people. He says they have scattered his flock and driven the sheep away, and that they have not attended to them. The sheep were not cared for. Because of this, God declares that he himself will attend to these leaders and hold them accountable for the evil of their deeds.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The leaders of Judah, especially its kings, had neglected and mistreated the people. The verses that follow show that God himself will gather his scattered sheep and give them good shepherds.

If you have some responsibility over others, whether in the family, the church, or at work, care for them with tenderness and attention. Ask yourself: whom do I need to visit, listen to, or encourage this week?
exp.34:18:
God promises that the family of the Rechabites will never lack a descendant of Jonadab who stands before Him. The phrase "to stand before me" means to serve God, to live at His disposal. The phrase "will never fail" speaks of a lasting promise.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Rechabites had for generations obeyed the command of their ancestor Jonadab not to drink wine or live in houses. God holds them up as an example before Judah, which did not obey its God. It is not known with certainty how this promise was fulfilled afterward; some think it speaks of continuous service, others of a descendance that would endure.

Today, this encourages us to be faithful and obedient. If we do so with God, who deserves more than any other authority, He sees and values our steadiness, even in the small things of each day.
exp.6:0:
This verse is only the opening of a new message. It says that a word from God came to Jeremiah. Here the content of the message is not yet stated; the verse only announces that it is coming.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives and passes on his word. According to what follows, God will send him to the gate of the temple to speak to the people of Judah who were coming in to worship. The message will be a call to change their conduct, not just to keep up their religion.

For today: before speaking, it is good to listen. We can ask God to let his word reach us first, and be willing to correct our ways, not just to attend church.
exp.12:15:
Give glory to the LORD your God means acknowledging and honoring him, and doing so before it is too late. The "darkness" and the "dusky mountains" stand for judgment and disaster, the kind of situation where a person walks blindly and stumbles. The "deep gloom and thick darkness" describe a dense, threatening darkness. The phrase "He turns it into" means that the light people hope for would be changed into darkness.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the word of the LORD to Judah. The people were proud and unwilling to obey. The verse that follows shows the prophet's grief, since the judgment would come in the form of captivity. Scholars agree that this is a warning given before the exile, although the exact date is debated.

For today: do not put off humbling yourself before God. If anything in your life has taken his place because of pride, acknowledge it today with simplicity and return to him, while there is still light.
exp.6:28:
God tells Jeremiah to cut off his hair and throw it away, and to raise a lament on the bare hills. It is a sign of mourning, because the Lord has rejected this generation that stirred up his anger. The verse says "cut off your hair," and the hills are the barren heights where the people carried out their rituals.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah just after telling him that the people will not listen to him. Judah had disobeyed, rejected correction, and practiced idolatry, even in the temple. Some understand that the cut hair may refer to the prophet or to the people; the text allows both readings.

For today: when we see that we are drifting away from God, or that others are, it is not enough to judge. God invites us to listen to his correction in time, and to weep sincerely and pray for those who have turned away.
exp.1:14:
The young lions have roared at him and sounded their voices. They have laid waste his land, and his cities lie in ruins, with no one living in them. For "roared," the verse uses the word "roared" itself; for "inhabitant," it refers to the one who lives in a place.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the words of God. He has just accused the people of two wrongs: leaving God, the fountain of living water, and digging broken cisterns. The "lions" are usually understood as enemy nations, such as Assyria or Egypt, though scholars debate exactly which ones. The passage presents the ruin as the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: when you feel emptiness or face problems, examine where you have placed your trust. Things that cannot sustain you, such as success or money, break apart. Return to God, who does satisfy.
exp.8:11:
This verse asks three questions: who is wise enough to understand what has happened, to whom has the LORD spoken so that he could explain it, and why has the land been destroyed and scorched like a desert, so that no one can pass through it? A "wise man" here means a person who has understanding.

Jeremiah speaks with a broken heart over the judgment that is coming upon Judah. The questions remain open until God himself answers in the verses that follow: the people abandoned his law, did not obey his voice, and followed the stubbornness of their own hearts and the Baals.

For today: true wisdom begins when we recognize that our choices have consequences and that God speaks with clarity. Today we can ask ourselves in what area we are following our own path instead of his Word, and return to him with humility.
exp.50:8:
This verse says that people tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed. That is why the call is to abandon her and for each person to return to their own land. "We tried to heal Babylon" means just that: we tried to heal her. The phrase "Abandon her" means leave her, and "let each of us go" means let each one go back to his own land. Her judgment is so great that it extends to the sky and reaches to the clouds, meaning her guilt is enormous and God already sees it.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, or the voice of the foreigners who lived in Babylon. Many understand that they are the exiles of Israel and other peoples who were cared for by Babylon, but she did not change. God had already decided to judge her for her pride and her violence. The text does not fully make clear who is speaking, and so it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: there are situations or environments that do not change even when we have done our part. After praying and doing what we can, we can let go of what is not ours to fix, step away with wisdom, and trust that God does justice.
exp.2:12:
God tells Israel to acknowledge its guilt. To "acknowledge" here means to admit it openly, and to have "rebelled against the LORD" means that it turned against God. The phrase about having "scattered your favors to foreign gods" speaks of spreading its love and loyalty to other gods, under "every green tree," that is, in the shady places where pagan worship was practiced. And it did not obey God's voice.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the northern kingdom, Israel, which was already in exile. Although he rebukes it, the invitation comes wrapped in mercy: God will not keep his anger forever, and he calls it to return, like a husband who longs to restore his people.

For today: God does not ask us to pretend that we are doing well, but to admit honestly where we have drifted away. Recognizing the wrong is not the end; it is the door back to a merciful God who receives us with grace.
exp.29:20:
This verse says that Israel's leader will come from within his own people; he will not be a foreigner. God says he will bring him near to himself and asks: who would dare on his own to approach me? In other words, no one would come near to God on his own; it is God who makes it possible.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises to restore Israel after the exile: he will multiply the people, punish their oppressors, and renew his relationship with them, so that they will be his people. Many Christians see here a sign of the Messiah, but the text also speaks of a future ruler in general, and it has been interpreted in various ways.

Drawing near to God does not depend on our courage or our merits, but on his initiative. If today you feel a desire to pray or to seek God, thank him, because he himself has been softening your heart. Come near with confidence.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that those who follow idols become senseless and lose good judgment. The phrase "altogether senseless" means that they become completely unable to think clearly, and the word "foolish" means that they end up acting as fools. The word translated as "worthless" points to things that are empty and without any real value. The idols in this verse are made of wood, so what they teach is pure emptiness.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking to Israel, which was surrounded by peoples who worshiped images. Before this, he praises the LORD as incomparable, and afterward he describes how the craftsman covers the idol with silver, gold, and fine cloth. Even though it may look beautiful, it is still human work. In the end, Jeremiah contrasts it with the living and true God.

Today, an idol can be anything we trust more than God: money, fame, or success. Ask yourself: where am I seeking security? Lay it before God in prayer and trust Him.
exp.5:21:
This is what the LORD says: an army is coming from the land of the north, and a great nation is being stirred up from the ends of the earth. God is announcing an invasion that is about to come.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was offering incense and sacrifices, but its heart was far from Him and it lived in injustice. For this reason God says that those rituals do not please Him. Many understand that the enemy from the north was Babylon, although the text does not name it here. Some scholars debate how this image was first applied.

For today: God is not satisfied with a religion that is only outward appearance. Examine whether your daily life, your dealings with others, and your obedience match what you sing and offer in church.
exp.5:1:
God says that though Jerusalem, called "the daughter of Zion," is beautiful and delicate, that is, refined and accustomed to comfort, he will destroy her. The verse sets the beauty and the destruction side by side, so the contrast is the point: the city's loveliness will not spare it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the invasion from the north by Babylon. He warns Jerusalem, which felt secure and at ease, that its beauty will not protect it. The shepherds with their flocks who come to camp are an image of armies surrounding the city.

For today: comfort and success are no guarantee of safety before God. Today you can ask yourself whether you have stopped listening to his warnings because you feel at ease, and return to him with humility before a greater shaking becomes necessary.
exp.17:6:
It says that God has the right to announce judgment against any nation or kingdom. The words "at any time" show that He may speak such a word whenever He decides. The verbs "uprooted, torn down, and destroyed" are like those of a farmer who pulls a plant out of the ground and ruins it.

The Lord speaks to the prophet Jeremiah, who is in the potter's house watching how the clay is worked. God uses that scene to tell Israel that He is the one who shapes the nations. But the verses that follow make clear that the warning is not a fixed fate: if the people turn from their evil, God changes His mind and does not send the punishment.

For today: when God warns us through His Word or through our conscience, we should not take it as a final sentence, but as an invitation to turn back. Right now we can recognize a wrong path and ask Him for help to change.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah once again. "Then the word of the LORD came to me" means "I received a message from God." It is a transition: the account of the ruined belt ends, and now the verse comes.

The speaker is Jeremiah, a prophet of Judah. God had told him to hide a linen belt by the Euphrates, and when he went back to get it, it was ruined. That object was a visible sign. The following verses explain that Judah, because of its pride and because it followed other gods, would be ruined just like that belt. Scholars debate exactly where that place was.

God does not stay silent: he explains what he is doing and why. Today we can approach his Word with humility, letting him correct us in time, before pride wears us down from the inside.
exp.3:24:
Jeremiah says that he looked and no one was left, and that all the birds of the air had fled. It is a picture of complete desolation: the land was left without people and without life. The phrase "no man was left" means that no one remained to be seen.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, describing in a vision the judgment that would come upon Judah for its idolatry and its rebellion against God. The images recall creation undone: an empty earth, skies without light, mountains trembling. Many understand that it foretells the invasion from the north. Even so, God makes clear in verse 27 that he will not finish off his people completely.

For today: God is patient, but he takes sin seriously. If something in your life is drifting away from him, do not ignore it; return to him soon, because his mercy remains open to anyone who repents.
exp.30:15:
God tells Rachel to stop weeping. He asks her to keep her voice from weeping and her eyes from tears, because the reward for her work will come. The word "salary" from the older text is replaced by reward, which is what your verse says. And he promises that her children will return from the land of the enemy, that is, from exile.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Rachel appears as a figure of the mother who weeps for her children carried away captive; she was the ancestor of Ephraim and Benjamin, northern tribes. This belongs within the promises of Israel's restoration. Later, Matthew 2:18 quotes the weeping of Ramah in another context, and interpreters relate it in different ways.

God does not mock pain, but neither does he let pain have the last word. Today you can weep honestly before him and, at the same time, hope that God is at work and that your faithfulness is not lost.
exp.47:33:
This verse describes a cry of grief heard across the land of Moab. Several towns are named, from Heshbon to Elealeh, Jahaz, Zoar and Horonaim, and Eglath-shelishiyah. The sound is one of mourning rising from town to town. The reference to the waters of Nimrim, which once gave life, points to their drying up, so that the land is left in ruin.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, known for its pride and its trust in its riches and its gods. God announces judgment on it, but he also shows sorrow: the prophet weeps over the ruin of its vineyards and of its joy.

For today: we should not trust in what seems secure, such as money or success, because everything can come to an end. And when others suffer, even those who went wrong, we can have compassion, as God did.
exp.49:19:
It says that when the time God has set comes, a search will be made for Israel's guilt and Judah's sins, and none will be found. It does not mean they never sinned, but that God will forgive them completely. The phrase "a search will be made" means "they will be looked for" or "they will be searched out." The phrase "the remnant I preserve" refers to those God keeps safe, a remnant that remains.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Babylon, which had oppressed his people, and promises to bring Israel back to its land. Many understand that forgiveness is part of that restoration. Some Christians also see here a sign of the complete forgiveness God offers in Christ.

For today: if you have confessed your sin to God, you can rest in his forgiveness. Do not keep carrying guilt that he has already chosen to wipe away. Come to him with humility and confidence.
exp.40:17:
This verse explains why the people wanted to go to Egypt: they were trying to escape the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians. Ishmael had struck down Gedaliah, the governor whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land. The people feared that Babylon would punish them.

The account is told by Jeremiah. After the killing, Johanan rescued the people that Ishmael had carried off, and he stopped near Bethlehem. They planned to flee to Egypt, but they had not yet asked God for direction. The Bible shows here a very strong human fear.

Today, when something frightens us, it is easy to decide quickly and look for an escape of our own. Before acting, let us pray, ask for wise counsel, and seek the will of God. Fear should not be our guide; trust in God should.
exp.23:3:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah once more. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means that a message from God came to him. After asking him what he saw, God is going to explain the meaning of the two baskets of figs.

Jeremiah is the prophet speaking. God had just shown him two baskets in front of the temple. This happens after the king of Babylon carried some of the people of Judah into exile, around 597 B.C. God uses the image of the figs to explain what was happening to those who had been taken away.

For today: God does not leave us with only what we see. When something seems confusing or painful, we can ask him to help us understand it from his perspective and listen to his word with patience.
exp.10:22:
This verse says that none of that group will be left alive. God announces that he will bring disaster on the people of Anathoth, and he calls that moment "the year of their punishment." Here the word "punishment" means a time when God acts to judge what people have done.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Anathoth, his own townspeople, wanted to kill him if he kept prophesying in the name of the LORD. God responds by defending his servant and announcing judgment on those who wanted to silence his word. The Bible presents this as God's justice, not as Jeremiah's revenge.

For today: it is not wise to keep quiet about the truth out of fear of pressure, even from family or acquaintances. And whoever rejects God should not take his patience lightly. We can trust that God cares for those who are faithful to him and acts with justice in his time.
exp.21:12:
God pronounces a warning cry: woe is coming upon the one who builds his palace through wrongdoing and his upper rooms without fairness. The word "justice" here means acting with fairness and uprightness. The phrase "makes his countrymen serve without pay" means having people work for nothing, refusing to pay them what they have earned. "Countrymen" refers to a fellow citizen, the person right beside us. In other words, it means taking advantage of someone else's labor and withholding the wages they are owed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses the royal palace of Judah, right after speaking about Shallum, the son of Josiah. The next king, Jehoiakim, was expanding his luxurious palace with cedar and red paint, while exploiting his workers. God reminds him that his father Josiah did justice and things went well for him.

Today: if you have employees or work alongside others, pay them with fairness and on time. No progress, house, or business is worth anything if it is built on the abuse of others.
exp.30:20:
Here the people are told to set up road markers and signposts along the way, so that they do not lose the route back. The stone markers that serve as signs are the road markers, and the road itself is the highway. The "virgin Israel" is asked to keep in mind the road she has traveled, the way by which she went into exile, because it is by that same road that she will return to these cities of hers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was in captivity, and the Lord promises them restoration. He had earlier said that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, remains a precious son to him, and that he has compassion on him. The call to return comes from that love, not from rejection.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, he calls you to come back. Remember the point where you turned aside, take a concrete step toward him, such as prayer or asking forgiveness, and set up signs that help you not lose your way, such as daily Bible reading or a community of faith.
exp.7:3:
God tells Jeremiah to ask the people two plain questions. Do men fall and not get up again? Does one turn away and not return? The answer that anyone would give is no; getting up and coming back is the natural thing to do.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Just before this, the text announces judgment on a people who served the stars and other false gods. With these questions, God shows how strange Judah's attitude is: falling and wandering are part of being human, but refusing to come back is not. The verses that follow say that even so, the people would not repent.

For today: if you have fallen or wandered away from God, do not stay there. He invites you to come back. Acknowledge your mistake, ask yourself "what have I done?" and today take a step back toward Him.
exp.48:28:
It says the enemies will carry off everything the people of Kedar had: their tents, their flocks, their tent curtains, all their goods, and their camels. They will also shout at them, "Terror is on every side!"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Kedar were nomadic tribes of the desert, rich in livestock, who lived confidently and without defenses. God announces that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would attack them. Scholars agree that the judgment falls on a people secure in themselves; the exact historical details of that campaign are not well known.

For today: our possessions and securities can disappear quickly. It is wise to guard the heart so that we do not trust in what we have, but in God, who sustains life when everything else is lost.
exp.21:14:
God asks a king whether he truly rules well just because he lives in a luxurious palace with cedar walls. He points out that the king's father also ate and drank, meaning he enjoyed a normal and good life, but he also acted justly and righteously and stood up for what was right. That is why things went well for him.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Jehoiakim, king of Judah. The king was building a large palace while not paying his workers and oppressing the people. His father, King Josiah, is held up as an example, because he cared for the needy and the poor. God says that this is what it truly means to know him.

For today: greatness is not measured by what we have, but by how we treat others. If you have a business or people under your charge, pay fairly and on time, and treat everyone with dignity.
exp.48:22:
Concerning Damascus. This verse says that the cities of Hamath and Arpad were put to shame and filled with fear because they had received bad news. The picture of their anxiety is like a restless sea that cannot be calmed, and their courage is gone.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a series of messages about the nations neighboring Judah. Damascus, the capital of Syria, would face judgment. Hamath and Arpad were cities in northern Syria, and their panic announces that disaster is approaching. Scholars often connect this with the advance of Babylon, although the text does not give all the details.

For today: bad news can overcome someone who trusts only in their own strength or in their city. Let us learn to place our security in God, and in the face of sudden fear, to pray before we let ourselves be overwhelmed.
exp.12:26:
God tells Jerusalem that he has seen all her sin. Her "adulteries" and her "shameless prostitution" are a picture of spiritual unfaithfulness: turning away from God to worship idols. Her "lustful neighings" describe an uncontrolled desire, like a horse in heat. The "hills and in the fields" are the high places where idol worship took place. At the end, God cries out, "How long will you remain unclean?" It is a cry of grief and of waiting.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah during a time of spiritual decline in Judah. Earlier, the people had forgotten God and trusted in lies, in false securities. God uses strong language because the people had broken their covenant with him, but his words also show a desire to see them made clean.

For today: God sees what we do in secret and still hopes that we will return. You can confess to him honestly whatever has taken his place in your heart and ask him to cleanse you.
exp.29:21:
This verse is a promise of relationship: God says that his people will truly be his, and that he will be their God. The phrase "you will be My people" means that they will belong to him as his people. It is a covenant promise, like a pledge of belonging to one another.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel were under judgment and in captivity because of their disobedience. Even so, in this chapter God promises to restore them, to punish their oppressors, and to raise up a ruler from among them. Some believers see here a sign of the Messiah; others read it mainly as a promise for Israel in its history. The verses that follow remind us that God also judges wickedness.

For today: God does not only want to forgive; he wants a close relationship. If you feel far away, draw near to him with a humble heart, and remember that his desire is to be your God and for you to live as his.
exp.3:14:
It speaks of a voice that resounds from Dan, the far north of the land, and of another that proclaims disaster from the hills of Ephraim, farther south. Disaster here means a great misfortune. These are messengers who warn, from place to place, that danger is already drawing near.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. The enemy comes from the north, and the news travels on, passing through Dan and Ephraim, right along the road to Jerusalem. God gives a clear warning because the people had turned away from Him, and before that He says: "Wash your heart clean of wickedness." Many understand the enemy to be Babylon, although the passage does not name it here.

For today: God warns before the consequences arrive. Let us not wait until the trouble reaches our door. If there is something crooked in our heart, let us go to God today and ask Him to cleanse us.
exp.21:29:
God commands that Coniah be recorded as "childless," meaning that none of his descendants would sit on the throne and rule. "Descendants" are his offspring, and "rule" means to govern. None of his line would prosper on the throne of David.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was king of Judah and was taken into exile in Babylon because of the disobedience of the people and their kings. He had children, so the text is understood to mean that none of them would reign. Some see here a difficulty for the line of Jesus, and scholars explain it in different ways.

Today we can remember that titles, inheritances, and family names do not secure the future. What sustains life is obeying God with humility and trusting in his promises.
exp.50:20:
God says he will use someone as his "hammer" to break the military strength of his enemies: horses, riders, chariots, and the drivers who ride in them. "Shatter" means to smash into pieces. Horses and chariots were the most powerful weapons of that time.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in a long message against Babylon. Scholars debate who the "hammer" refers to: some think of Cyrus and the Medes and Persians, others of God's people or of a more general instrument. What is clear is that God directs history, and that Babylon, so feared, would not last forever.

For today: when evil seems invincible, remember that no human power is beyond God's control. Trust in him and do not let fear dominate you.
exp.30:21:
God asks his people, "How long will you wander, O faithless daughter?" The word translated "faithless" here is the one your verse uses, and it describes someone who has turned away from loyalty. Then he announces that he will do something new on the earth: "a woman will shelter a man." This phrase is difficult, and it has been understood in several ways: as a Israel that returns and seeks God with strength, as an unexpected situation of safety, or, in the Christian tradition, as a sign of the Messiah. There is no single certain explanation.

The Lord speaks to the exiles of Israel. Tenderly he calls them to return to their land, for he promises restoration, forgiveness, and a new beginning.

For today: if you are far away or going around in circles without direction, God does not reject you. He invites you to return, and he can begin something new in you. Today, pray with sincerity and take one concrete step toward him.
exp.37:17:
This verse states the reverse of the earlier promise. If King Zedekiah does not surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, the city will be handed over to the Chaldeans, the Babylonians. They will burn it down, and the king himself will not get away from their grasp. The phrase "surrender to the officers" means going out to them and giving yourself up.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in God's name to Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. Jerusalem was under siege. Jeremiah had already been imprisoned for saying that surrender was the way to save lives. The king consults him in secret, but he is afraid of what others will think.

For today: God shows us clearly the consequences of our decisions. Obeying him may be frightening and may cost us pride, but the fear of people should never weigh more than his word.
exp.14:7:
He says that God would make the widows so many they would outnumber the grains of sand on the seashore. He would bring a "destroyer" (an invading army) at noon, in the full light of day, against the mothers of young men. Suddenly anguish and dismay would fall on the people. The word "destroyer" speaks of an attacker who lays waste.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah, his people. He had warned them many times, but they turned away and did not change their ways. God says he is "weary of relenting," that is, of holding back his judgment. Some believe this refers to the Babylonian invasion, though the text gives no further details.

For today: God speaks in earnest, but his patience is long. Do not harden your heart against his call. If something in your life is pulling you away from him, return today with sincerity, because God receives whoever turns back to him.
exp.13:20:
Here Israel asks God not to abandon his people. "Do not despise us" means "do not reject us." "Do not disgrace Your glorious throne" means that God should not let it fall into dishonor; the throne may refer to the temple or to Jerusalem, and it is interpreted in different ways. "Do not break Your covenant" means: do not cancel Your promise.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, praying on behalf of the people in the middle of a great drought. First they acknowledge their sin and that of their fathers. Then they do not rely on their own merits, but on the name of God and on His covenant, that is, on His faithfulness.

For today: when you have failed, do not hide from God. Come near with sincerity, acknowledge your mistake, and rely on who God is and on what He has promised, not on how good you yourself are.
exp.31:15:
This verse tells how Jeremiah, after giving the deed of purchase to Baruch, son of Neriah, began to pray to the LORD. The deed of purchase was the document that proved the buying of a piece of land. "LORD" is the name of God, written in capital letters in your Bible.

Jeremiah speaks. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon, and he himself was a prisoner. On God's command he had bought a field from his cousin, something that seemed absurd, since the land was about to fall into enemy hands. God told him to keep the documents in a clay jar as a sign that one day land would be bought again in Israel. Jeremiah, filled with doubt and wonder, brings everything before God in prayer.

For today: when what God asks of you seems to make no sense, do not hide your doubts. Pray honestly, remembering who God is and what he has done, and obey, trusting that his promises still stand.
exp.49:22:
This verse says that Babylon, which was like a mighty hammer striking all the nations, now lies broken and shattered. It expresses amazement at how an empire so strong has become a ruin, something the other nations look upon with horror. The word "was" is the simple past of "be," and "nations" refers to the peoples or nations of the earth.

The prophet Jeremiah announces, on God's behalf, judgment against Babylon. God had used this empire to correct other peoples, but Babylon was proud and cruel. Because of this, according to the text, it provoked the LORD. The verses that follow say that God himself brings about its fall.

For today: no human power lasts forever. If we have strength, money, or influence, let us use them with humility and justice, remembering that we answer to God. And if someone suffers from injustice, they can trust that God sees it.
exp.40:10:
This verse says that Johanan and the army commanders who were with him heard about all the crimes that Ishmael had committed. The phrase "the commanders of the armies with him" refers to the military leaders serving alongside Johanan. The "crimes" here refer to the murders and the taking of the people of Mizpah as captives.

The book of Jeremiah recounts here what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had left Gedaliah as governor, and Ishmael murdered him and carried the people away captive. The narrator reports that Johanan learned of this, and so he gathered his men to go after Ishmael, as the account goes on to tell.

For today: when we learn of an injustice, it is not enough simply to grieve over it. God calls us to act with wisdom and courage, according to what we are able to do, to help those who are suffering, whether by praying, by speaking out against wrong through proper means, or by coming to the aid of the victims.
exp.27:2:
It says that, in just two years, God would bring back to this place all the articles of the Lord's house that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had taken from here and carried to Babylon.
