The idea of restoring what was taken matches the verse's wording. The phrase "within two years" means the return would happen within two years.

The speaker is Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, in the temple, before priests and the people. He says he speaks on behalf of the Lord, but Jeremiah had announced a long exile. Hananiah offered a pleasant and quick message. Later, Jeremiah shows that Hananiah was not speaking on God's behalf.

For today: not every hopeful message comes from God. Before believing easy promises, compare them with what the Bible teaches and pray for discernment. God's true hope does not avoid reality, but sustains us within it.
exp.13:17:
The verse describes a land where suffering is everywhere. If a person goes out into the country, they see those killed by the sword; if they enter the city, they see those ravaged by famine. The phrase "those slain by the sword" points to people killed in war. Also, the prophet and the priest travel to a land they do not know: they move from place to place, but without understanding what is happening. Some take this to mean they were carried off as captives; others, that they wander aimlessly.

Jeremiah speaks, a man who feels the pain of God and of the people. Judah suffers drought, hunger, and war because of its sin. The religious leaders gave false security and did not guide the people back to God.

For today: it is not enough to hold an office or to have a religious appearance. Seek God with sincerity, ask for wisdom, and acknowledge your mistakes, as the people do later in the text, so that you do not go about without understanding.
exp.25:20:
King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and officials heard Uriah's words, and the king looked for a way to put him to death. Uriah found out about it, and in fear he fled to Egypt. The phrase "sought to put him to death" means that the king looked for a way to kill him. "Mighty men" and "officials" refer to the men of authority in the government.

The speakers here are the leaders and the people of Judah, who bring up the case of Uriah while they debate whether Jeremiah deserves to die. Uriah had prophesied the same thing as Jeremiah: judgment against Jerusalem. Jehoiakim, instead of repenting, pursued him. Later they caught up with him in Egypt and killed him.

For today: speaking the truth can cost dearly, and even the faithful feel fear. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to speak with humility and firmness, and let us listen to correction instead of silencing the one who gives it to us.
exp.17:21:
Jeremiah asks God to let cries of pain be heard in the houses of his enemies when an army suddenly arrives. The reason is that they dug a pit to capture him and hid traps for his feet. The verse uses "raiders" for the attackers, "capture" for the act of seizing him, and "snares" for the traps.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. The people of Judah, angry over his messages from God, planned to harm him, even though he had pleaded on their behalf. This is one of his most raw and sincere prayers. Some understand these words as a cry for justice, and others as a human outpouring of pain. The Bible does not hide it.

For today: when someone repays you evil for good, bring your pain honestly to God, without holding it in or taking revenge yourself. Then let Him be the judge, and ask Him for a heart free of resentment.
exp.50:28:
The earth shakes and writhes in pain, because the LORD's intentions against Babylon stand firm: to leave the land of Babylon a desolate place, with no one living there.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing the word of the LORD. God calls several nations, such as Ararat, Minni, Ashkenaz and the Medes, to attack Babylon. Babylon had dominated and oppressed many peoples, and God declares that its power will come to an end. The text uses poetic and strong language to describe that judgment.

For today: even when it sometimes seems that the powerful will never fall, the Bible reminds us that God governs history and his purposes are fulfilled. We can rest in him, live with humility and trust that his justice comes in its time.
exp.42:9:
God tells Jeremiah to say to the Jews that He will send for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, whom He calls "my servant." This king will set his throne over the stones that Jeremiah hid, and he will spread his royal pavilion over them.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah at Tahpanhes, in Egypt, where many Jews had fled out of fear of Babylon, even though God had told them not to go. The stones hidden in the clay at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace were a visible sign: Egypt would not be a safe refuge. Calling Nebuchadnezzar "servant" does not mean he was righteous, but that God would use him to accomplish His purpose.

For today: do not look for security in places or people that God did not direct you to. Trusting and obeying God, even when it is frightening, is safer than any refuge we choose on our own.
exp.6:16:
God asks Jeremiah a question: "Do you not see what they are doing?" He does not ask because He does not know, but so that the prophet will understand why the judgment is just. Judah and Jerusalem are named, and the word "streets" shows that the sin was public, not hidden.

God speaks to Jeremiah in the well-known message at the temple. He has just told him not to pray for the people, because they kept worshiping the "queen of heaven" and other gods. The verses that follow show that the whole family took part. God grieves, and He also warns that the greatest harm will fall on themselves.

For today: Ask God to open your eyes to see honestly what things occupy the place that only He should have in your life and in your home, and be steadfast in returning to Him.
exp.48:27:
This verse announces God's judgment against Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, desert peoples whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would defeat. God gives the command: "Rise up, advance against Kedar, and destroy the people of the east." The "people of the east" were nomadic tribes of the desert, living east of Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter gathers messages against several nations that were neighbors of Israel. These peoples lived confident in their tents, their flocks, and their remoteness, but God showed that none of them was beyond his reach. Scholars do not know in detail how this attack happened, but the text presents it as part of God's plan.

For today: there is no true security in what we possess or in living far from everything. Let us trust in God, who governs over all the nations.
exp.3:1:
If Israel returns to him, God says, they will be able to swear "as surely as the LORD lives" truthfully: with truth, with justice, and with righteousness. To swear is to affirm something by calling God as witness. The verse says the nations will be blessed by God, and that they will glory in him, meaning they will rejoice in him and take pride in him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Many people used God's name with their mouths, yet they kept their idols and their injustices. God asks for a real change, not just words.

For today: let us make sure that what we say about God matches how we live. This week, try to keep your promises and be honest, even when no one notices.
exp.49:24:
The passage says that the LORD has opened His armory and brought out the weapons of His wrath. An armory is the place where weapons are kept, and the weapons here stand for the tools God uses to carry out His justice. The verse also says that this is the work of the Lord GOD of Hosts in the land of the Chaldeans, which means Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed many peoples, including Judah, and had grown proud against God. Now judgment is coming to it. Scholars understand that God uses other nations as His instruments, although this verse does not name them.

For today: God does not overlook injustice, even when it takes time. This invites us to trust that He will do justice, and to live with humility, without abusing whatever power we have.
exp.20:11:
God speaks to the royal family of Judah, the descendants of King David. He commands them to administer justice "every morning," meaning promptly, without putting it off. They must rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor. If they do not, God's wrath will burn like a fire that no one can put out, because of their evil deeds.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at a time when Jerusalem was threatened by Babylon. God denounces that the rulers had allowed injustice. Even so, this message offers an opportunity: if they changed, there was hope. Some scholars think the punishment was already very near; others see here a sincere call to repentance.

For today: if you have any authority or influence, even a small amount, do not delay in doing what is right. Defend the person who is mistreated or ignored, and do it soon.
exp.6:19:
God says that his anger and fury will be poured out on "this place," meaning Jerusalem and Judah. The judgment will reach people and animals, the trees of the field, and the produce of the land. "Will be poured out" describes something that falls with force. "Will burn and not be extinguished" means it will be a fire that no one can put out.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. He says it at the temple in Jerusalem, where the people felt secure. Yet the whole family took part in worshiping "the queen of heaven," a foreign goddess. Many scholars connect her with Ishtar, though not all agree. God warns them that their sin would harm themselves.

Today: God is not satisfied with a religion that is only for show. Examine what things are taking the place of God in your home, and return to Him in humility before the harm grows.
exp.15:19:
This verse asks a question that already contains its answer: can a person make gods for himself? Of course a person can make images, but those images are not real gods. The phrase "for himself" means he made them to suit his own taste and convenience, which the verse itself conveys in the words "for himself."

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, in the middle of a prayer. God has just announced punishment for the idolatry of Judah. Jeremiah looks ahead and says that people from other nations will recognize that their fathers inherited nothing but falsehood. Then God promises to show his power so that they will know that his name is the LORD.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can still make "gods" to our own measure: money, fame, success, or comfort. Ask yourself honestly what thing gives you more security than God does, and hand it over to him in prayer.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that lying and deceit had become so common in Judah that no one could be trusted, not even a friend or a brother. The verse's word for the close companion is the one the reader sees as "neighbor," meaning a neighbor or close friend. Deceit is described as craftiness, and the slander is spoken of as lies spread about others. The phrase "every brother deals craftily" shows that betrayal reached even into one's own family.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, grieved over his people, and at the same time conveys the message of the LORD. Earlier he says he would wish to go off to the wilderness. The verses that follow explain that the people had learned to lie and did not want to know God. Some think the warning "do not trust any brother" describes the situation rather than being a general command to distrust everyone.

Today we can examine our own words. Before asking for trust, let us strive to be people who speak truthfully, including in small things, at home and at work.
exp.22:7:
This verse says that God will bring back the descendants of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the other lands where he had banished them. They will live again in their own land. People will then say "As surely as the LORD lives" because of this new deliverance, more than because of the rescue from Egypt.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The kings and leaders of Judah had failed, and the people would go into exile. Even so, God promises a future of return and hope. This appears alongside the promise of a righteous King, "the LORD our righteousness," whom many Christians see fulfilled in Jesus.

For today: even if you feel far away or lost, God remains faithful to restore. Trust that he can raise up a new story, and remember with gratitude his past and present rescues.
exp.2:24:
They say the people recognize their shame and their guilt. "Lie down" means they are cast down, defeated. "Shame" and "disgrace" speak of dishonor, which covers them like a heavy cloak. They admit they have sinned against the LORD their God, both they and their ancestors, from their youth until today, because they have not obeyed the voice of the LORD their God.

Here Israel speaks, the repentant people, responding to God's call in the preceding verses, which invited them to return to Him. They acknowledge that the hills and mountains where they worshiped idols were false, and that help is found only in God. Some scholars see this as a genuine prayer of repentance, and others as the confession God was hoping to hear from them.

For today: confessing our failures honestly, without excuses, is the first step toward returning to God. He receives those who acknowledge their sin and wants to hear from them again.
exp.50:56:
God says he will make the leaders of Babylon drunk: her princes and wise men, along with her governors, officials, and warriors. Here "make drunk" is a picture of judgment: they will be left without strength or clear judgment, like a drunk man. Then they will fall into a sleep from which they will not wake, which is death. The one who speaks is the King, the LORD of Hosts, that is, God with authority over all powers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a proud empire that oppressed other peoples, including Judah. The message, sent with Seraiah, announces that God will repay with justice and that not even the most powerful will be able to escape it.

For today: let us not place our trust in human power, fame, or intelligence, because all of that is temporary. Let us trust in God, the just King, and live with humility, knowing that he has the last word.
exp.17:1:
God tells Jeremiah to go down at once to the potter's house, the place where the clay is shaped. There God will give him his message.

The Lord speaks, and the message is for his prophet Jeremiah. The verses that follow show that God uses an everyday scene: the potter reshapes a damaged vessel. Later the text applies the image to Israel and the nations, although scholars debate how some details are to be applied.

For today: God can speak to us in the simple and ordinary things of daily life. Today you might pause in the middle of a common task, with an attentive heart, and ask him what he wants to teach you. He also knows how to remake us when something breaks.
exp.45:14:
Why have Egypt's warriors been laid low? The verse asks what has happened to its strong ones, and it answers that they could not stand, because the LORD has thrust them down.

The strong one here may be a mighty warrior, or it may be the bull Apis, an Egyptian god. The Hebrew allows both readings, so we cannot be certain which is meant.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah and announces that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will come to attack Egypt. Egypt trusted in its army and in its gods, but this defeat will not be only a military event. God himself allows it and directs it.

For today: human strength, whether money, position, or ability, is not a secure foundation. You can ask yourself what you are trusting in most, hand it over to God in prayer, and ask him to be your true support.
exp.6:14:
God says he will cast the people of Judah out of his presence, just as he has already cast out their "brothers," that is, the tribes of the north. "Ephraim" was the largest tribe and stood for the whole kingdom of Israel. Being cast out of God's presence means being driven away, losing his favor and his nearness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah trusted that the temple in Jerusalem would protect them, even though they kept living in disobedience. God reminds them that he had spoken to them many times and they did not listen. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been taken captive by Assyria, and God uses that example as a warning.

For today: it is not enough to have religious things or to feel secure because of our tradition. God looks for a heart that listens and obeys. If you feel that God is speaking to you today, respond quickly and with humility.
exp.9:11:
This verse says that the LORD made the earth by his power, established the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding. The words "power," "wisdom," and "understanding" name the qualities behind each act of creation: power is strength, wisdom is knowledge, and understanding is good judgment. Everything God has made shows that he works with both strength and a thoughtful mind.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah. Around this passage, he compares the living God with idols made by human hands, which cannot do anything. He wants to remind them that only the Creator deserves trust and worship, and that they should not let themselves be impressed by the religions and customs of the neighboring nations.

Today we can remember that the God who holds up the universe is also wise enough to guide our lives. When something worries us, we can pray and trust that his power and his wisdom never fail. And we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts.
exp.2:7:
Here God says that he saw everything Israel, the northern kingdom, had done. Through her unfaithfulness she "committed adultery," that is, she went after other gods. For this reason he sent her away and gave her a "certificate of divorce." But Judah, her unfaithful sister, saw this and had no fear; she also prostituted herself.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the days of King Josiah. God uses the image of a broken marriage to show that Israel was unfaithful to him through idolatry. Israel had already been taken into captivity, and Judah should have learned from that, but it did not.

For today: let us not minimize sin because others have already suffered its consequences. God invites us to return to him with our whole heart, not merely in appearance, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.15:15:
God says he will send for many fishermen, and they will catch his people. After that, he will send for many hunters, and they will hunt them down on every mountain and hill, even from the clefts of the rocks. No one will be able to hide.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the exile in Babylon. Judah had fallen into idolatry and wickedness. This verse follows a promise of return to the land, but the text that comes next makes clear that judgment will come first. Some understand the fishermen and hunters as the invaders who would lead the people into exile. Others also see a later search to restore them. There is more than one interpretation.

Today: we cannot hide from God, but there is no place where his mercy does not reach us. If you have turned away, return to him with sincerity.
exp.21:1:
God tells Jeremiah to say to the king of Judah: "Hear the word of the LORD." The message is meant not only for the king but also for his officials and for the people who come in through these gates. "Sits on the throne of David" means he rules as a descendant of David.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. God sends him to the royal palace to call the rulers to account. The verses that follow explain the reason: God requires justice, help for the oppressed, and protection for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. Whoever reigns is not an absolute owner; he answers before God.

Whoever has authority, whether in government, at work, or in the home, must listen to God. Today we can ask ourselves: do I use my influence to protect the weak, or only for my own benefit?
exp.25:0:
At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and king of Judah, God gave a message to the prophet. The phrase "this word came from the LORD" means that God spoke directly. "The LORD" is the usual English name for God, written in capital letters in this translation.

The one speaking is God, and he is speaking to Jeremiah. This was a delicate moment: a new king was beginning his reign, and the people needed to return to God. According to the verses that follow, God asks Jeremiah to speak in the temple, holding nothing back, in the hope that the people will turn from their ways. Some scholars see here the start of a message that continues through the rest of the chapter.

For today: God still speaks with clarity and with hope that we will return to him. Today we can hear his word with humility, without trimming it or bending it to suit ourselves, and let it correct us with love.
exp.38:9:
It says that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard for the king of Babylon, left behind in the land of Judah some of the poorest people, those who had no property. At that time he also gave them vineyards and fields to work.

This is part of the account of the fall of Jerusalem. The narrator tells that the Babylonians burned the city and took most of the people away into exile. The poor were left behind, perhaps because they did not seem a threat, and so someone had to care for the land. The text does not explain the captain's exact reasons, so it is best not to claim more. It is striking that, in the middle of the ruin, those with the least received provision.

For today: God can care for the most needy even in times of crisis. We can ask ourselves whom we are overlooking and, where possible, help them with something concrete, such as food, work, or companionship.
exp.22:16:
They keep telling those who despise God, "The LORD says you will have peace." To those who walk in the stubbornness of their own hearts, they promise, "No harm will come to you." Despising God means treating him with contempt and rejecting him, and the stubbornness of the heart is a refusal to bend to God's will and a preference for one's own way.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Before the exile in Babylon, Judah was living in sin, and many prophets offered comforting messages that God had never given them. That is why God rebukes them, since their words came from their own thinking and not from the LORD.

Today it is wise to be cautious about messages that only tell us what we want to hear. Measure what you hear against the Bible, and remember that sometimes God corrects before he comforts.
exp.28:7:
God warns his people not to be led astray by the prophets and diviners who live among them. He also tells them not to listen to the dreams that these people bring to them. Being "deceived" means being led down a wrong path. "Diviners" are people who claim to know the future through means that God does not approve of.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the Jews who were taken into exile in Babylon. God asks them to live normal lives, start families, and seek the good of the city. But some false prophets were telling them that the exile would end soon. God states that he did not send them, and that the return would come only after seventy years.

Today, before you believe a spiritual message, a "prophecy," or a hunch, check it against the Bible. If it does not agree with what God has already said, do not follow it, even if it sounds encouraging.
exp.15:12:
God tells the people of Judah that he will drive them out of their land and take them to a country that neither they nor their ancestors have known. There they will serve other gods all the time, and God will show them no favor. The word "favor" in the verse means kindness or mercy, and "other gods" means false gods.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had abandoned God, worshiped idols, and followed the desires of their stubborn hearts, even more than their fathers did. This is the warning of exile. But the next verse shows that punishment would not be the final word: God promises to bring them back to their land.

For today: when we turn our backs on God, we end up serving other things that enslave us. We can return to him with humility today, trusting that his discipline seeks to restore us, not destroy us.
exp.4:19:
God commands the prophet to announce a message to the whole people. "House of Jacob" and "Judah" refer to God's people, that is, to the entire nation. The verse uses two words for speaking out: "declare" means to announce clearly, and "proclaim" means to make the message known publicly, so that no one can say they never heard it.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. The people had turned away from God to serve other gods, and yet they wondered why hard things were happening to them. This verse opens a warning: what follows is a call to listen, because the people had eyes and ears but did not want to see or hear.

For today: God speaks to us clearly, but sometimes we pretend not to hear. Today you can take a quiet moment, open the Bible, and ask God for a heart willing to listen and obey, without excuses.
exp.17:0:
God spoke to Jeremiah. This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD. The name of God in this translation is "the LORD." The verse is only the introduction, and the teaching comes in the verses that follow.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. Jeremiah ministered in Judah in very difficult times, before the fall of Jerusalem. God sends him to the potter's house to teach him a lesson through something he could see. Later in the text, that image is used to speak about the way God deals with his people.

God still speaks today through his Word. We can ask him for an attentive heart and read the Bible calmly, willing to listen and obey, even in the simple things of each day.
exp.1:21:
God says that even if Israel tries to clean itself with lye and a large amount of soap, its guilt remains, like a stain that will not come out. No human effort can remove that guilt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses his people of abandoning their love for Him to worship other gods, the Baals, at high places and under leafy trees. Even so, the people insisted, "I am not unclean." God uses strong images, such as a faithless wife and a good vine that turned into a wild one, to show the pain of betrayal.

For today: hiding guilt behind a good appearance, religion, or our own effort does not help. The healthiest thing is to honestly admit what we have done and turn to God, who truly forgives and cleanses those who return to Him.
exp.50:47:
It says that the whole universe will shout for joy when Babylon falls. The verse names the direction the destroyers come from, and the verse's sentence about it is rewritten here: the destroyers coming from the north are the armies that will attack from that direction, and the LORD himself declares that he is sending them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and taken its people into exile. God promises that this proud empire will also fall, and he encourages the exiles not to lose heart at news of war. Many understand that the army from the north refers to the Medes and Persians, although the text gives no further detail here.

For today: when you see that evil and injustice seem very strong, remember that God still governs history. Do not despair or take revenge. Trust that he will do justice in his time, and meanwhile remain faithful and keep your heart in him.
exp.28:22:
It says that God judges Ahab and Zedekiah for three things: they committed an outrage in Israel, they committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they spoke lies in God's name, words He never told them to speak. God affirms that He knows this and is a witness to all of it, even though no one else has seen it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He writes to the Jews taken captive to Babylon. There, these two men were giving them false hopes that the exile would be short. God announces that Nebuchadnezzar will punish them. The text says nothing more about how these sins became known, only that God saw them.

For today: God sees what we do in secret, and speaking in His name is something very serious. Before saying "God says this," let us examine His Word and live with integrity, knowing that He is a witness to everything.
exp.33:12:
God begins to speak and reminds them of something important: he made a covenant with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery, the place where they had been enslaved. "The LORD" is God's name, and a covenant is a solemn, binding promise.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had freed their Hebrew slaves, but later changed their minds and enslaved them again. God reminds them that their freedom came from him, and that the law about releasing servants was part of the covenant.

For today: if God has forgiven us and set us free, we should treat others with justice and compassion. Keeping what we have promised, even when it costs us, shows that we truly remember his goodness.
exp.12:14:
This verse says that the people must pay attention and not be arrogant, because the LORD himself has spoken. The words "listen and give heed" mean the same as "listen." The phrase "do not be arrogant" means not becoming full of yourself or thinking you are better than others. It is an urgent call to listen with humility.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the words of the LORD to Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier, God announced a severe judgment on kings, priests, and the whole people because of their rebellion. Even so, in the verses that follow, Jeremiah invites them to give glory to God before the darkness comes, and he says he will weep in secret if they do not listen. His warning comes from pain, not coldness.

For today: when the Bible or our conscience confronts us, let us not defend ourselves with pride. Let us ask God for a humble heart, listen in time, and change our course.
exp.13:14:
This verse says that God speaks sternly against certain prophets. They spoke as if they came from God, but He had not sent them. They said there would be no war or famine, and God answers that these same prophets will die by war and famine.

"Sword" here means war, and "consumed" means destroyed. The Berean Standard Bible puts the first part as "No sword or famine will touch this land," so the prophets' claim is that the land will be safe from both war and hunger.

The one speaking is the LORD, and He says it to Jeremiah. At that time there was a great drought and a threat of invasion. Jeremiah was praying for the people, but there were prophets who gave false comfort. God warns them that their lies will not stop the punishment, and that the people who believed them will also suffer.

For today: let us not believe something just because it sounds comforting or because someone with religious authority says it. Let us compare what we hear with the whole Bible and ask God for wisdom. The truth sometimes makes us uncomfortable, but it cares for us better than a pleasant lie.
exp.31:25:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah once more. The message came directly from God, and the colon at the end of the line introduces what God wants to tell him right away.

Jeremiah has just prayed with doubts. Babylon is already surrounding Jerusalem, and God had asked him to buy a piece of land, even though everything seemed lost. The prophet does not understand why he should make that purchase. Then God answers. He reminds Jeremiah that he is the God of all flesh, that is, of all human beings, and that nothing escapes his knowledge.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening and have questions, bring them honestly to God, as Jeremiah did. God is not troubled by your doubts, and he can answer you with words that restore your confidence in him.
exp.12:20:
God asks Judah, pictured here as a woman, "What will you say when He sets over you close allies whom you yourself trained?" The question points to the reckoning that is coming. The allies she once shaped and relied on will now be the ones who rule over her. And the pain that follows will be like the anguish of a woman in labor: sudden, gripping and intense.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah before the fall of Jerusalem. Judah had sought alliances with other nations instead of trusting in God. Many understand that these allies were powers such as Babylon, which would come from the north. The exact details of who is meant are debated.

For today: the decisions we make without God can turn against us. Today you can examine what you have placed your trust in and return to God with humility before problems grow.
exp.8:13:
They say that the people not only abandoned God's law, but also followed the stubbornness of their own hearts. They also went after the Baals, false gods worshiped by the peoples of Canaan and linked to rain and harvests. That worship had been passed down to them by their fathers. Here the word translated "stubbornness" points to a hardened will and one's own desires, not to mere fantasy.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He explains why the land was laid waste: the people disobeyed his voice and his law. This verse shows the root of the problem, which was following their own impulses and inherited customs. That is why the judgment announced afterward comes.

For today: examine whether what you do comes from the Word of God or only from your desires and from what has "always been done" in your family. Compare it with the Bible, keep what is good, and humbly set aside what does not please God.
exp.28:6:
The verse says that the exiles were to seek the prosperity of the city where God had sent them, and to pray to the LORD on its behalf. The word "seek" means to strive to obtain something. "Exiles" refers to people who have been forced to live away from their homeland. To "pray" is to ask earnestly. The reason given is simple: if the city prospers, they too will prosper.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the Jews who were taken to Babylon. God tells them to settle down, start families, and live normal lives, because the exile would last a long time. At the same time, he warns them not to believe prophets who promised a quick return. Those promises were false.

For today: even when we are not in the place we hoped for, we can serve and pray for our city, work with honesty, and care for our neighbors. God can use that place to provide for us and to shape us.
exp.29:10:
The LORD tells his people, "I am with you to save you." The nations where he scattered them will be completely destroyed, but he will not completely destroy Israel. He will discipline them justly, and he will by no means leave them unpunished.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was under God's judgment and would soon be taken into exile. Even so, God promises restoration: the people will return and live in peace. The verse that follows shows that the wound is serious, but God does not abandon his people.

For today: when God corrects us, his aim is not to destroy us but to heal and restore us. If you are going through discipline or a hard consequence, do not lose hope. Come to God with humility, because he remains with you.
exp.18:1:
God tells Jeremiah to go out to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, near the entrance of the Potsherd Gate of Jerusalem. There he is to proclaim the message that God gives him. "Proclaim" means to announce openly and clearly. The gate's name is sometimes explained as the potters' gate, but its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The LORD speaks, and Jeremiah is his prophet. God sends him with a clay jar and with elders of the people and of the priests, so that they may be witnesses. The valley was a place where the people had worshiped false gods and shed innocent blood. For this reason God warns them of a judgment that is near.

For today: God calls us to speak the truth with courage and love, even when it is not popular. Ask him to show you what to say and when, and do it with humility and without fear.
exp.31:4:
He says that King Zedekiah will be taken to Babylon, where he will stay until God attends to him. Then comes a question: "If you fight against the Chaldeans, will it not go well with you?" That question expects the answer no, since it will not go well for them. "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, who was imprisoned because King Zedekiah could not bear his message. Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah said that resisting would be useless. Some understand "attend to him" as a possible time of God's care or judgment. The text gives no further detail here.

Today it reminds us that God tells the truth even when it is uncomfortable. We can ask him for humility to hear his correction in time, instead of resisting it out of pride or fear.
exp.36:1:
This verse says that King Zedekiah, his officials, and the people of the land of Judah refused to obey the words that God had spoken through the prophet Jeremiah. The verse begins with "But," and it refers to God as "the LORD."

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Zedekiah had been placed as king by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, when Judah was already under his rule. Jeremiah had been warning the people for years, but they would not heed him. Soon after, the king asks Jeremiah to pray for them, which shows that they wanted God's help without being willing to obey his word.

For today: it is not enough to ask God for help in a crisis if we are not willing to obey him in our everyday lives. Today we can ask ourselves what his Word tells us and take a concrete step of obedience.
exp.22:39:
This verse says that God will bring upon them shame that will last forever and humiliation so deep that no one will be able to forget it. The words "everlasting shame" and "perpetual humiliation" here refer to a deep loss of honor and dignity.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, at a time of great corruption. False prophets and the people were using the phrase "burden of the Lord" in a mocking way, or to give authority to their own ideas. Whether it refers to a message or a weight, God had asked them to stop using it. Since they kept speaking in His name without respect, the judgment is severe.

For today: let us be very careful about how we speak in God's name. Before we say "God told me" or use the Bible to support our own opinions, let us pray, study with humility, and speak with reverence.
exp.1:8:
God says he will once again bring his case against his people. "I will contend with you" and "I will bring a case against" are the language of a courtroom: God acts like someone formally making an accusation. He speaks not only to the people of that time but also to their children's children, that is, to future generations. The word "again" shows that God had already spoken to them before.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just recalled that he brought them into a fertile land, but they defiled it. Priests, teachers of the law, shepherds (leaders), and prophets stopped seeking him and followed Baal. This complaint is not from a God who wants to destroy, but from one wounded because his people exchanged what is good for what does not profit them.

For today: God speaks to us with patience before he corrects us. Honestly ask yourself whether anything has taken God's place in your life, and return to him today, before that habit passes on to your children.
exp.29:8:
This verse says that the people will no longer serve foreign oppressors. Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom God himself will raise up for them. David died centuries ago, so many understand this as a future king from his line.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel and Judah, a people who were suffering punishment and exile. He promises to free them from their yoke, that is, from slavery. Christians often see in this "David" Jesus, a descendant of David. Jews interpret it in other ways, as a future king of that line.

For today: when you feel bound by guilt, fear, or a difficult situation, remember that God promises to rescue and restore. Serve him with confidence, because his king does not oppress but sets free.
exp.13:3:
This verse describes a severe drought. The ground is cracked open because no rain has fallen on the land, and the farmers, not knowing what to do, cover their heads. The word "cracked" in the verse means split open. The farmers are the ones who work the fields. Covering the head was a gesture of shame, sorrow, and despair.

Jeremiah records this drought as part of a lament over Judah. Everyone suffers: the nobles, the farmers, and even the animals. Later, the people acknowledge their sin and cry out to God. Many understand this drought as a sign that the people had turned away from Him, although the text shows above all the pain and anguish of the people.

There are moments when our resources run out and we do not know what to do. Instead of hiding our faces in shame, we can lift them up and come to God with sincerity. He receives those who come with empty hands.
exp.15:2:
This verse explains the reason for a hard command God gave to Jeremiah: not to marry or have children in that place. God speaks of the children who would be born there, and of the mothers who gave birth to them and the fathers who had them. The phrase "the mothers who bore them" refers to the women who gave birth, and "the fathers who fathered them" refers to the men who had children. "This place" is the land of Judah.

God speaks to Jeremiah, His prophet, at a time when the people had turned away from Him through idolatry and wickedness. Jeremiah's solitary life was a visible sign of the judgment that was coming. The verses that follow describe a disaster so severe that there would not even be normal funerals.

For today: God speaks with seriousness about sin, but He also gives warning before He acts. If we sense His correction today, let us not ignore it; let us return to Him with humility, because His desire is to restore us.
exp.9:18:
Here someone cries out in pain: "Woe to me because of my brokenness! My wound is grievous!" Then the speaker says to themselves: "This is truly my sickness, and I must bear it." The Hebrew words behind "brokenness" and "wound" are not explained here.

The speaker seems to be the people of Judah, or the prophet speaking on their behalf, facing the invasion and exile that God had announced. Interpreters understand this in different ways, but the next verse describes a ruined tent and lost children, so the pain is real. The cause is mentioned afterward: the shepherds, or rulers, did not seek the Lord.

For today: when pain comes, do not minimize it or bear it in silence. Be honest with God about your wound, and humbly examine whether there is something you should correct, without ceasing to trust in his mercy.
exp.51:30:
This verse tells that, after thirty-seven years of exile, the new king of Babylon, Evil-merodach, pardoned Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and released him from prison. The king did not simply free him; he showed him mercy and restored him to a place of honor. This took place on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, in the first year of that king's reign.

Jeremiah 52 is the end of the book and repeats much of what is told in 2 Kings 25. The account closes with this news, after speaking of the fall of Jerusalem and the deportations. Many understand that the author leaves a sign of hope: the family of David had not been forgotten.

Even in long and dark times, God can open an unexpected door. We can keep trusting and waiting with patience, without thinking that everything is lost.
exp.18:2:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the kings of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem. He announces that he is going to bring disaster on this place so severe that everyone who hears of it will have their ears ring, meaning the news will be so shocking it will leave people reeling. Here "disaster" refers to calamity, not wickedness.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in the valley of Hinnom, next to Jerusalem, with some elders as witnesses. God accuses the people of having abandoned him, of worshiping other gods, of shedding innocent blood, and of burning their children as offerings to Baal. For this reason he announces judgment.

For today: God takes injustice and idolatry seriously. Let us ask him to show us what things have taken his place in our hearts, and let us return to him before we harden ourselves.
exp.4:11:
They have lied about the LORD. The verse says they said, "He will not do anything," meaning that they rejected him or did not take him seriously. They also said that harm would not come to them, and that they would not see sword or famine.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Israel and Judah of rebelling against him. The people felt secure and believed God would not judge them. So God says that his words in the prophet's mouth will be like fire, and the people like wood. Scholars understand that the verse points to the coming invasion of Babylon, though the text gives no further details here.

Today it is easy to live as if God does not see or does not matter, especially when everything is going well. We can ask ourselves honestly: do I listen to his word, or do I ignore it because it makes me uncomfortable? Let us return to him with humility before life forces us to.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that the survivors of this wicked people will choose to die rather than to live. The phrase about choosing death over life is worded here as the verse reads in the Berean Standard Bible. "The remnant" are those who are left alive after the judgment, and "the LORD of Hosts" is the LORD, ruler over all heavenly armies and powers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had worshiped the sun, the moon and the stars, and would not turn back to God even though they were called many times. For this reason he announces a harsh judgment: exile and shame. The verses that follow show that God still asks them why they do not return.

For today: let us not harden our hearts. If we feel that something is pulling us away from God, let us return to Him soon, because God still receives whoever truly repents.
exp.45:4:
God asks in wonder: "Why am I seeing this? They are terrified, they are retreating." The Egyptian soldiers, even their warriors, were defeated and fled in haste without looking back. The words "they flee in haste" describe people running quickly and without stopping. The phrase "terror is on every side" describes a fear that surrounded them on all sides, as the verse says: "terror is on every side."

Jeremiah speaks a message from the Lord about Egypt. The verses before it show the army proudly preparing for war. Here we see the result: defeat. The text connects this with the battle of Carchemish beside the river Euphrates, where Babylon defeated Egypt. The message teaches that no human power is above God.

For today: do not place your security only in your strength, your money, or your preparation. Do your part well, but trust first in God, because He sustains what human effort cannot.
exp.6:17:
This verse shows whole families working together in idolatry: the sons gather the wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead the dough. Together they make cakes for the Queen of Heaven, a pagan goddess (many believe she was Astarte or Ishtar, though this is not certain). They also pour out drink offerings to other gods, and the purpose is stated plainly: to provoke God to anger.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He tells him that he should no longer pray for the people, because they do not want to return to Him. What is serious is that the whole family takes part, and this is not a hidden sin but one in plain sight in the streets.

For today: ask yourself what things your family does together. Make sure their faith, their customs, and their example at home point toward God and not toward other things that take His place.
exp.45:20:
Egypt's hired soldiers, who were well fed and comfortable like fattened calves, did not stand their ground in the battle. They turned back and fled together, all at once, because the day of their calamity had come upon them. In this verse, "the time of their punishment" means the moment when God acts to judge them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD has said. Egypt relied on its strength and its reputation, but God declares that the enemy will come against it. Many understand this as a reference to the Egyptian defeat before Nebuchadnezzar. Some scholars debate whether these soldiers were foreign mercenaries, since the text does not make this completely clear.

For today: do not place your security in your comfort, your money, or your strength. All of these can fail in a difficult day. Trust in God, who sustains life when everything else collapses, and live with humility and responsibility.
exp.36:18:
Here Jeremiah asks King Zedekiah: where are the prophets who told you that the king of Babylon would not come against you or this land? "Your" refers to the people and the king, and "who prophesied to you" means they spoke to them on God's behalf.

Jeremiah speaks from prison, where they had put him for saying that Jerusalem would fall. The king consults him in secret, and Jeremiah repeats God's message to him without softening it. With this question he shows the king that the prophets who promised peace were wrong, while what Jeremiah had said was coming true.

For today: let us not seek only voices that reassure us. It is good to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible and to be willing to hear the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, because God corrects us to help us return to Him.
exp.16:9:
In this verse God says that He examines the deepest part of each person. "Searching the heart" means investigating thoughts and desires thoroughly. "Examining the mind" refers to looking closely at the inner thinking and motives behind what people do. God rewards each person according to their way, and what they receive reflects what their deeds deserve.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. He has just said that the human heart is deceitful and that no one knows it well. Here He answers that He does know it. Earlier He contrasted the one who trusts in God, like a tree beside the water, with the one who trusts in man.

For today: do not be content with looking good on the outside, nor trust only in your feelings. Ask God to examine your heart and correct you with love, and trust in Him sincerely.
exp.1:25:
Jeremiah 2:26 says that Israel will be put to shame, just as a thief is ashamed when he is caught. The shame will reach everyone: the people, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets. No one is spared, not even those who were supposed to lead and guide the nation.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of having turned away from the living God to follow other gods. He compares them to a wild donkey in heat, running out of control. They answer stubbornly, "We have loved strangers, and after them we will go." Then they call a piece of wood "father," yet in their distress they ask God for help.

For today: it is not enough to turn to God only when there are problems. Examine what you place your trust in, such as money, success, or the approval of others, and return to God from now on, not only in the crisis.
exp.36:3:
Jeremiah was moving freely among the people, going where he liked, because they had not yet put him in prison. The prison he would later be held in is simply called the prison here.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans, also known as the Babylonians. King Zedekiah had not obeyed God, yet he still asked Jeremiah to pray for the nation. The narrator makes clear that Jeremiah was still free, but it will soon be seen that they would imprison him. It is also mentioned that the army of Egypt came and the Chaldeans withdrew for a time, which gave the people false hope.

For today: we often seek God only when we are in trouble, without wanting to obey him the rest of the time. God invites us to listen to his word always, not only in crisis, and to obey it sincerely.
exp.28:27:
It says that Jeremiah sent a message to the exiles in Babylon: the exile will be lengthy. For that reason they are to build houses and settle down, and plant gardens and eat their produce. The verse notes that the wording means "it will be long," that one word means "build," another means "settle down," and another means "plant."

The one speaking here is Shemaiah, a false prophet who was in Babylon. From there he wrote to Zephaniah, the priest in Jerusalem, complaining about Jeremiah. He quotes Jeremiah's letter as if it were a nuisance. For Shemaiah, that advice discouraged the hope of a quick return. Jeremiah was telling them that God would care for them even there.

For today: when you go through a difficult season that will not end soon, do not put your life on hold. With God's help, keep working, caring for your family, and serving where you are, without ceasing to trust his promises.
exp.31:11:
He says that Jeremiah handed Baruch the deed of the purchase for the field. He did this in front of his cousin Hanameel, the witnesses who had signed the purchase agreement, and all the Jews sitting in the courtyard of the guard. "Deed" means the written document recording the sale. "Signed" means the witnesses had put their names to the agreement.

Jeremiah speaks while he is imprisoned in Jerusalem, as the army of Babylon surrounds the city. God asked him to buy a field in Anathoth, even though the land seemed lost. It was a sign that, after the judgment, the people would return to their land. Baruch, his secretary, would keep the documents with care.

For today: God invites us to trust his promises even when the situation looks dark. We can take concrete steps of faith, with order and honesty, waiting for God to fulfill what he has said.
exp.50:30:
It says that couriers will arrive one after another, racing to tell the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end. Here "courier" means a messenger who travels on foot.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what the LORD had decided against Babylon. This power had oppressed Judah and other nations. Many understand that the verse describes the fall of the city, and the Greek historian Herodotus recounts that it was taken quickly and by surprise, although the details are debated.

For today: no human power is eternal, however secure it may seem. We can trust that God acts with justice and in his own time. This invites us not to place our security in riches, fame, or strength, but in him.
exp.48:7:
Turn and run, the Lord tells the people of Dedan. Hide in the low places and stay out of sight, because judgment is coming. The verse says God will bring disaster on Esau, the ancestor of Edom, at the time He punishes him. Dedan was a neighboring people, probably allied with or related to Edom, so they too were in danger. The word "disaster" points to the ruin that falls on Edom, and "punish" means that God comes to call them to account for what they have done.

Jeremiah delivers this message against Edom, and God makes clear that neither the wisdom for which Teman was known nor any hiding place could save Edom when its time came.

For us today, the lesson is plain. We cannot hide from God, and we cannot rely on our own wisdom or sense of security to protect us. It is far better to come to Him now with humility and seek His forgiveness while there is still time.
exp.30:25:
He says that someone wakes up from a sleep and realizes it was pleasant and restful. "At this I awoke and looked around" means that he woke up and took in his surroundings, and the rest had been good for him. The sleep was pleasant and did him good.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks after receiving a message of hope for Judah and Israel, who were suffering under judgment and exile. God promises comfort to the weary and joy to the sorrowful. Some understand the sleep as a vision God gave him; others, as an expression of relief after so many harsh announcements. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when you are exhausted or sad, remember that God can bring rest and hope into your life. Trust his promises, even if you do not yet see the complete change.
exp.35:4:
Jeremiah gives an instruction to Baruch, his assistant. He tells him that he is "restricted," meaning that he is prevented from moving freely, and so he cannot enter the house of the LORD, which is called here the temple. The word "commanded" means that he gave him a task to carry out.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He had already dictated to Baruch all the words that God had given him, and now he wants them read in public. Jeremiah could not go to the temple, although the text does not explain in detail the reason for his restriction. God wanted the people to hear, to repent, and to be forgiven.

For today: when a limitation keeps you from doing what you would wish, do not sit idly by. Ask God what you can do with what you still have, and trust that He can use other people to carry forward His message.
exp.24:19:
This verse follows a list of nations to whom God commands that the cup of his anger be given to drink. Named here are "all the mixed tribes," meaning foreign peoples who were mixed together or allied; all the kings of Uz; all the kings of the Philistines (the land of the Philistines is meant here); and the cities of Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and what remained of Ashdod. Exactly who the "mixed tribes" were is not known for certain.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, around 605 B.C. He warns that Babylon would come as an instrument of judgment, not only against Judah but against many neighboring nations.

For today: God rules over all nations, not only over his own people. This invites us to live with humility, not to trust in human power, and to listen to his voice in time, seeking his forgiveness and guidance.
exp.26:20:
Yes, this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says about the articles that remain in the house of the LORD, in the palace of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem. The verse opens by stressing that what follows is the word of God, not the prophet's own opinion. It names the articles still left in the temple, in the royal palace of Judah, and in Jerusalem. "Articles" here means objects of value, such as vessels and containers, used in worship.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. Jeconiah and many of the nobles had already been carried off to Babylon, along with some objects from the temple. False prophets were claiming that everything would soon be returned. Jeremiah contradicts them: what remains will also be taken away, and God will bring it back in his own time.

For today: when someone promises quick and easy solutions, it is wise to ask what God really says. His word sometimes corrects us, but it also offers hope. We can trust that He keeps His times and does not forget us in our trials.
exp.16:20:
God tells Jeremiah to warn the people. Their very lives depend on it. They must not carry a load on the Sabbath day, nor bring it through the gates of Jerusalem.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the kings of Judah and all the people living in Jerusalem. The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant with God. Carrying loads and doing business on that day showed a heart that did not trust in Him. The verses that follow say that their ancestors would not listen or accept correction.

For today: God invites us to rest and to trust that He sustains our lives. We can set aside a weekly time free from worry and work, to be with Him, with our family, and with the church, and to let Him correct us with humility.
exp.2:22:
What it says: Here "deception" means something false that promises help but delivers nothing. The "hills" and "mountains" were the high places where the people worshiped idols. "Salvation" means rescue or deliverance. The verse admits that those places of false worship do not save; only the LORD our God can save Israel.

Context: Jeremiah tells of a weeping heard on the heights, and God calls the rebellious children to return so that he can heal them. This verse is the answer of the repentant people, who admit their mistake. The lines that follow show their shame at having followed idols, just as their ancestors did.

For today: We can ask ourselves what things we have placed our hope in, such as money, success, or the approval of others. If they fail us, we can return to God sincerely, knowing that he does receive the one who comes back to him.
exp.31:29:
This verse says that God's people, both Israel and Judah, had done nothing but evil from their youth as a nation. To "provoke" God to anger means to stir up his displeasure, and "the work of their hands" points above all to the idols they made.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by the Babylonians and will soon fall. God explains that this judgment is not unjust: the people had been turned to idols for a long time, even burning incense to Baal on the rooftops. Yet in this same chapter God promises to restore his people.

For today: we should not take sin lightly or let it become a habit. We can ask what things made by our own hands or desires have taken the place of God, and turn back to him with humility, trusting that his mercy is still open.
exp.40:2:
This verse tells that Ishmael, after murdering Gedaliah, also killed all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, as well as the Chaldean soldiers who were there. "Killed" here means that he put them to death, and "Chaldean soldiers" are the Babylonians.

The one telling the story is the book of Jeremiah, which recounts what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Ishmael, who was of royal lineage, took advantage of a shared meal to betray and kill. The Bible does not fully explain his motives; many think resentment and political ambition played a part, and that he may have had foreign backing (the king of the Ammonites is mentioned in verse 40:14).

Today, this account warns us how destructive resentment is when it is not surrendered to God. It also invites us to seek peace and not to let ambition or bitterness lead us to harm others.
exp.30:16:
God tells Rachel, who is weeping for her lost children, that there is hope for her future. "Your future" means what comes next, the outcome of her story. "Your land" means her homeland. Her children will return to their land.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Rachel appears as an image of the mothers of Israel who weep for their children carried off into exile. Ramah was a place near where the captives were gathered. God answers their grief with a promise of return, within a broader message of restoration for his people.

For today: when you go through a loss or a painful wait, you may weep without guilt, but you can also bring your pain before God and trust that he has the final word. His promise does not deny your sadness; it accompanies it with hope.
exp.45:13:
Here God commands that a warning be announced throughout the cities of Egypt: Migdol, Memphis, and Tahpanhes. The message is to take your positions and prepare yourselves, because the sword is about to devour everyone around you. The call to prepare means to ready yourself for what is coming. "Those around you" refers to the people and places surrounding the cities.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah about the coming attack by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who would strike Egypt. Egypt trusted in its military strength, but the text says its strong soldiers would stumble over one another. The message shows that no human power stands above God.

Today we can learn not to rest only on our security, money, or strength. If God warns us in time, it is wise to listen and adjust our lives. Trusting in Him gives us a firmer foundation than any army.
exp.7:20:
He says the prophet is crushed inside as he sees the harm done to his people. The word "brokenness" points to something shattered and wounded. The words "I mourn" describe deep grief, a heavy sorrow that weighs on him. The phrase "horror has gripped me" means that dread seized him and left him without strength. "The daughter of my people" is a tender way of naming Judah.

The speaker is Jeremiah, though some think the voice of God can also be heard in the chapter. Judah had given itself to carved images and other gods, and judgment was coming. The people complain that the summer has passed and no rescue came. Jeremiah, instead of mocking, weeps with them.

For today: when we see the pain or sin of others, let us not respond with coldness or pride. Let us ask for a compassionate heart, pray for them, and look for ways to help them return to God, the true healer.
exp.25:15:
This verse says that the officials and the people defended Jeremiah before the priests and prophets who were accusing him. They declared that he did not deserve death, because what he had spoken came in the name of the LORD our God. The "officials" are the leaders of Judah. The phrase "worthy of death" describes a person who has committed an offense punishable by execution.

Jeremiah had preached in the temple that God would destroy Jerusalem if the people did not repent. The priests and prophets grew angry and demanded his death. Jeremiah answered calmly and warned that killing him would mean shedding innocent blood. Then the officials and the people recognized that he was speaking for the LORD. Afterward, some elders recalled the case of the prophet Micah.

For today: when an uncomfortable truth comes from the Word of God, let us not reject it out of irritation. Let us listen with humility, and if necessary, repent.
exp.21:26:
Here it says that Coniah and his mother will long with all their heart to return to their land, but they will never get back there. The phrase "lift up their soul" is an old expression that means to long for, to desire eagerly. In your verse, the word "long" is the one that carries this sense.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was a king of Judah. God announces that he will be handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar and taken captive to Babylon. This happened because of the kingdom's disobedience. The text says he would die there, far from his homeland.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and God invites us to listen to Him in time. Even when we go through losses or difficult periods of exile, we can draw near to Him with humility, knowing that He hears us and cares for us.
exp.11:6:
God himself speaks and says that he has forsaken his house, that is, the temple and the land where he dwelt among his people. He says he has abandoned his inheritance. The word "inheritance" refers to what is received as property, and here it means Israel, the people of God. The phrase "the beloved of my soul" shows his deep affection for them. Even so, he gives them into the hands of their enemies.

Jeremiah complains that the wicked prosper. God answers him that his people have turned against him, and that even the prophet's own family will betray him. God suffers in judging, because he loves what he punishes. Scholars agree that this is about the judgment on Judah for its rebellion.

God takes no pleasure in punishment; his judgment is painful to him. Today we can trust that, when he corrects us, he does so with a heart wounded by love, and we can respond in time with sincere repentance.
exp.3:23:
Jeremiah describes what he sees in a vision: the mountains were quaking, and all the hills were swaying. What seems most solid in the land was shaking and collapsing. "Quaking" means shaking hard, and "swaying" means moving back and forth.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. God has just said that his people are foolish: they knew how to do evil, but not how to do good. The vision shows the effect of God's judgment, as if everything were returning to emptiness. Many think it speaks of an invasion that was approaching, and the image is very poetic.

For today: do not put your security in things that seem firm, such as money, success, or your own wisdom. Seek to know God truly and to obey him, because only he does not move.
exp.37:7:
This verse tells that Ebed-melech went out from the king's palace and went to speak to the king. He had heard that Jeremiah was in a dungeon, that is, a deep, dark cistern used as a prison. There was no water there, only mud. An official of the court was called a "eunuch," and the word "Ethiopian" indicates that he came from Ethiopia, a land south of Egypt.

The narrator tells that the leaders of the people had thrown Jeremiah there because they did not like his message from God. Ebed-melech, a foreigner with a position in the palace, saw the injustice and decided to act. The king was sitting at the gate of Benjamin, so Ebed-melech went to find him to defend the prophet.

For today: when we see an injustice, let us not wait for someone else to speak. Ebed-melech did not have the power of the leaders, but he used his position and his voice with courage. We can do the same on a small scale, defending someone who suffers mistreatment.
exp.17:22:
Here Jeremiah speaks to God and tells Him that He knows well the plans of his enemies to kill him. He asks God not to forgive them or wipe away their guilt, that is, not to let them go unpunished. The words "let them be overthrown" mean that they should be brought down before God's justice. The "time of your anger" is the moment when God acts in judgment.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. The people of his own town rejected him and plotted against him because he announced hard messages on behalf of God. This is one of his strongest prayers, sometimes called a "confession." Some see in it sincere pain brought before God; others, a cry that reflects the justice of prophetic judgment.

For today: when someone hurts you, you can bring your pain to God with complete honesty, without hiding what you feel. But leave justice in His hands, and remember that Jesus taught us to pray also for those who harm us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.28:25:
The passage says that God appointed Zephaniah as priest in place of Jehoiada, to serve as the chief officer in the house of the LORD. His responsibility was to deal with any madman who acts like a prophet. Such a man was to be put in the stocks and in neck irons, a wooden device that held the body fast.

Here Shemaiah speaks, a false prophet exiled in Babylon. He wrote this letter to Zephaniah and the priests of Jerusalem to pressure them into silencing Jeremiah. Jeremiah had advised the exiles to settle down and wait, since the exile would be long. Shemaiah called him mad, but Jeremiah's message came from God.

For today: do not dismiss a message just because it is uncomfortable or unpopular. Test it against Scripture and ask God for wisdom before you judge.
exp.17:17:
Jeremiah's opponents say: "Come, let us make plans against him." They believe they do not need his message, because there will always be priests to teach the law, wise people to give advice, and prophets to speak. "Let us denounce him" means attacking him with words, accusing and condemning him, and "pay no heed to any of his words" means they will refuse to pay attention to what he says.

The speakers are some of the people who reject Jeremiah's message. He had announced judgment because of Judah's unfaithfulness, and instead of turning back, they choose to silence him. Afterward, Jeremiah prays to God and reminds him that he had pleaded on their behalf.

For today: when a correction makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to attack the messenger. Let us ask God for humility to examine what we hear, and if we are criticized for speaking the truth in love, let us bring that burden to prayer, as Jeremiah did.
exp.47:25:
It says that God tells Moab to be "made drunk," meaning to stagger under his judgment, like someone who drinks a cup of punishment. The reason is that Moab "magnified himself" against the Lord, which means he set himself up proudly against Him. Therefore he will wallow in his own vomit, a picture of complete humiliation. "Laughingstock" means someone mocked and put to public shame.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and the chapter announces its fall because of its arrogance and its trust in itself. The following verse recalls that Moab also mocked Israel, the people of God.

For today: pride that defies God ends in shame. We can examine whether we trust our achievements more than Him, and ask Him for humility to depend on God each day.
exp.38:7:
This verse tells that the armies of Babylon, called Chaldeans, set fire to the king's palace and to the houses of the people. They also broke down the walls of Jerusalem. The phrase "set fire to" in this verse refers to lighting the buildings on fire.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah records the fall of Jerusalem in the year 586 BC, according to the most widely accepted date. For years, Jeremiah had warned that if the people did not return to God, this judgment would come. The verses before this one show the sad end of King Zedekiah, and the verses that follow describe how many were taken captive.

For today: God speaks clearly and is faithful to his word, even when we do not always want to listen. If we feel that he is correcting us, let us not wait until everything falls apart; let us return to him today with humility, because his mercy remains open.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that when God's people have grown in number and prospered in the land, the ark of the covenant will no longer be talked about. It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made. "When you multiply and increase" points to a future time of growth, and "declares the LORD" tells us God Himself is speaking.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to an unfaithful people, yet He invites them to return. The ark was the symbol of God's presence. Here He promises a new time when Jerusalem itself will be called "the throne of the LORD." Some see in this a closer divine presence; others, an announcement of the Messiah. Interpreters explain it in several ways.

For today: do not cling to symbols or traditions as if they were God Himself. Seek His presence sincerely, because He wants to be near you.
exp.43:27:
It says that a few survivors from Judah will escape the sword and return from Egypt to their land. Then all those who went to live in Egypt will know whose word will stand: God's or theirs. The "remnant" means those who are left over, the rest. The "sword" refers to war.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem kept worshiping the queen of heaven and said things were going better for them that way. God warns them that his judgment will come upon them, and the outcome will show who was right.

For today: we can ask ourselves whose advice we are following more, our own ideas and excuses or the word of God. Opinions change, but what God says endures. It is wise to obey him before we learn the hard way.
exp.8:17:
It says the mourning women, women who were skilled at weeping at funerals, should come quickly and raise a lament over the people. The verse uses the words "come quickly," meaning they should hurry. The "eyelids" are the edges of the eyes, and "overflow" and "gush" describe tears flowing out in great amounts. It is a weeping that does not stop.

The LORD of hosts speaks through Jeremiah. He announces that Judah will be scattered and destroyed because of its unfaithfulness. He calls for the women who knew how to lament, because the pain will be so great that it will take a deep and shared weeping. Some believe Jeremiah himself joins in that grief, since he is known as the prophet who wept for his people.

Today we can learn that weeping in the face of sin and suffering is not weakness. If there is pain in your family or your community, do not hide it: bring it to God and tenderly accompany the one who suffers.
exp.16:16:
Jeremiah asks God not to become something that terrifies him. He says to God, "You are my refuge," meaning that he trusts in God and runs to him for shelter when hard times come. The phrase "day of disaster" refers to a time of distress, danger, or calamity.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. People mocked him and said, "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come now!" Jeremiah announced judgment, and that is why they rejected him. He insists that he did not seek this work or desire the disaster, and that he spoke with sincerity before God. For this reason he clings to God as his refuge.

For today: when you are criticized or feel pressured for doing what is right, speak to God with complete honesty. Tell him your fear, and place your trust in him again, because he can sustain you when the difficult day comes.
exp.23:2:
God asks Jeremiah what he sees, and the prophet answers that there are figs: the good figs are very good, but the bad figs are so bad that they cannot be eaten. The Berean Standard Bible has Jeremiah answer "Figs!" and then describe the two kinds, which is how the image is set up for the reader.

The Lord speaks, and Jeremiah answers him. This happens after Nebuchadnezzar carried King Jeconiah and many of the leaders and craftsmen of Judah away to Babylon. With this simple image, God wants to teach something about the exiles. He himself makes clear that he looks with favor on those taken to Babylon and has good plans for them, even though their situation may look like punishment.

For today: do not judge your life only by what you see. A hard season can be a time when God is caring for you and preparing you. Ask him for eyes to see as he sees.
exp.5:6:
As a well keeps gushing out its water, so the city keeps pouring out its evil. Violence and destruction can be heard all around it. Sickness and wounds are always before God.

This verse says that the evil of Jerusalem is like a well that never runs dry: it keeps flowing out without stopping. "Evil" is the word the verse uses for wrongdoing. The phrase about violence and destruction being heard in the city means that abuse and harm can be heard on every side. The phrase about sickness and wounds speaks of the damage and pain this evil causes, which God sees continually.

God speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah, to Jerusalem. A few verses earlier, God announces an attack against the city because of its violence. Even so, in the following verse he calls it to turn from its ways, so his judgment also brings an invitation to return. Scholars debate the exact timing, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not let small evil become a habit. Ask God to show you which attitudes or injustices you have come to accept as normal, and deal with them soon, with humility and change.
exp.5:18:
God calls the whole earth to witness what he is about to do. He says he will bring disaster upon Judah, and that this disaster is "the fruit of their own schemes," the natural result of their choices and their hearts.
