The reason is clear: they have paid no attention to God's word and have rejected his instruction.

The verse says they rejected God's instruction, meaning they turned it away.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he had sent watchmen, that is, prophets who warned of danger, but the people answered, "We will not listen." Afterward, God says that their sacrifices and their incense do not please him, because their religion was only outward and their lives did not obey.

For today: it is not enough to practice religious rituals if we close our ears to the voice of God. Today you can read his Word with humility and obey something concrete that it shows you.
exp.49:2:
For a nation from the north will come against Babylon and make its land a desolation. The verse says it plainly: no one will live in it, and both man and beast will flee. The phrase "from the north" tells us the direction of the attack. "Desolation" here means total ruin, a land left empty of people and animals alike.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and taken Judah into captivity. Its idols, Bel and Merodach, are called powerless. Scholars often see the Medes and Persians in this, although the prophecy also speaks of a broader fulfillment. Then God promises that Israel will return, weeping and seeking him.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, stands above God. We can trust that he does justice and restores those who return to him in humility.
exp.50:24:
God speaks directly against Babylon, which he calls the "destroying mountain" because it devastated many nations. He declares that he is against it, that he will stretch out his hand against it, that he will roll it over the cliffs, and that he will turn it into a charred mountain, a scorched and lifeless ruin like a burned-out volcano.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and God promises to repay Babylon for the wrong done to Zion. Some understand the image of the mountain as the power of the empire; others see it as a reference to its lofty capital. The text does not specify.

For today: do not lose heart when pride and injustice seem to prevail. God sees, and no human power is eternal. Trust in his justice, refrain from taking revenge on your own, and seek to live with humility.
exp.16:22:
This verse says that the people of Judah did not listen to God or pay attention to him. "Stiffened their necks" means they became stubborn, like an ox that will not let the yoke be put on it. "Would not listen" and "incline their ear" go together: they refused to listen or to let themselves be taught.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who addresses the people of Jerusalem. He had asked them to keep the Sabbath as a day set apart, without burdens or work, as he had commanded their ancestors. The Sabbath was a sign of trust and obedience to God. This verse shows that their underlying problem was not just a rule, but a heart that did not want to listen. God offers them blessing if they obey.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are willing to listen to God when something makes us uncomfortable. This week, choose a moment to read the Bible calmly, and ask God for a heart willing to receive his discipline.
exp.13:11:
Even if the people fast, God says He will not listen to their cry. He will not accept their burnt offerings or their grain offerings either. Here "finish them off" means to destroy them. The "sword" stands for war, "famine" is a shortage of food, and "plague" refers to diseases that spread quickly among people.

The LORD speaks to Jeremiah during a severe drought and the threat of war. The people kept up religious practices on the outside, but their daily lives were far from God. The false prophets promised them peace without any need to turn back to Him. For this reason God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them.

For today: religious acts, such as praying, fasting, or giving, do not replace a heart that turns back to God. You might ask yourself honestly: is there something God is asking me to change while I only go through the outward motions?
exp.24:10:
This verse says that the whole land of Judah would become a desolate wasteland, and that these nations would have to serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. A desolate wasteland is an empty, abandoned place, left bare and lifeless.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After years of warning that went unheeded, he announces that the people will suffer the consequences of their rebellion. He calls Nebuchadnezzar "my servant" because he would use him as an instrument of judgment, though that does not excuse the wickedness of Babylon. For this reason, after the seventy years, God would also judge Babylon. Scholars understand in different ways how to count those seventy years.

For today: God speaks clearly and is patient, but he takes our decisions seriously. If you have ignored one of his warnings, do not wait any longer: return to him today. Even judgment has a limit, and God remains the one in control.
exp.5:15:
God tells the people of Judah to stop, like someone who has come to a crossroads, and to look and ask about the ancient paths, that is, the ways of faithfulness God showed them from the beginning. Where is the good way? Walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls, that is, peace and inner calm. But the people answer firmly: "We will not walk in it!"

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God denounced leaders who healed the wound of the people lightly, saying "peace, peace" when there was no peace. Later, God sends watchmen to warn them of the danger, and they also refuse to listen. It is a call to return before judgment.

For today: before making an important decision, stop for a moment, pray, and seek God's guidance in the Bible, instead of following only what is fashionable or what comforts you for a little while.
exp.14:3:
It says that God will make his people a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. The word "horror" points to something so dreadful that others are appalled by it and shudder at the sight. The cause it gives is what Manasseh, son of Hezekiah and king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.

The words are spoken by the LORD through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. Manasseh had promoted idolatry and violence (2 Kings 21). Although his grandson Josiah carried out reforms, the people kept walking the same path. Interpreters explain in different ways how Manasseh's guilt relates to that later generation, but the text shows that his sin left deep marks.

For today: our decisions can affect others, even those who come after us. Take care what you sow in your family, and return to God with sincerity while there is still time.
exp.23:5:
God promises to care for a group of people with kindness. "I will keep my eyes on them for good" means that he will look on them with favor. He says he will return them to their land, will build them up and not tear them down. He will also plant them and not uproot them, like someone tending a garden.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks for God. Judah was carried off captive to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans. God uses the image of two baskets of figs: the good figs represent those taken into exile, whom God did not abandon, and the bad figs represent those who stayed behind with King Zedekiah. In this way he gives them hope in the middle of exile.

For today: even when you go through a painful season, God may be working for your good. Trust that he has not forgotten you, and turn back to him with your whole heart.
exp.22:34:
This verse says that people should ask one another in a simple way: "What has the LORD answered?" and "What has the LORD spoken?" The words "each man to his friend and to his brother" mean that each person speaks to his friend or relative. God is teaching them the right way to talk about his message.

God speaks through Jeremiah. At that time, some false prophets used the phrase "burden of the LORD" to give weight to their own ideas. God corrects this misuse, because they were twisting his words. That is why he asks them to ask again what he actually said.

Before repeating what others say God has spoken, it is wise to ask: what does the Bible really say? We can examine the Scriptures with humility and not use God's name to support our own opinions.
exp.0:9:
God tells Jeremiah that he has appointed him today over nations and kingdoms. "To uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow" speaks of removing what is wrong; "to build and plant" speaks of raising up something new.

The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, a young man called to be a prophet. He had just touched his mouth and put his words in it. Jeremiah had no power of his own: his authority consisted in announcing what God said, and those words would bring judgment and also hope. God promises to be with him, so that he would not fear.

For today: God does not call us only to point out what is wrong, but also to build. Ask him to show you what attitude you should let go of and what good habit you should sow, and trust that he walks with you.
exp.50:59:
Jeremiah had written on a single scroll all the disaster that would come upon Babylon, all these words that had been written concerning Babylon. The message gathered everything God had spoken against that city and its empire. Here the disaster means judgment, not wickedness.

Jeremiah was God's prophet in Judah. He wrote this message for Seraiah, an official who traveled to Babylon with King Zedekiah in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was to read it there, aloud, as a sign that God would carry out what had been announced. Many believe it was also a message of hope for the exiles.

For today: God does not forget what He promises, so it is worth writing down and keeping His words. Even when evil seems strong, we can trust that God has the last word.
exp.48:4:
God says he will bring terror on the Ammonites from every side. People will be driven out in panic, each one rushing straight ahead, and no one will be left to bring back those who have fled and scattered.

The Lord, the LORD of Hosts, speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is against Ammon, a people living next to Israel. They trusted in their fertile valleys and their wealth, and they said, "Who will come against me?" God warns them that this sense of security is false.

For today: let us not place our security in money, in work, or in what we own. All of that can change suddenly. Let us trust in God, who gives true peace and who gathers up the one who is lost.
exp.3:6:
A fearsome enemy is described here, advancing like a lion that has left its hiding place. He is called a destroyer of nations, meaning someone who lays whole peoples to ruin. He has set out to leave the land of Judah in ruins, with its cities reduced to rubble and no one living in them. To be "reduced to ruins" means to be destroyed completely, and to be "uninhabited" means to have no one living there.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what God says. God warns Judah that judgment is coming from the north because of their disobedience. Many understand the lion to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. The alarm is meant to wake the people and move them to act.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings, hoping that everything will simply pass. If you sense that something in your life is drifting away from Him, do not put it off. Come to Him today with humility, ask for forgiveness, and correct your course, trusting in His mercy.
exp.33:1:
God commands Jeremiah to go to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and deliver a clear message: Jerusalem is about to be handed over to the king of Babylon, and he will burn the city down. "Burn it down" here means to destroy it completely by fire. "Deliver into the hand" means to put something under another's power.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD, the God of Israel. Babylon, under Nebuchadnezzar and his army, was already attacking Jerusalem and the cities of Judah that remained. God sends this word because the people and their kings had turned away from Him. Even so, the message goes on to include a personal word for Zedekiah: he would not die by the sword.

For today: God sometimes speaks hard truths, but He does so that we will listen and respond. If you feel corrected by something today, do not harden your heart; come near to God with humility.
exp.30:33:
It says that a time is coming when no one will need to tell another, "Know the LORD," because everyone will know him, from the least to the greatest. The reason is that God will forgive their wrongdoing and will remember their sins no more. The words "neighbor" and "brother" in the verse refer to a fellow citizen and a companion. Saying God will "remember their sins no more" means that God will not hold their sins against them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who had broken the covenant and were suffering the consequences. God promises a new covenant, with his law written on the heart. Christians see its fulfillment in Jesus (Hebrews 8); others interpret it in other ways.

For today: you can draw near to God without fear, trusting in his forgiveness. Knowing him is not only learning facts, but living in relationship with him, and asking that his word transform your heart each day.
exp.12:24:
This is your lot, the share God has measured out to you, Jerusalem. The word "lot" means what falls to a person as their portion, and the phrase "the portion I have measured to you" refers to the fair share she receives. The reason is clear: the people forgot God and put their trust in a lie, that is, in false gods and deceptive securities.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier He said they were so used to doing wrong that it was hard for them to change, just as a leopard does not change its spots. Then He announces that their shame will be exposed, and yet He asks with sorrow, "How long?"

For today: check where you place your trust. When we forget God, false securities fail us. Today, spend a few minutes in prayer and leave in His hands what worries you most.
exp.50:58:
This verse presents a message that the prophet Jeremiah gave to Seraiah, son of Neriah. Seraiah was accompanying King Zedekiah of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign. He is called "the quartermaster," a title whose exact meaning is uncertain.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God. He entrusts to Seraiah, who was travelling to Babylon, the great city that ruled over Judah, the word of judgment against it. In this way the message would reach the very place it spoke about. The Bible gives no further details about the reason for the king's journey.

For today: God can use ordinary people, in difficult places, to carry his word. Trust that he rules over the powers of this world, and obey faithfully wherever you find yourself.
exp.22:33:
It says that if a prophet, a priest, or anyone else claims, "This is the burden of the LORD," God himself will punish that person and his household. The Hebrew word for "burden" (massa) can mean "weight" or also a "solemn message." The phrase "I will punish" means "I will call to account."

God speaks through Jeremiah in the days of Judah before the exile. There were prophets who claimed to speak for God, but they were making up their messages. Some probably used that phrase mockingly or to give false authority to their own words. For this reason God forbids the expression and judges those who distort his word.

For today: before saying "God told me" or "the Bible says," let us think with humility and check whether what we say is truly faithful to Scripture. Using God's name to back up our own ideas is something very serious.
exp.20:5:
God himself says he will strike down the people who live in Jerusalem, and that both people and animals will die in a terrible plague. A plague is a deadly disease that spreads quickly from one person to another.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. King Zedekiah had asked for a hopeful word while the army of Babylon was surrounding Jerusalem. God answers with judgment, because the people had turned away from him. Even so, the passage ends by setting before them a way of life and a way of death: there was still a choice to be made.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God corrects us. If he shows us a mistake, we can listen and turn back to him with humility, because his warning is also an invitation to choose the path of life.
exp.32:9:
God says that the place people call a wasteland, with neither people nor animals, in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that lie deserted, will once again be filled with life. The words "there will be heard again" point to the sound of life returning to the place. The verse does not say what that sound will be, but the verses that follow describe it: voices of joy and praise.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had suffered the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile, and Jeremiah himself was in prison. God answers with a promise of forgiveness and restoration, just when everything seemed lost.

Today, you may see areas of your life as a wasteland. This verse invites you not to let what you see have the last word. God can forgive, heal, and restore joy. Bring to him in prayer whatever seems hopeless, and trust in his goodness.
exp.27:14:
Jeremiah speaks directly to Hananiah, another prophet, and tells him that the LORD did not send him. Hananiah had persuaded the people to trust in a lie.

Jeremiah had carried a wooden yoke to show that Judah had to submit to Babylon. Hananiah broke it and promised that God would soon free the people. But God told Jeremiah to say that this yoke would be replaced by one of iron. Hananiah offered false hope, and the text tells us that he died that same year.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we hear, even when it is pleasant, agrees with the Word of God. Not every comfortable message comes from Him. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible, to pray with humility, and to prefer the truth, even when it costs us.
exp.0:18:
God tells Jeremiah that the people will fight against him, but they will never overcome him. The reason is a promise: "I am with you." "Deliver" means to rescue you and keep you safe. God does not promise that there will be no opposition, but that opposition will not have the final say.

The Lord, who is speaking, calls Jeremiah as a prophet. He sends him to speak to kings, princes, priests, and the people of Judah, who had turned away from God. His message would be harsh and would not be well received. That is why God compares him to a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall.

If you do what is right and are criticized or rejected, you are not alone. Obey with humility and confidence, remembering that God's presence sustains you even when others oppose you.
exp.24:25:
God says he will make all the kings of the north, both near and far, drink the cup of his judgment one after another, along with all the kingdoms on the face of the earth. The north is the direction referred to here, and the face of the earth is the whole world. At the end, the king of Sheshach will drink it too. Many understand "Sheshach" to be a code name for Babylon, although the text does not explain this here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around 605 B.C. Judah and the neighboring nations had rejected the calls to turn back to God. The "cup" is an image of divine punishment: no one is left out, not even Babylon, which would be used as an instrument.

For today: God is just with everyone, without favoritism. Instead of believing that our power or our nation protects us, it is wise to live with humility, listen to his correction in time, and repent with sincerity.
exp.37:15:
King Zedekiah made a solemn promise to Jeremiah in private. He swore by the Lord, the God who gives us life, that he would not kill him and would not hand him over to the men who were trying to kill him. "Seeking your life" means they were looking to take his life. The word "swore" means he made the promise with an oath.

The king speaks with Jeremiah at one of the entrances of the temple, in the last days of Jerusalem before it fell to Babylon. Jeremiah had been mistreated for announcing hard messages from God. Zedekiah was afraid and wanted to hear a word from the prophet, but he did it in secret, because he feared his own officials. Jeremiah did not trust him, and with good reason.

For today: a promise is worth as much as the obedience that goes with it. Zedekiah promised to protect the prophet, but he did not obey his counsel. Let us ask God for courage to listen to his truth and live it, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.43:0:
This verse introduces a message from God to Jeremiah. It is addressed to all the Jews living in Egypt, in the cities of Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Memphis, and in the land of Pathros, which was southern Egypt.

Jeremiah was a prophet of God. After the fall of Jerusalem, many Jews fled to Egypt, and Jeremiah was taken there with them. God gives him this message because the people were still caught up in idolatry, even after seeing the punishment that fell on Jerusalem. The verses that follow explain this clearly.

For today: God speaks to us to correct us and also to protect us. If we have seen the consequences of turning away from Him, let us not repeat the mistake. Today you can ask yourself, with humility: what things are pulling me away from God? Listen to His word and return to Him.
exp.15:20:
God himself says he is going to show his power. "I will make them know my power" means he will make his strength visible in action, so that there is no room for doubt. "This time" means "now, on this occasion." The purpose is that they will know that his name is the LORD, that is, the true God, the LORD who acts.

God speaks here in response to Jeremiah's prayer, in which Jeremiah has just said that the LORD is his strength and refuge. Jeremiah announces that even distant nations will recognize that the idols are a lie. God speaks in this way in the midst of judgment on Judah, which had followed false gods. Scholars debate exactly who the "them" refers to, whether Judah, the nations, or both.

For today: when something takes the place of God in your trust, whether money, success, or fear, hand it over to him. Ask him to show you his power, and trust that you can truly know him.
exp.5:24:
This verse is a very serious warning: it is not safe to go out into the fields or travel the roads. "For the enemy has a sword" means there are armed soldiers ready to kill, and "terror is on every side" means fear surrounds everyone. There is no quiet place.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, and the message comes from God. He announces that an invading army from the north will come against Jerusalem, the city called the daughter of Zion, because of the people's persistent disobedience. The verses before and after show anguish, mourning, and a call to repent. Scholars often connect the enemy with Babylon, though the text describes it without naming it.

For today: let us not ignore God's warnings until disaster arrives. If He calls us to return to Him, let us answer now with humility and sincerity, trusting that His mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.33:2:
He says that King Zedekiah will not be able to escape from the Babylonians. He will be captured and handed over to the king of Babylon. He will look the king of Babylon in the eye and speak with him face to face, directly and personally, and he will end up taken away to Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was already attacking Jerusalem and other cities of Judah. God tells Jeremiah to warn the king that the city would fall. Zedekiah had earlier ignored the prophet's warnings. The following verse adds a note of mercy: he would not die by the sword, but would die in peace and with honor. Other passages in the Bible describe a harsher end for Zedekiah, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God speaks the truth even when it hurts, and his warnings aim to get us to respond in time. Today we can ask ourselves what advice we have been avoiding hearing, and respond with humility and obedience, trusting in his mercy.
exp.11:2:
Jeremiah tells God that He knows him completely: He sees him and tests his heart. Then he asks that the wicked be dragged away like sheep being led to slaughter, and set apart for the day of carnage.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He is confused and hurt because the wicked prosper while he suffers for being faithful. His own neighbors had betrayed him. His prayer is very intense, and some understand it as a sincere outpouring of grief before God, not as a wish for personal revenge. God answers him afterward by calling him to persevere.

When it hurts to see the unjust doing well, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it to God honestly, trusting that He knows your heart and will do justice in his time.
exp.35:2:
God says that perhaps the people of Judah will hear about the disaster he plans to bring on them, and that each of them will turn from his wicked way. The word "perhaps" shows that God gives them a real chance. If each person turns from his wrong way of living, God promises to forgive their wickedness and their sin. "Plan to bring" means God has already decided what he will do.

God speaks, giving instructions to Jeremiah in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. He asks him to write on a scroll all the messages he had given him over many years. Jeremiah was in prison and could not go to the temple, so he used Baruch to write. God did not want only to punish; he wanted the people to respond and return to him.

For today: when God shows us something wrong in our lives, it is an invitation to change, not only a threat. Today you can recognize a bad habit, ask for forgiveness, and trust that God hears those who return to him with sincerity.
exp.20:13:
God says he will punish Jerusalem as its people's deeds deserve. Here "punish" means holding them accountable, not paying a friendly visit. The phrase about their deeds means that the people will face the consequences of what they have done. The fire God sends into "your forest" points to the city and its proud sense of safety, and the fire that consumes everything around it speaks of a destruction that reaches beyond the city itself.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. He had called the royal house of David to do justice and to rescue the oppressed. But the people trusted that their city, set high up, could not be reached by any enemy, asking who would dare come against them. God answers that no wall protects them from his judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use our position, work, or influence to help those who suffer injustice. God does not ask us for our own security, but for justice and mercy toward others, beginning today.
exp.29:0:
This verse is an introduction. It says that what follows is a word that the Lord gave to Jeremiah. The phrase "came to Jeremiah" means the word was given to him. And the verse's wording "This is the word" signals that the message is about to be stated.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. The verses that follow explain that God asks him to write it in a book and promises that he will bring Israel and Judah back from captivity. Many understand this chapter to be a message of hope for a people who had been punished. Scholars discuss which parts were fulfilled when the people returned from exile and which parts look further ahead.

For today: God speaks with purpose and wants his words to be preserved. We can read the Bible with confidence, trusting that he offers hope even after difficult times. Today, before you read, ask him to speak to you, and write down one promise that encourages you.
exp.45:3:
This verse gives orders for war: harness the horses, mount the steeds, take your positions with helmets on, polish the spears, and put on armor. The "helmets" here are metal headgear, and the armor is the protective gear worn over the body.

God speaks through Jeremiah about Egypt. Pharaoh Necho was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, beside the Euphrates River, around 605 B.C. The orders sound like a call to get ready, but many read them with irony: Egypt prepares with everything it has, and still it will fall, as the verses that follow say. Some think it describes the preparation before battle; others see it as a mockery of Egyptian pride.

For today: we can prepare well and work hard, but our final security is not in our own resources. It is in God, who rules over all nations and all outcomes.
exp.51:1:
This verse says that Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done. The phrase "in the sight of the LORD" means that God saw and judged his conduct. Jehoiakim was another king of Judah, known for his disobedience and for rejecting God's word.

This passage closes the book of Jeremiah with a historical summary. The writer, probably someone close to the prophet, explains why Jerusalem fell: it was no accident, but the result of years of rebellion. Zedekiah also rebelled against Babylon, and that brought on the siege of the city.

For today: our decisions carry weight, and copying the bad examples we see does not excuse us. It is worth asking ourselves whom we are imitating and seeking God sincerely before the consequences arrive.
exp.16:7:
This verse says that the person who trusts in God is like a tree planted by the water. Its roots reach toward the stream, so when the heat comes it does not fear, its leaves are always green, and in a year of drought it does not worry and does not stop producing fruit.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he warned that whoever trusts only in people is like a dry shrub in the desert. Then he contrasts that life with the life of the one who leans on the Lord. Afterward he speaks of how deceptive the heart can be.

For today: in your hard times, do not wait for the drought to arrive before seeking God. Set aside time each day to pray and read the Bible, so that your roots are firm and you find calm when the pressure comes.
exp.32:3:
This verse says that the Lord, the God of Israel, speaks about the houses of Jerusalem and the palaces of the kings of Judah. Those houses were torn down to make defenses against the siege ramps and the sword, so the buildings were pulled apart to protect the city during the attack.

Jeremiah is imprisoned, and Jerusalem is surrounded by the army of Babylon (the Chaldeans). God acknowledges that the city suffers because of its wickedness, but in the same message he announces that he will not abandon it: he promises healing, forgiveness, and restoration.

For today: when you see something in your life or your family reduced to ruins, do not stay silent. God invites you to cry out to him, to acknowledge what needs to be corrected, and to trust that he can rebuild what seems lost.
exp.41:11:
It says that God promises to deal with the people with compassion. The phrase "I will show you compassion" means that He will treat them with kindness, and "he will have compassion on you" means that the king of Babylon will also treat them with leniency. Finally, "and restore you to your own land" means that He would bring them back or would let them continue living in their land. Note: in some readings, the subject is God working through the king.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors fear Babylon's revenge and want to flee to Egypt. They ask God for counsel, and He answers that they should stay in Judah and not be afraid.

For today: when fear pushes you to look for a quick way out, stop and ask God what He wants. Obeying sometimes means staying still and trusting, even when the situation seems threatening.
exp.51:5:
On the ninth day of the fourth month, the hunger in Jerusalem became so severe that the common people had no food left at all. The old explanation of a word like "prevailed" does not apply here, since your verse says "so severe" and "had no food," and the phrase "people of the land" is described in plain words as the common people of the country.

This chapter is a historical account that summarizes the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. No one knows for certain who wrote it; some think it was Jeremiah and others think it was a later editor. It shows the end of the long siege, which Jeremiah had announced as the consequence of the people's disobedience.

For today: God speaks to us patiently before crises arrive, and it is wise to listen in time. In addition, this verse reminds us that the poorest suffer the most, so we can generously help those who are going hungry today.
exp.36:14:
The verse tells how the officials were angry with Jeremiah, beat him, and placed him in jail. The words "they beat him" carry the meaning of the first phrase, and "they placed him in jail" carries the meaning of the second. The house of the scribe Jonathan had been made into a prison.

Jeremiah was God's prophet in the final days of Jerusalem, when Babylon had the city surrounded. As he went out through the Benjamin Gate, a guard accused him of defecting to the enemy. Jeremiah denied it, but no one believed him. The officials punished him, perhaps because his message of surrendering to Babylon seemed to them like treason. This last point is an interpretation, but it fits the account.

For today: sometimes telling the truth brings misunderstanding and unjust punishment, even when a person is sincere. Jeremiah remained faithful and, when the king called for him, he spoke again without changing the message. Let us ask God for courage to be honest and patience when we are not believed.
exp.6:20:
This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves. The burnt offerings were burned completely on the altar, while the other sacrifices were partly eaten. God speaks with irony, inviting them to gather everything together and eat it, as if it no longer had any worth to Him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who carried out religious rituals but lived in disobedience. The verses that follow explain that the main thing God asked of them when He brought them out of Egypt was: "Listen to my voice." Many understand that He does not reject sacrifices in themselves, but rejects them when there is no obedience.

For today: faith does not consist only of attending, singing, or keeping religious customs. God seeks a heart that listens and obeys. Today you might ask yourself: "What is God asking of me that I have not yet obeyed?"
exp.32:15:
In those days, as God has prepared them, Judah will be saved and Jerusalem will live in safety. "Will dwell securely" means that the city will live with confidence, without fear. And the city will be called "The LORD Our Righteousness," that is, the LORD is the one who makes us righteous.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Jerusalem was under threat and the people lived in distress. God promises to keep his good word and to raise up for David a Branch of righteousness, that is, a righteous descendant who will rule well. Many Christians see here a promise fulfilled in Jesus.

For today: our security does not depend on what we do or on our circumstances, but on God, who gives us his righteousness. Trust in him and rest in his promise.
exp.48:1:
This verse announces that God will bring a time of judgment on Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. The battle cry will be sounded against the city, it will be reduced to a heap of ruins, and its villages will be burned. Destruction here means complete ruin. In the end, Israel will drive out those who had taken its land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Ammonites had taken over the territory of Gad, which belonged to Israel, as though Israel had no claim to it. God does not overlook that injustice. Scholars debate exactly how and when this prophecy was fulfilled, but the message is clear: God judges pride and abuse.

For today: do not lose heart when you see injustice or abuse that seems to go unanswered. Trust that God sees, and avoid taking advantage of others, because He holds people accountable.
exp.6:5:
God asks his people for three things: to stop oppressing the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow; to stop shedding the blood of innocent people in this place; and to stop following other gods, which would bring them harm. To oppress means to mistreat someone through abuse. Other gods are the idols of other nations.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they lived in injustice and idolatry. God tells them that repeating "the temple of the LORD" is not enough; they must change their behavior. If they do, they will be able to keep living in the land.

For today: true faith shows in how we treat the most vulnerable. This week, you could concretely help someone who is alone or in need, instead of relying only on going to church.
exp.11:3:
Here Jeremiah asks how much longer the land will suffer. It is dry, the grass has withered, and the animals and birds have been swept away. The cause, he says, is the evil of the people who live there. They were saying, "He cannot see what our end will be," that is, "God cannot see what will become of us" or "Jeremiah cannot see what will become of us." The phrase can be understood in both ways.

Jeremiah speaks with God, complaining because the wicked seem to prosper while the land suffers. This takes place in Judah, probably during a time of drought. Many people spoke about God with their mouths, but their hearts were far from him. Jeremiah was also rejected by his own family.

For today: you can bring your questions and your pain to God with sincerity, as Jeremiah did. And remember that God does see how we live and how we will end, so it is worth living with honesty before him.
exp.22:38:
God says that, because of what the people had done, he will forget them, meaning he will set them aside, and he will cast them out of his presence. He also speaks of the city, Jerusalem, which he had given to them and to their ancestors.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Hebrew word for "burden" can also mean "message," and people used it mockingly or carelessly to speak of supposed messages from God, even though he had asked them not to do so. Some understand that they were mocking God's word; others understand that false prophets were making up messages. The text shows a serious judgment against the disrespectful use of his name.

Today we can be careful about how we speak of God. Before saying "God told me," it is wise to pray, to compare it with the Bible, and to speak with humility and respect.
exp.6:9:
God asks with sorrow and irony: how can they come to the temple, which bears his name, and say, "We are safe," while they keep on doing so many evils? The phrase "we are delivered" means "we are free from danger." "Abominations" are things that God hates.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people stole, murdered, swore falsely, and worshiped Baal, yet they thought the temple would protect them, as if simply being there were enough. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh, where his sanctuary was destroyed because of the people's wickedness.

Today, going to church, praying, or invoking God's name does not replace an obedient life. Let us ask God to examine our hearts, and let us live in a way that is consistent with what we say we believe.
exp.30:12:
It says that a time will come when the young women will dance with joy, and the young men and the old will celebrate together. God promises to turn their mourning into joy and to give them comfort. In this verse, the young woman is the maiden, and mourning is the grief that God will turn into joy.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was suffering the consequences of its disobedience and of the exile. In this chapter, sometimes called the book of comfort, God announces that he will rescue his people and restore them. Christians often see in this promise a foretaste of salvation in Christ, although there are different ways of interpreting it.

For today: if you are going through pain, bring it honestly to God. He does not ignore your tears, and he promises comfort. While you wait, lean on others, both young and old, and keep hope alive.
exp.13:15:
The verse says that the people who listened to the false prophets will be thrown into the streets of Jerusalem, dead from famine and war. No one will bury them, nor their wives, sons, or daughters. "Sword" means war, and "I will pour out their own evil upon them" means they will receive the consequences of their own wrongdoing.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah during a time of drought and threat. The false prophets promised peace and said there would be no war or famine, but God had not sent them. The people believed them because it was what they wanted to hear, so they also share the responsibility. Even so, God himself grieves for his people in the verses that follow.

For today: let us not believe something just because it sounds pleasant. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and ask God for discernment, even when the truth is difficult.
exp.48:38:
Here Jeremiah says that, although God will punish Elam, in the end he will restore its people from captivity. "In the last days" means "in the distant future" or "at the end of time." "Restore from captivity" means bringing back the exiles.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the nations that bordered Judah. Elam lay east of Babylon, in what is today Iran. Just before this verse, God announces severe judgment against them. Here he adds a promise of hope. The Bible does not explain in detail how or when this would happen; some see it in historical events, and others see it as a future fulfillment.

For today: even when God corrects, his final word does not have to be destruction. We can trust that he is just and also merciful, and that he can restore what seemed lost.
exp.36:19:
Jeremiah respectfully asks King Zedekiah to listen to him. He pleads that the king not send him back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, because he fears he will die there. He is making a humble request, and "May my petition come before you" means "I hope you will consider what I am asking."

He speaks as God's prophet, who had warned that Babylon would defeat Jerusalem. For this he had been accused and locked away in a harsh place that had been turned into a prison. Jeremiah maintains that he has done no wrong and asks for fair treatment. The king agrees and has him kept in the prison courtyard, with a daily portion of bread.

For today: it is not a lack of faith to ask for help with humility and clarity when we suffer injustice. We can remain faithful to God, speak the truth with respect, and seek protection without bitterness.
exp.28:11:
This verse says that the people, living far from their land, will again call out to God. The phrase "call upon Me" means calling to God asking for help. The words "come and pray to Me" speak of drawing near to Him in prayer. And God promises, "I will listen to you," meaning He will hear them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He writes a letter to the Jews exiled in Babylon. He tells them that the exile will last about seventy years and that God has not forgotten them. His plans for them are for peace and hope. The promise to listen is given within that setting: God will bring them back to their land.

For today: even in difficult times or far from what we know, we can pray with confidence. God listens. Today you can take a few minutes to speak to Him honestly about what weighs on you, remembering that He invites us to seek Him with all our heart.
exp.44:1:
This verse opens God's message to Baruch. The words "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says" announce that what follows comes from God. "to you, Baruch" shows that the message is personal, addressed to him by name.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Baruch was his helper and wrote down what Jeremiah dictated to him, in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. It was a difficult time, full of warnings of judgment. Baruch felt worn out and distressed, and God, who knew his complaint, decides to speak to him directly.

God does not see people as a faceless crowd. He knows your name, your weariness, and what you say inside yourself. You can be honest with Him when you are discouraged, and be attentive to His answer, even when it is not the one you expected.
exp.3:19:
Disaster after disaster is proclaimed, and the whole land lies in ruin. The reader is told that the tents and curtains, the coverings of the homes, are destroyed in an instant. The word "laid waste" here means total destruction, a complete collapse.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, the prophet. He sees in vision the invasion coming from the north because of the sin of the people of Judah. His grief is so strong that he feels anguish in his heart. Some think the prophet speaks "my tents" on behalf of the people; others think God is the one speaking. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: the decisions we make have consequences, and God does not take pleasure when we suffer. If there is something in your life that you know needs to be corrected, do not wait for everything to collapse. Return to God today, with humility, and ask for his help.
exp.33:19:
God says that he will hand over those who broke their covenant to their enemies, the people who want to kill them. Their corpses will be left unburied and will become food for the birds of the air and the animals of the earth. "Seek their lives" means that these enemies are trying to take their lives away.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. The people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law commanded, but then they enslaved them again. They had sealed that agreement with an ancient rite: passing between the parts of a calf that had been cut in two. By breaking the promise, they took on the curse that this rite symbolized.

For today: God takes our promises seriously, especially those made before him. Before promising something, let us think carefully; and if we have already promised, let us keep our word with integrity and justice toward others.
exp.1:17:
The verse says that Judah goes looking for help in Egypt and in Assyria, as if traveling there to drink from their rivers. "The Nile" is the river of Egypt, and "the Euphrates" is the great river of Assyria. God asks with sorrow: what will you gain by going there?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people had turned away from the LORD and were seeking protection from foreign powers. Earlier in this chapter, God reminds them that the Egyptian cities of Noph and Tahpanhes had already brought them harm. Interpreters explain the political details in various ways, but the central rebuke is clear: they had abandoned God.

Today, when we are afraid or in need, it is easy to run to sources that seem secure: money, influence, or the approval of others. Ask yourself honestly: to which "river" do I go first? Seek God first in prayer, and then use other resources wisely.
exp.26:10:
This verse says that any nation that agrees to submit to the king of Babylon and serve him, God will leave in its own land. There it will be able to cultivate the ground and live in it. A "yoke" is the wooden frame placed on the necks of working animals. The phrase "I will leave" means that God will allow them to stay where they are, and "to cultivate it" means they will work the land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah and its neighbors faced the power of Babylon. False prophets claimed there would be no submission, but God says those words were a lie. Accepting the yoke was the way to survive.

Today we can learn to tell apart what sounds encouraging from what truly comes from God. Before following any voice, let us compare its message with Scripture and seek wise counsel. Sometimes humble obedience, even when it costs us, protects us more than an easy promise.
exp.31:3:
Zedekiah king of Judah will not escape from the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians. He will be handed over to the king of Babylon, and the two will speak face to face and see each other eye to eye. It is a way of saying that Zedekiah will be captured and brought before him to be judged.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf. Babylon had Jerusalem surrounded, and King Zedekiah had shut the prophet up in the courtyard of the prison because he did not like his message. Jeremiah kept saying what God commanded him, even though he was punished for it.

Today we can learn that God's truth does not change because it makes us uncomfortable. It is better to listen to it humbly in time than to reject it and suffer the consequences later.
exp.24:23:
This verse says that God will make all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mixed tribes who live in the desert, drink the cup of his judgment. "Mixed tribes" refers to groups of different origins who lived side by side, though scholars are not sure exactly who is meant.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, a few years before Babylon conquered Judah. In this chapter, God uses the image of a cup of wrath that many nations must drink. In this way he shows that Babylon would be his instrument, and that no people, near or far, stands outside his justice.

For today: God rules over all nations and all people. No one is so powerful or so distant that they do not owe an account to him. This invites us to live with humility and to trust that his justice is perfect.
exp.50:57:
This is what the LORD of Hosts declares: Babylon's thick walls will be leveled, and her high gates will be consumed by fire. The work of the people will amount to nothing, and the nations will wear themselves out only to feed the flames.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in a message against Babylon. This city was a powerful empire that had oppressed Judah. God promises it justice, for He is the God who repays. The verses that follow say that Jeremiah put these words in writing to send them to Babylon with Seraiah.

For today: We can rest in the knowledge that no human power, however strong it may seem, is above God. Trust Him when you see injustice, and avoid placing your security in things that do not last.
exp.28:28:
This verse tells us that the priest Zephaniah read the letter that Shemaiah had sent from Babylon to Jeremiah the prophet. In the Berean Standard Bible the words are placed in parentheses, which marks them as an aside in the narrative. Jeremiah learned directly of the accusations against him.

Shemaiah was a false prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He had written to Jerusalem demanding that Jeremiah be corrected for saying that the captivity would be long. Zephaniah, a priest, received that letter, but instead of acting against Jeremiah, he read it to him. We do not know for certain why he did this; some think he respected Jeremiah or wanted to warn him. Afterward God answers and exposes Shemaiah.

Today we can learn not to react with fear to unjust criticism. The best course is to bring it honestly before God, who knows the truth and knows how to defend his own in his time.
exp.33:15:
This verse says that the people of Judah first obeyed God and set their Hebrew servants free, but afterward changed their minds. "Profaned My name" means they showed disrespect toward the God in whose name they had made the agreement. "Taken back the menservants and maidservants" means they enslaved again those they had set free, forcing them once more to serve them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Babylon. It seems that King Zedekiah and the people made a solemn covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew brothers, as the law required. But when the danger seemed to pass, they broke their promise. God judges them for not keeping what they had promised before Him.

For today: when we promise something to God or to others, let us not keep it only while it suits us. Think of a commitment you have neglected and ask God for help to keep it with integrity.
exp.17:20:
Jeremiah asks God to hand the children of his enemies over to hunger and the sword. He asks that their wives be left childless and widowed, that their husbands be slain by disease, and that their young men be struck down by the sword in battle. "Pour out the power of the sword" means to give them over to violence. The phrase about young men being struck down in battle means the same thing as the sword.

Jeremiah is the one speaking. Some people of Judah, angry at his message, were planning to harm him (verses 18-20). He had interceded for them, and they repaid good with evil. This prayer is a very raw lament, and its words sound like a request for judgment, not an example of forgiveness. Many understand it as announcing the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: when you are wronged unfairly, you can bring your pain and your anger to God honestly, without taking revenge yourself. Then look to Jesus, who on the cross asked forgiveness for his enemies (Luke 23:34).
exp.31:20:
This verse reminds us that God brought his people out of Egypt in a powerful way. "Signs and wonders" were miracles that showed his power. "A strong hand and an outstretched arm" is a way of saying that God acted with great strength on Israel's behalf. "Great terror" speaks of the fear the Egyptians felt when they saw what God was doing.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, praying to God. Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonians, and the prophet had just bought a piece of land at God's command. Before receiving an answer, Jeremiah goes over the history: God had rescued and cared for his people, but the people did not obey him.

For today: when you find yourself in a situation with no way out, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. Before asking him for help, thank him for his past faithfulness. That strengthens trust and helps you obey him with more humility.
exp.20:4:
God says that He Himself will fight against Jerusalem. The phrases "outstretched hand" and "mighty arm" are images of power; they were once used to speak of how God delivered Israel from Egypt, but now they are turned against the people. The words "anger," "fury," and "great wrath" show a very serious judgment. The word "you" in this verse refers to the people.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God to King Zedekiah while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. The king hoped that God would rescue him, but the people remained in sin and did not repent. God warns them that their resistance will not save them, because He Himself opposes that rebellion.

For today: we cannot ask for God's help while we ignore His voice. If there is something in our lives that God has shown us, the best thing is to turn back to Him with humility and sincerity, because He remains just and also merciful toward those who repent.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah. The opening words mean that a message from God came to him. The name "LORD" in this verse refers to God, written in capital letters in the Old Testament. Here the message itself has not yet been given; the verse only announces that God is about to speak.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, a prophet who lived in Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. This phrase often marks the start of a new message from God. In the verses that follow, God asks him to do something very hard: not to marry or have children, as a sign of the difficult times coming upon the people.

For today: God speaks, and listening is the first step. Before asking him for answers, we can set aside a moment to read his Word with attention and a willingness to obey, even when it is not easy.
exp.28:31:
God says he will surely punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. The word "visit" here means coming to call someone to account. None of his family will remain among the people, and he will not see the good that God will bring to his people, because Shemaiah preached rebellion against the LORD, that is, he taught people to disobey God.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah at a time when the Jews were exiled in Babylon. Jeremiah had written to them telling them to settle there and wait seventy years. Shemaiah sent letters telling them the opposite, as if God had sent him. In this way he gave them a false hope. The text does not explain the exact details of how this punishment was carried out.

For today: before believing someone who claims to speak on God's behalf, compare what they say with the Bible. And if you teach others, do it with humility and truth, because God takes seriously the words we use in his name.
exp.41:2:
This verse is the people's request to Jeremiah. They want him to pray that God will show them the path they should follow and what they should do. The phrase "tell us the way we should walk" means that God would point out the right course for them. Notice that they say "the LORD your God," speaking to Jeremiah, not "our God."

The speakers are the army officers, Johanan, and all the people, a small group that remained after the fall of Jerusalem. They are uncertain and afraid, and they ask Jeremiah to pray for them. They promise to obey. However, later in the account it shows that they did not keep what they promised, and they went down to Egypt.

For today: asking for God's guidance is good, but we must do it with a heart willing to obey, even if the answer is not what we hoped for. Before we pray, let us ask ourselves whether we are truly open to whatever He says.
exp.15:14:
It says that God will do something so great that people will swear by him in new words: "As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north." The phrase "land of the north" refers to Babylon, from where the people would return. God promises to bring them back from all the places where they had been banished and to return them to the land he gave to their forefathers.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had worshiped false gods, and for that reason God announces the exile. But in the midst of judgment he promises a new beginning. Just as the exodus from Egypt was the great memory of his rescue, the future return would be another act of salvation just as memorable.

For today: God disciplines, but he does not completely abandon. If you are going through the consequences of your mistakes, do not lose hope. Return to him sincerely, because he is faithful to restore and to make a new start.
exp.47:0:
God declares judgment against Moab, a people who lived next to Israel. He names several Moabite places: Nebo, Kiriathaim, and the fortress. Nebo is pronounced a woe, meaning it is about to be devastated. Kiriathaim will be captured and disgraced, and the fortress will be shattered and dismantled. These words describe a complete collapse of what Moab had built and relied on.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, but in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel. This message is a warning to Moab, a nation that trusted in its pride, its strongholds, and its wealth. Later in the chapter, the text mentions that self-reliance. The exact historical details of how this was fulfilled are debated, so it is wise not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: what seems strong, such as money, reputation, or achievements, cannot save us. Today you can examine what you truly trust in and give that place to God.
exp.30:24:
He says that God will give rest and joy to the one who is worn out and sad. "Refresh" means to restore strength and energy, the way a cool drink revives someone who has been working in the heat. God promises to refresh the weary soul and to fill those who are weak.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were living in exile in Babylon, tired and with broken hearts. God promises them that they will return to their land, that there will be blessing and normal life again. Some think the following verse, "awoke," is Jeremiah saying that his vision of comfort was sweet to him.

Today, if you feel exhausted or sad, bring that weariness to God honestly. He does not tire of you. Ask Him to fill you with peace and strength, and seek to rest in His faithfulness, one day at a time.
exp.28:23:
This verse is a brief command from God to Jeremiah: he is to carry a message to Shemaiah, a man from Nehelam. The text says nothing more about him here; the content of the message comes in the following verses. "You are to tell Shemaiah the Nehelamite that" means "you are to say to him that."

God speaks through Jeremiah to the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, Jeremiah had sent them a letter with God's word. Shemaiah, also in exile, answered by sending letters of his own to Jerusalem, and he pressed the priests to punish Jeremiah. God responds and confronts Shemaiah for speaking with an authority he did not have. Of Nehelam we know no more; some think it indicates his origin or family, but this is not certain.

Today we can learn not to speak in God's name lightly. Before we correct or silence others, it is wise to examine whether what we say agrees with his Word.
exp.14:5:
God speaks to Jerusalem and Judah. He says: "You have forsaken me and turned your back." Because of this, he announces that he will stretch out his hand against them and destroy them. The phrase "I am weary of showing compassion" means that God had already held back many times, giving more chances, but he will no longer do so.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Judah fell to Babylon. The people had practiced idolatry and injustice for a long time, and the text mentions the sin of King Manasseh. God does not act suddenly: he had warned and waited, but the people did not return to him.

For today: God's patience is real, but it is not an excuse to put off change. If today you feel that you have drifted away from him, do not wait any longer. Come back, and trust that his mercy will receive you.
exp.41:7:
Jeremiah, after receiving God's answer, summoned Johanan son of Kareah, the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. The word "summoned" means the same as "called," and "commanders" refers to the leaders of the army.

Jeremiah is the one who speaks and acts here. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors asked him to pray for them, promising to obey God whatever his answer might be. Ten days later, the word of God came, and Jeremiah gathered everyone to announce it. His message was not only for the leaders but for everyone.

For today: when we ask God for direction, it is good to be willing to obey before we hear his answer. Praying with an open heart, and not merely seeking approval for what we have already decided, prepares us to receive his guidance with humility.
exp.4:8:
God asks a question here, and the answer is clearly no. He wants the people to see that a just God cannot ignore such behavior. The BSB wording, "Should I not punish them for these things?", makes the point plain: God will bring consequences for wrongdoing. The phrase "avenge Myself" means that God responds with justice because He is the one who has been wronged.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. Earlier in this chapter, He accuses them of abandoning Him, of swearing by false gods, and of living in unfaithfulness and excess. Even after receiving prosperity, they turned away from Him. Then He announces judgment, yet He does not ask to destroy them completely. So the warning comes after great patience, not from a sudden anger.

For today: God takes faithfulness seriously, but He is also patient. Do not take advantage of His goodness; if He shows you something you need to change, respond quickly with repentance and return to Him.
exp.1:10:
God asks whether any nation has ever changed its gods. He answers that none has, even though those gods are not gods at all, meaning they have no real power. Yet his people exchanged their Glory, which is God himself, for useless idols.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Israel of abandoning him to follow idols. He points them to the pagan peoples, both west toward the islands of Kittim and east toward Kedar, to show that even those nations did not act this way. God speaks with pain, like someone who has been betrayed.

For today: we can exchange God for things that promise a great deal, such as money, success, or the approval of others, but these cannot sustain us. Today you can ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart and return to him with sincerity.
exp.6:33:
God announces that he will silence, in the towns of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, the sounds of celebration: the sounds of joy and gladness, and the voices of the bride and bridegroom. The phrase "I will remove" means "I will take away." The word "wasteland" describes a place that has been ruined and left empty, where nothing lives or grows.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in his message at the temple. The people mixed the worship of the LORD with idols, and even practiced terrible sacrifices at Topheth. God warns that judgment would come because of that rebellion. Many understand this as a reference to the Babylonian invasion and the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: let us not take lightly what God says about sin or his call to return to him. Examine whether there is something in your life that you keep tolerating, and come back to God sincerely, because he is the one who gives true joy.
exp.17:9:
It says that if a nation God intended to bless does evil and does not listen to his voice, then God will relent of the good he had planned to do for it. The word "relent" is used here, and in this verse it describes a change of direction, not a mistake on God's part. "Intended" here means "decided" or "planned."

Speaking through the prophet Jeremiah after the visit to the potter, who reshapes the damaged clay, God teaches that his warnings depend on how people respond. For this reason he calls Judah and Jerusalem to turn from their evil way, but they answer with stubbornness, set on following their own desires.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted while we live ignoring his voice. Today you can ask yourself where God is speaking to you, and obey him with humility, without hardening your heart.
exp.3:3:
Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart. God is calling the men of Judah and the people of Jerusalem to a change that goes deeper than the body. The foreskin is the skin cut away in circumcision, and here it stands for whatever clings to the heart and keeps it from obeying God. If they do not change, God's wrath will break out like a fire that no one can put out, because of the evil of their deeds.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier He had asked them to truly turn back to Him and to break up the fallow ground, that is, to prepare the soil of the heart and not sow among thorns. Judah kept up outward rituals, but remained in sin. The verses that follow announce an invasion from the north.

For today: it is not enough to appear religious. Ask God to show you which attitude or habit is hardening your heart, and give it over to Him sincerely, letting Him change it from within.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that God tells the prophet Jeremiah to go down to the palace of the king of Judah and proclaim a message from Him there. "LORD" is the name of God, and "go down" shows that Jeremiah was to travel from where he was to the king's palace. The words "This is what the LORD says" show that the message was not Jeremiah's own idea, but God's.

The one speaking is God, and the message is addressed to the king of Judah, his servants, and the people. We do not know with certainty which king is meant at the beginning, although the following verses suggest that the kingdom of David was in danger because of its injustice. God wants rulers to act with justice and to protect the weak.

For today: if you have authority, even if it is only in your home or at work, use it to protect and treat well those who have less power.
exp.11:14:
1) What it says: God promises that, after he uproots the nations that were neighbors of Israel, he will once again have compassion on them. He will return each one to its own inheritance and its own land. "I will once again have compassion" shows that God's mercy comes back to them after judgment, and "return each one to his inheritance" means that he restores each people to the land that belongs to them.

2) Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Those neighboring nations had mistreated Israel and, according to the text, had even taught his people to swear by Baal. God will judge them, but he leaves a door open: if they learn to follow him, they will be established among his people. If not, they will be destroyed.

3) For today: God's justice does not close the door to his mercy. If someone has hurt you or pulled you away from God, trust that God judges with justice. And remember that you too need his compassion. Pray today for someone you find hard to forgive.
exp.1:23:
It says that Israel is like a wild donkey, raised in the wilderness, that sniffs the wind in the heat of her desire, and no one can restrain her. "Who can restrain her passion?" speaks of an impulse no one can hold back. "The heat of her desire" refers to her strong urge, and "mating season" is the time when that urge is at its peak. When that time comes, there is no need to wear yourself out searching for her, because she is easy to find.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses his people of idolatry, of running after the Baals, false gods of Canaan. They denied their guilt, but God shows them with this image how unrestrained their desire is to go after other gods.

For today: when a passion dominates us and we justify it, it is wise to stop, be honest before God, and ask him for help. He does not condemn us to humiliate us, but to bring us back to himself.
exp.31:36:
God promises that he will surely gather his people from all the lands where he sent them. He says he banished them in his furious anger and great wrath, strong words that show how deeply he was displeased by their sin. But now he promises to return them to this place and to make them live in safety.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and the people have turned to idols, including the terrible child sacrifices made to Molech. The exile was a just punishment. Even so, God does not end with judgment: he adds a promise of restoration and of a renewed covenant.

For today: God disciplines, but he does not abandon. If you have turned away from him or are living through the consequences of your mistakes, you can return to him with confidence. His discipline seeks to heal and restore, not to destroy. Pray sincerely today and let him lead you back.
exp.33:5:
This verse says that the prophet Jeremiah personally passed on to Zedekiah, king of Judah, the whole message God had given him. He did this in Jerusalem, the capital. The phrase "all these words" refers to what came before: the warning that Babylon would conquer the city and the promise that the king would not die by the sword. Zedekiah is the king named in the verse, and Jerusalem is the city where it all took place.

Jeremiah was the prophet who spoke on behalf of God. Babylon already had Jerusalem surrounded, and the king was in a very difficult situation. Even so, Jeremiah did not soften the message or change it to please the king. He delivered it to him directly, just as he had received it. Some scholars debate exactly how the promise that the king would die "in peace" would be fulfilled, but the text emphasizes that God had spoken.

For today: when you must say a hard truth, do it with respect, but do not distort it out of fear. And when God speaks to you through his Word, listen with humility, even when it is not comfortable.
exp.31:2:
This verse explains why Jeremiah was in prison. King Zedekiah had imprisoned him and confronted him: "Why are you prophesying like this?" Jeremiah was declaring that the LORD was about to hand Jerusalem over to the king of Babylon, and that the king would capture it.

The one speaking is the narrator, who recalls the king's words. Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonian army, and Jeremiah was held in the guard's courtyard, next to the palace. The king was troubled by the message, since it discouraged the soldiers and he did not want to hear that his city would fall. Jeremiah, however, kept speaking what the LORD told him.

For today: sometimes the truth is uncomfortable and tempts us to silence the one who speaks it. Let us ask God for humility to receive correction in time, without anger, and for courage to speak the truth with love even when it costs us.
exp.4:13:
Because of what the people have said, God declares that he will make the words he gives Jeremiah like a fire in his mouth, and this people will be like wood that the fire consumes. "Therefore" means "for this reason." "Wood" refers to pieces of dry timber. "Consume" means to burn them up completely.

The LORD, the God of hosts, speaks to Jeremiah. The people had denied God, saying: "He does not exist, and nothing bad will happen to us." They also looked down on the prophets, saying they were only wind. God answers that his message will be real and powerful, and that judgment will come through a foreign nation, as the following verses say.

For today: do not make light of God's word or think there will be no consequences for ignoring it. Read the Bible with humility, let yourself be corrected, and respond quickly when God speaks to your heart.
exp.22:11:
The verse says that the path of these prophets and priests will become slick, like ground that gives way beneath the feet in total darkness. They will not see where they are going, they will be driven away, and they will fall. The BSB speaks of their path becoming slick and of being driven away into the darkness, so the picture is of people who cannot see and cannot keep their footing. God himself declares that he will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The religious leaders of Judah had claimed to serve God, but they lived in wickedness, even inside the temple. They encouraged the people to keep sinning instead of calling them back to God. For this reason he announces certain judgment against them.

For today: whoever teaches or guides others carries a great responsibility before God. Let us examine whether our lives match what we say we believe, and ask God to let his light guide our steps so that we do not walk in darkness.
exp.9:14:
They say the idols are worth nothing. "Worthless" means something empty, without value or power. "A work to be mocked" means they are a thing fit for ridicule, something deceptive. "In the time of their punishment" is the moment when God steps in to judge. Then those idols will perish, because they have no life or strength to save.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, who were surrounded by nations that worshiped images made by craftsmen. Earlier, the text shows the great power of God over the rain, the clouds, and the wind. It compares this with cast idols, which have no breath. He wants the people not to be impressed by those religions and to trust only in the true God.

Today we do not usually carve statues, but we can still put our trust in things that cannot sustain life: money, success, or the opinions of others. Today you can ask yourself where your security rests, and turn your trust back to the God who truly has power and endures.
exp.40:12:
It says that the people who were with Ishmael rejoiced when they saw Johanan son of Kareah and the army commanders with him coming toward them. The phrase "the commanders of the army" refers to the leaders of the military forces, and "they rejoiced" shows the relief of people who had been hoping to be rescued.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks. Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and carried off the people of Mizpah as prisoners. Johanan and the commanders heard about it and went out to pursue him as far as Gibeon, beside the great waters, a place with a large pool. The captives saw in Johanan their deliverer.

For today: when someone goes through an unjust or frightening situation, our help can bring real joy. We can ask ourselves whom we might accompany, defend, or rescue through concrete action, without waiting for others to do it.
exp.45:15:
He made many stumble, and they fell over one another. They said, "Get up! Let us return to our own people and to the land of our birth, away from the oppressor's sword."

This verse says there were so many fallen soldiers that they stumbled over one another. The ones still standing urged each other to go home, to their own people and the land where they were born, away from the sword of the oppressor. The phrase "he made many stumble" refers to God, who allowed many to fall.

Jeremiah announces a message from God about Egypt, defeated by Babylon (see verse 2). The people speaking in this verse appear to be foreign soldiers serving in the Egyptian army, either hired fighters or allies. They see that everything is lost and want to flee home. Some interpreters understand "he made many stumble" to refer to God, and others to the disorder of the army itself.

For today: no human force, however great it may seem, can stand against God. Trust in Him more than in your own strength, your money, or your alliances, and return to Him before everything falls apart.
exp.49:28:
God calls for archers to be gathered, all those who string the bow, to surround Babylon with a camp, so that no one escapes. The phrase "to string the bow" is the reader's wording for drawing a bow, and "to encamp" means to set up camp with an army around a city. God commands that Babylon be repaid according to her deeds and done to as she has done, because she has defied the Lord, "the Holy One of Israel."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the peoples who would attack Babylon. That nation had been cruel to Judah and had destroyed the temple. The text presents her as having defied God, and for that reason she receives judgment.

For today: pride, the belief that we do not need God, puts us in danger. Today you can ask God for a humble heart and trust that he does justice in his own time, without you having to take revenge.
exp.26:21:
This verse says that the sacred objects still left in Jerusalem would also be carried off to Babylon. There they would remain until God attends to them again, that is, until he takes notice of them and acts. Afterward God promises to bring them back and restore them to this place. As for the words "I will restore them," the verse says "Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At that time, false prophets were saying that the objects from the temple would soon return.
