Jeremiah contradicts them: Babylon had already taken Jeconiah and the nobles, and more loss would come. Even so, God adds a promise of return. Traditionally this is linked to the return after the exile, although the text gives no dates.

For today: when you go through a loss or a long wait, do not take easy promises as hope. God may allow a difficult time, but his final word is not abandonment. Trust that he knows when to restore.
exp.16:15:
Jeremiah tells God that he did not run away from being His shepherd, that is, from leading the people in God's name, and that he did not want the day of despair to come upon them. "Run away" means he did not avoid the calling. He affirms that God knows what he spoke, because he spoke it in God's presence.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He is accused of announcing judgments that do not come to pass, and people mock him, asking where the word of the LORD is. He defends himself before God, not before the people. He makes clear that his message was harsh, but he did not deliver it for pleasure or out of ambition. Some understand "shepherd" as his office as a prophet; the Hebrew term allows more than one translation.

When you are misunderstood for doing what is right, do not defend yourself with resentment. Bring your heart to God in prayer; He knows your motives and can give you peace.
exp.42:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah while he was in Tahpanhes, a city in Egypt. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah" means that the LORD gave him a message. The message simply arrived for him.

Jeremiah had warned the people not to flee to Egypt, but they did not obey, and they took the prophet with them. Even there, God kept speaking. After this verse, the LORD tells him to set up a sign with stones to announce that Nebuchadnezzar would reach Egypt. Scholars agree that this is an announcement of judgment, although they discuss the historical details of how it was fulfilled.

For today: God does not stop speaking even when we go wrong or are far from where we should be. We can listen to him again and obey him today.
exp.9:17:
He says God himself will sling out the people who live in the land, the way someone hurls a stone from a sling. To "sling out" means to throw them far away, that is, to pull them from their place. To "bring distress upon them" means to make them suffer. The phrase "so that they may be captured" is hard: it may mean that they will be taken prisoner, or that through their capture they will come to understand what is happening.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Judah for its idolatry, and the verse that follows sounds like the people's lament before the destruction. Interpreters connect it with the exile to Babylon.

For today: when a hardship pulls us out of our comfort, we can ask God what he wants to show us. He can use pain to wake us up and draw us closer to himself, and he does not leave us alone.
exp.24:2:
Jeremiah reminds the people that for twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of King Josiah until now, God has been speaking to him, and that he has passed that message on to them again and again. The phrase "again and again" points to persistence: Jeremiah did not give the warning once and stop, but kept delivering it, and the people still did not listen.

Jeremiah, God's prophet, speaks in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, when Nebuchadnezzar was beginning to reign in Babylon. He addresses Judah and Jerusalem. He reminds them that God had called them many times to turn from their evil ways, and that the coming judgment was not a sudden blow but the result of having ignored so many warnings.

For today: God often speaks with patience and more than once. If we sense that something in our life needs to change, let us not put it off. Listening humbly today, and obeying, is a way of responding to his love.
exp.49:32:
This verse says that God sees the suffering of his people. The sons of Israel and the sons of Judah, the northern and southern kingdoms, were oppressed, that is, treated with harshness and violence. Their captors kept them firmly held and refused to release them. The verse says the captors "hold them fast," meaning they kept them tightly bound, and to release them means to set them free.

The phrase "the LORD of Hosts" shows his power over all things. This prophecy announces judgment against Babylon, the power that carried Judah into captivity. God promises to act on behalf of his people. The following verse calls him "their Redeemer," the strong one who defends their cause.

For today: if you feel trapped by an injustice or a burden you cannot shake off, remember that God sees your situation and is stronger than the one who oppresses you. Pray with confidence, keep doing good, and wait for his justice.
exp.37:22:
He says that if King Zedekiah does not surrender, everything he loves will be lost. His wives and children will be handed over to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). He himself will not escape their grasp, but the king of Babylon will seize him, and the city will be burned down. "Will be seized" means that he will be captured.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in a private conversation with King Zedekiah while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. God was asking him to surrender in order to save lives and the city. Zedekiah was afraid of his own officials and hesitated to obey. Jeremiah warns him that if he does not obey, the very women of the palace will say that his friends deceived him.

For today: obeying God out of fear of what others think usually costs far more than obeying him with humility. When God shows us a path, it is better to trust him now than to regret later having listened to the wrong voices.
exp.24:7:
God, here called "the Lord of Hosts" (the Lord who has power over all), begins to pronounce a judgment. The reason is simple: "you have not obeyed my words." In other words, the people did not want to hear or do what he had told them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. For many years he had warned them to give up their idols and return to him, but they kept on as before. That is why this "therefore" introduces the consequences: the coming of Babylon, which God would allow as a judgment.

Today, this verse reminds us that listening to God is not only hearing, but obeying. If we feel that his Word corrects us, we should not ignore it: let us respond with humility and change, while there is still time to return to him.
exp.47:8:
It says Moab should put salt on itself, because it is going to be laid waste, and its cities will be left desolate with no one living in them. "Put salt on Moab" is a vivid way of saying that the land would be ruined and left barren, the way salted ground was seen as unable to bear life.

It is the Lord speaking through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and it trusted in its riches, its fortresses, and its god Chemosh. The message announces that a destroyer would come and that this false sense of security would not save it. Scholars debate which invasion is in view; the text presents it as a judgment from God.

For today: check where you truly rest your trust. Money, achievements, or comfort may seem secure, but they do not sustain life when crises arrive. Trusting God gives you a foundation that does not collapse.
exp.6:18:
God says that his people think they are offending him with their idolatry, but in reality they are harming themselves. The question is a way of saying: "Is it really me they are hurting?" The phrase "to their own shame" means disgrace and ruin. "Provoking" means stirring up his anger.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah practiced a cult of the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess (scholars debate exactly who she was). Entire families took part. God warns them that his judgment will come because they abandoned him.

For today: when we turn away from God, the greatest harm falls on us ourselves. His commands protect us. Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking God's place in our lives and return to him with sincerity.
exp.7:14:
We hoped for peace and well-being, but nothing good has come. We expected a time of healing and relief, but all we found was terror. The word "terror" in the verse describes fear, confusion and distress.

These words come from a lament of the people of Judah, who faced the threat of an enemy coming from the north. Before this, God had warned through Jeremiah that his people would suffer for having turned their backs on him. Many expected that everything would turn out well without changing their lives. Some scholars think Jeremiah also speaks with grief on their behalf, but the text does not always make clear who is speaking in each line.

For today: it is not enough to wish that things would get better if we keep ignoring God. True hope begins when we return to him with sincerity and humility.
exp.4:2:
God says he looks for truth among his people, and he does not find it. Jeremiah tells God that you struck them, but they felt no pain; you finished them off, but they refused to accept discipline. They have made their faces harder than stone and refused to repent.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in prayer, just after God asked for a search of Jerusalem for even one honest person. God said that if such a person were found, he would forgive the city. Jeremiah sees that neither the poor nor, according to the verses that follow, the leaders want to obey. They said "As the LORD lives," yet they swore falsely.

For today: when God corrects us through hardships, his Word, or wise people, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask him for humility to listen, to recognize our error, and to return to him sincerely, not merely with religious words.
exp.18:12:
God says that the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah will be defiled, just like that place, Topheth. This will happen because of the houses where the people burned incense on their rooftops to all the host of heaven, the stars, and poured out drink offerings to other gods.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah broke a clay jar in front of the people as a sign that God would shatter the city. Topheth was a place where idolatry was practiced, and God uses it as an image of judgment. The people had hardened their hearts and did not want to listen.

For today: examine what, or who, you give first place in your home and in your heart. God invites us to return to Him with humility, before habit hardens us.
exp.50:62:
It says that, when he had finished reading the scroll in Babylon, Seraiah was to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates River. The words "finished" and "tie" are plain in this wording. The scroll contained the announcement of God's judgment against Babylon.

Jeremiah gives this command to Seraiah, an official who was traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah. It was a symbolic act, like those prophets used to deliver a message. The scroll sinking represented the fall of Babylon, which would never rise again. Interpreters see in this the certainty of God's word, not a ritual with magical power.

For today: when evil seems great and unstoppable, remember that God has the final word. Trust in his promises and do not let fear defeat you, because he is faithful and just.
exp.50:38:
He says that God will prepare a feast for the Babylonians while they are flushed with heat, that is, in the middle of their celebration and confidence. He will serve them a feast and make them drunk so that they revel, but they will end in a sleep that lasts forever, meaning death, with no waking up. "I will serve them a feast" refers to God's own action in arranging this.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed its people. The images of lions, jackals and ruins show that its power will come to an end. Many think the feast is a figure of judgment, though history also records a feast on the night Babylon fell (Daniel 5). Scholars do not agree on whether this text refers to that exact event.

For today: do not trust in success, pleasure or power as though they were eternal. Live with humility, do justice, and rest in God, who governs every nation and cares for his own.
exp.20:3:
God tells the people of Jerusalem that the weapons they are using to defend themselves against the king of Babylon will be turned back against them. "The weapons of war that are in your hands" refers to the soldiers and the strength they are relying on. The Chaldeans, the Babylonians, are surrounding the city from outside its walls, and God says He will bring them in to the very center of it.

King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah to seek God's answer, hoping for a miracle like those of the past. But God answers through the prophet with a message of judgment: the city had kept on in disobedience, and now He Himself would not fight on its behalf.

For today: it is not enough to ask God for help when trouble comes if we keep ignoring His voice. Today you can examine your heart, admit where you have failed, and return to Him with humility, before seeking only quick solutions.
exp.21:6:
He says God will send "destroyers," that is, those who bring ruin, each one with his weapons of war. They will cut down the choicest cedars and throw them into the fire. The cedars may speak of the trees of the royal palace, and also of the greatness and pride of Judah. Scholars understand the image in different ways.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the house of the king of Judah. He warns that if they do not keep justice and the covenant, their palace will be left desolate. The verses that follow explain the reason: they abandoned God's covenant and served other gods. The text does not name the destroyers here, but the biblical story connects them with Babylon.

For today: let us not trust in what we have built, in power, or in prestige. What seems as firm as a cedar does not protect us if we turn away from God. Listening to his word and obeying it is what gives true security.
exp.50:25:
It says that Babylon will be so completely destroyed that no one will ever again take from its ruins a cornerstone or a foundation stone. In that time, the cornerstone and the foundation stone were the strongest and most valuable parts of a building. "Desolate" here means left completely empty and in ruins. The phrase "forever" means the destruction will last without end.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon, here called "the destroying mountain," had laid waste to nations and also to Jerusalem and its temple. God promises to bring justice to his people. The verses that follow call on peoples such as the Medes to rise up against it. Scholars understand the prophecy in different ways as to how and when it was fully fulfilled.

For today: do not despair before the abuse or injustice of the powerful. God sees, remembers, and judges with justice. Rest in Him, and avoid personal revenge.
exp.49:10:
Babylon rejoiced and grew proud when she plundered "my inheritance," that is, God's people and their land. The phrase "you frolic like a heifer treading grain" describes her wild, careless delight, and the picture of stallions neighing pictures her loud, confident celebration. It was a proud joy, without compassion.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had allowed Babylon to punish Judah, but she went too far: she enjoyed the violence and considered herself superior. For this reason God announces that he will raise up nations from the north against her. The verses that follow describe her shame and her ruin.

For today: God sees how we treat others, especially the weak. It is never good to rejoice in the harm of others or to boast of our power. Let us ask him for a humble and compassionate heart, and trust that he will do justice.
exp.43:28:
God says he will give a sign to the Jews who went to Egypt. The sign is that he will visit them, that is, step in to punish them. In this way they will know that his threats of harm really come true. "Threats of harm" means the punishment he has announced. The word "visit" here is not a friendly visit, but an intervention by God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews fled to Egypt in disobedience to God, and there they practiced idolatry, worshiping "the queen of heaven." God warns them that their punishment will be certain. The sign that follows is the downfall of the pharaoh Hophra, which is mentioned in the next verse. Scholars agree that it is a future sign, but they do not all date it the same way.

For today: God's words do not depend on what we think or wish. Today we can listen to him with humility and obey him, without waiting for the consequences to teach us the way.
exp.2:8:
It says that Israel was indifferent to her own unfaithfulness, and that this defiled the land. Her betrayal of God is pictured as adultery, and she carried it out with stones and with trees, meaning the idols made of stone and of wood. The verse shows that she simply did not take her sin seriously, and treated her faithlessness as a small matter.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares his people to an unfaithful wife. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been punished and sent away. Even so, Judah, the southern kingdom, saw this and did not learn from it, but did the same. God calls them to return, but they do not do so from the heart.

For today: It is easy to treat sin as something small, and it becomes a habit. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts. If there are any, let us return to Him with sincerity, not just with words.
exp.51:13:
The verse says that the whole Babylonian army, under the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls around Jerusalem. The Chaldeans were the Babylonians. Without walls, the city was left defenseless and exposed.

This chapter is a historical account that closes the book of Jeremiah. It tells how Jerusalem fell, approximately in the year 586 BC. Jeremiah had warned for years that, if the people kept turning away from God, this judgment would come. Here the narrator simply describes the events: first the temple and the houses were burned, and then the walls were broken down.

For today: God's warnings are not empty threats but calls to return to Him in time. If today we feel that God is speaking to our hearts, let us not put it off. Let us respond with humility, and He is patient and generous in forgiving.
exp.46:6:
This verse is the answer to a question. The prophet had asked the sword of the Lord to rest, and now he is given a reply: how can it rest when the LORD has commanded it? He has appointed it against Ashkelon and the shore of its coastland. The phrase "the shore of its coastland" refers to the edge of the sea along that land. "It" refers to the sword, and "He has appointed it" means that God assigned it that place.

Jeremiah speaks of God's judgment on the Philistines, who lived in coastal cities such as Gaza and Ashkelon. The text does not say precisely which army carried this out, and scholars have interpreted it in different ways. What is clear is that the prophet presents the punishment as something God directs, not as a simple accident of war.

For today: we can trust that God governs justice with purpose and timing. When we see violence or injustice that seems never to end, let us pray honestly, yet rest in the knowledge that God remains in control.
exp.3:4:
This verse is a command to sound the alarm. The people are told to announce in Judah and proclaim in Jerusalem that the ram's horn should be blown throughout the land, that the people should cry aloud and gather together, and that they should flee to the fortified cities, the cities with walls. The words "announce" and "proclaim" both mean to say something publicly and loudly.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, He called Judah to turn back to Him wholeheartedly, and warned that His anger would come like fire because of the people's wickedness. Now the warning becomes urgent: a disaster is coming from the north. The following passages describe it as a destroying lion, and many relate it to Babylon.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings or put off repentance until tomorrow. If you sense that something in your life or in your heart needs to change, return to Him today, with sincerity and humility.
exp.51:3:
It says that in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, marched against Jerusalem with his entire army. They encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it.

This chapter is the historical account that closes the book of Jeremiah. The one telling the story is not God speaking directly, but the writer recounting the events. It explains that Zedekiah did evil and rebelled against Babylon, and that the fall of Jerusalem came as God's judgment after much disobedience. This matches what Jeremiah had warned about for years.

For today: God is patient, but our choices have consequences. If you feel that God is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Listen to His voice with humility and return to Him while there is still time.
exp.8:8:
Here God asks two strong questions. "Punish" means to hold someone accountable for what they have done. "Avenge Myself" means that God cannot remain indifferent in the face of such wrongdoing. The answer the question expects is: yes, he will have to act.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people used friendly words and spoke of peace with their neighbor, but they planned to deceive him. God had already said he would test them as metal is refined in a furnace. His judgment is not a whim; it arises from the lies and betrayal among them. The verses that follow also show the grief of God and of Jeremiah over what was coming.

Today we can examine whether our words match our hearts. God cares about truth and justice in everyday life. Let us ask his help to speak with sincerity and to treat others without a double face.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the word of the Lord also came to Jeremiah during the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, and kept coming until the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, another son of Josiah. That period ended when the people of Jerusalem went into exile. The phrase "and through the days of" means the message continued across that whole stretch of time, and "went into exile" refers to the removal of the city's people from their home.

The one speaking is the writer of the book, who sets the stage for Jeremiah's ministry. Earlier he mentioned its beginning in the time of Josiah; now he summarizes his long labor up to the fall of Jerusalem. Many understand this to be about forty years, although the text does not give that number. In this way the reader knows that Jeremiah spoke in difficult times, full of warnings.

For today: God asks us for faithfulness even when we do not see quick results. Jeremiah kept speaking for years amid rejection. Today we can keep obeying God with steadiness, trusting that He sustains those who serve Him.
exp.21:3:
God tells the king of Judah that if he truly carries out these commands (to act with justice, to rescue the one being mistreated, and not to harm the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow), the line of David will keep ruling. The words "if you will indeed carry out these commands" mean that the promise depends on doing what God has just asked. Kings who sit on David's throne would enter through the gates of this palace with honor, security, and authority, riding on chariots and on horses, together with their officials and their people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who is to carry this message to the royal palace. God offers a conditional promise: the continuation of the throne depends on obedience. He then warns that if they do not obey, the palace will be left in ruins. History shows that Judah eventually fell before Babylon.

For today: those who hold some kind of authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, should use it to protect the vulnerable. God's blessing is not sustained by religious appearance, but by practical justice and mercy.
exp.42:5:
This verse continues the list of the people whom Johanan and the military leaders took with them to Egypt: the men, the women, the children, and the king's daughters. It also includes everyone whom Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, had allowed to remain with Gedaliah son of Ahikam. Among them were the prophet Jeremiah and Baruch son of Neriah, his helper.

The narrator is describing what happened after Gedaliah was murdered. The people had asked God for counsel through Jeremiah, and God told them to stay in Judah. But Johanan and the leaders did not believe that word, and they went to Egypt out of fear of Babylon. Jeremiah and Baruch were taken along with them as well, though we do not know in detail how this happened.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we seek God's direction only so that he will confirm what we have already decided. Obeying his word when it frightens us is better than fleeing toward a false sense of safety.
exp.24:21:
This verse continues a list of nations that must drink the cup of God's anger. Here all the kings of Tyre and Sidon are named, important cities of the Phoenician port, and also the kings of the coastlands across the sea, that is, lands along the Mediterranean.

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks around 605 B.C. God announces that Babylon will bring judgment, first on Judah and then on many nations. The neighboring peoples will also answer for their pride and their wickedness. Scholars do not agree on exactly which coastlands are meant.

For today: God rules over all nations, not only over his own people. This invites us to live with humility, not to trust in power or riches, and to place our trust in God, who is just and patient.
exp.49:14:
Raise a war cry against Babylon from every side. She has thrown up her hands in surrender. Her towers have fallen, and her walls have been torn down. This is the vengeance of the LORD, so take your vengeance on her. As she has done, do the same to her.

The message comes from the prophet Jeremiah, who speaks on God's behalf. Babylon had destroyed nations and oppressed Israel, and judgment is announced against it because it sinned against the LORD. Some see here a fall of Babylon that was already near, and others also see a broader fulfillment. Scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: you can trust that God sees injustice and does not leave it without a response. This helps you let go of resentment and not take revenge yourself, leaving God to be the judge, and at the same time to examine your own treatment of others.
exp.29:4:
This verse says that God himself announces a cry that is heard: a cry of panic, a cry of terror, not of peace. The words "a cry of panic" describe people overwhelmed with fear, and "is heard" shows that the message reaches the whole people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Just before this, he promises that he will bring Israel and Judah back from captivity. But before that restoration there will come a very hard time, which the text calls "a time of trouble for Jacob." Interpreters apply it in different ways: to the fall of Babylon, to other historical events, or to a time still future. Even so, the passage ends with the promise that Jacob will be delivered.

Today it reminds us that pain does not have the final word. If you are going through fear or distress, you can hold on to the fact that God still guides your story and has a purpose of rescue.
exp.30:22:
This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: when he restores his people from captivity, they will once again speak this blessing in the land of Judah and in its cities: "May the LORD bless you, righteous dwelling place, holy mountain." Bringing back the captives means restoring them to their own land. "Righteous dwelling place" refers to Jerusalem or Zion, the place where God lived among his people.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in exile, or were about to be, because of their sin, and these chapters bring comfort and hope. God promises that punishment will not be the final word: there will be a return, rest for the weary, and joy for the sorrowful.

For today: if you are going through a time of pain, failure, or exile, remember that God knows how to restore. While you wait, pray with confidence and bless again what belongs to God, without losing hope.
exp.22:35:
God says that the phrase "the burden of the LORD" should no longer be used. The word in the original can mean "burden," but it can also mean "a solemn prophecy or message." God says that whatever each person says becomes a burden to that very person, because they had twisted the words of the living God. The phrase "refer no more" means "stop bringing up" or "stop repeating." "Pervert" means "distort" or "change."

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against prophets, priests, and people who used that phrase in a mocking way or to give authority to their own ideas. Many interpreters see a play on words here, though some understand it in a slightly different way.

Today, we should be careful not to say "God says" to support our own opinions. Before speaking on God's behalf, it is wise to listen to his Word with humility and to compare it with the whole Bible.
exp.22:28:
God asks whether his word is not like fire and like a hammer that smashes a rock. With these images he says that his word has power: it burns away what is false, purifies, and breaks down hardness of heart.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Some prophets shared their own dreams as if they came from God, and in this way they led the people away from him. God distinguishes between the chaff (human dreams, which have no value) and the wheat (his word, which nourishes). Then he rebukes them for stealing messages from one another and saying "This is what the LORD declares" when God had not spoken.

For today: it is not enough that something sounds beautiful or spiritual. Test what you hear in the light of the Bible, and let it confront you and transform you, even when it sometimes makes you uncomfortable.
exp.5:10:
Jeremiah says he is full of the Lord's wrath and is tired of holding it back. That wrath will fall on everyone: children out in the streets, groups of young men, husbands and wives, the old and the very old alike. The very old are those who have lived a long time, and being "captured" here means being taken away in the invasion.

Jeremiah speaks, but he expresses God's feelings. Judah had spent years rejecting the warnings; its ears were closed. They despised God's word and lived in greed and deceit, including their religious leaders. The judgment would come through an invading army. Some understand the wrath to be God's, and others understand that it also reflects the prophet's grief.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God speaks to us. If something in his Word makes you uncomfortable today, listen to it with humility and change in time, before the consequences arrive.
exp.42:12:
Here it says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will demolish the sacred pillars of the temple of the sun in Egypt and burn down the temples of Egypt's gods. The "sacred pillars" are stone columns set up for worship. The place named here is Beth-shemesh, which means "house of the sun," and it is usually identified with Heliopolis.

God speaks through Jeremiah. A group of Jews fled to Egypt seeking safety, even though God had told them not to go. Jeremiah warns them that Egypt will not save them, and that the gods they trusted there will be unable to defend themselves or defend them. God uses Babylon as an instrument of judgment.

For today: let us ask ourselves where we look for security apart from God, whether in money, power, or our own plans. All of that can fail, but God remains faithful. Trusting in Him and obeying Him is the firmest refuge.
exp.12:10:
God said he had joined all of Israel and all of Judah to himself, the way a loincloth clings close to a man's waist. The waist is the middle part of the body, where a belt or cloth would be worn. God wanted them to be his people, bringing him renown, praise, and glory. But they did not listen. They did not pay attention to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah was told to hide a linen loincloth near the Euphrates River, and later he went back and found it ruined and good for nothing. Through this picture, God shows that his people had become spoiled because of their pride and because they followed other gods.

God desires closeness with us, not just obedience to rules. We can ask ourselves today: am I truly holding on to God and listening to his voice, or have pride or other priorities pulled me away? Today you can return to him with a sincere heart.
exp.22:21:
If those prophets had stood in God's council, they would have proclaimed his words to his people. In this way they would have helped them turn back from their evil ways and deeds. The phrase "stood in my council" points to being admitted into God's presence and counsel, so that the message comes from him and not from the prophet's own imagination.

God speaks through Jeremiah at a time when Judah had gone astray. God accuses prophets who spoke comfortable and false messages without having been sent by him. A true message does not lull the conscience to sleep, but calls for change.

For today: before accepting or repeating a spiritual message, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God and invites you to correct your course. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and spend time with God in prayer and reading, so that you come to know his voice.
exp.27:9:
Hananiah, who claimed to be a prophet, takes the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it. A yoke is the wooden frame placed on oxen for work.

Jeremiah wore the yoke as a sign that God allowed Babylon to rule over Judah. Hananiah contradicted that word and promised that within two years the yoke would be broken. He broke the symbol in front of all the people, and Jeremiah left without arguing. Afterward, God gave Jeremiah a message about this event.

For today: not every pleasant message comes from God. Before believing a promise of comfort, compare it with what the Bible says and ask God for wisdom. God's truth sometimes hurts, but it takes care of us.
exp.1:19:
God says that long ago he broke the yoke and tore off the chains that held his people, meaning he set them free from slavery. But the people answered, "I will not serve!" Instead of following God, they went to every high hill and under every green tree and lay down as prostitutes, giving themselves to idolatry.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of abandoning him after he had rescued them, and of seeking security in Egypt and Assyria and in false gods. High hills and green trees were common places of pagan worship. The image of a prostitute shows the pain of a betrayed love.

For today: the freedom God gives us is not meant for living without him, but for serving him in love. Ask yourself what things you seek to feel secure or satisfied in place of God, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.26:12:
He says God asks King Zedekiah a question: "Why should you and your people die?" The words "by sword and famine and plague" mean death by war, by hunger, and by disease that spreads. God had already declared that this would happen to any nation that does not serve the king of Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks to King Zedekiah of Judah. Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke as a sign that Babylon would rule over those nations. Other prophets were saying the opposite, that there would be no submission. With this question, God invites the king to choose to live and not to harden himself.

For today: sometimes we prefer the voices that tell us what we want to hear. This week, compare any advice with what God says in his Word, even when it is hard to accept, and choose the obedience that gives life.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that the invaders urge one another on: "Rise up!" and they plan to attack by night and destroy the fortresses of Jerusalem. "Let us attack" means they are moving toward the city, which stood on high ground. The "fortresses" are the strongholds and important buildings.

Here the enemy armies speak, the ones God announces from the north. Earlier, in verse 4, they had wanted to attack at midday, but the time has run out on them, so now they decide to attack by night. According to the next verse, it is the LORD who backs them, for Jerusalem is full of violence, injustice and robbery. It is a judgment for the people's persistent wickedness, after many calls to return to God.

For today: let us not think that God's time of grace is endless. If God points out something wrong in our life, let us not leave it for later. Let us repent today, while there is still time.
exp.31:40:
God says that he will delight in doing good to his people. In the original, the verb is the same one translated "I will rejoice," so the sentence reads "I will rejoice in doing them good." "I will plant them" is an image: God will settle them in the land the way someone plants a tree so that it takes root. He will do this faithfully, with all his heart and with all his soul, meaning with his whole will and his full commitment.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians (Chaldeans), and the people were heading into exile because of their disobedience. Even so, God promises an everlasting covenant and a return to the land. Jeremiah had bought a field as a sign of that hope.

For today: God does not help you grudgingly. He takes joy in doing you good. If you feel you have failed or that everything is lost, trust that his love is steadfast. You can come to him with humility, knowing that he desires to restore you and to let you take root in him.
exp.42:0:
This verse says that Jeremiah finished speaking to the people. He had told them everything the LORD their God had sent him to say, leaving nothing out. The verse stands as a pause before the people's response. The phrase "the LORD their God" is the way the verse names God, and "everything that the LORD had sent him to say" is how the verse describes the message he delivered.

Jeremiah speaks after the fall of Jerusalem. The survivors, together with their leaders, had asked him to pray and to tell them God's will. He told them that they should remain in Judah and not flee to Egypt. As the following passage shows, the leaders accused him of lying and rejected the message.

For today: it is easy to ask for God's guidance while already having decided what we want to do. Before we pray, let us ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey even when the answer is not what we hoped for.
exp.43:25:
God says he swears by his great name, that is, by who he is. His oath is that no man of Judah living in Egypt will ever again invoke his name or say, "As surely as the Lord GOD lives." That was a solemn way of affirming something. God takes away from them the right to call on his name as though everything were fine between them and him.

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah who fled to Egypt against God's command. There, together with their wives, they kept burning incense and pouring out drink offerings to the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess, and they promised to keep doing so. God answers with a firm warning about the consequences of their idolatry.

For today: it is not enough to speak God's name with the mouth. He desires sincere faith, without dividing the heart with other idols.
exp.50:42:
It says that the cities of Babylon would be destroyed. Its land would be dry and arid, a place where no one would live or even pass through. "Desolation" means complete ruin. "Son of man" simply means "a human being." "Where no one lives" is the plain wording here.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what the LORD says against Babylon, the power that had subjected Judah. The passage, with images of sea and desert, shows that its great power would come to an end. Sheshach is a coded name for Babylon. God also calls his people to leave there and save themselves. Scholars discuss how and when each detail of this prophecy was fulfilled.

For today: nothing that humanity builds with pride is eternal. Today you can ask yourself where you are placing your security, and trust more in God, who endures forever.
exp.27:4:
This verse says that the prophet Jeremiah replied to the prophet Hananiah. He did so in public, in the presence of the priests and of all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD. The house of the LORD is the temple in Jerusalem. The word "replied" here means that Jeremiah then spoke in answer to what Hananiah had just said.

Hananiah had just announced that God would break the power of Babylon within two years and bring back the exiles and the vessels of the temple. Jeremiah, who had announced a long period of submission to Babylon, responds calmly. He says "Amen," since he would wish it to be true, but he will soon make clear what God has shown him.

For today: when someone says what we would like to hear, we can respond with respect and without mockery, but also with honesty, measuring everything against what God has actually said.
exp.24:36:
This verse says that the peaceful meadows, which seemed safe, will be silenced by the burning anger of the LORD. The meadows are the grazing lands where the flocks rest, and the flock itself is also pictured in the image. The word for "silenced" points to ruin, the quiet that follows destruction. The shepherds and chief herdsmen, that is, the leaders of the people, cry out and weep because they have no way left to escape.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, sent by God. In this chapter he announces judgment on Judah and on several nations. The "shepherds" represent kings and rulers. God judges them for their rebellion and injustice, and for not having listened to the prophets over many years. Scholars understand the images of flock and shepherd as figurative language about leadership.

Today it reminds us that outward calm does not always mean we are right with God. It is a good time to examine the heart, listen to His Word, and turn back to Him with humility, for He is patient and desires to forgive.
exp.30:18:
Here he says Ephraim, that is, the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, acknowledges his sin. First he returned to God and felt sorrow for what he had done. Afterward he struck his thigh in grief and regret, much like beating one's chest. The word "youth" refers to the sins of his younger days, and "shame" is the sense of disgrace. He feels ashamed and humiliated for bearing the disgrace of his past mistakes.

Here Ephraim speaks, lamenting his rebellion. This comes after God promises hope and restoration. God had said he disciplined him like a stubborn young bull, and the people respond with humility. Immediately God calls him "a dear son" and promises mercy.

For today: when you recognize your error, do not remain sunk in shame. Come before God with sincerity, for his discipline seeks to restore you, and his heart is moved to compassion for you.
exp.43:12:
God says that he will punish the Jews who went to live in Egypt, just as he punished Jerusalem. The three forms of punishment are the sword (war), famine, and plague (diseases that spread from person to person). The word "visit" in the older translations does not appear in this verse, so the sense here is simply that God will punish them as he punished Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, even though God had told them not to go. There, moreover, they were burning incense to other gods. God warns them that Egypt would not be a safe refuge.

For today: running away from God does not keep us safe. When He asks something of us, trusting and obeying is safer than seeking protection on our own. If we have turned away, His Word invites us to return and to ask for forgiveness.
exp.22:37:
This verse says that God had commanded the people not to use the expression "the burden of the LORD," but they kept saying it anyway. That is why God responds with judgment. The word "burden" comes from a Hebrew word that can mean a weight or also a prophetic message. The sense here is simply that God had sent word to them forbidding that phrase.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Some people used "the burden of the LORD" mockingly or to give authority to their own ideas, and false prophets claimed to speak on God's behalf when He had not spoken to them. Many understand that the expression became a kind of wordplay and a way of despising the true word. God warns them that treating His message this way will have serious consequences.

Today we can be careful about how we speak of God. Before saying "God told me" or using spiritual phrases, it is good to examine whether we are honoring His word or only defending our own desires.
exp.35:10:
This verse says that Micaiah, son of Gemariah and grandson of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD read from the scroll. The phrase "heard" means that he had already listened to the full message. The sentence is left open, and the following verse tells what he did afterward.

Baruch, Jeremiah's helper, read the scroll containing God's messages aloud, on a day of fasting and in front of many people in the temple. Micaiah was among the listeners. His father Gemariah had a room in the temple, from which the reading was done. Micaiah went right away to tell the palace officials what he had heard.

For today: when we hear the Word of God, it is not meant to be kept to ourselves. Micaiah took it seriously and shared it. We can ask ourselves what we are hearing from God today, and to whom we can share it with humility.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that although God is going to punish his people very severely, he will not destroy them completely. The phrase "I will not make a full end of you" means there will be judgment, but a remnant with hope will also remain. The word "yet" introduces the contrast.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had left the Lord and served other gods. Because of this, the announcement is that a foreign army will invade the land, eat its harvests, and destroy its cities. Even so, in the middle of this strong warning, God leaves a promise: his discipline has a limit.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not think that God has already abandoned you. His correction is serious, but it is not the end. Return to him sincerely, because his desire is to restore you, not to destroy you.
exp.48:30:
God calls an army to rise up and attack a people who live at ease and feel secure, with no walls and no defenses. "Rise up" and "advance against" mean the same thing: go on the attack. The "gates or bars" are the locks and barriers that would normally keep an enemy out, and "they live alone" suggests they dwelt apart, trusting in their distance from others.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in his message against Kedar and Hazor, peoples of the desert of Arabia. According to the text, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would attack them. Their false sense of security would not save them. Scholars cannot determine with certainty all the historical details of these places.

For today: feeling secure is not the same as being safe. If we trust only in our calm, our wealth, or our isolation, we can neglect what matters most. Let us put our trust in God, who is a firm refuge, and live with humility, attentive to his voice.
exp.47:29:
God says he knows very well the insolence of Moab, its pride and arrogance. But that insolence will accomplish nothing. Its boasting, its false assurances, will not help it either. The phrase "it is futile" means that what Moab intends will not come to pass.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message of judgment against Moab, a nation neighboring Israel. The preceding text speaks of its pride and haughtiness. God does not overlook that attitude. But afterward we see that God also grieves over the ruin that is coming, for he says he will weep for Moab.

Today we can remember that pride and empty words do not protect us. If we have trusted in our own strength or in excuses, it is wise to acknowledge this with humility before God, who sees the heart, and to seek his mercy.
exp.36:10:
This verse tells us that the Chaldean army, meaning the Babylonians, withdrew from Jerusalem. They pulled back because the army of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, was coming to help Judah. The siege was lifted for a time.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book. Earlier, God had told Jeremiah not to let the people deceive themselves into thinking the danger was over. The Chaldeans would return and burn the city. This is where the account of what Jeremiah did during that pause begins.

For today: a temporary relief does not always mean the problem has been solved. When a crisis passes, let us not become complacent or ignore what God tells us. Let us use the calm to listen to his voice and correct whatever needs correcting.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that Jeremiah is to give a message to the envoys so that they carry it back to their kings. It is a command with authority: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel." The phrase "the LORD of hosts" presents God as the Lord of all power.

God speaks, and Jeremiah is his messenger. Envoys from several neighboring nations were in Jerusalem, probably to plan a rebellion against Babylon. Through Jeremiah, God sends them a message: it is not the time to rebel. The verses that follow say that God is the Creator and that he allowed Nebuchadnezzar to have authority for a time.

For today: before making ambitious plans, it is good to stop and listen to God. He sees beyond what we see, and his word calls us to humility and trust.
exp.30:2:
God says that he appeared to his people in the past. His message is: "I have loved you with an everlasting love," meaning a love that has no end and no beginning in time. Therefore, "I have drawn you with loving devotion," which here means that God drew, sustained, and treated them with kindness even when the people failed.

Speaking through the prophet Jeremiah, God addresses Israel, which was going through exile and judgment, and many felt that God had abandoned them. This message of comfort reminds them that their history with God is rooted in love, and it promises that He will restore and rebuild them.

When you feel that your mistakes or your trials have pulled you away from God, remember that his love does not depend on your performance. Return to Him with confidence, knowing that his loving devotion sustains you.
exp.4:28:
God asks a pointed question: will he not punish these things? The Berean Standard Bible renders the verse with "punish them," so the idea is that God steps in to judge and set things right. The question is not a passing mood. It is God declaring that he will respond to evil with justice, and the question carries a clear answer: yes, he will.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. The powerful were growing rich through deceit, and they did not defend the orphan or the poor. In addition, prophets and priests were failing in their duty. God does not ignore injustice, even when it seems the guilty are doing well.

Today, this invites us to examine how we gain what we have, how we treat the weak, and whether we defend what is right. It also comforts us: God sees injustice and does not forget it.
exp.21:10:
God announces that Shallum, son of King Josiah, has gone out of Judah and will never return. The phrase "who succeeded his father Josiah" means that he became king in place of his father. "Has gone forth from this place" refers to his being taken away from Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Shallum is usually identified with Jehoahaz, who reigned only a few months and was taken captive to Egypt by Pharaoh Necoh (2 Kings 23:31-34). The previous verse explains the cause: the people abandoned their covenant with God and worshiped idols. That is why the consequences came.

For today: turning away from God has consequences, even when we have power or a good inheritance. Ask him today to keep you faithful, and to make your decisions just and honoring to his word.
exp.49:37:
A drought will fall on Babylon's waters, and they will dry up. The reason is that it is a land full of carved images, or idols, and its people have gone mad over them. Carved images are figures made to be worshiped, and to go mad over them means to lose good judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment against Babylon, the power that had destroyed Jerusalem. The waters may refer to the rivers and canals that sustained the city; some scholars also see a symbolic meaning. The sword in the previous verse and the desert that follows show that its fall would be total.

For today: idols are not always statues. Anything that takes the place of God, such as money, fame, or success, eventually leaves us empty. Today you can ask yourself what your heart holds above God, and give it to him sincerely.
exp.19:4:
God says that everything of value in Jerusalem will be handed over to its enemies. The wealth and goods of the city are what he means by "all its products and valuables," and "all its products" refers to what the people had produced with their own work. The "valuables" and "treasures" are objects of great worth, including those belonging to the kings of Judah. The enemies will plunder them, seize them, and carry them off to Babylon.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Pashur, a priest with authority in the temple, had struck Jeremiah and left him imprisoned in the stocks, an instrument of punishment, for announcing judgment. When he was released, Jeremiah answered him firmly: God was warning that Judah would be taken captive to Babylon because it did not turn back to him.

For today: what we value most, such as money, position, or security, is not firm forever. It is good to ask ourselves where we are placing our trust and to return to God, even when his word is sometimes hard to hear.
exp.13:8:
Here the people ask God why he seems to be like a man taken by surprise, unable to act, or like a warrior powerless to save. Then they affirm that God is among them and that they are called by his name, meaning they belong to him. They close with a plea: "Do not forsake us!"

The one speaking is Jeremiah, praying on behalf of the people during a great drought. He acknowledges Israel's sin, but appeals to the character of God. In the response that follows, God says the people have not wanted to return to him, and he tells Jeremiah not to pray for them.

For today: when you feel that God is silent, be honest with him and pray with humility. Acknowledge your failings, remember that you belong to him, and ask for his help, but also allow him to correct your course.
exp.24:18:
This verse continues the list of nations that Jeremiah was to give the cup of God's wrath to drink. Here Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is named along with his officials, his leaders, and all his people. The word "cup" stands for the cup of God's judgment, and drinking from it represents receiving God's judgment.

Jeremiah, the prophet of Judah, speaks here by recounting a symbolic vision that God gave him. The cup begins with Jerusalem and Judah, and then reaches other nations. The message is that God rules over all peoples, and that no king, not even the powerful Pharaoh, escapes his justice.

For today: no one stands above God, whether by their power or their position. We can live with humility, trusting that God is just, and examine our hearts without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.24:11:
God says that when the seventy years of service to Babylon are complete, He will call the king of Babylon and his nation to account for their guilt. The sentence that explains one of the source phrases is rewritten here: God will come to judge them. He also says that the land of the Chaldeans will become an everlasting desolation, meaning a total and lasting ruin.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around the year 605 BC. Judah had disobeyed God, and Babylon would be the instrument to discipline her. But Babylon was also responsible for its cruelty and pride. Many understand that "everlasting" speaks of a definitive fall, though some see it as prophetic language of great force.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered. We can rest in the fact that He judges with righteousness, so we do not need to take revenge. Entrust your grievances to God and seek to live with humility.
exp.14:9:
Here Jeremiah laments with great pain. He cries out, "Woe to me, my mother, that you have borne me," because he feels that being born brought him a life of quarrels and conflict throughout the land. He says, "I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses me," which means he never lent money or took out loans, so he had no entanglements of debt with anyone, and yet everyone curses him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a message of judgment upon Judah. Because he announced hard words on behalf of God, the people rejected him. His words are a sincere complaint, and God answers him right away with a promise to take care of him in times of distress.

For today: if people reject you for doing what is right, do not hide your pain. Tell God honestly, as Jeremiah did, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.34:12:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the people of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem. He asks them a question that sounds like a rebuke: will they not accept discipline and obey his words? Here the sentence simply refers to the men of Judah and the people living in Jerusalem, and the city is named Jerusalem.

The Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel, speaks through Jeremiah. The Rechabites, a family that fled to Jerusalem because of the Babylonian invasion, had faithfully kept the command of their ancestor Jonadab not to drink wine. God uses their example to show that Judah, by contrast, did not listen to God, even though he spoke to them again and again.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I obey God with the same constancy with which I respect the people I esteem? A good practice is to read the Bible every day and choose one specific thing God asks of you, so you can put it into practice that same week.
exp.27:5:
Jeremiah answers the prophet Hananiah by saying "Amen," which means "so be it." He wishes that God would fulfill what Hananiah announced: that the objects from the temple and all the exiles would return from Babylon to this place. The exiles are the people carried away by force, and the objects are the articles of the LORD's house.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, in front of priests and the people. Hananiah has just said that God would break the yoke of Babylon within two years. Jeremiah had announced a long exile. His "Amen" does not seem to be approval, but a sincere wish that it would be true, although he then warns that a prophecy is tested when it comes to pass. Some also read it with a touch of irony; the text does not make this clear.

For today: we can wish for good news without ceasing to seek the truth. When messages sound appealing, it is wise to pray, to compare them with Scripture, and to speak with humility and compassion.
exp.33:13:
God reminds his people of an old law: when a Hebrew sold himself to another person because of debt, he was to serve six years and go free in the seventh year.

The Lord adds that their ancestors did not obey or listen; in other words, they did not pay attention.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was threatened by Babylon, and King Zedekiah and the people had freed their Hebrew servants. Later they changed their minds and enslaved them again. God reminds them that this law was tied to the covenant made when he brought them out of Egypt. The verses that follow show that their disobedience was serious.

For today: if we make a promise before God, we should keep it even when it costs us. We can also ask ourselves whether we are treating with justice and compassion those who depend on us, such as employees or people in debt.
exp.1:31:
Would a young woman forget her jewelry, or a bride her wedding sash? In this verse God uses the picture of a bride who would never forget her clothing and jewelry. The words for "jewelry" and "wedding sash" are the ones in the verse: the jewelry is what she wears to adorn herself, and the sash is the wedding band she would never leave behind.

God compares this to his people. Something as natural as remembering what belongs to you has become impossible for Israel, which has forgotten him for countless days.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He accuses them of ignoring correction, of rejecting the prophets, and of saying, "We are free, we will not return to you." His pain is that of a forsaken husband, and so he asks whether he had ever been a desert or a dark land to them.

For today: do not let everyday concerns fill your heart and make you forget God. Set aside a moment each day to remember him with gratitude, prayer, and his Word.
exp.12:25:
God says that He Himself will lift up the skirts of Jerusalem and leave them exposed for all to see, so that its shame will be seen. The word "skirts" refers to the edges of long clothing, and "shame" means public disgrace or humiliation. It is a strong image of exposure.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had forgotten Him and trusted in a lie, that is, in idols and false securities. In the Bible, unfaithfulness to God is often compared to adultery. This image announces the consequences of that sin, but the closing question of the context ("how long?") shows that God still desires to cleanse them.

For today: God sees what we try to hide. Instead of covering our failures, we can confess them honestly to Him and return to Him, for He wants to cleanse us.
exp.51:8:
This verse says that the Chaldeans seized King Zedekiah as he was trying to escape from Jerusalem. They brought him before the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah, in the land of Hamath. There, the king "pronounced judgment on Zedekiah," meaning he passed sentence on him and set out his punishment. "Seized" means that they took hold of him by force.

Chapter 52 summarizes the fall of Jerusalem, and the author is not identified with certainty in this passage. For years Jeremiah had warned that Judah would fall if it kept rejecting God and refused to submit to Babylon. Zedekiah did not heed those words, and here what had been announced comes to pass.

For today: ignoring a clear warning does not make it disappear. If God speaks to us through his Word or through wise counsel, it is wise to obey in time, before the consequences arrive. His correction seeks to care for us, not to destroy us.
exp.14:12:
God says he will hand over the wealth and treasures of the people as plunder. "Give up as plunder" means letting others take everything and carry it away. It will be "without charge": the people will receive nothing in return. And this will reach throughout all their land (the "borders" are the boundaries or regions).

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The reason he gives is "for all your sins": the people had turned away from God. The verses before this are hard to understand, and some scholars debate exactly who is being addressed, but most see here a judgment on the nation.

For today: let us not place our security in money or possessions, because they can be lost. Let us seek God sincerely and live with a faithful heart.
exp.47:3:
Moab will be shattered, meaning completely defeated. The most painful part is that her little ones will cry out, that is, the children, or perhaps the weakest and most humble people of the city.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what God says against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Moab trusted in its pride, its riches, and its fortresses. The message announces that this security will fall, and that ruin will come to cities such as Heshbon, Madmen, and Horonaim. The text describes the suffering with great vividness.

For today: God takes pride seriously, but he also hears the crying of the weak. We can examine what we truly trust in and be sensitive to the suffering of those who have no voice.
exp.19:6:
He says Jeremiah feels deceived and overpowered by God. The word translated "deceived" can also be rendered "persuaded" or "enticed"; some understand it as "you deceived me." "Overcome" means defeated by a stronger force. Jeremiah admits that God was stronger and that he could not resist his call, but now he is a laughingstock all day long, and everyone mocks him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks just after the priest Pashur struck him and put him in the stocks for announcing judgment on Jerusalem. Alone now, Jeremiah opens his heart to God with a very sincere complaint. Interpreters debate how strong the word "deceived" is, but all see here an honest prayer, not unbelief.

For today: when obeying God costs you mockery or weariness, do not hide what you feel. Tell it to him frankly in prayer, as Jeremiah did. God is not alarmed by your complaints, and he can sustain you even when you feel weak.
exp.12:11:
God commands Jeremiah to tell the people that every wineskin, the leather bag used to store wine, will be filled with wine. The people reply with a mocking or weary tone: "Don't we surely know that every wineskin should be filled with wine?"

The LORD, the God of Israel, speaks through Jeremiah. The people had refused to listen and kept following false gods. What seems like an obvious statement is a coded message: in the following verse, the wine stands for God's judgment, which would fill everyone, from the kings down to the common people, until they stagger and fall.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly just because they sound familiar. Listening with humility, and not with an attitude of "I already know that," leads us to change course in time.
exp.8:15:
It says that God will scatter the people of Judah among nations they had never known, nations that neither they nor their ancestors had known. In addition, He will send war after them, and the phrase about the sword going after them means that it will pursue them until they are finished off. The word translated here as "finish off" means to bring to an end or to consume completely.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had turned away from God to follow their own desires and to worship the Baals, false gods, just as their ancestors had taught them. That is why this judgment comes, which history shows fulfilled in the exile in Babylon. The verses that follow speak of mourning over this tragedy.

For today: what we inherit or follow out of habit is not always what is right. It is wise to examine our lives in the light of God's Word, and to return to Him with humility before error costs us dearly.
exp.51:0:
This verse introduces Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He became king at the age of twenty-one and ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother is also named, Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah (she is not known to be the prophet Jeremiah, who was from Anathoth). The phrase "became king" means that he took the throne and began to rule.

This final chapter of the book of Jeremiah reads like a historical summary, very similar to 2 Kings 24 and 25. It is not a speech from God, but an account that explains how Jerusalem fell. The verses that follow show that Zedekiah did what was evil, and that the judgment came because of the people's disobedience and their leaders. The details of his age and his mother place his reign in real history.

Today we can learn that holding an office or a position is not enough; what matters is obeying God. Let us ask him for humility to listen to his voice in time and not to harden our hearts.
exp.30:0:
This verse says that God promises to be the God of all the families of Israel, and that they will be his people. "Families" refers to the family groups or tribes. The statement describes a close, two-way relationship: God belongs to them, and they belong to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had been wounded by judgment and exile, but here God announces restoration. The words "at that time" point to a future of renewal. The verses that follow explain the reason: God has loved them with an everlasting love and has dealt with them in mercy.

For today: our relationship with God does not begin with our effort, but with his steadfast love. If you feel far away or weary, you can return to him with confidence, because his desire is to be your God and to have you near.
exp.28:14:
This verse records what the exiles were saying: "The LORD has raised up prophets for us here in Babylon." The phrase "raised up" means that God caused them to rise up, or stand up, in that place. The people leaned on those prophets to believe that their situation would soon change.

God speaks through Jeremiah, in a letter to the Jews taken captive to Babylon. He had promised them restoration after seventy years. But in Babylon there were prophets announcing an immediate return, and the people believed them. God warns that those words did not come from Him, and that judgment would still reach those who stayed behind in Jerusalem.

For today: it is not enough for someone to speak in God's name or to say what we want to hear. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and seek God with all your heart, with patience, even in difficult times.
exp.17:19:
Here Jeremiah brings a complaint to God: "Should good be repaid with evil?" He says that they have dug a pit for him, that is, they have prepared a trap to make him fall or to kill him. Then he asks God to remember how he stood before Him to speak good on their behalf and to turn away His wrath from them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a very sincere prayer. Some people of Judah were planning to silence him with accusations and slander, because they did not want to hear his message of judgment. Jeremiah feels hurt because he had interceded for them. What follows is a very harsh prayer against them; it is an honest cry, not a model to imitate without thought.

For today: when people repay you with evil for having done good, do not keep the pain to yourself. Bring it to God with sincerity, as Jeremiah did, and let Him take care of your cause and heal your heart.
exp.32:20:
It says that God's covenant with David is as firm as day and night. The word "broken" means to cancel or annul. Just as no one can stop the order of day and night, no one will be able to cancel the promise that a son of David would reign on his throne, nor the promise that there would be Levites who are priests serving God. "My ministers" refers to those who serve him in worship.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The people were living through the disaster of the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, and it seemed that everything had been lost. God answers with hope: his word will stand. Christians see in Jesus, a descendant of David, the fullest fulfillment of this promise, though some interpreters understand it in other ways.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, remember that God is faithful to what he has promised. Each sunrise can remind you that his faithfulness does not change, and that you can entrust your future to him.
exp.43:22:
Jeremiah tells the Jews living in Egypt that the disaster that fell on them was no accident. They burned incense to other gods. By doing so they sinned against the LORD, did not obey his voice, and did not walk in his instruction, his statutes, or his testimonies. The phrase "as you see today" means: "as you can see now."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of Jews fled to Egypt and kept worshiping the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess. They believed this would bring them better fortune. Jeremiah answers that the ruin of Judah came from abandoning God.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for security outside of God. Instead of blaming luck, it is wise to listen to his Word, recognize our mistakes, and obey him again with humility.
exp.44:2:
Baruch says he is worn out by grief. He feels that the Lord has piled sorrow on top of his pain. His words "I am worn out with groaning and have found no rest" mean that he has exhausted himself with so much sighing and weeping, and still he finds no relief.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Baruch, his assistant, who wrote down the prophet's words. This was in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when the messages were harsh and announced judgment. Baruch was overwhelmed, and perhaps he also wanted a safer life or a more important place. God does not ignore his complaint, but speaks to him frankly and promises to watch over his life.

When you feel tired and sad, do not hide your pain from God. Tell him honestly. And let him also examine your expectations, because trusting him is safer than chasing greatness.
exp.25:19:
This verse introduces another prophet, named Uriah, the son of Shemaiah, from the town of Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied in the name of the LORD, that is, he spoke on God's behalf. He spoke the same message of judgment against Jerusalem and the land of Judah that Jeremiah had spoken. The verse says he prophesied "the same things that Jeremiah did," so his message matched Jeremiah's.

Here some of the elders and common people speak up to defend Jeremiah, who was in danger of death because of his message. Earlier they had recalled Micah, whom no one put to death. Now they mention Uriah, but his case ended badly: according to the verses that follow, King Jehoiakim pursued him, he fled to Egypt, and they caught up with him. He is cited as an example of what could happen.

For today: telling the truth can be costly, and even so God calls us to be faithful. Let us ask him for courage, but also for wisdom and humility to speak with love.
exp.21:17:
God announces that when Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and king of Judah, dies, no one will truly mourn him. His family will not cry out, "Alas, my brother! Alas, my sister!", and the people will not cry out, "Alas, my master! Alas, his splendor!" It will be a death without grief or honor.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Shortly before, he compared Jehoiakim with his father Josiah, who defended the poor and the needy, and that was what it meant to know God. Jehoiakim, on the other hand, sought his own gain, shed innocent blood, and oppressed others. That is why he receives this judgment.

For today: greatness is not measured by position or money, but by how we treat the weak. Ask God to show you whom you can defend or help this week, and do it with justice and kindness.
exp.7:11:
Does God ask whether his people felt shame after doing detestable things? The answer is no: they had lost even the ability to blush. The words "they will fall" describe what will happen to them, and "when I punish them" means that God is coming to call them to account. For this reason they will fall together with those who fall in the judgment.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. God accuses everyone, from the least to the greatest, including prophets and priests, of deceit and greed. They kept saying "peace, peace" to calm the wounds of the people, without truly healing them, even though there was no peace.

For today: do not get used to sin or treat it lightly. If you feel conviction, do not put it out; it is a gift of God. Come to Him with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and let Him truly heal you.
exp.49:6:
This verse says that everyone from Israel's enemies who came across the scattered people devoured them. Their enemies also justified themselves, saying, "We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the Lord." In the Berean wording, "devoured" is a picture of destroying or taking advantage of someone, and "their true pasture" describes the Lord as the place where his people find safety and nourishment, and "the hope of their fathers" describes him as the one their ancestors trusted.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing the fall of Babylon. His people were like lost sheep, badly led by their shepherds. The enemies used Israel's sin as an excuse, but God does not leave them without blame: he will judge Babylon for its violence. Then he calls his people to return to him.

For today: to recognize our own failings without using other people's failings as an excuse to do harm. And if we have drifted away from God, we can return to him with humility, because he remains our hope.
exp.50:44:
God tells his people to leave Babylon and save their lives before his judgment arrives. "Come out of her" means to leave that city behind. "The fierce anger of the LORD" speaks of God's strong judgment against evil. "The LORD" is the name of God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was a powerful empire that had oppressed Israel and worshiped idols, such as Bel. God announces that he will judge Babylon and bring about its fall. His people were scattered among them, and God asks them to leave so they will not be caught up in that judgment. The historical details of how it was fulfilled are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God invites us not to settle into what opposes him. Today you can ask yourself what habit or environment is pulling you away from God, and take a concrete step to leave it, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that both Israel, the northern kingdom, and Judah, the southern kingdom, were utterly unfaithful to God. The word here means more than a slip. It describes a loyalty that was deliberately broken.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, He announces that He will punish a people who turned away from Him, and that their walls will be torn down because they do not belong to Him. Then their unfaithfulness is shown: they denied God, said that no harm would come upon them, and despised the prophets.

For today: God does not settle for a faith of words alone. Honestly examine whether there is something you know God is asking of you and that you have decided to ignore. Return to Him soon, without excuses, because His patience seeks to lead us to repentance.
exp.9:3:
What it says: The verse describes how a wooden idol is made. It is adorned with silver and gold, and it is fastened with hammer and nails so that it will not totter or fall from its place.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people, surrounded by nations that worship idols and practice astrology. He warns them not to imitate those customs or fear those signs. With a certain irony, he shows that a god made by human hands, which needs nails so that it does not fall, has no power at all. At the end, the text contrasts this with the greatness of the Lord.

For today: Today idols can be money, success, or image. Ask yourself: what do you trust more than God? What we build and adorn cannot sustain us; only God, living and powerful, can do that.
exp.3:11:
It says that a wind even stronger than the earlier one is coming, and that God himself is sending it. "Violent" means harsh, very intense.
