The statement that God will pronounce judgments means that He will announce His verdict against them for their wickedness. The phrase "a wind too strong for that" is describing a wind stronger than the one just mentioned.

The one speaking is God, in the middle of the words of the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah complains that the people expected peace and received a threat. This dry desert wind represents the invasion that was drawing near. It was not meant to winnow the wheat, but to destroy. God warns that the punishment would be worse, because the people did not want to leave their sin.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with approval. If He points out something to us in our conscience, it is wise to repent soon, before the consequences grow.
exp.24:20:
This verse continues a list of nations. God names Edom, Moab, and the Ammonites, neighboring peoples of Israel, located to the east and southeast of the Jordan River. In this list, all are called to drink the cup of God's wrath (v. 15).

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks around 605 B.C., when Babylon was growing in power. God announces that his judgment would reach Judah first and then many neighboring nations. These peoples had their own history of pride and violence.

For today: God rules over all nations, not only over his people. We can live with humility, remembering that we all answer to him, and trust that his justice is perfect, even when we do not fully understand it.
exp.31:37:
This verse says that the people of Israel will be God's people, and that God will be their God. It is a promise of close relationship and of belonging to one another. The phrase "They will be My people" and the idea that God is "their God" express the same bond from both sides, and the wording shows how completely God commits himself to them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was about to fall to Babylon because of the people's disobedience, and God had allowed it. Even so, he promises to gather them again, bring them back to their land, and give them a heart and a way to fear him. This promise is repeated in other passages of the Bible, and many Christians see it fully fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ.

Today, even when you have failed or feel far away, God invites you to return to him. Take a few minutes to tell him sincerely: "You are my God, and I want to live as yours."
exp.41:8:
This verse is the beginning of God's answer. Jeremiah reminds everyone that he speaks in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, the one they themselves asked him to bring their requests to. "To present your petition" means bringing their requests before God.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors, led by Johanan, was afraid of the king of Babylon. They asked Jeremiah to pray so they would know what to do. After ten days, Jeremiah brings them God's answer, just as they had asked.

When we ask God for direction, it is good to do so with a willingness to obey, even when the answer is not the one we hoped for. Prayer is listening, not only speaking.
exp.22:15:
This verse is a warning from God to his people. It tells them not to listen to prophets who bring them comforting messages. The phrase "they are filling you with false hopes" means that these prophets fill people's minds with empty illusions. Those prophets speak whatever comes from their own minds, not what the LORD has actually told them.

God himself speaks, through Jeremiah, in a time of sin in Judah. The prophets of Jerusalem were living wickedly and encouraged the people to continue in their evil, telling them that everything would be fine and that no punishment would come. That is why God rebukes them so sharply, and the people were in danger for believing them.

For today: before accepting a spiritual message, let us compare it with the Bible. That a message is pleasant does not prove that it comes from God. Let us seek the truth, even when it sometimes confronts us.
exp.14:15:
Jeremiah says that he found God's words and took them in, meaning he received them and held them deep within himself. Those words became his joy and his heart's delight. The reason is that he bore God's name: he was God's prophet, belonging to him.

The word "ate" in the verse is a figure of speech for taking something in fully and making it part of oneself. The phrase "LORD God of Hosts" is a title that highlights the power of God.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the midst of rejection and mockery for announcing God's message. Before and after this verse he complains, asks for help, and feels deep pain. Even so, he remembers that God's word was his joy. Some think it refers to a moment of his calling, but the text does not say so with certainty.

For today: when you are tired or hurt, do not leave the Bible aside only as a duty. Read it slowly, as one who is nourished, and honestly tell God what you feel.
exp.30:6:
This is what the Lord says: sing with joy for Jacob, and shout for the foremost of the nations. Make your praises heard, and pray, "O Lord, save your people, the remnant of Israel." The remnant are those who survived and were left behind.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had suffered exile and destruction because of their disobedience. In this chapter God promises to restore them, bring them back, and comfort them. This joy is announced before the full fulfillment is seen; it is a hope based on God's promise.

For today: even in difficult times, we can praise God in advance, trusting that he keeps what he promises. As you pray for what you need, add gratitude and song, because God hears and rescues his own.
exp.20:9:
God says he has decided to act against Jerusalem, not to bless it but to bring disaster on it. The city will be handed over to the king of Babylon, who will destroy it with fire. To "set one's face against" someone means to confront them firmly. The phrase "will burn it with fire" is the same idea the reader sees in "will destroy it with fire."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians, and the people refused to change course. Earlier, God offered them a choice between life and death: surrendering meant living. Then he calls the house of David to do justice and rescue the oppressed. The punishment is presented as the result of their wickedness.

For today: God warns us out of love before the consequences arrive. If something in your life pulls you away from justice or truth, do not harden yourself with pride. Listen, acknowledge your mistake, and change today.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the people of Israel betrayed God, just as a wife who is unfaithful to her husband betrays him. The phrase "may betray" means breaking a promise of loyalty. The husband is the one she was bound to in faithfulness. When God says "you have betrayed Me," he means that Israel acted with betrayal, failing to keep their word to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just recalled that he wanted to treat Israel as his children and give them a good land, hoping they would be faithful to him. Here he expresses his pain because they left him. But the text that follows shows that it does not end in condemnation: God calls them to return and promises to heal them.

For today: if you notice that you have moved away from God, do not hide yourself. He grieves over betrayal, but he still invites you to come back. Today you can speak to him honestly, acknowledge where you have failed, and ask him to heal your heart.
exp.18:4:
They built the high places of Baal, that is, altars on hilltops, to honor the god Baal. There they burned their own sons as an offering. "Holocaust" refers to offerings that were burned up completely. God makes clear that he never commanded this, never said it, and never even thought of it.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the Valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. He accuses the kings and the people of abandoning him, worshiping other gods, and shedding innocent blood. For this reason he announces judgment on that place. Scholars agree that this refers to the sacrifice of children, although not all of them specify how widespread the practice was.

For today: We should examine whether what we do in God's name truly comes from him. Let us compare our customs with the Bible, and take care of the weakest among us, especially children.
exp.21:2:
God commands the king of Judah and his people to act with justice and righteousness. They must rescue the one suffering abuse from the hands of the one who mistreats him. They must not cheat or take what belongs to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow, nor kill innocent people. The phrase "administer justice" means deciding cases fairly, and "rescue" means to free someone or defend them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who receives the order to go to the royal palace. The message is for the king, his servants, and the people. God reminds them that ruling is not only about having power, but about caring for the most defenseless. He then promises blessing if they obey, and warns that the palace would fall into ruins if they do not.

Today we can ask ourselves who near us is at a disadvantage: an immigrant, a child without support, or a widow. We can help them, deal with them honestly, and defend their rights.
exp.22:31:
God says he is against those who tell false dreams as if they came from him. These so-called prophets retold their dreams to lead God's people astray with reckless lies. God makes clear that he did not send them or command them, and that they are of no benefit at all to the people.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the days before the fall of Judah. Several prophets were assuring everyone that all would be well, even though the people were living in sin. They claimed to speak for the Lord, but their words were made up or taken from others. God rebukes them for turning the people away from repentance.

Today we can compare what we hear, even when it sounds beautiful or spiritual, with what the Bible says. A true word from God may comfort, but it also corrects and leads us to obey him.
exp.39:1:
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard for the king of Babylon, found Jeremiah and spoke to him. He acknowledged that the LORD, the God of Israel, had decreed the disaster that was now falling on Jerusalem. The phrase "so he took" can be read as "then he took," and "said to him" simply means "told him." The phrase "this place" refers to Jerusalem and Judah.

The speaker is a foreign officer. Jeremiah had been bound among the captives being taken to Babylon, and he was set free at Ramah. For a long time Jeremiah had warned that the people would be punished for their disobedience. The text does not explain how Nebuzaradan knew that prophecy.

For today: God's truth is sometimes recognized where we least expect it, and when trouble comes, people do not always listen to us. If God speaks to us through his Word, it is better to respond in time with humility, rather than waiting to see the consequences.
exp.12:6:
Jeremiah obeys God and goes to the Euphrates River. There he digs up the loincloth he had hidden in the rock, and he finds it ruined. It was of no use at all.

God had asked Jeremiah to use this loincloth as a sign for the people. A loincloth is worn close to the body, and God wanted Judah close to Him. But the people became proud and turned away from God. The verses that follow explain that in the same way, the pride of Judah and Jerusalem would be ruined. Some scholars debate whether the journey was real or a vision, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: pride pulls us away from God and leaves us useless. We can ask Him for a humble heart and stay close to Him every day, in prayer and in His Word.
exp.8:4:
They betray one another and no longer tell the truth. They have trained their tongues to lie so thoroughly that it is as if they had taught them to do it. "Friend" here means a close companion. "Iniquity" describes twisting what is right and doing wrong with effort and persistence. They wear themselves out committing sin.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, his people. He is grieved because lying has destroyed trust between friends and even between brothers. The verses that follow say that this deceit grew out of refusing to know God. For that reason he announces that he will refine them as metal is melted and purified, though his sorrow over his people is evident.

Today we can examine our own words: do I exaggerate, conceal, or tell half-truths? Resolve to speak with honesty and kindness this week, even when it is costly. Ask God to help you become someone others can trust.
exp.50:51:
God himself says he is going to step in. The word "punish" here means to hold someone accountable for what they have done. The idols of Babylon are the ones the verse calls "her idols." The people who suffer under that judgment are the wounded, and their groaning will be heard throughout the land of Babylon. God announces that the false gods will not be able to defend anyone.

Jeremiah prophesies against Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and defiled the temple. Earlier, the people confessed their shame over that humiliation. God responds by promising that Babylon too will be held accountable. The verses that follow say that neither its height nor its strength will save it.

For today: no power and no modern "idol", such as money, fame or control, can save us. We can trust that God sees injustice and will act in his time. In the meantime, let us place our security in him alone.
exp.10:19:
Jeremiah is speaking to God. He addresses him as "O LORD of Hosts," the one who judges righteously and "examines the heart and mind," meaning he knows the most inward things: thoughts and feelings. He asks to see God's vengeance on his enemies, that is, that God would bring about justice. He says he has "committed my cause" to God, which means he has placed his case in God's hands.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He had just learned that the men of his own town, Anathoth, were plotting to kill him to silence his message. He did not know it, and he was like an innocent lamb. Scholars debate how to understand his request for vengeance; it is a cry for justice, not a command.

When you are treated unjustly, bring your case to God honestly, including your pain and anger. He sees the heart and can do justice better than you can, so there is no need for you to take revenge.
exp.41:6:
It says that ten days passed before God spoke to Jeremiah. The verse's wording "after ten days" points to the time that had gone by, and the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah at the end of that period. The answer from God did not come right away.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors, with Johanan and the military leaders, asked Jeremiah to pray for them. They promised to obey God, whether what he said was good or bad. Jeremiah waited ten days until he received the word. The Bible does not explain why it was exactly ten days, so it is better not to invent a reason.

Today too, God sometimes seems slow to answer. That waiting can be a time to examine our hearts and ask ourselves whether we are truly willing to obey, even if the answer is not the one we want. Let us wait with patience and with a willing heart.
exp.21:27:
God asks with sorrow whether Coniah is like a shattered pot, a jar that no one wants. He asks why he and his descendants have been hurled out and cast into a land they do not know. "Despised" means held in contempt, and "a jar that no one wants" means a thing no one values or desires.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, king of Judah, also called Jehoiachin, was taken captive to Babylon because of the disobedience of the people and their kings. The message says that none of his descendants would sit on the throne. Some understand the phrase about having no children to mean that none of them would hold the throne.

For today: power, position, and prestige do not last, and God does not measure worth by them. Live with humility and obedience, and remember that God remains the one who gives and takes away.
exp.17:8:
And if at another time I announce that I will build up and establish a nation or kingdom, God can, at any moment, announce his blessing over a nation or kingdom: to build it up is to raise it and strengthen it, and to establish it is to give it firm roots and lasting growth. "I announce" means that God declares what he will do.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, the prophet saw the potter reshape a damaged vessel. God teaches that his announcements are not a blind fate: they depend on how the people respond. If a nation turns from its evil, God changes the punishment announced; if it turns away from him, he changes the blessing. It is a call to Judah to turn back.

For today: do not give up on your future, and do not rely on your past blessings. Today you can return to God, correct a wrong path, and obey his voice with humility.
exp.15:1:
God commands the prophet Jeremiah not to marry or have children in this place, that is, in the land of Judah. It is a personal instruction and a very hard one. "Marry" here means to get married.

The Lord speaks and tells Jeremiah this a few years before the fall of Jerusalem (around 587 B.C.). His solitary life was a visible sign for the people: a judgment so terrible was coming that bringing children into that place would mean condemning them to suffering. The passage that follows describes death by disease, sword, and famine. Jeremiah bore that pain as a living message.

For today: God sometimes calls his servants to difficult and lonely paths. If you are going through one, remember that he sees your sacrifice and does not leave you alone. He also invites us to take his word seriously and not to ignore his warnings.
exp.29:19:
God promises that the people of Israel will live again as in the old days, secure and blessed. Their congregation, that is, the people gathered together, will be made firm and stable before God. And to punish their oppressors means that God will act to hold them accountable for the harm they caused. "As in days of old" means "as at the beginning."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This passage belongs to what is called the "book of consolation" (chapters 30 and 31). Judah faced ruin and exile because of its unfaithfulness, but God promises to restore the city, the temple and the joy of the people, and to renew the relationship: "You will be my people, and I will be your God."

For today: if you are going through a time of loss or injustice, remember that God knows how to restore what is broken and also how to defend those who suffer. Trust in Him, and leave justice in His hands, without holding on to resentment.
exp.48:8:
In the verse, the prophet says that when grape harvesters come to a vineyard, they usually leave some gleanings behind. Even thieves in the night take only what they want. But with Edom it will be different: the destruction will be complete, as the next verse shows. The phrase "only what they wanted" in the verse means that a thief's aim is limited, while Edom's judgment will go beyond what is normal.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah with a message of judgment against Edom, the people descended from Esau. Teman and Dedan were regions or cities connected with Edom and its reputation for wisdom. God announces that neither their wisdom nor their hiding places will save them. Many understand that the judgment comes because of their pride, although here the text focuses on the punishment.

For today: let us not trust in our intelligence, resources, or security as if they were our refuge. Let us place our trust in God, who also cares for orphans and widows, and use what we have with humility.
exp.38:15:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to Ebed-melech the Cushite, a man from Cush. The message is that God is about to carry out what He has said against Jerusalem, bringing harm and not good. The words "before your eyes" mean that Ebed-melech will see with his own eyes the fulfillment of what was announced.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who was being held in the courtyard of the prison. Ebed-melech, an official of the palace, had stood up for the prophet and helped pull him out of a cistern (chapter 38). This word came before the fall of Jerusalem. Although it announces judgment, it opens the way to a promise of protection for him, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: God sees acts of courage and kindness, even when no one else notices them. If you do what is right and trust in Him, you can rest in the knowledge that He will not forget you, even in difficult times.
exp.32:2:
God invites his people to call out to him, that is, to call on him sincerely and out of real need. He promises that he will answer and that he will show them "great and unsearchable things," meaning things that are vast and hard to grasp, things the person does not yet know. The word "unsearchable" points to things that are hidden or beyond the reach of human understanding.

The one speaking is the LORD, and he speaks to Jeremiah while the prophet is imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard. Jerusalem is surrounded by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and everything seems lost. Even so, God promises something beyond the ruin: in the verses that follow he speaks of healing and restoration. Scholars understand that promise mainly as applying to Israel at that time.

For today: when you feel shut in or without a way out, pray to God honestly. He will not always give the result you hope for, but you can trust that he hears and guides.
exp.21:28:
Jeremiah 22:29 repeats the word "land" three times to draw attention with force. It is like a solemn cry: "Hear!"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was king of Judah and was taken captive to Babylon. God announces that his fate will be harsh and that none of his descendants will reign successfully on the throne of David. The whole land is called to hear this judgment. Some understand it to refer to the land of Judah; others, to the whole earth as a witness.

For today: God speaks with seriousness, and it is worth listening before the consequences arrive. Today you can set aside a moment to read the Bible with a heart willing to obey.
exp.17:7:
This verse says that if a nation turns away from its wrongdoing, God will change the disaster he had planned for it. The word "But" at the start of the verse is a connecting word meaning "however" or "yet." To "turn" from evil means to turn around and change direction. When the verse says God will "relent," it means he changes his mind and does not carry out the punishment he had announced.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has sent him to the potter's house to show that God is like one who shapes clay. His message to Israel and to other nations is clear: his warnings of judgment are not fixed sentences, but calls to return. The verses that follow show that the opposite can also happen: if a people turns away from what is good, God will change the blessing he promised.

For today: God responds to the heart that changes. If there is something in your life that does not please God, do not think it is too late. Today you can leave it behind and return to him with sincerity.
exp.22:9:
The land of Judah, the verse says, is full of adulterers, and this is probably meant both literally and as unfaithfulness to God. Because of the curse, the land mourns and dries up. The pastures of the wilderness have withered. Their "course," meaning the direction of their lives, is evil, and their power is misused.

Jeremiah speaks, grieved by the false prophets. God fills him with deep anguish, like someone staggering from wine. The religious leaders were deceiving the people and living in wickedness. Some understand the curse as the consequence of sin, and others see it as a reference to false oaths; the text allows several readings.

For today: examine how you use your influence, whether at home, at work, or in church. Ask God that your life be faithful and that your strength be used to do good and to speak the truth.
exp.47:42:
Jeremiah 48:43 says that terror, a pit, and a snare await the people of Moab. The "pit" is a trap dug in the ground, like the ones used to catch animals. The "snare" is a net or cord that catches whatever steps into it. "Dweller" means someone who lives in a place. The picture is of a people with no way out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring nation of Israel, and the text just before this verse explains that Moab was judged because it set itself up proudly against the Lord, through its arrogance and rebellion. The verses that follow describe how whoever flees from one danger falls into another. It is poetic language about a judgment that is very real.

For today: pride makes us believe we do not need God, but in the end it traps us. Today you can be humble, recognize the things in which you have trusted yourself more than Him, and ask Him sincerely for direction.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that Jerusalem must wash the evil from its heart if it wants to be saved. God asks, "How long will you harbor wicked thoughts within you?" because the people kept holding on to thoughts of wrongdoing, that is, crooked plans and ideas. To be saved means to be delivered or rescued.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had turned away from God, and the arrival of an enemy army, swift as a whirlwind and coming from the north, was being announced. Even so, God offers a way out: a change within, not only in outward behavior. Many understand that the judgment was coming because of the people's rebellion, but the invitation to repentance remained open.

Today we can ask ourselves what wicked thoughts we are feeding, such as resentment, envy, or deceit. Instead of justifying them, let us ask God to cleanse our hearts and obey him today.
exp.39:5:
It says that Jeremiah went to Mizpah, where Gedaliah, the son of Ahikam, was, and he stayed with him. The people who had been left behind in the land, the poor who had not been taken away to Babylon, were there too.

This is the account of the prophet after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonian captain Nebuzaradan had freed him from the chains and gave him the choice of going to Babylon or staying. Jeremiah chose to stay with his people, beside Gedaliah, whom Babylon had appointed as governor. No other reason is given here, but his decision shows his love for those who were suffering.

Today we can learn that serving God often means staying beside people in need, even when more comfortable options exist. We can ask ourselves: whom can I accompany with patience and faithfulness?
exp.39:2:
This verse says that the Lord carried out what he had warned. The phrase "lo ha traído" is what the Hebrew original looks like, and it means that he has brought the punishment on them, that is, he has caused it to come. The reason is plain: the people sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, so this disaster has happened to them.

The speaker is Nebuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, addressing Jeremiah after the fall of Jerusalem. It is striking that a foreign officer acknowledges that the LORD had announced this. Some think he knew Jeremiah's words; the Bible does not explain how he knew them. Then he sets Jeremiah free from his chains.

God speaks to us with patience, and his warnings are real. Today we can ask ourselves what correction we have ignored, and obey it with humility before the consequences arrive.
exp.5:28:
What it says: Jeremiah uses the image of a silver refiner. The bellows is the tool that blows hard to fan the fire. Here the bellows blow fiercely, and the fire is intense enough to blast away the lead. The lead was added to help clean the silver of impurities, but it was also consumed in the process. "The refining proceeds in vain" means the refiner worked for nothing, because the wicked were not purged and did not come out clean.

Context: God speaks to Jeremiah, whom he placed as a tester of his people. Judah was a rebellious people, full of deceit. God had tried to cleanse them with warnings and punishments, but they did not change. That is why the next verse says they will be called rejected silver.

For today: God corrects in order to cleanse, not to destroy. If He points out something in us, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask Him today to show us what needs to be removed from our lives, and respond with humility and repentance.
exp.44:0:
This verse introduces a message that the prophet Jeremiah gave to Baruch, son of Neriah. Baruch was the one who wrote down on a scroll what Jeremiah dictated to him. This happened in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah. The word "saying" at the end signals that the message follows right after.

Baruch was Jeremiah's scribe. That year, the fourth of Jehoiakim, was a time of great tension in Judah, and writing down Jeremiah's words was a risky task. The one speaking here is Jeremiah, but on God's behalf, and the message that follows answers the discouragement Baruch was feeling.

For today: God sees the people who serve quietly and grow weary. If you are exhausted or sad, bring Him honestly what you feel, because He listens to you and knows how to speak to you with care.
exp.8:23:
If someone wants to boast, the verse says, let it be that they truly know God. God says that He is the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth. And He adds: "for I delight in these things," meaning this is what pleases Him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah trusted in their wisdom, their strength and their money, while the nation was heading toward disaster. God shows them that none of that would save them, and that what mattered most was knowing Him and living as He is.

For today: instead of boasting about your achievements, seek to know God through His Word, and practice loving devotion and justice with the people around you.
exp.24:22:
This verse follows a list of peoples who must drink the cup of God's wrath. It names Dedan, Tema, and Buz, places and tribes of Arabia. The last phrase describes those who cut the corners of their hair, a custom belonging to those peoples, although scholars do not always agree on how to understand that expression.

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks while Babylon was growing in power. God announces that his judgment will reach Judah and also many neighboring nations, great and small, near and far. No one stands outside his sight.

For today: God is just with everyone, and no one lives hidden from him. Instead of judging others with pride, we can examine our own hearts, live with humility, and seek his mercy in Christ.
exp.1:11:
God calls the heavens to be stunned by this, to be shocked and utterly appalled. It is a poetic way of saying that what his people have done is so serious that even creation should be amazed. To be appalled means to be left empty or ruined by the shock.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God asked his people to look far and wide, across the western and eastern lands, to see whether any nation had ever changed its gods, even though those gods were false. Israel, however, abandoned the true God, their glory, for things that cannot help them. God's pain is that of someone who has been betrayed.

For today: examine where you place your trust and your heart. God is the source of life; if we exchange him for money, success, or approval, we are left empty. Return to him with sincerity.
exp.13:10:
God said to Jeremiah, "Do not pray for the well-being of this people." That is, do not ask God any longer to bless them or to spare them from punishment. "Do not pray" is plain enough, and "the well-being of this people" means asking good things for them.

The Lord spoke to his prophet. Judah was suffering a great drought, and Jeremiah had prayed for the people. But they loved to wander, that is, they liked to stray far from God, and they did not change. Their fasts and offerings were only outward, and the false prophets promised them peace without repentance. God, therefore, announces judgment.

For today: God takes sin seriously, and he is not pleased with rituals while the heart remains far away. Examine whether your life of faith goes beyond the outward, and turn to God with sincerity while there is still time. He always receives those who truly repent.
exp.35:29:
God announces judgment against King Jehoiakim. He will have no one to sit on David's throne, and his body will be thrown out and exposed to the heat by day and the frost by night, left without a proper burial. "Descendants" here refers to his offspring.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jehoiakim had cut up and burned the scroll that contained God's warnings, as if destroying the message could cancel what it said. His son Jehoiachin reigned only three months before being taken captive to Babylon. The biblical texts do not detail how Jehoiakim died, so we do not know exactly how this was fulfilled.

Today, ignoring, silencing, or rejecting what God says does not change the truth. When faced with an uncomfortable word of Scripture, we can choose the humility to listen and correct our course, rather than resisting it.
exp.41:1:
Here the people come to Jeremiah and ask him to pray for them. The request "May our petition come before you" means that they hope he will receive their plea with attention. They refer to the Lord as "your God," and they describe themselves as a remnant, that is, a small group that survived. They say they were many and now are few, as the prophet can see for himself. The phrase "this entire remnant" shows that they are speaking for the whole group together.

Here speak the military leaders, Johanan, Jezaniah, and all the people. Jerusalem had fallen before Babylon, and this group of survivors was frightened and without direction. They seek God's guidance through the prophet. Later, the story shows that they did not obey what God told them, so their request was not entirely sincere.

For today: asking God for advice is good, but we must be willing to obey his answer before we ask him. Today you can pray, saying: "Lord, tell me what to do, and I want to do it."
exp.27:15:
God, through Jeremiah, tells Hananiah that he is about to remove him from the earth. "I am about to remove you from the face of the earth" means he will be taken out of this world. Hananiah would die that same year, and the reason is that he preached rebellion against the LORD, that is, a message that went against what God had said.

Jeremiah speaks to Hananiah, a prophet who had promised that Babylon would soon fall and that everything would return to normal. But God had said that the people must submit to Nebuchadnezzar. Hananiah gave the people false hope in God's name. The following verse tells that he died in the seventh month of that year.

Speaking in God's name is a serious matter. Before repeating or teaching something as "the word of God," it is wise to compare it with the Bible, even when the message is more comfortable or pleasant to hear.
exp.28:20:
God speaks against two men, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah. They claimed to speak for God, but they were telling lies in his name. God announces that he will hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and that the king will kill them before your very eyes.

Jeremiah writes to the Jews who were taken captive to Babylon. Some false prophets were promising them a quick return, which went against what God had said through Jeremiah. The verses that follow say that their end would be remembered as a curse, and that God also knew about their wrongdoing. The Bible gives no further details about them.

Today we can learn to test what we hear in God's name. A pleasant message is not always true. Let us compare what is taught with all of Scripture, and pray for wisdom.
exp.32:0:
This verse says that God spoke again to Jeremiah. The phrase "the word of the LORD came" means that the message came from God. The phrase "a second time" shows that he had already spoken to Jeremiah before, in chapter 32. The phrase "while Jeremiah was still confined in the courtyard of the guard" means that Jeremiah was still being held in a courtyard inside the palace. The words "to him" and the colon at the end show that what follows is the message God is about to give.

God speaks, and Jeremiah is the one who receives it. The prophet was in prison for announcing that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon, something that troubled the authorities. Even so, God did not abandon him. He spoke to him in the middle of the crisis, and the message that follows brings hope and restoration for the people.

For today: even when you feel shut in by problems, God is not far away. You can pray with confidence, expect his voice, and listen to him through his Word, even when your situation seems to have no way out.
exp.26:19:
This verse says that when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried Jeconiah (son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah) into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon, along with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem, he did not take certain objects from the temple: the pillars, the bronze sea, the stands, and other vessels.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf, around the year 594 B.C. Some false prophets were claiming that the objects from the temple would soon be returned. Jeremiah answers them: if you truly have a word from God, then pray that what is still left will not be taken away. God warns that Babylon will take those things too.

For today: do not cling to comfortable promises that merely sound good. Test what you hear against the Word of God, and trust that He has a plan even in difficult times, and that He keeps what He promises.
exp.22:19:
This verse says that God's anger will not turn back until he has fully carried out the purposes of his heart. The word for his anger is rendered in the verse as "anger," and "the purposes of his heart" refers to what he has planned. The phrase "in the days to come" points to later times, and the verse says that people will understand this clearly. God promises that when everything happens, the people will grasp what he did and why.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were listening to prophets who said that everything would be fine, but God declares that he did not send them and did not speak to them. For this reason he announces judgment like a storm falling on the wicked. Some understand "the days to come" as the near time of the exile in Babylon, and others see a broader scope as well. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

Today we can learn to measure every religious message by the Word of God, and not only by what pleases us to hear. If God corrects, he does so so that we will return to him. Let us listen to his voice with humility and obey.
exp.29:14:
God asks his people why they cry out over their pain. A "wound" is a deep injury, and "no cure" means there is no way to heal it. God says this suffering comes because of their great iniquity and many sins. "Iniquity" means doing what is wrong and crooked.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel and Judah were in crisis, and their allies had abandoned them. God explains that the punishment was the result of their sin. But the message does not end here: later God promises to judge the oppressors and heal his people.

For today: when you suffer, do not stop at crying out. Ask God whether there is something you need to acknowledge, though not every suffering is punishment for a specific sin. If there is something, confess it sincerely, and remember that God corrects in order to heal, not to destroy.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that when the announced day of judgment comes, the king and his officials will lose their courage. "Lose their courage" means they will lose their nerve and their strength. "Tremble in fear" means the priests will be shaken with terror, and "astounded" describes the prophets being struck with amazement and horror, not admiration.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. The lion and the destroyer of nations are commonly understood to refer to an invader from the north, though the text does not give its name here. The people had trusted false promises of peace, and the leaders who were meant to guide them did not see the danger coming. That is why the blow catches them unprepared.

For today: do not rest in easy assurances. If you have any responsibility, whether at home, in the church, or at work, seek God's truth with humility, even when it is uncomfortable, and not only what soothes you.
exp.25:11:
Jeremiah speaks to the officials and to all the people. He tells them that the LORD sent him to announce a message against the temple and against Jerusalem. "Officials" are the leaders or those in authority. "Prophesy" means that he spoke on behalf of God.

The priests and the prophets had just accused Jeremiah and were demanding that he be put to death, because he announced that the temple and the city would be destroyed if the people did not change. Now Jeremiah defends himself before the judges, without denying anything. He makes clear that he does not speak on his own, but because the LORD commanded him.

For today: speak the truth with courage, even when it costs, and do so with humility. Jeremiah does not mock or attack; he calls for change and trusts in the LORD. We can ask him to give us courage and gentleness together.
exp.12:17:
God commands Jeremiah to tell the king and the queen mother to take a lowly seat, sitting down on the ground, because their glorious crowns have already fallen from their heads. Sitting low was a sign of mourning and humility. "Take a lowly seat" means setting aside pride.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah and to their royal family. He warns them that their arrogance will lead them into captivity. Many scholars think the "queen mother" held a position of real influence in the court, though there is no complete certainty about exactly who they were. The prophet himself weeps in secret for the people who will not listen.

For today: humility comes best when we choose it ourselves before life imposes it on us. Today you can acknowledge before God the areas where you have believed yourself self-sufficient, and ask him to teach you to depend on him.
exp.12:23:
God says he will scatter his people like chaff, the light husk of the grain that comes loose when it is threshed. The wind carries it away without any effort. The "desert wind" was hot, dry, and strong, so the image speaks of a quick scattering with no way back.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had grown so used to evil that, as the text says, the leopard does not change its spots. God reminds them that they forgot the Lord and trusted in falsehood. The scattering is the result of that path. Many understand that it foretells the exile in Babylon.

For today: the habits we repeat shape us. Today you can honestly recognize some habit that pulls you away from God and ask him for help to change it. His correction seeks to bring you back to him.
exp.50:4:
This verse says that Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, the LORD of Hosts. Even though their land is full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel, God did not leave them or break his relationship with them. To be abandoned is to be left alone by someone who should stay; here it means that God remains faithful to his people.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God, announcing judgment on Babylon, the power that had subdued Judah. The verses nearby describe the fall of Babylon and call people to flee from it. God shows that his people, though disciplined for their sin, were not forgotten, and that he will also judge those who punished them.

For today: when you fail, do not think that God has abandoned you. His correction seeks to restore you, not to destroy you. Return to him with sincerity and trust in his faithfulness.
exp.16:21:
God tells the people of Judah not to carry a load out of their houses on the Sabbath day and not to do any work. He asks them to keep that day holy, just as he commanded their forefathers. "Holy" means set apart for God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the kings and people of Jerusalem, who gathered at the city gates. At that time there was a great deal of trade and the moving of goods. God reminds them of an ancient command to rest. The verses that follow show that the problem was the hardness of their hearts: they did not want to listen or to be corrected.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and let go of your worries, trusting that God cares for you. Ask yourself whether work or money is occupying the place that belongs to him. Obeying gladly matters more than keeping a practice out of habit.
exp.2:4:
The verse says the people speak as if God would be angry forever and never let his anger end. But the reality is shown in what follows: they have spoken words of rebellion and have kept doing all the evil they could.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He confronts them about their unfaithfulness, compared to that of a wife who betrays her husband. Just before, he invites them to call on him as "my Father." Many understand that the statement about anger reflects the people's excuse: to sin and think that God will not be angry, or that his anger will change nothing. The text is not entirely simple, and some read it differently.

For today: do not use God's patience as an excuse to stay in what is wrong. If there is something you know you must leave behind, come to him today with sincerity and ask him for forgiveness.
exp.25:23:
He says that Ahikam, son of Shaphan, supported Jeremiah so that he was not handed over to the people to be killed. The word "supported" means that he stood with him and gave him shelter. "Nevertheless" introduces the contrast with what came before, and "the people" here refers to those who wanted him dead.

The narrator tells us that Jeremiah had announced judgment against Jerusalem and Judah, and this stirred up anger. Shortly before, it is told that King Jehoiakim had ordered the prophet Uriah put to death for saying the same thing. Jeremiah faced a similar danger. Ahikam was an influential man; his family appears in other passages helping Jeremiah. The Bible does not detail exactly how he protected him.

God can use particular people to care for those who speak the truth. We can be like Ahikam: to stand beside and defend, with prudence, someone who suffers for doing what is right. And if you feel alone in your faithfulness, remember that God often provides support, sometimes in unexpected ways.
exp.41:19:
This verse says that the people deceived themselves. The phrase about going off course means that they wandered away from what was right and did harm to themselves. They asked Jeremiah to pray to the LORD on their behalf and promised to do whatever the LORD said. The phrase tell it to us means "let us know," and the phrase we will do it means "we will obey."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors wanted to flee to Egypt out of fear. They asked God for guidance, but God told them to stay in the land. Jeremiah warns them that their hearts already seemed set on going to Egypt, even though they said the opposite.

For today: let us not ask God for direction if we have already decided not to obey. Before we pray, let us truly surrender our plans to him, and be willing to follow his answer, even when it is difficult.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that the religious customs of the neighboring peoples are worthless. Their practices and beliefs are what the verse calls "the customs of the peoples." The word "worthless" means having no real value or substance. The prophet describes how they make an idol: they cut down a tree from the forest, and a craftsman shapes it with a chisel, a tool for carving wood.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel, his people. The Israelites were surrounded by nations that worshiped idols and feared the signs of the sky, such as the stars. God warns them not to imitate those customs. The verses that follow show that the idol cannot speak, cannot walk, and cannot do either good or harm.

For today: let us ask ourselves which things made by human hands, such as money, fame, or success, have taken God's place in our hearts. Let us place our trust in the living God, not in what we ourselves make.
exp.37:4:
Zedekiah, king of Judah, answers the officials who are asking for Jeremiah's death. He says to them, "Here he is; he is in your hands." He admits that the king can do nothing to stop them.

Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon. Jeremiah has said that the city will fall, and the officials accuse him of discouraging the soldiers. Zedekiah, a weak and fearful king, does not defend the prophet and leaves him in their hands. They throw him into a cistern full of mud.

For today: when we know what is right, fear of people can lead us to keep silent or to give in. Let us ask God for courage to defend the truth and the innocent, even when it costs us.
exp.50:53:
This verse describes a cry heard from Babylon and a great destruction in the land of the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans were the people who ruled Babylon. The word used for this destruction means ruin, total destruction.

The prophet Jeremiah announces what God has said about Babylon. This empire had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed Israel. God promises that no fortress, not even one that seemed to reach to heaven, would save it. The verses that follow explain that God is the one who judges Babylon and gives it what it deserves.

For today: human powers may seem firm, but they are not eternal. If you suffer injustice today, you can rest in the fact that God sees and governs history. Trust in Him, do not repay evil with evil, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.50:1:
It says that God will send strangers to Babylon to winnow her, that is, to fan the grain the way someone tosses wheat into the air to separate the chaff. In this way they will empty her land. They will come against her from every side "in her day of disaster," that is, the day of her ruin and judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was a powerful empire that had mistreated other peoples, among them Judah. God announces that this power will not last forever. The image of winnowing, along with the destroying wind of the previous verse, shows a judgment that sweeps away and scatters.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, stands above God. If you see injustice today, trust that God governs history and in his time judges. Meanwhile, live with humility and justice, without relying on pride or on force.
exp.19:3:
God tells Pashur that He will make him a "terror," meaning a cause of dread, to himself and to all his friends. They will fall by the sword of their enemies, and Pashur will see it before his very eyes. In addition, all of Judah will be handed over to the king of Babylon, who will carry the people away into Babylon and put them to the sword. Here "sword" is the weapon the verse names, and "friends" refers to his companions and close associates.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Pashur, an official of the temple, had struck the prophet and put him in the stocks for announcing judgment. Jeremiah answers him with this message and gives him a new name, which is usually understood to mean "terror on every side." Pashur denied God's warning and trusted in a false sense of security.

Today: do not silence or ignore correction just because it is uncomfortable. Ask God for a humble heart, willing to hear His truth even when it hurts, because His warning seeks our good.
exp.5:2:
Shepherds and their flocks will come against Jerusalem. They will set up their tents all around the city, and each one will take charge of his own portion, letting his animals graze there as if the land were already divided among them. The image is of an army settling in for a long stay, with the city treated as a field to be shared out.

God speaks through Jeremiah and announces a judgment coming from the north. The "shepherds" here are usually understood as the leaders of enemy armies, and their flocks would be their troops. They surround the city as though it were a pasture to be divided among them. The "daughter of Zion" is Jerusalem, described as delicate and confident. Some scholars see here an image of siege; the text uses symbolic language.

For today: let us not confuse comfort with security. If God calls us to correct something, let us listen promptly, before the problems grow and surround us.
exp.37:27:
He says that Jeremiah stayed in the courtyard of the guard until Jerusalem was captured. The word translated "courtyard" here is the one the verse uses for the guard's courtyard. The phrase "Jerusalem was captured" describes the same event the verse names. In other words, he was not released earlier, and he was still there when the city fell.

The narrator tells what happened after Jeremiah spoke privately with King Zedekiah and then gave a careful answer to the officials who questioned him. Jeremiah had been warning for a long time that Jerusalem would fall if it did not surrender to Babylon. That is why he had been mistreated. This verse closes that episode and prepares the account of the city's fall, which most historians date to 586 B.C.

Jeremiah remained faithful even though his situation did not improve. God does not always rescue us from difficulties right away, but he is with us in them. Today we can keep doing what is right even when things seem stuck, trusting that God sustains those who obey him.
exp.3:22:
He says that the prophet looked at the earth and saw it in ruin and empty, that is, wrecked and without life. He also looked up at the heavens and there was no light. The word "destroyed" means leveled, left in ruins. The phrase recalls Genesis 1:2, where the earth was formless and empty.

Jeremiah speaks here, recounting a vision God gave him. Judah had become foolish: it knew how to do evil but not how to do good. For this reason the prophet announces a judgment that would be like a return to chaos. Scholars agree that it is an image of the disaster that was coming, probably through an invasion; not all agree on how literal the scene is.

For today: sin undoes what God has ordered, but He continues calling us to return. Today you can ask yourself in what area you have ignored God and take a concrete step of repentance and obedience.
exp.33:16:
God says that, since the people did not obey him by proclaiming freedom to their fellow Hebrews, he will now proclaim a different kind of "freedom" for them: they will be left free to the sword, the plague, and the famine. To proclaim means to announce officially. The phrase "I will make you a horror" means they will be shaken and scattered, becoming an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. The leaders had made a covenant to free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but then they enslaved them again. In doing this they broke a promise made before God, in his house and with a solemn ceremony.

For today: God expects us to keep what we promise, especially when it comes to treating others with justice. Check whether there is any promise or debt of justice you have failed to fulfill, and seek to make it right with humility.
exp.7:7:
God asks how the people can claim to be wise and to have the law of the Lord. He says that the lying pen of the scribes has produced a deception. The word "lying" points to writing that twists the truth, so the scribes' work did not serve the people but misled them. There are two ways to understand this: either the scribes wrote or taught the law falsely, or, although the law was written down, the people did not obey it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Earlier he compared the people to the birds, which know their seasons, while they did not recognize God's judgment. They boasted of having the law, but they followed greed and deceit, and rejected his word.

Having a Bible, knowing verses, or going to church is not enough. Ask yourself today: which command of God have I read and still not obeyed? Ask him for humility to repent and put it into practice.
exp.8:19:
He tells the women to listen closely to what God says. He asks them to teach their daughters and their neighbors to sing wailing, which are songs of mourning and sorrow, and lament, that is, weeping put into words. It is not advice for easing pain, but a call to recognize how serious what is coming is.

Jeremiah announces God's judgment on Judah, and the disaster is so great that death enters even the palaces. In that culture there were women who led the mourning laments. Here God charges them to teach the lament to the next generation, because the grief will be very widespread.

For today: do not flee from grief or hide it. Learn to weep honestly before God, teach your children to do the same, and accompany those who suffer with your presence and your words.
exp.45:12:
This verse serves as a heading. It says that the Lord gave Jeremiah a message about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who would come to strike the land of Egypt. The phrase "the word that the LORD spoke" points to a message from God, and "strike" means attack and defeat.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, the text describes Egypt as a nation wounded beyond cure, and afterward it announces the alarm in several Egyptian cities. Many understand this to refer to the Babylonian campaigns against Egypt, but scholars debate the exact moment it refers to. What is clear is that God directs history, including the history of the great powers.

For today: do not place your final security in power, money, or prestige, because all of these can fall. Trust in God, who remains in control and cares for those who seek him.
exp.29:9:
God tells his people, here called "Jacob" and "Israel," not to be afraid or dismayed. He himself will save them, even though they are far away, in the land where they were taken as prisoners. He will bring them back, they will live in quiet and ease, and no one will make them afraid.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were suffering the consequences of their disobedience and were living in exile, far from their home. God promises them freedom, restoration, and a future of peace. He also makes clear that he will discipline them, but he will not destroy them completely.

For today: when you feel trapped by guilt, fears, or difficult circumstances, remember that God corrects with love and does not abandon you. Pray with confidence and rest in his promise to help you.
exp.11:16:
It says that if a nation will not obey God, He will uproot that nation completely, the way a tree is pulled up by its roots, and destroy it. The words "I will uproot it and destroy it" repeat the same warning for emphasis, and "declares the LORD" marks these as God's own words.

God is speaking, answering Jeremiah's complaint about Israel's neighboring peoples who mistreated them. God says that although He will judge them, afterward He will have compassion on them. If they learn to follow His ways and to swear by Him instead of Baal, they will be included among His people. This verse is the final warning: the offer of mercy is real, but rejecting it has consequences.

Today, this verse reminds us that God's mercy is an invitation, not something we can ignore without consequences. If there is something in your life that God is asking you to correct, do not postpone it: respond to Him today with humility.
exp.26:1:
God tells Jeremiah to make a yoke out of leather straps and to put it on his neck, a sign that everyone could see. The yoke was the kind used to harness animals to their work.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah obeys as a prophet. The message was addressed to Judah and the neighboring kingdoms. With that yoke, God was showing them that they must submit to Babylon. The text names "Jehoiakim," but the rest of the chapter speaks of Zedekiah, and some scholars believe there is an old copying error in that name.

Today, God may ask us for obedience even when we do not fully understand his plan. This week, choose one concrete action that you know God is asking of you, and do it with humility, even if it costs you.
exp.29:13:
Israel's lovers, the allied nations she had relied on for security, have forgotten her and no longer care for her. God says he struck her as an enemy would, with harsh punishment, because of her great wickedness and her many sins. The phrase "because of your great iniquity" gives the reason for the punishment: the suffering was a consequence of what she had done.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Israel and Judah, who were living in crisis and exile. Their allies did not help them, and God explains that their suffering is connected to their rebellion. But the passage continues with a promise: God will judge their oppressors, and restoration will come.

For today: when the things or people we trust fail us, it is a good time to return to God honestly, acknowledge our faults, and ask him for healing. He corrects, but he also restores.
exp.47:16:
This verse calls on the neighboring peoples around Moab, and everyone who knew its reputation, to mourn its fall. The images of the "mighty scepter" and the "glorious staff" stand for power and splendor: the scepter was a symbol of authority, and the staff was a sturdy walking stick. The question "How is it shattered?" expresses amazement that something so strong has fallen.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment on Moab, a nation neighboring Israel. The texts in this section point to its pride and its trust in its own riches and fortresses (for example, Jeremiah 48:7 and 48:29). The tone mixes judgment and sorrow, since the prophet himself weeps for Moab later in the chapter.

For today: nothing we admire or trust in, such as success, power, or fame, is as firm as it seems. Let us trust in God, not in our own strength, and learn to feel compassion, not mockery, when others fall.
exp.41:9:
It says that if the people stay settled in Judah, God will build them up and plant them, and will not tear them down or uproot them. "Stay" means to remain in place, without running away. The phrase "I will relent of the disaster" does not speak of an error on God's part; many understand that it expresses his grief over the punishment he had to bring, and his desire to restore.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the people were afraid of the king of Babylon and planned to escape to Egypt. Johanan and the leaders asked Jeremiah to pray, and ten days later this answer came: trust God and stay.

For today: when fear pushes us to look for quick ways out, we can stop, pray, and obey what God has already shown us. His protection often lies in trusting him, not in fleeing on our own.
exp.19:14:
This verse says that the man who brought the news to Jeremiah's father, "A son is born to you," deserves a curse, because with that announcement he brought him great joy. The phrase "brought the news" simply means he delivered the message. It is a very strong cry, full of pain.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah. He had just been beaten and placed in the stocks for preaching God's message (Jeremiah 20:1-2). He is exhausted and discouraged. Even so, just before this, he had praised God, and then suddenly he falls into this complaint. The Bible shows his emotions without hiding them. This is not a teaching to curse others, but the sincere prayer of someone who is broken.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not pretend to be strong. Tell God honestly what you feel, as Jeremiah did. He listens, and you can also seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters.
exp.47:44:
This verse says that the Moabites who were fleeing from their enemies stopped in the shadow of Heshbon, a strong city, thinking they would be safe there. But fire and flame came out of that same city and consumed the land. The phrase "the foreheads of Moab" refers to the top of the head, and "the sons of tumult" describes proud and rebellious people. In other words, the judgment reached from the far edges of the land to the heads of the proud.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment on Moab for its pride and its trust in itself and in its god Chemosh. This verse recalls an ancient song in Numbers 21:28, where fire came out of Heshbon. Some think it points to a past defeat, and others to a new judgment. In the end, God promises restoration.

For today: do not place your security in places, money, or human strength. Seek refuge in God, who is the only one who never fails.
exp.41:3:
Jeremiah answers them plainly: "I have heard you," meaning he has understood their request. He says he will surely pray to the LORD their God as they asked, and that he will tell them everything the LORD answers. "I will not withhold a word from you" means he will hide nothing from them, whether it is pleasant or hard.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a small group of survivors asks Jeremiah to seek God's guidance. They fear Babylon and are unsure whether to stay or flee to Egypt. They promise to obey. Later in the chapter it becomes clear that their hearts were already leaning toward Egypt, although here they sound sincere.

For today: before asking God for direction, honestly decide that you will obey his answer, even if it is not what you hope for. And if someone advises you from the Bible, be thankful that they speak to you with frankness.
exp.28:26:
This verse is part of a question with a tone of rebuke. Someone asks Zephaniah: "So now, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who poses as a prophet among you?" The word "rebuked" means correcting with authority, and "Anathoth" is Jeremiah's hometown.

The one speaking here is Shemaiah, a false prophet who was in Babylon. He wrote a letter to Jerusalem to pressure the priests. He wanted them to silence Jeremiah, because Jeremiah had sent the exiles an uncomfortable message: the captivity would be long, and they should settle down there. Shemaiah calls "false" the man who was in fact telling the truth from God.

For today: not everyone who sounds confident speaks the truth, and not every uncomfortable word is a lie. Before rejecting a correction, compare it with what Scripture says, and ask God for the humility to listen.
exp.5:16:
God says that he appointed watchmen over the people, meaning lookouts who sounded a warning when danger was near, so that they would listen for the ram's horn. But the people answered plainly: "We will not listen."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, shortly before judgment came. God had already shown them the good way and promised them rest, but they said: "We will not walk in it." Watchmen are usually understood as the prophets who warned the people. Their refusal brought consequences, as the following context shows.

Today, God still speaks through his Word and through people who advise us with love. Think of some warning you have been ignoring, and ask God for a humble heart to listen to it and obey in time.
exp.5:14:
Here God asks whether his people are ashamed of the terrible things they have done. The answer is no: they have no shame at all, and they do not even know how to blush. "Abomination" refers to things God hates. "I punish them" here means that God will come to hold them accountable. That is why the verse says they will fall along with the others who fall.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He accuses everyone, from the least to the greatest, including prophets and priests, of greed and deceit. They kept saying "peace, peace" to calm the people, without addressing the real wound. God offers them the chance to return to the ancient paths, but they refuse.

For today: when our sin no longer troubles us, it is a warning sign. Let us ask God for a sensitive heart, and accept his correction with humility, before hardening drives us away from him.
exp.4:5:
God says he will allow the people to be attacked as if by wild animals: a lion from the forest, a wolf from the desert, and a leopard that lies in wait near their cities. Anyone who ventures out will be torn to pieces. The word "strike" means hit, and "ravage" means attack and destroy. The cause is that their rebellious acts and unfaithful deeds had multiplied.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah. Earlier, Jeremiah looked first among the poor and then among the leaders, hoping to find someone who knew the way of God, but all of them had broken free of His yoke, that is, they refused to submit to Him. The animals are a picture of the judgment that would come; many connect them with invaders, although the text does not name them here.

For today: rebellion almost never grows all at once, but little by little. Ask God to show you the areas where you have been giving in, and return to Him soon, before the habit hardens.
exp.9:5:
It says that there is none like You, O LORD. You are great, and Your name is mighty in power. The word translated "mighty" here speaks of real strength and power. "Like" means similar or equal.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, who were surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. Just before this verse, he describes how an idol is made: from wood, decorated with silver and gold, and fastened so that it will not fall. Such idols cannot speak or walk. Jeremiah contrasts that powerlessness with the living God, to encourage the people not to fear false religions or be drawn in by them.

For today: when something seems greater than God to you, such as money, success, other people's opinions, or fear, remember that nothing can be compared to Him. Set aside a few minutes today to tell Him in prayer, "LORD, there is none like You," and hand over that worry to Him.
exp.43:23:
Jeremiah speaks again to all the people, and he specifically includes the women, who had been among those most involved in worshiping the "queen of heaven." He calls them to hear the word of the LORD. His message is addressed to all of Judah who were living in Egypt.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God to the Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, even though God had told them not to go. They kept offering incense to another deity and refused to acknowledge their error. That is why Jeremiah calls them to hear a message of judgment.

For today: listening to God is not just hearing, but being willing to change course. Today you can ask yourself whether there is something God shows you in his Word that you have been putting off obeying.
exp.41:5:
This verse says that the people promise to obey whatever God answers, whether it is pleasant or unpleasant. The phrase "whether it is pleasant or unpleasant" means the same as the phrase "whether it is good or bad." The word "so" in the verse simply introduces the result that follows, and "it may go well with us" means things may turn out well for us. They recognize that obeying God is the way to have things go well for them.

The people speaking are those who remained in Judah, together with Johanan and the military leaders. After the fall of Jerusalem, they are afraid of Babylon and plan to flee to Egypt. They ask Jeremiah to pray for them and they promise to be loyal to God. But the verses that follow and the rest of the chapter show that, when the answer arrives, they do not like it and do not obey as they promised.

It is easy to say "I will do whatever God says" before knowing what he will say. Today you can examine your heart: am I willing to obey even when the answer is not convenient for me? Pray with sincerity and ask God for a heart that is willing beforehand.
exp.28:0:
This verse introduces a letter that the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon. It was addressed to the elders who had survived among the exiles, to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the others whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. To be carried into exile means being forced to leave your homeland and live in another country.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God. This happens after the first deportation, when King Jeconiah and many leaders and craftsmen were taken to Babylon, around 597 B.C. The people were wounded and confused, and the letter, carried by Elasah and Gemariah, would give them God's word for that situation.

God does not stay silent when we live through hard times or far from what we know. We can seek his word with confidence, because he has something to say to us also in the midst of trial.
exp.0:5:
Jeremiah responds to God with surprise and fear: "Ah, Lord GOD!" He says he does not know how to speak, for he is only a child. That word does not always mean a baby; it can refer to a young man without experience. Jeremiah feels too young and inexperienced for such a great task.

God has just told him that He knew him and set him apart before he was born, to be a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah does not argue with the calling, but he feels he is not ready. Then God answers that he should not use that excuse, because He will send him, will give him what to say, and will be with him. Scholars do not know his exact age.

When God asks something of you and you feel small or incapable, do not stay in your excuses. What matters is not your ability, but that God goes with you. Take the step, trusting in his help.
exp.10:17:
The passage says that the LORD informed Jeremiah, so he knew, and that God then showed him what his enemies were doing, that is, their deeds and hidden plans.

Jeremiah speaks as God's prophet in Judah. The verses that follow show that some of his own people were plotting to kill him because of his messages. He was like an innocent lamb who suspected nothing, until God opened his eyes. Some scholars think these were people from his hometown, but this verse only speaks of "they."

Today we can ask God for wisdom to see reality clearly, without naivety or bitterness. When someone hurts or deceives us, we can do what Jeremiah did: bring our case to God in prayer, and trust that he judges with justice.
exp.3:17:
It says that what is happening to Jerusalem is no accident: its own ways and its deeds have brought this upon it. The "punishment" is the consequence of its sin, and the bitterness is a deep pain that pierces to the heart. The "watchmen" are soldiers who surround the city.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the Babylonian invasion. Judah had rebelled against God, and He warns that an enemy army is coming from afar. Immediately, the prophet expresses his own grief, so the message joins justice and sorrow for the people.

For today: when we face painful consequences, it is wise to ask ourselves honestly whether there are decisions we should recognize and correct. God does not take pleasure in our pain; He invites us to return to Him with humility and to change direction.
exp.50:40:
It says that Babylon, which the verse also calls "Sheshach," has been captured and taken. It was a city admired by the whole world, but now it has become a horror among the nations. "Has been captured" means that it was taken by force. "Sheshach" appears to be a coded name for Babylon, a kind of secret writing used in Hebrew; many scholars understand it this way. "Horror" refers to the dismay and shock at its ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon, the powerful empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed its people. The text shows that God is just and that no human kingdom, however great, is beyond his control. The nearby verses describe its fall with strong images, such as a feast that ends in a deathlike sleep and a sea that covers it.

For today: do not place your security in prestige, power, or success, because these pass away. Trust in God, who sustains what truly endures, and live with humility.
exp.48:15:
This verse says that Edom was deceived by its own pride. It lived in the clefts of the rocks and on high mountain summits, and it felt secure, like an eagle with its nest set high above the ground. But God says that even from there he will bring it down. The words "terror" and "pride" describe a fearful reputation and an inflated sense of self-importance. "Rocks" are large stones.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Edom, a nation neighboring Israel. Its land was mountainous and hard to attack, and that gave it a false confidence. God announces that he will make it small and that it will be left desolate, as happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. Scholars do not agree on all the historical details of when this was fulfilled.

For today: pride makes us believe we are safe because of what we have or what we achieve. Today you can be humble and trust in God, not in your money, your position, or your strength.
exp.33:6:
This verse tells us that the army of Babylon was attacking Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah, namely Lachish and Azekah. "Fighting against" means that they were waging war and attacking. The verse also explains that these two were the only fortified cities still left in Judah, which means the other strong cities had already fallen.

Jeremiah is speaking to King Zedekiah in Jerusalem while the Babylonian siege was advancing. God had warned him that the city would be handed over, but he also promised that the king would die in peace and with honor. The verse shows how serious and how near the situation was. Shortly afterward, the people made an agreement to free their Hebrew servants, but then they did not keep it.

For today: when the pressure is great, it is easy to promise change and forget it once the danger has passed. God expects sincere and steady obedience, not only in a crisis. Today you can keep a pending promise you made to God or to someone else.
exp.43:17:
This verse says that the people, from the time they stopped burning incense and pouring out drink offerings to the Queen of Heaven, felt that they lacked everything and were perishing by the sword and by famine. "By the sword" means by the sword.

The speakers are Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt, and they respond to Jeremiah with rejection. They believed that their past prosperity came from that worship. Scholars often think the Queen of Heaven was a goddess, but they are not sure which one. Jeremiah will explain to them that the ruin came because of their idolatry, not because they had abandoned it.

For today: sometimes we blame God or doing what is right for our difficulties, when the problem lies elsewhere. Before interpreting our trials, let us ask God for humility to see the truth and to return to Him.
exp.48:5:
According to the verse, after the punishment God will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites. This means he will bring back what they lost and return them to their land. The "Ammonites" are the descendants of Ammon, a people who lived next to Israel, east of the Jordan River.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Before this verse, God announces judgment on Ammon for its pride: they trusted in their valleys and their riches and thought no one would attack them.
