Even so, the final word is not only punishment but a promise of restoration. Scholars debate when or how this was fulfilled, and the Bible does not give details.

For today: God corrects pride and false security, but his final desire is to restore. If today you trust your resources more than God, return to him with humility. And if you are going through a correction, do not lose hope: his mercy has the last word.
exp.28:5:
They say that the exiles in Babylon should build families: marry, have children, and help their children find spouses too. "Take wives and have sons and daughters" and "take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage" refer to arranging marriages for their children, as was customary then, and "multiply there; do not decrease" means that they should not shrink in number.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a letter to the Jews taken captive to Babylon. Some prophets were saying that the exile would be short. God tells them to live normally, because the stay would be long (the text speaks of seventy years ahead).

For today: even if you are in a difficult season or one you did not choose, God invites you to live with hope, to build relationships, and to sow life where you are, without becoming paralyzed while waiting for everything to change.
exp.11:12:
The passage says that the people worked hard and sowed wheat, but harvested thorns. They wore themselves out and gained nothing from it. The phrase "harvested thorns" means they reaped only what they had planted, and what they planted was worthless. In the end, they will bear shame for what they produced, because of the Lord's fierce anger.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, describing the Lord's judgment on Judah for turning away from Him. The land was left desolate, and no one took it seriously. Even so, the verses that follow show that God does not abandon them completely: He promises to have mercy and to bring them back to their land.

For today: whatever we do without God, however much effort it takes, can end in emptiness. Before you keep running ahead, ask yourself whether your plans are placed before Him. And if you have wandered away, remember that His mercy remains open for the one who returns.
exp.1:15:
The verse says that the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes, cities of Egypt, have shaved the crown of your head. The crown of the head is the top of the skull, so the image is of Israel being humiliated and brought low by the very nations it turned to.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people. He shows them that their trouble was no accident: they had turned away from God and looked for protection to Egypt and Assyria. The nations they trusted ended up harming them. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical event the verse refers to, but the message is clear.

For today: when we look for security in money, people, or human power instead of in God, sooner or later those things fail us and hurt us. Today you can hand over to God whatever you trust most and return to him with sincerity.
exp.22:26:
God says that the prophets he is addressing want his people to forget his name through the dreams they tell one another. The comparison is to what Israel's ancestors did: they too forgot his name by worshipping Baal, a false god of Canaan.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. There were prophets who claimed their dreams were messages from God, but the dreams were their own ideas and they were false. By sharing them, these prophets led the people away from the true word of God. God makes it clear that his word is like fire and like a hammer, not like a mere dream.

Today we should examine what we hear claimed in God's name. An experience, a strong impression, or a personal opinion does not carry the same weight as Scripture. The safest course is to test everything against the Bible and ask God for the humility to obey it.
exp.22:25:
God asks a question filled with sorrow and firmness: "How long will this continue?" He is speaking about prophets who spread falsehood. He says they prophesy the delusion of their own minds, that is, their own ideas and inventions, and not what God has told them.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The religious leaders of Judah were saying "I dreamed, I dreamed" and using the name of God to give comfortable and false messages. In this way they led the people of God astray, as they had done before with Baal. God reminds them that nothing is hidden from him.

Today we can examine what we hear, and also what we say, in the light of the Bible. An impression, an experience, or a pleasant idea does not carry the same weight as the Word of God. Let us ask God for a humble heart to hear the truth, even when it is not comfortable.
exp.2:13:
This verse is a call from God to his unfaithful people. "Return" means coming back to God with your whole heart. "Faithless children" are those who have wandered away from him. God says, "I am your master," meaning he remains their rightful Lord and keeper, and he still holds them in covenant love. He promises to take one from a city and two from a family, that is, a remnant, and bring them to Zion, the place where he dwells.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had worshiped idols "under every green tree", and yet God calls them to return. He reminds them that he is merciful and will not keep his anger forever. Some understand this as referring to the return from exile, while others also see a broader hope for the future.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you are perfect to come back. He calls you with tenderness. Acknowledge your failing sincerely and take a step of return today in prayer.
exp.30:1:
This verse says that the LORD speaks of a people who survived the sword and found his favor in the wilderness. "Found favor" means they received kindness they did not deserve. The "sword" refers to war and violence. And when Israel went to find rest, it describes Israel seeking peace and security.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter brings hope to a people struck by judgment and exile. Some understand that the "wilderness" recalls the departure from Egypt; others, that it refers to the exile. Perhaps it includes both ideas. In any case, God promises to be their God again and to restore them with everlasting love.

Even in your dry seasons or after deep wounds, God can meet you with his favor. If today you feel worn out, do not strain to appear strong: draw near to him and find your rest.
exp.10:4:
God says he will keep the promise he swore to Israel's ancestors: to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, meaning rich and fruitful. The words "as it is to this day" show that the promise was already seen as being kept in the present. Jeremiah answers "Amen, LORD," meaning "Yes, let it be" or "I agree."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, and Jeremiah replies. God recalls the covenant made when he brought Israel out of Egypt, a place of hard suffering under slavery. The people enjoyed the land, but they did not obey. So God reminds them that his faithfulness was joined to the call to obey.

For today: God has been faithful to you in many things. Respond as Jeremiah did, with a sincere "Amen," that is, with gratitude and with concrete obedience. Today, choose one thing God asks of you and do it.
exp.20:7:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the people of Jerusalem. He places two ways before them: one that leads to life and one that leads to death. "I set before you" means "I place in front of you," so that they may choose.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the army of Babylon, and King Zedekiah had asked for a word from God. The answer is hard: the city would fall. Even so, God leaves a door open. According to the verses that follow, whoever went out and surrendered to the Chaldeans would save his life. It was a call to accept the judgment with humility.

For today: God does not force us down only one road; He invites us to choose with responsibility. When He corrects us, the wisest thing is to listen in time, even if it costs our pride, because His correction seeks that we may live.
exp.48:3:
God asks the Ammonites, "Why do you boast in your valleys?" Their valleys were rich and fruitful land. The verse here notes that this valley had gone to waste, so the boast was empty. "Faithless daughter" describes the nation of Ammon as unfaithful, a way of speaking about the people as a whole. She trusted in her riches and asked, "Who can come against me?"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, with a message of judgment against the Ammonites, neighbors of Israel. Their capital was Rabbah. The verses before this one announce war and ruin upon her. Scholars debate which valleys are meant, but the idea is clear: Ammon felt secure because of what she had. Even so, the text ends with a promise of restoration.

Today we can ask ourselves what our security rests on. Money and achievements can fail. Let us trust in God first.
exp.29:17:
God promises that he will restore the fortunes of the people of Israel, here called "Jacob." Their "dwellings" are their homes, and the exile they had suffered is what he is turning around. God will have compassion on them. The city, Jerusalem, will be rebuilt on its own ruins, and the palace will stand in its rightful place.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in exile, or were about to be, because of their disobedience. Others mocked Zion, saying that no one sought her. God answers with a promise of healing and restoration. Scholars see a partial fulfillment in the return from Babylon, and many Christians also see a broader hope in Christ.

Even if something in your life seems ruined or abandoned, God can rebuild it. Today you can bring that area to him with confidence and wait patiently for his mercy.
exp.17:18:
Jeremiah asks the Lord to pay close attention to him and to hear what his accusers are saying. The request "Attend to me" is simply the plea itself, and those who oppose him are people who are arguing against him and setting themselves against him.

The prophet is speaking. The people of his town, together with religious leaders, were planning to harm him and silence him, because his message of judgment troubled them. He does not defend himself alone but brings his case before God. The verses that follow show his pain and a very harsh prayer against them. This can be understood as a sincere complaint, which God allows him to express before him.

For today: when someone criticizes you or treats you unfairly for doing what is right, you do not have to repay blow for blow. Bring your case to God honestly, tell him how you feel, and ask him to see and to act.
exp.35:25:
This verse tells that King Jehoiakim, angry at the message of the scroll, ordered three men to seize Baruch, the scribe, and the prophet Jeremiah. The king's command was to seize them, and he wanted them arrested. But the LORD had hidden them, and they could not be found.

It is part of the account where Jeremiah dictated to Baruch the words of God, and Baruch read them publicly. The king, instead of repenting, burned the scroll and tried to silence the messengers. The text does not say where or how God hid them, only that it was God who protected them.

For today: when obeying God brings opposition, remember that He cares for His own and that His word cannot be erased. Remain faithful, trusting in His protection, even when you do not always know how He will provide it.
exp.49:4:
They will ask the way to Zion and turn their faces toward it. They will urge one another, "Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on what the Lord says. The message announces the fall of Babylon, the people from the north, who would be destroyed. Then Israel and Judah, once divided, would return together, weeping and seeking God. Many understand this as the return from exile, and others see in it a broader hope that is fulfilled in Christ. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: if you have drifted away, you can return to God with humility and without delay. Ask for the way, seek the company of other believers, and renew your commitment to Him.
exp.31:12:
This verse says that Jeremiah gave an instruction to Baruch, his secretary, and did so in the sight of everyone present. The phrase "I instructed" means "I gave a direction" or "I commanded." "In their sight" means there were witnesses.

Jeremiah is speaking while he is imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard while Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon. God had asked him to buy a field from his cousin Hanamel, even though the land seemed lost. Jeremiah did everything with documents and witnesses, and now he passes on what God wants Baruch to do: keep the deeds as a sign that there will be restoration.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, we can act with faith and order, doing things with clarity and honesty, trusting that God's promises will be fulfilled in his time.
exp.51:14:
Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of Babylon, led away into exile the common people who were left in Jerusalem. The phrase "the poor of the people" refers to ordinary folk, people without high office or position. He also took those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, along with the craftsmen.

This chapter is a historical account of the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 BC. The one who narrates it describes the judgment that Jeremiah had announced for years, because the people had turned away from God. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. It is very similar to 2 Kings 25.

For today: God takes his warnings seriously, but he never stops seeing ordinary people. If you are going through a loss or a hard change today, do not feel forgotten. Pray sincerely and trust him again.
exp.39:3:
Jeremiah, who had been bound in chains, is now set free, the verse says. Nebuzaradan gives him two choices: come with him to Babylon, where he would take care of him, or stay in his own land. If it pleases him to go to Babylon, he may go, and if it seems wrong to him, he may stay. The whole land lies open before him, and he may go wherever he judges right.

The speaker is Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, after the fall of Jerusalem. He had found Jeremiah bound among the captives. He acknowledges that the Lord had announced this punishment because of the people's sin. Jeremiah had warned of this for years, and in the end he decides to stay with those who remained in the land.

For today: God can use even unexpected situations to bring freedom and direction. When you face a decision, pray, weigh what is faithful to God and not only what is comfortable, and choose with wisdom.
exp.49:20:
God commands an army to attack Merathaim and the people of Pekod, two names that here point to Babylon. "Kill them and devote them to destruction" means to pursue them until the task is completely finished. "Do all that I have commanded you" asks for full and faithful obedience to God's orders. Many scholars note that Merathaim and Pekod sound like Babylonian place names, and their meanings may also be read as wordplays: "double rebellion" and "punishment."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Judah, and now God announces its fall. This is connected to his promise to restore Israel and forgive its sin.

For today: God is just and does not forget injustice, but he also forgives his own people. We can rest in the knowledge that he governs history, and leave in his hands the wrong that hurts us, without seeking personal revenge.
exp.28:12:
It says that God promises to let himself be found by those who seek him sincerely. "You will seek Me and find Me" means that when you look for him, you will find him. "When you search for Me with all your heart" means seeking him with your whole will and desire, not halfheartedly or out of habit.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He is addressing the Israelites who were carried off captive to Babylon. He had already told them the exile would be long, but he promises them that he has not forgotten them and that he has plans for peace for them. Then he announces that he will bring them back to their land.

For today: if you are going through a difficult time, do not turn away from God. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible sincerely, without rushing, trusting that he answers those who seek him truly.
exp.28:30:
God sends a message to all the exiles in Babylon. The word "captivity" here refers to the people who had been taken away from their homeland. God speaks about Shemaiah the Nehelamite and says that this man prophesied to them even though God had not sent him. In this way he has made them trust in a lie.

Jeremiah had written to the exiles, telling them to settle down in Babylon and remain there for many years. Shemaiah, on the other hand, sent letters from Babylon to Jerusalem criticizing that message. When Zephaniah read the letter to Jeremiah, God answered and declared Shemaiah to be a false prophet.

Today we can learn not to believe something just because it sounds encouraging or comes from someone with authority. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and pray with humility. God's truth can be difficult, but it sustains better than a comfortable lie.
exp.6:21:
When God brought Israel out of Egypt, his first request was not that they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices. A "burnt offering" was an offering burned whole on the altar, and the animals offered are called the "victims." God does not deny that sacrifices exist; he marks what mattered most from the beginning.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the temple at Jerusalem. The people carried out their ceremonies, but they lived in disobedience. So God tells them, with irony, to add more offerings and eat the meat: without an obedient heart, these are of no use. Interpreters explain this statement in various ways, but almost all agree that God puts obedience first.

For today: it is not enough to attend church, give, or sing. Ask God to show you where you need to obey him from the heart, and start there.
exp.22:30:
God says that he is against certain prophets. The phrase "who wag their own tongues" describes people who speak in a smooth, flattering way, the way someone talks when they want to win you over. Then they announce, "The LORD declares it," meaning they present their own words as if God had given them that message.

The speaker is the LORD, speaking through Jeremiah. Judah was surrounded by prophets who said what the people wanted to hear, even though God had not sent them. Shortly before, God compares his word to fire and to a hammer that breaks the rock: it is powerful, not merely pleasant.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are looking for messages that comfort us or for the truth of God. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.50:52:
Even if Babylon were to climb up to the heavens and make her lofty stronghold secure, God says he would send destroyers against her. The verb for "climb" simply means to rise or ascend, and the idea of fortifying her stronghold means making it stronger and harder to reach. Those who tear down and lay waste are the destroyers. Nothing, however high it may seem, is beyond God's reach.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had invaded Judah and defiled the temple in Jerusalem, and the people felt shame and grief. God answers by promising that he will judge Babylon and its idols. The image of rising to the heavens recalls the pride of those who think they are untouchable. The verses that follow announce the fall of the city.

For today: when pride, injustice, or power seem unbeatable, do not lose hope. God is just and has the final word. Trust in him, keep doing good, and do not rely on your own strength.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that God gave a message to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent two men, Pashhur son of Malchijah, and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, to ask something of him.

The verse is clear in its own wording, so the older-style phrases from other editions do not need explaining here.

Context: Jeremiah is the prophet who speaks, and Zedekiah is the king of Judah. Babylon, led by Nebuchadnezzar, was attacking Jerusalem. The king wanted Jeremiah to consult God, hoping for a miracle. The verses that follow show that God's answer was not the one they were expecting.

For today: It is easy to seek God only when a crisis arrives. We can approach Him with steadiness and a willingness to obey, not only asking Him to get us out of trouble.
exp.6:27:
This verse says that the people did not obey the voice of the Lord their God and would not accept correction. To "receive correction" means to let oneself be taught and to change. The statement that truth has perished means that truth and faithfulness had disappeared. The statement that truth has disappeared from their lips means that they no longer even spoke of it.

God speaks to Jeremiah at a time when the people trusted in the temple and its rituals, yet lived in injustice and idolatry. God tells him in advance that his message will be rejected. Even so, Jeremiah must keep speaking faithfully. Then comes a call to mourn over the judgment that is approaching.

For today: when a word from God makes us uncomfortable, let us not set it aside right away. Let us ask for humility to listen, to recognize what we need to change, and to obey. A sincere faith shows itself in how we respond to correction.
exp.24:35:
Listen to the cry of the shepherds and the wailing of the leaders of the flock, because the LORD is destroying their pasture. This verse says that a cry and a wail are heard from the shepherds and the leaders of the flock. The reason is that the LORD is ruining their grazing lands. "Cry" means a loud outcry, "wailing" is a heartbreaking lament, "leaders" are the chief leaders, and "pasture" is the land where the sheep feed.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in God's name within an announcement of judgment on Judah and the nations. The "shepherds" are the rulers and leaders of the people, who, according to the context, did not care well for the flock. Many understand that the judgment came through Babylon, although this verse does not name it.

For today: whoever has some responsibility over others, in the church, the family, or the workplace, should care for it with humility and truth, remembering that one day they will give an account to God.
exp.10:9:
This verse says that the people repeated the same sins as their ancestors. It refers to the people who have returned to their old ways, which means they have gone back to the sins of their forefathers. They refused to obey God's words and followed other gods to serve them. So both Israel (the northern kingdom) and Judah (the southern kingdom) broke the covenant that God had made with their forefathers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The covenant was the agreement made in the time of Moses: God would be their God, and they would obey him. God accuses them of a conspiracy, a shared agreement to rebel. For that reason he announces the consequences of having broken what was promised.

Today we can learn that it is not enough to know what God has said; we must obey him. Ask yourself whether there is something God has already shown you that you keep putting off. Ask him for help today to take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.32:6:
God promises that he will bring back those who were taken away as prisoners, both from the kingdom of Judah and from the kingdom of Israel. He says "I will restore Judah and Israel from captivity," that is, he will bring them back from exile. And he says "I will rebuild them as in former times," so he will rebuild them as they were before, in their earlier strength.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks for God while he himself is imprisoned, as Jerusalem falls to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). The people were living with the consequences of their sin, and God had hidden his face from them. Even so, in the middle of the ruin, he promises healing, forgiveness, and peace. Scholars see this fulfilled in the return from exile, and many Christians also see its fullness in Christ.

For today: if you are going through a season of ruin or difficult consequences, God has not left you without hope. Draw near to him with sincerity; he restores, and he can rebuild what seemed lost.
exp.1:9:
God tells his people to cross over to the coasts of Cyprus and look, and to send messengers as far as Kedar, a desert people to the east, and to think carefully. They are to check whether anything like this has ever happened before. The coasts of Cyprus stand for the lands across the sea to the west.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Its leaders, priests, shepherds, and prophets had forgotten God and were following Baal. God points to the far west and the far east to show that no nation changes its gods the way Judah did with the living God.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have put in place of God, even if they seem good or ordinary. It is good to spend time in prayer and in the Bible in order to return to Him, who is the source that never fails.
exp.11:8:
God compares his people to a bird of prey with unusual markings, and other birds of prey circle around her to attack. Then he tells the beasts of the field to gather and come to devour her. "Inheritance" means his cherished possession, and "circling" means coming at her from every side.

God speaks through Jeremiah about Judah. The people had turned against him, and for this reason he allows enemy nations to attack them. The image of the bird is difficult: some understand it as a spotted bird of prey, others as a bird attacked for being different. Even so, the tone shows God's grief, not coldness.

Today, do not take your relationship with God lightly. If you have drifted away, return soon, because he suffers over what he loves. And take care of what he has entrusted to you: your faith, your family, your service.
exp.34:3:
Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the house of the LORD and led them to a room used by the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, who is called "a man of God," meaning a man known as a servant of God, perhaps a prophet. That room was near the room of the officials and above the room of Maaseiah, the son of Shallum, the doorkeeper.

Jeremiah acts here on God's command. The place is public and clearly identified, so there would be witnesses. God wanted to use the faithfulness of the Rechabites, who obeyed their ancestor Jonadab, to show by contrast that Judah was not obeying God.

Today we can ask ourselves: if these people keep the word of a human father, how do I obey the Word of God? Choose a clear command of God today and keep it faithfully.
exp.41:13:
This verse shows what some of the people might say: "We will not stay here; it is better for us to go to Egypt." There, they believe, there will be no war, no sound of the ram's horn (the alarm signal in battles), and no hunger for bread. "Live there" means "settle down and remain in Egypt."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, bearing the word of the LORD. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors of Judah ask him to pray for them. God promises to care for them if they remain in their land, but He warns them what would happen if they disobey and go to Egypt seeking safety.

Today, we sometimes look for security by our own way and not by God's way. Before deciding out of fear, ask yourself: "Am I seeking comfort or obeying God?" His direction is always safer than our plans.
exp.18:11:
This is what the Lord says he will do to this place and to the people who live in it: he will make this city like Topheth. The word "residents" refers to those who live there. Topheth was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, outside the city.

Jeremiah speaks for the Lord, and just before this he broke a clay jar in front of the elders. That act pictured a judgment that could not be undone. The people had turned away from God, worshiped other gods and, according to the passage, shed innocent blood. Topheth was a place tied to those practices, which is why God uses it as a picture of what was coming.

For today: let us not take lightly turning to other loyalties. If anything takes in our hearts the place that belongs to God, it is wise to stop, repent and return to Him while there is time, trusting in His mercy.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that the exiles from Judah in Babylon will use the fate of two men as a curse. They will say: "May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire!" Being exiles means being taken away from home and forced to live in Babylon. "Roasted in the fire" describes an execution by fire ordered by the king of Babylon.

God speaks through Jeremiah to the exiles. Ahab and Zedekiah were false prophets who claimed to speak in God's name, but gave messages of peace that He had not sent them. The text says they also committed wickedness and adultery. This Ahab is not the king of Israel. The Bible does not tell more about how his death happened.

Today, this passage invites us not to believe every message just because it sounds spiritual or encouraging. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and look for teachers who live with integrity.
exp.31:17:
This verse says that God shows loving devotion to thousands of people, and also that the consequences of the wrongdoing of the parents are laid on their children after them. The word "thousands" simply refers to the number of people meant, and the picture of the iniquity being laid "into the laps" of the children is a way of saying that those consequences fall on them. Then it calls God great and mighty, and names him the LORD of Hosts, the Lord of all the armies and powers of heaven and earth.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, in prayer. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon and he is a prisoner, but God had told him to buy a field as a sign that one day the people would return to their land. Jeremiah prays by remembering who God is.

For today: when everything seems lost, remember that God is loving and at the same time just. Pray as Jeremiah did, trusting in God's character, and think too about the example you leave to those who come after you.
exp.22:13:
God says that he has seen a horrible thing among the prophets of Jerusalem. They commit adultery and live by lies, and they support evildoers so that no one turns away from their wickedness. Where the source said that they "strengthened the hands" of the wicked, the meaning is that they gave encouragement and support to them. That is why God compares them to Sodom, and the people of Jerusalem to Gomorrah, cities known for their sin.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Earlier he had condemned the prophets of Samaria, who followed Baal. Now he says that those of Jerusalem are even more serious, because they were meant to guide the people and instead deceived them with false messages. Then comes the judgment against them and the warning not to listen to them.

For today: it is not enough for someone to speak about God with confidence. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and also look at how that person lives. If you have influence over others, take care that your life and your words do not encourage wrongdoing.
exp.29:1:
God speaks to Jeremiah and tells him to write down everything He has said to him. "Write in a book" means that he should record those words so they will not be lost. "The LORD" is the name of the God of Israel.

God Himself is speaking, and the one who listens is the prophet Jeremiah. According to the verses that follow, what he must write is a promise: God will bring back Israel and Judah from captivity and will make them return to their land. Many understand that it is written so that the people, in the middle of exile, would have something firm to trust in. The book serves as a witness that God will fulfill what He has promised.

God wants His words to be kept safe. Today we can do something similar: write down what God teaches us in the Bible and go back to it in difficult moments, to remember that His promises still stand.
exp.31:26:
He says that the Lord is the God of "all flesh," that is, of all humanity, not only of Israel. Then he asks: "Is anything too difficult for Me?"

God speaks to Jeremiah while Jerusalem is under siege by the Babylonians. Jeremiah, at God's command, had bought a field, and now he doubts and prays in confusion: why buy land if the city is going to fall? God answers by reminding him of his power. He announces judgment for idolatry, but later promises restoration.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, you can pray honestly, as Jeremiah did, and trust that nothing escapes him and nothing is impossible for him.
exp.38:11:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, gave orders for Jeremiah to be looked after. "Take him" means "take him away," "look after him" means "take good care of him," and "do not let any harm come to him" means that no one should harm him at all. "Do for him whatever he says" means that they were to give him whatever he asked for.

The king speaks, and gives the order to Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, when Jerusalem fell. Jeremiah had been imprisoned by his own people for announcing this judgment on behalf of God. Now the enemy king orders that he be protected. The Bible does not explain why he did this; it may be that he knew what Jeremiah had said, but that is not stated clearly. What we do see is that God took care of his servant.

For today: God knows how to care for those who are faithful to him, even in difficult times and in unexpected ways. Remain faithful, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.48:17:
It says that Edom will be destroyed in the same way as Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, which were "overthrown," meaning completely torn down. No one will live there, and no man will dwell in it, meaning no one at all.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom was a neighboring nation of Israel, and it lived with confidence in its rocky mountains, as if it could never be reached. God denounces its pride and says that no height will free it from His judgment. Sodom is mentioned as an example of total ruin. Scholars understand in different ways how literal the fulfillment was, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not place your security in your achievements, your position, or your resources. Ask God for a humble heart, because only He is truly firm and no one can withstand Him.
exp.21:19:
This verse is a painful command. Jerusalem is told to climb the mountains of Lebanon and the land of Bashan, and to cry out loudly from there. "Lovers" refers to the political allies the people trusted, and "crushed" means they were defeated and broken.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. He has just announced a shameful end for King Jehoiakim. God reminds Jerusalem that He spoke to her when everything was going well, but she would not listen. Scholars usually understand that those high places serve to make the cry heard far away, and that the lovers were the neighboring nations.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, people, or reputation. All of these can fail. Let us listen to God today, in the good times, and not wait until the crisis arrives.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that God promises to let his people live in the land he gave to their ancestors, "forever." But this promise comes after an "if": if they change the way they live. The phrase "forever" can also be understood as "for a long time" or "from generation to generation."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people thought the temple would protect them, even though they oppressed the weak, killed the innocent, and worshiped idols. God asks them for a real change, not just trust in empty religious words.

For today: true faith shows in how we treat others. Think of someone near you who is in need, and help them with justice and kindness this week.
exp.16:4:
This verse says that the LORD declares a curse on the person who puts their trust in other people and depends on mere human strength, that is, on what is weak and temporary. "Mankind" means people in general, and "strength" refers to the support a person leans on. The core problem is that such a person turns their heart away from the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had fallen into idolatry, with altars on high places, and they sought security in alliances with other nations instead of turning to God. The next verse compares such a person to a dry shrub in the desert, and then contrasts them with the one who trusts in the LORD.

For today: value the help of other people, but do not make them your final foundation. Before deciding something important, pray and ask whether your heart is resting in God or only in your own resources and connections.
exp.35:12:
Micaiah, after hearing Baruch read, went and reported everything he had heard to the princes. The words "to them" point to the princes. The phrase "in the hearing of the people" means Baruch read the scroll aloud, so that the people gathered could listen.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Baruch was the assistant of the prophet Jeremiah, and he had read in the temple the words that God had given to Jeremiah. Micaiah, the son of a man known among the officials, told it to the princes gathered in the scribe's chamber. That is why they sent for Baruch so they could hear it directly from him.

For today: when we hear something valuable from the Word of God, we should not keep it to ourselves. Sharing it with humility and faithfulness, without adding or taking anything away, can open the way for another person to hear God.
exp.8:21:
This verse describes a very harsh scene: the bodies of the dead will lie scattered across the open field like dung, or like newly cut grain left behind the reaper, and no one will gather them. "Open field" refers to the bare ground outside the town. The picture is of a harvest with no one left to bring it in.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces the judgment that would come upon Judah for its rebellion, with death and mourning everywhere. For this reason he calls the women to raise laments. Many scholars connect this with the Babylonian invasion, although the text gives no further details.

For today: the things we tend to trust in, such as talent, strength or money, do not save us from everything. What is most valuable is to know God and to live as he pleases, with mercy, justice and righteousness.
exp.0:7:
God tells Jeremiah not to be afraid of the people he will be sent to. The reason is simple: God himself is with him and will deliver him, that is, rescue and protect him. "The LORD" is God's name, and "declares the LORD" stresses that the promise comes from him.

God speaks and answers Jeremiah, a young man who felt unable to speak in public. God does not accept the excuse of his young age, for he will give him the words and send him with a difficult message for the people and the kings. The promise does not say there will be no opposition, but that God will be with him.

When God calls you to do something difficult, such as telling the truth in love or standing firm, do not wait until you feel capable. Take the step trusting that he is with you.
exp.13:21:
This verse asks three questions to show that only God can send rain. "The worthless idols of the nations" are nothing, and they cannot bring rain. The skies cannot send showers on their own either. So the people say, "Is this not by You, O LORD our God?" and declare that they put their hope in Him, because He has done all these things.

The people of Judah are speaking, and the prophet Jeremiah prays on their behalf. There is a severe drought (Jeremiah 14:1-6). Before this verse they confess their sin and ask God to remember them. Here they stop looking to idols and place their hope in God alone.

For today: when something important is missing, such as work, health, or peace, do not run first to what cannot help you. Honestly acknowledge your failings and put your hope in God, who has power over all things.
exp.22:32:
Here God teaches how to respond when someone asks, "What is the burden of the LORD?" The Hebrew word for "burden" (massa) can mean "weight" or "prophetic message." There seems to be a play on words: God answers, "What burden?" and then says that He Himself will cast them off, like someone who sets down a heavy load.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against false prophets who invented messages and said "Thus says the LORD" without His having sent them. They used the phrase "burden of the LORD" to give weight to their words and to mock the true prophet.

For today: before saying "God told me" or repeating what others say God said, let us examine whether it agrees with Scripture. Using God's name lightly is serious; it is better to ask humbly, "What has the LORD answered?"
exp.7:10:
They say the leaders dressed the wound of the people as if it were something minor. A "wound" here is a serious injury, and treating it "with very little care" means not taking it seriously. They kept saying "peace, peace," but there was no peace at all.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. The prophets and priests, instead of calling for repentance, gave comforting messages while the people continued in greed and deceit. That is why God announces judgment, for they were not even ashamed.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we prefer words that soothe us or the truth that heals us. True peace begins when we acknowledge our sin, repent, and return to God, instead of covering the wound with pleasant phrases.
exp.2:16:
At that time people will call Jerusalem "The Throne of the LORD," and all the nations will gather in Jerusalem to honor the name of the LORD. They will no longer follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts. The nations are the "all the nations" the verse mentions, people from across the world who come together there.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who had turned away from him. But in the midst of the rebuke he offers hope: faithful shepherds and a restored future. He says that the ark of the covenant will no longer be spoken of, as if God's presence depended on an object. Interpreters debate whether this points to a spiritual fulfillment, a future one, or both.

For today: God does not want only rites or symbols, but a heart surrendered to him. Ask him to soften your stubbornness and teach you to truly obey him.
exp.50:48:
Babylon has caused many of Israel's people to be killed, and because of that, people from across the earth will now be killed in Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah announces what the LORD says against Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and carried the people into exile. God promises that he will call Babylon to account for its violence and its idols. The exiles receive hope: God has not forgotten their suffering and does not ignore the injustice. The text does not say that Israel was innocent; other passages show that God also disciplined them.

For today: when you suffer an injustice, do not take revenge. Hand your pain over to God, who judges with justice, and ask him to help you forgive and to keep trusting in him.
exp.31:10:
Here Jeremiah describes how he took the documents of the purchase of the field. The deed of purchase is the contract, and this reader's verse describes it as having two copies: the sealed copy, which holds its terms and conditions, and the open copy, which was left unsealed. So there was one copy kept protected and another in plain view.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon and he himself was imprisoned in the court of the guard. God asked him to buy the field of his cousin in Anathoth, even though the land seemed lost. It was a sign that, after judgment, God would restore his people to that land.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, we can take concrete steps of faith, done with order and honesty, trusting that God keeps his promises even when we do not yet see the result.
exp.35:28:
This verse is a message from God to King Jehoiakim. God reminds him of what he did: he burned the scroll where Jeremiah had written the warnings. Jehoiakim was angry because the scroll said that the king of Babylon would surely come and destroy this land and leave it without people or animals. The phrase "You are to proclaim" means Jeremiah is to announce this message to the king, and "destroy" speaks of wiping out the country.

The Lord speaks, and He speaks to Jeremiah so that he will tell the king. Baruch had written down the words that Jeremiah dictated. Jehoiakim rejected them by burning the scroll, but God commanded that they be written again. Burning the paper did not change what God had said.

Today we can learn that ignoring a warning does not make it disappear. If God's Word makes us uncomfortable, it is better to listen to it with humility and correct our course than to try to silence it.
exp.47:41:
Moab will be destroyed as a nation. The reason is clear: "he vaunted himself against the LORD," that is, Moab became proud and rose up with arrogance against God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and this chapter announces its judgment. Before that, the text describes an enemy that falls like an eagle on its cities, and then speaks of terror, pit, and snare, images of a trap from which there is no escape. The sin named here is pride before God.

Today we can examine our hearts: do we trust in our strength, achievements, or money as if we did not need God? Let us ask Him for humility and live thankful, knowing that all we have comes from Him.
exp.2:0:
This verse refers to an old law: if a man divorced his wife and she married another man, he could not take her back again (see Deuteronomy 24:1-4). Doing so would defile the land, meaning it would make the land unclean. God compares this to Israel, who went off with many lovers, meaning other gods and alliances. Even so, God says, "you would return to Me."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, which had turned to idol worship. He describes that unfaithfulness as adultery. What stands out is that, according to the law, returning would be impossible, yet God offers to receive his people back. Some read the opening question as carrying a tone of rebuke; the overall meaning is clear.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, do not think it is too late. He invites you to return with sincerity. You can pray, confess your failure, and begin again today.
exp.24:34:
This verse says that the shepherds and the leaders of the flock will have nowhere to run and nowhere to hide. "Shepherds" and "leaders of the flock" refer to the rulers and leaders of the people and of the nations.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the word of the LORD. Just before this passage, God announces judgment on many nations for their wickedness, and calls their leaders to weep. Many readers understand that the image of the shepherd who cannot escape shows that neither power nor position spares anyone from being held accountable before God.

For today: if you have responsibility over others, in your home, your work, or your church, carry it out with humility and honesty, remembering that God sees how you care for those who have been entrusted to you.
exp.48:36:
God says he will shatter Elam before their enemies, before those who want to take their lives. He will bring disaster upon them, along with his fierce anger, and he will send out the sword after them until he finishes them off. "Seek their lives" means that these enemies want to take their lives. "Shatter" means that they will be broken down completely.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against several nations. Elam lay east of Babylon, and was famous for its archers. Breaking their bow shows that God would take away their strength. It is not known with precision how each detail was fulfilled. But the passage ends with hope: God promises to restore Elam in the end.

For today: no human strength is as secure as it seems. Trust in God, not in your own power, your money, or your success. And remember that his judgment is not the final word, because he also offers restoration.
exp.4:6:
God asks how he could forgive a people who had turned away from him. His children abandoned him and swore by gods that are not gods. The words "I satisfied their needs" mean that God provided for them fully, and yet they committed adultery. They gathered in large numbers at the houses of prostitutes. Some understand this as literal unfaithfulness, and others also as idolatry, which the Bible often calls spiritual adultery.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, shortly before Babylon invaded it. God accuses the people of rebellion and of lying when they swear by idols. Even so, the question shows pain, not only anger.

For today: when God blesses us, it is easy to forget him. Think about what he has given you, and thank him with a concrete decision of faithfulness, such as keeping your promises and your honesty.
exp.13:4:
Verse 5 says that even the doe, an animal that is very tender toward its young, gives birth in the field and leaves her newborn fawn behind. She does this not because she lacks affection, but because there is no grass to eat.

The prophet Jeremiah describes a severe drought that has fallen upon Judah. The verses before this one show nobles, farmers, and servants ashamed because of the lack of water. Then Jeremiah prays to God and acknowledges that the people have sinned and turned away. The drought is presented as a serious sign, and the text connects it with the spiritual condition of the people.

When hard times come, we can be honest before God, as Jeremiah was. Instead of blaming others or hardening ourselves, we can admit our failures, ask for forgiveness, and trust in his mercy.
exp.43:13:
God says that the Jews who went down to Egypt to live there will not get away from the punishment. None of them will be left alive to return to Judah, even though they long to go back. The final phrase, "no volverán sino los que escaparen," suggests that only a few fugitives would manage to return.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group went to Egypt, against God's counsel, and there they worshiped other gods. God warns them that Egypt will not be a refuge. Instead of repenting, the people reject the message, as the next verse shows.

For today: do not seek security far from God, and do not harden your heart when He corrects you. Listening in time and returning to Him is wiser than insisting on our own way.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah. "Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying," is the way the Berean Standard Bible puts it. The word "saying" announces that the message Jeremiah is to carry follows right away.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, a prophet of Judah, who tells how God gave him a message. Here the first great speech of the book begins. From what follows, God wants to remind his people of the affection and faithfulness of earlier times, before he rebukes them for their unfaithfulness. The verse does not say exactly when he received it, and that does not change the meaning.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Before we begin reading the Bible, we can pray quietly and ask him for an attentive heart, ready to obey what he says.
exp.5:23:
It says that the people of Judah heard the report of the enemy army coming from the north, and fear left them paralyzed. Their hands "hang limp" means they became weak and without strength, as if they had been disarmed. Anguish gripped them with an intense pain, compared to the pain of a woman in labor.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, identifying himself with his people. God had already warned that an invader would come from the north, as a consequence of Judah turning away from Him. Many scholars see Babylon here, though the text does not yet name it. The verse shows the fear that comes when the warning is ignored.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to return to God. Heed His warnings with humility, and when fear leaves you paralyzed, bring it to Him in prayer.
exp.33:20:
God says that he will hand King Zedekiah and his officials over to their enemies, that is, to those who are out to kill them. He will also hand them over to the army of the king of Babylon, which had pulled back from Jerusalem for a time.

The phrase "those who seek their lives" means that these enemies are trying to take their lives.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had made a solemn agreement to free their Hebrew slaves, passing between the parts of a divided calf, but later they enslaved them again. God judges them for breaking their word and for not obeying his law. The pullback of Babylon was only temporary.

For today: God takes seriously what we promise. If we make a promise before him, we should keep it, especially when it concerns treating others with justice and freedom. Let us ask him for help to be people of our word.
exp.25:4:
He says that God asks the people to listen to the words of the prophets whom he has sent to them. The phrase "again and again" means that God kept sending them, with persistence, without growing tired. The word "á" is an old form, and "no habéis oído" means that they have not paid attention to them.

Here the LORD speaks, and he tells Jeremiah to repeat it in the temple. It is a warning: God wants the people to turn away from their evil way so that he will not have to punish them. If they do not listen, Jerusalem will suffer the fate of Shiloh, a place where the sanctuary once stood and which lay in ruins. Many understand that God gives them another chance because of his mercy.

For today: God still speaks to us with patience, through his Word and through people who advise us. Let us not harden our hearts. Today, read the Bible with a desire to obey and correct something that God shows you.
exp.45:16:
The Egyptian soldiers, defeated, cry out that Pharaoh was all noise, like a man who made a great deal of commotion but let his chance slip by. The phrase "all noise" points to a king whose loud claims were never matched by action. The appointed time would be the right moment to act or to resist.

Jeremiah announces the defeat of Egypt before Babylon, near the Euphrates River. The soldiers, who once trusted their king, now blame him for his empty words and his failure to act. Scholars discuss some details of the Hebrew text, but the general sense is that Egypt promised much and could not deliver.

Today we can learn not to place our trust in people who talk a lot and do little. Let us trust in God, whose word always comes to pass, and let us also be people who respond in time when He calls us.
exp.48:24:
This verse is a lament: someone asks with grief how it is possible that Damascus, the city of praise, the town that brings Me joy, has been forsaken. The exact sense of the original is not entirely clear.

God speaks through Jeremiah against Damascus, a city neighboring Israel. The verses before describe panic over bad news of war. The verses after announce judgment: fire and death. It is not known with certainty who speaks this lament: it may be the prophet, God, or someone from the city itself.

For today: no city, fame, or success is secure in itself. Put your trust in God, not in what looks strong, because only He endures.
exp.15:8:
God announces that he is going to remove the sounds of celebration from this place. The sounds of joy and gladness will be gone, along with the voices of the bride and bridegroom at their weddings. This would happen soon, "before your very eyes" and "in your days," meaning while the people themselves were still living.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He tells him not to marry, and not to join in mourning or in feasting, as a sign to the people. The people had turned away from God to other gods, and judgment was coming as the result. Even so, God gives warning in advance, and that shows his patience.

For today: let us not take everyday blessings and joys for granted. Let us thank God for them, and humbly examine whether our hearts still remain close to him.
exp.50:22:
He says that God will use Babylon like a hammer to destroy all kinds of people: the shepherd with his flock, the farmer with his oxen, and also the governors and officials. No one is left out, neither the countryside nor the government.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been an instrument of God and had also oppressed many peoples, including Judah. This passage announces that its power will come to an end and that God will repay it for the evil it did in Zion. Some understand that God will use another people, the Medes, to carry this out.

For today: no human power is eternal or escapes the justice of God. If you suffer from an injustice, you can rest in the knowledge that God sees and judges with righteousness. And if you have authority, use it with humility and justice.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that the people did not ask, "Where is the LORD?", even though He had brought them up out of Egypt and led them through a very harsh wilderness. The words "a land of deserts and pits, a land of drought and darkness" describe a dangerous, lifeless place. "A land where no one travels and no one lives" describes a region that was empty of people.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He complains to the people of Israel because their ancestors turned away from Him and followed worthless idols. God reminds them of His past care: He freed them from slavery, went with them through the wilderness, and brought them to a good land. Even so, they forgot Him.

For today: it is easy to forget God when things are going well. We can remember in prayer how He has helped us in hard times, thank Him, and seek Him every day, not only in times of need.
exp.24:6:
This verse says that the people did not listen to God. The word "But" marks a contrast with what came before, and "provoked Me to anger" means they made him angry. "The works of your hands" refers to the idols they made and worshiped. In doing so, they were harming themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. For many years, God had asked them to give up their evil ways, stop following other gods, and live in peace in their land. Since they paid no attention, God announces that he will bring Babylon, with its king Nebuchadnezzar, as the consequence of their rebellion.

For today: God warns us out of love, not to annoy us. If there is something in your life that you have put in God's place, such as money, fame, or an addiction, listen to his voice today and change course before it causes you more harm.
exp.16:12:
It says that the Lord is the hope of Israel, and that all who abandon him will be put to shame. "All who turn away" refers to those who draw away from the Lord. "Will be written in the dust" means that their names will soon be erased, like something written on the ground. "Fountain of living water" is a spring of fresh, flowing water, and that spring is God himself.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a people who trusted in riches and other supports. First he praises God as Israel's hope, and then he warns about the consequences of leaving him. The shift to "for me" makes it seem that God himself is speaking, though some understand it as Jeremiah speaking. Right after this, the prophet asks to be healed, and the people mock him.

For today: when you feel dry inside, do not look first to other sources. Return to God with simple prayer and reading of his Word.
exp.9:19:
It says that the home of the one speaking has fallen into ruin. The tent was the dwelling of shepherds and ordinary people in that time, and its ropes held it up. When the ropes are snapped, everything collapses. Its sons have departed and are no more, meaning its people have gone away or died, and no one is left to pitch the tent again or set up its curtains.

The one speaking is the voice of Judah, the people, or perhaps the prophet Jeremiah speaking on their behalf. They mourn the destruction that comes with the invasion from the north and the exile. The text that follows says that their leaders did not seek God.

For today: when everything falls apart, we do not need to pretend we are fine. We can lament honestly before God. And if the leaders, or we ourselves, have stopped seeking Him, this is a good moment to return to Him.
exp.12:18:
The verse says that the cities of the Negev, the dry region in the south of Judah, have been shut tight, and no one can open them. The Berean wording makes clear that this is the Negev, so the verse names that region directly. "Have been carried into exile" means that the people were taken away from their land as prisoners. All of Judah, without exception, has been carried into exile and wholly taken captive.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, with grief, on behalf of God. Earlier he called the people to humble themselves, because their pride would bring judgment. Here he describes that fall as though it had already happened. The shut-tight cities may indicate that they were under siege, or that there was no one to defend or help them. The message is that the punishment would reach everyone, even the most distant places.

For today: God warns us with love before the consequences arrive. If something in your life pulls you away from Him, such as pride, do not wait until you have lost everything. Humble yourself today, listen to His voice, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.0:15:
God says he will pronounce his judgments against his people for all their wickedness. In the reader's wording, God announces that he will speak his judgment against them because they have forsaken him and burned incense to other gods, and worshiped the works of their own hands. Burning incense means offering incense in worship, and the works of their hands are the idols they made themselves.

The Lord speaks, and answers Jeremiah, a young prophet called to speak in Judah. God explains why he will bring an army from the north: the people abandoned him and worshiped other gods. The judgment is not arbitrary; it has a clear reason. Even so, God strengthens Jeremiah so that he speaks without fear.

For today: examine what things are occupying the place of God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Right now you can return to him sincerely and put him first in your decisions.
exp.6:22:
This verse says that the most important thing God asked of his people was obedience, not just rituals. "Obey Me" means to act on what is said, not merely to hear it. The words "I will be your God, and you will be My people" express a covenant relationship, a bond of mutual belonging. "Walk in all the ways I have commanded you" means living according to his instructions, and "so that it may go well with you" means that things may go well for them in life.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in the temple in Jerusalem. The people offered sacrifices, but they lived in disobedience. God tells them, with irony, to eat even the flesh of the burnt offerings, since without obedience those acts were of no value. Some understand that he does not reject the sacrifices, but places them in second place.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or do religious things. Ask yourself today: what has God asked me to do that I have not yet obeyed? Take one concrete step today.
exp.45:10:
He says that Egypt, called the "Virgin Daughter of Egypt," must go up to Gilead, a region famous for its balm, a resin used as medicine to heal wounds. But God warns her that it will be useless: no matter how many remedies she tries, there will be no healing. "In vain" is the sense here, meaning to no purpose. "Virgin" here points to a nation that thought itself unspoiled and invincible.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Egypt had been defeated by Babylon at Carchemish, beside the river Euphrates. The text presents that fall as a judgment of God, and with irony it shows that no human resource could undo that wound.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, reputation, or resources to fix what only God can heal. When we recognize our need and return to Him in humility, there is hope, because He is able to restore.
exp.50:45:
God tells his people not to let their hearts grow faint or be afraid when reports of war reach them. The word "rumor" here means news or a report. First one report will come in one year, and then another the next year, bringing violence in the land and one ruler rising against another ruler.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people who live among the Babylonians. He announces that Babylon will fall and that God will judge its god Bel. He warns them ahead of time that there will be disturbing news and violent changes, so that they will not lose heart or be caught off guard.

For today: when alarming news arrives, do not let fear rule your heart. Remember that God sees everything and still governs. Breathe, pray, and trust that his word will be fulfilled.
exp.45:2:
He says: "Deploy your shields, small and large; advance for battle!" "Deploy" means to position your forces and get them ready. The small shield was carried by the soldier, and the large shield was a great one that covered nearly the whole body. It is a military command given to the Egyptian soldiers.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Egypt. It refers to the battle of Carchemish, near the river Euphrates, where Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, defeated the army of Pharaoh Necho. The tone is ironic: Egypt prepares with all its equipment, but the verses that follow show that it will flee in defeat.

For today: we can have good preparation, plans, and resources, but none of them saves us if God is not on our side. Prepare yourself with responsibility, but place your trust in God and not only in your own strength.
exp.19:2:
The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, a wooden device that held the body fast and punished it, Jeremiah told him that the LORD does not call him Pashhur, but Magor-missabib. This name is usually understood as "terror on every side."

Pashhur was a priest and an authority in the temple. He was angered by the message of judgment that Jeremiah preached, and he punished him. Jeremiah, without fear, spoke for the LORD and gave him a new name that announced what would come: the invasion of Babylon and the suffering of the people.

For today: holding a religious position does not make us right. If someone corrects us with God's truth, it is better to listen with humility than to silence them or defend ourselves with pride.
exp.7:6:
It says that even the birds of the sky know when it is time to migrate: the stork, the turtle dove, the swift, and the thrush keep their seasons and return at exactly the right time. But God's people do not know "the requirements of the LORD," that is, what God asks of them and what He rightly requires.

The passage records God speaking through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had turned to idolatry and injustice, and no one repented. God compares the instinct of the birds with the stubbornness of the people, who reject His word even though they should know better.

For today: it is not enough to know things about God; we need to return to Him with humility. Today, think of an area where you sense God calling you to change, and respond with a sincere prayer and one concrete step.
exp.24:1:
This verse says that the prophet Jeremiah spoke God's message to all the people of Judah and to all the residents of Jerusalem. The words "spoke" and "residents" show that he delivered it aloud to the people who lived in the city. No one was left out: it was a message for everyone.

Jeremiah speaks in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, when Nebuchadnezzar was beginning to reign in Babylon. God sends him to warn the people that, after so many years of not listening, serious consequences would come. Jeremiah had kept up this warning for twenty-three years, according to the verses that follow, but almost no one paid him any attention.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are listening to God when he speaks to us through his Word, even when the message is uncomfortable. A good practice is to read the Bible with a heart willing to obey, not just to receive information.
exp.3:30:
He says the prophet hears a cry of pain, like that of a woman in labor with her first child. It is the "daughter of Zion," that is, Jerusalem and its people, who gasps for breath and stretches out her hands, crying, "Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers." The murderers are the killers who have come to destroy. The word "faints" means she has no strength left.

Jeremiah is the one speaking, announcing God's judgment on Judah for its unfaithfulness. Earlier, the people tried to dress up and make themselves attractive to win allies, but it was in vain. Many understand that the invasion comes from the north, and it is later identified with Babylon. Jeremiah feels deep pain over what he announces.

For today: let us not wait until anguish comes to turn back to God. Today we can seek him with sincerity, instead of trusting in appearances or in human supports that fail.
exp.1:6:
God says he brought his people into a fertile land to eat its fruit and bounty. The word "Carmel" here means a land of orchards and fruitful fields, and "inheritance" is the property God gave them as their portion. The words "defiled" and "detestable" describe making the land unclean and turning what was given into something repugnant. God gave them blessing, but they answered with contempt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Israel of forgetting him after he brought them out of Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. The leaders also failed: priests, shepherds and prophets went after Baal, a false god. So God brings a formal charge, as in a court case.

For today: it is easy to forget God when everything is going well. Today we can stop and thank him for what we have, and care honestly for what he has entrusted to us: family, work, health and faith.
exp.1:3:
This verse is a call to listen. God asks the attention of all his people: "house of Jacob" and "all you families of the house of Israel" refer to the descendants of Jacob, that is, to the whole nation. "Hear" means "listen," and "the LORD" is the name of God used in this verse.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf. Just before this, God fondly recalls how Israel followed him in the wilderness, like a faithful bride. Then, in the verses that follow, he asks the people what wrong they found in him that led them to turn away and follow empty things, such as idols. This verse opens that complaint with tenderness and seriousness.

For today: before deciding or following what attracts us, we can pause to listen to the voice of God in his Word. Remembering how he has cared for us in the past helps us not to run after things that promise much and give nothing.
exp.25:21:
This verse tells how King Jehoiakim sent a group of men all the way to Egypt, led by Elnathan, son of Achbor. They were going to bring back Uriah, the prophet who had fled there. The words "sent men to Egypt" simply mean that the king personally dispatched them to that country.

The passage is part of the book of Jeremiah and serves as a defense of the prophet. Uriah is mentioned as an example of what could happen to anyone who spoke God's word with firmness. Jehoiakim did not want to hear the message and preferred to silence the messenger. The text does not explain all the details of Elnathan's mission.

For today: when a truth makes us uncomfortable, it is tempting to attack the one who speaks it. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his correction, even when it comes by means we do not like.
exp.19:8:
He says that Jeremiah wanted to stop speaking: "I will not mention Him or speak any more in His name." But God's message was in his heart like a fire burning inside his bones. The phrase "I become weary of holding it in" shows that he tried hard to keep it inside and could not.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He delivered hard messages on God's behalf, and every day people insulted and mocked him. Even his friends were waiting to see him fall. Tired and wounded, he complains to God and thinks about giving up. Even so, at the end of the passage he trusts that God is with him.

For today: if you feel worn out from doing good or from speaking the truth, you can tell God honestly how you feel, as Jeremiah did. God does not become angry at your honesty. Ask him for strength to remain faithful, and surround yourself with people who encourage you.
exp.24:5:
This verse is a call not to worship other gods. The word "follow" describes going after something and staying close behind it, and bowing down in worship is simply the act of bowing down. The phrase "the works of your hands" refers to the idols that people made. God promises that if they give that up, he will do them no harm.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. God had sent them prophets again and again, and they did not listen. He asked them to turn away from their evil ways and to keep living in the land he had given them. The next verse shows that they did not obey, and for that reason judgment would come.

For today: an idol can be anything that takes the place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today you can ask yourself what has been capturing your heart, and place it back in God's hands through a sincere prayer.
exp.30:26:
God promises that the days are coming when He will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah. In other words, He will repopulate them and make them grow. The phrase "the seed of man and of beast" speaks of people and livestock: the land will once again have families, herds, and life.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had suffered destruction and exile. That is why, in this chapter, God announces hope and restoration. The verses that follow say that just as God watched over them to uproot and tear down, now He will watch over them to build and plant.

For today: if you are going through a season of loss or ruin, remember that God knows how to sow again. Trust that He can raise up something new in your life, and walk with patience while He makes it grow.
exp.24:17:
Jeremiah was told to hand the cup of God's judgment first to Jerusalem, to the cities of Judah, to its kings and to its officials. The result would be ruin: they would become a ruin, an object of horror and contempt and cursing. The phrase "as they are to this day" suggests that, at the time this was written, that ruin was already seen or regarded as fulfilled.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, sent by the LORD. The "cup" is an image of God's anger. Judah had rejected many warnings and practiced idolatry. That is why the judgment begins with God's own people and then reaches the other nations, as the following verses show.

For today: God takes seriously the faithfulness of those who say they believe Him. Ask God to show you what you should correct, and respond promptly, because His warning is also an invitation to return to Him.
exp.32:10:
This verse promises that in the places that are now empty, the sounds of joy and gladness will be heard again: the voices of the bride and bridegroom at weddings, and people bringing thank offerings to the house of the LORD and saying, "Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever." The bridegroom and the bride are the groom and the bride. "Restore the land from captivity" means that God will bring his people back from exile, as he did in former times.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem and Judah were in ruins, and the people saw them as deserted, without people or animals. Jeremiah announces this message of hope while the punishment still weighs heavily. God promises to restore what seemed lost forever.

For today: when a situation looks empty or without a way out, you can keep thanking God for his goodness. He can bring back joy where there was pain. Today, write down one specific reason to thank him and say it to him in prayer.
exp.7:8:
Those who thought themselves wise will be put to shame, left dismayed and trapped like prisoners. The reason is that they rejected the word of the LORD. Then God asks: since they have rejected his word, what wisdom do they really have?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people said, "We are wise, and we have the law." But God says that the scribes handled the law in vain, because they did not obey it. Even the birds know when to migrate, yet the people did not recognize God's judgment coming upon them.

Having the Bible or knowing a great deal about it is not the same as obeying it. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has already told me clearly that I am avoiding? True wisdom begins by listening to him and heeding him.
exp.1:26:
The verse says the people speak to a tree and call it "You are my father," and to a stone and say, "You gave me birth." They have turned their backs to God and not their faces. Yet when trouble comes, they cry out, "Rise up and save us!"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He accuses them of turning away from the living God to follow idols. With a sharp irony, he shows them as inconsistent: they ignore him in calm times and seek him only in crisis. In the verses that follow, he tells them to ask the gods they have made for help.

For today: examine what you place your trust in, such as money, success, or approval. Seek God also in the good days, not only when there is distress, and trust that He still welcomes whoever returns with sincerity.
exp.7:18:
Listen to the cry that comes from a land far away. The people ask: "Is the Lord no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?" Then God answers with grief: why have they provoked me with their carved images and their worthless foreign idols? "Carved images" are idols that have been shaped by hand. "Worthless foreign idols" are gods of other nations that have no real power.

Jeremiah writes before the exile in Babylon. Many understand that he hears in advance the weeping of those who will be carried away. The questions express surprise: how can this be happening to us if God dwells among us? God responds that the problem was their idolatry. Some think the voice asking the questions is Jeremiah's, and others think it is the people's. In any case, the grief of the prophet and the grief of God are mixed together.

Today: it is not enough to say "the Lord is with us" while we give our hearts to other things. Ask him to show you what has taken his place, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.35:24:
This verse tells us that three officials at court, Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah, urged the king not to burn the scroll containing God's word. But the king would not listen to them. "Urged" means they pressed him earnestly, and "would not listen to them" means he refused to heed them.
