We are in the time of King Jehoiakim of Judah. Jeremiah had spoken God's words, and his assistant Baruch wrote them on a scroll. When the scroll was read to the king, he cut it up and threw it into the fire. These officials, unlike the king, were alarmed and tried to stop him. Even so, God's word was not destroyed, because afterward God commanded that it be written again.

For today: do not harden your heart when the Bible confronts you. If someone warns you with care, listen to them, and before the word of God respond with humility rather than rejection.
exp.15:18:
He says that Jeremiah turns to God and calls him his strength, his fortress, and his refuge when distress comes. He also announces that people from distant nations, "the ends of the earth," will come to God. They will say that what their ancestors handed down to them was nothing but lies, worthless idols with no benefit at all.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a harsh message of judgment against Judah for its idolatry. God has just said that he sees everything and will punish their sin. But here, in the midst of judgment, Jeremiah expresses trust in God and hope that other nations will also come to know him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, run to God before things that promise security, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask him to be your refuge, and examine where you are placing your trust.
exp.45:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book. It says that God gave a message to Jeremiah, his prophet, and that this message concerns the nations.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks through Jeremiah. Chapters 46 to 51 gather messages about several foreign peoples. The verses that follow begin with Egypt and recall its defeat by Babylon at Carchemish. In this way it is shown that God rules over all the nations, not only over Judah.

For today: although the powers of the world may seem immense, none of them is outside the care and authority of God. We can trust that he remains just and sovereign when the news frightens us.
exp.6:2:
Thus says the LORD, through Jeremiah, to the people: "Correct your ways and deeds." That is, change the way you live and act. If they do, God promises to let them keep living in this land.

Jeremiah speaks at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem, and the message is for the people of Judah who came in to worship. God warns them not to trust in empty religious phrases like "the temple of the LORD," for they believed the temple would protect them even while they lived wrongly. God asks for a real change, above all justice toward one's neighbor.

Today we can ask whether our lives match what we say we believe. Going to church or using spiritual words is not enough. Let us ask God for help to change one specific attitude or habit, and to treat those around us with justice and kindness.
exp.11:11:
It says that destroyers have come over all the barren heights in the wilderness. The "sword of the LORD" is an image of God's judgment, which sweeps across the land from one end to the other. "Destroyers" means those who plunder and ruin. "No flesh has peace" means no human being has peace; no one is left untouched.

The Lord speaks, in the middle of Jeremiah's lament about the people of Judah. God calls the land "my vineyard" and describes how invaders laid it waste because of the people's disobedience. Many understand this to refer to enemy armies, such as Babylon, though the text gives no names here.

For today: God takes seriously the direction we follow. His judgment is not whim, for He always calls people to repentance. Ask yourself whether there is something in your life that He is asking you to correct, and return to Him today with humility, trusting in His mercy.
exp.28:10:
God says that he knows very well the plans he has for his people. They are plans to prosper them and not to harm them. The word "plans" in this verse refers to his purposes, and the promise of "a future and a hope" points to a good outcome that he intends for them.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the Jews exiled in Babylon. False prophets were telling them the exile would be short, but God says it will last seventy years. Even so, he promises that he will not abandon them and that he will bring them back. This promise was first given to that people in that specific situation.

For today: even if you go through long and difficult times, you can trust that God remains good and faithful. This does not mean everything will come easily, but it does mean you can seek him in prayer, as the next verse says, with all your heart.
exp.4:25:
Among God's people, wicked people are found. They watch in secret, like the hunter who waits and sets snares and traps to catch birds. But here the prey is not animals but men. These are people who plan and set traps against others.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of not honoring Him, even though He gives them the rain and the harvest. The verses that follow describe the traps: deceit, unjust riches, and neglect of the fatherless and the poor. God does not overlook injustice among His own people.

For today: examine whether, in your work, your business, or your relationships, you take advantage of others through deceit or half-truths. Ask God for a heart that honors Him and cares for the weakest.
exp.39:4:
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, was still speaking with Jeremiah as Jeremiah was about to leave when he gave him another choice: he could return to Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the cities of Judah, and stay with him among the people. Or he could go anywhere else that seemed right to him. The captain then gave him food and a gift, and let him go.

A Babylonian officer speaks here after the fall of Jerusalem. He had removed Jeremiah's chains and given him freedom to choose. Jeremiah had announced this judgment for years. According to the text that follows, he went with Gedaliah to Mizpah, alongside those who remained in the land.

God can use even difficult circumstances to care for us and guide us. When you have to make a decision, pray, think about where you can serve best, and choose with humility, even if it is not the easiest or most impressive path.
exp.35:16:
The princes of Judah, alarmed by what they heard, ask Baruch to explain how he wrote down all those words. They want to know whether Jeremiah dictated them to him. The question "How did you write all these words?" asks for the method, and "Was it at Jeremiah's dictation?" asks whether Jeremiah was speaking them as Baruch wrote.

Jeremiah was prevented from entering the temple, so he sent Baruch, his scribe, to publicly read God's message. The princes heard the scroll and became alarmed, because it announced judgment. Before taking it to King Jehoiakim, they wanted to confirm where it came from. Afterward, they advised that Baruch and Jeremiah go into hiding, since the king might react with violence.

For today: when the Word of God unsettles us, let us neither ignore it nor argue it away. Let us listen with humility, and if need be, act with wisdom and courage to obey it.
exp.4:0:
God invites the people to go up and down the streets and squares of Jerusalem to look for just one person who acts justly and seeks the truth. If they find one, God promises to forgive the city. "Go up and down" means to walk back and forth through the streets. "Acts justly" means treating others fairly and doing what is right.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people considered themselves faithful, but they lived in deceit and refused to correct themselves. The verses that follow say that they swore in God's name without sincerity and hardened their faces. The request shows how serious the situation was, and also the mercy of God, who is ready to forgive.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are people who seek the truth and act justly, even when no one else does. Begin with one concrete act of honesty today.
exp.22:17:
This verse asks a pointed question: which of those prophets has truly stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word? The implied answer is that none of them has.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The false prophets said "you will have peace" and "no harm will come," even though the people were living in sin. They made up pleasing messages from their own hearts. God reminds them that he will judge, and that his storm will fall on the wicked.

For today: before accepting a message as coming from God, compare it with the Bible. A word that only sounds comforting is not necessarily from God. Set aside time to hear his Word with careful attention, and to obey it.
exp.26:5:
He says that God himself has placed all those lands under the authority of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He calls him "My servant," meaning someone God uses to carry out his purpose. Even the beasts of the field are made subject to him. "I have placed" means "I have put under his authority."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message was meant to reach the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, and also Judah. God was asking them to accept Babylonian rule and not rebel. Calling him "My servant" does not mean that Nebuchadnezzar was righteous, but that God directs history, and the passage itself says his time would also come to an end.

Even when governments seem strong, God is still the one in charge. We can trust that he guides history, and ask him for humility to obey him when his ways are not easy for us to understand.
exp.49:13:
The verse tells the archers to line up in formation all around Babylon and shoot at her without holding back. "Line up in formation" means get into position; "draw the bow" means pull back the string to fire; "arrows" are the shafts shot from the bow; and "spare no arrows" means do not hold any back. The reason given is that Babylon has sinned against the LORD.

This is a prophecy by Jeremiah about the fall of Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem. God speaks of judgment against a proud and cruel nation. The text does not clearly name the attackers here; many think of the Medes and Persians, and others also see a broader meaning. It stresses that this is God's justice, not simply human revenge.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. We can rest in the fact that he judges with justice, and so we do not need to repay evil with evil. Rather, we can pray for justice and live with humility.
exp.48:32:
It says that Hazor will become an abandoned place, where only jackals will live, wild animals that look like dogs. The phrase "a desolation forever" means it will be left empty, without people. The words "no man will abide there" show that no one will stay or live in it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is against Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, desert tribes who lived in confidence, without walls or gates, believing themselves safe. Hazor here is not the city in Canaan, but refers to those Arab settlements; scholars are not certain of their exact location. Babylon would be the instrument of judgment.

For today: the security that comes from our riches or our own strength is fragile. Let us place our trust in God, not in what we have, because only He truly sustains our life.
exp.31:38:
God promises to give his people "one heart and one way," that is, one shared desire and one direction for life. The words "I will give them" are the verse's own wording. "So that they will always fear Me" does not speak of terror, but of respect and reverence toward God. And "for their own good" means that things will go well for them. This blessing would reach their children as well.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah faced exile because of their disobedience, but God promises to gather them, bring them back, and make an everlasting covenant with them. Here the change comes from God himself: he puts that heart and that reverence within them.

For today: if you find it hard to obey or to keep a steady course, ask God to give you a united heart to follow him. And remember that your faithfulness can also bless your family.
exp.5:5:
The verse says that the LORD of Hosts commands that trees be cut down and a siege ramp be raised against Jerusalem. A siege ramp is a mound of earth or wood built up to attack a city wall. Here, "punished" means receiving judgment, not a friendly visit. The reason is stated plainly: there is nothing but oppression within the city.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that an enemy army will come against Jerusalem. The nearby verses present this as the result of the people's constant wickedness: injustice, robbery, and harm. Even so, God calls them to turn back before He leaves the city desolate. His judgment comes with a warning and an open door.

For today: let us not downplay the injustice we see or practice. Ask God to show you where you need to change, and do it soon, treating those around you with justice and respect.
exp.3:12:
It says that an enemy is approaching quickly and with great power. He advances like the clouds, his chariots are like the whirlwind, and his horses are swifter than eagles. Then the people cry out, "Woe to us, for we are ruined!" They will be plundered and destroyed.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, and the voice of God is also heard announcing judgment. Judah and Jerusalem had turned away from God. For this reason an invasion is coming, which many understand to be that of the army of Babylon, although the text does not give the name here. Then God calls Jerusalem to cleanse its heart so that it may be saved.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to arrive before you turn back to God. Ask him today to examine your heart, and sincerely let go of whatever you know does not please him.
exp.51:26:
This verse tells that the king of Babylon had those prisoners struck down and put to death at Riblah, a place in the land of Hamath, north of Israel. The words "struck them down" and "put them to death" point to an execution. So the people of Judah were taken into exile, away from their own land.

The one who tells the account is the author of the book, who closes Jeremiah's prophecy with a historical summary. Many believe this chapter is very similar to 2 Kings 24 and 25. The prisoners were military leaders and officials, taken when Jerusalem fell. The account confirms that what Jeremiah had warned about for years came to pass.

For today: God speaks in earnest, and his warnings are not empty words. If he corrects us through his Word, it is wise to respond soon with humility. And even in dark times, we can trust that his mercy does not run out.
exp.50:26:
God calls for a banner to be raised and a ram's horn to be blown to gather armies against Babylon. He names the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, peoples to the north of Babylon. "Summon" means to call together. "Captain" is a military leader. The image of horses coming up like swarming locusts suggests an unstoppable multitude.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed nations and plundered Judah. God announces that he will judge her and will use other peoples to do it. The verses that follow mention the Medes, and this was fulfilled with the fall of Babylon before the Medes and Persians.

For today: God rules over empires, and injustice will not last forever. If you suffer something unjust, trust that God sees and acts in his time, and avoid taking revenge on your own.
exp.50:17:
They are worthless, meaning empty and without any real value. They are "a work to be mocked," that is, something fit for ridicule. "Punishment" refers to the moment when God steps in to judge. When that time comes, the idols will be destroyed and will not be able to save anyone.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on God's word against Babylon, a nation full of idols. Just before this verse, the Creator is shown sending rain, clouds, and wind. Then it says that the God of Jacob is the Former of all things. The contrast is clear: God creates; idols are only made by human hands.

For today: ask yourself what you are truly trusting in, whether money, success, or image. All of that can fail. Put your trust in the living God, who truly sustains your life.
exp.31:32:
They have turned their backs to God and not their faces. Turning the back is a picture of refusing him outright. "Again and again" in the Berean wording points to the same idea as "rising up early and teaching": God instructed them persistently and from the start. Even so, they would not listen or respond to discipline.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is about to fall to Babylon, and God explains the reason: it was not for lack of warning, but because kings, priests, prophets and people rejected his word for a long time. Then he mentions their idolatrous practices, even in the temple.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we face God when he corrects us. Sometimes his voice comes through the Bible, a wise counsel or a restless conscience. A good practice is to respond with humility: to listen, acknowledge the mistake and change course without delay.
exp.17:12:
God tells the people to ask the nations around them whether anyone has ever heard of anything like this. The word for the surrounding peoples refers to those who are not Jewish. A most terrible thing is something hideous and disgraceful. The phrase "Virgin Israel" is a poetic way of naming God's people, as if they were a pure young woman who ought to have been faithful. What they did is so strange that not even the nations around them would do it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had just offered Judah a way out: to turn from their evil path. They answered with stubbornness, saying it is no use, that they will keep following their own desires. So God points out how absurd it is to abandon Him.

For today: when God calls us to change, let us not harden our hearts by saying it is too late or that we will do as we please. Today you can ask Him to show you a crooked path and take one concrete step to correct it.
exp.4:24:
This verse says that the people's sins were the reason God held back good things. Their "wrongdoings" are their crooked actions, and "diverted" means that they turned these things aside, keeping them from reaching the people. "These things" refers to the rain and the harvest of the previous verse. "Good things" are the blessings God wanted to give them, which his bounty provided.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on God's message to Judah. He rebukes them because, although God gave them rain and harvest in their season, they did not honor or thank him for it. Furthermore, the text that follows shows that there was deceit and injustice among them. Some scholars see here a covenant-style language, where disobedience brought consequences.

For today: not all suffering comes from a personal sin, but it is wise to examine our hearts. We can thank God for what we receive each day and humbly correct what displeases him, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.29:6:
How awful that day will be! No day will be like it. It is the time of Jacob's distress, the people of Israel, but he will be saved out of it. The phrase "none will be like it" means no other day compares to it, and "saved" means rescued.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were under the threat or weight of judgment and exile, and the verses before it describe a fear so great that men press their hands to their waist like a woman in labor. Interpreters disagree about whether "that day" refers only to the fall of Babylon and the return from exile, or also to a broader time in the future. The next verse promises to break the yoke and restore the people.

For today: even when a trial seems to be the worst of all, God can bring deliverance. We can ask him for help with confidence and wait on his faithfulness.
exp.4:26:
This verse says that the houses of the wicked are full of deceit, like a cage full of trapped birds. Just as a hunter fills his cage with what he catches, they filled their homes with wealth gained through traps and lies. Because of this, they became powerful and rich.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He accuses people within his own nation who lie in wait and set traps for others. According to the verses that follow, they did not defend the orphan or the poor. God shows that these injustices do not go unnoticed and that there will be consequences.

For today: let us examine how we earn our money and how we treat the weak. Prosperity does not prove that God approves of everything we do. Let us ask God for honesty in our work and practical compassion toward those who have no one to defend them.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that the leaders of the people, called "shepherds," have become senseless. They do not seek the LORD, that is, they do not ask him for direction or take him into account. For this reason they have not prospered, and the people they looked after are scattered, like sheep without a guide.

Here Jeremiah speaks, and in these verses he expresses the grief of Judah before the ruin that is coming. The broken dwelling and the lost children show a home destroyed, with its children gone. Interpreters often see in the shepherds the kings, priests and rulers. The prophet explains that the disaster came in part because they turned away from God.

For today: if you guide others at home, at church or at work, seek God first in prayer and in his Word. Without that, even the best plan can leave others confused and scattered.
exp.20:6:
This verse announces a very harsh judgment. God says that after the plague, the famine, and the sword, he will hand over King Zedekiah, his officers, and the people left alive in this city to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and to their enemies who seek their lives. He will put them to the sword and will not spare them or show pity or compassion. The sword here is the sword itself, and the statement that he will show no pity means that the enemy will show no mercy.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah shortly before the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. King Zedekiah had asked for a favorable word, but God answered with a warning. This came after years of refusing his calls to repentance. Even so, the next verse offers a way out: surrender and live.

For today: when God warns us, it is wise to listen in time and not to trust in our own defenses. His truth may hurt, but it always leaves a door open to return to him.
exp.22:36:
This verse gives instructions on how to ask about God's word. The prophet should be asked with respect: "What has the LORD answered you?" and "What has the LORD spoken?" These are simple questions, aimed at hearing what God actually said.

God speaks through Jeremiah to a people who often used the phrase "the burden of the LORD." The Hebrew term can mean "message" or "burden," and it seems to have been used mockingly and carelessly. God corrects that habit and asks that what He said be repeated faithfully, without twisting it.

Today we can take care with what we say in God's name. Before claiming "God told me," it is good to return to the Bible, examine carefully what it says, and speak with humility. That way we do not use His name for our own ideas.
exp.13:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book. It says that God spoke to Jeremiah about a great drought, a time without rain. The name for God here is "the LORD," and the phrase "came to Jeremiah" means that the message reached the prophet.

Here Jeremiah is not speaking on his own. He presents what God made known to him. The verses that follow show the suffering of the people: Judah is in mourning, the cities have grown weak, and even the nobles cannot find water. In the Bible, lack of rain sometimes appears as a warning from God to a people who had turned away from Him. The text, however, here only announces the drought.

For today: when times of scarcity or pain come, do not stay only in complaint. Stop, pray, and ask God whether there is something you should correct or entrust to Him, trusting that He hears.
exp.16:8:
The human heart, meaning the innermost part of a person (their desires, thoughts and decisions), can deceive us more than anything else. Here the heart is described as beyond cure, and the question "who can understand it?" means that no one can fully grasp it by themselves.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah, who trusted in human alliances and in their own strength. Earlier, the person who trusts in God is compared to a tree planted by the water. Then God says that He indeed searches the heart and gives to each one according to his deeds.

For today: do not blindly trust your feelings or your justifications. Before deciding, pray, ask God to examine your heart, and compare your decisions with His Word.
exp.48:16:
It says that Edom will become an object of horror. "Desolation" means complete ruin and destruction. Whoever passes by it will be appalled, that is, left shocked and horrified, and will scoff, mocking the ruin of all her wounds. The wounds are the blows and damage left by the judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, Israel's neighbor, lived in rocky mountains and felt secure and untouchable. God warns that its pride deceived it. The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah shows that the punishment would be complete. Scholars agree on the general message, though they debate exactly when it was fulfilled.

Today we can learn that no human security, whether money, position, or strength, protects us from God. Examine where you place your trust. Cultivate humility, and rest in the Lord, who is the only truly firm refuge.
exp.0:6:
God answers Jeremiah: "Do not say, I am only a child." He explains that Jeremiah must go to everyone he sends him to and must speak all that God commands him.

The Lord speaks, answering Jeremiah, who has just said that he does not know how to speak. God had just told him that he knew him and had set him apart before he was born to be a prophet. Jeremiah feels insecure, but God does not stop at his excuse. Immediately he promises to be with him and to put his words in his mouth.

For today: when God asks something of you and you feel very young, inexperienced, or unable, do not stay focused only on your limits. Obey step by step, trusting that God is with you and gives you what is needed for what he asks.
exp.21:25:
He says that God himself will drive out Coniah and his mother from their own country and carry them off into a foreign land, where neither of them was born. There they will both die. The phrase "hurl you" means God will force them out with great violence, and "another land" means a foreign country.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin or Jeconiah, was king of Judah. God had earlier compared him to a signet ring on his hand, a sign of honor and authority, and yet now he rejects him because of the wickedness and pride of the kingdom. He was taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and his mother went with him.

For today: holding a place of power or privilege does not protect us from the consequences of turning away from God. It is better to live with humility and to listen to his voice in time, before things are lost.
exp.16:3:
God tells his people that they will lose the land he himself gave them. The phrase "relinquish the inheritance" means that they will no longer hold it. They will be enslaved to their enemies in a country they do not know. The "anger" is his burning wrath, and the fire that "will burn forever" is an image of judgment. Some understand "forever" as a very long and harsh punishment, not necessarily one without end.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had built altars and high places to worship idols, and their children grew up remembering them. That is why the punishment comes, which was fulfilled in the exile to Babylon.

For today: God calls us to trust in him alone, not in false gods or in passing things such as money or people. Today you can ask yourself where you are placing your security, and hand it over to God in prayer.
exp.5:13:
This verse says that the leaders treat the wound of the people as if it were something minor. A serious injury is what is meant, and to dress it with very little care is to handle it carelessly. They keep saying "Peace, peace," but the peace they announce is not real at all.

It is God speaking through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He accuses prophets and priests of deceiving the people, because out of greed they told them that everything was well while sin kept growing. For this reason God later calls them to return to the ancient paths, but they answered: "We will not walk in it."

For today: do not settle for comforting words that ignore what is truly wrong. Ask God for humility to hear the truth, to recognize your wounds, and to return to his way, where there really is rest for the soul.
exp.49:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book. It says that what follows is a word the LORD spoke through Jeremiah the prophet, concerning Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans were the people who ruled Babylon. The phrase "through Jeremiah" means that God used the prophet as his messenger to deliver this message.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah passes on what he receives. Babylon was then the power that had conquered Judah and carried people off into exile. This message announces that this empire would also be judged. Many understand it as a comfort to God's people, for it showed them that Babylon's power was not eternal. Chapters 50 and 51 are devoted entirely to this theme.

For today: when evil seems powerful and unbeatable, remember that God still governs history. Trust that his justice will come in its time, and in the meantime remain faithful.
exp.44:4:
God asks Baruch whether he is seeking great things for himself, and tells him not to seek them. He will bring disaster on every living creature, so the whole world is facing judgment. But to Baruch he promises that his life will be granted to him as a spoil of war: like plunder rescued from a battle, he will survive wherever he goes.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, probably in the days of King Jehoiakim, when Judah was about to fall. Baruch, the scribe who wrote down the prophet's words, was exhausted and discouraged. God corrects him with tenderness and invites him to see the whole picture.

For today: in difficult times, be careful not to dream only of your own success or comfort. Ask God to help you be content with his daily care. He does not promise an easy or famous life, but he does promise to sustain you and keep you safe in the middle of trial.
exp.42:1:
Here we see that Azariah, Johanan, and all the arrogant men accuse Jeremiah of lying. They say that the LORD our God has not sent him to tell them, "You must not go to Egypt to reside there." The verse of "proud" is not needed for this translation, and the verse of "sojourn" is replaced by the verse's own wording: "to reside there" means to live there for a time as a foreigner.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors asked Jeremiah to pray so that they could know what to do. They promised to obey. But when God told them to stay in Judah and not go to Egypt, they already had another decision in their hearts. That is why they reject the message and blame the prophet, later saying that Baruch is manipulating him.

For today: before asking God for direction, let us check whether we are truly willing to obey. If we have already decided everything, it is easy to call what God tells us a falsehood.
exp.24:32:
This verse says that on the day of the LORD's judgment there will be many dead spread across the whole earth, from one end to the other. No one will mourn them, gather them, or bury them. They will lie on the ground like dung, which is to say, like worthless waste.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God had announced judgment on Judah and on many nations for their wickedness and their refusal to listen. Here it is shown that God is Judge of all humanity. The "shepherds" who come afterward are the rulers, who will also be judged.

For today: God takes justice seriously, and no one escapes it. Instead of ignoring his voice, we can repent with humility and trust in his mercy, which is still offered in Christ.
exp.9:0:
Listen closely to this verse. The word "Hear" means "listen," the name of the God of Israel is "the LORD," and "you" refers to the people being addressed. God speaks to the whole "house of Israel," that is, to all his people, and asks them to pay attention to what he tells them.

The book of Jeremiah records the messages God gave through this prophet to his people before and during the fall of Jerusalem. Here God speaks and prepares the message that follows: he warns Israel not to imitate the religious customs of other nations or to fear the signs of the heavens, and he reminds them that idols are the work of human hands.

Today, before we are carried along by what others fear, believe, or follow, it is good to stop and listen to God in his Word. Reading it attentively each day helps us live with trust rather than fear.
exp.43:3:
God says that he sent all his prophets to the people again and again, with persistence, warning them not to do that detestable thing he hates. The phrase "again and again" shows that he kept on, repeating his warnings without letting up, like someone who keeps calling out to a friend who will not stop what is harming them. The "detestable thing" is offering incense to false gods.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to the Jews who had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. He reminds them that the ruin of their land was no accident, but the result of idolatry. God shows them that his patience and his warnings were constant, but they would not listen.

For today: when God warns us through his Word, or through wise counsel and our conscience, let us not take it lightly. His correction is a sign of his care. Today we too can give up something we know grieves him.
exp.42:8:
God tells Jeremiah to pick up large stones and bury them in the clay of the brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, while the Jewish people watch. Tahpanhes is an Egyptian city. The instruction to bury the stones in the clay can be understood as setting them into the brick pavement.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. A group of Judeans had fled to Egypt out of fear of Babylon, disobeying God's word. With this action, God shows them that Egypt would not be a safe refuge either: Nebuchadnezzar, whom God calls "my servant," would come and set his throne over those very stones. Scholars debate the exact details of the place.

Today: running away from what God asks of us, looking for security somewhere else, does not protect us. It is better to obey and trust in Him, who is the true refuge.
exp.5:22:
It says that an enemy army is coming against Jerusalem, called here "O Daughter of Zion." Its soldiers grasp the bow and spear. They are cruel and merciless. The noise of their advance roars like the sea, and they come riding on horses, lined up like men in formation, ready to fight.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. For a long time the people ignored his warnings and continued in their sin. Therefore he announces a judgment coming from the north. The text does not name the invader here; many think of Babylon, though some debate this.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings out of convenience. If something in your life draws you away from him, do not put it off; return to him sincerely, because God corrects in order to restore, and his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.47:39:
God announces that an enemy will swoop down on Moab suddenly, like an eagle that dives onto its prey with its wings spread out. The picture is of a sudden attack, one that comes without warning.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel, east of the Dead Sea. The text does not say here who the eagle is; many think it refers to an invading army, probably Babylon. God explains the reason for the judgment: Moab stood against the Lord in its pride. Its arrogance and its refusal to honor God led it toward its fall.

For today: pride makes us trust in our own strength, achievements, or security. Today you can hand over to God whatever you trust in most and ask him for a humble heart that depends on him.
exp.23:1:
Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs. One holds very good figs, like those that ripen early, which are the first figs of the season and highly valued. The other holds very poor figs, so bad that they could not be eaten.

Jeremiah is speaking, recounting a vision that God gave him. It takes place after the first deportation to Babylon, when Nebuchadnezzar carried away King Jeconiah, the princes, and the craftsmen. God will use these baskets, set in front of the temple, to explain his judgment and his care for two groups of people.

For today: God sees reality beyond appearances and circumstances. Those who go through hard trials are not forgotten by Him. Ask Him to teach you to look at your life and the lives of others as He sees them, with truth and hope.
exp.49:27:
Listen to the people fleeing and escaping from Babylon as they arrive in Zion with a report: the LORD our God has already carried out justice. "Vengeance" here means a just punishment from God, not a vengeance driven by resentment. It is "vengeance for His temple" because Babylon had destroyed the temple in Jerusalem.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who lived through the exile. Babylon had been very proud and cruel toward Israel. For this reason the text announces its fall and says that the survivors will carry the news to Jerusalem. Some scholars see here the Jews returning from exile, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when you see injustice and feel that no one responds, remember that God sees and that he has the final word. You can leave your pain in his hands, pray for justice, and refrain from taking revenge yourself.
exp.3:15:
This verse is a command to give warning. The message must be announced to the nations, and also to Jerusalem, that a besieging army is coming from a distant land. Here "a besieging army" refers to the force that surrounds a city. The phrase "they raise their voices against the cities of Judah" describes the army shouting its battle cry against the towns of Judah. The cities of Judah will be attacked.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he called Jerusalem to cleanse its heart so that it might be saved. Now he warns that judgment is drawing near because of its rebellion. Many understand this to be the army of Babylon, although the text does not give the name in this verse.

For today: God gives warning before he corrects, because he desires that we return to him. Today you can examine your heart with sincerity, acknowledge what you need to leave behind, and come to God without delay.
exp.1:18:
The verse says that the consequences of doing wrong will fall on the very people who did it. "Your own evil" means the harm your choices bring on you. "Your own apostasies" means your turning away from God. "Will reprimand you" means that this very path will show that you were wrong. God invites you to consider and realize how evil and bitter it is to forsake the LORD your God, and to have no fear of Him, that is, reverence and awe.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had left God to seek help from Egypt and Assyria, neighboring powers, and to follow other gods. God reminds them that He had cared for them, and that their choices were hurting them.

For today: when you feel yourself drifting away from God, stop and examine what you are asking to keep you safe. Return to Him sincerely, because far from Him, what seems like freedom ends in bitterness.
exp.48:12:
God makes a solemn promise, swearing by himself: Bozrah will become a ruin. It will be a thing of disgrace and horror, a lonely wasteland, and a word people use when they pronounce a curse. "Desolation" means complete destruction, and "disgrace" means shame and dishonor. Its surrounding cities will also be left in ruins forever.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in his message against Edom. Bozrah was an important city of that people. God declares that Edom will be judged, as others were, and that it will not escape. Scholars understand the punishment as the consequence of its pride and its hostile treatment of Israel.

For today: God takes pride and injustice seriously, even when he is slow to act. Examine whether you trust in your own strength or in God, and treat others with humility and compassion.
exp.37:14:
Jeremiah answers King Zedekiah plainly. He tells him that if he shares what God is saying, the king will likely put him to death, and that if he offers advice, the king will not listen to it. To "tell" someone something means to make it known to them; to "listen" here means to really hear and act on what is said.

Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, and Babylon was already surrounding Jerusalem. Shortly before this, the officials had thrown Jeremiah into a cistern for announcing the defeat. Now the king calls for him in secret, and the prophet, with good reason, is cautious: he had already spoken before without anyone paying attention. Even so, the king immediately swears to protect him.

Today we can learn to be honest even when it costs us. And we can also ask ourselves whether, when we seek advice, we are truly willing to act on what we hear, even when it is not what we hoped for.
exp.0:17:
God tells Jeremiah that he has made him like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls. These are images of strength and firmness. A fortified city is a city built with strong defenses. Jeremiah is to stand firm against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land. That firmness will be needed in the face of every level of the nation.

God speaks when he calls Jeremiah, who was young and afraid. He entrusts him with a message of judgment against a people who worshiped idols. He knew they would reject him, so God promises him strength to endure. The next verse assures him: "they shall not prevail against you; for I am with you."

For today: when obeying God brings opposition or mockery, do not rely on your own character alone. Ask God for the firmness that he gives, and go forward with humility, remembering that he is with you.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that God compares the two kingdoms of the Hebrew people. Israel, the northern kingdom, was openly unfaithful and turned away from God. But Judah, the southern kingdom, was unfaithful in a deceptive way, pretending to be loyal. The phrase "has shown herself more righteous" means that Israel was less guilty than Judah.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had already fallen to Assyria, and Judah saw it, but did not learn from it. Judah returned to God only in pretense, with a religion that was merely for show. With this comparison God does not excuse Israel; rather, he shows how serious Judah's falsehood is. Right after this, God invites Israel to return, because he is merciful.

For today: it is not enough to appear faithful before others. God looks for a sincere heart. If we know the truth and still pretend, our failure is serious. But the door remains open: we can admit our sin and turn back to God with all our heart.
exp.4:3:
Then the prophet says: "I thought, surely these are only the poor; they have played the fool, because they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God."

Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a complaint to God. He sees that the people do not change, not even after punishment. At first he thinks the common people fail for lack of teaching. Then, in the next verse, he will go to the leading men, but they too have broken free of God's rule and rebelled against him.

For today: learning God's word is important, but knowing it is not enough. Let us examine whether, besides knowing what God asks, we are willing to obey him and to receive his correction with humility.
exp.14:6:
God says that he will scatter his people with a winnowing fork at the gates of the land. A winnowing fork was a tool used to toss threshed grain into the air so the wind could carry off the chaff. In this picture, God sends his people far off, to the very edges of the land, to its gates and borders.

The verbs describe the consequences plainly. To bereave means to leave someone without children, and to destroy means to bring to ruin. These are the losses God says will fall on people who have not turned from their ways.

The Lord speaks here through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah and Jerusalem had turned away from God for a long time, and he had repeatedly warned them of judgment. The verses around this one speak of widows, losses, and terror. Scholars understand this as the announcement of the invasion that would come upon Judah.

For today, let us not mistake God's patience for permission to carry on as before. If you sense God calling you to return to him, do not put it off. He receives with grace anyone who truly repents.
exp.3:5:
Tell the people to raise a warning flag in Zion, to seek refuge and not delay, because God is about to bring disaster from the north, a terrible destruction. The meaning of "north" here is clear from the verse itself, and the word for destruction describes complete ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier He called them to return to Him wholeheartedly, but they did not do so. Now He warns of the judgment that is coming. Many understand that the enemy from the north was Babylon, though the text does not name it here.

For today: do not put off what God asks you to correct. If you feel He is calling you to come back to Him, respond today with humility and sincerity, before the consequences arrive. His warning is a sign of care, not only of anger.
exp.42:11:
He says that God himself will set fire to the temples of the gods of Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar will burn those temples and take the gods away as captives. Nebuchadnezzar will wrap the land of Egypt around himself the way a shepherd wraps himself in his garment: he will take it with ease. Then he will depart from there unscathed, that is, without being stopped or harmed.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf in Tahpanhes, Egypt. A group of Jews had fled there, against the prophet's advice, out of fear of Babylon. God warns them that Egypt will not be a safe refuge. He calls Nebuchadnezzar "my servant," because he would use him as an instrument of judgment, even though that king did not know the Lord.

For today: do not place your security in places, people, or things that seem strong. Only God is a firm refuge. Before making a decision out of fear, pray and seek his guidance.
exp.31:6:
Jeremiah recounts what God had told him: his cousin Hanamel, the son of his uncle Shallum, would come to ask him to buy a field in Anathoth. The phrases "my field" and "the right of redemption" refer to the family land and the right of a relative to buy it back, so that it would stay within the family.

Jeremiah is held prisoner in the courtyard of the guard, while Jerusalem is under siege by the Babylonians. God warns him beforehand, and when Hanamel arrives, Jeremiah recognizes that it was the word of the LORD. Buying that field in a land about to be conquered was a sign that, after the punishment, God would bring His people back to the land.

For today: even when everything seems lost, we can take small steps of faith and obedience, trusting that God keeps His promises. He warns us and guides us, even in difficult times.
exp.12:16:
He says that if the people do not listen to this warning, the prophet will weep in secret, with deep sorrow, because of their pride. His eyes will overflow with tears because God's people, compared to a flock, have been taken captive. The word "pride" here refers to a stubborn, arrogant attitude, and the picture of tears overflowing shows how much he grieves.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the message of the Lord to Judah. Earlier he had urged them to humble themselves and give glory to God, but they resisted. The verses that follow announce the exile. Some think the weeping belongs only to the prophet, while others hold that it also reflects the grief of God; the text allows us to see both.

When someone turns away from God out of pride, we should not look on them with contempt but with compassion. We can warn them with humility, pray for them, and weep over them with love, not with harshness.
exp.25:7:
It says that when Jeremiah had finished telling all the people everything the Lord had commanded him to say, the priests, the prophets, and all the people seized him. "Seized him" means they grabbed hold of him and took him into custody. They were shouting, "You must surely die!" That is, they were certain he was going to be put to death.

The context is Jeremiah's message in the temple, in the time of King Jehoiakim. God warned that if the people did not repent, the temple would be destroyed like Shiloh, a place where the tabernacle once stood. The religious leaders were offended because they trusted that the temple would protect them. They rejected the message and wanted to silence the messenger.

For today: God's truth sometimes makes us uncomfortable, especially when it touches our pride or our false sense of security. Instead of responding with anger, we can listen with humility, examine our hearts, and turn back to God.
exp.30:7:
God says that He Himself will bring His people back from the north and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth. He will leave no one behind: not the blind, not the lame, not the women who are expecting or who are in labor. They will return together as a great assembly.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel were scattered and exiled because of their sin, but God promises them restoration. Ephraim names the northern kingdom, and the passage calls it God's firstborn, that is, a very beloved son. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of complete salvation in Christ, although this is understood in various ways.

For today: God takes special care of the weak and the weary. If you feel far away or without strength, you can return to Him with confidence, because He Himself seeks you out and walks with you on the way.
exp.6:31:
God announces that a time is coming when the place called Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, will no longer be known by that name. It will be called the Valley of Slaughter. So many will die that they will be buried there until there is no more room.

The word "defile" in the verse means to make something dirty or unclean.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had done terrible things: in Topheth they burned their own children in rituals, something God never commanded. They had also filled the temple with their idols. The announcement is a judgment: the place of their sin would become the place of their punishment.

For today: God takes seriously the harm we do to the innocent and false worship. It is worth asking ourselves what things we put above God, and whether for their sake we neglect those we are called to care for. He also always calls people to repentance before judgment.
exp.7:12:
God says he will completely bring an end to his people. The phrase about gathering them all together, the way a harvest is gathered in, describes destroying them all at once. He uses the picture of a vine with no grapes, a fig tree with no figs, and leaves that wither: signs of a dry field with no fruit. The words about what he has given them being lost to them mean that they will lose the blessings God had given.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were living in sin, and their leaders kept saying "peace, peace" to calm the people, even though there was no true peace. They felt no shame for their wrongdoing. Some scholars see here a warning of the judgment that would come upon Judah.

For today: God looks for real fruit, not just appearance. If something in your life is wrong, do not cover it with pretty words. Acknowledge it with humility, ask God for forgiveness, and let yourself be corrected before the damage grows.
exp.6:25:
This verse says that the people would not listen to God or pay attention to him. The Berean Standard Bible speaks of stiffening their necks, which means becoming stubborn, like someone who holds his neck rigid so as not to bow his head. Paying attention with a willingness to obey is what the verse says they refused to do. The verse also says that this generation did more evil than their fathers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in Jerusalem, before the fall of Judah. The people believed they were secure because they had the temple, but they continued in injustice and idolatry. God reminds them that for generations he had sent them prophets persistently, and yet there was no change.

For today: when a word from God makes us uncomfortable, we should not reject it out of pride. Let us ask him for a heart ready to listen, and let us obey promptly, even when changing is costly.
exp.24:31:
This verse says that God's judgment will spread from one nation to another, like a violent storm rising from the most distant parts of the earth. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" is a title that presents God as the Lord who commands all power.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf, probably shortly before Babylon came to rule the region. Before this chapter, the people of Judah had for years refused the calls to turn back to God. Here the message widens: God, as Judge of the whole earth, calls all the nations to account, and their leaders will also be held responsible.

For today: God takes justice seriously and does not overlook evil. You can examine your life with humility, correct what He shows you, and trust that He is a righteous Judge.
exp.41:16:
It says that all who decide to go to Egypt to live there as foreigners will die by war, famine, or disease. "Resolve to go" means deciding to go; "reside" means living there for a time; "sword" is war; "plague" is a deadly outbreak of disease. Not one of them will survive or escape the disaster God brings on them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon, and the survivors of Judah were afraid and wanted to flee to Egypt. They asked Jeremiah to pray for them and promised to obey. God answers that they should stay in the land, and warns them that fleeing would not save them. Some scholars note that they were already inclined to go to Egypt even before hearing the answer.

We often look for security in a place or plan of our own, instead of obeying God. Before deciding something important, ask God sincerely, and be prepared to obey his answer, even when it is frightening.
exp.49:1:
The passage tells the reader that God commands the announcement to go out to all the nations, without holding anything back, and that a banner is to be raised as a signal, declaring that Babylon has been captured. "Bel" and "Marduk" were the names of Babylon's chief god, and the carved images and idols were the figures the people bowed down to. The text affirms that these gods were put to shame and shattered.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had overpowered Judah and destroyed Jerusalem, and it trusted in its strength and in its gods. This message announces that its fall comes from the hand of the God of Israel. It is spoken as though it had already happened, to show that it is certain. The verses that follow speak of God's people returning in tears to seek him.

For today: Whatever we put in place of God, such as money, success, or power, sooner or later falls. Today you can ask yourself what you truly trust in, and place your hope again in God, who does not fail.
exp.47:2:
This verse describes a cry of anguish heard from Horonaim, a city of Moab. The words "devastation" and "great destruction" speak of total ruin, like something smashed to pieces. It is as if the prophet hears from a distance the weeping of a people who are losing everything.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, announcing what the LORD says about Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Moab trusted in its cities, its strongholds, and its pride, and the chapter declares that all of it will fall. Scholars do not agree on every historical detail of when and how this happened, but the central message is clear: no human strength is secure without God.

For today: check where you place your security, whether money, work, or achievements. Those things can fail, but God remains. Trust Him first, with humility.
exp.50:60:
Jeremiah tells Seraiah that, when he gets to Babylon, he is to see the city and read aloud all the words Jeremiah has written against it.

Jeremiah is the prophet who is speaking. Seraiah was an officer who traveled with King Zedekiah to Babylon. The exact role he held is uncertain: some think he helped organize the trip and the places where they would stop. Jeremiah asks him to read the message out loud there, so that it would be clear that God would judge Babylon, the power that then ruled the world.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever, and that God's words are fulfilled in their time. When evil seems strong, we can trust God and remain faithful, as Seraiah did, even in difficult places.
exp.7:13:
Here the people ask themselves, "Why are we just sitting here?" They propose to gather together and flee to the fortified cities, but their words reveal a grim expectation: that they would perish there. Then they admit that the Lord has doomed them and given them poisoned water to drink. They acknowledge that all of this has happened because they sinned against the Lord.

Here the people of Judah speak, although some understand it to be the prophet Jeremiah speaking on their behalf. God has just said that judgment is coming because of their rebellion and because they did not even feel shame. The fortified cities seemed like a way out, but the verses that follow show that the enemy would come anyway.

For today: when a crisis arrives, let us not first run to our human refuges. Let us honestly acknowledge our faults and return to God, who forgives those who repent.
exp.12:13:
God says that he will smash his people, causing them to crash against one another, fathers and sons alike. He declares that he will allow no mercy, pity, or compassion to stand in the way of the punishment. The statement that nothing will keep him from destroying them is the heart of the verse: no one will be spared.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem, including kings, priests, and prophets. The image of wineskins full of wine announces that everyone will be left reeling from the judgment, stumbling with no way out. The cause is their pride and their persistent rebellion, despite the warnings. The verses that follow call them to humble themselves and give glory to God before the darkness comes.

For today: do not harden your heart when God speaks to you. If He corrects you through His Word, respond quickly with humility and repentance, while there is still time and light.
exp.50:9:
The LORD has brought forth our vindication, that is, he has shown everyone that his people were in the right and that he defends them. That is why everyone is invited: "Come, let us tell in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem, what the LORD our God has accomplished." To bring something out into the open means to make it visible, to reveal it.

Here the Israelites in exile are speaking, or the prophet on their behalf, in view of the fall of Babylon. That nation had oppressed them, and now God is acting against it. Some understand the "vindication" as the proving of the people's innocence, not as meaning they were perfect; the text does not elaborate further.

For today: when you go through injustice, trust that God sees and can act in his own time. And when he works in your favor, do not keep it to yourself: tell it in your church or with your family, to encourage others and to give him thanks.
exp.16:10:
It says that whoever gains wealth unjustly is like a partridge that sits on eggs it did not lay. In the end, what he has gathered does not stay with him. "Gathers" here means collects or piles up. The end of life is the close of one's days, and a fool is someone who lacks sense. His riches will desert him in the middle of his days, and in the end he will be seen as a fool. Scholars explain the image of the partridge in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he reminded them that the heart deceives and that God examines everything. He gives to each person according to his deeds. For this reason he warns that gaining by injustice brings no security, and that only God is the true hope.

For today: before you earn money, ask yourself whether you are doing it with honesty. Work with integrity and place your security in God, not in what you have.
exp.43:26:
God says he is "watching over" the Jews who went to Egypt, but not to care for them. He is watching to bring harm on them. "Watching over" here means keeping close and careful attention. "By sword or famine" means they will die by the sword or by hunger, and "until they are finished off" means that almost all of them will perish. Even so, the next verse mentions that a few will escape and return to Judah.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Jews had fled to Egypt, and there they were worshiping the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess, and keeping vows made to her. God warns them because they had turned away from him despite many earlier warnings.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously. It is worth examining whether we give him first place or look for security in other things, and returning to him with humility while there is still time.
exp.49:35:
It says God will send judgment, like a sword, against the false prophets of Babylon. They will become fools, because their predictions will fail. The sword will also fall on her warriors, and they will be filled with terror, overcome by fear and destroyed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Israel and Judah, and trusted in its military power and in its wise men and diviners. God promises to defend his people, for their Redeemer is strong. Scholars understand that the passage announces the fall of Babylon, and some also see a broader meaning about judgment on all human pride against God.

For today: do not put your security in horoscopes, fortune-tellers, or your own strength. Trust in God, who cares for his people and rules over every human power.
exp.49:31:
The verse says the arrogant one, that is Babylon, will stumble and fall with no one to pick him up. God promises to kindle a fire in his cities that will consume all those around him. The word "arrogant" here refers to someone who thinks himself above everyone else.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon. This empire had oppressed Israel and Judah and refused to release the captives. God presents himself as the strong Redeemer who will defend the cause of his people. The fire can be understood as an image of judgment, and scholars debate how it was fulfilled in history.

For today: pride prepares us for a fall, but God cares for those who suffer injustice. Today you can ask him to free you from pride and trust that he defends the oppressed.
exp.0:11:
God tells Jeremiah that he has observed correctly. The phrase "I am watching over my word" means that God stays alert to what he has said and is active in making sure it is carried out. "To accomplish it" means to carry it through and make it come true.

God has just called Jeremiah as a prophet and shows him a branch of an almond tree. In Hebrew, the word for "almond tree" sounds like the word for "watching" or "being awake." The almond is one of the first trees to bloom at the end of winter. Through this, God assures a frightened young man that he is not speaking into empty air: what he has promised and warned will happen. Afterward comes the announcement of judgment that will come from the north.

We can trust that God does what he says. When one of his promises seems slow in coming, let us remember that he watches over his word, and in the meantime let us stay faithful with patience.
exp.18:9:
God gives Jeremiah a command: he is to shatter a clay jar while the men who are with him watch. "Men" here means the men who accompany him, and the "jar" is a clay vessel that has been fired and hardened. It is a sign that everyone present could see and understand.

The LORD speaks, and he gives the order to the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah had taken some elders and priests to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where the people had practiced idolatry and shed innocent blood. God wanted them to see a clear sign: just as a broken clay jar cannot be repaired, Jerusalem would be destroyed because of its rebellion. Some scholars point out that the jar was dry and hardened, which underlines how final the judgment would be.

Today we can learn that God speaks to us with seriousness and calls us to return to him while there is still time. Let us not harden our hearts; let us hand over to him today whatever pulls us away from him, and let him shape us.
exp.50:63:
In this verse, Babylon is said to "sink," meaning she will go under like something dropped into deep water and never come back up. She will not rise again from the disaster that God brings upon her. "Her people will grow weary" means they will be worn out, defeated, and without strength. The final sentence marks the end of Jeremiah's words in this book.

Jeremiah gave Seraiah, an officer who was traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah, a scroll announcing that city's fall. He was to read it there, tie a stone to it, and throw it into the Euphrates. It was a symbolic act: just as the scroll would sink, Babylon would fall. Interpreters see here a sign that God judges proud empires, even though today they appear powerful.

For today: no human power lasts forever. We can trust that God acts with justice, so we do not need to fear those who seem invincible or live with envy or bitterness.
exp.21:22:
It says that someone lives calm and secure, like a bird that builds its nest high in the cedars of Lebanon. But that comfort will not last. When the pains come, they will groan with anguish, a pain as strong as that of a woman in labor. The word "groan" here means they will cry out with deep suffering.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jerusalem and its royal family, and the following verse mentions Coniah, king of Judah. The cedars of Lebanon probably point to the luxurious royal palaces, built with that wood. God spoke to them when things were going well, but they would not listen to him. That is why judgment will come through Babylon.

For today: when everything is going well, it is easy to ignore God. Use times of calm to listen to him and obey him, instead of trusting only in your own security.
exp.50:23:
God promises that he will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea for all the evil they did in Zion, and he will do it before his people's very eyes. Here "repay" means to give just recompense. "Chaldea" is another name for the land and people of Babylon.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and taken the people of Judah into exile. Earlier in this chapter, God uses Babylon as a hammer that breaks nations, and now he says that she too will answer for her violence. Scholars understand that the fulfillment came with the fall of the empire, though some also see a broader meaning.

For today: when we are wronged unjustly, we can hand our pain over to God and not take revenge ourselves. He sees every injustice, and his justice comes in its time. That frees us to forgive and to keep trusting.
exp.1:35:
The verse says the people are constantly changing direction and running from one plan to another. The reader's wording "How impulsive you are, constantly changing your ways!" captures this restlessness, and the next line warns that Egypt will disappoint them just as Assyria did before. Their shifting of plans and alliances is what the prophet is pointing to.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people considered themselves innocent and, instead of turning back to God, sought protection from powerful nations. God tells them those alliances will fail. Scholars agree on the general point, although the exact historical details of those alliances are explained in several ways.

For today: when you face a problem, do not jump from one solution to another looking for security everywhere except in God. Before deciding, stop, pray, and honestly acknowledge your faults. He offers a firm trust that will not leave you disappointed.
exp.51:12:
This verse tells that Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, set fire to the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. The phrase "every significant building" refers to every important structure in the city.

Jeremiah 52 is a historical summary that closes the book. The writer records the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, just as Jeremiah had warned for years. The people had ignored God's calls to return to Him, and judgment came. It is a sad account, but it shows that God's words are fulfilled.

For today: let us not take the voice of God lightly. If He corrects us through His Word or through wise people, it is better to listen in time and return to Him. His correction seeks to heal us, and His mercy is always waiting for us.
exp.51:7:
This verse tells that the army of Babylon chased King Zedekiah, who was fleeing from Jerusalem. They caught up with him on the plains of Jericho, a low area near the Jordan River. There his whole army deserted him: his soldiers left him and each went off on his own. The word "overtook" means they caught him, and "deserted" means his soldiers abandoned him and scattered rather than standing with their king.

This final chapter of Jeremiah recounts the fall of Jerusalem. The text presents it as a historical record, and several scholars think its author may have been Jeremiah or another writer who gathered these events. For years Jeremiah had warned that the king should surrender to Babylon, but Zedekiah did not heed him. Here we see the result of ignoring those warnings.

For today: when we ignore the voice of God and trust our own plans, the support we thought secure can vanish. It is better to listen in time and obey with humility.
exp.3:20:
Here the question is asked: "How long must I see the signal flag and hear the sound of the horn?" The signal flag was a sign to gather troops or to warn of danger, and the horn sounded the alarm. The words "How long must I" are a cry of weariness and anguish before a war that does not end.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, the prophet, and his grief is very deep, as his earlier words about his inner being show. He announces the judgment that is coming upon Judah. The verses that follow explain the cause: the people did not know God and became skilled at doing evil. Some understand that Jeremiah also expresses God's grief over his people.

For today: do not ignore the alarms God sends, such as your conscience or his Word. And if the evil around you grieves you, weep and pray for others, as Jeremiah did.
exp.42:6:
This verse tells how the group led by Johanan went down to Egypt, even though God had told them not to go. Tahpanhes is an Egyptian city, today written Tafnes, in the Nile delta. The phrase "because they did not obey the voice of the LORD" means they ignored what God had commanded through Jeremiah.

After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and Gedaliah, the governor, was killed, the people feared reprisals. They asked Jeremiah to pray, and they promised to obey God. He answered that they should stay in Judah and that God would protect them. But Johanan and the others said Jeremiah was lying, and they left anyway, taking him with them by force.

For today: sometimes we ask God for direction, but we have already decided what we want to do. Before we pray, let us ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey, even when his answer frightens us.
exp.43:20:
Jeremiah asks a question to show that the answer is obvious: of course God remembered. The incense here means smoke offered as a sacrifice. He says that everyone, from the common people up to the kings and officials, burned incense to other gods in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. God saw all of it and did not forget.

Jeremiah is speaking to the people who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. They say that things went better for them when they worshiped the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess, and that their husbands agreed with them. Jeremiah answers that the ruin of their land was the result of that sin and of not obeying God.

For today: do not think that God overlooks what becomes custom. Examine which practices you have accepted only out of tradition or because they are common, and return simply to obeying his Word.
exp.22:20:
God says that there were prophets who rushed out to speak in his name, but he never sent them and never gave them any message. The word "have run" describes people who were in a hurry, very busy and active. "Prophesied" means they announced messages as if they came from God.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah in the days before the fall of Judah. Many prophets told the people that everything would be fine, even though they were still living in sin. God rebukes them because their words came from their own imagination and not from his presence. That is why the people did not repent.

Today we can learn not to trust a voice just because it sounds confident or is full of activity. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible and to spend time in God's presence. And if we speak on his behalf, let us do it with humility and faithfulness to his Word.
exp.16:18:
God tells Jeremiah to go and stand at the gate of the people, the gate through which the kings of Judah go in and out. He is also to stand at all the other gates of Jerusalem.

Here "the LORD" is the name God uses for himself.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the assignment. The gates were very busy places, where kings and ordinary people passed through. That made them an ideal place to deliver a message to everyone. What follows is a call to keep the Sabbath. It is not known for certain which gate this was.

For today: God wants his word to reach everyone, without distinction. We can speak of him simply in the places where we live each day, with respect and with love, and first obey him ourselves.
exp.5:26:
God tells Jeremiah that he has appointed him to examine his people the way someone tests ore. That means Jeremiah is placed as someone who watches closely and tests what he finds. "So you may know" means he will observe them carefully, and "try their ways" means he will assess how they live and what conduct they follow.

God speaks to Jeremiah just before the enemy invasion he announced. The people resist changing. For this reason, the prophet must look honestly at their condition, the way a tester examines ore. The verses that follow show the result: the people are like metal that is not refined.

For today: before judging others, examine your own way honestly before God. Ask him to show you what you need to correct, and respond with humility and obedience.
exp.49:39:
It says that Babylon will be destroyed just as Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were, when God overthrew them, that is, brought them down completely. No one will live there again, not a single person, and no man will remain there.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a proud empire, full of idols, that oppressed Judah. The prophet announces that a people from the north will come to judge it. Scholars explain that the total desolation was fulfilled gradually, and some still debate how to understand each detail.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, is above God. This invites us not to trust in money, success, or modern idols, but in the One who is just and cares for his people.
exp.40:16:
They went and stayed at Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, as a stop on the way to Egypt. Their plan was to move on, so the stay was meant to be temporary. The verse says they "stayed," which means they remained there for a while. The name Geruth Chimham is usually taken to mean a place of lodging or an inn, though its exact meaning is uncertain.

This is where the narrator comes in. Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, had been murdered by Ishmael. Johanan rescued the people, but he feared the Chaldeans would take revenge. That is why they were thinking of fleeing to Egypt. Later, in chapter 42, they ask God for guidance through Jeremiah, though it seems they were already inclined to leave.

For today: fear can lead us to decide before we pray. Before we act, let us seek God with a heart willing to obey, even if his answer is not the one we were expecting.
exp.39:11:
This verse tells that the Jews who had been scattered to other countries came back to the land of Judah. They arrived where Gedaliah was, at Mizpah, and gathered an abundance of wine grapes and summer fruit. The word "returned" in the verse means coming back, and "banished" means forced to leave their homes, and "gathered" here means harvested.

It is part of the account of the prophet Jeremiah after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonians had left poor people in the land and had appointed Gedaliah as governor. When they heard this, many scattered Jews came back. The text does not say that God approved everything that happened afterward, but it shows a brief time of calm and provision.

Today we can see that God can give us moments of rest and abundance after difficult times. We should receive them with gratitude, but also with attention, because the account that follows shows that Gedaliah did not heed the warnings. Let us be thankful and wise.
exp.33:17:
God says he is going to hand over the people who broke his covenant. They had made a solemn promise in his presence, cutting a calf in two and passing between its pieces. "Broke" means violated the terms, and the promise was not kept.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. The people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but then they took them back into slavery. Passing between the pieces of the animal was an ancient way of sealing a covenant, as if saying: "may this happen to me if I do not keep my word." God takes that promise seriously.

Today, this reminds us that our word matters before God. If we have promised something, especially something that protects or frees others, we should keep it. If we have failed, it is good to acknowledge it and make it right with humility.
exp.7:1:
