Jeremiah 8:2 says that bones taken out of the tombs will be spread out under the sun, the moon, and all the stars of heaven. These are the very things this people loved, served, followed, consulted, and worshiped. Their bones will not be gathered up or buried, but will lie on the ground like dung.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before Jerusalem fell. Judah had turned away from God to worship the heavenly bodies and idols. For that people, being left unburied was a terrible dishonor. The punishment shows how serious their idolatry was, and their own "gods" could not help them.

For today: examine what you give your love, your time, and your decisions to. What we put in God's place cannot save us. Return today to serving Him alone.
exp.24:16:
Jeremiah tells that he obeyed God. He took the cup from the LORD's hand and made all the nations drink from it, each one to whom the LORD had sent him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks and tells what he did after receiving God's command. The cup represents God's judgment, called "the cup of wrath." To drink from it means to receive the consequences of sin. The list begins with Jerusalem and Judah, and continues with Egypt and other nations. Many understand this as a symbolic or prophetic vision, not a literal journey through all those places, although the text does not fully clarify this.

God speaks with seriousness, but also with justice, and no one stands outside his gaze. Today we can listen to his Word with humility, without thinking ourselves exempt, and turn back to him in time. If he sends us to say something difficult, may we do so with faithfulness and love.
exp.5:27:
These verses say that the people's leaders have become hardened rebels against God. "Hardened rebels" means people who refuse to obey God and will not turn back. "Walking around as slanderers" means they go about spreading false accusations and deceiving others. "Bronze and iron" are common, hard metals, not precious ones: this is how God describes their character, hardened and without worth. "Corrupt" means they damage and spoil the people around them.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Just before this verse, he announces that a destroyer is coming upon Judah and calls the people to mourning. God appointed Jeremiah as one who tests the people, like someone who examines metals. The image continues: the refiner's fire fails to remove the impurity, and the people are left as rejected silver.

For today: when we have influence over others, at home, in the church, or at work, let us ask God for a sincere heart. May our words and example build up, not corrupt. Let us allow Him to examine and correct us.
exp.21:15:
This verse says that Josiah, the king's father, took up the cause of people who were suffering and of those who had nothing. Because of this, it went well with him. A person who is "afflicted" is someone who suffers or is mistreated, and a "needy" person is someone who lives in want. Then God asks: "Is this not what it means to know Me?" That is, knowing God is not only talking about Him, but acting as He does, with justice and compassion toward the weak.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jehoiakim, king of Judah, who was building a luxurious palace with cedar and vermilion (red paint) while he oppressed the people and sought his own gain. God compares him with his father Josiah, who did practice justice. The verses that follow announce judgment on Jehoiakim.

Today, knowing God shows in how we treat the vulnerable. Think of someone close to you who is in need or being treated unfairly, and help them in a concrete way this week.
exp.49:26:
It tells the attackers to kill all of Babylon's young bulls and send them to the slaughter. The young bulls are strong and well fed. The phrase "the time of their punishment" marks the moment when God steps in to judge. That is why the words "Woe to them!" announce that their day has come to face the consequences.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. Interpreters often see in the young bulls an image of the empire's warriors or leaders, though the text uses poetic language. The reason the passage gives is Babylon's pride against the Holy One of Israel and its treatment of his people.

For today: power and prosperity do not make us untouchable before God. We can live with humility and justice, and trust that he sees every injustice and acts in his own time.
exp.13:9:
God answers the people of Judah with judgment. "Loved to wander" means they delighted in going from place to place, chasing after other gods and alliances, and they did not restrain their feet, that is, they did not stop or turn back to God. For this reason the LORD "does not accept them," meaning He takes no pleasure in them. "Punish them for their sins" means He will hold them accountable for what they have done.

Jeremiah has just prayed for the people during a great drought, asking that God not abandon them. Here God responds. The people were saying "do not forsake us," but their lives remained far from Him. For this reason, in what follows, God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them.

For today: it is not enough to ask God for help in a crisis if we are not willing to change course. If there is something God shows you that you must leave behind, stop your feet today and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.14:4:
God asks Jerusalem three questions: who will have pity on you? Who will mourn for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare? The phrase "to ask about your welfare" was a way of greeting someone and showing concern for their well-being. The implied answer is that no one will.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces the punishment coming upon Judah for its idolatry and its rebellion. He mentions the sin of Manasseh, the king who led the people into great evil, and recalls that the people did not turn from their ways. The verse shows the pain of a judgment that would leave the city alone.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God calls us to return. And in the meantime, let us be people who care about others, who visit, comfort, and ask with kindness how they are.
exp.23:8:
He says that God will hand over Zedekiah, his officials, and the rest of the people to become a horror, an offense, a disgrace, an object of scorn and ridicule, and an object of cursing among all the kingdoms of the earth. "Horror" means something that provokes deep dread and revulsion. Their name would be used as an example of misfortune, and people would speak of them with mockery and contempt. "Banishing" them means that God will scatter them far from their homeland.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah after the first deportation to Babylon. With the image of two baskets of figs, the good ones are the exiles whom God will care for and bring back; the bad ones are Zedekiah and those who stayed behind or fled to Egypt. It was a judgment for their rebellion and their false sense of security.

For today: God is serious when he calls us to turn back to him, but he also offers a new heart. Do not harden your heart against his correction; return to him today with sincerity.
exp.45:11:
The nations have heard of Egypt's shame, and her outcry fills the earth. The word "shame" here means humiliation, and the cry spreads through the whole earth. A warrior stumbles over another warrior, and both of them fall down together.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Egypt had been defeated by Babylon at Carchemish, beside the Euphrates River. Egypt trusted in its power and its fame, but God tells them that their defeat is unavoidable. It has no cure, like a wound without remedy.

For today: let us not place our trust in strength, money or prestige, because all of that can fall in a moment. Let us instead seek refuge in God, who is the only one who never fails and who sustains the humble.
exp.26:16:
It says that the people of Judah should not listen to the false prophets. Instead of resisting Babylon, they should serve the king of Babylon and so keep their lives. Jeremiah asks: "Why should this city become a ruin?", that is, why let Jerusalem lie in ruins? Here "listen" means to pay attention and obey, and "live" means to stay alive.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God to King Zedekiah, to the priests, and to the people. The false prophets said that the vessels of the temple, carried off to Babylon, would soon be brought back. Jeremiah warns them that this is a lie. God offers them a hard path, but one that saves lives.

For today: before following a voice that tells us what we want to hear, let us compare its words with what the Bible teaches and seek wise counsel. The truth sometimes makes us uncomfortable, but it cares for us.
exp.13:19:
We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the guilt of our fathers. Here the people speak to God and admit their own wrongdoing. "Wickedness" describes a life turned away from God, and "guilt" points to the wrong that deserves blame. They recognize that they, and also their ancestors, have done wrong, and they state it plainly: "indeed, we have sinned against You."

These words come in the middle of a great drought, with famine, sickness, and war in Judah. Many understand that Jeremiah prays on behalf of the people, though some think it is the people themselves who speak. They ask for mercy, but their repentance may be incomplete, since later God does not immediately change his decision.

For today: when things go wrong, it is not enough to ask only for relief. It is good to stop, to be honest with God, and to call sin what it is, without excuses. That honesty opens the way to his forgiveness.
exp.27:6:
Jeremiah asks Hananiah to listen to him. He begins with "Nevertheless," and then goes on to say what follows in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people, that is, publicly, with everyone present.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, in front of the priests and the people. Hananiah had just prophesied that Babylon would soon fall and that the exiles and the objects of the temple would return. Jeremiah answers with a sincere "Amen," for he would very much like it to be true. But now he remembers that a prophet is tested over time and by what God actually says.

Today we may heartily wish for good news, but we should not believe something only because it pleases us. Let us weigh every message in the light of the Bible, with humility, patience, and prayer.
exp.20:8:
Whoever stays in this city will die by the sword, by famine, or by plague. But whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) who are besieging the city will live, and he will keep his life like a spoil of war.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Jerusalem falls to Nebuchadnezzar. The people had disobeyed again and again, and God sets before them a choice: the way of life or the way of death. It was a hard message, which many saw as betrayal, but it offered a way out to anyone who would believe.

For today: sometimes God asks us to trust his word even when it sounds difficult or humbling. Letting go of pride and obeying may be the path that saves us.
exp.47:38:
They will cry out in grief, "How shattered Moab is! How they wail! How Moab has turned its back in shame!" Moab will become an object of ridicule and horror to all the nations around it.

This verse says that Moab has fallen completely, and that everyone should weep aloud. Crying out is a loud wail of pain. "Shattered" means broken to pieces. Turning its back is what Moab does when it flees in defeat. The neighboring nations look at Moab and respond with mockery and amazement.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a prophecy against Moab. Earlier, the text mentions Moab's pride and its trust in itself. God says he has broken Moab like a vessel that is not pleasing. The gestures of mourning, such as shaving the head and wearing sackcloth, show deep grief. The verses that follow announce the invasion.

For today: do not trust in your success or your pride, because they can fall. Place your security in God, and treat with humility those who suffer, without mocking them.
exp.4:12:
The verse says the prophets are nothing but wind, with no message from God in them. Their wording in this version says "The prophets are but wind," so the idea is that their words are empty and carry no true word from God.

The last part of the verse is a plain statement of what should happen to them. The reader's version says, "So let their own predictions befall them." This reads as a wish that the things they announce would fall back on them.

These are probably words from the rebellious people, who mocked Jeremiah's warnings. They said that God would do nothing and that no harm would come. Some believe the statement is a kind of irony from God that turns back against them. Then God answers: his word in Jeremiah's mouth will be like fire, and the judgment would indeed come.

Today, when a truth from God makes us uncomfortable, it is tempting to call it exaggeration. It is better to listen with humility, compare it with the Bible, and let God correct our course in time.
exp.30:4:
The verse says that the people will once again plant vineyards on the hills of Samaria. Those who plant will enjoy the fruit of their labor. The idea of enjoying what they planted means they will be free to eat from it. In the law, the fruit of a newly planted tree was not eaten until the fifth year (Leviticus 19:23-25), so this speaks of waiting and reward.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Israel, the northern kingdom, whose capital was Samaria and which had been taken into exile. In the middle of pain, God promises restoration, because he loves them with an everlasting love. The vineyards speak of peace, stability, and normal life returning.

For today: when you feel that what was lost will not come back, trust that God can restore hope. Keep sowing with patience in your family, your work, and your faith, knowing that God is faithful and can bring fruit in its time.
exp.22:12:
God says he saw an offensive thing among the prophets of Samaria, meaning foolish and shameful conduct. They prophesied by Baal, a false god, and so they led God's people Israel astray. Here "astray" means led off the right path.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom, Israel, which had already fallen to Assyria. God uses it as an example to accuse the prophets of Jerusalem, who according to the context were even worse. The leaders who were supposed to guide the people led them down the wrong path, and God announces that he will hold them accountable.

For today: do not follow someone just because they speak with confidence or hold a religious position. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and if you teach others, do so with humility and faithfulness to the Word of God.
exp.29:11:
God says that the injury of his people is incurable, meaning there is no hope of cure by human means. An "injury" is a severe blow or break, and a "wound" is an open sore. The word for "incurable" means very hard to heal. The harm runs deep, and no remedy people can offer reaches it.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel, who was suffering punishment for their sin and exile. Earlier, God had promised to save them and not destroy them completely. Here he explains that their allies had abandoned them and that he himself had disciplined them for their wickedness. In this passage God is honest about how serious the problem is, and that honesty sets the stage for his promise of healing (v. 17).

For today: do not minimize your wounds or your sin, and do not look only for human remedies. Acknowledge honestly what hurts you and bring it to God, the only one who can heal what seems beyond repair.
exp.51:28:
In Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year, 832 people from Jerusalem were taken away by force into exile in Babylon. The word "exile" here means being forced to leave one's home and live in another country.

These are the final figures in the book of Jeremiah, which carefully records the three deportations of Judah. The one who records them looks back, now that Jerusalem has fallen. The numbers are small compared with other accounts, and scholars explain the difference in several ways: perhaps only a certain group of people is counted here. There is no single certain answer.

God warned through Jeremiah, and everything was fulfilled with exactness. His Word is worthy of trust, both in its warnings and in its promises. Today we can listen to him in time and obey him, knowing that he counts and remembers every person, even in the midst of pain.
exp.10:7:
They would not obey God or pay attention to what he said. Instead, each one followed the stubbornness of his own evil heart. So God says he has brought on them the curses of the covenant, the consequences he had told them would follow if they did not keep it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He asks him to proclaim in Judah and Jerusalem the words of the covenant that God made with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt. God had warned them again and again, and even so the people refused to obey. For this reason the judgment that the covenant itself warned of is coming.

For today: God speaks to us with love and patience, but we can become used to ignoring him. Today you can choose to listen to his Word and obey one specific thing, instead of only following what seems right to you or what comes naturally.
exp.6:15:
God tells the prophet Jeremiah to stop praying for the people of Judah. A "plea" here is an earnest, heartfelt request. "I will not listen to you" means that God would not grant what Jeremiah asked on their behalf at that time.

God speaks here in the well-known sermon at the temple. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they worshiped idols, such as the queen of heaven, and did not live in justice. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh and warns that judgment is coming. After a long time of rebellion and of refusing to change, the opportunity to repent was running out. Some scholars see here a judgment already decided; others see a sign of how serious their sin was.

For today: let us not trust in what is religious, such as a building or a custom, while the heart remains far from God. Right now we can turn back to Him with sincerity.
exp.8:5:
The passage says that the people live surrounded by lies. The word for "dwell" points to the place where one lives, so deception is the very air of everyday life. Because they practiced deceit so much, they refused to know God. The name of God in the verse is the LORD, written in capitals.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was full of deception, even among brothers and friends. The verses before this one show that they had grown used to lying. God says this falsehood kept them from Him. Then He announces that He will test them the way metal is tested in fire, and it grieves Him to have to do it.

For today: honesty brings us closer to God. Today you can choose to tell the truth with love, even in small things, and ask God to cleanse you from all deceit.
exp.6:1:
God tells Jeremiah to stand at the entrance of the temple and announce a message to all of Judah. The old wording is easy to clarify: "Stand in the gate" is in the verse as "stand in the gate," "proclaim" is in the verse as "proclaim," and "Hear" is in the verse as "Hear." The message is addressed to those who came in to worship God.

God is speaking, and Jeremiah is his messenger. The place was chosen on purpose: that is where the religious people were. According to the verses that follow, God wanted to correct the false confidence of those who believed they were safe simply because they had the temple, while they lived without obeying him.

For today: before going to church or praying, ask yourself whether your everyday life reflects what you say you believe. Truly worshiping includes listening to God and obeying him, not only keeping a religious custom.
exp.28:2:
This verse tells us who carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon: Elasah, son of Shaphan, and Gemariah, son of Hilkiah. King Zedekiah of Judah had sent them to King Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon. The letter was entrusted to these two men, and the verse introduces the message they carried.

Jeremiah, a prophet in Jerusalem, writes to the exiles who were already in Babylon after the first deportation. These two men were traveling on official business, and so the letter reached the captives. What follows is God's message: they should settle down and live there, because the exile would be long. The Bible gives no further details here about these messengers.

God often uses simple means and ordinary people to carry his word. Today you can be a messenger too: a phone call, a letter, or a timely word of advice can encourage someone going through a hard season.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that God's land was turned into a ruin. Laid waste and left as a wasteland is the sense here. In the reader's wording, the land is "desolate before Me, it mourns," as if it were lamenting in God's sight. And all the land is laid waste because no man takes it to heart, meaning nobody took it seriously or cared about it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His inheritance is the people of Judah and their land. God describes how the shepherds, who were the leaders, trampled it, and how the enemies came to devour it. What is serious is that no one saw it as a judgment from God or turned back to Him. Some believe that "takes it to heart" means taking it seriously.

For today: do not overlook the signs that something is wrong in your life or your surroundings. Stop, pray, examine your heart, and return to God before the harm grows.
exp.49:36:
A sword is against its horses and chariots, and against all the foreigners living among its people. They will become like women, left without strength or courage. A sword is also against its treasuries, and they will be plundered.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon for its pride, its idolatry, and its mistreatment of God's people. The verses before speak of its wise men, diviners, and warriors, and the verses after speak of idols and desolation.

For today: let us not place our security in money, strength, or fame, because all of that is fragile. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and hand our security over to God.
exp.31:14:
This verse is a promise from God: even though everything seems lost, one day people will again buy houses, fields and vineyards in that land. The word "bought" here means property being purchased and paid for, the way land changes hands in a real market. The verse does not include the phrase "the Lord of hosts" in its wording, so that is not the focus of this comment.

Jeremiah speaks by the command of God. The armies of Babylon surrounded Jerusalem, and the prophet was in prison. Even so, God asked him to buy a field from his cousin. Jeremiah instructs Baruc to keep the documents in a clay jar, so that they would last a long time. It was a sign that there would be restoration after the judgment.

For today: when you pass through a dark season, do not stop trusting God or taking steps of faith. Plan with hope, pray sincerely, and leave the future in his hands, because he keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.50:35:
God promises his people that he himself will be their defender. "I will plead your case" means that God will take up their cause and do justice. "I will take vengeance on your behalf" means that he will punish the one who wronged them. The images of drying up Babylon's sea and making its springs run dry stand for Babylon losing what supported it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem and Zion have just complained that Nebuchadnezzar devoured them and left them empty like a vessel. God answers that cry. Some think the "sea" and the "spring" refer to the Euphrates River, which ran through Babylon, though they may also be a picture of his power in general.

When you suffer an injustice, you can bring your pain to God in prayer instead of taking revenge yourself. He sees, he hears, and he will do justice in his time.
exp.1:24:
God asks his people to stop chasing idols until their feet are bare and their throat is parched. It is as if he were saying, "Stop, you are wearing yourself out." But the people answer, "It is hopeless," meaning there is no remedy. They say, "I will not stop," because they love foreign gods and intend to go after them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just compared Israel to a wild female camel or donkey in heat, running out of control. Israel denied its idolatry, and God shows them what they are really doing. The people's answer sounds like stubbornness and false hopelessness.

For today: when something wears us down and we still say, "I can no longer change," let us remember that God keeps calling. It may be an addiction, an anxiety, or an idea that has taken the place of God. Today you can stop, be honest with him, and ask him for help.
exp.28:4:
This verse says that the exiles in Babylon are to live normally: to build houses and settle down in them, to plant gardens and eat what they produce. The verb here means "build," and the call to settle down is a call to live in the houses they build. Planting gardens means sowing trees and vegetables.

It is part of a letter from the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon. He speaks in the name of the LORD. Some false prophets were saying the exile would be short, but God tells them it will be long (Jeremiah 29:10 speaks of seventy years). For that reason he asks them to put down roots and not to live waiting for an immediate way out.

For today: even in difficult times, or in circumstances we did not choose, God calls us to live with faith, working, caring for our families, and serving where we are, without putting life on hold while we wait for things to change.
exp.26:7:
This verse says that God warns any nation or kingdom that refuses to serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. A yoke is the wooden frame placed on the neck of working animals; here it stands for submission. Plague is a deadly sickness that spreads. Resistance would bring the sword, famine, and disease.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the days of King Zedekiah of Judah. God had allowed Babylon to rule the region for a time, and the false prophets were saying there would be no submission. Jeremiah urged people to accept this reality in order to save lives.

For today: when God allows a difficult situation, listening to his voice with humility is worth more than comfortable but false words. Before following a popular message, compare it with what the Bible teaches.
exp.41:10:
God tells the people not to be afraid of the king of Babylon. "Do not be afraid of him" means the same as "Be not afraid of him." God promises, "I am with you," to save them and deliver them from the king, here described as "his hand."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors feared Babylon's revenge and planned to flee to Egypt. They asked Jeremiah to consult God. The answer was to stay in the land, with the promise of protection and that God would build them up again.

For today: when fear pushes us to look for ways out on our own, we can stop and ask what God is asking of us. Obedience can be frightening, but his promise to be with us is firmer than any threat.
exp.6:12:
God says that the people have done all these evil things, even though he has spoken to them again and again. The phrase "again and again" shows that God kept pressing them with urgency and persistence, like someone who keeps returning to a message because it matters so much. Even so, they would not listen when he spoke, and they did not answer when he called.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, probably at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they were living in injustice and idolatry. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh, where the ancient sanctuary once stood, to warn them that a religious place saves no one without sincere obedience.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly listen to God or only go through the motions of religion. This week, set aside a few minutes to read the Bible calmly and ask him what he wants you to change. Then obey him in one concrete thing.
exp.1:20:
God says he planted his people like a choice vine, from the very best seed. Then he asks with grief how it could happen that they have turned into a rotten, wild vine. The question is not really asking for information. It shows sorrow and accusation, because what has grown does not match what he planted.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He reminds them that he rescued them and gave them a good beginning, yet they said "I will not serve" and went after other gods, the Baals. His question expresses how painful it is that the fruit does not match what he planted.

For today: God has given us his care and a good beginning. It is worth asking ourselves what fruit our lives are bearing, and returning to him sincerely, without excuses, so that our lives reflect the care he has shown us.
exp.35:14:
The princes, that is, the leaders and officials of the kingdom, ask Baruch to sit down and read the scroll aloud, so that they themselves may hear it. The phrase "in our hearing" means "before us." Baruch obeys and reads.

Baruch was Jeremiah's secretary, and he had written down Jeremiah's messages from God. He had already read the scroll to the people in the temple. Micaiah told what he heard, and the princes sent for him. Notice the respectful treatment: they invite him to sit down and they listen carefully. Afterward they become frightened, because they understand that the message is serious and that the king must know about it.

Today we can do the same with the Bible: listen to it calmly, without rush and with humility. Set aside a quiet moment, read a passage aloud, and ask yourself what God is asking of you.
exp.1:27:
God asks Judah with irony: "Where are the gods you made for yourselves?" He invites them to rise up and save them in their time of trouble, if they can. And he adds that Judah's gods were as numerous as its cities.

Here "save" is simply the idea of rescuing someone from danger, and "time of trouble" is a season of distress. The question "if they can" means the same as "if they are able."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people had turned away from him to worship idols of wood and stone, but when crisis came they cried out to God: "Arise and deliver us." God exposes that contradiction: they had turned their backs on him, not their faces, and yet they still expected to be rescued.

For today: we can ask ourselves where we truly place our trust: money, work, reputation, and other things. These things may help a little, but they do not sustain the soul in a crisis. It is wise to seek God now, not only when trouble arrives.
exp.49:30:
Here God says he himself is against Babylon, which he calls "you, O arrogant one," meaning proud and full of itself. The phrase "your day has come" means the time of judgment has arrived. "The time when I will punish you" makes clear that this is not a friendly visit; God comes to hold Babylon accountable. "The Lord GOD of Hosts" is a title that emphasizes his power over all things.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Israel and Judah, and the nearby passages say it grew proud against the Holy One of Israel. God promises that its pride and its violence will not go unanswered. Scholars connect this with the historical fall of Babylon, though some also see in it a symbol of human pride in general.

For today: pride makes us believe we do not need God. Today you can ask him to give you humility and to recognize that everything you have comes from him.
exp.10:3:
God reminds the people of the covenant he made with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt, out of what he calls the "iron furnace," a place of intense suffering. He told them: "Obey Me, and do everything I command you," and promised: "you will be My people, and I will be your God."

Here the LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who must announce this message to Judah and Jerusalem. God reminds them of what they promised in the covenant, because the people were not obeying him. He warns that disobedience brings consequences, but he also reminds them of his faithfulness in rescuing them.

For today: God has shown us his love and wants a relationship with us, not just words. We can ask ourselves what God has already told us in his Word that we have not yet put into practice, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.49:23:
Babylon is pictured here as a creature that walks straight into a trap without seeing it. God says he set snares for her, meaning hidden nets or traps, and she was caught before she realized what was happening. "You were found" means that she was discovered, and "caught" means she was taken captive. The reason given is that she challenged the LORD. She defied him and set herself against him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on what God said against Babylon. This empire had dominated and destroyed other peoples, including Judah, and it felt secure. The message announces that God would call it to account. The Bible says that its pride and its wickedness had consequences. Scholars often connect the fall with the arrival of the Medes and Persians, although the text is written in poetic language.

Today we can remember that feeling secure does not mean being free from error. It is wise to ask God for humility and to examine our hearts before pride blinds us.
exp.29:23:
God's fierce anger will not turn back until he has fully accomplished the purposes of his heart. His righteous wrath against sin will run its full course, and his plans will be carried out. And "in the days to come" points to a future time when the people will understand what they cannot see clearly today.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the name of the LORD. The people of Judah faced judgment for their sin, but this chapter also announces restoration. God promises that he will be their God and they will be his people. The storm falls on the wicked, and the verse shows that God finishes what he begins. Interpreters differ on what exact time "the days to come" refers to.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, trust that he has a just and good purpose. Keep obeying him with humility and ask him for patience, because some answers come with time.
exp.41:14:
Here God speaks to the small group that survived in Judah. He tells them: "Hear the word of the LORD." If they are determined to go to Egypt and live there, a serious consequence will follow. The sentence is left open, and the next verse completes it. The survivors are the ones who were left behind, the remnant.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the people fear Babylon and ask Jeremiah to pray so they will know what to do. They promise to obey. But God has already told them to stay in the land, and here he warns them against fleeing to Egypt to seek safety on their own.

Today, we sometimes ask God for direction when, deep down, we have already decided what we want. Before praying, ask yourself whether you are truly willing to obey, even if the answer frightens you. The security God gives is worth more than the security we try to find for ourselves.
exp.26:9:
What it says: God declares that the prophets who announce that Judah will not have to serve Babylon are lying. "To remove" means to take the people away from their land, and "to banish" means to force them out. These false promises would end in exile and ruin for the people.

Context: The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, toward the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah. Babylon already dominated the region. Many prophets, diviners, and enchanters claimed that everything would turn out well. God asks the people to accept the yoke of Babylon as the way to keep living in the land.

For today: Do not believe something just because it sounds encouraging. Before following a message, compare it with what the Bible teaches and ask God for wisdom. Sometimes the truth is hard, but it leads to life.
exp.37:3:
The leaders of the kingdom ask the king to put Jeremiah to death. They say he is discouraging the soldiers who are still in the city, and all the people, by the things he tells them. They accuse him of not seeking the well-being of these people, but their ruin.

The officials are speaking while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. Jeremiah was repeating what God said: the city would be handed over, and whoever surrendered would save his life. They heard a message of defeat and betrayal; in truth it was a warning from God to save lives.

Today, we sometimes reject the truth simply because it hurts or contradicts what we want to believe. Before accusing the one who corrects us, let us ask ourselves humbly whether they speak with love, and whether God may be speaking to us through that voice.
exp.46:4:
Gaza is said to be shaved bald, and Ashkelon is said to be silenced. In that time, shaving or cutting the hair was a sign of deep mourning, and the verse's images of shaved heads and self-cutting picture that grief. The prophet asks, "how long will you gash yourself?", as if to say that their sorrow seems to have no end.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against the Philistines, who lived along the coast. An invading army is announced that comes with chariots and a loud uproar, and it brings such terror that fathers do not even stop to help their children. It is not stated here with certainty who the invader is; some think of Egypt and others of Babylon. What is clear is that God allows it.

For today: let us not trust in our own strength or security, because everything can fall suddenly. It is better to trust in God and to live in humility before Him.
exp.37:23:
Zedekiah tells Jeremiah not to let anyone know about their private conversation. If Jeremiah keeps it secret, he will not die. The words "Do not let anyone know about this conversation, or you will die" mean that no one should find out what was discussed.

King Zedekiah is speaking, and he was afraid of his officials and of the Babylonians. Jeremiah had warned him that if he did not surrender, Jerusalem would be burned. The king wanted to hear from God, but he did not dare to obey in public. So he asks for silence and suggests to Jeremiah what to say if the officials ask questions.

For today: fear of other people can keep us from obeying God with courage. Let us ask him to give us faith to do what is right, even when it costs us, and to speak with truth and wisdom.
exp.6:4:
If you truly correct your ways and your deeds, and if you act justly toward one another, then God says you will be allowed to stay in this place. The verse has three key ideas to explain. "Correct" here means changing your conduct for the better. "Really" means genuinely, not just on the surface. "Act justly" means treating others fairly.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses those who came into the temple in Jerusalem confident that the place would protect them, while they lived unjustly. God asks them for a real change, not just religious words. The promise is that they could continue living in that land.

For today: faith is not measured only by attending church or saying the right phrases. Think of a relationship or task where you have been unfair or careless, such as at work, in your family, or in a dealing with a neighbor, and this week make it right with honesty.
exp.16:2:
God speaks to Judah, whom he calls "My mountain in the countryside," most likely meaning Jerusalem and its land. He announces that their wealth and treasures will be given over as plunder. The word "wealth" refers to their possessions, and "high places" were raised spots where people worshiped, often other gods. The reason given is that sin spread throughout the whole territory.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had their sin deeply marked, as if engraved in iron, and they kept worshiping idols beside trees and hills. God announces the consequences: loss of wealth and of the land, and serving their enemies. He then contrasts this with trusting in people instead of in Him.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, possessions, or people. All of that can be lost. Trust God first and ask Him to be your true foundation.
exp.1:29:
It says that God struck the people's children, but the striking was in vain, because they did not accept the discipline. The phrase "in vain" means without result, and that is why it is used here. Being "struck" speaks of painful correction. The verse also says that their own sword devoured the prophets, like a voracious lion tearing apart its prey. The prophets were messengers of God, and the people rejected them and killed them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, accusing Judah of having abandoned him to worship idols. God reminds them that the earlier punishments did not bring them back to him. Some understand that this refers to prophets killed by the people's own violence, as other passages of the Bible also tell; the text does not give names here.

Today, this verse invites us not to harden our hearts when God corrects us, whether through his Word, through wise counsel, or through the consequences of our mistakes. Ask yourself: what is God trying to teach me through this? Listening with humility leads us back to him.
exp.49:29:
It says that the young men of Babylon will fall in her streets, that is, in the public spaces of the city. Her warriors will also be silenced, meaning they will be stopped and no longer able to fight, the way a voice is silenced. This will happen "in that day," the time of God's judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, and had grown proud against the Holy One of Israel. For this reason God announces that he will judge her, and his people receive hope that evil will not have the last word.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, success, or power, because none of these protects us from God. We can ask him for humility in what we do, and rest in the knowledge that he will do justice in his own time, without our having to take revenge.
exp.2:6:
God says he waited for Israel, the northern kingdom, to come back to him after all her unfaithfulness. He said to her, "Turn back to me," but she did not return. The word "rebellious" in the older translations describes a person who turns her back and walks away. Meanwhile, her sister Judah, the southern kingdom, was watching what was happening.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the days of King Josiah. God compares the idolatry of his people to an unfaithful wife. Israel had already fallen, and God wanted Judah to learn from that example. As we will see in the verses that follow, Judah saw, but did not repent.

For today: it is not enough to see the consequences in the lives of others; God invites us to correct our course in time. If there is something that pulls you away from him, listen today to his call to return, because his patience is real.
exp.50:0:
God says that he himself will stir up a destroying spirit against Babylon and against the people of Leb-kamai. The image is of a force that sweeps through and clears everything away.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been used by God to discipline Judah, but it had also been proud and cruel toward the nations. So God announces that now Babylon itself will face judgment. The verses that follow speak of winnowers who scatter and empty the land, the way grain is cleaned.

For today: no human power or pride lasts forever. We can trust that God sees injustice and has the last word. In the meantime, let us ask him for humility so that we do not set ourselves against him.
exp.30:38:
A measuring line, meaning a cord used to mark out land and buildings, will once again stretch out straight to the hill of Gareb and then turn toward Goah. The word for "hill" is the same as the word used in the verse. It is not known for certain where Gareb and Goah were. They were probably places near Jerusalem, but scholars do not agree on their exact location.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises that Jerusalem will be rebuilt and dedicated to the Lord, even after the punishment. Measuring the city shows that God has a detailed plan to restore it. Earlier he said that he will not reject Israel forever, and this promise is part of the new covenant of this chapter.

For today: when you feel that your life has been left in ruins, remember that God knows how to restore with care and purpose. Place yourself in his hands and trust that he leaves nothing unmeasured.
exp.26:18:
This verse begins a message from God about the bronze objects that were still in the temple: the pillars, the sea (a large basin of water for the priests), the bases (wheeled stands for the basins) and the other articles. The word "articles" refers to the utensils or containers used in worship.

Jeremiah speaks to the people and to the priests. Some false prophets were saying that these objects, which Nebuchadnezzar had earlier carried away, would soon be returned. Jeremiah warns them not to listen, because that hope was an illusion. God announces that what remained would also be carried off to Babylon. The message aims to lead Judah to submit and live, instead of staying deceived.

For today: Before believing a religious message that sounds pleasant, let us compare it with what God has said in his Word. The truth, even when it hurts, protects us and leads us to obey and to live.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that the people of Jeremiah's time had done more evil than their ancestors. The phrase "stubbornness of his evil heart" describes a heart inclined toward wrong, and each person followed his own inclinations instead of obeying God. The last clause of the verse, "instead of obeying Me," shows that the problem was refusing to listen to God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, before the exile in Babylon. The people would ask why such punishment was coming. God answers that their fathers abandoned him to serve other gods, and that they, instead of learning from that, followed their own path even more. For this reason he announces that they will be carried off to another land.

For today: it is not enough to say that we are better than others or that we have inherited a good faith. It is worth asking ourselves honestly whether we really obey God or simply follow what our heart dictates. Read his Word, pray, and ask for direction to obey him.
exp.35:6:
Jeremiah hopes that the people will bring their petition humbly before the LORD and that each one will turn away from his wicked way. The words "perhaps" and "it may be" mean that their plea might reach God, though nothing is certain. The word "turn" in the verse means turning back from the wrong path. Jeremiah also warns that the anger and fury the LORD has pronounced against this people are very great.

Jeremiah speaks from prison and cannot go into the temple. So he asks Baruch, his scribe, to read the scroll with God's messages aloud in public. He takes advantage of the day of fasting, when many people would be gathered together. He says "perhaps" because the turning back depended on the people's response; it was not guaranteed.

For today: God speaks to us clearly because he desires that we turn back to him. If there is something in your life that God shows you, do not harden your heart against it. Come to him with sincerity, pray, and take one concrete step of change.
exp.38:10:
This verse says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had given orders about Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard. The "captain of the guard" was a high official of the king. The orders themselves are given in the next verse.

The narrator of the book explains what happened when Jerusalem fell. While many were taken to Babylon, Jeremiah had announced for years that this would happen. Here we see that the Babylonian king gave instructions to protect him. The text does not explain why he did this; some think he had heard of Jeremiah's words about submitting to Babylon, but this is not stated here.

God can care for his faithful servants even in very difficult times, and even use people who do not know him. We can trust that he sustains us, even when everything around us seems to be falling apart.
exp.1:34:
The people of Judah claim: "I am innocent, so God's anger will turn away from me." But God answers that he will judge them, precisely because they say "I have not sinned." Judging someone means presenting a formal case against them. "His anger will turn from me" means they expect God's anger to have already passed.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had sought other gods and political alliances, and even had the blood of innocent people on her clothes. Even so, she considered herself free of guilt and did not repent. That is why God confronts her.

For today: denying our failures keeps us from forgiveness. We can ask God to show us honestly what is in our hearts, and confess it without excuses, trusting that he forgives those who repent.
exp.35:15:
This verse tells how the officials, when they had heard the message of the scroll, turned to one another in fear and looked at each other in alarm. Their reaction shows that each of them was frightened, and that they felt the fear together. Then they said to Baruch that they must report all these words to the king.

The officials were the senior ranking men of King Jehoiakim. Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, had just read to them the warning words that God had given through the prophet. They understood that the message was serious and that the king needed to know it. Later on we see that the king reacted very differently.

For today: when God's Word touches our hearts, let us not ignore it or let it pass by. Let it move us to respond with reverence, and let us answer with obedience and humility.
exp.50:36:
This verse says that Babylon will be turned into ruins. A "heap of rubble" is broken stone and debris piled up; "jackals" are wild animals of the wild dog family; "object of horror" is something that makes whoever sees it shudder; and "scorn" is the mocking contempt people show toward something they despise. "Without inhabitant" means without people living in it.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Judah and destroyed Jerusalem, and the people cried out for justice. God answers that he will judge the cause of his people. It is a prophecy of judgment against a proud and violent nation. Scholars debate how and when it was fulfilled in exact detail, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. We can hand our pain over to him without taking revenge, trusting that he judges with justice, and examine whether we ourselves walk in pride.
exp.32:16:
God promises that there will always be a descendant of David to rule over the people of Israel. "David will never lack a man" means that the line of kings will never come to an end. "Sit on the throne" speaks of ruling with authority. The words "the LORD" name God himself, written in capital letters in this translation.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were living through a painful time, close to the fall of Jerusalem, and it seemed that everything had been lost. God answers with hope: he announces the "Branch of righteousness," a shoot from David. Many Christians see here a promise fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, remember that God keeps what he promises, even when it takes time or seems impossible. You can rest in his faithfulness and pray with confidence, waiting on Christ, the King who never fails.
exp.50:6:
Babylon was like a gold cup in the LORD's hand. It was glorious and powerful, but God was the one who used it. Its wine made the whole earth drunk, that is, left the nations confused and under its control. The verse says the nations went mad, meaning they were left stunned and unable to think clearly.

The prophet Jeremiah announces a message from the LORD against Babylon, the empire that had conquered Judah. God had not abandoned his people, even though they had sinned. Now he calls them to leave Babylon, because its punishment was coming. Some understand that God used Babylon as an instrument and then judged it for its wickedness.

For today: The bright and powerful things of this world can confuse us and dull the heart. Ask yourself what influences are making you drunk on ideas or desires that pull you away from God, and take one concrete step to separate yourself from them.
exp.9:23:
This verse is a prayer. The speaker asks God to correct him, but only with justice and measure, not in anger. "Justice" means fair and balanced, not harsh. "Anger" here is strong wrath, and "bring me to nothing" means being utterly destroyed.

The one praying is Jeremiah, speaking on behalf of his people. An invasion is announced from the north that will leave the cities of Judah in ruins. Jeremiah acknowledges that human beings do not control their own path and asks for mercy in the midst of punishment. Some understand that he prays for himself, and others, that he prays as the voice of the people.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not run from God. Come near with humility and ask him to correct you with fairness and mercy, trusting that his purpose is to restore you, not to destroy you.
exp.0:8:
God reaches out his hand, touches Jeremiah's mouth, and tells him that he has put his words in it. The phrase "and said to me" simply means that God told him. It is a gesture that shows Jeremiah will not speak on his own, but will carry God's message.

The Lord speaks, and he speaks to Jeremiah, a young man who has just been called as a prophet. Jeremiah felt very small and afraid, and he had said that he was only a child. God answers by promising that he will be with him and will deliver him. Then he gives him a very great task for his people and the nations. Many understand the touch on the mouth as a symbolic sign of his calling, not necessarily as something physical.

Today, when God asks us to speak or act and we feel unable, we can remember that he does not leave us alone. Before speaking, it is good to listen to his Word and let it guide what we say.
exp.49:15:
This verse says that Babylon will be left without those who sow and reap. "Cut off" can be read as "removed" or "cut down." The sickle is the curved tool used to cut the grain at harvest. The "oppressor's sword" speaks of the violence of a cruel ruler. The foreigners who lived in Babylon, frightened by the war, would each turn back to his own people and his own land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon, which had dominated many nations and mistreated Israel, would be judged for its pride and its sin. The verses that follow recall that Assyria and Babylon had devoured Israel, but God would also call them to account.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered forever. If someone has hurt you, trust that God is just, bring your pain to him, and avoid taking revenge on your own. Ask him to help you live with humility and to treat others well.
exp.21:16:
It says that Jehoiakim had his eyes and his heart set on nothing except his own dishonest gain. He also sought to shed innocent blood, to practice extortion and oppression, and to do others harm.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, king of Judah, was building a luxurious palace while the people suffered. God compares him with his father Josiah, who defended the poor and the afflicted. For God, knowing Him is seen in doing justice. So He announces that Jehoiakim will have a dishonorable end.

For today: examine where you set your heart and your time. If you have any power, whether at home, at work or in the church, use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them.
exp.48:23:
Damascus has become weak and has turned to run. Panic has gripped the city. Anguish and pain have seized it, like a woman in labor. The city loses its courage. To become weak here means to be left without strength because of fear. The city wants to flee, but a trembling takes hold of it. The picture is of sudden suffering that cannot be stopped, like the pain of a woman giving birth.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is part of a series of warnings against nations that border Israel. Damascus, capital of Syria (Aram), receives news of a judgment that is coming. Nearby passages mention cities that melt with fear at the "bad news." The text does not say here who would carry out the punishment, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: the strongest cities can fall in a moment. Our true security is not in power, fame, or money, but in God. Today you can bring your fears to Him in prayer and trust in Him.
exp.8:24:
This verse says that God announces a time when he will call to account, or "punish" in judgment, all who are circumcised only in the flesh. "Punish" here means that God will step in to judge. The verse speaks of people who carry the outward sign of circumcision but whose hearts are not right with God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he had said that the only thing worth boasting about is knowing him and his mercy, justice, and righteousness. The verses that follow name Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, and Moab, and say that Israel was "uncircumcised in heart": having an outward sign without a heart given to God.

For today: having religious signs, such as baptism, church membership, or customs, is not enough. Ask yourself honestly whether your heart truly seeks to know God and to live with mercy and justice.
exp.9:1:
God tells his people not to copy the religious customs of the nations around them. They also must not be terrified by the signs in the heavens, such as eclipses, comets, or the movements of the stars, even though the other nations are terrified by them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Israel. Many in that time saw the stars as signs that directed their destiny, and this was mixed up with idol worship. The verses that follow show how foolish it is to worship idols made of wood, decorated and nailed down so they will not fall over.

For today: do not let fear of the future, horoscopes, trends, or the pressure of other people guide you. Trust in God, who is greater than any sign or circumstance, and ask him for wisdom before you follow what everyone else is doing.
exp.25:8:
Here the people challenge Jeremiah: "How dare you prophesy in the name of the LORD that this house will become like Shiloh, and this city will be desolate and deserted?" Their word for "desolate" is the one in the verse that reads "desolate," meaning laid waste and ruined. "Deserted" refers to having no one living in it. Then all the people assembled against him in the house of the LORD.

The priests, the prophets, and the people are speaking. Jeremiah had just announced that, if they did not repent, God would leave the temple like Shiloh, a place where the sanctuary once stood and which, according to Jeremiah 7, was judged. They trusted that the temple would protect them, so his message seemed to them an offense.

For today: sometimes God's truth is uncomfortable, especially when it touches what we believe is secure. Let us ask for humility to hear correction without attacking the messenger, and for courage to speak the truth with love.
exp.38:1:
This verse tells that, after a long siege, the walls of Jerusalem were breached. "The city was breached" means that the Babylonians broke through the wall and were able to enter. About eighteen months passed from the start of the siege, and the date is the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

The one who tells the story is the book of Jeremiah, which records what the prophet had warned about for years. God had called Judah to return to Him, but the king and the people did not heed it. The fall of the city shows that God's words are fulfilled, even though it takes time.

For today: let us not postpone obedience, thinking there will always be time. When God speaks to us through His Word, listening in time spares us much pain. He remains merciful to whoever turns back to Him.
exp.30:3:
God promises his people that he will build them up again, like someone rebuilding a house that has fallen. He calls Israel "virgin," a tender way of speaking of a beloved people. The "tambourines" are instruments of celebration, and the "joyful dancing" is a gathering of people dancing with delight. The promise is that the celebration will come back.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in pain, struck down by destruction and exile. God reminds them of his everlasting love and announces restoration. Scholars often see here the people of the northern kingdom (Ephraim and Samaria), though the promise embraces all of Israel.

For today: if you feel your life has been left in ruins, God has not forgotten you. He knows how to rebuild. Trust in his love and leave room for joy to return, even if it comes slowly.
exp.12:4:
He says Jeremiah obeyed God's command. He took the linen belt and hid it at Perath, just as the LORD had commanded him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, recounting a symbolic act that God asked him to perform. The belt represented the people of Judah, whom God wanted close to himself, but who became proud and drew away. Later the belt rots, as a sign of judgment for that pride. It is not known with certainty whether the journey was literal or a vision, and scholars have interpreted it in both ways.

For today: Jeremiah obeyed without yet understanding the meaning. We can practice that trust, doing with faith what God shows us, even when we do not yet see the reason why.
exp.43:15:
This verse is the people's answer of refusal to Jeremiah. They say: "As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you!" In other words, they refuse to obey what Jeremiah told them on God's behalf.

The ones speaking are the Jews who had gone to live in Egypt, men and women alike, including those who knew that their wives were burning incense to the queen of heaven, a pagan goddess. Jeremiah had just warned them that God's judgment would reach them because of their idolatry. Instead of repenting, they challenge him and defend their custom.

Today we might ask ourselves whether there is any word of God that we prefer to ignore because it makes us uncomfortable. Listening with humility, even when it hurts, is the first step toward returning to Him.
exp.24:12:
God says he will carry out against Babylon, "that land," everything he has declared against it. That includes what Jeremiah wrote down in this book about the nations. "Bring upon" means to make these words come to pass. "All the nations" refers to the peoples Jeremiah prophesied against.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around the year 605 BC. Judah had ignored his warnings for years. God announces that Babylon would be used to discipline Judah and other peoples, but that afterward Babylon too would have to answer for its own wickedness. The seventy years can be understood as a literal or approximate period; interpreters explain it in different ways.

God takes justice seriously and does what he says. We can trust that no injustice is forgotten before him, and so we can entrust our wrongs to him and live with humility, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.5:3:
This verse says that the enemies urge one another to attack Jerusalem. Preparing for battle means calling for war and getting ready to fight. "Against her" refers to the city, the daughter of Zion, the one under attack. "Rise up, let us attack at noon" means they want to strike at midday, in the full heat of the sun. Then they complain that the daylight is fading and the evening shadows are growing long, so they will not be able to attack in time. That is why, in the next verse, they propose attacking by night.

Jeremiah passes on what God showed him: an army from the north will come as judgment on Jerusalem. Here the prophet imitates the voice of the invaders, who are in a hurry and eager to destroy. The cause, according to the text, is the violence and wickedness in the middle of the city. Some understand the "woe" as mockery or the impatience of the enemies.

For today: let us not postpone the correction God asks of us. If today we feel his call to change, let us listen to it with humility, before the day is over.
exp.30:17:
God listened closely to Ephraim's moaning. Ephraim here stands for the northern people, Israel. They admit that God disciplined them severely, and they describe themselves as an untrained young calf that will not let itself be led. They ask God himself to bring them back, because they cannot return on their own, and they confess that the LORD is their God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in exile because of their disobedience, but God promises comfort and return. Before and after this verse, God asks them to stop weeping, and then calls them a precious son, with a heart moved by mercy.

For today: when you feel far from God or ashamed of your mistakes, do not wait until you have fixed yourself on your own. You can pray sincerely: "Restore me, LORD." He listens, corrects with love, and receives the one who returns to him.
exp.21:4:
He says that if the king and his people do not obey what God has just commanded, God himself promises, with an oath, that this house will become a pile of rubble. The phrase "a pile of rubble" shows what is meant: a place torn down and left in ruins. The words "I swear by Myself" show that God makes this promise with total seriousness.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the king of Judah and his court. He had asked them for justice, to defend the oppressed and to care for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. He offered them blessing if they obeyed, but he also warned them of the consequences if they did not. The warning seeks to bring them to repentance before it is too late.

For today: God is concerned with how we treat the weak. Today we can ask ourselves whom we can help or defend, and obey God's word through deeds, not only by hearing it.
exp.47:1:
It says that Moab will no longer be a source of pride or fame. Against Heshbon, a Moabite city, others planned evil and said to one another: "Come, let us cut her off from nationhood." "Devised" means that they made plans. You too, people of Madmen, will be silenced, and the sword will pursue you. The name Madmen resembles a Hebrew word meaning "dung," and some believe there is a play on words here, though this is not certain.

The one speaking through Jeremiah is the LORD, the God of Israel. This message announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring people who trusted in their cities, their riches, and their pride. The texts do not say exactly who the attackers would be, and interpreters explain this in various ways.

Today we can remember that no human fame, strength, or security lasts forever. It is wise to place our trust in God and not in what we boast of, and to live with humility.
exp.6:11:
The verse says that God invites his people to go to Shiloh, the place in the land where he first made a dwelling for his Name. He asks them to see what he did to that place because of the wickedness of his people Israel. The word "dwelling" in the verse is the idea of setting up a place where his Name would live.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people thought the temple would protect them, even though they lived in injustice, idolatry and deceit. Shiloh had been a center of worship in ancient times, and the Bible does not describe here how it was destroyed; God uses it as a warning: if Shiloh fell, Jerusalem can also fall.

For today: let us not trust in places, rituals or religious traditions as if they were a shield. God seeks a heart that obeys and lives in justice, not merely a presence in the temple.
exp.22:8:
Here Jeremiah says that his heart is broken within him because of the prophets. His bones tremble, and he feels like a drunken man, that is, without strength and staggering. Because of the LORD, and because of His holy words, he has become like a man overcome by wine.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. God has just promised that he will bring his people back, but Jeremiah sees that many prophets and priests are false and are leading the people down the wrong path. That is why he trembles before the holiness of God and the seriousness of that sin.

For today: let us take God's Word seriously, and those who teach it. We can compare what we hear with the Bible, pray for our leaders, and ask God for a heart that grieves over sin, not one that ignores it.
exp.12:1:
Jeremiah did exactly what God commanded him. He bought a loincloth and put it around his waist. A loincloth is a piece of cloth worn around the hips, which is what is meant by the belt in this verse. The waist is the lower part of the body. The phrase "in accordance with the word of the LORD" means "in line with what God said."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, recounting his obedience. God asked him for a symbolic action, a kind of living picture to be seen. Later the belt is ruined, and God uses it to show how Judah, which was meant to be joined to Him, had been corrupted by its pride. Some scholars debate exactly where the river in this account was located, but the central message is clear.

Obeying God sometimes involves doing things we do not fully understand. Jeremiah first obeyed, and afterward God explained the meaning. Today we can trust and take the next step that we know God is asking of us.
exp.50:49:
Says that the survivors of the sword, those who managed to escape the slaughter, must depart without delay and not linger. It also asks them to remember the LORD even from far away, and to let Jerusalem come to mind. The phrase "do not linger" conveys the sense of moving on, and "remember" means to keep something in mind.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon, which had destroyed Israel and defiled the temple, would be judged. The Israelites living in exile there receive an order: leave before the city falls. Scholars understand this as a literal call to leave Babylon, and some also see it as a message of faithfulness in a foreign land.

When God rescues us from danger, it is not wise to keep looking back or hesitating. We can act with obedience and keep the memory of God alive: set aside a moment each day to thank him and to recall what he has done for us.
exp.39:13:
This verse tells how some men warned Gedaliah that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, had sent Ishmael to take his life. Johanan asks whether Gedaliah is aware of this. But Gedaliah did not believe them.

The ones speaking are Johanan and the military leaders. Babylon had left Gedaliah as governor over the Jews who remained in the land, and he lived in Mizpah. Johanan feared that if Gedaliah were killed, the whole group would scatter. Gedaliah, according to the text, thought the accusation was false. Ishmael did later murder him (Jeremiah 41), so his trust turned out to be a serious mistake.

For today: when someone warns us of danger, it is wise to listen with humility and ask God for wisdom. Being trusting is not wrong in itself, but ignoring a serious warning can cost dearly.
exp.21:11:
This verse says that Shallum will die in the foreign land where he is taken, and that he will never see his own land again. The word "exiled" in the verse means that he will be taken away by force and sent to live in another country.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Shallum, also called Jehoahaz, was the son of King Josiah and reigned for a very short time. According to 2 Kings 23, the king of Egypt took him prisoner. God announces that there will be no return, and for that reason he calls for weeping over the one taken away more than over the one who has died. Then the text speaks of the injustice of kings who built palaces without paying their workers.

For today: having power or success is not enough; God looks at how we treat others. Today you can ask yourself whether you pay what is fair and whether you act with honesty and respect toward those who work with you.
exp.34:0:
This verse tells us that a message came from the LORD to the prophet Jeremiah. The name "LORD" in this verse is the personal name of God, and the verse makes clear that this happened during the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the one who receives his word and delivers it. Jehoiakim ruled during a time when the people had turned away from God, and Jeremiah had spent years warning them. The verses that follow show that God will use the Rechabites, a family faithful to the instructions of their ancestors, as an example for Judah.

For today: before we listen to opinions or pressure, let us look carefully at what God says in his Word. If he speaks clearly, our response should be to obey him with sincerity and steadiness.
exp.8:6:
God himself says he will refine them and test them, the way metal is heated to prove it and burn away its impurities. The closing question, "What else can I do because of the daughter of My people?", can be read as: "What else can I do with my beloved people?" Many read it with sorrow, as if God saw no other way out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah lived full of lies: they deceived their neighbors, spoke peace with their mouths while plotting harm within, and did not want to know God. That is why this judgment comes, aimed at purifying and correcting.

For today: ask God to examine the way you speak. Try to tell the truth with love, without false words or deceit. If God corrects you, remember that He does it to cleanse you and draw you close to Him.
exp.6:23:
Jeremiah 7:24 says that the people did not listen to God or pay attention to him. Instead of obeying, they followed the stubborn inclinations of their own evil hearts. The verse's wording about not inclining the ear means listening closely and being willing to obey. Going backward and not forward means that instead of growing, they got worse.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, probably in the temple in Jerusalem. The people trusted in religious rituals, but they lived in disobedience. God reminds them that from the beginning he asked them for something deeper than sacrifices: that they listen to him and obey him. He sent them prophets again and again, and they ignored them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only fulfill our religious duties or whether we truly listen to God. This week, read a passage of the Bible calmly, ask God to speak to you, and decide to obey one concrete thing he shows you.
exp.48:13:
The prophet says he heard a message from God: an envoy was sent among the nations, calling them to assemble and march against Edom. The word "message" here means a report or a piece of news. The call "Assemble yourselves to march against her!" summons the nations to come together, and "Rise up for battle!" calls them to get ready to fight.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God against Edom, whose chief city was Bosra. Edom trusted in its mountains and its rocky strongholds, and believed it could not be touched. God announces that its pride will be brought low. Scholars understand in different ways how and when this was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: God rules over the nations.

For today: do not place your security in your position, your possessions, or your strength. All of that can fall. Live with humility and trust in God, who is the only refuge that never fails.
exp.25:3:
This verse is the beginning of the message Jeremiah was to deliver. God tells him to say: "If you do not listen to Me and walk in My law, which I have set before you..." The sentence is left unfinished and continues in the next verse. "Listen" means to pay attention and take to heart, and "say" here means to tell or deliver a message.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He commands him to go to the court of the temple and speak to the people who came to worship, holding nothing back. God wanted them to turn back, and so He says that perhaps they would listen and turn away from their evil way. In this way He could hold back the punishment He had planned.

For today: it is not enough simply to go to a place of worship; God expects us to listen to His word and put it into practice. This week, read a passage of the Bible and decide on one concrete action to obey it.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that although the people of Jerusalem say, "As surely as the LORD lives," a phrase used to make a solemn oath, they are actually swearing falsely. "They are swearing falsely" means that their words sound religious but are not true. They use God's name without honoring it with their lives.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God challenges them to search Jerusalem for a single person who practices justice and seeks truth, and promises to pardon the city if such a person is found. Then Jeremiah laments that the people did not accept correction. The problem was a faith of lips, without obedience.

For today: it is not enough to say religious words or to name God. Today you can examine whether your words, promises and daily decisions agree with what you say you believe, and ask God to make you a sincere and faithful person.
exp.50:2:
God gives an order against the army of Babylon. It tells the archer not to bend his bow and the soldier not to put on his armor. The order is not to spare its young men, and to devote all its army to destruction.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been an instrument of judgment against Judah, but it grew proud and mistreated God's people. Now God himself judges it. The verses that follow remind us that Israel was not abandoned by its God, even though it had sinned.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, stands above God. Trust that he does justice in his own time, and avoid the pride that puts its confidence in its own armor.
exp.11:9:
Jeremiah 12:10 says that many shepherds, meaning rulers or leaders, have destroyed God's vineyard. The word for "trampled" means to crush or trample underfoot, and "plot of ground" refers to the land and people that belong to God. What was precious to Him has been turned into a desolate wasteland.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. God laments that his people turned away from him, and for that reason he allowed them to suffer. The "shepherds" are usually understood as kings and leaders, although some think they also include invading armies. Even so, the passage shows God's grief over what has been lost.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in the family, the church, or at work, care for those under your charge with humility. And pray for leaders, that they will care for people and not destroy them.
exp.25:5:
