God says he will do to the temple in Jerusalem what he did to Shiloh, and that the city will become an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth. The idea is that other peoples would point to Jerusalem as an example of punishment.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who is standing in the temple courts. He warns that if the people continue to refuse to obey his law or to listen to the prophets he has sent them again and again, they will lose the temple. Shiloh was an ancient place of worship that was destroyed, and the Bible remembers it as a warning. The leaders and the people reacted with violence and wanted to kill Jeremiah.

For today: religion without obedience does not protect us. When God corrects us through his Word, it is wise to listen with humility, even when it hurts, instead of defending ourselves or rejecting the message.
exp.27:3:
It says that God will bring back Jeconiah, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon. The phrase "I will restore" means that God will return them to their homeland; the exiles are those taken away from Judah to Babylon; the "yoke" is the heavy burden of control that Babylon put on Judah. The promise is that this yoke will be broken.

The one speaking here is Hananiah, a prophet who presents himself as a spokesman for God, and he says it in the temple in front of the people. Jeremiah had announced that Babylon would rule for a long time. Later, the text shows that God had not sent Hananiah and that his message was false (Jeremiah 28:15-16). Hananiah offered quick relief, but it was not true.

For today: not every hopeful message comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible and ask for wisdom. True hope does not ignore reality, but rests on what God has actually said.
exp.28:13:
He says that God promises to let himself be found by his people. He assures them that he will restore them from captivity, that is, he will bring their exile to an end. He will gather them from all the nations and places where he had banished them, and he will bring them back to the land from which he sent them into exile. The phrase "I have banished you" shows that God recognizes the exile as part of his judgment.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a letter to the Jews who were carried into exile in Babylon. They wanted to return soon, and false prophets were promising them exactly that. God tells them that the return will come, but later on (verse 10 mentions seventy years). In the meantime, they are to seek him with their whole heart.

For today: when you are in a difficult season that does not get resolved quickly, do not stop seeking God sincerely. He has not forgotten you. Pray with perseverance and trust that his timing and his restoration are more reliable than your hurry.
exp.4:20:
This verse is a strong call from God to his people. He tells them to listen, though he calls them "foolish" and "senseless." In biblical language, the "heart" is the mind and the will, meaning that they do not think or understand. They have eyes and ears, but they do not see or hear what God shows them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Judah, which had left God to serve other gods. He warns them that this decision would have consequences. Then he asks them why they do not fear him, since he set limits to the sea by his power.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are really listening to God or only hearing words. Before reading the Bible or praying, we can ask him: "Lord, open my eyes and my heart." Then, obey what he shows us.
exp.41:20:
Jeremiah says that he has already told them today what God commands, but they have not obeyed. Here "told" simply means that he made it known to them. God had sent his message to them through the prophet, and they did not carry it out.

Jeremiah speaks to the survivors of Judah, after the fall of Jerusalem. They had asked him to pray and promised to obey whatever God said. God answered that they should not go to Egypt, but they had already made up their minds to go. Jeremiah shows them that their words did not match their actions.

For today: let us not ask for God's guidance only to receive permission for what we already want. Before we pray, let us decide to obey his answer, even when it costs us or is different from our plan.
exp.28:8:
These men spoke in God's name and claimed to be prophets, but they were lying. God Himself makes this clear: "I have not sent them." "They are falsely prophesying to you" means they announce messages as if they came from God, and "falsely" means they speak a lie.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Israelites who had been carried off captive to Babylon. False prophets were promising them that they would soon return home. God tells them to settle down, seek the peace of the city, and wait, because the return would come after seventy years. In this way He protected them from false hopes.

Today, not every message spoken "in God's name" comes from Him. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray for wisdom, and be wary of anyone who only promises what you would like to hear. God is faithful, and His truth sustains us even when the wait is long.
exp.32:18:
God spoke again to Jeremiah. "And the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah" means that the message did not come from the prophet himself, but from God. It is a short phrase that marks the beginning of a new declaration. "The LORD" is the name of God, and the colon that follows announces that what He wants to communicate is coming.

Jeremiah is imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, and Jerusalem is under threat from Babylon. Even so, God gives him words of hope about restoration. The verses before this one promise that there will not be lacking a descendant of David or priests who serve. This verse introduces the assurance that follows: God's faithfulness is as firm as day and night.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, seek the Word of God before the news or your fears. He continues to speak and fulfills what He promises, even in difficult times.
exp.41:12:
This verse begins a warning from God. It says: "But if you say, 'We will not stay in this land,' and you thus disobey the voice of the LORD your God." The word "but" means "yet" or "however," and the verse's wording shows that refusing to stay is the same as refusing to obey.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors was afraid of Babylon and asked Jeremiah to pray so they would know what to do. God answered: stay, do not be afraid, I am with you. But the people were already planning to leave for Egypt, looking for safety.

For today: sometimes we ask God for direction when we have already decided what we want. We can pray with a heart willing to obey, trusting that his presence sustains us more than any plan that seems safe.
exp.12:21:
God tells Judah that when they ask, "Why has this happened to me?", the answer is the magnitude of their wrongdoing. The verse pictures their skirts being stripped away and their bodies left exposed, an image of shame and public humiliation, as captives often suffered.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people have ignored his warnings, and an invasion is coming from the north. Some understand this to refer to Babylon. God wants Judah to see that their suffering is not chance, but the result of their persistent sin.

For today: when trials come, it is good to humbly ask whether there is something we should acknowledge before God. Not every difficulty is punishment, but honesty opens the door to forgiveness and change.
exp.30:10:
This verse says that God rescued Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, and freed them from the hand of a power that had overwhelmed them. The word "redeemed" means that God acted with power and paid the cost to set his people free from slavery or oppression.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter is a message of hope for Israel, a people scattered and suffering in exile. God promises to bring them back, to lead them with care, and to turn their weeping into joy. Many understand the power that had overwhelmed them to refer to the nations that dominated Israel, such as Babylon. The text does not name it here, so this is a reasonable interpretation.

For today: when you feel trapped by something stronger than you, such as fear, debt, or an addiction, remember that God knows how to rescue. Ask him for help with confidence and take the step you can take, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.18:3:
God says that the people abandoned him and made this place a foreign place, somewhere that no longer belonged to him. There they burned incense to other gods, gods that neither they, nor their ancestors, nor the kings of Judah had ever known. They also filled this place with the blood of the innocent.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the Valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. He warns the kings and people of Judah that punishment is coming because of their idolatry and violence.

Today we can ask what things occupy the place that belongs to God in our lives. Returning to Him means leaving behind what harms others and living with justice and compassion.
exp.50:46:
He says that God will punish Babylon, that is, step in to judge her. Her idols are the carved images she trusted in. Her whole land will suffer shame, because those gods cannot save her, and her slain will lie fallen within her.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a proud and idolatrous empire that oppressed other peoples, among them Israel. The text announces that God does not overlook that injustice and calls his people to leave the city. Many understand it as referring to the fall of Babylon before peoples from the north.

For today: do not place your trust in things that seem strong but cannot save, such as money, prestige or power. Trust in God, who is just and cares for his own.
exp.40:5:
Ishmael son of Nethaniah left Mizpah to meet some travelers. He was weeping as he went, but his tears were not genuine. When he met the men, he said, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam," even though he had already killed Gedaliah. "Went out to meet them" means that he went out to welcome them.

The narrator recounts the event. Gedaliah was the governor appointed by Babylon over those who remained in Judah, and Ishmael murdered him in secret. The eighty men were coming in mourning, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, to bring offerings to the temple in ruins. Ishmael pretended grief to draw them into the city, and there he killed them. The text does not explain all of his motives.

Today the passage warns us that tears and kind words do not always reveal a sincere heart. Let us ask for wisdom to discern, and let us make sure that our own compassion is genuine.
exp.39:8:
Gedaliah swears an oath to the military leaders and their men. He tells them not to be afraid to serve the Chaldeans, the Babylonians. He asks them to stay and live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and he promises that it will go well with them.

Jerusalem had already fallen, and many had been taken captive to Babylon. Babylon appointed Gedaliah as governor over the poor who were left behind. He speaks from Mizpah to calm the leaders who feared reprisals. His message agrees with what Jeremiah had taught: accept the situation and live in peace. However, the account goes on to a tragic ending, for Gedaliah was murdered.

When life changes in painful ways, God invites us not to act out of fear, but to live with diligence, peace, and trust in Him, day by day.
exp.33:4:
God tells King Zedekiah that he will not die in battle but will die in peace. When he dies, he will be honored as his ancestors were: spices will be burned at his funeral, and people will mourn him with cries of lament, saying, "Alas, master!"

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf while Babylon attacks Jerusalem. God announces that Zedekiah will be taken captive, but he promises that Zedekiah will not die by the sword. The Bible does not tell how this was fulfilled, and it is not clear what "in peace" means here.

Even in times of judgment, God offers mercy to the one who listens. Today we can trust that his word is fulfilled, and respond with humility when he speaks to us.
exp.6:24:
God says that, from the day Israel came out of Egypt until the days of Jeremiah, He sent them all His servants, the prophets, again and again. The phrase "again and again" shows that He did this with persistence and care, never tiring, like a father who keeps reaching out to his children. "Your fathers" refers to their ancestors.

God speaks through Jeremiah in his message at the temple. The people trusted in their rituals and in the temple, but they did not obey. God reminds them that from the beginning His covenant was simple: listen to My voice, and I will be your God. The prophets were a sign of His patience, but the people hardened their hearts.

Today, God still speaks with patience. Ask yourself: is there something God has already shown you in His Word that you have put off obeying? Today you can listen to Him with an open heart and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.24:27:
Some nations will refuse to take the cup that Jeremiah offers them. The cup represents God's judgment, like a drink that leaves a person staggering. Then God tells Jeremiah to say to them that they have no choice: "You most certainly must drink it."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the time when Judah was falling. God announces that the punishment will begin with his own people, and that the other nations will not be free either. No one can escape his justice.

For today: we should not believe that we can avoid the consequences of our decisions just because we do not want to see them. It is better to humble ourselves, acknowledge our faults and seek God while there is still time, for his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.49:44:
Therefore listen to the plans that the LORD has drawn up against Babylon, and the strategies He has devised against the land of the Chaldeans. Even the little ones of the flock will be dragged away, and their pasture will be made desolate because of them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD has resolved. Babylon had dominated Israel and other nations. The chapter announces its fall before a people coming from the north. The king trembles, and God presents himself as the shepherd whom no one can resist. Some think that "the little ones of the flock" shows how easy the defeat will be; others see it as a picture of total humiliation.

For today: even when evil seems strong and impossible to stop, God still governs history. We can trust His justice, wait with patience, and not respond with pride or revenge.
exp.46:3:
It says a day is coming that will bring destruction on all the Philistines. That same day will also cut off every ally that Tyre and Sidon could offer them. "Destroy" means to lay waste or wipe out completely. "Coasts of Caphtor" points to the island of Crete, though some think of another region of the Mediterranean; the Philistines came from there.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The flood that rises from the north is an army that comes down like an overflowing river. Many understand this to be Babylon, though the text does not name it here. God announces judgment on a nation neighboring Judah, and the grief is so great that parents do not even turn to look at their children.

For today: do not trust in alliances, money, or people as your ultimate security. When every human helper fails, God remains the firm refuge. Place your trust first in Him.
exp.50:21:
God says he will use an instrument of his, like a hammer, to destroy Babylon. The phrase "shatter" means to smash into pieces. The words for "young man" and "maiden" refer to young people, and the unmarried girls are included. The list covers every age and both sexes, to show that the judgment would be total.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed nations and had harmed Judah and Jerusalem. Scholars do not agree on who the "hammer" is: many think of the Medes and Persians who would defeat Babylon, and others see a more general image. What is clear is that God promises justice for the wrong that was done.

Today we can trust that God sees injustice and does not forget it. Instead of taking revenge, we can hand our pain over to him and wait for his justice, without losing compassion for people.
exp.25:12:
Jeremiah asks the people to correct the way they live and act, and to obey the LORD their God. If they do, He may relent of the disaster He has announced against them. This does not mean that God made a mistake, but that He changes His decision about judgment when people turn back to Him. "Obey the voice of the LORD" here means listen and act on what He says.

Jeremiah speaks before the princes and the people. The priests and prophets were accusing him of deserving death for announcing judgment against Jerusalem and the temple. He does not defend himself out of fear, but repeats that God sent him and offers a way out: return to God.

Today, when a word of God makes us uncomfortable, we can get angry or we can correct our course. Let us think of one habit or decision that does not please God, and take a concrete step of change today, trusting in His mercy.
exp.16:11:
It says that the place where God makes himself present among his people is glorious and exalted, and that it has been so from the very beginning. "Exalted" means raised up and worthy of great honor. A "sanctuary" is the holy place where God is worshiped. The verse calls it a "glorious throne," as if God himself reigned there.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. Earlier, God warned that unjust riches are lost, and that he examines the heart of every person. Then Jeremiah says that whoever abandons God will be put to shame. Between those two warnings, the prophet praises God as a secure refuge. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of the temple in Jerusalem or of God's throne in general.

For today: when you feel that what you have could be lost, return to God as your secure place. Set aside a moment each day to pray and remember that he reigns and does not change.
exp.48:37:
He says God will set his throne in Elam, as one who comes to rule and to judge. There he will destroy its king and officials.

He speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, within messages addressed to several nations. Elam lay east of Babylon, in the region of present-day Iran. The text presents its downfall as a judgment of God. But the following verse adds a promise of restoration "in the latter days." Scholars debate how and when this was fulfilled.

For today: God is the true King, and no human power lasts forever. We can trust that he judges with justice, but he also offers hope. Today you can hand over to him your concerns about rulers and injustices.
exp.19:15:
He says that the man who brought the news of Jeremiah's birth should be like the cities that the Lord overthrew without compassion. "Overthrew" here means wiped out or left in ruins. "Without compassion" means the Lord showed them no mercy. And that this man should hear "an outcry in the morning," that is, alarm and weeping from early hours, and "a battle cry at noon," that is, a roar of attack in the full light of day.

Jeremiah speaks at the height of his anguish. He had just been beaten and put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur for announcing God's judgment. His pain is so great that he curses the day of his birth. It is often read as an exaggerated outburst rather than a calculated wish. Some see here poetic language of lament.

For today: God is not shocked when we honestly tell Him our pain. Bring your complaints to Him in prayer, and do not carry them alone.
exp.9:9:
It says that, unlike idols, the LORD is the true God. He is the living God and the eternal King. The earth quakes at his wrath, and the nations cannot endure his indignation. The verse's "wrath" is his righteous anger, and the nations are the peoples who cannot withstand it.

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, who saw the nations worship idols of wood covered with silver and gold. The prophet mocks those images, made by craftsmen, and contrasts them with the God who created everything. This verse is the center of that contrast.

For today: modern idols, such as money, success, or the approval of others, are also our own handiwork and cannot save us. Today you can place your trust in the living God, acknowledge his authority, and rest in the fact that he still reigns.
exp.22:6:
God announces that days are coming when people will no longer use as their main oath the familiar phrase: "As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt." Swearing "as the LORD lives" was a way of affirming something with seriousness. The exodus will not be forgotten, but it will be overshadowed by something even greater.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, while Judah faced exile in Babylon. Just before this, he promises a righteous King, a descendant of David, who is called "The LORD our righteousness." Then he says he will gather his people from the north and from all the lands where he had scattered them, and bring them back. Many Christians see Jesus in that King.

For today: God does not stay in the past. If you are going through a season of loss or scattering, remember that he knows how to rescue again. Give thanks for his past works, but trust that he can still open a new path.
exp.2:5:
God spoke to Jeremiah in the days of King Josiah and asked him to consider what faithless Israel, the northern kingdom, had done. He calls her "faithless" because she had been disloyal to him. Her unfaithfulness was spiritual: she worshiped other gods. The high hills and the green trees under which she prostituted herself were places where pagan worship was practiced.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Israel had already fallen before Assyria, and God compares her to an unfaithful wife. He shows this to Judah, the southern kingdom, which saw what had happened and still followed the same path. God wants Judah to learn and to turn back.

For today: let us learn from the mistakes of others before we repeat them. If anything takes the place of God in our hearts, let us return to him soon, because he still calls us with patience.
exp.51:32:
It says that the king of Babylon had Jehoiachin change out of his prison clothes, that is, he freed him from his appearance as a captive. Moreover, Jehoiachin dined at the king's table regularly, for the rest of his life. The phrase "changed out of his prison clothes" means that he put on different clothes in place of the ones he wore as a prisoner, and "dined" refers to the meals he shared with the king.

This is the end of the book of Jeremiah, and it was most likely added by a later writer, since it speaks of events that happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Jehoiachin, king of Judah, had been held prisoner in Babylon for about thirty-seven years. The new king, Evil-merodach, treated him with kindness. Some see here a sign that God had not forgotten the family of David, although the text does not explain this.

For today: even in long times of difficulty, God can open a door of relief when we least expect it. We keep trusting and waiting, and we give thanks for small gestures of kindness.
exp.22:5:
This verse promises that, in the days of the righteous King whom God will raise up from David's family, Judah will be saved and Israel will live in security. The phrase "will dwell securely" means he will live calm and without fear. The King will be called "The LORD Our Righteousness," meaning the Lord is our righteousness.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were being misled by unjust shepherds (leaders), and soon they would be carried into exile. God promises better shepherds and a righteous King. Christians see in this branch Jesus; Jews have understood it in other ways.

For today: when you feel guilty or insecure, remember that your worth before God does not depend on your achievements, but on Christ, our righteousness. Rest in Him and live with confidence, doing good.
exp.48:34:
God says, the LORD of Hosts, that he will shatter the bow of Elam. The bow was that people's main weapon, so it stands for their military strength. The phrase "the mainstay of their might" means that this was where the core of their power lay.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the beginning of Zedekiah's reign in Judah. Elam was a nation east of Babylon, known for its archers. The message is part of the prophecies against several nations. The verses that follow say that Elam will be scattered and will suffer judgment. Scholars do not agree on all the historical details of how this was fulfilled.

For today: no human strength, whether money, power, or skill, is absolute. It is wise to trust God and not in what we think makes us invincible.
exp.28:9:
God has not forgotten his exiled people, says this passage. When seventy years are complete in Babylon, he will attend to them, meaning he will act on their behalf. He will confirm his promise to restore them and bring them back to Jerusalem. The phrase about bringing them back refers to returning them to their homeland, and "to this place" refers to Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a letter addressed to those taken into exile in Babylon. False prophets were telling them the exile would be short and filling them with hopes of a quick return. God corrects that lie: the exile would be long, but it would have an end. Scholars debate whether the seventy years is an exact figure or an approximate one.

For today: God sometimes allows long seasons of waiting, but he does not abandon us. Instead of clinging to easy promises, trust his true word, pray with patience, and keep serving him where you are while you wait.
exp.11:7:
God says that his people, whom he calls his "inheritance," have turned against him like a lion in the forest. The lion roars against God, meaning it challenges him with its words and its conduct. That is why God says, "I hate her," a strong word that shows his painful rejection of that rebellion.

Here God himself speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah, whom God loved, had abandoned him and even opposed him. God laments that his people, instead of being a treasure, had become hostile. Some understand this "hating" as a wounded love that withdraws its favor, not as a hopeless hatred, since the book also promises restoration.

For today: God grieves when we reject him. If you notice hardness or rebellion in your heart, return to him with humility. He continues to offer forgiveness to anyone who repents.
exp.28:15:
This verse introduces a message from the LORD to those who stayed in Jerusalem: the king who sits on David's throne, and all the people who remain in this city. They are the brothers of the exiles, the ones who did not go with them into exile. The word "but" in this verse simply connects it to what came before, and the phrase "this is what the LORD says" means that this is a direct message from God.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the exiles in Babylon. Some prophets there were promising a quick return. God asks them for patience, because restoration would come later. Now he also speaks to those who remained in Jerusalem, who believed they were safe and did not listen to his warning. The next verse announces the judgment that awaited them.

For today: let us not trust in our position or in voices that only say what is comfortable. Let us receive the Word of God with humility, even when it corrects us.
exp.15:17:
God says that, before he restores his people, he will justly punish their wickedness and their sin. "Repay them double" most likely means a full and abundant repayment, though some read it as a way of expressing great severity. He speaks of "carcasses": this refers to their lifeless idols, which polluted the land God had given them, the land that was their inheritance, their own possession.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had filled the land with idolatry, and God announces that exile will come, for he sees all their ways. But the nearer context also points to hope: afterward, nations will come to acknowledge that the idols are a lie.

For today: God sees what we hide and calls us not to fill our lives with empty things that take his place. Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting first, and bring it honestly to God, who forgives and restores.
exp.22:24:
God says that He has heard those prophets. They spoke lies, yet they used God's name to give authority to their words. Their excuse was: "I had a dream! I had a dream!" as if a dream were the same thing as a message from God. Here, "prophesy" means speaking in God's name.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. Earlier, He reminded the people that He sees everything and fills heaven and earth, so no one can hide from Him. These prophets were leading the people with dreams that came from their own hearts, and that drew them away from God, as had happened before with Baal. God does not condemn every dream, but the false use of His name.

Today we can test every teaching, impression, or "word" in the light of the Bible. Before saying "God told me," it is wise to ask for wisdom, to be humble, and to check whether it agrees with what God has already revealed in His Word.
exp.31:8:
Jeremiah tells us that he bought the field in Anathoth from his cousin Hanamel. He paid by weighing out seventeen shekels of silver. Silver was weighed rather than counted as coins, because coins were not used in the way they are today.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He is confined in the courtyard of the prison, because Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon. God had told him that his cousin would come and ask him to buy the field, in keeping with the family law of redemption. When Hanamel arrived, Jeremiah recognized that this was the word of God. His purchase was a sign of hope: someday the people would live again in that land.

For today: even when everything seems lost, we can take concrete steps of faith and obedience. Trusting God does not mean ignoring difficulty, but acting with hope in his promises.
exp.39:15:
Gedaliah firmly answers Johanan, "Do not do such a thing!" He does not believe that Ishmael is a traitor, and he tells him that what Johanan is saying about Ishmael is a lie. With this, he rejects the plan to kill Ishmael in secret.

Gedaliah was the governor whom the Babylonians left over the poor people who remained in Judah. Johanan and other leaders warned him that the king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael to murder him. Gedaliah did not believe them. Afterward, Ishmael did kill him (Jeremiah 41), so his trust proved to be a serious mistake. His intention seemed good, but he was naive.

For today: kindness and trust are valuable, but they need wisdom. When someone warns you of a danger, listen with humility, pray, and investigate carefully, instead of dismissing it just because you don't want to think badly of others.
exp.41:0:
Here it says that all the military commanders, along with Johanan son of Kareah, Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, approached Jeremiah. The word "approached" is the verse's own wording, and the next verse explains why: they wanted him to pray for them.

The narrator tells what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. After the murder of the governor Gedaliah, the survivors were afraid of retaliation from Babylon. They seek out Jeremiah, the prophet, to ask for direction on God's behalf. Later it becomes clear that some were already thinking about going to Egypt.

For today: when you are afraid or do not know what to do, seek God's guidance with humility. But do not ask for direction only to hear what suits you; pray with the resolve to obey, whatever it is.
exp.41:17:
This verse says that the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, warns the people: just as his anger and wrath were poured out on the residents of Jerusalem, so his wrath will be poured out on them if they go to Egypt. The words "object of cursing and horror," "vilification and disgrace" are the terms the verse uses for what they would become. And they would never see this place again.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors feared Babylon and planned to flee to Egypt. They asked Jeremiah to pray and promised to obey God. But he noticed that they were already inclined to leave, and that is why he speaks to them with such firmness.

For today: before asking God for direction, let us check whether we are truly willing to obey the answer, even when it is not the one that gives us the most security.
exp.9:22:
A person cannot fully steer their own life or be certain of every step they take. The BSB reads "a man's way is not his own" and "no one who walks directs his own steps," so the course of a person's life does not rest in their own hands. The one speaking recognizes that we need God's guidance.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks in prayer to the LORD. He has just announced that the shepherds, that is, the leaders of Judah, did not seek the LORD and therefore failed. An invasion from the north is also foretold. Jeremiah admits human limitation and then asks that God correct him with justice, not with anger.

For today: before you make plans, pray and ask God for direction. Make your plans with humility, and trust that He can guide you even when things do not turn out as you expected.
exp.25:2:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the people without holding anything back. He says, "Perhaps they will listen and turn," meaning they might hear and change their ways. If each person turns away from his evil way of life, God says he will relent from the disaster he is planning to bring on them. In other words, he would change his decision to judge them. The word "turn" means to turn back or change direction.

God speaks, and gives Jeremiah the command at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Jeremiah is to go to the courtyard of the temple and say everything God commanded him. The people had rejected the prophets again and again. Even so, God offers them one more chance before judging them. How God's "relenting" should be understood is explained in several ways, but all of them show his willingness to forgive.

For today: if there is something in your life that you know does not please God, do not wait any longer. God still opens the door to anyone who wants to return to him.
exp.4:22:
This verse says the people of Judah had a heart that was "false," meaning twisted and stubborn, and "rebellious," a heart that does not want to submit to God. "Turned aside and gone" means they turned around and walked away from Him instead of drawing near.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier He showed them that the sea keeps the limit He set for it, yet His people, who can think and decide for themselves, do not obey Him or fear Him. Then He reminds them that God gives them the rain and the harvest, and that their sins have taken good things away from them.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has spoken to me about, and have I turned away from it? Today we can return to Him with humility, thank Him for what He gives us each day, and obey Him in something specific.
exp.21:20:
God says that he warned his people while things were going well for them, when they felt safe and secure. But they answered, "I will not listen." God adds that this has been their way since youth: they did not obey his voice.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jerusalem, which here appears as a woman with lovers, that is, allies and powers she trusted in instead of trusting in God. Before this verse, judgment is announced against the king of Judah. God reminds him that the disaster comes after many warnings that were ignored.

For today: let us not wait until a crisis arrives to listen to God. When things are going well, it is a good time to read his Word and obey it with humility.
exp.50:3:
This verse announces that many of the people of Babylon will die in their own land. "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians. The phrase "pierced through" means struck down by weapons, and "in her streets" shows that the blow will reach into the heart of the city.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. In context, Babylon had been an instrument of God, but it was also proud and cruel, and now it receives judgment. God promises that he has not abandoned Israel or Judah, even though they too had sinned. The verses that follow call the people to leave Babylon and save their lives.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. That invites us to trust his justice instead of taking revenge, and to turn away from anything that drags us into living far from him.
exp.6:13:
God says that he will do to the temple in Jerusalem, the house that bears his name and the place where the people put their trust, what he did to Shiloh. The phrase "the house that bears My Name" means that the place belongs to him and carries his name.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they kept living in injustice and idolatry. Shiloh had once been an ancient center of worship in Israel, and God reminds them that this place was left in ruins. The details of its destruction are not explained here, but the message is clear: a holy place does not protect those who do not obey.

For today: let us not trust in outward things, such as a church, a tradition, or a religious custom, as if they guaranteed God's favor. Let us examine whether our hearts and our lives truly listen to him and obey him.
exp.37:1:
Jeremiah says that God announces what will happen in Jerusalem. Whoever stays in the city will die by the sword, by famine, or by plague. But whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) will live. He will keep his life like a spoil of war, with nothing more, and he will live.

Jeremiah, God's prophet, speaks while Babylon besieges Jerusalem. Years of rebellion and of ignoring God brought this judgment. The officials hear it and become angry, because they believe his message weakens the courage of the soldiers. Jeremiah does not seek the harm of the people; he calls them to obey so that they may be saved.

For today: sometimes God asks us for something that wounds our pride, such as surrendering, asking forgiveness, or changing course. Hearing an uncomfortable truth can save us from greater harm. Let us pray for humility to obey, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.30:9:
This verse calls all the nations, even the most distant ones, to hear a message from God: the same God who scattered Israel will gather his people again and take care of them. The word "nations" refers to peoples, and "distant coastlands" refers to faraway lands. The image of a shepherd who keeps his flock shows constant protection.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who suffered exile because of their sins. This chapter is part of what is called the "Book of Consolation," where God promises to restore his people with tenderness. God himself is presented as the Father of Israel. Some see here the return from Babylon; others also see a broader and future hope.

For today: if you feel that your life is scattered or broken, trust that God cares like a good shepherd. Tell him your situation in prayer, and take a step of obedience today, trusting that he knows how to gather what was lost.
exp.42:4:
This verse tells how Johanan and all the army commanders gathered the survivors of Judah. These were people who had been scattered among other nations and had come back to live in their land. The commanders are the men in charge of the armed forces. The phrase "scattered" means spread out or dispersed among the nations.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. God, through Jeremiah, had told them to stay in Judah and not to fear Babylon. But Johanan and the others accused Jeremiah and Baruch of lying, and they did not obey. So they took everyone, including the prophet, and set off toward Egypt.

For today: fear can lead us to disobey God even when He has already shown us the way. Before deciding something under pressure, it is wise to pray, search the Bible, and listen to wise counsel, rather than choosing what seems safest.
exp.10:15:
God once called you a flourishing olive tree, beautiful and full of well-formed fruit. But with a mighty roar, God will set that tree on fire, and its branches will be consumed.

The phrase "called you" in the verse is about how God described or regarded you. The word "beautiful" points to how the tree looks, and the word "well-formed" points to the quality of its fruit.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had a special relationship with God, but they broke the covenant and worshiped Baal. That is why judgment comes. Some understand the "fire" as an enemy invasion; the text does not give exact details.

For today: having a good appearance or a good start in faith is not enough. God looks for constant faithfulness. We can ask him to examine us and help us remain in him with a sincere heart, not merely with religious habits.
exp.40:7:
This verse tells how, among a group of men that Ishmael was about to kill, ten of them begged him not to do it. They told him they had supplies hidden in the field: wheat, barley, oil, and honey. Ishmael spared them and did not kill them along with the others. The phrase "hidden treasure" here means hidden stores or reserves of food.

Ishmael, of the royal family, had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon. Then he deceived a group of pilgrims who were coming from the north, pretending to weep and offering to take them to Gedaliah. The ten men spoke to save their lives. The text does not explain why Ishmael accepted; perhaps he wanted that food, but the Bible does not say so.

For today: in the middle of a dangerous situation, what we have can help us save lives, but the account reminds us that violence and deceit are terrible. Let us ask God for wisdom, and use our resources to care for others, not to bargain with evil.
exp.32:19:
It speaks of God having a covenant (or agreement) with day and night, that is, the fixed order in which they follow one another. And it asks: "If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night no longer come at their appointed time?" The sentence is left unfinished here and is completed in the following verse. To "break" a covenant means to cancel or undo it. "At their appointed time" means "at the right time."

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who was in a time of crisis for Judah. God promises to restore his people. He uses something no one can change, the order of days and nights, to show that his promise to David and to the Levites is just as certain.

For today: every sunrise is a reminder that God keeps what he promises. When you feel doubt or fear, look at the rising sun and rest in the fact that his faithfulness is firmer than any circumstance.
exp.47:9:
This verse says that cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, that is, careless, halfhearted, or slack in carrying it out. Cursed too is the one who withholds his sword from bloodshed. The word "sword" here means the blade of war, and to withhold it means to hold it back or refrain from using it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The judgment on Moab was a task God entrusted to human agents, and it was not to be carried out with indifference. Some understand the "bloodshed" as the warfare of judgment in that specific historical moment, not as a rule for all time.

Today, when we serve God, let us do it with sincerity and devotion, without neglect or leaving unfinished what he asks of us. Serve God with a whole heart and with perseverance.
exp.9:4:
Jeremiah 10:5 compares the idols of the nations to scarecrows standing in a cucumber patch. They cannot speak. They have to be carried because they cannot walk. That is why the verse says not to fear them: they can do no harm, and they can do no good either. (Some understand the comparison as a stiff, upright figure set up to frighten birds, which is the picture the verse brings to mind.)

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to his people, Judah. They lived surrounded by nations that worshiped idols, and they were tempted either to be afraid of those gods or to copy them. The prophet describes how these idols are made: wood cut from a tree, decorated with silver and gold, and fastened down so it will not fall. He then sets all of this against the LORD, who has no equal.

For today, ask yourself what frightens you, or what you trust more than God, such as money, status, or the opinions of others. Anything we make ourselves falls short. Place your trust in the living God, who speaks, and who acts.
exp.37:24:
Here King Zedekiah, the king of Judah, tells Jeremiah that the officials might learn about their private conversation. If they do, he asks Jeremiah to picture how they will question him: "Tell us what you said to the king and what he said to you; do not hide it from us, or we will kill you." The word "hide" in that demand means "keep back."

Jeremiah had announced that Jerusalem would fall into the hands of Babylon if the people did not surrender. The officials wanted him dead for this. The king, afraid of them, asks Jeremiah to keep quiet and suggests an answer to protect himself. Jeremiah, according to the text, said what the king had told him to say about his request not to be sent back to the house of Jonathan, though he did not tell them everything that had been discussed.

For today: fear of people can lead us to crooked decisions. Let us ask God for the courage to act with wisdom and truth, without letting what others think control us.
exp.19:17:
Here Jeremiah asks: why was I born? Only to see trouble and sorrow, and to end my days in shame? The womb is the mother's body, where a child is formed. "Trouble" means hardship and distress. "Shame" means mockery and disgrace.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. God had called him to announce judgment, and the people mocked him. Shortly before this, the priest Pashhur struck him and put him in the stocks. Jeremiah, worn out, pours out his pain before God. The Bible does not hide this complaint, and many see it as a sincere prayer, not as a lack of faith.

When you are discouraged, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Jeremiah did. Then look for someone you trust who can stand with you and listen.
exp.45:6:
It is a question that God asks to draw attention. It compares a great army advancing with a river that rises and overflows. The Hebrew word for "rises" means that it lifts itself up and spreads out, like the Nile when it floods.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD about Egypt. Pharaoh Necho led his army toward the Euphrates, and there he was defeated by Babylon, as the verses before this one show. Egypt boasted of being unstoppable, but God shows that its strength was not secure. Scholars generally agree about this battle, although some details are debated.

For today: We can be impressed by power, money, or success, and put our trust in them. But all of that can fall in a day. Let us place our trust in God, who does remain.
exp.0:13:
God tells Jeremiah that disaster will come from the north. This disaster will be poured out, like something released all at once, and it will fall on all who live in the land, that is, on the people of Judah and its cities.

The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, who had just been called as a prophet. He shows him the vision of a boiling pot tilting from the north. The verses that follow explain that God will call peoples from the north, and they say the reason is the idolatry and disobedience of Judah. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text here does not name it.

For today: God warns before he acts. Let us not ignore the warnings; if anything in our lives is pulling us away from him, let us return to God sincerely, today.
exp.2:2:
God had held back the rains because of the people's sin. The spring rain was the one needed for the harvest to ripen, and without it the fields were left dry. The people also had the brazen look of a prostitute, an openness about their wrongdoing that showed no sense of shame. "You refuse to be ashamed" means that they refused to admit their error.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He compares the people to an unfaithful wife who went after other "lovers," that is, other gods. The drought appears as a warning from God, who still keeps inviting them: "return to me."

For today: when we feel that something is drying up in our lives, it is worth asking ourselves humbly whether there is something we should confess. God does not call us to humiliate us, but to restore us. Today we can return to Him with sincerity.

sum.46: God announces through Jeremiah that an invasion coming from the north, like a flood, will destroy the Philistines and reach as far as Gaza, Ashkelon, Tyre and Sidon. There will be so much terror that fathers will be unable to help their children. It is God's judgment: his sword will not rest until it accomplishes what he has commanded.
sum.29: God tells Jeremiah to write down his words. Although Israel and Judah are suffering great distress because of their sins, God promises to break their yoke, heal their wounds, and bring them back to their land. He will punish their oppressors, raise up a ruler from among them, and renew their relationship: "You will be my people, and I will be your God."
sum.40: Ishmael, a member of the royal family, murders Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and kills many others as well, including pilgrims who had come to worship. He then takes the people captive, but Johanan catches up with him and rescues the people. Out of fear of the Chaldeans, they make preparations to flee to Egypt.
sum.48: God announces judgment on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam for their pride and for trusting in their riches, their mountains, or their strength. No nation can escape when God decides to act. Even so, he promises to restore Ammon and Elam, and to care for the orphans and widows of Edom.
sum.25: God commands Jeremiah to warn the people in the temple that, if they do not repent, Jerusalem will become like Shiloh. The priests and prophets want to kill him, but the officials and the elders defend him, recalling Micah. God protects Jeremiah through Ahikam, and it is taught that God calls people to repentance.
sum.44: In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, God speaks through Jeremiah to Baruch, his scribe, who was worn out and full of sorrow. God tells him that He is going to tear down what He Himself built, so Baruch should not seek greatness for himself. Even so, He promises that his life will be spared wherever he goes.
sum.49: God announces through Jeremiah that Babylon will fall along with its idols, because it has been filled with pride and has mistreated his people. Israel and Judah, like lost sheep, will return weeping to seek God, and he will forgive them. God, their strong Redeemer, will defend their cause.
sum.14: God tells Jeremiah that the people of Judah will be punished for their rebellion, even if Moses and Samuel were to plead on their behalf. Jeremiah complains about the pain and rejection he suffers, but he finds joy in God's word. God calls him to return to Him and promises to make him strong, like a wall of bronze, and to rescue him.
sum.23: Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs: some very good, and others so bad they could not be eaten. God says the good figs are the exiles taken to Babylon, whom he will watch over, bring back to their land, and give a heart to know him. The bad figs are King Zedekiah and the people who stayed behind or fled to Egypt, and they will face judgment.
sum.12: God commanded Jeremiah to buy a linen belt and hide it by the Euphrates. Later he went back and found it rotten and good for nothing. Through this, God showed that the pride and idolatry of Judah and Jerusalem would leave them worthless, even though he had bound them to himself. He warned them to humble themselves before punishment and exile came, and Jeremiah wept for them.
sum.10: God tells Jeremiah to remind Judah of the covenant he made with their ancestors, but the people broke it and followed false gods such as Baal, so God announces punishment and will not listen to their cry. In addition, the people of Anathoth plan to kill Jeremiah, and God declares that they will be judged.
sum.22: God condemns the false shepherds and prophets who scattered his people with lies and false peace, and he promises to gather his remnant and raise up a righteous King from the line of David. His word is like fire and a hammer, and it is different from invented dreams. Those who twist it will face judgment.
sum.30: In Jeremiah 31, God promises to bring his scattered people back home, turn their weeping into joy, and rebuild them with everlasting love. He announces a new covenant: he will put his law in their hearts, everyone will know him, and he will forgive their sins. He also assures them that Israel will not be rejected forever.
sum.45: God announces through Jeremiah that the mighty army of Egypt will be defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Neither its strength nor its gods will be able to save it. But to his people Israel he says, "Do not be afraid, for I am with you," and he promises to rescue them from captivity and discipline them without destroying them completely.
sum.39: Nabuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, sets Jeremiah free and lets him choose where he wants to live. Jeremiah stays with Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and many Jews return to the land. Johanan warns that Ismael intends to kill Gedaliah, but Gedaliah does not believe him.
sum.18: God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar and to take the elders of the people to the Valley of Hinnom. There he announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and for sacrificing innocent children. Jeremiah breaks the jar as a sign that the people will be shattered, and then he repeats the message in the temple: they would not listen to God.
sum.28: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, raise families, and seek the welfare of the city, because God promises to bring them back after seventy years, with plans for peace. He also warns them against false prophets, and God announces punishment for them and for Shemaiah.
sum.2: God compares the unfaithfulness of Israel and Judah to a wife who leaves her husband, yet still calls them to return, because he is merciful and does not keep his anger forever. He promises to restore them, give them good shepherds, and gather his people together. In the end, the people acknowledge their sin and declare that salvation is found only in God.
sum.33: While Babylon was attacking Jerusalem, Jeremiah warned King Zedekiah that the city would fall and that he himself would be taken away as a prisoner, though he would die in peace. The people had set their Hebrew servants free, but then they enslaved them again, breaking their covenant with God. Because of this, God says that they will receive "liberty" to face the sword, famine, and plague.
sum.34: God told Jeremiah to offer wine to the Rechabites, but they refused, because they faithfully keep the command of their ancestor Jonadab to live in tents and not drink wine. God uses their example to rebuke Judah, which did not obey his prophets, and he announces punishment for Judah, but he promises that the family of Jonadab will always serve him.
sum.3: God calls Judah and Jerusalem to turn back to Him wholeheartedly and to give up their wickedness, or an enemy army will come from the north to destroy the land. Jeremiah is distressed by the suffering he sees coming, and God explains that the people are foolish when it comes to doing evil. Even so, He promises not to bring a complete end to them.
sum.42: When Jeremiah finishes delivering God's message, the proud leaders accuse him of lying, and they take all the rest of Judah off to Egypt, disobeying the Lord. While they are in Tahpanhes, God tells Jeremiah to hide stones there and announce that Nebuchadnezzar will come to conquer Egypt and burn its gods. No one escapes God's judgment by running away from his word.
sum.19: Pashur, a chief priest, struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks because of his message. Jeremiah told him that Babylon would carry Judah off into exile. Then Jeremiah, worn down by the mockery, admitted that he could not keep silent about God's word. He trusted that God was with him, and he ended by cursing the day he was born.
sum.11: Jeremiah asks God why the wicked prosper. God answers that even greater trials await him, including betrayal by his own family. God laments that his people will be destroyed by their enemies, but he promises mercy and restoration. Whoever learns his ways will be blessed, and whoever refuses to obey will be uprooted.
sum.27: Hananiah prophesies that God will break the yoke of Babylon within two years. But Jeremiah replies that true prophets used to announce judgment, and that a prophet of peace will be known as genuine only if his words come true. Hananiah then breaks the wooden yoke, and God announces iron yokes in its place. Jeremiah tells him that God did not send him, and Hananiah dies that same year.
sum.9: God warns Israel not to imitate the nations or fear their idols, because they are the work of human hands, mute and powerless. Only Jehovah is the living God, the Creator of all things, and Jeremiah sees judgment coming upon Judah. He acknowledges that a person does not direct his own steps, and he asks to be corrected with justice.
sum.47: God announces judgment on Moab: its cities will be destroyed because it trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh, and it grew proud against the LORD. The prophet himself weeps over its ruin. Even so, the passage ends with hope: at the end of time, God will bring back the captives of Moab.
sum.31: Jeremiah, who was being held prisoner while the Babylonians surrounded Jerusalem, buys his cousin Hanamel's field out of obedience, and he has the deeds of purchase stored in a clay jar. God explains that the city will fall because of the people's sin, but that one day he will bring them back, make an everlasting covenant with them, and people will once again buy land.
sum.41: After the fall of Jerusalem, the people and their leaders ask Jeremiah to pray for them and promise to obey whatever God says. Ten days later, God answers: if they stay in the land, he will look after them and protect them from the king of Babylon; if they flee to Egypt, war and famine will overtake them there. Jeremiah warns them that their promise was not sincere.
sum.36: King Zedekiah did not obey God, yet he asked Jeremiah to pray for them. God warned that even though the Chaldeans would withdraw for a time, they would come back and burn the city. Jeremiah was falsely accused, beaten, and thrown into prison, but he continued to tell the king the truth.
sum.7: God warns that Judah will be judged because its people rejected his word, clung to deceit and greed, and its leaders gave false peace without any shame. Even the birds know their seasons, yet the people do not understand God's judgment. Jeremiah weeps in grief and asks why there is no healing for his people.
sum.26: God tells Jeremiah to put on a yoke and to warn the kings of the neighboring nations, and Zedekiah as well, that they must submit to Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God has given those lands for a time. The prophets who say otherwise are lying, and whoever submits will live in their own land. The remaining objects from the temple will also be taken to Babylon, but God promises to bring them back someday.
sum.15: God tells Jeremiah not to marry, and not to attend funerals or feasts, as a sign that a terrible judgment is coming on Judah because of its idolatry, which is worse than that of its ancestors. But God promises that after punishing them and sending them into exile, he will bring his people back. In the end, even the nations will recognize that the idols are a lie.
sum.20: When Babylon besieged Jerusalem, King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah to inquire of God, hoping for a miracle. God answered that He Himself would fight against the city, and that whoever surrendered to the Chaldeans would live, while whoever stayed in the city would die. He also called the house of David to do justice and rescue the oppressed from the hand of their oppressor, because of their wickedness.
sum.35: God tells Jeremiah to write his warnings down on a scroll, hoping that the people will turn back from their wrongdoing. Baruch reads it aloud in the temple, but King Jehoiakim cuts it up and burns it, showing no fear. God protects Jeremiah and Baruch, and the word of God is written out again, this time with even more content.
sum.37: Jeremiah announces that whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live, but the officials throw him into a muddy cistern so that he will die. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian, persuades the king and rescues him. Jeremiah pleads with Zedekiah to surrender, but the king is afraid, and Jeremiah remains in custody until the fall of Jerusalem.
sum.21: God tells Jeremiah to say to the king of Judah that he must practice justice and protect the oppressed, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. If he does not obey, the palace will be left empty, and the city will fall because it abandoned the covenant with God. The kings Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah are judged for their injustice and greed, and they will be taken into exile.
sum.4: God searches Jerusalem for even one honest person and cannot find one, because the people have rebelled, sworn falsely, oppressed the poor, and followed lying prophets. So he announces that a foreign nation will come to destroy them, though he promises not to finish them off completely. He reminds them that the sea obeys the limit he sets, yet they do not fear him.
sum.16: God accuses Judah of a sin so deep that it seems carved into their heart, and announces punishment. He blesses the one who trusts in Him, like a tree planted by the water, and warns about the deceitful heart. Jeremiah asks for healing, and God calls the people to keep the Sabbath, with the promise of blessing or of fire.
sum.8: Jeremiah weeps for his people, because lies, deceit, and the rejection of God's law have filled them with wickedness. God announces punishment: the land will be laid waste and the people scattered. Even so, He teaches that no one should boast in their wisdom, strength, or riches, but in knowing God, who delights in mercy and justice.
sum.17: God sends Jeremiah down to the potter's house to show him that he can reshape nations the way a potter reshapes clay, and that he changes his plans depending on whether people repent or not. Judah refuses to turn back to God and plots against Jeremiah, who cries out to God and asks him for justice against them.
sum.43: Jeremiah warns the Jews who were living in Egypt that Jerusalem was destroyed because of their idolatry, and that if they keep worshiping other gods, it will lead them to ruin. They refuse to listen and say they will keep honoring the "queen of heaven." God responds that his word will be fulfilled, and that only a few will escape.
sum.24: Jeremiah reminds Judah that for twenty-three years they rejected the warnings from God and from his prophets. Because of this, God will send Nebuchadnezzar, and the nations will serve Babylon for seventy years; afterward, Babylon will also be judged. Through the image of the cup of God's fury, God shows that his judgment will reach everyone.
sum.13: A great drought strikes Judah, and the people cry out and confess their sin. But God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them, because they still have not repented, and the false prophets are deceiving them with promises of peace. Even so, Jeremiah weeps and asks God not to abandon them, since only He can give the rain.
sum.5: God warns that a cruel army from the north is coming against Jerusalem, because the people are full of violence, deceit, and false peace. He offers them the chance to return to the ancient paths and find rest, but they refuse to listen, and God rejects their empty sacrifices. Jeremiah weeps and calls for mourning.
sum.38: Jerusalem falls to Babylon just as God had warned. King Zedekiah tries to flee, but he is captured, forced to watch his sons die, and then blinded and taken prisoner. Even so, God looks after Jeremiah, and He also promises to save Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, because he trusted in Him.
sum.51: Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, and because of this Nebuchadnezzar laid siege to Jerusalem until hunger overcame the city. The city and the temple were burned, its treasures were stolen, and many people were taken into captivity. In the end, King Jehoiachin was released and treated with kindness, a small sign of hope.
sum.50: God announces that he will destroy Babylon for its wickedness and for what it did to Jerusalem, using other nations as his instrument. He calls his people to leave her and not to forget him, because he is the Creator and idols are worthless. Jeremiah orders this message to be read in Babylon and the book to be sunk in the Euphrates, as a sign of its fall.
sum.0: God calls Jeremiah, a young priest from Anathoth, to be a prophet to the nations, and promises to put his words in his mouth. Although Jeremiah says he is too young and feels afraid, God assures him that he will be with him to deliver him. Through two visions, the almond branch and the boiling pot, God announces that judgment will come from the north because of the people's idolatry.
sum.32: Jeremiah, still under guard, receives a promise from God: although Jerusalem lies in ruins because of its sin, God will heal it, forgive His people, and bring them back from captivity. Joy and flocks will return, and a righteous Branch from David's line will come. God affirms His covenant with David and the Levites, as firm as day and night.
sum.1: God reminds Israel of the love of her youth, when she followed Him through the wilderness, and asks what wrong they found in Him that made them abandon Him. His people left Him, the fountain of living water, for broken cisterns and for idols. Although they say, "We have not sinned," God announces judgment and shame.
sum.6: God sends Jeremiah to the gate of the temple to warn Judah not to put their trust in the temple while they continue to live in injustice, steal, murder, and worship idols. If they change their ways, they will remain in the land; if they do not, God will do to the temple what He did to Shiloh. God demands obedience rather than sacrifices, and He announces judgment and desolation.
